s.b: Everyone who walks through the Gospels, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude and Revelation, from Mary and Joseph to Pilate, Peter, Stephen, Paul and Phoebe.
Towns, regions, islands, lakes, hills and rooms where the story happens, with the events that took place there.
The stories Jesus told, with their themes, where they appear and what they connect to.
Healings, exorcisms, rescues and signs in the Gospels and Acts, with where each is told.

What the prophets promised and where the Gospels, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude and Revelation say it came true.
The events of Jesus’ life and of the early church, in order, each tied to a spot on the map.

Key Greek words from the four Gospels, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude and Revelation, plus Aramaic phrases and puzzling expressions.
Sin, holiness, love, grace, faith, justification, the kingdom and the other great themes, and how Jesus and Paul speak of each.
The names of God, the titles of Jesus and the Spirit, and the seven “I am” sayings.
The Sabbath, the feasts and the other sacred days that shape the Gospel story.
God’s promises through Noah, Abraham, Moses, David and the new covenant.
Pharisees, Sadducees, the Twelve, tax collectors, the council, Roman officials and the other groups in the story.

Coins, clothing, food, ships, tools and objects mentioned in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude and Revelation.
Excavated sites, inscriptions and objects that touch the Gospel story.
How people ate, dressed, worshiped, mourned and lived in Jesus’ world.

Rulers, politics, groups and events behind the Gospels, Acts, Romans, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews, James, 1 Peter, 2 Peter, 1 John, 2 John, 3 John, Jude and Revelation.
The voices in the Commentary library, and the terms used in Bible study.
The Bible translations, how they differ, and the manuscripts behind them.

t: A young woman of Nazareth, betrothed to Joseph, who is told by the angel Gabriel that she will bear the Son of the Most High. Luke gives her song, the Magnificat. She is with Jesus at the wedding at Cana and stands near the cross, where he entrusts her to the beloved disciple. In Acts 1:14 she is with the believers in the upper room.
f: Wife of Joseph; relative of Elizabeth

t: A builder (Greek tekton, often rendered “carpenter”) from Nazareth, a descendant of David. In Matthew he obeys dreams to take Mary as his wife, to flee to Egypt and to settle in Nazareth. He disappears from the story after Jesus is twelve.

Son of Zechariah and Elizabeth, he preached repentance in the Judean wilderness and baptized in the Jordan. He pointed to Jesus as the Lamb of God, rebuked Herod Antipas for his marriage and was beheaded at Machaerus.
f: Son of Zechariah and Elizabeth; relative of Mary

t: An elderly priest of the course of Abijah who is struck silent when Gabriel announces John’s birth in the Temple. His speech returns at the naming of the child, when he sings the Benedictus.
A relative of Mary from a priestly family, who conceives in old age. When Mary visits, the child leaps in her womb and she blesses Mary as “the mother of my Lord”.
f: Wife of Zechariah; relative of Mary

t: The angel who stands in God’s presence, who announces the births of John and Jesus. He also appears in Daniel.
A devout man in Jerusalem who was promised he would see the Messiah. He takes the baby Jesus in his arms and speaks the Nunc Dimittis, warning Mary that a sword will pierce her own soul.
An elderly widow of the tribe of Asher who worshipped night and day in the Temple. She thanks God at the sight of the child and speaks of him to all who await redemption.
The first Roman emperor. Luke dates Jesus’ birth to a census decreed in his reign. Herod the Great ruled Judea as his client king.
Augustus’s successor, in whose fifteenth year (about AD 28–29) John began to preach. His image was on the silver denarius of Jesus’ question about taxes.

A brilliant, brutal builder who rebuilt the Temple, the fortresses of Masada and Herodium, and the port of Caesarea. Matthew shows him trying to kill the child Jesus after the visit of the Magi. He died in 4 BC.

e.u: Tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, 4 BC – AD 39
t: A son of Herod the Great who ruled Galilee through Jesus’ whole ministry. He founded Tiberias, imprisoned and killed John the Baptist, and questioned Jesus before the crucifixion. Jesus called him “that fox”.
f: Husband of Herodias; son of Herod the Great

t: A granddaughter of Herod the Great who left her first husband, Antipas’s half-brother, to marry Antipas. John the Baptist condemned the marriage, and she arranged his death.

The Roman governor who sentenced Jesus to be crucified. Josephus and Philo describe him as harsh and provocative. A building inscription found at Caesarea names him “Prefect of Judea”. First Timothy 6:13 speaks of “Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate.”

Joseph Caiaphas was high priest through Jesus’ ministry and presided over the trial before the Sanhedrin. A richly decorated ossuary found in Jerusalem in 1990 is inscribed with his family name. In Acts he is among the rulers who question Peter and John (4:6).
The powerful former high priest (AD 6–15) whose sons and son-in-law held the office after him. John says Jesus was taken to him first. In Acts he is named with Caiaphas as high priest (4:6).

A fisherman from Bethsaida who lived at Capernaum, brother of Andrew. Jesus renames him “Peter” (the Rock). He confesses Jesus as the Christ, denies him three times, and is restored on the shore of the lake after the resurrection. In Acts he leads the Jerusalem church: he preaches at Pentecost, heals a lame man, stands before the council, takes the gospel to Cornelius, and is freed from prison by an angel. Paul calls him Cephas in 1 Corinthians. Some at Corinth said “I follow Cephas.” Paul lists him first among those to whom the risen Christ appeared (15:5) and notes that he travels with a believing wife (9:5). In Galatians Paul calls him Cephas. He stayed with him for fifteen days (1:18), is among the “pillars” in Jerusalem (2:9), and at Antioch was opposed “to his face” for drawing back from the Gentiles (2:11-14). The first letter of Peter opens “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1) and presents him in chapter 5 as “a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed” (5:1). He says he writes from “Babylon” (5:13), which many early writers took to mean Rome. Clement of Rome (about AD 96) and later writers say Peter was put to death there. The letter has many echoes of the sayings and acts of Jesus that Peter had known, among them the Chief Shepherd (John 21:15-17) and the stone the builders rejected (Mark 12:10).

In 2 Peter the writer calls himself “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1), says he lives “in the tent of my body” and expects to lay it aside soon (1:13-14), and tells of hearing the voice from heaven “when we were with Him on the holy mountain” (1:18). Many scholars doubt that he wrote the letter and think it was written in his name after his death; others hold that he wrote it near the end of his life.
A former disciple of John the Baptist who first followed Jesus and brought his brother Peter to him. He brings the boy with loaves and fish and brings Greeks to Jesus.

Fishermen partnered with Peter, nicknamed “Sons of Thunder”. With Peter they are the inner circle at the raising of Jairus’s daughter, the Transfiguration and Gethsemane. Herod Agrippa I executed James around AD 44. In Acts, John goes with Peter to the temple and to Samaria. Herod Agrippa kills James with the sword (12:2), the first of the Twelve to die. Paul names “John” among the pillars who gave him the right hand of fellowship (Galatians 2:9).
In 1 John: Early tradition ascribes 1 John to John the son of Zebedee. The letter itself does not name its writer.
f: Sons of Zebedee and probably Salome

t: Called on the day after Andrew and Peter. He brings Nathanael to Jesus, is asked where to buy bread for the five thousand and asks to see the Father at the Last Supper. He is named in the list of the eleven in Acts 1:13.
Brought by Philip and astonished that Jesus saw him under the fig tree. He is named at the end of John among the disciples at the lakeshore. Many identify him with the apostle Bartholomew.
A customs agent at Capernaum who left his booth to follow Jesus and hosted a dinner for tax collectors and sinners. Matthew’s Gospel calls him Matthew; Mark and Luke call him Levi.

Called “the Twin”. He is ready to die with Jesus in John 11, asks “how can we know the way?” and refuses to believe in the resurrection until he sees the marks of the nails, then declares “My Lord and my God!”

The disciples’ treasurer, who agreed to hand Jesus over to the chief priests for thirty pieces of silver. Matthew says he returned the silver and hanged himself. Acts 1 tells how he died and how Matthias took his place.
A woman from Magdala whom Jesus had freed of seven demons. She supported his ministry, stood at the cross and was the first to see the risen Lord.
She sat at Jesus’ feet to listen while Martha served. John says she poured expensive perfume on his feet six days before Passover.
Hosted Jesus at Bethany and made the confession “I believe that you are the Christ, the Son of God.” John 11 pictures her meeting Jesus on the road after her brother’s death.
Raised from the tomb after four days. The raising prompts the plot to kill Jesus. His tomb is shown at Bethany today. (The poor man in Luke’s parable has the same name but is a different character.)
A woman of means, wife of Chuza, a manager of Herod Antipas’s household, who supported Jesus out of her own funds and was at the empty tomb.
Named by Mark among the women at the cross and the tomb. She is probably the “mother of the sons of Zebedee” in Matthew’s list, who asks Jesus for places for her sons.
f: Probably mother of James and John

e.u: Pharisee and member of the council
t: He comes to Jesus by night, speaks up for him before the council, and after the crucifixion brings about a hundred pounds of spices for the burial.
A rich, righteous member of the council who did not consent to Jesus’ condemnation. He asked Pilate for the body and laid it in his own new tomb.

A short, wealthy toll official who climbed a sycamore-fig to see Jesus. Jesus invited himself to his house, and Zacchaeus promised to give half his goods to the poor and repay fourfold anyone he had cheated.
A leader of a synagogue, probably at Capernaum, who begged Jesus to come and heal his dying twelve-year-old daughter. Jesus raised her up.
Mark names him “son of Timaeus”. He called out to the “Son of David,” was healed and followed Jesus on the road. Matthew mentions two blind men; Luke does not give a name.
A non-Jewish officer, likely in Herod Antipas’s service, who built the local synagogue. He asked Jesus to heal his servant and said “just say the word.” Jesus marveled at his faith.
A Greek woman of Syrian Phoenicia whose daughter was oppressed by a demon. She pressed Jesus to help, saying even the dogs eat the children’s crumbs. Matthew calls her a Canaanite.
A woman who came to draw water at noon at Sychar. Jesus told her about living water and about worship in spirit and truth; she became the first witness to the Samaritans.

e.u: Healed in the country of the Gerasenes
t: A man living among the tombs, with so many spirits that they called themselves “Legion”. After he was healed, Jesus sent him home to tell his own people, and he proclaimed it across the Decapolis.
A widow whose only son was being carried out of the village for burial when Jesus touched the bier and told him to rise.

e.u: Healed at the Pool of Siloam
t: Jesus makes mud, applies it to the man’s eyes and sends him to wash in the Pool of Siloam. His healing leads to a debate with the Pharisees and his own parents.
He lay by the pool with the sick, and Jesus told him to take up his mat and walk. The healing was on a Sabbath.
She put two small copper coins (lepta) into the Temple treasury. Jesus said she had given more than all the rest, because she gave out of her poverty.

e.u: Man who asked about eternal life
t: A wealthy man who had kept the commandments from his youth. Jesus loved him and told him to sell his possessions and follow; he went away grieving.
A man in prison for insurrection and murder. At the Passover amnesty the crowd chose him over Jesus.
A man from the Jewish community of Cyrene, in modern Libya, pressed by the soldiers to carry Jesus’ cross. Mark calls him the father of Alexander and Rufus.

e.u: Disciple on the road to Emmaus
t: One of two followers who walked from Jerusalem on Easter afternoon and failed to recognize Jesus until he broke bread with them.
The officer who watched Jesus die and said, “Truly this man was the Son of God.”

Cited for the Law, the bronze serpent, the manna and the commandment about divorce. He appears with Elijah at the Transfiguration. In Acts 3:22 and 7:20-44 Moses is a prophet like Jesus. Paul says death reigned “from Adam until Moses” (5:14), recalls God’s word to Moses about mercy (9:15), and cites Moses on the righteousness that comes from the law (10:5, 19). Paul says the forefathers “were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2) and quotes “the Law of Moses” about the ox (9:9). In 2 Corinthians 3:7-16 Paul uses the veil over Moses’ face to show the difference between the old covenant and the new. Ephesians 6:2-3 quotes the fifth commandment given at Sinai, “Honor your father and mother,” which Paul calls “the first commandment with a promise.” In 2 Timothy 3:8 Paul says “Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses.” Hebrews 3:1-6 says Moses was faithful “as a servant” in God’s house, and Christ as a Son over it. Chapter 8 says that Moses was warned to make the tabernacle according to the pattern shown him on the mountain (8:5). Chapter 11 tells how Moses’ parents hid him, how he chose to suffer oppression with God’s people, and how he kept the Passover (11:23-28).
Jude 9 refers to a Jewish story in which the archangel Michael “disputed with the devil over the body of Moses.” Deuteronomy 34:6 says that no one knows where Moses was buried.

The prophet who was expected to return before the Day of the Lord. Jesus says John the Baptist is that Elijah, and Elijah appears with Moses at the Transfiguration. Paul recalls Elijah’s complaint and God’s reply about the seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal (Romans 11:2-4). James 5:17-18 says that Elijah “was a man just like us.” He prayed earnestly that it would not rain, and it did not rain for three and a half years, and then he prayed again and the heavens gave rain. James uses him as proof that “the prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.”

The patriarch of Genesis. Jesus’ opponents claim him as their father; Jesus says he saw Abraham’s day and, “Before Abraham was, I am.” In Acts 3:25 and 7:2-8 Peter and Stephen speak of Abraham. Romans 4 argues that Abraham was credited with righteousness by faith before he was circumcised, so that he is father of all who believe. Galatians 3 argues from Abraham: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (3:6), “those who have faith are sons of Abraham” (3:7), and the blessing comes to the Gentiles in him (3:8-9). In chapter 4 Paul reads the story of his two sons as a picture of two covenants. Hebrews 6:13-18 says that when God made a promise to Abraham he swore by himself. In chapter 7 Abraham gives a tenth to Melchizedek and is blessed by him, which shows that Melchizedek is greater. In chapter 11 he obeys the call without knowing where he is going, lives in tents, and is ready to offer Isaac (11:8-19). James 2:21-23 appeals to Abraham twice: he was “justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar,” and the Scripture that says “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” was fulfilled, and he was called a friend of God.

Israel’s great king, ancestor of the Messiah. The title “Son of David” appears often; archaeology offers the Tel Dan stele’s mention of the “House of David”. In Acts, Peter and Paul read the Psalms as David’s words about the Messiah. Romans 4 quotes David on the blessing of the person whose sin is not counted (Psalm 32), and Romans 11 quotes his curse on those who stumbled (Psalm 69). In 2 Timothy 2:8 Paul tells Timothy to remember Jesus Christ, “raised from the dead, descended from David.” Hebrews 4:7 says that God speaks “through David” in Psalm 95, and Psalm 110, quoted in chapters 1, 5 and 7, is also a psalm of David. David is named in the list of the faithful (11:32).

The prophet Jesus quotes most. Luke has him read from the Isaiah scroll in the Nazareth synagogue, and the Gospels cite him for John the Baptist’s ministry. In Acts, Philip explains Isaiah 53 to the Ethiopian, and Paul closes by quoting Isaiah 6. Paul quotes Isaiah more than any other prophet in Romans, on the remnant (9:27-29), the stone of stumbling (9:33), the beautiful feet of the messengers (10:15) and the root of Jesse (15:12). Ephesians 2:17 echoes Isaiah’s words about “peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near” (Isaiah 57:19; 52:7), and the armor of 6:14-17 borrows from Isaiah 11:5, 52:7 and 59:17. A Jewish tradition says that Isaiah was sawn in two under King Manasseh, and some readers think this is behind Hebrews 11:37, which speaks of those who were “sawed in two.” The Old Testament does not record how Isaiah died.
Jesus calls his own resurrection after three days “the sign of Jonah” and says the men of Nineveh will rise at the judgement because they repented at Jonah’s preaching.

The builder of the first Temple, celebrated for wisdom and splendor. Jesus says the lilies are more beautiful and that “something greater than Solomon is here”. In Acts 7:47 Stephen says Solomon built the house, yet the Most High does not dwell in houses made by hands.

The adversary who tempts Jesus in the wilderness, and whom Jesus pictures falling like lightning as God’s kingdom advances. The name means “accuser”. In 2 Corinthians Paul does not want to be outwitted by him (2:11), calls him “the god of this age” who “has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (4:4), says he “masquerades as an angel of light” (11:14), and links him to the “messenger of Satan” that torments Paul (12:7). Ephesians speaks of “the ruler of the power of the air” (2:2), warns “do not give the devil a foothold” (4:27), and tells believers to “make your stand against the devil’s schemes” (6:11). It also speaks of “all the flaming arrows of the evil one” (6:16). In 1 Thessalonians Paul says “Satan obstructed us” from coming back to the church (2:18) and fears “the tempter” had tempted them (3:5). In the second letter the coming of the lawless one is “accompanied by the working of Satan” (2 Thessalonians 2:9), and the Lord will “guard you from the evil one” (3:3). In 1 Timothy Paul says he has “handed over to Satan” Hymenaeus and Alexander (1:20). A new convert may “fall under the same condemnation as the devil” (3:6), and “some have already turned aside to follow Satan” (5:15). In 2 Timothy 2:26 Paul hopes that opponents will “escape the snare of the devil, who has taken them captive to his will.” Hebrews 2:14-15 says that Christ shared flesh and blood so that through death he might destroy “him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil” and free those held in slavery by the fear of death. James 4:7 tells the readers to “resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” In 2:19 even the demons believe in one God “and shudder,” and in 3:15 the wisdom that comes from jealousy and selfish ambition is called “earthly, unspiritual, demonic.” In 1 Peter 5:8 he is “your adversary the devil,” who “prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.” Peter tells the readers to be “sober-minded and alert” and to resist him, “standing firm in your faith” (5:9).

In 1 John he is “the devil,” who “has been sinning from the very start”; the Son of God “was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil” (3:8). The letter also speaks of “the evil one” (2:13-14; 3:12; 5:18-19) and says that “the whole world is under the power of the evil one” (5:19).
In Jude 9 the archangel Michael “disputed with the devil over the body of Moses” and left the rebuke to the Lord.

In Revelation he is the great red dragon, “that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9). He is thrown down from heaven, makes war on the woman’s children, gives his power to the beast, is bound for a thousand years, and is finally thrown into the lake of fire (12:7-17; 13:2; 20:1-10).

A Jew born in Tarsus, trained in Jerusalem under Gamaliel, and a Roman citizen. As Saul he approves Stephen’s death and arrests believers, until the risen Jesus meets him on the road to Damascus. He then takes the gospel to Cyprus, Asia Minor, Macedonia and Greece in three journeys, is arrested at the temple, appeals to Caesar, and reaches Rome in chains. In Romans he writes as an apostle who has not yet been to Rome, explains the gospel for Jew and Gentile, and describes his plans for Jerusalem and Spain. In 1 Corinthians he answers a church he founded, writing from Ephesus. He calls himself the one who laid the foundation, tells how he works with his hands, and says he became “all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some.” In 2 Corinthians he writes from Macedonia after a painful visit, a sharp letter and a long wait for Titus. He defends his ministry, lists his sufferings, tells of his escape from Damascus and of a thorn in the flesh, and says “when I am weak, then I am strong” (12:10). In Galatians he opens with “an apostle—sent not from men nor by man” (1:1), tells how he came to the gospel and met the Jerusalem leaders, and confronts Peter at Antioch. He then argues for faith over works of the law, writes with “large letters” in his “own hand” (6:11), and says “I bear on my body the marks of Jesus” (6:17). In Ephesians he calls himself “an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God” (1:1) and “the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles” (3:1). He says he is “less than the least of all the saints” (3:8), and asks the readers to pray that he will speak boldly, “an ambassador in chains” (6:19-20). In Philippians he writes with Timothy as “servants of Christ Jesus” (1:1), is in chains (1:7, 13), and says, “to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21). He lists his old credentials as a Pharisee and “a Hebrew of Hebrews” (3:5) and counts them as loss (3:7-8). He has “learned to be content regardless of my circumstances” (4:11). In Colossians he writes with Timothy (1:1) to a church he has not met (2:1). He is “a servant” of the gospel (1:23, 25), rejoices in “my sufferings for you” (1:24), asks for prayer for “which I am in chains” (4:3), and ends with a greeting “in my own hand” (4:18). In 1 and 2 Thessalonians he writes with Silvanus and Timothy to a church he had to leave soon after founding it (1 Thessalonians 2:17). He reminds them that he worked “night and day” (2:9), calls himself “like a nursing mother” and “as a father” (2:7, 11), and wrote the closing greeting of the second letter “in my own hand” (2 Thessalonians 3:17). In 1 Timothy he writes to Timothy at Ephesus, as “an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior” (1:1). He calls himself “formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man” who “was shown mercy” (1:13), and says Christ came to save sinners, “of whom I am the worst” (1:15). Scholars disagree on whether Paul wrote the letter or a later follower did. In 2 Timothy he writes in chains, as “an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus” (1:1). He asks Timothy not to be ashamed “of me, His prisoner” (1:8), and says, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith” (4:7). Many take it as his last letter. Scholars disagree on whether Paul wrote it or a later follower did. In Titus he is “a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ” (1:1). He tells Titus, “The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished” (1:5), and says, “I have decided to winter” at Nicopolis (3:12). Scholars disagree on whether Paul wrote it or a later follower wrote in his name. In Philemon he is “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” (verse 1) who prefers to “appeal on the basis of love” (verse 9). He writes “with my own hand” (verse 19), promises to repay anything Onesimus owes, and asks for a guest room because he hopes to be “restored” to the church (verse 22). The letter does not say where he was held.

2 Peter 3:15-16 calls him “our beloved brother Paul,” says he wrote to the readers “with the wisdom God gave him,” and adds that “some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures.”
f: Companion of Barnabas, Silas, Timothy and Luke

t: A Levite from Cyprus whose given name was Joseph. He sells a field and gives the money to the apostles, vouches for Saul in Jerusalem, brings him to Antioch, and travels with him on the first journey. After a sharp disagreement over John Mark he sails again to Cyprus. Paul mentions Barnabas as one who, like himself, works for a living (1 Corinthians 9:6). In Galatians he goes up to Jerusalem with Paul and Titus (2:1), receives the right hand of fellowship (2:9), and at Antioch is “led astray” with Peter by the hypocrisy of the others (2:13). Colossians 4:10 names Mark as “the cousin of Barnabas.” Tertullian, in the early 200s, named Barnabas as the writer of Hebrews, and some scholars still favor him, since he was a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36) and a “son of encouragement,” and Hebrews calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22). The letter does not name its author.

e.u: First martyr; one of the Seven
t: A Greek-speaking believer “full of faith and the Holy Spirit,” chosen to serve the widows. Accused before the council, he retells Israel’s history and says the Righteous One has come. He sees Jesus standing at God’s right hand and is stoned, praying for his killers.

Chosen with Stephen to serve the widows, he preaches in Samaria, explains Isaiah 53 to an Ethiopian official, and baptizes him. He later lives in Caesarea with four daughters who prophesy, where Paul stays with him.
f: Father of four daughters who prophesied

t: A disciple in Damascus, “well spoken of by all the Jews.” The Lord sends him to the street called Straight to lay hands on Saul, who has been blind for three days. Though afraid because of Saul’s reputation, he obeys and calls him “Brother Saul.”

e.u: A couple in the Jerusalem church
t: A husband and wife who sell a piece of property and bring part of the price to the apostles while claiming to give all of it. Peter says they lied to the Holy Spirit; both die, and fear falls on the whole church.

The high priest who orders Paul struck on the mouth at the council, and who later goes to Caesarea with Tertullus to accuse him before Felix. Josephus names an Ananias son of Nedebaeus as high priest in about AD 47-59.

A centurion of the Italian Cohort at Caesarea, “devout and God-fearing,” who prays and gives to the poor. An angel tells him to send for Peter. When Peter preaches in his house the Holy Spirit falls on his whole household, and they are baptized.

A man who amazed the Samaritans with magic and who believed and was baptized after Philip’s preaching. When he sees the Spirit given through the apostles’ hands he offers money for the power, and Peter rebukes him.

A eunuch and chief treasurer of the queen of the Ethiopians, returning from worship in Jerusalem. He is reading Isaiah 53 aloud in his chariot when Philip joins him, explains the passage, and baptizes him in water along the road.
A disciple known for good works and charity, especially the clothing she made for widows. When she dies, the believers send for Peter, who prays, says “Tabitha, arise,” and presents her alive.
A Joppa craftsman whose house is by the sea. Peter lodges with him, sees the vision of the sheet on his roof, and leaves with the men sent from Cornelius.

e.u: Pharisee and teacher of the law
t: A Pharisee honored by all the people. In the council he tells his colleagues to leave the apostles alone, for if this plan is from men it will fail, but if from God they cannot stop it. Paul later says he was trained at his feet.
A prophet who predicts a great famine, and later binds his own hands and feet with Paul’s belt to show that the Jews of Jerusalem will bind its owner and hand him over to the Gentiles.

A brother of Jesus who did not follow him during his ministry but is named a leader in Jerusalem. After Peter leaves, James presides at the council on the Gentiles and later receives Paul and the elders. The letter of James is traditionally his. Paul saw “James, the Lord’s brother” on his first visit (Galatians 1:19) and counts him among the pillars (2:9). The men “from James” at Antioch changed Peter’s table (2:12). The letter of James calls its writer only “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1). Tradition from early on has taken him to be James the brother of the Lord. Josephus says that he was stoned in Jerusalem about AD 62. Some scholars believe the letter was written in his name by a later Christian, and others that it comes from him, perhaps through a secretary who wrote good Greek.
The letter of Jude begins, “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (Jude 1). James was well enough known that his name alone told readers who Jude was.
f: Brother of Jesus and of Jude

t: The son of Mary, whose Jerusalem home hosted the church. He goes with Barnabas and Saul on the first journey but turns back at Perga. Paul refuses to take him again, so Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus. Mark is traditionally the author of the second Gospel. Colossians 4:10 calls him “Mark the cousin of Barnabas” and tells the church, “If he comes to you, welcome him.” Paul writes, “Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11). Philemon 24 calls him one of Paul’s “fellow workers” who send greetings. Paul and Barnabas had parted over him (Acts 15:37-39), and here he is again with Paul. Peter calls him “my son Mark” (1 Peter 5:13). Early writers such as Papias said that Mark was Peter’s interpreter, and that his Gospel is built on what Peter taught.
The servant girl who recognizes Peter’s voice at the gate of Mary’s house and in her joy forgets to open it. The believers, who are praying for him, first say she is out of her mind.

Grandson of Herod the Great and ruler of a kingdom nearly as large as his grandfather’s. He has James killed, jails Peter at Passover, and dies at Caesarea after accepting the cry that his voice was a god’s, not a man’s.
f: Father of Agrippa II, Bernice and Drusilla

t: A Roman governor “a man of intelligence” who summons Barnabas and Saul to hear the word of God. When Elymas the magician tries to turn him away and is struck blind, the proconsul believes, astonished at the teaching about the Lord.
A Jewish false prophet attached to the proconsul. Paul calls him “full of all deceit and fraud” and a son of the devil, and he is struck blind for a time.

A leading man in the Jerusalem church who carries the Council’s letter to Antioch, then goes with Paul on the second journey. He is beaten and jailed with Paul at Philippi, and later stays at Berea. Paul names “me and Silvanus and Timothy” as the ones who preached Christ in Corinth (2 Corinthians 1:19). In 1 and 2 Thessalonians he is “Silvanus,” named with Paul and Timothy in the greeting (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). In 1 Peter 5:12 the apostle writes, “Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly.” The phrase may mean that Silvanus carried the letter, wrote it as Peter’s secretary, or both.

A disciple from Lystra, the son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father. Paul has him circumcised and takes him along. He travels with Paul and Silas, stays on at Berea, and is later sent to Macedonia from Ephesus. Timothy sends greetings from Corinth in Romans 16:21. Paul calls Timothy “my beloved and faithful child in the Lord” and says he has sent him to remind the Corinthians of his way of life. He asks that Timothy “has nothing to fear while he is with you.” He is named with Paul as sender of 2 Corinthians (1:1) and as one who preached in Corinth (1:19). Timothy is named with Paul as a sender of Philippians (1:1). Paul writes, “I have nobody else like him who will genuinely care for your needs” (2:20), and says that “as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel” (2:22). He hopes to send Timothy to Philippi soon (2:19, 23). Timothy is named with Paul as a sender of Colossians (1:1), “Timothy our brother.” Paul sent Timothy back to Thessalonica “to strengthen and encourage you in your faith” (1 Thessalonians 3:2), and Timothy returned “with the good news about your faith, your love” (3:6). He is named with Paul in both greetings. First Timothy is addressed to “Timothy, my true child in the faith” (1:2), left at Ephesus to deal with false teaching (1:3). Paul tells him, “Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers” (4:12), to “fight the good fight” (1:18; 6:12), and to “guard what has been entrusted” to him (6:20). Second Timothy calls him “my beloved child” (1:2), recalls “your tears” (1:4) and tells him to “fan into flame the gift of God” (1:6), to “be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (2:1) and to “Preach the word” (4:2). Paul asks him to “make every effort to come to me quickly” (4:9) and “before winter” (4:21). Philemon 1 names him as co-sender: “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother.” Hebrews 13:23 says “our brother Timothy” has been released and that the writer will come with him if he arrives soon. This is usually taken to be Paul’s coworker, but the letter says nothing more.

A God-fearing woman from Thyatira who deals in purple cloth. At a riverside prayer meeting in Philippi ’the Lord opened her heart,’ and she and her household are baptized. She then hosts Paul and his companions.

Wakened at midnight by an earthquake, he sees the doors open and draws his sword to kill himself, until Paul calls out that all are there. He asks, “What must I do to be saved?” and is baptized that night with his household.

A man who hosts Paul and Silas. When the mob cannot find them it drags Jason and some believers before the politarchs, accusing them of saying there is another king, Jesus. Jason posts bond and they are released. Paul says Jason sends greetings from Corinth in Romans 16:21 and calls him a fellow countryman.
A member of the Areopagus council who believes after Paul’s speech. A woman named Damaris and others also believe. Later tradition made him the first bishop of Athens.

A Jewish couple who left Rome when Claudius expelled the Jews. They work with Paul at Corinth, go with him to Ephesus, and explain the way of God more accurately to Apollos. Paul calls them coworkers in Romans 16. In Romans 16 Paul greets “Prisca and Aquila,” who “have risked their lives for me,” and “the church that meets at their house.” They are back in Rome after Claudius’s edict. From Ephesus Paul sends greetings from “Aquila and Prisca,” and “the church that meets at their house” (1 Corinthians 16:19). They had first met him in Corinth. Paul writes, “Greet Prisca and Aquila” (2 Timothy 4:19). They appear to be back in the east, probably at Ephesus. Adolf von Harnack suggested that Priscilla was the writer of Hebrews, and that the name was left out because a woman had written it. The suggestion is old and unproved, and the writer uses a masculine form of a word for himself in 11:32.

A Jew from Alexandria, ’mighty in the Scriptures,’ who teaches accurately about Jesus though he knows only John’s baptism. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain more. He then helps the believers in Achaia. Paul says, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.” Some Corinthians said “I follow Apollos,” but Paul treats him as a fellow servant and says he “strongly urged him” to visit Corinth again. Paul asks Titus to help “Zenas the lawyer and Apollos” on their way (Titus 3:13). The two are probably passing through Crete. Martin Luther suggested that Apollos wrote Hebrews, since Acts 18:24 calls him an eloquent man who knew the Scriptures well and who came from Alexandria, which fits the style and the use of the Greek Old Testament. The letter does not name its author.

Brother of the philosopher Seneca. He dismisses the Jews’ charge against Paul as a dispute over words and names, and ignores the beating of Sosthenes in front of his court. An inscription at Delphi helps date his term.
A maker of silver shrines of Artemis who rallies fellow craftsmen: Paul’s preaching threatens both their trade and the greatness of the goddess. The crowd fills the theater and shouts for two hours.
A different Demetrius, with “a good testimony from everyone,” is commended in 3 John 12. Nothing links the two.

He quiets the crowd by saying that Ephesus is guardian of the temple of Artemis, that the Christians have not robbed temples, and that any complaint should go to the courts. He then dismisses the assembly.
A young man seated in a third-story window while Paul talks until midnight. He falls asleep, falls to the ground and is taken up dead. Paul bends over him and says “his life is in him.”

Paul calls him ’the beloved physician.’ The ’we’ passages in Acts (from Troas to Philippi, and from Philippi to Jerusalem, and in the voyage to Rome) suggest the writer joined Paul at those points. Luke and Aristarchus are with him on the sea voyage. In Colossians 4:14 he is “Luke, the beloved physician.” Paul says, “Only Luke is with me” (2 Timothy 4:11). Philemon 24 lists him among Paul’s “fellow workers” who send greetings, with Mark, Aristarchus and Demas.

The commander of the garrison at the Fortress of Antonia. He rescues Paul from the mob, learns that he is a Roman citizen, and after hearing of a plot sends him with a strong escort to Felix at Caesarea with a letter.
A young man who hears about the plot of the forty men and tells Paul and the tribune. He is the only member of Paul’s family mentioned in Acts.

Antonius Felix, a freed slave who rose to be procurator. He hears Paul’s case, keeps him in custody for two years, and with his wife Drusilla listens to Paul speak about faith, justice and judgment, until he sends Paul away.
A Jewish princess, daughter of Herod Agrippa I and sister of Agrippa II and Bernice. She hears Paul speak with her husband.
f: Sister of Agrippa II and Bernice

t: The advocate who accuses Paul before Felix, opening with flattery and calling him a ’plague’ who stirs up riots among all the Jews.
Porcius Festus succeeds Felix. Wanting to please the Jews, he asks if Paul will go up to Jerusalem; Paul appeals to Caesar. Festus consults King Agrippa and sends Paul to Rome.

e.u: King of territories east and north of Galilee
t: Son of Herod Agrippa I, expert in Jewish customs and questions. He hears Paul with his sister Bernice and Festus, and answers, “In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?” He tells Festus that Paul could have been set free if he had not appealed to Caesar.
Daughter of Herod Agrippa I. She accompanies her brother to Caesarea “with great pomp” and sits with him as Paul speaks.

The Roman officer who takes charge of Paul and other prisoners on the voyage to Italy. He treats Paul kindly, trusts the pilot over Paul, and later stops the soldiers from killing the prisoners so as to save Paul.
The leading Roman official on the island, who welcomes the shipwrecked party for three days. Paul heals his father of fever and dysentery.
A follower of Jesus from the beginning, nominated with Joseph Barsabbas. The believers pray and the lot falls to him, so he is counted with the eleven apostles in place of Judas.

e.n: The man at the Beautiful Gate
t: A man over forty, carried each day to the temple to beg. Peter and John take his hand and he walks in the name of Jesus, and enters the temple leaping and praising God.
A man who had never walked. He listens to Paul, who sees that he has faith to be made well and tells him to stand up. The crowd takes it as proof that the gods have come down.

e.u: Servant of the church in Cenchrea
t: A woman whom Paul commends at the end of Romans as “our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea.” He asks the Romans to “welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints” and to help her with anything she needs, because she “has been a great help to many people, including me.” Many scholars think she carried the letter to Rome.
f: Fellow worker of Paul, from the harbor town of Corinth

t: Paul spoke the letter and Tertius wrote it down. Near the end he adds his own greeting: “I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.” It is the one place where a scribe of Paul’s letters names himself.

“Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church,” sends greetings from Corinth. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 1:14 that he baptized a Gaius there, and many think it is the same man. Gaius was a very common name, and Acts 19:29 and 20:4 mention other men called Gaius. Paul says he baptized Gaius (1 Corinthians 1:14).
The Third Letter of John is written to another “beloved Gaius” (3 John 1). Nothing shows he is the same man, though Bede in the 8th century thought so.

Paul sends greetings from “Erastus, the city treasurer.” A man of that name appears in Acts 19:22 as one of Paul’s helpers and in 2 Timothy 4:20 as staying in Corinth. A paving stone near the Corinth theater records an Erastus who paid for the pavement in return for his office. Paul says, “Erastus has remained at Corinth” (2 Timothy 4:20).
f: Believer with a public post in Corinth

t: Paul greets “Andronicus and Junia, my fellow countrymen and fellow prisoners.” He says “they are outstanding among the apostles, and they were in Christ before I was.” Early writers took Junia to be a woman, and many scholars think the pair were a couple. Paul does not say where or when he was imprisoned with them.
f: Jewish believers, probably from before Paul’s own conversion

t: Paul greets “my beloved Epenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in the province of Asia.” Since the letter greets him in Rome, he had moved there. The note shows how freely Christians traveled across the empire.

Paul greets “Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who has been a mother to me as well.” Mark 15:21 names Rufus and Alexander as the sons of Simon of Cyrene, and some think this is the same Rufus because Mark was probably written for Rome. That cannot be proved, since Rufus was a common name.
f: Possibly the son of Simon of Cyrene

t: In Romans 5 Paul sets Adam beside Christ: “just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin,” so the free gift of grace comes through one man, Jesus Christ. Paul says death reigned “from Adam until Moses,” even over those who had not broken a command as Adam did. Paul says “as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive,” and calls Christ “the last Adam” (1 Corinthians 15:22, 45). In 1 Timothy Paul says “Adam was formed first, and then Eve,” and “it was not Adam who was deceived” (2:13-14).

Romans 4 mentions “the lifelessness of Sarah’s womb” along with the age of Abraham’s body, and says that Abraham did not waver in unbelief about God’s promise. In Romans 9:9 Paul recalls the promise “At the appointed time I will return, and Sarah will have a son.” In Galatians 4 she is the “free woman” whose child was born “through the promise” (4:22-23), and Paul says “the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (4:26). Hebrews 11:11 says that Sarah, though barren and past the age, received power to conceive because she considered the one who promised to be faithful. In 1 Peter 3:6 she is held up to Christian wives because she “obeyed Abraham and called him lord.” Peter says that the readers are “her children if you do what is right and refuse to give way to fear.”
f: Wife of Abraham, mother of Isaac

t: In Romans 9 Paul recalls that God’s promise came through Isaac, “not the children of the flesh,” and then through Jacob rather than his twin Esau, before either was born. Paul quotes Malachi: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.” He uses them to show that God’s purpose rests on his call and not on human descent. Hebrews 11:9 says that Abraham lived in tents, “as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise.” Isaac and Jacob blessed their sons by faith (11:20-21), and 12:16-17 warns against Esau, who “for a single meal sold his birthright” and later “could find no ground for repentance, though he sought the blessing with tears.”

e.u: The king of Egypt in the Exodus
t: Paul quotes God’s word to Pharaoh from Exodus 9:16: “I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.” Romans 9 uses him as an example of God’s sovereign choice in showing mercy or letting hearts harden.
f: Ruler of Egypt in the time of Moses

e.u: Her household told Paul of the quarrels
t: Paul writes, “My brothers, some from Chloe’s household have informed me that there are quarrels among you.” Nothing else is known about her. The wording suggests she was a woman of some means whose household members, perhaps slaves or freed people, traveled between Corinth and Ephesus.
f: Believer known to Paul and the Corinthians

t: Paul says, “I thank God that I did not baptize any of you except Crispus and Gaius.” Acts 18:8 calls Crispus the ruler of the synagogue, who believed “together with his entire household.” Many think this Gaius is the host of Romans 16:23, since Gaius was a very common name.

Paul opens the letter “Paul, called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and our brother Sosthenes.” Acts 18:17 names a Sosthenes as the synagogue ruler who was beaten in front of Gallio, and he may be the same man, though the name was not rare.

Paul baptized “the household of Stephanas” (1:16) and says “Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia, and they have devoted themselves to the service of the saints” (16:15). He urges the church “to submit to such as these,” and is glad that Stephanas, with Fortunatus and Achaicus, has come to him.

e.u: Visitors who came to Paul at Ephesus
t: Paul writes, “I am glad that Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you. For they refreshed my spirit and yours as well.” Nothing more is known of them. Fortunatus is a Latin name and Achaicus means “from Achaia.”

e.u: A member living with his father’s wife
t: Paul has heard that “A man has his father’s wife,” and he tells the church to remove the man: “hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord.” His name is not given. Scholars disagree whether he is the same person whom Paul asks them to forgive in 2 Corinthians 2:5-8.

A Greek believer who works with Paul. Galatians 2:1-3 says he went up to Jerusalem with Paul and was not made to be circumcised. In 2 Corinthians Paul waits anxiously for him at Troas, is comforted when he arrives in Macedonia with good news, and sends him back to Corinth to finish the collection. Many think he carried the sharp letter. Paul calls him “my partner and fellow worker among you” (8:23). Acts never names him. Paul took him to Jerusalem, and “not even Titus, who was with me, was compelled to be circumcised, even though he was a Greek” (Galatians 2:3). Paul says, “Titus to Dalmatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). Paul addresses him as “my true child in our common faith” (Titus 1:4) and says he left him on Crete to “appoint elders in every town” (1:5). He tells him to “speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine” (2:1), says “Let no one despise you” (2:15), and asks him to come to Nicopolis once Artemas or Tychicus arrives (3:12).

Paul writes, “if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you.” The majority had punished him, and Paul asks them to “forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow” (2:5-8). In 7:12 he speaks of “the one who did wrong” and “the one who was harmed.” The man is not named, and scholars still disagree whether he is the man of 1 Corinthians 5 or someone who insulted Paul during the painful visit.

Paul writes, “I am afraid, however, that just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ” (11:3). The story is in Genesis 3, and Adam named her Eve because she would be “the mother of all the living” (Genesis 3:20). In 1 Timothy 2:13-14 Paul refers to Eve in giving reasons for his instruction about teaching, and writes that “the woman who was deceived” fell into transgression. How this argument applies is debated.

Aretas IV ruled the Nabataean kingdom from Petra for about forty-eight years, from about 9 BC to AD 40. Paul says that in Damascus “the governor under King Aretas secured the city of the Damascenes in order to arrest me” (2 Corinthians 11:32). How an official of Aretas came to hold power in Damascus is debated.

e.u: Sarah’s slave and mother of Ishmael
t: Abraham’s wife Sarah gave her slave Hagar to Abraham, and she bore Ishmael (Genesis 16). Paul reads the story as a picture: “One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery: This is Hagar” (Galatians 4:24). He then says she “corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem, because she is in slavery with her children” (4:25).
f: Slave of Sarah, mother of Ishmael

t: Paul calls him “the beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord” and says, “I have sent him to you for this very purpose, that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts” (6:21-22). Acts 20:4 names him as a man of Asia who traveled with Paul. He also carries the letter to the Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9) and is later sent to Crete or Ephesus (Titus 3:12; 2 Timothy 4:12). Colossians 4:7-8 gives his job: “Tychicus will tell you all the news about me. He is a beloved brother, a faithful minister, and a fellow servant in the Lord.” Paul sends him “that you may know about us, and that he may encourage your hearts.” Paul says, “Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus” (2 Timothy 4:12). Paul says he will send “Artemas or Tychicus” to Titus (3:12), probably to take his place on Crete. The letter does not say which of them came.

e.u: The slave who returned with Tychicus
t: Ephesians does not name him. Colossians 4:9 says, “With him I am sending Onesimus, our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you.” Paul’s letter to Philemon asks Philemon to receive Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16). He is a living example of what Ephesians 6:5-9 says about slaves and masters. Paul calls him “our faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you” (4:9) and sends him with Tychicus. Philemon 10-16 tells why he was away. In Philemon he is the slave for whom Paul appeals: “my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains” (verse 10). Paul says, “Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me” (verse 11), and plays on the meaning of his name, “useful.” He is to be received “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (verse 16). The letter does not say how he came to Paul or whether Philemon set him free. Ignatius names a bishop of Ephesus Onesimus about AD 110, but a link to this man is only a guess.
f: Slave, later a brother in Christ

t: Paul calls him “my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger and minister to my needs” (2:25). He fell “sick indeed, nearly unto death” (2:27), and he was distressed that the Philippians had heard of it (2:26). Paul sends him back, so that they may “welcome him in the Lord with great joy,” because he nearly died “risking his life” (2:29-30). He brought the church’s gifts (4:18). The name was common, and Epaphras in Colossians 1:7 is probably a different man.

e.u: A fellow worker named in the letter
t: Paul names him among “the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the Book of Life” (4:3). Nothing else is said about him. Some later writers thought he was Clement of Rome, but the name was very common. Eusebius says that some in the early church, according to Origen, named Clement of Rome as the writer of Hebrews, and Clement’s own letter to the Corinthians draws on Hebrews at length. That shows that Hebrews was known in Rome by the end of the 1st century, though it does not show who wrote it.

e.u: The person asked to help Euodia and Syntyche
t: Paul writes, “I ask you, my true yokefellow, to help these women” (4:3). The Greek word (syzygos) could be a title or a name, and some have wondered whether it was a man named Syzygus. The letter does not say who is meant.

e.u: The Colossian who brought the gospel and the news
t: Paul calls him “our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf” (1:7). The Colossians “learned it from Epaphras” (1:7), and he told Paul of their “love in the Spirit” (1:8). He “is one of you” (4:12). Paul says he is “always wrestling in prayer for you” (4:12) and “goes to great pains for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis” (4:13). Philemon 23 calls him Paul’s fellow prisoner. The name may be a short form of Epaphroditus, but most scholars think the man of Philippians 2:25 is someone else. Paul calls him “my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus” and says he sends greetings (Philemon 23). The word is the one used of Aristarchus in Colossians 4:10.
f: Founder and pastor of the church at Colossae

t: Paul calls him “my fellow prisoner” (4:10). Acts names him as a Macedonian from Thessalonica who was seized in the riot at Ephesus (19:29), who traveled with Paul (20:4), and who sailed with him to Rome (27:2). Philemon 24 also lists him among Paul’s fellow workers. Philemon 24 lists him among Paul’s “fellow workers” who send greetings.

e.u: A Jewish co-worker with a Roman second name
t: Paul writes, “Jesus, who is called Justus, also sends greetings” (4:11). He, Aristarchus and Mark are “the only Jews among my fellow workers for the kingdom of God,” and Paul says “they have been a comfort to me” (4:11). Nothing else is known of him. Jesus is the Greek form of Joshua, and Justus was a common Roman name.

Paul lists him with Luke: “Luke, the beloved physician, and Demas send you greetings” (4:14). Philemon 24 names him as a fellow worker. In 2 Timothy 4:10 Paul says that Demas has deserted him because he loved the present world. Paul says, “Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica” (2 Timothy 4:10). Philemon 24 lists him among Paul’s “fellow workers” who send greetings. He is not called a fellow prisoner.

e.u: A woman of Laodicea who hosted a church
t: Paul writes, “Greet the brothers in Laodicea, as well as Nympha and the church that meets at her house” (4:15). Some manuscripts read “his” or “their” house, and the name could be read as Nymphas, a man, but many editors prefer Nympha and “her house.” Nothing else is known of her. She is one of several women named as hosts of house churches in the New Testament (Acts 12:12; 16:15; Romans 16:3-5).
f: Host of a house church at Laodicea

e.u: A man told to finish his ministry
t: Paul tells the church to say to Archippus that he should “complete the ministry you have received in the Lord” (4:17). The letter does not say what the ministry was. Philemon 2 calls him “our fellow soldier.” Because Philemon and Colossians were sent together, many suppose he lived in or near Colossae and belonged to Philemon’s circle. Paul calls him “our fellow soldier” and greets him with Philemon and Apphia (Philemon 2). Colossians 4:17 tells him to complete the ministry he received. Some suggest he was Philemon’s son, but the letters do not say.

e.u: A figure Paul says will be revealed before the Day
t: Paul writes that “the Day of the Lord” will not come “until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness—the son of destruction—is revealed” (2 Thessalonians 2:3). He “will oppose and exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship” and “seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God” (2:4). The Lord Jesus “will slay” him “with the breath of His mouth and annihilate” him “by the majesty of His arrival” (2:8). Readers disagree on whether this is one person, a series of rulers or a power in history.
1 John 2:18 recalls the teaching that “the antichrist is coming,” and says “many antichrists have appeared.” The letter does not use the title “man of lawlessness.”
f: An opponent of God in the last days

e.u: What holds back the lawless one for now
t: Paul writes, “you know what is now restraining him, so that he may be revealed at the proper time” (2 Thessalonians 2:6), and “the one who now restrains it will continue until he is taken out of the way” (2:7). The Thessalonians knew what Paul meant because he had told them (2:5), and the letter does not repeat it. Suggestions include the Roman order, the preaching of the gospel and an angel, and none is certain.
f: Something or someone that holds back the lawless one

e.u: The one Paul says came to save sinners
t: The letter names him “Christ Jesus” and “our Lord Jesus Christ.” Paul says “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst” (1 Timothy 1:15), and that there is “one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all” (2:5-6). He is the one “who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate” (6:13), and the hymn in 3:16 says “He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory.” In 2 Timothy he is the one who “has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel” (1:10), who is “raised from the dead, descended from David” (2:8), and who “will judge the living and the dead” (4:1). In Titus he is “Christ Jesus our Savior” (1:4) and “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (2:13), a phrase many read as calling Jesus God. He “gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness” (2:14). In 1 Peter he is the “living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight” (2:4), the one who “committed no sin” (2:22), who “bore our sins in His body on the tree” (2:24), who “suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God” (3:18), and the “Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (2:25). He is also the “Chief Shepherd” who will appear (5:4). The readers are to “sanctify Christ as Lord” in their hearts (3:15).

In 2 Peter he is “our God and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:1) and “our Lord and Savior” (3:2, 18). The writer speaks of his “power and coming” (1:16) and of the Day of the Lord (3:10), and asks the readers to “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).

In 1 John he is “the Word of life” (1:1), “His Son, Jesus Christ” (1:3), “the Righteous One” (2:1), “the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (2:2; 4:10), and the one who “came by water and blood” (5:6). The letter says “Whoever has the Son has life” (5:12), and “He is the true God and eternal life” (5:20).
In 2 John he is “Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father” (3), who came “in the flesh” (7), and whose teaching one must remain in: “Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son” (9).
In 3 John he is never named. The letter speaks only of “the Name,” for whose sake the brothers went out (7).

In Jude he is “our only Master and Lord” (Jude 4). The readers are “kept in Jesus Christ” (Jude 1) and wait for his mercy “to bring you eternal life” (Jude 21), and glory is given to God “through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Jude 25).
f: The Lord Paul serves and the subject of the hymn

t: Paul writes of “your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well” (2 Timothy 1:5). They are named only here. Acts 16:1 says Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer and his father was a Greek. Paul also says Timothy has known “the Holy Scriptures” “from infancy” (3:15), and the letter does not say who taught him, though the family is the likely answer. The letter does not say how the two women came to faith.
f: Three generations of faith: Lois, Eunice, Timothy

e.u: A friend who searched Rome for Paul
t: Paul prays, “May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me” (2 Timothy 1:16-17). He had also “ministered” to Paul “in Ephesus” (1:18). In 4:19 Paul greets “the household of Onesiphorus,” and Paul prays for the Lord to grant him mercy “on that day” (1:18), so some readers think he may have died, but the letter does not say. He is not named elsewhere in the New Testament.
f: Ephesian friend who was not ashamed of the chains

e.u: The man at Troas who kept Paul’s cloak
t: Paul asks Timothy, “When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments” (2 Timothy 4:13). Carpus is named only here, and the letter says nothing more about him.

e.u: A co-worker who went to Galatia
t: Paul says, “Crescens has gone to Galatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). Some early manuscripts read “Gaul” instead. He is named only here.
f: A worker sent or gone abroad

e.u: A man who opposed Paul’s message
t: Paul writes, “Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message” (2 Timothy 4:14-15). Alexander was a common name. The letters do not say whether he is the Alexander of Acts 19:33 or of 1 Timothy 1:20.
f: An opponent Timothy was to avoid

e.u: An Ephesian companion left sick at Miletus
t: Paul says, “Trophimus I left sick in Miletus” (2 Timothy 4:20). Acts 20:4 names Trophimus among those from Asia who went with Paul, and Acts 21:29 calls him “the Ephesian.” The letter does not say what the illness was or when this happened.

Paul calls him “one of their own prophets” (Titus 1:12). Later writers name Epimenides as the poet behind the Cretan saying and describe him as a poet and seer from Crete, usually placed about 600 BC. The letter itself does not give his name.
f: Cretan poet whose saying Paul quotes

e.u: One of the two men Paul might send
t: Paul writes, “As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis” (Titus 3:12). Artemas is named only here. The letter does not say who he was, or whether he or Tychicus went to Crete.
f: Possible replacement for Titus on Crete

e.u: A traveler Titus is to equip
t: Paul asks Titus, “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need” (Titus 3:13). Zenas is named only here. In the New Testament “lawyer” usually means an expert in the law of Moses (Luke 7:30; 10:25), but the letter does not say what kind of lawyer he was.

e.u: The slave owner Paul writes to
t: Paul calls him “our beloved fellow worker” (Philemon 1) and thanks God for his “faith in the Lord Jesus” and “love for all the saints” (verse 5). The church met in his house (verse 2). He owned Onesimus, and Paul asks him to receive Onesimus back “as a beloved brother” (verse 16). Paul also says, “you owe me your very self” (verse 19), which suggests Paul had a part in Philemon’s own faith. The letter does not say where he lived. Colossians 4:9 and 4:17 point to Colossae. Church tradition, written down much later, makes him a bishop and a martyr, but the New Testament says nothing about the end of his life.
f: Wealthy believer and slave owner at Colossae (probably)

t: Paul greets “Apphia our sister” (Philemon 2). She is named only here. Many readers think she was Philemon’s wife, and the Greek word “sister” only means a fellow believer, so the letter does not say. She is greeted by name in the same verse as Archippus and the house church, so she was known to the church that met in the house.
f: Believer greeted by name; perhaps Philemon’s wife

e.u: King of Salem and priest of God Most High
t: Genesis 14:18-20 tells of him in three verses: he met Abraham after a battle, brought out bread and wine, and blessed him, and Abraham gave him a tenth. Psalm 110:4 says the Lord’s king is “a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews 7 builds on these two passages. The writer reads his name as “king of righteousness” and “king of Salem” as “king of peace,” and notes that Genesis gives no father, mother or genealogy for him, so that he is “like the Son of God” and remains a priest for all time (7:1-3). Because Abraham gave him a tenth and was blessed by him, the writer argues that his priesthood is greater than the Levitical priesthood.
f: Priest-king; a picture of the Son’s priesthood

e.u: Moses’ brother, the first high priest
t: Hebrews 5:4 says no one takes the honor of high priest on himself, but is called by God “just as Aaron was.” Aaron’s priesthood is the standard against which the writer sets Melchizedek (7:11), and Aaron’s budding rod is listed among the contents of the ark (9:4).

e.u: Moses’ successor who led Israel into the land
t: Hebrews 4:8 says that if Joshua had given Israel rest, God would not have spoken of another day. The writer takes this to mean that the entry under Joshua was not the final “rest,” which still lies ahead. Joshua is the Greek form Jesus, though the writer does not play on the two names here. The fall of Jericho under Joshua is named in 11:30.
f: Led the people across the Jordan into the land

e.u: The woman of Jericho who welcomed the spies
t: Hebrews 11:31 says that Rahab the prostitute, “because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient.” She is the only woman other than Sarah to be named in the list of the faithful in chapter 11, and James 2:25 also names her. Matthew 1:5 lists her in the genealogy of Jesus. James 2:25 asks whether even Rahab the prostitute was not justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route. She follows Abraham as a second example, a foreign woman beside the father of the nation.
f: A foreigner who hid the spies and was spared

e.u: An unnamed teacher with a deep knowledge of Scripture
t: The letter does not give its author’s name. The writer calls it “my word of exhortation” (13:22) and writes in some of the finest Greek in the New Testament, quoting the Greek Old Testament. He says Timothy has been released and sends greetings from “those from Italy.” He speaks of the message as “confirmed to us by those who heard Him” (2:3), so he was not one of the first hearers. Paul, Barnabas, Apollos, Priscilla and Luke have each been suggested; Origen, as Eusebius reports him, said only God knows.
f: Unknown author; Paul, Barnabas, Apollos and others suggested

e.u: The sufferer of the book of Job
t: James 5:11 says, “You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy.” Job is named only here in the New Testament. In the Old Testament Job also complains and questions God, but James picks out what he endured and the way the story ends. A Jewish writing called the Testament of Job, from about the same period, also makes Job a model of endurance.

Peter recalls “the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water” (3:20). He pairs the flood with baptism: “this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also” (3:21). Peter does not name the mountains where the ark came to rest. Genesis 8:4 puts it on the mountains of Ararat. 2 Peter 2:5 calls Noah a preacher of righteousness.

2 Peter 2:5 calls him “a preacher of righteousness” and says God “preserved” him “among the eight” when He brought the flood on the ungodly world; 3:5-6 recalls that “the world of that time perished in the flood.”

e.u: The God Peter tells the readers to trust
t: Peter ends chapter 4 by saying that “those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good” (4:19). Elsewhere in the letter God is the Father who foreknew (1:2), who raised Christ from the dead (1:3, 1:21), who “judges each one’s work impartially” (1:17), who “opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (5:5) and who is “the God of all grace” (5:10).
f: Faithful, and the God of all grace

e.u: The seer who loved the wages of wickedness
t: A seer from Pethor on the Euphrates whom the king of Moab hired to curse Israel (Numbers 22-24). His donkey saw the angel of the LORD and spoke, and instead of cursing he blessed Israel. Numbers 31:16 says his advice led Israel into sin at Peor, and Revelation 2:14 speaks of the teaching of Balaam. Peter says the false teachers “have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness” (2:15-16). Jude 11 also mentions Balaam’s error. A wall inscription from Deir ‘Alla, about 800 BC, names a seer called Balaam son of Beor.
Jude’s words are, “they have rushed headlong into the error of Balaam” (Jude 11).

In the letter to Pergamum some hold “the teaching of Balaam,” who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before Israel, so that they ate food sacrificed to idols and committed sexual immorality (Revelation 2:14).

Abraham’s nephew, who chose the plain of the Jordan and settled near Sodom, and who was led out of the city before it was destroyed (Genesis 13; 19). Genesis does not call him righteous, but 2 Peter does: God “rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard)” (2:7-8). The letter uses him to show that “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials” (2:9). Jesus joined the days of Noah and the days of Lot (Luke 17:26-30).

a: John, the writer of the letters
t: The letter does not give a name. It speaks in the first person plural of what “we have heard, … seen with our own eyes, … gazed upon and touched with our own hands” (1:1), and in the singular as “I am writing” (2:1). From the second century, church writers such as Irenaeus say that it came from John the apostle, who lived at Ephesus. The Second and Third Letters are written by “the elder,” and Papias mentions a John the Elder, so some scholars think that was the writer; others hold that the apostle is meant. The letter also leaves out any greeting and any closing.

The Second and Third Letters name their writer only as “the elder.” Many take him to be the same person as the writer of 1 John, and the sense of the three letters is hardly doubted; who the elder was is still argued.

The first son of Adam and Eve, who brought an offering from the ground, was angry when God looked with favor on his brother Abel’s offering, and killed him in the field (Genesis 4:1-16). God marked him and sent him to wander. In the New Testament he is named in Hebrews 11:4, Jude 11 and 1 John 3:12, which says he “belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did Cain slay him? Because his own deeds were evil, while those of his brother were righteous.”
Jude says of the intruders, “They have traveled the path of Cain” (Jude 11).

The letter says, “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One” (2:1). The Greek word is paraklētos, the word the Gospel of John uses of the Holy Spirit as “Helper” (John 14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7); it occurs five times in the New Testament, four in the Gospel and here. The next verse calls Him “the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (2:2).

e.u: The writer, who gives no name
a: The elder of 2 John and 3 John
t: The letter opens “The elder” (1:1) and gives no other name, and the Third Letter opens the same way. Church writers from the second century on, Irenaeus among them, quote 2 John as the work of John, the Lord’s disciple. Papias, a bishop at Hierapolis, spoke of an elder named John besides the apostle, and some scholars think this elder wrote the Second and Third Letters; others hold that the apostle called himself “the elder” as an older man with standing in the churches. He loves the readers “in the truth” (1:1), is “overjoyed” to find their children “walking in the truth” (1:4), and hopes “to come and speak with you face to face” (1:12).

3 John opens the same way, “The elder, To the beloved Gaius” (3 John 1). There he speaks of “my children,” says he has “written to the church,” plans a visit, and expects to deal with Diotrephes when he comes (3 John 4, 9-10, 14).
f: Writes as “the elder”; called John by early tradition

e.n: Gaius, the friend the elder writes to
t: The letter is addressed “To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth” (1:1), and it calls him “Beloved” three more times. Brothers who visited him “testified about your devotion to the truth” (1:3), and he is “faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you” (1:5). The elder may count him among “my children” (1:4). He belongs to a church in which Diotrephes has refused the brothers, and the elder asks him to keep on receiving them and to “send them on their way in a manner worthy of God” (1:6). Gaius was a very common Roman name. The New Testament has a Gaius of Macedonia, a Gaius of Derbe and a Gaius of Corinth, and nothing shows that this is any of them. A church manual of about AD 380 calls a Gaius the bishop of Pergamum, a late tradition that cannot be checked.
f: Friend, and perhaps convert, of the elder

e.u: The man who loves to be first
a: Diotrephes, who loves to be first
t: A leading man in the church the elder wrote to. The letter says, “Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction” (1:9). The elder charges him with “malicious slander against us,” and says that “he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church” (1:10). The letter does not accuse him of false teaching; the complaint is about ambition and the way he treats others. Readers differ over what he was: the host of a house church, a leader who had taken sole control, or a man who distrusted outsiders. His name means nourished by Zeus and is rare. He is known only from these two verses.
f: Opposes the elder; refuses the traveling brothers

e.u: The man with a good testimony
t: The elder writes, “Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true” (1:12). He is probably the man who carried the letter to Gaius, and perhaps one of the traveling brothers, so that the verse works as a letter of recommendation. Nothing links him with the silversmith Demetrius of Acts 19, and the name was common. A church manual of about AD 380 makes a Demetrius the bishop of Philadelphia, a late tradition that cannot be checked.
f: Commended by the elder to Gaius

e.u: Writer of the letter of Jude
a: Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ
t: The letter opens, “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (1:1). Jude is the same name as Judas and Judah. Most readers take him to be the Judas whom the Gospels list among the brothers of Jesus (Mark 6:3; Matthew 13:55), and the James he names to be the leader of the church in Jerusalem. He calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and does not mention the family tie. He does not claim to be an apostle and speaks of “the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ” as others (1:17). He had meant to write “about the salvation we share,” but “felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith” (1:3). He knows the Old Testament well and also uses two Jewish books outside it. The brothers of Jesus did not believe in him during his ministry, were among the believers after the resurrection, and later traveled as missionaries. Hegesippus, in the 2nd century, tells of two grandsons of Jude who farmed in the land of Israel and were questioned under Domitian. Some scholars think the letter was written later in his name.
f: Brother of James, and by the usual reading a brother of Jesus

t: Jude writes, “even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, ‘The Lord rebuke you!’” (1:9). The name means “Who is like God?” In the book of Daniel he is the great prince who stands guard over Israel (Daniel 10:13, 21; 12:1), and in Revelation 12:7 he and his angels fight the dragon. Jewish writings of the time count him among the chief angels. The story of the body of Moses is not in the Old Testament; early Christian writers say Jude took it from a Jewish book called the Assumption of Moses. Only here in the Bible is Michael called “the archangel,” and the only other use of that word is 1 Thessalonians 4:16.
In Revelation 12:7-9 “Michael and his angels” fight the dragon, and the dragon is thrown down to the earth.
f: Disputes with the devil over the body of Moses

t: A Levite of the family of Kohath who, with Dathan, Abiram and 250 leaders, rose against Moses and Aaron and claimed that the whole community was holy and needed no such leaders (Numbers 16:1-3). The ground opened and swallowed the rebels, and fire consumed the 250 who offered incense (Numbers 16:31-35). His sons did not die (Numbers 26:11), and several psalms carry the name of the sons of Korah. Jude says of the intruders, “they have perished in Korah’s rebellion” (1:11): they reject authority in the church as he did, and Jude speaks of their end as certain.

e.u: The man who walked with God
t: Enoch is the seventh name in the family line from Adam through Seth (Genesis 5:3-18). Genesis says that he walked with God and that God took him (Genesis 5:24), and Hebrews 11:5 says he was taken up so that he did not see death.
