In the centuries before Jesus a large body of Jewish writing grew up under his name, telling of his journeys through heaven and his warnings of judgment. Jude quotes from it: “Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: ‘Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones to execute judgment on everyone’” (1:14-15). The words are from 1 Enoch 1:9. Jude is the only New Testament writer to quote the book by name.
f: Son of Jared, father of Methuselah

t: The writer names himself four times as John (1:1, 4, 9; 22:8) and gives himself no title but servant, brother and prophet: “I, John, your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus, was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (1:9). He knows the seven churches of Asia closely and expects them to accept his authority. His mind is soaked in the Old Testament; he never quotes it formally, yet most verses echo it. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus, in the 2nd century, say he was John the apostle, the son of Zebedee, and that is the main tradition of the church. Dionysius of Alexandria, in the 3rd century, pointed to the differences in Greek style between Revelation and the Gospel of John and concluded that another John wrote it; many modern scholars agree, and some speak of a prophet John otherwise unknown. Early writers say he was banished to Patmos under Domitian and later returned to Ephesus.
f: Brother and fellow servant of the seven churches; by tradition the apostle John

t: Christ says to the church at Pergamum, “you have held fast to My name and have not denied your faith in Me, even in the day when My faithful witness Antipas was killed among you, where Satan dwells” (2:13). Nothing else is known of him. He is the only person in the seven churches named as having died for the faith, and he is given the title that 1:5 gives to Jesus, “the faithful witness.” The Greek word for witness is martys, and from deaths like his it came to mean martyr. A later legend says he was bishop of Pergamum and was burned inside a bronze bull.
f: A member of the church at Pergamum

e.u: A teacher in the church at Thyatira
t: Christ says to Thyatira, “You tolerate that woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess. By her teaching she misleads My servants to be sexually immoral and to eat food sacrificed to idols” (2:20). Jezebel is almost certainly not her real name. It is the name of the queen of Israel who promoted the worship of Baal and persecuted the prophets (1 Kings 16:31; 18:4; 21:25). The woman at Thyatira was a Christian with a following in the church who claimed to speak for God, and she taught that believers could join in the meals of the guilds and their gods. Women did prophesy in the early churches (Acts 21:9; 1 Corinthians 11:5); the fault found here is what she taught. She had been given time to repent and refused.
f: Tolerated by the church at Thyatira

e.u: Jesus Christ as John sees him
a: The Lion of the tribe of Judah
t: John hears of a Lion and turns to see a Lamb: “Then I saw a Lamb who appeared to have been slain, standing in the center of the throne” (5:6). From then on “the Lamb” is the book’s chief name for Jesus, used 28 times. The picture joins the Passover lamb (Exodus 12), the servant led like a lamb to the slaughter (Isaiah 53:7) and John the Baptist’s “Lamb of God.” The Lamb has been killed and stands alive. He alone can open the scroll of God’s purposes, he is worshiped with God (5:13), he shepherds his people (7:17), the kings make war on him and he defeats them, he has a bride, and with God he is the temple and the lamp of the new Jerusalem (21:22-23). Heaven sings, “Worthy is the Lamb, who was slain, to receive power and riches and wisdom and strength and honor and glory and blessing!” (5:12).
f: Jesus Christ, shown as the slain and living Lamb

e.u: The devil, as Revelation pictures him
a: The deceiver of the whole world
t: John sees an enormous red dragon with seven heads, ten horns and seven crowns, whose tail sweeps a third of the stars from the sky. He is named plainly: “the great dragon was hurled down—that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan, the deceiver of the whole world” (12:9). He tries to devour the Messiah at his birth, loses a war in heaven to Michael, and is thrown down to earth, where he pursues the woman and her children. He gives his power and throne to the beast from the sea (13:2), and with the beast and the false prophet he forms a counterfeit of God, the Lamb and the Spirit. He is bound for a thousand years, released, and at last thrown into the lake of fire (20:10). In the Old Testament the sea monster Leviathan or Rahab stands for the powers of chaos that God defeats (Isaiah 27:1; Psalm 74:13-14).
f: Satan; the power behind the two beasts

t: “Then I saw a beast with ten horns and seven heads rising out of the sea. There were ten royal crowns on its horns and blasphemous names on its heads” (13:1). It looks like a leopard with a bear’s feet and a lion’s mouth, the four beasts of Daniel 7 in one. The dragon gives it his power; one of its heads has a mortal wound that has healed; the whole earth worships it; it makes war on the saints for 42 months. Its number is 666 (13:18). It carries the prostitute Babylon and later destroys her (17:3, 16), and it is captured by the rider on the white horse and thrown into the lake of fire (19:20). John’s first readers would have seen in it the Roman Empire and its emperors, who were given divine titles. Many readers also, or instead, see a final ruler at the end of the age, the Antichrist, a name Revelation itself does not use.
f: Empowered by the dragon; worshiped by the earth

e.n: The beast from the earth, the false prophet
e.u: Makes the world worship the first beast
t: “Then I saw another beast rising out of the earth. This beast had two horns like a lamb, but spoke like a dragon” (13:11). It acts for the first beast, works signs, has an image of the beast made, and sees to it that no one can buy or sell without the beast’s mark. Later it is called “the false prophet” (16:13; 19:20; 20:10), and it shares the first beast’s end. Where the first beast is power, the second is persuasion: religion and propaganda in the service of the state. For the churches of Asia this was the network of priests and officials who ran the worship of the emperor. Jesus warned of false prophets who would work great signs (Matthew 24:24).

e.n: Abaddon, the angel of the Abyss
e.u: King of the locusts of the fifth trumpet
t: The locusts that rise from the Abyss at the fifth trumpet “were ruled by a king, the angel of the Abyss. His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in Greek it is Apollyon” (9:11). Abaddon means destruction, and in the Old Testament it is a name for the realm of the dead (Job 26:6; Proverbs 15:11). Apollyon means destroyer. Some think John chose the Greek name to recall Apollo, the god the emperor Domitian favored, one of whose signs was the locust. He may be the same as Satan or one of Satan’s angels; the text does not say. John Bunyan made Apollyon the fiend whom Christian fights in The Pilgrim’s Progress.
f: King over the locusts from the Abyss

e.n: The woman clothed with the sun
e.u: Mother of the child the dragon hunts
a: A woman clothed in the sun
t: “And a great sign appeared in heaven: a woman clothed in the sun, with the moon under her feet and a crown of twelve stars on her head” (12:1). She is in labor, and a dragon waits to devour her child, who is “a male child, who will rule all the nations with an iron scepter” (12:5), the Messiah. The child is caught up to God, and she flees to the wilderness, where God feeds her. The dragon then makes war on “the rest of her children, who keep the commandments of God and hold to the testimony of Jesus” (12:17). The sun, moon and twelve stars recall Joseph’s dream about the family of Israel (Genesis 37:9). Most readers take her as the people of God: Israel, from whom the Messiah came, and the church, his persecuted family. In Catholic and Orthodox tradition she is also Mary, the mother of Jesus.
f: Mother of the male child; pursued by the dragon

t: A fertile, densely settled region ruled by Herod Antipas. Most of Jesus’ ministry took place here, among villages around the lake and on the road between Tiberias and Sepphoris. In Acts 9:31 the church has peace in Judea, Galilee and Samaria.

The southern region, ruled directly by a Roman prefect from AD 6. It includes Jerusalem, Bethlehem, Bethany, Jericho and the wilderness. In Acts “all Judea” hears the word and the church is scattered through it. Paul says the Thessalonians “became imitators of the churches of God in Judea” (1 Thessalonians 2:14).

The hill country of the old northern kingdom. Pilgrims often detoured east through the Jordan Valley to avoid it, but Jesus goes through. In Acts it is the second ring of the mission: “Jerusalem, all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.”

A group of ten cities, mostly east of the Jordan, with Greek culture and pagan temples. Scythopolis (Beth Shean) was the only one west of the river. Jesus visits the region and sends a healed man to proclaim the good news there.
The strip of land east of the Jordan, ruled by Antipas. It contained Machaerus, where John was killed, and the place where John had baptized.

Two ancient Phoenician ports in what is now Lebanon, outside Herod’s territory. People from these cities came to hear Jesus, and he withdrew there at one point. In Acts Paul lands at Tyre and finds disciples, and later his ship calls at Sidon.

A large Jewish community lived in Egypt, especially in Alexandria. Matthew says Joseph took Mary and the child there to escape Herod and later returned to Nazareth. Coptic tradition places their stay around Old Cairo. In Acts 7 Stephen retells the stories of Joseph and Moses in Egypt. The story of Jannes and Jambres, Pharaoh’s magicians, is set here (2 Timothy 3:8).
A small farming village in the lower Galilean hills, probably a few hundred people, near the larger city of Sepphoris. Excavations show terraced fields, wine presses and simple houses.

e.u: Town of David, six miles south of Jerusalem
t: A small village in Judea, linked to David and to Micah’s prophecy of a ruler from there. The Church of the Nativity stands over a grotto honored since the 2nd century.

A fishing and farming village on the north shore, with a customs post and a Roman garrison nearby. Jesus taught in its synagogue and healed in Peter’s house. Excavations show black basalt houses and a later white limestone synagogue.
The site of Jesus’ first sign at a wedding and a later healing. Two villages claim the name, Kafr Kanna (traditional) and Khirbet Qana, which has more first-century remains.
A small village on the slope of the Hill of Moreh, where Jesus raised a widow’s son. The village still exists as Nein.

e.u: Fishing village near the lake’s north end
t: The home of Peter, Andrew and Philip. It lay just east of the Jordan in Philip’s territory and was rebuilt as a Greek-style city. The leading candidate is et-Tell.
A basalt town two miles north of Capernaum. Jesus names it with Bethsaida as a city that saw his deeds and did not repent.

e.u: Fishing town on the western shore
t: The home of Mary Magdalene. Excavations have uncovered a first-century synagogue with a carved stone, a market, a harbor and ritual baths. Matthew calls the place Magadan.
A rich crescent of farmland between Magdala and Capernaum, which gave the lake one of its names. Jesus landed here after walking on water, and crowds brought him the sick.

e.u: Pagan city at the foot of Mount Hermon
t: Philip’s capital, built near a spring and a cave shrine of the god Pan. Peter confesses Jesus as the Christ in this region.
A gentile district east of the lake, with a steep bank beside the water. The Gospels name it differently (Gerasa, Gadara, Gergesa), perhaps because the area was linked to more than one city.

e.u: Oasis city in the Jordan Valley
t: One of the oldest cities in the world. Herod built a winter palace on the new site, about two miles from the ancient mound. Jesus heals the blind and visits Zacchaeus here on his way up to Jerusalem.

e.u: Village on the Mount of Olives
t: Home of Lazarus, Martha and Mary, about two miles east of Jerusalem. Jesus stays here during Passion Week.

e.u: Village near the Mount of Olives
t: The village where Jesus sent two disciples to find a colt for his entry into Jerusalem.
Where the risen Jesus broke bread with two disciples. Its location is uncertain, and several sites have been proposed.
A Samaritan village below Mount Gerizim. Jacob’s Well, honored since early times, is the setting for the long talk with the Samaritan woman.
The city whose destruction becomes Jesus’ standard for judgement. Its location is debated, but traditions place it at the southern end of the Dead Sea.
2 Peter 2:6 says God condemned “the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly,” and 2:7-8 tells of Lot’s rescue.
Jude 7 says that “Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them” are “on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire.”
The great Assyrian city on the Tigris, to which Jonah was sent. Jesus holds up its people as examples of repentance.

e.u: Freshwater lake, also Gennesaret and Tiberias
t: About 13 miles long and 8 wide and nearly 700 feet below sea level. It is a harp-shaped lake that supported a fishing industry, with sudden storms funneled down by the hills.
Flows from Mount Hermon through the lake and down to the Dead Sea. John baptized on it, and two sites, Qasr al-Yahud and Al-Maghtas, claim Jesus’ baptism.

e.u: Dry hills between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea
t: A rocky desert of limestone ridges and canyons. John preached here, Jesus fasted here, and the Qumran community withdrew to its edge.
Matthew sets the Sermon on “the mountain” and Luke on “a level place”. Tradition places it on the northern hills above Tabgha, where the Church of the Beatitudes now stands.
The Gospels say only that Jesus took three disciples up “a high mountain”. Tradition since the 4th century says Mount Tabor, while some scholars prefer Mount Hermon.
2 Peter 1:18 recalls the voice from heaven “when we were with Him on the holy mountain,” which most take to be the Transfiguration.

A city of perhaps 30,000–60,000 people, packed with pilgrims at festivals, built on two ridges around the Temple Mount. It lay about 2,500 feet above sea level, and Gospel writers often say people “go up” to it. In Acts it is the home of the first church, the city of the council, and the place where Paul is arrested. Paul is about to take the collection from Macedonia and Achaia to Jerusalem (Romans 15:25-28). The Corinthians are to set aside money each week for the saints in Jerusalem (1 Corinthians 16:1-3). In 2 Corinthians 8-9 Paul asks the Corinthians to finish the gift for the poor believers here. In Galatians Paul went up here after three years, and again after fourteen years. He also contrasts “the present-day Jerusalem” with “the Jerusalem above” (4:25-26).

The great sanctuary rebuilt by Herod the Great on a vast platform, with courts for Gentiles, women, Israel and priests. Jesus teaches here, drives out the merchants and predicts its destruction, which came in AD 70. In Acts the believers meet daily in the temple courts, Peter heals a lame man at the gate, and Paul is seized there. Ephesians 2:19-22 says believers are being built together “into a holy temple in the Lord,” “a dwelling place for God in His Spirit.” The letter also says the “dividing wall” has been removed (2:14).
In Revelation John is told to measure the temple of God and the altar (11:1), and in the new Jerusalem he sees no temple, because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple (21:22).

A ridge across the Kidron Valley from the Temple, where Jesus approached Jerusalem, taught about the end, prayed on the night of his arrest and, in Acts, ascended. In Acts 1:12 the apostles return from this mountain after the Ascension. Ephesians 4:8-10 speaks of Christ who “ascended on high” and who also “descended to the lower parts of the earth,” using words from Psalm 68. The Mount of Olives is where Acts 1:9-12 places the ascension.
An olive press and garden at the foot of the Mount of Olives. The name means “oil press”. Jesus prayed here and was arrested.
An Aramaic name meaning “skull”, where Jesus was crucified outside the city walls. The Church of the Holy Sepulchre stands on the traditional site.
A double pool with five colonnades near the Sheep Gate, excavated north of the Temple Mount. A man waited here thirty-eight years.

e.u: Pool at the south end of the city
t: A large stepped pool at the end of Hezekiah’s tunnel, where pilgrims purified themselves. The blind man washed here.

A large furnished room in Jerusalem where Jesus ate the Passover meal with his disciples, washed their feet and gave the long farewell talk in John 13–17. The tradition on Mount Zion is old, but the actual house is unknown. In Acts 1:13 the believers stay in an upper room, and wait for the Spirit.

On the Orontes River, the city where believers were first called Christians, where Barnabas and Saul taught for a year, and from which the first journey is launched. Paul reports back here after each journey. In Galatians 2:11-14 Paul opposes Peter here. Some place the Jerusalem meeting of 2:1-10 before this event.

A Roman colony in the highlands of what is now Turkey. Paul preaches in the synagogue, a crowd gathers the next Sabbath, and he and Barnabas turn to the Gentiles before opposition drives them out. If the churches of Galatia were in the south, this Roman colony was among the first Paul reached (Acts 13:14-50). Paul recalls “the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra” (2 Timothy 3:11).

The ancient city where Saul goes to arrest believers, is healed by Ananias, preaches in the synagogues and escapes in a basket. He later retells the Damascus road story twice. Paul remembers the escape from this city in 2 Corinthians 11:32-33. Paul says he “returned to Damascus” after going to Arabia (Galatians 1:17).

A great trading and university city in south-east Asia Minor. Paul says he was born here and is “a citizen of no obscure city.” Barnabas fetches him from Tarsus to work in Antioch. Paul says he “went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia” (Galatians 1:21), and Tarsus was the main city of Cilicia.
Herod’s harbor city on the coast, with the governor’s palace. Philip lives here, Cornelius is baptized here, Herod Agrippa dies here, and Paul is tried before Felix, Festus and Agrippa.
The harbor town (modern Jaffa) where Peter raises Tabitha, stays with Simon the tanner, and sees the vision of the sheet before the men from Cornelius arrive.
Barnabas’s home. Paul, Barnabas and Mark cross the island from Salamis to Paphos on the first journey, where Sergius Paulus believes. Later Barnabas and Mark sail there again.

Where Paul heals a lame man, is called Hermes, and is stoned and dragged out as dead. Timothy comes from here, and Paul picks him up on the second journey. Paul’s stoning here (Acts 14:19) is probably what he means by “once I was stoned” (2 Corinthians 11:25). Some read “you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God” (Galatians 4:14) and “the marks of Jesus” (6:17) in the light of what happened here (Acts 14:11-19), if the Galatians were southern. The letter itself does not make the link. Timothy was from Lystra or the area (Acts 16:1-2). First Timothy speaks of “the previous prophecies about you” (1:18) and “the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders” (4:14). The letter does not say where this happened. Timothy’s grandmother Lois and mother Eunice (2 Timothy 1:5) belonged to this area, and Paul recalls his sufferings “in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra” (3:11).

Where Paul and Barnabas speak in the synagogue and a great number believe, before a plot to stone them sends them to Lystra and Derbe. Paul recalls “the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra” (2 Timothy 3:11).
The last town on the first journey, where Paul and Barnabas make many disciples. Gaius of Derbe travels with Paul later.

The first city Paul preaches in on European soil. Lydia believes by the river, a slave girl is freed from a spirit, and Paul and Silas are jailed and released by an earthquake. Philippians is addressed to the church here (1:1). Paul says that “in the early days of the gospel, when I left Macedonia, no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving” (4:15). Paul says he had “already endured suffering and shameful treatment in Philippi” before he came to Thessalonica (1 Thessalonians 2:2).

Where Paul reasons from the Scriptures in the synagogue for three Sabbaths and a mob forms. Paul writes two letters to the church here. Philippians 4:16 says, “even while I was in Thessalonica, you provided for my needs again and again.” First and Second Thessalonians are letters to the church here. The first one says the message of the Lord “ring out from you to Macedonia and Achaia” (1 Thessalonians 1:8), and the second shows a church still under pressure (2 Thessalonians 1:4). Paul says Demas “has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica” (2 Timothy 4:10).
Where the Jews are “more noble” than those in Thessalonica, receiving the word eagerly and examining the Scriptures every day.

The home of philosophy. Paul argues in the synagogue and the marketplace and speaks to the Areopagus, using an altar to an unknown god, and Greek poets, to introduce the God who raised Jesus. Paul says he was “left on our own in Athens” and sent Timothy to Thessalonica from there (1 Thessalonians 3:1-2).

A busy commercial city on a narrow isthmus with two harbors. Paul stays eighteen months, working with Aquila and Priscilla, and writes at least two letters to the church here. Romans was probably written from Corinth, in the home of Gaius, with Tertius as scribe. The Roman colony where Paul founded the church and to which 1 Corinthians is addressed. In 2 Corinthians Paul writes to this church after a painful second visit here, and says he is coming “a third time” (12:14). Most readers think Paul wrote both letters to Thessalonica here, soon after Timothy returned from Macedonia (1 Thessalonians 3:6; Acts 18:5). Paul says, “Erastus has remained at Corinth” (2 Timothy 4:20).

The great port and the center of the worship of Artemis. Paul stays about three years, working in the hall of Tyrannus, and the whole province of Asia hears the word. Paul writes 1 Corinthians from Ephesus, where he stays “until Pentecost” because “a great door for effective work has opened” (1 Corinthians 16:8-9). Paul’s hardship in Asia (2 Corinthians 1:8) may refer to trouble here, though the letter does not say. Ephesians is addressed “to the saints in Ephesus” (1:1), though some oldest copies omit the city’s name. Paul spent about three years here (Acts 20:31), and Timothy was later left in charge (1 Timothy 1:3). Paul spent two or three years here (Acts 19:8-10), and the church at Colossae may have come out of that work, since he writes to them as people he had not met (Colossians 2:1). Some scholars suggest he wrote Colossians from an Ephesian prison. First Timothy is set here: Paul asks Timothy to “stay on at Ephesus” (1:3). The letter seems to place Timothy here. Onesiphorus had “ministered” to Paul “in Ephesus” (1:18), Paul says he has sent Tychicus “to Ephesus” (4:12), and he sends greetings to Prisca and Aquila (4:19). It does not say outright where Timothy is.
In 1 John: Early writers, among them Irenaeus, say John lived at Ephesus in his last years and wrote his Gospel there. 1 John names no place, but is usually linked to the churches around Ephesus.
In 2 John, no place is named. Tradition puts the elder who wrote 1 John and the short letters at Ephesus, and the churches of Asia are the usual guess for his readers.
In 3 John, again no place is named. Tradition puts the elder at Ephesus, and Gaius lived somewhere within reach of a visit.
The first of the seven letters is to Ephesus (Revelation 2:1-7): a church that tests false apostles and works hard, but has abandoned the love it had at first.

Where Paul sees the vision of the man from Macedonia and later raises Eutychus. Paul found an open door here but could not rest because Titus was missing (2 Corinthians 2:12-13). Paul says he left his cloak “with Carpus at Troas” (2 Timothy 4:13).

Where Paul gives his farewell to the elders of Ephesus, and kneels with them on the beach to pray. The elders of Ephesus met Paul at Miletus (Acts 20:17-38). He told them, “Be shepherds of the church of God” (Acts 20:28), and Ephesians 4:11 lists “pastors and teachers” among Christ’s gifts. Paul says, “Trophimus I left sick in Miletus” (2 Timothy 4:20).
Called Melite in Acts. The wrecked ship’s company comes ashore in a bay, and Paul is bitten by a viper, heals the father of Publius, and stays three months.

The ship’s course runs under Crete. Paul advises wintering at Fair Havens, and the ship is driven off by the storm. Paul says he left Titus “in Crete” (Titus 1:5), and quotes a Cretan poet (1:12). The letter does not name any town on the island.

The goal of the book. Paul has been told “you must bear witness also in Rome.” He lives there under guard in his own rented house for two years, welcoming all who come. Romans is Paul’s letter to the church in the capital, which he plans to visit on his way to Spain. If Ephesians was written from Rome, Paul wrote “the prisoner of Christ Jesus” (3:1) and “an ambassador in chains” (6:20) while under guard here (Acts 28:16, 30). If Philippians was written from Rome, Paul’s chains had become known “throughout the whole palace guard” (1:13), and “the household of Caesar” sent greetings (4:22). If Colossians was written from Rome, Paul was “in chains” here (4:3, 18) with Aristarchus, Mark, Luke and others (4:10-14). In 2 Timothy Paul is a prisoner here. Onesiphorus “searched diligently until he found me” (1:17), Paul is “chained like a criminal” (2:9), and he expects his “departure” (4:6). Friends there send greetings (4:21).
Revelation never names Rome, but most readers see the city behind “Babylon the great,” the woman seated on seven mountains (17:9), the city that rules over the kings of the earth (17:18).

The region of northern Greece that includes Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. Paul crosses to it after his vision at Troas. Macedonia gave to the poor among the saints in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26). Paul plans to come to Corinth after going through Macedonia (1 Corinthians 16:5). In 2 Corinthians Paul goes on here from Troas and meets Titus (2:13; 7:5). The churches give “according to their ability and even beyond it” out of deep poverty (8:1-5), and “the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied my needs” (11:9). Philippians 4:15 speaks of the time “when I left Macedonia,” when the church at Philippi alone partnered with Paul in giving and receiving. The Thessalonians became “an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia” (1 Thessalonians 1:7), and they showed love “to all the brothers throughout Macedonia” (4:10). Paul says he urged Timothy to stay at Ephesus “on my departure to Macedonia” (1 Timothy 1:3).

Southern Greece, with Athens and Corinth. Gallio is proconsul here. Achaia gave with Macedonia to the poor among the saints in Jerusalem (Romans 15:26). The Roman province whose capital was Corinth. Paul calls the household of Stephanas its first converts (1 Corinthians 16:15). Paul addresses 2 Corinthians to “all the saints throughout Achaia” (1:1) and says his boasting “will not be silenced in the regions of Achaia” (11:10). The Thessalonians became “an example to all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia” (1 Thessalonians 1:7).

The western part of what is now Turkey, with Ephesus as its main city. Paul is forbidden by the Spirit to preach in Asia on the second journey, then stays there about three years on the third. The province whose churches send greetings in 1 Corinthians 16:19. In 2 Corinthians 1:8 Paul tells the church of hardships “in the province of Asia” that left him despairing “even of life.” The Roman province whose capital was Ephesus. Because some of the oldest copies of Ephesians leave out “in Ephesus,” some scholars think the letter was meant for several churches in Asia. Paul says, “everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes” (2 Timothy 1:15).

The port on the Saronic Gulf, about eight miles from Corinth. Phoebe was a servant of the church there (Romans 16:1), and Acts 18:18 says Paul shaved his head at Cenchrea because of a vow before sailing for Syria.

The region across the sea from Italy, later organized as Dalmatia. Paul says that “from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum” he has fully proclaimed the gospel (Romans 15:19). Acts does not mention it.

e.u: The western end of the empire
t: Paul hoped to visit Rome and then go on to Spain (Romans 15:24, 28). The New Testament does not say whether he got there, though 1 Clement says he reached “the limit of the west.”
The sanctuary of Poseidon about ten miles east of Corinth, where the games were held every two years. Paul draws his picture of racing and discipline from the athletes there (1 Corinthians 9:24-27).

e.u: Churches Paul organized the collection in
t: The central highlands of what is now Turkey. Paul tells the Corinthians to do as he “directed the churches of Galatia” about the collection for the saints (1 Corinthians 16:1). Acts 18:23 says he strengthened the disciples there. Paul addresses his letter to “the churches of Galatia” (Galatians 1:2). Some scholars place them in the north, near Ankara; others in the Roman province’s southern cities where Acts 13-14 shows Paul preaching. Paul says, “Crescens has gone to Galatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). Some early manuscripts read “Gaul.”

The mountain where God met Israel after the exodus. Paul recalls the people there “sat down to eat and to drink, and got up to indulge in revelry” (1 Corinthians 10:7, quoting Exodus 32:6). The exact location is uncertain; Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai is the traditional site. Moses came down from the mountain with a shining face, and Paul uses the veil he wore as a picture in 2 Corinthians 3:7-18. Paul says “Hagar stands for Mount Sinai in Arabia” (Galatians 4:25).

e.u: The Nabatean lands east and south of Judea
t: Paul says that after his call he “went into Arabia and later returned to Damascus” (1:17). In his day Arabia usually meant the Nabatean kingdom, whose capital was Petra. The letter does not say where he stayed or what he did, and he also says Hagar stands for “Mount Sinai in Arabia” (4:25).

e.u: A wealthy city in the Lycus Valley
t: Paul does not mention Laodicea in Ephesians, but Colossians 4:16 speaks of “the letter from Laodicea,” which some scholars have connected to this one. Tychicus carries both letters. Revelation 3:14-22 later addresses the church here. Paul says he is struggling for “those at Laodicea” (2:1), greets “the brothers in Laodicea, as well as Nympha” (4:15), and asks that Colossians be read there and that the Colossians read “the letter from Laodicea” (4:16).
The last of the seven letters is to Laodicea (Revelation 3:14-22): neither cold nor hot, the church that says it is rich and needs nothing, with Christ outside knocking at its door.

e.u: A smaller town up the Lycus Valley
t: Onesimus and Tychicus travel to Colossae (Colossians 4:7-9), the same trip on which Tychicus carries Ephesians (6:21-22). The town was once a center of the wool trade but had fallen behind its neighbors Laodicea and Hierapolis by Paul’s day. Colossians is addressed to the church here (1:2). Epaphras, Onesimus and Archippus are from this town or its neighborhood (4:9, 12, 17). Philemon is usually placed at Colossae, since Archippus (Philemon 2) and Onesimus (Colossians 4:9, 17) belong to that church.

e.u: A hot-spring city across the river from Laodicea
t: Colossians 4:13 is the only verse in the New Testament that names the city. Paul says that Epaphras “goes to great pains for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis.” The city lay on a ridge above the Lycus, known for its hot springs, its cloth and its dyers. Later Christian tradition says the apostle Philip died there.

e.u: The region where Titus had gone
t: Paul says, “Titus to Dalmatia” (2 Timothy 4:10). Dalmatia was the Roman province on the east shore of the Adriatic, a part of the older Illyricum, which Paul names in Romans 15:19. The letter says nothing about why Titus went there.
Fortress east of the Dead Sea, built by Herod the Great, where Josephus says John the Baptist was imprisoned and executed. The Gospels say only that Herod Antipas had him imprisoned and beheaded.
A town on the edge of the wilderness north of Jerusalem where Jesus withdrew with his disciples after the raising of Lazarus, before the final Passover.

A village in the hill country west of Jerusalem, by tradition the home of Zechariah and Elizabeth and the birthplace of John the Baptist. Luke says only “a town in Judah.” It is traditionally where Mary visited Elizabeth and sang the Magnificat.
A place with plenty of water where John the Baptist was baptizing, near Salim. Its exact location is debated.

On the east shore of the Sea of Galilee, a site with a Byzantine monastery and church built on a steep slope by the shore. Tradition connects it with the healing of the man from the tombs and the herd of pigs rushing into the lake.

A Roman fortress at the northwest corner of the temple courts, built by Herod the Great, where soldiers watched over the crowds. Tradition has placed Pilate’s judgment hall near it, though some scholars place the trial at Herod’s palace.
A covered walkway along the east side of the temple courts. Jesus walked here at the Feast of Dedication, and the apostles later gathered here.
The “potter’s field” bought with the thirty pieces of silver Judas threw into the temple. Matthew says it was called the Field of Blood. It is in the Hinnom Valley south of the Old City.
The home of the high priest in Jerusalem, where Jesus was taken for questioning and where Peter denied him three times.
A rounded mountain in Lower Galilee, traditionally the Mount of Transfiguration. The Gospels do not name the mountain, and some think Mount Hermon is more likely.
A settlement on the northwest shore of the Dead Sea near the caves where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found, linked by many scholars with the Essenes.
A gate of the temple where a lame man begged. Its exact identity is debated; many scholars link it with the Nicanor Gate on the east, others with the Shushan Gate.

A lecture hall in Ephesus where Paul taught daily for two years after leaving the synagogue. Some manuscripts add that he taught from late morning to mid-afternoon, when the hall was free. Its location is not known.
A rocky hill below the Acropolis in Athens and the name of the council that met there. Paul addresses it and quotes Greek poets.
A long east-west street in Damascus where Saul was led after meeting Jesus and where Ananias found him at the house of Judas.
A town in the plain near Joppa (modern Lod), where Peter healed Aeneas. It was a day’s walk from Jerusalem and the road to the coast.
The Greek name of Ashdod, a Mediterranean coastal city south of Joppa, where Philip was found after baptizing the Ethiopian official.
A city Herod rebuilt for his father Antipater, about halfway between Jerusalem and Caesarea. The soldiers stop here with Paul on the night ride.
The port of Antioch on the Orontes, from which Barnabas and Saul sail for Cyprus.
The port of Philippi (modern Kavala), where Paul first lands in Europe.
A port on the Aegean coast where Paul meets his companions after walking from Troas.
A harbor on the south coast of Crete where the ship stops. Paul warns that the voyage will end in loss, but the ship sails on.
The main city of Sicily, where Paul’s ship stays three days on the way to Rome.
A port on the Bay of Naples where Paul lands in Italy and stays seven days with believers.

e.n: The Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns
t: Two stops on the Appian Way, 43 and 33 miles from Rome, where Roman believers came to meet Paul.

A small rocky island in the Aegean Sea, about 34 square kilometers, some 60 kilometers off the coast of Asia, in the Dodecanese islands of modern Greece. John writes that he “was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (1:9). Early writers say he had been banished there, a common Roman penalty, and that he returned to Ephesus after Domitian died.

A cave halfway up the hill is shown as the place of the vision, and the Monastery of St John, founded by the monk Christodoulos in 1088, stands on the summit. The tradition of the cave is late, but the island itself is the one place the book names as its setting.

A large and beautiful harbor city about 55 kilometers north of Ephesus, now Izmir in Turkey. Smyrna was loyal to Rome from early days, built one of the first temples to the goddess Roma in 195 BC, and in AD 26 won a contest among the cities of Asia for the right to build a temple to the emperor Tiberius.

The letter to Smyrna (2:8-11) speaks of poverty, slander and coming prison, and promises the crown of life to those faithful to death. About AD 155 Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, was burned in the city’s stadium after refusing to call Caesar lord.

An old royal city on a steep hill about 25 kilometers from the Aegean, now Bergama in Turkey. It had a famous library, a healing center of the god Asclepius, the great Altar of Zeus (now in Berlin), and in 29 BC the first temple in Asia to Augustus and Roma. It was a leading center of the emperor’s worship in the province.

Christ says the church lives “where the throne of Satan sits” (2:13), which has been explained by the altar, by the imperial temple, or by the Roman governor’s court. The letter names the martyr Antipas, the teaching of Balaam and the Nicolaitans, and promises hidden manna and a white stone (2:12-17).

A trading town in the Lycus valley of Lydia, now Akhisar in Turkey, on the road between Pergamum and Sardis. Inscriptions show many trade guilds: dyers, wool workers, linen workers, leather workers, potters and bronze smiths. Lydia, the seller of purple cloth whom Paul met at Philippi, came from Thyatira (Acts 16:14).

The letter to Thyatira (2:18-29) is the longest of the seven. Christ appears with eyes like fire and feet like burnished bronze, and rebukes the church for tolerating a prophetess called Jezebel who leads believers into immorality and eating food sacrificed to idols, probably at guild feasts.

The old capital of the kingdom of Lydia and of King Croesus, now Sart in Turkey, below a steep acropolis that was thought impossible to take. Twice it fell by surprise, to Cyrus of Persia in 547 BC and to Antiochus III in 214 BC, when attackers climbed the cliffs at night. An earthquake destroyed the city in AD 17, and the emperor Tiberius helped rebuild it.

Christ says to Sardis, “you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead” (3:1), and warns, “If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief” (3:3), a warning that fits a city whose walls had been taken while its guards slept. A large synagogue of the 3rd century shows that the Jewish community there was strong.

A city on the road east from Sardis, now Alaşehir in Turkey, founded by King Attalus II, whose love for his brother gave him the name Philadelphus. It lay in a region of frequent earthquakes; the geographer Strabo says its walls were always cracking and many people lived outside the city. After the great earthquake of AD 17 it took the name Neocaesarea in thanks for the emperor’s help.

The letter to Philadelphia (3:7-13) has no rebuke. Christ holds “the key of David” and sets before the church an open door. He promises that the one who overcomes will be a pillar in God’s temple who will never again leave it, and will bear God’s name and the name of the new Jerusalem: promises that fit a city that had to flee its buildings and changed its name.

The great river of Mesopotamia, which runs from the mountains of eastern Turkey through Syria and Iraq to the Persian Gulf. It was the northeast border of the land promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18), the river of Babylon, and in John’s day the frontier between the Roman Empire and the Parthians, the one power Rome feared in the East.

At the sixth trumpet four angels bound at the Euphrates are released with a vast army of horsemen (9:14-16); at the sixth bowl the river dries up to prepare the way for the kings from the East (16:12). For readers in Asia the river meant invasion from beyond the empire’s edge.

A farmer scatters seed on a path, rocky ground, thorns and good soil. Only the good soil bears a crop. Jesus explains that the seed is the word of the kingdom and the soils are the different ways people hear it.

An enemy sows weeds in a field of wheat. The master tells his servants to let both grow until the harvest, when they will be separated. Jesus explains it as the end of the age, when the angels sort the righteous from the wicked.
The smallest of seeds grows into the largest garden plant, big enough for birds to nest in its branches. The kingdom begins small and becomes large.
A woman mixes a little yeast into a large amount of flour until all of it is worked through. The kingdom spreads quietly from within.
A man scatters seed and goes about his life while it sprouts and grows without his understanding how. When the grain is ripe he puts in the sickle. Only Mark tells this one.
A man finds treasure in a field, hides it again, and in his joy sells everything to buy the field. The kingdom is worth everything.
A merchant looking for fine pearls finds one of great value and sells everything he has to buy it.
A net is thrown into the sea and gathers fish of every kind. The good are kept and the bad are thrown away, as the angels will separate the righteous from the wicked at the end of the age.
One man builds his house on rock and another on sand. When the storm comes, only the house on the rock stands. Hearing Jesus’ words and doing them is the rock.
A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find the one that is lost, and rejoices when he finds it. There is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.
A woman with ten silver coins loses one, lights a lamp, sweeps the house and searches until she finds it, then calls her friends to celebrate. Only Luke tells this one.

A younger son takes his inheritance, wastes it far from home, and returns hoping to be a hired servant. His father runs to meet him, restores him as a son and throws a feast, while the older brother resents it. Often called the parable of the loving father or the two sons.
A king forgives a servant a huge debt. That servant then refuses to forgive a fellow servant a small one and is handed over for punishment. Jesus tells it after Peter asks how many times to forgive.
A moneylender cancels the debts of two men, one owing ten times what the other owed. Jesus asks Simon the Pharisee which will love him more, and applies it to the woman who anointed his feet.
A man beaten by robbers is passed by a priest and a Levite. A Samaritan stops, cares for him and pays for his recovery. Jesus tells it in answer to the lawyer’s question, “Who is my neighbor?”

A landowner hires workers at different hours and pays all of them a denarius. Those who worked all day complain, and he answers that he is free to be generous. The last will be first and the first last.
A father asks two sons to work in the vineyard. One says no and goes anyway; the other says yes and does not go. Tax collectors and prostitutes are entering the kingdom ahead of the chief priests.

A landowner sends servants and finally his son to collect fruit from his vineyard, and the tenants kill them. Jesus quotes Psalm 118: the stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone. The religious leaders realize he is speaking about them.
A king invites guests to his son’s wedding. They refuse and some mistreat his servants, so he opens the invitation to everyone in the streets. One guest without wedding clothes is thrown out.
Revelation 19:9 reads, “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb.”

A man prepares a great banquet but invited guests all make excuses. He brings in the poor, the crippled, the blind and the lame, and then people from the roads. Luke’s version is told at the table of a leading Pharisee.
Seeing guests choose the best seats, Jesus says to take the lowest place and let the host move you up. Those who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.

e.n: The cost of building a tower
t: Before building a tower or going to war, a person sits down to count the cost. Anyone who would follow Jesus should do the same.
Ten bridesmaids wait for the bridegroom. Five bring extra oil and five do not, and when he arrives at midnight the unprepared are shut out. The lesson: stay awake and be ready.
A master gives his servants five, two and one talent before traveling. Two put the money to work; the third buries his. On return, the faithful are rewarded and the fearful servant loses what he had.
A nobleman leaves to receive a kingdom and gives ten servants a mina each. Luke tells it near Jericho, as people think the kingdom is about to appear, and it includes citizens who refuse the king.

The Son of Man separates the nations like a shepherd dividing sheep from goats. What was done, or not done, for the hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick and imprisoned was done, or not done, to him.

A servant left in charge of the household is blessed if the master finds him faithful on his return, and punished if he has abused the others. Jesus calls the disciples to stay ready for a day they do not know.
A man leaves home and tells his doorkeeper to stay alert, because no one knows when the master of the house will return. “Watch.”
When a fig tree puts out leaves, you know that summer is near. In the same way, when you see the signs Jesus described, know that the end is near.
A man comes looking for fruit on his fig tree for three years and finds none. The gardener asks for one more year to dig around it and fertilize it. If it still bears no fruit, then cut it down.
A man knocks on his neighbor’s door at midnight to borrow bread for a guest. The neighbor gets up because of the man’s persistence. How much more will the Father give to those who ask?
A widow keeps demanding justice from a judge who neither fears God nor respects people, and he finally gives it to her. Jesus tells it so that his followers will pray and not lose heart.

e.n: The Pharisee and the tax collector
t: Two men pray in the temple. The Pharisee thanks God that he is not like other people; the tax collector beats his chest and asks for mercy. The tax collector goes home justified.

A wealthy farmer plans to build bigger barns and take life easy. God says, “This night your soul is required of you.” Life does not consist in the abundance of possessions. Jesus tells it in answer to a man who wanted him to settle an inheritance dispute.

A manager about to lose his job quickly reduces what his master’s debtors owe so that they will welcome him later. His master praises his shrewdness. Jesus ends with the saying about two masters: you cannot serve God and money.

A rich man ignores the beggar Lazarus at his gate. After death, Lazarus is comforted and the rich man is in torment, and Abraham says that if they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they would not be persuaded even if someone rose from the dead.
A servant who comes in from the field does not expect to be thanked for doing his duty. When you have done all that you were told, say, “We are unworthy servants.”
No one lights a lamp and hides it under a basket. It is put on a stand so that everyone can see. What is hidden will be brought to light.
No one sews a patch of new cloth on an old garment or pours new wine into old wineskins, or both will be ruined. Jesus says this when asked why his disciples do not fast.

Children call out to one another, “We played the flute and you did not dance.” Jesus says this generation rejected both John the Baptist, who came fasting, and the Son of Man, who came eating and drinking.
No one can plunder a strong man’s house unless he first ties him up. Jesus tells this when accused of casting out demons by the power of Beelzebul.

e.n: The return of the unclean spirit
t: When an unclean spirit leaves a person, it wanders, then returns with seven worse spirits to find the house swept and empty. A cleaned life with nothing in it is not safe.
John records a figure of speech rather than a parable: the shepherd enters by the door, calls his sheep by name, and lays down his life for them. Jesus says, “I am the good shepherd.”
Jesus says, “I am the true vine.” Branches that remain in him bear fruit, and branches that do not are cut off. John also calls this a figure of speech.
When the disciples ask why he speaks in parables, Jesus says the secrets of the kingdom are given to them, while those outside see and do not see. He quotes Isaiah 6:9-10.

At a wedding in Cana, the wine runs out. Jesus has servants fill six stone jars with water, and it becomes wine better than what was served first. John calls it the first of his signs, and it revealed his glory.
A royal official from Capernaum asks Jesus to come heal his dying son. Jesus tells him, “Go, your son will live,” and the boy recovers at the same hour. John calls it the second sign in Galilee.
After a night of catching nothing, Simon Peter lets down his nets at Jesus’ word and nearly breaks them with fish. He falls at Jesus’ knees and Jesus calls him to catch people.

e.n: The man with an unclean spirit
t: In the synagogue at Capernaum, a man cries out, “I know who you are, the Holy One of God.” Jesus commands the spirit to be silent and come out, and the crowd marvels at his authority.
Simon’s mother-in-law lies sick with a fever. Jesus takes her hand and lifts her up, the fever leaves, and she begins to serve them.
A man with leprosy kneels and says, “If you are willing, you can make me clean.” Jesus touches him and says, “I am willing; be clean,” and tells him to show himself to the priest.

e.n: The paralyzed man lowered through the roof
t: Four friends dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus. Jesus says, “Your sins are forgiven,” then heals him to show that the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins.

e.n: The man at the pool of Bethesda
t: A man who has been ill thirty-eight years lies by the pool in Jerusalem. Jesus tells him to take up his mat and walk. It was a Sabbath, which started the controversy that John records afterward.

e.n: The man with the withered hand
t: On a Sabbath in the synagogue, Jesus asks whether it is lawful to do good or to do harm on the Sabbath. He heals the man’s hand, and his opponents begin to plan against him.

A Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his servant but says he is not worthy to have Jesus under his roof; Jesus only needs to speak the word. Jesus marvels, “Not even in Israel have I found such faith.”

e.n: The widow’s son raised at Nain
t: At the gate of Nain, Jesus meets a funeral procession for a widow’s only son. He touches the bier, says, “Young man, arise,” and gives him back to his mother.
A storm swamps the disciples’ boat while Jesus sleeps in the stern. He rebukes the wind and sea, and there is a great calm. The disciples ask, “Who then is this?”
A man possessed by a legion of spirits lives among the tombs in the region of the Gerasenes. Jesus sends the spirits into a herd of pigs, and the man is found sitting, clothed and in his right mind.
A synagogue ruler begs Jesus to heal his dying daughter. News comes that she has died, but Jesus says, “Do not fear, only believe,” takes her hand and says, “Talitha cumi.” The girl gets up.

e.n: The woman who touched Jesus’ cloak
t: A woman who has bled for twelve years pushes through the crowd and touches Jesus’ cloak. Power goes out from him. He says, “Daughter, your faith has made you well.”
Two blind men follow Jesus calling, “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” He touches their eyes and says, “According to your faith let it be done to you.”
After Jesus casts out a demon from a man who could not speak, the man speaks. The crowds marvel, while the Pharisees say he casts out demons by the prince of demons.

With five loaves and two fish, Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men on a grassy hillside and the disciples gather twelve baskets of leftovers. It is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, recorded in all four Gospels.
In the fourth watch of the night, Jesus comes to the disciples walking on the lake. In Matthew, Peter steps out on the water and begins to sink. When Jesus enters the boat, the wind stops.
People bring the sick on mats to Gennesaret, and as many as touch the fringe of his cloak are healed.
A Gentile woman near Tyre persists in asking Jesus to heal her daughter, even answering that “even the dogs eat the crumbs.” Jesus honors her faith and the girl is healed from a distance.
In the Decapolis, Jesus puts his fingers in the ears of a deaf man with a speech impediment, touches his tongue and says, “Ephphatha” (be opened). Mark preserves the Aramaic word.
With seven loaves and a few small fish, Jesus feeds four thousand men, and they collect seven baskets of leftovers. It happens in a largely Gentile region.

Jesus leads a blind man out of the village, spits on his eyes and lays hands on him. The man first sees people “like trees walking,” then Jesus touches him again and he sees clearly. Only Mark records it.

On a high mountain, Jesus’ face shines like the sun and his clothes become white. Moses and Elijah appear and speak with him, and a voice from the cloud says, “This is my beloved Son; listen to him.” Not usually counted as a healing, but it is one of the Gospels’ great revelations of his glory.

2 Peter 1:16-18 recalls the voice “from the Majestic Glory” and says, “we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain.” The letter does not name the event, but most take it to be the Transfiguration.

e.n: The boy with an unclean spirit
t: At the foot of the mountain, a father brings his son, whom the disciples could not heal. “I believe; help my unbelief!” Jesus rebukes the spirit and the boy is healed. This kind comes out only through prayer.

e.n: The coin in the fish’s mouth
t: When collectors ask whether Jesus pays the temple tax, he sends Peter to the lake to catch a fish with a coin in its mouth, enough for both of them. Only Matthew tells this one.

Jesus makes mud with spit, puts it on a man’s eyes and sends him to wash in the pool of Siloam. The man sees. The Pharisees interrogate him and put him out of the synagogue, and Jesus tells them, “I am the light of the world.”

On a Sabbath in a synagogue, Jesus lays hands on a woman who has been bent over for eighteen years, and she stands up straight and praises God. He answers the synagogue ruler’s protest by pointing to how people water their animals on the Sabbath.
At a meal at a leading Pharisee’s house on the Sabbath, Jesus heals a man with swollen limbs and asks whether it is lawful to heal on the Sabbath.
Ten men with leprosy cry out for mercy and are healed on their way to the priests. Only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Jesus.

Lazarus of Bethany has been dead four days when Jesus arrives. He says, “I am the resurrection and the life,” weeps at the tomb, and cries, “Lazarus, come out.” John says this event led the leaders to plot Jesus’ death.
A blind beggar by the road near Jericho shouts, “Jesus, Son of David, have mercy on me!” and will not be silenced. Jesus calls him, asks what he wants, and restores his sight.

e.n: The cursing of the fig tree
t: Jesus finds a fig tree with leaves but no fruit and says it will never bear fruit again. The next morning it has withered. Mark frames it around the cleansing of the temple.
When a disciple strikes the high priest’s servant with a sword in Gethsemane, Jesus says, “No more of this,” and touches the man’s ear and heals him. John names the servant Malchus.

e.n: The second great catch of fish
t: After the resurrection, seven disciples fish all night without success. A man on the shore tells them to cast on the right side and they catch 153 large fish. John says they recognize the Lord, and Jesus has already made breakfast on a charcoal fire.

On the third day, the tomb is empty and Jesus appears to the women, to the disciples and to many others. All four Gospels end with it, and the rest of the New Testament proclaims it. Not a miracle he performed on someone else, but the sign to which all the others point.

e.n: Pentecost: wind, fire and many languages
t: Fifty days after Passover the believers are gathered in Jerusalem when a sound like a rushing wind fills the house, flames rest on each of them, and they begin to speak in other languages. Pilgrims from across the world hear “the mighty works of God” in their own tongues.

e.n: The lame man at the Beautiful Gate
t: A man lame from birth, carried daily to the temple gate to beg, is told by Peter, “In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, rise up and walk.” He leaps up and enters the temple praising God. The council later cannot deny that a notable sign has happened.
People bring the sick into the streets on cots so that at least Peter’s shadow might fall on them. Acts says crowds came from the towns around Jerusalem and that they were all healed.

e.n: Peter and the apostles freed by an angel
t: The high priest has the apostles jailed. During the night an angel of the Lord opens the prison doors and sends them back to the temple to teach. In the morning the guards find the cells locked and empty.
A husband and wife sell a field and bring part of the money, saying it is all. Peter says they have lied to the Holy Spirit; each falls dead. Luke says great fear came on the whole church.
Philip preaches the Messiah in a Samaritan city. Unclean spirits come out of many with loud cries, and paralyzed and lame people are healed. The city is filled with joy.

e.n: Philip carried away by the Spirit
t: After baptizing the Ethiopian official, Philip is taken away by the Spirit of the Lord and found at Azotus. The official goes on his way rejoicing.

On the road to Damascus a light from heaven flashes around Saul, who falls to the ground and hears a voice: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” He is blind for three days. Paul retells the story twice and treats it as an appearance of the risen Lord.

Ananias lays his hands on Saul and says, “Brother Saul, the Lord Jesus has sent me so that you may regain your sight and be filled with the Holy Spirit.” Something like scales falls from Saul’s eyes, and he is baptized.
Aeneas has been bedridden for eight years. Peter says, “Jesus Christ heals you. Rise and make your bed.” He gets up at once, and everyone who lives in Lydda and Sharon turns to the Lord.

Tabitha (Dorcas) is a disciple known for her works of charity. When she dies, Peter is called from Lydda. He sends everyone out, kneels, prays, and says, “Tabitha, arise.” She opens her eyes and sits up.

e.n: The Spirit falls on Cornelius’s household
t: While Peter is still speaking at Caesarea, the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear the word, and they speak in tongues and praise God. Peter says they have received the Spirit just as the apostles did, and orders them baptized.

Herod Agrippa jails Peter for Passover with four squads of soldiers. An angel wakes him, his chains fall off, and the iron gate opens by itself. Peter goes to the house of Mary, where the church is praying, and Rhoda is so happy she forgets to open the gate.

At Paphos the magician Elymas tries to turn the proconsul from the faith. Paul looks at him and says the hand of the Lord is against him; mist and darkness fall on him and he gropes for someone to lead him. The proconsul believes.
A man crippled from birth listens to Paul, who sees that he has faith to be made well and calls, “Stand upright on your feet.” He leaps and walks. The crowds call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes.

e.n: A slave girl freed from a spirit
t: At Philippi a slave girl with a spirit of divination follows Paul for days, until he turns and tells the spirit, “I command you in the name of Jesus Christ to come out of her.” Her owners lose their profit and drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates.

At midnight, as Paul and Silas pray and sing in the inner cell, a violent earthquake shakes the foundations, opens the doors and unfastens everyone’s chains. The jailer, ready to kill himself, asks how to be saved and is baptized with his household.

e.n: Handkerchiefs, aprons and the sons of Sceva
t: At Ephesus God does extraordinary miracles by Paul’s hands; cloths he has touched are carried to the sick, and diseases and evil spirits leave. Seven sons of the priest Sceva try to use the name of Jesus as a formula, and the evil spirit overpowers them.

A young man falls asleep in a third-floor window during Paul’s long talk and falls to the ground, picked up dead. Paul goes down, throws himself on him, and says, “Do not be alarmed, for his life is in him.” The believers are greatly comforted.

e.n: Spared in the storm and shipwreck
t: In the fourteenth night of the storm an angel stands by Paul and says, “Do not be afraid, Paul; you must stand before Caesar. And God has granted you all those who sail with you.” All 276 on board reach land, though the ship is lost.
A viper fastens on Paul’s hand as he adds sticks to the fire. The islanders expect him to die, then decide he is a god when he shakes the creature off and suffers no harm.
Paul prays, lays his hands on the father of Publius, who lies sick with fever and dysentery, and heals him. The rest of the sick on the island then come and are cured.
Isaiah told King Ahaz that a young woman would conceive and bear a son named Immanuel, “God with us.” Matthew applies it to Mary and the birth of Jesus.
Micah named Bethlehem Ephrathah as the place from which a ruler of Israel would come. The chief priests and scribes quote it to Herod when the Magi ask where the king is to be born.
God promised David that his throne and kingdom would be established forever through his offspring. The Gospels open by tracing Jesus to David.
God told Abraham that all the families of the earth would be blessed through his offspring. Matthew begins with “the son of Abraham,” and Mary and Zechariah both sing of this promise.
In Acts, Peter tells the crowd at the temple they are heirs of this promise: “In your offspring shall all the families of the earth be blessed.”

Paul quotes it in Galatians 3:8: “The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham: ‘All nations will be blessed through you.’” He says Christ redeemed us “in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles” (3:14).
Hosea wrote of Israel, “Out of Egypt I called my son.” Matthew sees Jesus’ return from Egypt as a replay of Israel’s story and applies the verse to him.
Jeremiah pictured Rachel weeping for her children as they went into exile. Matthew hears it again in the grief of Bethlehem’s mothers after Herod’s massacre.

e.n: He will be called a Nazarene
t: Matthew says the prophets said Jesus would be called a Nazarene, but no single Old Testament verse says this. Many link it to the Hebrew word for “branch” (netzer) in Isaiah 11:1, or to the low esteem of Nazareth.
Isaiah spoke of a voice crying out in the wilderness to prepare the way of the Lord. All four Gospels identify this voice with John the Baptist.

e.n: The messenger who prepares the way
t: Malachi promised a messenger to prepare the way before the Lord. Jesus says John is this messenger.

Malachi said God would send Elijah before the great and terrible day of the Lord. Jesus says that Elijah has come in John the Baptist, and the angel Gabriel tells Zechariah that John will go in the spirit and power of Elijah.
Isaiah said that the people in darkness in Zebulun and Naphtali, the land by the sea, would see a great light. Matthew applies it to Jesus starting his ministry in Capernaum.

e.n: The Spirit upon the anointed one
t: Isaiah wrote of one anointed to preach good news to the poor and proclaim freedom for captives. In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus reads this passage and says, “Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing.”
After Jesus heals many in Capernaum, Matthew says this fulfilled Isaiah’s words that the servant took up our infirmities and bore our diseases.

Isaiah’s servant would not quarrel or cry out, would not break a bruised reed, and would bring justice to the nations. Matthew quotes it when Jesus heals the crowds and asks them not to make him known.
God told Isaiah that the people would hear and not understand, see and not perceive. Jesus quotes it to explain why he teaches in parables, and John uses it to explain why many did not believe.
In Acts, Paul closes the book by quoting the same passage of Isaiah to the Jewish leaders in Rome.

Moses told Israel that God would raise up a prophet like him from among them, and that they should listen to him. In the Gospels people ask whether Jesus is “the Prophet,” and the voice at the transfiguration says, “Listen to him.”
In Acts, Peter and Stephen both say Jesus is the prophet Moses promised.
f: John 1:45; John 6:14; John 7:40; Luke 9:35; Matthew 17:5; Acts 3:22-23; Acts 7:37

t: In the wilderness, Moses lifted a bronze serpent on a pole and everyone who looked at it was healed. Jesus tells Nicodemus that the Son of Man must be lifted up in the same way, so that everyone who believes may have eternal life.

God gave Israel manna in the wilderness. After the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus says the true bread from heaven is not what Moses gave but what his Father gives, and then, “I am the bread of life.”

The prophets pictured water poured out on the thirsty land and rivers flowing from the temple. At the Feast of Tabernacles, Jesus cries, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” and John explains it as the Spirit.
Ezekiel condemned Israel’s false shepherds and promised that God would shepherd his sheep himself and set one shepherd over them. Jesus calls himself the good shepherd.
Jeremiah promised a new covenant in which God would write his law on people’s hearts and forgive their sins. At the Last Supper, Jesus gives the cup as the new covenant in his blood.
In 2 Corinthians 3:6 Paul says God “has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit.”
Hebrews quotes Jeremiah 31 at length (8:8-12; 10:16-17) and calls Jesus “the mediator of a new covenant” (9:15; 12:24).
f: Luke 22:20; Matthew 26:28; Mark 14:24; 2 Corinthians 3:3-6; Hebrews 8:8-13; Hebrews 10:16-17

t: Zechariah told Jerusalem that her king would come humble and riding on a donkey. Matthew and John both describe Jesus entering the city this way.
The crowds greet Jesus with words from Psalm 118: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord.” Jesus later tells Jerusalem they will not see him again until they say it.
Psalm 118 speaks of a stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone. Jesus quotes it after the parable of the tenants, and the leaders realize he is speaking of them.
In Acts, Peter tells the council that Jesus is “the stone that was rejected by you, the builders, which has become the cornerstone.”
In Ephesians the church is built “with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone” (2:20), and the whole building grows into a holy temple.
1 Peter 2:7 quotes Psalm 118:22: “The stone the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.” Peter had used the verse before the council (Acts 4:11).
f: Matthew 21:42; Mark 12:10-11; Luke 20:17; Acts 4:11; Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Peter 2:4-8

t: Isaiah called the temple a house of prayer for all nations, and Jeremiah called it a den of robbers when it was misused. Jesus combines the two when he drives out those buying and selling in the temple.
The psalmist laments that even his close friend, who ate his bread, has lifted his heel against him. At the Last Supper, Jesus applies it to the one who would betray him.
Zechariah was paid thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the house of the Lord. Matthew connects this with Judas’ payment and the purchase of the potter’s field.
Zechariah wrote, “Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered.” On the way to Gethsemane, Jesus tells the disciples that all will fall away.
Isaiah’s servant was led like a lamb to the slaughter and did not open his mouth. Before Pilate and the high priest, Jesus mostly stays silent.
The servant in Isaiah gives his back to those who strike him and does not hide his face from mocking and spitting. The Gospels describe the guards and the soldiers doing exactly this to Jesus.
Isaiah says the servant was counted among transgressors. Jesus quotes it at the Last Supper, and he is crucified between two criminals.
The psalmists complain of enemies who hate them without a cause. Jesus tells the disciples that it is written in their law that people hated him without a cause.

e.n: My God, why have you forsaken me?
t: On the cross, Jesus cries out the first line of Psalm 22 in Aramaic: “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani.” That psalm also describes mocking crowds, pierced hands and feet, and the dividing of garments.
Psalm 22 describes the sufferer’s garments being divided and lots cast for his clothing. John says the soldiers who crucified Jesus did exactly this.
The sufferer in Psalm 22 is mocked: “He trusts in the Lord; let him deliver him.” The chief priests, scribes and elders say nearly the same words to Jesus on the cross.
The psalmist says that for his thirst they gave him vinegar to drink. On the cross, Jesus says, “I thirst,” and a sponge of sour wine is lifted to him on a hyssop branch.
The Passover lamb’s bones were not to be broken, and the psalmist says the righteous person’s bones are kept. John notes that the soldiers did not break Jesus’ legs.

e.n: They will look on the one they pierced
t: Zechariah says the people would look on the one they pierced and mourn. John sees it in the soldier’s spear thrust into Jesus’ side.
Isaiah says the servant was assigned a grave with the wicked but was with a rich man in his death. Jesus is buried in the new tomb of Joseph of Arimathea, a rich man.

Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12 describes a servant who is despised, bears the sins of many and is exalted. The Gospel writers apply parts of this passage to Jesus again and again, and Jesus himself says it must be fulfilled in him.
In Acts, Philip starts from Isaiah 53 and tells the Ethiopian official the good news about Jesus.
1 Peter 2:21-25 draws more on Isaiah 53 than any other passage in the letters: no sin, no deceit, no retaliation, bearing sins, healed by his stripes, sheep gone astray.
f: Luke 22:37; Matthew 8:17; John 12:38; Mark 10:45; Acts 8:32-35; 1 Peter 2:21-25

t: Jonah spent three days in the belly of the great fish. Jesus tells those asking for a sign that the only sign they will be given is the sign of Jonah, and that as Jonah was in the fish three days and nights, so the Son of Man will be in the heart of the earth.

David wrote that God would not abandon his holy one to the grave. On Easter evening, Jesus tells the disciples that everything written about him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled, and that the Messiah would suffer and rise on the third day.
In Acts, Peter at Pentecost and Paul at Pisidian Antioch both use Psalm 16:10 to argue that David spoke of the Messiah’s resurrection.

e.n: The Son of Man coming with the clouds
t: Daniel saw one like a son of man coming with the clouds of heaven and receiving an everlasting kingdom. Jesus applies this to himself before the high priest and in his teaching on the end.
Revelation 1:7 joins Daniel 7:13 and Zechariah 12:10: “Behold, He is coming with the clouds, and every eye will see Him—even those who pierced Him.”
Daniel spoke of an abomination that causes desolation set up in the holy place. Jesus tells the disciples that when they see this in the temple, those in Judea should flee to the mountains.

Psalm 110 begins, “The Lord says to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.” Jesus asks how the Christ can be both David’s son and David’s Lord, and later tells the high priest that the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of Power.
In Acts, Peter quotes Psalm 110:1 at Pentecost: David did not ascend into the heavens, but he says, “The Lord said to my Lord.”
Hebrews returns to Psalm 110:1 again and again: “Sit at My right hand until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet” (1:13; compare 8:1; 10:12-13; 12:2).
f: Matthew 22:41-46; Mark 12:35-37; Luke 20:41-44; Mark 14:62; Acts 2:34-35; Hebrews 1:13; Hebrews 8:1; Hebrews 10:12-13

t: Jesus says he has not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets but to fulfill them, and after the resurrection he says all that was written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms must be fulfilled.
Isaiah says all your children will be taught by the Lord. Jesus quotes it in the bread of life discourse: everyone who hears and learns from the Father comes to him.

Peter says the Scriptures had to be fulfilled about Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus. He reads the verses about a deserted house and another taking his position as pointing to the choice of a twelfth apostle.

e.n: The Spirit poured out on all flesh
t: Joel looked ahead to a day when God would pour out his Spirit on sons and daughters, young and old. Peter says the sound and the languages at Pentecost are that day, and that anyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.

Psalm 2 pictures nations raging and rulers plotting against the Lord and his Anointed. After Peter and John are released, the believers pray that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and Israel’s people have done what God’s hand had already planned.

In the synagogue at Pisidian Antioch Paul says God has fulfilled for the children what he promised the fathers by raising Jesus, as it is also written in the second Psalm: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you.”

Hebrews opens its argument with this verse: “For to which of the angels did God ever say: ‘You are My Son; today I have become Your Father’?” (1:5). It is quoted again in 5:5, in connection with Christ’s call to be high priest.
Paul quotes Isaiah 55:3 and Psalm 16:10 together to argue that the promise to David could not be fulfilled in David, who died and saw decay, but in the one God raised.

Isaiah’s servant is not only to restore Israel but to be a light for the nations so that salvation reaches the end of the earth. Paul and Barnabas say it is their command, and the Gentiles of Pisidian Antioch rejoice.
In Ephesians the Gentiles who were “far away” are brought near in Christ (2:13) and made “fellow heirs” (3:6), which Paul calls the long-hidden mystery.

e.n: A work that you would never believe
t: Habakkuk warns scoffers of a work God will do that they will not believe even if told. Paul ends his sermon at Pisidian Antioch with this warning.

Amos says God will rebuild David’s fallen tent so that the rest of mankind may seek the Lord, including all the Gentiles called by his name. At the Jerusalem Council James uses this verse to say that Gentiles should not be burdened.
Isaiah says heaven is God’s throne and earth his footstool, so no house built by hands can contain him. Stephen uses it to say that the temple, however holy, is not where God lives.

e.n: The righteous will live by faith
t: Habakkuk, looking at a coming invasion, says the righteous will live by their faithfulness to God. Paul quotes it in Romans 1:17 to show that the gospel reveals God’s righteousness “by faith from start to finish.”
Galatians 3:11 uses it against relying on the law: “no one is justified before God by the law, because, ‘The righteous will live by faith.’”
Hebrews quotes Habakkuk 2:3-4 in 10:37-38 and applies the second half to the readers: “But My righteous one will live by faith; and if he shrinks back, I will take no pleasure in him.”

Genesis says that Abraham believed the LORD, “and He credited it to him as righteousness.” Paul uses the verse to show that Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, so that he is the father of all who believe.

Paul opens his argument in Galatians 3 with this verse: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (3:6), and concludes that “those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith” (3:9).

James 2:23 says that this Scripture was “fulfilled” in Abraham’s offering of Isaac: his faith “was working with his actions” and “was perfected by what he did” (2:22). Paul uses the same verse for a different purpose in Romans 4:3.

e.n: Blessed is the one whose sin is not counted
t: Psalm 32 begins with the happiness of the person whose lawless acts are forgiven and whose sin the Lord does not count against him. Paul says David speaks of “the blessedness of the man to whom God credits righteousness apart from works.”
God’s promise to Abram in Genesis 17 changes his name to Abraham, “a father of many nations.” Paul says Abraham is therefore “the father of us all,” both circumcised and uncircumcised believers.
Psalm 14 describes a world in which all have turned aside and no one does good. Paul strings together lines from this psalm and others to show that Jews and Gentiles alike are under sin.

e.n: The older will serve the younger
t: Before Esau and Jacob were born, God told Rebekah that the older would serve the younger. Paul adds Malachi’s “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” to show that God’s purpose rests on his call, not on birth or deeds.

Hosea named his children “Not My People” to show God’s judgment on Israel, and then promised that those who were not his people would be called sons of the living God. Paul reads it as including the Gentiles.
1 Peter 2:10 echoes Hosea: “Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.”

e.n: Only the remnant will be saved
t: Isaiah said that though Israel was as many as the sand of the sea, only a remnant would return, and that without God’s mercy Israel would have become like Sodom. Paul says a remnant still exists “chosen by grace.”

Isaiah calls the LORD a stone of stumbling and a rock of offense to Israel, and also a precious cornerstone laid in Zion for those who trust. Paul says Israel stumbled over the stone and that the one who believes in him “will never be put to shame.”
1 Peter 2:8 adds Isaiah 8:14: for those who do not believe, Christ is “A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense.”
Moses tells Israel that God’s commandment is not far off in heaven or across the sea, but “in your mouth and in your heart.” Paul applies the passage to the word of faith about Christ.

e.n: Everyone who calls on the name of the LORD
t: Joel’s promise that everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved. Paul uses it in Romans 10 to show that the promise is for Jew and Gentile alike, since “the same Lord is Lord of all.”
Isaiah pictures a runner arriving at Jerusalem with news that God reigns. Paul quotes the line to show that people cannot hear unless someone is sent to preach.

e.n: The Deliverer will come from Zion
