t: Isaiah promises a Redeemer who comes to Zion and a covenant with those who turn from sin. Paul cites it at the end of his argument about Israel: “all Israel will be saved.”
Moses’ song says the LORD will take vengeance and repay. Paul quotes it to tell Roman believers not to avenge themselves but to leave room for God.
Hebrews quotes Deuteronomy 32:35-36 in 10:30 to warn the readers: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay,” and again, “The Lord will judge His people.”

Isaiah says that every knee will bow to the LORD and every tongue swear allegiance. Paul uses it to remind the Romans that they will all stand before God’s judgment seat, so they should not judge each other.
Philippians 2:10-11 applies the same words to Jesus: “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.”

Isaiah looks ahead to a root of Jesse who will stand as a banner for the peoples, and the nations will seek him. Paul closes his letter’s main argument with it: “The Root of Jesse will appear, One who will arise to rule over the Gentiles; in Him the Gentiles will put their hope.”

e.n: Let him who boasts boast in the Lord
t: Jeremiah says the wise should not boast in wisdom, the strong in strength or the rich in riches, but in knowing the LORD. Paul quotes the saying to end his argument that God chose the weak and the foolish: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.”

Paul quotes the line again in 2 Corinthians 10:17 when he refuses to boast about work done by others: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord.” He adds that “it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends” (10:18).

e.n: I will destroy the wisdom of the wise
t: Isaiah says that God will make the wisdom of the wise perish when his people honor him only with their lips. Paul quotes it to show that the cross overturns the cleverness of the age: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise; the intelligence of the intelligent I will frustrate.”

Paul says “as it is written: ‘No eye has seen, no ear has heard, no heart has imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.’” His words echo Isaiah 64:4 and perhaps other passages in Isaiah, but they do not match the Hebrew or the Greek translation exactly. He says God has revealed these things by the Spirit.

e.n: Who has known the mind of the Lord?
t: Isaiah asks who has directed the Spirit of the LORD or instructed him as his counselor. Paul quotes the question to show that no one can teach God, and then adds: “But we have the mind of Christ.”

e.n: He catches the wise in their craftiness
t: Paul backs up his point that the wisdom of this world is foolishness in God’s sight with two quotations. The first is from Eliphaz in the book of Job, and the second is from the Psalms: “The Lord knows that the thoughts of the wise are futile.” Paul uses both to warn against trust in human teachers.

Deuteronomy repeatedly tells Israel to purge evil from among them, in cases like false witness and sexual sin. Paul ends his instruction on the man with his father’s wife with the line “Expel the wicked man from among you.”

e.n: The two will become one flesh
t: Genesis says a man leaves his father and mother and is joined to his wife, and the two become one flesh. Paul uses the line against joining the body to a prostitute: “he who unites himself with a prostitute is one with her in body? For it is said, ‘The two will become one flesh.’” Jesus quotes the same verse about marriage.

Ephesians 5:31 quotes the verse, “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh,” then says, “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (5:32).

Deuteronomy 25:4 says not to muzzle an ox while it treads out the grain. Paul asks whether God is concerned about oxen, and concludes that the law was written for those who work, such as preachers of the gospel.

e.n: They sat down to eat and to drink
t: After the golden calf, Exodus says the people sat down to eat and drink and got up to play. Paul quotes it as a warning to the Corinthians who join feasts in temples: “Do not be idolaters, as some of them were.”

Psalm 24 begins by saying that the earth and everything in it belong to the LORD. Paul uses the line to settle the question of market meat: since all food belongs to God, a believer can eat what is sold without asking where it came from.

Isaiah warned Israel that if they would not listen to prophets, God would speak to them through foreign speakers. Paul uses it in the argument about tongues: “By strange tongues and foreign lips I will speak to this people, but even then they will not listen to Me, says the Lord.”

e.n: He has put everything under His feet
t: Psalm 8 says God put all things under the feet of the human race, and Psalm 110 says the LORD will make the king’s enemies his footstool. Paul combines these when he says Christ must reign “until He has put all His enemies under His feet,” and quotes Psalm 8: “God has put everything under His feet.”
Ephesians 1:22 uses the psalm’s words: “God put everything under His feet and made Him head over everything for the church.”
Hebrews quotes Psalm 8 in 2:6-8 and says that “at present we do not see everything subject to him. But we see Jesus” (2:8-9).

e.n: The first man Adam became a living being
t: Genesis 2:7 says God formed the man from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life, “and the man became a living being.” Paul quotes it and adds “the last Adam a life-giving spirit,” to show that Christ is the source of the new life.
Isaiah describes people who answered a call to repentance with feasting: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.” Paul uses the line to show what life looks like if the dead are not raised.

e.n: Death has been swallowed up in victory
t: Isaiah promises that the LORD will swallow up death forever, and Hosea asks where death’s plagues and sting are. Paul joins the two as the song of the resurrection: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?” His wording of Hosea differs from the Hebrew.

e.n: I believed, therefore I have spoken
t: Psalm 116 is a psalm of thanks from someone who nearly died. Paul quotes it in the Greek translation to explain why he keeps speaking despite danger: “in keeping with what is written: ‘I believed, therefore I have spoken,’ we who have the same spirit of faith also believe and therefore speak.”

e.n: Written on tablets of human hearts
t: Jeremiah promises a new covenant in which God writes his law on his people’s hearts, and Ezekiel promises a new spirit and a heart of flesh in place of a heart of stone. Paul does not quote either, but his words echo them: “not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.”

e.n: In the time of favor I heard you
t: In Isaiah 49 God speaks to his servant, promising help and restoring Israel and calling the nations. Paul quotes the promise to urge the Corinthians: “In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you.” Then he says that this time is now.

e.n: I will dwell with them and walk among them
t: Leviticus 26 promises that God will put his dwelling among Israel and walk among them, and Ezekiel 37 promises a covenant of peace and a sanctuary among them forever. Paul applies it to the church: “I will dwell with them and walk among them, and I will be their God, and they will be My people.”

Isaiah 52 calls Israel to leave Babylon and keep clean the vessels of the LORD. Paul applies it to the Corinthians’ close ties with idol worship: “Therefore come out from among them and be separate, says the Lord. Touch no unclean thing, and I will receive you.”

e.n: I will be a Father to you
t: God’s promise to David’s son in 2 Samuel 7:14 is “I will be his Father, and he will be My son.” Paul shifts it to the whole people and adds daughters: “I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters, says the Lord Almighty.” Scholars note he may be combining it with Isaiah 43:6.

e.n: He who gathered much had no excess
t: Exodus 16 tells how Israel gathered manna in the wilderness: those who gathered a lot had nothing left over, and those who gathered little had no lack. Paul uses it to argue for fair sharing between churches: “He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall.”

e.n: He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor
t: Psalm 112 describes the one who fears the LORD and is generous. Paul quotes it to show that giving does not run out: “He has scattered abroad His gifts to the poor; His righteousness endures forever.” He then says God “supplies seed to the sower and bread for food” and will increase the harvest of the giver’s righteousness.

e.n: Every matter must be established by two or three witnesses
t: Deuteronomy 19:15 sets the rule that one witness is not enough to convict someone of a crime: a charge must be confirmed by two or three witnesses. Paul quotes the rule as he plans a third visit, to deal fairly with accusations: “Every matter must be established by the testimony of two or three witnesses.”
1 John 5:6-9 calls “the Spirit, the water, and the blood” three witnesses in agreement, and says “the testimony of God is greater.”

e.n: Let light shine out of darkness
t: Genesis 1 describes God’s first act of creation as the command “Let there be light.” Paul does not quote it exactly. He says, “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” The same God who made the first light makes the new one.

e.n: To you and to your seed
t: God’s promises to Abraham speak of land and descendants. Paul reads one word closely: “The Scripture does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ meaning many, but ‘and to your seed,’ meaning One, who is Christ” (3:16). He then says that those who belong to Christ are “Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (3:29). The Hebrew word for “seed” is a collective singular, and Paul’s argument reads it as pointing to Christ and to those in him.

e.n: Cursed is everyone who does not continue
t: Moses told Israel at Shechem that anyone who did not uphold all the words of the law would be cursed. Paul quotes it to show that relying on works of the law puts a person under a curse: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law” (3:10).

e.n: The man who does these things will live by them
t: Leviticus 18:5 promises life to the one who keeps God’s statutes. Paul quotes it to show that the law works by doing, not by faith: “The law, however, is not based on faith; on the contrary, ‘The man who does these things will live by them’” (3:12). He sets it beside Habakkuk 2:4 in the verse before.

e.n: Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree
t: The law said a man put to death and hung on a tree was under God’s curse, and had to be buried the same day. Paul uses it for the cross: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree’” (3:13).

Isaiah told the exiles in Jerusalem to sing because the desolate city would have more children than the one with a husband. Paul quotes it for the Jerusalem above: “Rejoice, O barren woman, who bears no children; break forth and cry aloud, you who have never travailed; because more are the children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband” (4:27).

e.n: Expel the slave woman and her son
t: Sarah told Abraham to send away Hagar and Ishmael, and God told him to listen to her (Genesis 21:10-12). Paul quotes it as Scripture’s verdict on the two covenants: “Expel the slave woman and her son, for the slave woman’s son will never share in the inheritance with the free woman’s son” (4:30). He then says, “we are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman” (4:31).

Leviticus 19:18 commands love for a neighbor. Paul says “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’” (5:14), and then warns the Galatians what happens when they do the opposite: “if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another” (5:15).

Paul quotes the psalm, “When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men” (4:8), and applies it to Christ, who “ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things” (4:10). Psalm 68 describes God going up to his holy hill as a conqueror. Paul reads that victory as Christ’s ascension and the gifts as the leaders he gives to the church.

e.n: Peace to those far and near
t: Isaiah promises peace to those far and near (Isaiah 57:19), and speaks of the messenger who proclaims peace (Isaiah 52:7). Ephesians 2:17 says Christ “came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near.” Paul reads the promise as fulfilled when Christ brought Jew and Gentile together.

Zechariah 8:16 tells God’s people to speak the truth to one another. Ephesians 4:25 draws on it: “each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another.” Paul turns the prophet’s call for honest courts and speech into a rule for life inside the body of Christ.

e.n: Be angry, yet do not sin
t: Psalm 4:4 tells the reader to be shaken and not sin. Ephesians 4:26 quotes the Greek version: “Be angry, yet do not sin. Do not let the sun set upon your anger.” Paul does not forbid anger, but warns against letting it harden and “give the devil a foothold” (4:27).

Paul introduces a saying with “So it is said”: “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” (5:14). The words are not found exactly in the Old Testament. They are close to Isaiah 60:1, which calls Zion to arise and shine, and to Isaiah 26:19 and 51:17. Scholars suggest it was an early Christian hymn, perhaps sung at baptism, that drew on these verses.

The fifth commandment tells Israel to honor father and mother, and attaches a promise of long life in the land (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16). Paul quotes it in Ephesians 6:2-3 and calls it “the first commandment with a promise.” He widens the promise “that it may go well with you and that you may have a long life on the earth,” so it no longer depends on living in the land of Israel.

Isaiah pictures God as a warrior who puts on righteousness like a breastplate and salvation like a helmet (Isaiah 59:17), with righteousness as the belt around his waist (Isaiah 11:5). The messenger’s feet bring peace (Isaiah 52:7). Ephesians 6:13-17 hands God’s armor to believers: the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation and feet fitted with “the readiness of the gospel of peace.”

e.n: To me every knee will bow
t: The LORD says through Isaiah that he has sworn by himself, and that to him every knee will bow and every tongue will swear loyalty (Isaiah 45:23). Paul writes that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (Philippians 2:10-11). In Romans 14:11 the same words are used about the judgment seat of God. In Philippians they are applied to Jesus, and the glory still goes to the Father.

e.n: This will turn out for my deliverance
t: Paul writes, “I know that through your prayers and the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ, my distress will turn out for my deliverance” (1:19). The words are close to Job 13:16 in the Greek Old Testament, where Job says that his case will turn out for his salvation. Paul seems to borrow Job’s words for his own hope while on trial. “Deliverance” can mean release from prison, vindication, or final salvation, and Paul probably leaves all three open.

Moses’ song accuses Israel of being a perverse and crooked generation (Deuteronomy 32:5). Paul turns the phrase around. The Philippians live “in a crooked and perverse generation,” but they are “children of God without fault” who “shine as lights in the world” (Philippians 2:15). The church takes the place of faithful Israel among a people that has lost its way.

James 4:6 quotes Proverbs 3:34 in the form of the Greek Old Testament: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” In Proverbs it is part of the wisdom teaching about those who mock and those who are humble. James uses it as the reason for the commands that follow: submit, resist the devil, draw near, purify, and humble yourselves (4:7-10). First Peter 5:5 quotes the same verse in almost the same words, which may point to a saying that circulated among early Christians, or to both writers drawing on the Greek text.
1 Peter 5:5 quotes Proverbs 3:34 in the same words as James 4:6: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”

e.n: Be holy, because I am holy
t: “But just as He who called you is holy, so be holy in all you do, for it is written: ‘Be holy, because I am holy.’” (1:15-16). The words come from Leviticus, where they are said four times (11:44-45; 19:2; 20:7, 26). In Leviticus they are the base of the laws that set Israel apart from the nations around them. Peter says they apply to the church: God’s call makes his people like him in conduct. He has just told them to “prepare your minds for action” (1:13), literally to gird up the loins of the mind. The holiness he has in mind has to do with food and clothes less than with obedience, love and honest speech (1:22; 2:1).

e.n: The word of the Lord stands forever
t: “For, ‘All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord stands forever.’ And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.” (1:24-25). Peter quotes Isaiah 40:6-8 almost word for word from the Greek Old Testament. In Isaiah the promise was spoken to people exiled in Babylon, who were told to expect the return of the Lord. Peter says that the word is now the gospel his readers heard. They too are exiles, and the word that outlasts all flesh is the one that made them new.

“For it stands in Scripture: ‘See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame’” (2:6). The quotation is Isaiah 28:16. In Isaiah, God lays a stone in Zion as the foundation of a trustworthy building, in contrast with the leaders of Jerusalem who trusted in lies. Peter says that the stone is Christ, and that those who believe will not be put to shame. Paul quotes the same verse in Romans 9:33 and 10:11 and speaks of Christ as the cornerstone in Ephesians 2:20.

e.n: A kingdom of priests and a holy nation
t: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession” (2:9). At Sinai, God told Israel through Moses that they would be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation (Exodus 19:6), and Isaiah 43:20-21 calls Israel God’s chosen people, formed for himself to declare his praise. Peter gives the titles to the church. He adds the words of Hosea 1:9-10 and 2:23, where God tells those called “Not My People” that they are his people, and the Gentile believers are now included in those words. Paul uses Hosea in the same way in Romans 9:25-26. Revelation 1:6 and 5:10 call the redeemed a kingdom and priests.

e.n: By His stripes you are healed
t: “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. ‘By His stripes you are healed.’ For ‘you were like sheep going astray,’ but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (2:24-25). Peter takes the language of Isaiah 53 phrase by phrase: no sin and no deceit in his mouth (53:9), healing by his stripes (53:5), the sheep gone astray (53:6), the bearing of the sins of many (53:12). The word for “stripes” is molops, a bruise or weal left by a whip. Peter’s readers include slaves who knew such beatings. “The tree” (xylon) is the cross, as in Acts 5:30 and Galatians 3:13. Peter’s use of Isaiah 53 is the most extended in the New Testament apart from Philip’s with the Ethiopian (Acts 8:32-35).

Peter ends his teaching on blessing by quoting Psalm 34:12-16 in 3:10-12: whoever wants to love life and see good days must keep the tongue from evil and the lips from deceit, turn from evil and do good, and seek peace and pursue it. “For the eyes of the Lord are on the righteous, and His ears are inclined to their prayer. But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.” David wrote the psalm when he escaped from Abimelech by pretending to be mad (1 Samuel 21:10-15). The same psalm gives Peter “the Lord is good” in 2:3 (Psalm 34:8).

e.n: Do not fear what they fear
t: “Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken. But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord” (3:14-15). Peter is using Isaiah 8:12-13. In Isaiah’s day, King Ahaz and the people of Judah were afraid of an alliance of hostile kings, and the Lord told Isaiah not to fear what the people feared but to regard the Lord of hosts as holy, and to let him be their fear. Peter makes one change: where Isaiah says “the Lord of hosts,” he writes “Christ as Lord,” a quiet claim about who Jesus is. The same chapter in Isaiah (8:14) is the source of the “stone of stumbling” in 1 Peter 2:8.

e.n: A priest forever in the order of Melchizedek
t: Psalm 110 begins with the oracle that Jesus quoted in the Gospels, in which the Lord invites David’s lord to sit at his right hand. Verse 4 adds a second oracle, in which the Lord swears an oath and names this figure a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek. Hebrews is the only New Testament book that uses the second verse. It quotes it in 5:6, 7:17 and 7:21, and makes it the key to Jesus’ priesthood. The writer reasons that a priest with an oath from God, in a different order from Aaron’s, shows that the first priesthood was not final.

e.n: A body You prepared for Me
t: Psalm 40:6-8 says that God did not desire sacrifices and offerings but opened the speaker’s ears, and the speaker answers, “I have come to do Your will.” Hebrews quotes the passage from the Greek Old Testament, which reads “a body You prepared for Me” where the Hebrew text speaks of ears opened or dug for the speaker. The writer puts the words in Jesus’ mouth as he comes into the world and reads them as the end of the sacrificial system: “He takes away the first to establish the second. And by that will, we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (10:9-10).

Psalm 8 praises God for the place he gave human beings: “You made him a little lower than the angels; You crowned him with glory and honor and placed everything under his feet.” Hebrews applies it first to humanity and then to Jesus, saying, “At present we do not see everything subject to him. But we see Jesus, who was made a little lower than the angels, now crowned with glory and honor because He suffered death” (2:8-9). In the New Testament the same verse about everything under his feet is used of Christ in 1 Corinthians 15:27 and Ephesians 1:22. Hebrews adds that he shared their “flesh and blood” (2:14).

Haggai spoke to the people rebuilding the temple after the exile, promising that God would once more shake the heavens, the earth, the sea and the dry land. Hebrews quotes the promise as “Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well” and says that the words “Once more” point to the removal of what can be shaken, “so that the unshakable may remain” (12:26-27). The writer reads the shaking as the last judgment that leaves only the kingdom of God.

e.n: An angel promises John the Baptist’s birth
t: The priest Zechariah is serving in the temple when Gabriel tells him that his aged wife Elizabeth will bear the forerunner of the Lord.

e.n: The angel Gabriel appears to Mary
t: Mary, engaged to Joseph, is told she will conceive and bear the Son of the Most High, and she answers, “Let it be to me according to your word.”
Mary travels south to Elizabeth, whose baby leaps at her greeting, and Mary answers with the song traditionally called the Magnificat.
The hill-country town is not named; Ein Karem is the traditional site.
f: Ein Karem, hill country of Judea

t: Elizabeth’s son is born and named John, and Zechariah, able to speak again, prophesies about his son and the coming salvation.
Town not named; Ein Karem is the traditional site.
Because of a Roman census Joseph and Mary go to David’s town, where Jesus is born and laid in a manger.
Angels announce to shepherds in the fields that a Savior has been born, and the shepherds go and find the baby.
Traditional site near Beit Sahour; the fields are not named.
Eastern wise men follow a star, ask Herod in Jerusalem where the king of the Jews is to be born, and worship the child with gifts.
Mary and Joseph bring the baby to the temple, where Simeon and Anna recognize him as the promised salvation.
Warned in a dream, Joseph takes Mary and Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod.
Exact place in Egypt is not given; this pin marks the country generally.

e.n: Herod kills the boys of Bethlehem
t: Herod, tricked by the Magi, orders the boys of Bethlehem killed, which Matthew links to Jeremiah’s mourning at Ramah.
After Herod’s death the family returns from Egypt and makes its home in Galilee, in Nazareth.

e.n: The boy Jesus in the Temple
t: At twelve, Jesus stays behind in the temple, and his parents find him listening to the teachers and asking questions.

e.n: John the Baptist preaches in the wilderness
t: John calls Israel to repent and be baptized, and says that someone far greater is coming after him.
Traditionally Bethany beyond the Jordan (Al-Maghtas); the exact spot is debated.
Jesus is baptized by John, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father’s voice calls him his beloved Son.
Traditional site; the exact location is debated.

e.n: Jesus is tempted in the wilderness
t: After forty days of fasting, Jesus resists the devil’s three temptations by quoting Scripture.
Traditional Mount of Temptation near Jericho; the wilderness spot is not named.
Andrew, another disciple, Peter, Philip and Nathanael begin following Jesus after John points him out as the Lamb of God.
Site debated.
At a village wedding Jesus turns water into wine, the first of the signs John records.
Kafr Kanna is the traditional site; Khirbet Qana is another candidate.
Jesus drives out the money changers and sellers and speaks of raising up the temple of his body in three days.
A Pharisee and member of the council comes by night, and Jesus tells him he must be born again and that God so loved the world.
Exact house not named.
Jesus’ disciples baptize in Judea while John baptizes at Aenon, and John says of Jesus, “He must increase, but I must decrease.”
Site debated.
Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for water and offers her living water, and many in the town come to believe.
A royal official begs Jesus to heal his dying son at Capernaum, and Jesus says, “Go; your son will live,” from Cana.
Hearing that John has been arrested, Jesus goes to Galilee and makes Capernaum his base, preaching that the kingdom is near.
In his hometown synagogue Jesus reads Isaiah and says it is fulfilled today, but the people turn against him.
Jesus calls Simon, Andrew, James and John to leave their nets and follow him, and Luke places this after a huge catch of fish.
Luke names the lake of Gennesaret; the exact shore is not named.
Jesus teaches with authority and drives an unclean spirit out of a man in the synagogue.

e.n: Peter’s mother-in-law and the evening healings
t: Jesus heals Peter’s mother-in-law, and that evening the whole town gathers at the door for healing.
Jesus travels through the towns of Galilee teaching, preaching and healing, and large crowds follow him.
Region marker; no single town.
A man with leprosy kneels and asks to be made clean, and Jesus touches him and heals him.
Town not named.

e.n: The paralytic lowered through the roof
t: Four friends lower a paralyzed man through the roof, and Jesus forgives his sins and heals him.

e.n: Jesus calls Matthew and eats with sinners
t: Jesus calls the tax collector Levi (Matthew) and dines with tax collectors and sinners, saying he came for the sick.

e.n: Healing at the pool of Bethesda
t: On a Sabbath Jesus heals a man who had been ill for thirty-eight years, then explains his relationship to the Father.

e.n: Lord of the Sabbath in the grainfields
t: When the disciples pick grain on the Sabbath, Jesus calls himself Lord of the Sabbath.
Field not named.

e.n: The man with the withered hand
t: Jesus heals a man’s withered hand on the Sabbath in a synagogue, and his opponents begin to plot against him.
Town not named.
After a night in prayer, Jesus names twelve disciples as apostles.
The mountain is not named.
Jesus teaches the Beatitudes, the Lord’s Prayer and much more; Luke’s parallel is set on a level place.
Traditional site.
A Roman centurion asks Jesus to heal his servant without coming to his house, and Jesus marvels at his faith.
At the gate of Nain Jesus stops a funeral and tells a widow’s dead son to rise.
After a healing, Jesus’ critics say he casts out demons by the prince of demons, and he answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand.
Setting is “the house” in Mark.
When his mother and brothers come for him, Jesus says that those who do God’s will are his family.
From a boat Jesus teaches the crowds in parables, including the sower, the weeds, the mustard seed and the yeast.
Traditional spot at Tabgha.
f: Shore of the Sea of Galilee

t: A violent squall hits the boat, and Jesus calms the wind and waves with a word.
Jesus frees a man from a legion of demons, who enter a herd of pigs that rushes into the lake.
Gerasenes, Gadarenes and Gergesenes appear in the manuscripts; Kursi is the usual site.
f: Kursi, east shore of the lake

e.n: Jairus’ daughter and the woman with bleeding
t: On the way to Jairus’ house a woman is healed by touching Jesus’ cloak, and Jesus then raises Jairus’ daughter.
Town implied by the context.

e.n: Woes on Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum
t: Jesus warns the towns where most of his miracles were done that they will face judgment if they do not repent.
Jesus sends the Twelve in pairs to preach and heal, with instructions about what to carry and how to respond to rejection.
Region marker.

e.n: John the Baptist is imprisoned and killed
t: Herod Antipas imprisons John for rebuking his marriage, and John is beheaded at Herodias’ request.
Josephus names Machaerus as the prison; the Gospels do not.
With five loaves and two fish Jesus feeds a crowd of about five thousand men, the only miracle recorded in all four Gospels.
Luke names Bethsaida; the exact site is debated.
Jesus comes to the disciples across the stormy lake, and Peter briefly walks toward him.
People bring the sick to touch the edge of Jesus’ cloak, and all who touch him are healed.
The crowd finds Jesus at Capernaum, and he says he is the bread of life; many disciples turn back at this teaching.
Pharisees ask why the disciples ignore tradition, and Jesus says what defiles a person comes from the heart.
Place not named.
Jesus enters Gentile territory, and a woman’s persistent faith leads him to heal her daughter.

e.n: Healing the deaf man in the Decapolis
t: Jesus heals a deaf man who could hardly speak, and many other sick people, in Gentile country.
Region marker.
A second large crowd is fed with seven loaves and a few fish.
Exact site not named.
Jesus lands at Magadan (Magdala or Dalmanutha) and refuses the Pharisees’ request for a sign.
Mark’s Dalmanutha is uncertain.

e.n: A blind man healed at Bethsaida
t: Jesus heals a blind man in two stages, in a story only Mark records.
Peter says Jesus is the Christ, and Jesus begins to speak of his coming suffering.
On a high mountain Jesus shines with glory and speaks with Moses and Elijah, and the Father calls him his Son.
Tradition favors Tabor; some scholars prefer Mount Hermon.

e.n: Jesus heals a boy with a spirit
t: Jesus casts out a spirit that the disciples could not, saying some kinds need prayer.
Place not named.

e.n: The temple tax and the coin in the fish
t: Asked about the temple tax, Jesus sends Peter to catch a fish with a coin in its mouth.
The disciples argue about who is greatest, and Jesus teaches humility, care for little ones and forgiveness.

e.n: Jesus teaches at the Feast of Tabernacles
t: At the autumn feast Jesus teaches in the temple, invites the thirsty to come to him, and sends away the accusers of a woman caught in adultery.

e.n: “I am the light of the world”
t: Jesus says he is the light of the world and that before Abraham was, he is.
Jesus sends a blind man to wash at Siloam and he sees, which leads to a sharp dispute with the Pharisees.
Jesus says he is the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep.
Setting continues from the Jerusalem feast.
Setting his face toward Jerusalem, Jesus is turned away by a Samaritan village, and he rebukes James and John for wanting to call down fire.
Village not named.
Jesus sends seventy-two ahead of him in pairs, and they return with joy.
Region marker.
Asked who his neighbor is, Jesus tells of a Samaritan who helps a man beaten on the road from Jerusalem to Jericho.
Told as a parable on the road down to Jericho.
Martha is busy serving while Mary sits at Jesus’ feet, and Jesus says Mary has chosen the better part.
Luke says only “a village”; Bethany is the traditional identification.
At the winter feast Jesus says he and the Father are one, and the crowd tries to stone him.
Jesus weeps and then calls Lazarus out of the tomb after four days.
After Lazarus is raised, the chief priests and Caiaphas decide Jesus must die.
Because of the plot, Jesus leaves public view and stays with his disciples in a town called Ephraim.
Site identified with et-Taybeh.
Ten men with leprosy are healed, and only one, a Samaritan, comes back to thank Jesus.
Pharisees test Jesus about divorce, and he points back to God’s design in creation.
Region marker.
Jesus welcomes children and says the kingdom belongs to such as these.
Region marker.
A rich man asks how to inherit eternal life and goes away sad when Jesus tells him to sell all.
Region marker.
Jesus tells the Twelve for the third time that he will be killed and rise, and he teaches that greatness is serving.
Region marker.
As Jesus leaves Jericho a blind beggar cries out to him and receives his sight.
Matthew mentions two men.
Jesus invites himself to the house of the chief tax collector Zacchaeus, who gives half his goods to the poor.
A woman pours expensive perfume on Jesus shortly before his death, and he says she has prepared him for burial.
Matthew and Mark place it in the house of Simon the leper.
Riding a donkey, Jesus enters Jerusalem to cries of “Hosanna” from the crowds.
f: Bethphage and the Mount of Olives

t: Jesus curses a fruitless fig tree, and the next day it has withered; he uses this to teach about faith.
Jesus overturns the money changers’ tables, saying the temple should be a house of prayer.

e.n: Questions and teaching in the Temple
t: Leaders challenge Jesus’ authority, and he answers about taxes, the resurrection and the greatest commandment.

e.n: Some Greeks ask to see Jesus
t: Greeks come to Philip wanting to see Jesus, and he speaks of the grain of wheat that must die and of being lifted up.

e.n: Woes on the scribes and Pharisees
t: Jesus sharply warns against the religious leaders’ hypocrisy and laments over Jerusalem.
Jesus watches the crowd give and says a poor widow gave more than all the rest.
On the Mount of Olives Jesus speaks of the temple’s fall, coming trials and his return, and tells parables about being ready.
Judas goes to the chief priests and agrees to hand Jesus over for thirty pieces of silver.
At the Passover meal Jesus washes his disciples’ feet, gives them the bread and cup, and says one of them will betray him.
Traditional site of the Upper Room.
Jesus comforts his disciples, promises the Spirit and says he is the vine and they are the branches.
Traditional site; the last parts are spoken on the way.
Jesus prays for himself, his disciples and all who will believe through them.
Exact place not named; spoken before crossing the Kidron.
Jesus prays in agony in the garden, asking that the cup pass but submitting to the Father’s will.
Judas leads a crowd with swords and clubs to arrest Jesus, and the disciples flee.

e.n: Jesus before the high priest; Peter denies him
t: Jesus is questioned by Annas and Caiaphas while Peter denies knowing him three times.
Traditional location.
Judas, seeing Jesus condemned, returns the silver and takes his own life, and the priests buy a field with the money.
Traditional site of Akeldama.
Pilate questions Jesus, finds no guilt, and finally gives him up to be crucified.
The location of the praetorium is debated.
Pilate sends Jesus to Herod, who mocks him and sends him back.
Place of Herod’s stay is not named.
Soldiers mock Jesus, and Simon of Cyrene is made to carry his cross.
Jesus is crucified between two criminals, forgives those who killed him, and dies.
Traditional site beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus lay Jesus in a new tomb, and a guard is set.
Women find the tomb empty, and Mary Magdalene meets the risen Jesus.
The risen Jesus walks with two disciples and is recognized when he breaks bread.
Site debated; Emmaus-Qubeibeh is one candidate.

e.n: Jesus appears in the upper room
t: Jesus appears to the gathered disciples, shows them his hands and side, and opens the Scriptures to them.
Setting is a locked room; the traditional site is the Upper Room.
A week later Jesus appears to Thomas, who says, “My Lord and my God!”
The risen Jesus cooks breakfast for seven disciples on the shore and restores Peter.
Traditional spot at Tabgha.
Jesus meets the eleven on a mountain and sends them to make disciples of all nations.
Mountain not named.
Jesus blesses the disciples and is taken up into heaven.
Luke says near Bethany; Acts 1 names the Mount of Olives.

e.n: Jesus’ last words and the promise of the Spirit
t: For forty days the risen Jesus teaches the apostles about the kingdom, tells them to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit, and is taken up into a cloud. Two angels say he will return the same way.
Luke’s Gospel ends with the Ascension near Bethany; Acts names the Mount of Olives, a Sabbath day’s walk from the city.

e.n: The believers pray and choose Matthias
t: About 120 believers wait and pray together. Peter reads Judas’s fall in the Psalms, and the lot falls to Matthias to join the Eleven.
The upper room is not located exactly. Tradition points to the Cenacle on Mount Zion.
Wind, fire and many languages. The disciples are filled with the Spirit and Jewish pilgrims from across the world hear God’s mighty deeds in their own tongues.
Luke does not say where in Jerusalem. A house or the temple courts are both possible.

e.n: Peter preaches and three thousand are baptized
t: Peter says the crucified Jesus is both Lord and Messiah, quotes Joel and David, and calls the crowd to repent. About three thousand are baptized that day.
The southern steps and the many ritual baths found beside them make this a likely setting, but Luke does not name the spot.

e.n: The first church shares life together
t: The new believers learn from the apostles, break bread in homes, pray, and share their goods with anyone in need.

e.n: A lame man healed at the Beautiful Gate
t: Peter and John, going up to the three o’clock prayer, tell a man lame from birth to walk in the name of Jesus. He enters the temple leaping and praising God.
The Beautiful Gate is not certainly identified. It was on the east side of the temple complex.
A crowd gathers. Peter says God has glorified the Servant they handed over, and calls them to repent so that times of refreshing may come.
Solomon’s Portico was the covered colonnade on the east side of the temple platform.

e.n: Peter and John before the council
t: Arrested by the temple guard, the two are questioned by Annas, Caiaphas and the council. Peter answers that there is salvation in no one else. They are warned and released.
Exact meeting place not given. The council often met in the temple precincts or at the high priest’s house.
The believers pray for boldness, the place shakes, and they are filled again. Barnabas sells a field and lays the money at the apostles’ feet.
A couple sell property and keep back part of the price while claiming to give all of it. Peter exposes the lie, and both die. Great fear falls on the church.

e.n: The apostles arrested and freed by an angel
t: Many are healed in the shadow of Peter. The high priest jails the apostles, but an angel opens the doors at night and sends them back to teach in the temple.
The apostles say they must obey God rather than men. The Pharisee Gamaliel urges caution: if this is of God, no one can stop it. They are flogged and released, rejoicing.
Greek-speaking widows are overlooked in the daily food. The apostles ask the church to choose seven, including Stephen and Philip, and the word of God spreads.
Stephen is accused of speaking against the temple and the law. He retells Israel’s story from Abraham to Solomon and says the Righteous One has now been betrayed and murdered.
Paul calls himself a Jew born in Tarsus, ‘no obscure city.’ Tarsus was a major trading and university city in southeastern Asia Minor. He was also a Roman citizen.
Acts tells this later, in Paul’s own defenses. We place it here as the start of his story.
Paul says he grew up in Jerusalem and was trained ‘at the feet of Gamaliel,’ the same teacher who urged caution in chapter 5. He lived as a strict Pharisee.
This is told later in Paul’s defenses and placed here to show where he came from.

Stephen sees the heavens opened and Jesus standing at God’s right hand. He is dragged out and stoned, praying for his killers. The witnesses lay their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul, who approves.
The place is not named. Tradition has located it at different spots outside the walls.
f: North of the city wall, Jerusalem

t: Scattered by persecution, Philip preaches in a Samaritan city. Many believe and are baptized. Peter and John come down, and the Spirit is given. Simon the sorcerer offers money for the power and is rebuked.
Luke says ‘a city of Samaria.’ Sebaste, the former capital, is one candidate; the city is not named.
An angel sends Philip to a desert road. He meets the treasurer of the Candace of Ethiopia reading Isaiah 53, explains it from the passage, and baptizes him. Philip is then found at Azotus.
The spot is unknown. The road from Jerusalem to Gaza is described as ‘desert.’

e.n: Saul sets out to arrest believers
t: Saul drags believers from their homes to prison and asks the high priest for letters to the synagogues in Damascus, so that he can bring any followers of ‘the Way’ back in chains.

e.n: Saul meets the risen Jesus on the Damascus road
t: A light from heaven flashes around Saul and he falls to the ground. A voice says, ‘Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?’ Blinded, he is led by hand into Damascus and fasts three days.
Tradition places the meeting near Kawkab, southwest of Damascus. Luke gives no precise spot.
The Lord sends a frightened disciple named Ananias to Saul, who is praying at Judas’s house on Straight Street. Ananias lays hands on him; scales fall from his eyes, and he is baptized.
A Roman street (Via Recta) still runs through the old city of Damascus.

e.n: Saul preaches and escapes in a basket
t: Saul proclaims in the synagogues that Jesus is the Son of God. When a plot forms to kill him, friends lower him in a basket through an opening in the wall at night.
Paul recalls the same escape in 2 Corinthians 11:32-33.
The disciples fear Saul until Barnabas brings him to the apostles and tells how he met the Lord. Saul speaks boldly, then is sent home to Tarsus when Greek-speaking Jews seek to kill him.
Galatians 1:18-24 gives Paul’s own account of this visit.
The quiet years. Saul goes to Tarsus and Syria and Cilicia. Barnabas later comes looking for him.
Luke tells almost nothing about these years. Paul mentions them in Galatians 1:21.
Peter finds a man named Aeneas who had been bedridden eight years. ‘Jesus Christ heals you,’ he says, and Aeneas gets up. Many in Lydda and Sharon turn to the Lord.
A disciple named Tabitha (Dorcas), known for her kindness, dies. Peter kneels, prays, and says ‘Tabitha, arise.’ She opens her eyes, and Peter stays in Joppa with Simon the tanner.
A Roman centurion who fears God and prays and gives alms sees an angel in a vision. He is told to send for Simon Peter at Joppa.
Caesarea Maritima was the Roman capital of Judea.
On the roof at noon Peter sees a sheet of animals let down from heaven and hears, ‘What God has made clean, do not call common.’ Three men from Cornelius arrive at the door.
Tradition shows a tanner’s house near the harbor. Luke gives no street.

e.n: The Spirit falls on Gentiles at Cornelius’s house
t: Peter says he now sees that God shows no partiality. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on all who hear, and they are baptized.

e.n: Peter explains to the church in Jerusalem
t: Believers criticize Peter for eating with uncircumcised men. He tells the whole story, and the church says, ‘Then to the Gentiles also God has granted repentance that leads to life.’

Believers scattered after Stephen’s death preach to Greeks in Antioch, and many turn to the Lord. Barnabas fetches Saul from Tarsus, and they teach there for a year. Here the disciples are first called Christians.
Antioch was the third-largest city in the empire, in what is now southern Turkey.

e.n: Relief for Judea and Herod’s persecution
t: A prophet named Agabus foretells a famine, and Barnabas and Saul carry a gift to Judea. Herod Agrippa I kills James the brother of John and jails Peter, but an angel frees him and he goes to Mark’s mother’s house.
The house of Mary, John Mark’s mother, is not located. Tradition points to Mount Zion.
Herod accepts a crowd’s cry that he speaks like a god, and an angel of the Lord strikes him down. The word of God grows and multiplies.
Josephus also describes his death at Caesarea in AD 44.

While the prophets and teachers worship and fast, the Holy Spirit says, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul.’ The church lays hands on them and sends them off. This is the start of the first missionary journey.
From Seleucia the team sails to Cyprus, Barnabas’s home island. At Salamis they preach in the synagogues, with John Mark as their helper.
The proconsul Sergius Paulus asks to hear the word of God. A sorcerer named Elymas opposes them and is struck blind. The proconsul believes. From here Luke calls him Paul.
A first-century inscription mentions a Sergius Paulus, but the match is debated.
The team sails to Perga on the south coast of Asia Minor. John Mark leaves them and returns to Jerusalem. Paul later refuses to take him on the second journey.

In the synagogue Paul retells Israel’s story to David and declares that through Jesus forgiveness is proclaimed. The next Sabbath the crowds come, many Jews contradict, and Paul turns to the Gentiles. They are driven out.
Near modern Yalvaç, Turkey. Not the same as Antioch on the Orontes.
Paul and Barnabas speak so that a great number of Jews and Greeks believe. The city splits, and when a plot to stone them forms, they leave for Lystra and Derbe.
Modern Konya.

e.n: Lystra: the crowd calls them gods
t: Paul heals a man who has never walked. The crowd calls Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes and tries to offer sacrifices. Paul tells them to turn from these vain things to the living God.
The site is a mound near Hatunsaray, south of Konya. An inscription found nearby is dedicated to Zeus and Hermes.
Jews from Antioch and Iconium win over the crowd, and Paul is stoned and dragged out of the city as dead. The disciples gather around him; he gets up and goes back in.
Paul later writes of this beating (2 Corinthians 11:25).
The next day Paul and Barnabas go to Derbe, make many disciples, then retrace their steps and appoint elders in every church with prayer and fasting.
The site of Derbe is debated. Kerti Hüyük is the leading candidate.
Paul and Barnabas sail from Attalia, gather the church, and tell how God ‘had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles.’ They stay a long time.

Some say Gentile believers must be circumcised. After debate, Peter reminds the council that God gave the Spirit to Gentiles, and James says the prophets agree. They write a letter: no extra burden beyond a few basic requirements.
Galatians 2:1-10 may describe the same meeting from Paul’s side. Scholars discuss how the two accounts fit.
A sharp dispute over taking John Mark ends their partnership. Barnabas takes Mark to Cyprus; Paul chooses Silas and heads through Syria and Cilicia. This begins the second journey.
Paul finds a disciple named Timothy, son of a Jewish mother and Greek father, well spoken of. Paul has him circumcised and takes him along.

e.n: The vision of the man of Macedonia
t: Forbidden by the Spirit to speak in Asia or Bithynia, Paul reaches Troas. In a night vision a man of Macedonia pleads, ‘Come over to Macedonia and help us.’ The narrative changes to ‘we’ here.
The ‘we’ passages (16:10-17, 20:5-15, 21:1-18, 27:1-28:16) are usually taken as signs that Luke the writer was present.
By the river on the Sabbath, Paul speaks to a group of women. Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth, opens her heart, and she and her household are baptized.
Philippi was a Roman colony. The river is likely the Gangites, west of the city.

Paul frees a slave girl from a spirit. Her owners drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and jailed. At midnight an earthquake opens the doors, and the jailer asks, ‘What must I do to be saved?’
Paul claims Roman citizenship the next morning.
For three Sabbaths Paul argues from Scripture that the Messiah had to suffer and rise. A mob accuses the believers of saying there is another king, Jesus.
Thessalonica was the capital of the province of Macedonia.
The Bereans receive the word eagerly and examine the Scriptures daily to see if these things are so. When agitators come from Thessalonica, Paul is sent to the coast.
Modern Veria.

e.n: Paul at the Areopagus in Athens
t: Distressed by the idols, Paul speaks in the marketplace and then to the Areopagus council. He points to an altar ‘to the unknown god,’ quotes Greek poets, and says God will judge the world by the man he raised from the dead.
The Areopagus is the rocky hill northwest of the Acropolis.

Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla, tent-makers, and teaches in the synagogue. When opposition rises he moves next door. The Lord says in a night vision, ‘I have many in this city who are my people.’ Gallio dismisses the charge against him.
Gallio’s proconsulship, known from an inscription at Delphi, helps date this to about AD 51-52.

e.n: A vow at Cenchreae; a short stop at Ephesus
t: Paul cuts his hair at Cenchreae because of a vow, sails to Ephesus where he reasons in the synagogue, leaves Priscilla and Aquila there, and returns by Caesarea and Jerusalem to Antioch.
The map pin is at Ephesus.
Apollos, a learned Jew from Alexandria, preaches fervently but knows only the baptism of John. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately.

e.n: Paul in Ephesus: the Spirit, Tyrannus, the burning scrolls
t: Paul finds twelve disciples who know only John’s baptism and baptizes them in Jesus’ name. For two years he teaches in the hall of Tyrannus. Handkerchiefs, exorcists and burned magic scrolls worth fifty thousand silver pieces mark the time.
Demetrius, a silversmith who makes shrines of Artemis, rouses the city. The crowd chants ‘Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!’ for two hours until the town clerk calms them.
The great theater still stands and held about 25,000.
After travelling through Macedonia and Greece, Paul meets the church at Troas on the first day of the week. A young man named Eutychus falls from a window during his long talk, and Paul raises him.
Paul summons the elders from Ephesus and tells them he is going to Jerusalem bound in the Spirit. ‘It is more blessed to give than to receive.’ They weep, embrace him, and walk him to the ship.
Sailing by Cos, Rhodes and Patara, Paul reaches Tyre. The disciples there warn him through the Spirit not to go on to Jerusalem. The families kneel with him on the beach and pray.

Paul stays with Philip the evangelist and his four prophesying daughters. Agabus binds his own hands with Paul’s belt and says the Jews will bind the owner of the belt. Paul says he is ready to die for the Lord.

James and the elders ask Paul to join four men in a vow. Jews from Asia see him in the temple, accuse him of bringing Greeks into the sacred area, and drag him out. Roman soldiers rescue him from the mob.
A warning stone found in 1871 forbade foreigners from entering the inner court on penalty of death.
From the barracks steps Paul addresses the crowd in Aramaic and tells his story. At the word ‘Gentiles’ they erupt. The tribune orders him examined by flogging until Paul says he is a Roman citizen.

Paul splits the council by saying he is on trial for the resurrection of the dead; Pharisees and Sadducees quarrel. That night the Lord says, ‘Take courage, for as you have testified about me in Jerusalem, so you must testify also in Rome.’

e.n: The plot and the night ride
t: Forty men vow not to eat until they kill Paul. His nephew hears and tells the tribune, who sends Paul with 470 soldiers by night to the governor Felix at Caesarea.
Antipatris was on the main road from Jerusalem to Caesarea, about halfway.

The high priest’s lawyer Tertullus accuses Paul. Paul replies that he came to worship, not to stir riots, and that the real issue is the resurrection. Felix keeps him in custody for two years, hoping for a bribe.
The Roman governor’s palace at Caesarea was the former palace of Herod the Great.
The new governor Festus asks if Paul will be tried at Jerusalem. Paul, knowing the danger, says ‘I appeal to Caesar.’ Festus replies, ‘To Caesar you shall go.’

King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice come to hear him. Paul tells of his Damascus road meeting and his commission, and asks Agrippa, ‘Do you believe the prophets?’ The king says Paul could have been set free had he not appealed to Caesar.
Paul, other prisoners, Luke and Aristarchus sail under the centurion Julius. At Myra they change to an Alexandrian grain ship and slowly reach Fair Havens on Crete.
Fair Havens (Kaloi Limenes) is on the south coast of Crete.

Against Paul’s advice the ship leaves for a better harbor. A northeaster seizes it and drives it for fourteen days. An angel tells Paul that all 276 aboard will be saved, and Paul encourages them to eat.
The pin marks the small island of Cauda (Gavdos), where the ship was first driven. The route afterwards is a drift.

The ship runs aground on a sandbar and breaks up. All reach shore. A viper bites Paul’s hand and he shakes it into the fire; the islanders call him a god. He heals the father of Publius and many others.
Malta is the traditional site; some scholars have proposed other islands.

After three months they sail in another Alexandrian ship, landing at Puteoli. Believers there host Paul for a week, and brothers from Rome meet him on the Appian Way. Paul thanks God and takes courage.
Puteoli (Pozzuoli) was the main port for the Egyptian grain fleet.

Paul calls the Jewish leaders together, explains his appeal, and from morning to evening testifies about the kingdom and Jesus. Then, for two years in his own rented house, he welcomes all who come, ‘proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness and without hindrance.’
Acts ends here with no verdict. Paul’s later years come from his letters and from early church tradition.

Paul says that “from Jerusalem all the way around to Illyricum, I have fully proclaimed the gospel of Christ.” He has aspired to preach “where Christ was not known, so that I would not be building on someone else’s foundation.”

Acts never mentions Illyricum (the Roman lands along the Adriatic, later called Dalmatia). It may mark the far edge of his work in Macedonia (Acts 20:1-2). The pin is Salona, the capital of Dalmatia, as a general marker. 2 Timothy 4:10 says Titus went to Dalmatia.

e.n: Macedonia and Achaia give for the poor
t: Paul says Macedonia and Achaia “were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem.” He sees it as a debt: if the Gentiles “have shared in their spiritual blessings, they are obligated to minister to them with material blessings.”

2 Corinthians 8-9 describes the Macedonian gift in more detail, and 1 Corinthians 16:1-4 the plan for Corinth. Acts 20:4 lists the men who went with Paul to carry it. The pin is Thessalonica, a Macedonian capital.

Timothy, Lucius, Jason and Sosipater send greetings. Tertius, “who wrote down this letter,” adds his own. “Gaius, who has hosted me and all the church,” sends greetings, and so do Erastus, “the city treasurer,” and “our brother Quartus.”

Romans does not name the place where it was written. Corinth fits best: Paul spends three months in Greece in Acts 20:2-3, Phoebe comes from nearby Cenchreae, and a paving stone inscribed “Erastus” lies near the Corinth theater. Most scholars date the letter to the winter of about AD 56-57.

Paul commends “our sister Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea” and asks the Romans to “welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the saints.” She “has been a great help to many people, including me.”

Cenchreae was Corinth’s eastern harbor. Phoebe is probably the one who carried the letter to Rome, but Paul does not say so. The Greek word for “servant” is diakonos, which some translations render “deacon.”

e.n: The letter reaches the church in Rome
t: Paul writes “To all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints,” a church he has not yet visited. In chapter 16 he greets more than twenty people by name, including Prisca and Aquila, “the church that meets at their house,” and the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus.

Many scholars think the church grew out of Rome’s Jewish community and was shaken when Claudius expelled Jews from the city in about AD 49 (Acts 18:2). Jewish believers returned after he died in AD 54, which would explain the strain between Jewish and Gentile believers in chapters 14-15.

e.n: Be subject to the governing authorities
t: Paul tells the Roman believers to be subject to the governing authorities, to pay taxes, revenue, respect and honor to those who are owed them, and to owe no one anything except love.

Nero became emperor in AD 54, and the first years of his reign were stable. Tacitus records that in AD 58 a public outcry over tax collectors led Nero to consider ending indirect taxes. Paul wrote Romans 13 before the persecution of AD 64.

Paul says he is “on my way to Jerusalem to serve the saints there” and asks the Romans to pray “that I may be delivered from the unbelievers in Judea, and that my service in Jerusalem may be acceptable to the saints there.”

Acts 24:17 has Paul tell Felix he returned to Jerusalem “to bring alms to my people and to present offerings.” Acts does not describe the handing over. His arrest in the temple follows (Acts 21:27-36), so the prayer in Romans 15:31 was answered in a way Paul did not expect.

e.n: On to Spain by way of Rome
t: Paul says there are “no further opportunities for me in these regions.” He hopes “to see you on my way to Spain. And after I have enjoyed your company for a while, you can equip me for my journey.” First he must deliver the gift to Jerusalem.
The Bible does not say whether Paul reached Spain. 1 Clement 5 (about AD 95) says he reached “the limit of the west.” The pin is Tarraco, the capital of the Roman province, but Romans names no city.

Paul argues that Abraham was counted righteous because he believed God (Genesis 15:6), before he was circumcised and long before the law came. So Abraham is the father of all who believe, Jew and Gentile.
Genesis 15 does not name the place of the vision, but Abraham was then living by the oaks of Mamre (Genesis 14:13). The site near Hebron is traditional.

Paul asks whether God has rejected his people. He recalls Elijah complaining that he alone was left, and God’s answer: “I have reserved for Myself seven thousand men who have not bowed the knee to Baal.” So now too there is a remnant chosen by grace.
The story is in 1 Kings 19. Horeb is another name for Sinai, and its exact location is uncertain. Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai is the traditional site.

e.n: Paul brings the gospel to Corinth
t: Paul reminds the church how he came: “I came to you in weakness and fear, and with much trembling.” He “resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified.” He laid the foundation, and others are building on it.

Acts 18:1-18 tells the same visit. Paul stayed with Aquila and Priscilla, who made tents like him, argued in the synagogue, and stayed a year and a half. A letter of Claudius found at Delphi names Gallio as proconsul of Achaia, which dates the visit to about AD 50-52. Corinth had been rebuilt as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar in 44 BC.

e.n: Planted by Paul, watered by Apollos
t: Paul writes, “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow.” He treats himself and Apollos as fellow servants, not rivals. At the end of the letter he says he “strongly urged” Apollos to visit Corinth, but Apollos “was not at all inclined to go now.”

Acts 18:24-19:1 describes Apollos, a learned Jew from Alexandria who was taught more fully by Priscilla and Aquila in Ephesus, then crossed to Achaia and helped the believers there. Paul was back in Ephesus by the time Apollos reached Corinth.

Paul says, “I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, because a great door for effective work has opened to me, even though many oppose me.” He sends greetings from “the churches in the province of Asia,” and from Aquila and Prisca and “the church that meets at their house.”

Acts 19 has Paul in Ephesus for about three years (Acts 20:31). Most scholars date 1 Corinthians to about AD 53-55. When Paul asks “If I fought wild beasts in Ephesus for human motives, what did I gain?” he may be speaking figuratively. 2 Corinthians 1:8-9 mentions a crisis in Asia that nearly cost him his life.

Paul writes, “some from Chloe’s household have informed me that there are quarrels among you.” Individuals are saying, “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ.” He thanks God that he baptized only Crispus, Gaius and the household of Stephanas.

Chloe is named nowhere else, and Paul does not say where she lived. Cephas is Peter, though nothing says he visited Corinth. Crispus was the ruler of the synagogue in Acts 18:8, and Gaius is probably the host in Romans 16:23.

Paul says “the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” Christ crucified is “a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles.” God chose what is weak, so that no one can boast except in the Lord.

Corinth admired polished speakers who traveled from city to city, and Paul answers them directly. Roman writers such as Cicero called crucifixion the cruelest and most shameful form of execution, so a crucified Messiah was a hard message in any city of the empire.

Paul has heard of “sexual immorality among you, and of a kind that is intolerable even among pagans: A man has his father’s wife.” He tells them to expel the man, and says “a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough.” He adds, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed.”

The woman is most likely the man’s stepmother (Leviticus 18:8). Paul also mentions an earlier letter (5:9) that has not survived. Some scholars connect this man with the offender in 2 Corinthians 2:5-8, but others disagree.

Paul asks, “how dare he go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints!” He says the saints “will judge the world,” and asks, “Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?” He reminds them: “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified.”

Cases in a Roman colony were heard by magistrates in the forum, where wealthy patrons tended to have the advantage. The raised platform (bema) in Corinth’s forum is where Gallio heard the case against Paul in Acts 18:12-17.

Paul quotes a slogan, “Everything is permissible for me,” and answers it. He says “Flee from sexual immorality,” and tells them their body “is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you.” “You were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body.”

The hill above Corinth carried a temple of Aphrodite. Strabo says it once had over a thousand temple slaves, but he describes the older Greek city, which Rome destroyed in 146 BC, and how much of that continued in the Roman city is debated. “Bought at a price” is the language of buying a slave.

Paul begins, “Now for the matters you wrote about.” He gives advice on marriage, divorce and staying single, marking what comes from “the Lord” and what is his own judgment. He tells slaves, “if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity,” and says “the time is short.”

“The present crisis” (7:26) is not explained. Some link it to the famine in Claudius’ reign (Acts 11:28), which Tacitus also mentions, but this is a guess. Slavery was common in Corinth, and many believers there would have been slaves or freed slaves.

Paul says “an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one,” but warns that “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” Believers must not eat in an idol’s temple or cause a weaker brother to stumble. In the market, “Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience.”

Excavations at Corinth uncovered dining rooms with couches in the Asklepieion, a healing sanctuary north of the city, and in the sanctuary of Demeter and Kore on the slope of Acrocorinth. Meat sold in the market often came from temple sacrifices.

Paul says that “in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize.” Athletes train “for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable.” He says, “I discipline my body and make it my slave.”

The Isthmian Games were held every two years at the sanctuary of Poseidon, about ten miles east of Corinth. Winners received a wreath of pine or celery. The stadium has been excavated. Paul’s time in Corinth may have overlapped with one of the festivals.

Paul recalls that “our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea.” He says “that rock was Christ,” and warns against idolatry: “The people sat down to eat and to drink, and got up to indulge in revelry.” He adds that “God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear.”
The feast and revelry belong to the golden calf at the foot of Sinai (Exodus 32:6). The exact location of Sinai is uncertain. Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai is the traditional site.

Paul says that when they meet, “it is not the Lord’s Supper you eat.” Some go ahead without sharing: “While one remains hungry, another gets drunk.” He then recalls what he received: the Lord Jesus “on the night He was betrayed, took bread,” and “you proclaim the Lord’s death until He comes.”

The church met in homes. A typical Roman dining room held only about nine people reclining, with more in the adjoining courtyard, so wealthier members may have eaten first. This is the oldest written account of the Lord’s Supper, earlier than any Gospel.

Paul says “There are different gifts, but the same Spirit,” and “Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.” Chapter 13 says “Love is patient, love is kind,” and ends: “the greatest of these is love.” In chapter 14 he says he would rather “speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.”

Mirrors in Paul’s day were polished metal, and Corinth was known for its bronze work, so “a dim reflection as in a mirror” (13:12) would have been familiar. Verses 14:34-35 are debated: some manuscripts place them after verse 40, and scholars differ over whether Paul is limiting disorder, quoting a Corinthian slogan, or whether they were added later.

e.n: What Paul received: Christ died and was raised
t: Paul passes on “as of first importance”: that Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and “appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve,” then to over five hundred, to James, to all the apostles, and “last of all He appeared to me also.”

Most scholars think the wording of verses 3-5 goes back to within a few years of the crucifixion. Paul probably heard it when he spent fifteen days with Peter in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18). The pin marks where that report began, not where Paul wrote it.

e.n: If Christ has not been raised
t: Some in Corinth said there is no resurrection. Paul answers: “if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith.” Christ is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep,” and “as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive.” At the last trumpet “the dead will be raised imperishable.”

Greek thought often hoped for the soul to escape the body, and the Athenians mocked Paul’s talk of resurrection in Acts 17:32. The practice of being “baptized for the dead” (15:29) is mentioned nowhere else, and scholars offer many explanations. The line “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” echoes Isaiah 22:13.

Paul tells the Corinthians to do as he directed the churches of Galatia: “On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income.” He will send their chosen representatives with letters “to carry your gift to Jerusalem.”

The collection began with the agreement in Galatians 2:10 to “remember the poor.” Paul writes more of it in 2 Corinthians 8-9 and Romans 15:25-27, and Acts 20:4 lists the men who traveled with him. The pin is the destination.
Paul says “Stephanas and his household were the first converts in Achaia.” He is glad that “Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus have arrived, because they have supplied what was lacking from you.”

These three may have brought the Corinthians’ letter (7:1) and carried Paul’s reply back. Fortunatus is a Latin name, and Achaicus means “from Achaia.” Acts 17:34 names converts in Athens, which was also in Achaia, so “first converts” probably means the first household.

e.n: Timothy, and the plan to come through Macedonia
t: Paul says “I have sent you Timothy, my beloved and faithful child in the Lord,” and asks the church to see that Timothy “has nothing to fear while he is with you.” He plans: “After I go through Macedonia, however, I will come to you.”

Acts 19:21-22 has Paul send Timothy and Erastus into Macedonia, with plans to go on to Achaia, then Jerusalem, then Rome. Paul later changed his plans, which caused hurt feelings (2 Corinthians 1:15-17). The pin is Philippi, a Macedonian city on his route.

e.n: Despairing even of life in Asia
t: Paul tells the church, “We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life. Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead.” He says, “We have this treasure in jars of clay.”

Paul does not say what happened in the province of Asia. Some link it to the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:23-41), but the letter gives no details, and 1 Corinthians 15:32 and 16:9 show he faced danger and many opponents there. Jars of clay were the everyday containers of his day, cheap and easy to break.

e.n: A changed plan, and a “Yes” in Christ
t: Paul had planned to visit Corinth twice, “so that you might receive a double blessing,” on his way to Macedonia and again on his way back. He did not come, and some said he said “Yes, yes” when he meant “No, no.” He answers: “all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ.” He says he stayed away “to spare you.”

In 1 Corinthians 16:5-7 Paul had said he would come through Macedonia. Plans then changed more than once. Silvanus is Silas, who came to Corinth with Timothy (Acts 18:5), and the letter says the three of them preached there.

Paul writes, “So I made up my mind not to make another painful visit to you.” Later he says, “I already warned you the second time I was with you.” The visit that hurt both sides is the second, so the next one will be the third.

Acts does not mention this visit. Most scholars place it between 1 Corinthians and 2 Corinthians, a short trip across the Aegean from Ephesus. The details are not known, but something went badly wrong between Paul and a member or group in the church.

Paul says, “through many tears I wrote you out of great distress and anguish of heart, not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.” Later he adds, “Even if I caused you sorrow by my letter, I do not regret it. Although I did regret it.”

Titus is usually thought to have carried it. This letter has not survived, or it survives in part. Some scholars say it is 1 Corinthians, some say it is lost, and some say it is chapters 10-13 of this letter. The pin at Ephesus is the most likely place it was written, not something the letter says.

Paul writes, “Now if anyone has caused grief, he has not grieved me but all of you.” The majority had punished him enough, so “you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.” He says this is so “that Satan should not outwit us.”

The offender is not named. Some scholars connect him with the man in 1 Corinthians 5, while others think he insulted Paul during the painful visit. The letter does not decide. Paul asks the church to “reaffirm your love for him.”

Paul writes that when he went to Troas “to preach the gospel of Christ and a door stood open for me in the Lord, I had no peace in my spirit, because I did not find my brother Titus there.” He says, “So I said goodbye to them and went on to Macedonia.”

Troas was the usual port for crossing to Macedonia. Paul wanted news from Corinth so badly that he left an open door. Acts 20:1-2 has him leave Ephesus for Macedonia after the riot, and says nothing of Titus.

e.n: Titus brings good news in Macedonia
t: Paul says, “when we arrived in Macedonia, our bodies had no rest, but we were pressed from every direction—conflicts on the outside, fears within. But God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus.” Titus “told us about your longing, your mourning, and your zeal for me.”

Paul does not name the city where he met Titus. Philippi is a likely guess because Paul had friends there, but Thessalonica and Berea are also possible. Titus is never named in Acts, though he appears often in Paul’s letters, and Galatians 2:1-3 shows he was a Gentile.

Paul tells the Corinthians “You yourselves are our letter,” written “not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts.” Moses put a veil over his face, but “whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away.”

The shining face and veil come from Exodus 34:29-35, when Moses came down from Sinai with the second tablets. The exact location of Sinai is uncertain, and Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai is the traditional site. Paul takes the story as a picture of the old covenant, not as a rebuke of Moses.

e.n: The judgment seat and the ministry of reconciliation
t: Paul says “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ,” and that “if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation.” God “reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation.” He adds, “we are ambassadors for Christ.”

The Greek word for “judgment seat” is bema, the same word Acts 18:12 uses for the platform in Corinth’s forum where Gallio sat. Paul’s readers walked past a real bema every day. An ambassador, in Roman times, spoke for a ruler who was not present.

e.n: Open hearts, and a warning about partners
t: Paul says “Our hearts are open wide” and asks the Corinthians to “Open wide your hearts also.” He warns, “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers,” and asks, “What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God.”

Many scholars hear an echo of Deuteronomy 22:10, which forbids plowing with an ox and a donkey together, in the picture of a yoke. “Belial” is a Hebrew word for worthlessness that later became a name for the evil one. Some scholars think 6:14-7:1 was inserted from another source, while others say it fits Paul’s argument.

Paul says that in “the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity.” He writes that “they gave according to their ability and even beyond it,” and “they earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints.”

The Macedonian churches were at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea (Acts 16-17). The pin is Thessalonica as one of them. Philippians 4:15-16 shows the Philippians had supported Paul before. Romans 15:26 says Macedonia and Achaia both gave.

e.n: Titus and the brothers are sent ahead
t: Paul writes that he is sending Titus and two other brothers. One “is praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel” and was “chosen by the churches to accompany us with the offering.” Paul says, “We hope to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift.”

Neither brother is named. Acts 20:4 lists the men who later traveled with Paul to Jerusalem: Sopater, Aristarchus, Secundus, Gaius, Timothy, Tychicus and Trophimus. The pin is Corinth, where the brothers were headed.

Paul says “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.” He asks each person to “give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver.” He ends, “Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!”

The gift was for believers in Jerusalem, as in Romans 15:25-27 and 1 Corinthians 16:1-4. Galatians 2:10 says the Jerusalem leaders asked Paul to “remember the poor.” Acts 24:17 has Paul say he came to Jerusalem to bring gifts for the poor of his nation. The pin is the destination.

Paul writes, “I, Paul, who am humble when face to face with you, but bold when away.” Some said, “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account.” He answers that “the weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world.”

Chapters 10-13 have a sharper tone than chapters 1-9. Some scholars think they come from a different letter, perhaps the “tearful” letter or a later one, while others think Paul changed tone after he heard how part of the church was still resisting. The manuscripts hand them down as one letter.

Paul fears that “just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ.” Visitors preach “a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed.” He calls them “false apostles, deceitful workers,” and says “Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light.”
