The letter does not say where the “prophecies” about Timothy were spoken (compare 4:14). The pin at Lystra stands for his home (Acts 16:1-2) and is a judgment call. In 1 Corinthians 5:5 Paul uses almost the same words for putting a man out of the church, and the aim there too is that he be saved. Second Timothy 2:17-18 names Hymenaeus as one who taught that the resurrection had already happened. An Alexander in 2 Timothy 4:14 is called a coppersmith who did Paul harm; the letters do not say whether he is the same man, and Acts 19:33 has another Alexander in Ephesus.

Paul writes, “First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone—for kings and all those in authority—so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity.” God “wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all.”

Jews prayed for foreign rulers (Jeremiah 29:7), and Josephus says sacrifices were offered at the Temple for the emperor until the revolt of AD 66 (Jewish War 2.409-410). If Paul wrote the letter in the 60s, the emperor was Nero. Ephesus was a center of emperor worship, and the church is told to pray for rulers and not to worship them. The words “one God” echo the great Jewish prayer, “The Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

e.n: Prayer, dress and women in the assembly
t: Paul writes, “I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension.” He asks the women to dress “with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, but with good deeds.” He also writes, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet,” and points to Adam and Eve.

This is one of the most debated passages in the letters. Some readers take the rule to be lasting, based on the order of creation. Others think it answers a local problem at Ephesus, where false teachers were at work (1:3-7; 2 Timothy 3:6-7) and women in the church may have been drawn to them. The verb for “exercise authority” (authentein) is rare and its sense is argued. Acts 18:26 shows Priscilla helping to teach Apollos at Ephesus, and Romans 16:1 and 16:7 name women who served. “Saved through childbearing” (2:15) has also been read in several ways, among them as a reference to the birth of Christ. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

Paul writes, “This is a trustworthy saying: If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task.” The list that follows is mostly about character: “above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach.” He “must manage his own household well” and “have a good reputation with outsiders.”

The Greek word for “overseer” (episkopos) means one who watches over, and in Acts 20:17 and 20:28 and Titus 1:5-7 it is used for the same people as “elders.” “The husband of but one wife” has been read as faithful to one wife, as not married again after a wife’s death, or as not having divorced and remarried; the church has differed. The household was the center of life in the city, and a church often met in someone’s house. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

Paul writes, “Deacons likewise must be dignified, not double-tongued or given to much wine or greedy for money. They must hold to the mystery of the faith with a clear conscience.” He says, “they must first be tested,” and that “those who have served well as deacons acquire for themselves a high standing and great confidence in the faith.”

The Greek word for “deacon” (diakonos) means a servant. Phoebe is called one in Romans 16:1 and Paul greets overseers and deacons together in Philippians 1:1. In 3:11 “the women” may mean the wives of deacons or women who were deacons themselves; the Greek can be read either way. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

e.n: “The pillar and foundation of the truth”: a hymn
t: Paul writes, “Although I hope to come to you soon, I am writing you these things in case I am delayed, so that you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth.” He then quotes what seems to be a hymn: “He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory.”

The letter names Macedonia (1:3) but no town, so the pin at Philippi is a judgment call for where Paul was. The lines in 3:16 are arranged in pairs, and most scholars think Paul is quoting an early hymn or creed. The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus was one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world, and ancient writers describe its many columns (Pliny counts 127), so the image of a “pillar” would have been vivid there.

e.n: Later times: forbidding marriage and foods
t: Paul writes, “Now the Spirit expressly states that in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons.” They “will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods that God has created to be received with thanksgiving.” He answers, “every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected.”

The letter does not name the group. Some Jewish groups, such as the Essenes, kept to strict rules about food, and some later Christian groups forbade marriage and meat. Paul’s answer goes back to Genesis 1:31, where God calls his creation good. “In later times” can mean the time that has already begun, since Paul says the teaching is already at work (4:6-7). The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

Paul writes, “reject irreverent, silly myths. Instead, train yourself for godliness. For physical exercise is of limited value, but godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come.” He says, “we have set our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe.”

The Greek verb for “train” (gymnazo) gives us “gymnasium.” Greek cities had gymnasia where young men exercised, studied and made connections, and Ephesus had several. Paul uses athletic pictures elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:24-27; 2 Timothy 4:7). The saying that God is “Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe” has been read in more than one way, and the first part echoes 2:4. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

Paul writes, “Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.” He tells Timothy, “devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching,” and not to “neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders.”

If Paul wrote the letter in the 60s, Timothy, who joined Paul about AD 49-50 (Acts 16:1-3), would probably have been in his thirties or so. The Greek word for “youth” was used loosely of men well into that range, so it is not clear how young he was. Scripture was read aloud in the assembly because few could read, and copies were scarce. Second Timothy 1:6 speaks of the same gift “through the laying on of my hands,” so Paul may have been among those who laid hands on him. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

e.n: The church as a family: honor widows
t: Paul writes, “Do not rebuke an older man, but appeal to him as to a father. Treat younger men as brothers, older women as mothers, and younger women as sisters, with absolute purity.” He says, “Honor the widows who are truly widows,” and, “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.”

In Greek and Roman cities a widow without a husband, sons or property had little security, and a family was expected to care for her. Acts 6:1 shows that widows needed help from the first years of the church. The church is pictured as a household with fathers, mothers, brothers and sisters, and the same picture appears in 3:15. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

Paul writes, “A widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, the wife of one man, and well known for good deeds.” He says, “refuse to enroll younger widows,” and advises them “to marry, have children, and manage their households, denying the adversary occasion for slander.” He adds, “If any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened.”

The “list” may be a roll of widows who received the church’s help, or a group who served the church in return, or both; the letter does not say. Roman law under Augustus pressed widows to marry again, which fits the advice to younger widows. “Washing the feet of the saints” (5:10) was a servant’s work (John 13:5-14). The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

e.n: Elders, “double honor” and a little wine
t: Paul writes, “Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching. For the Scripture says, ‘Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,’ and, ‘The worker is worthy of his wages.’” He adds, “Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments.”

The first saying is Deuteronomy 25:4, which Paul also uses in 1 Corinthians 9:9. The second matches Jesus’ words in Luke 10:7. “Double honor” can mean respect and pay. A charge against an elder needs “two or three witnesses,” as Deuteronomy 19:15 requires. Ancient doctors often prescribed a little wine for the stomach, and the advice in 5:23 is personal and brief. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

e.n: Slaves, and teachers who see godliness “as a means of gain”
t: Paul writes, “All who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited.” Those who teach another doctrine have “an unhealthy interest in controversies and semantics,” and “regard godliness as a means of gain.”

Slaves were a large part of the population in cities like Ephesus, and many churches had slaves and masters among their members (Colossians 3:22-4:1; Philemon). Paul does not say here that slavery is right. The advice aims to keep the church from being slandered, and it says that believing masters are “brothers” (6:2). Traveling teachers in the Greek world often charged fees, and the charge of teaching for gain was a familiar one. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

Paul writes, “godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these.” He warns, “the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows.”

The Greek has no word for “the” before “root,” so it can be read “a root of all kinds of evil,” and this is how many translations render it. The saying about bringing nothing into the world is close to Job 1:21 and Ecclesiastes 5:15. Ephesus was a rich trading city, and Paul says wealth was one of the teachers’ temptations. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

Paul writes, “But you, O man of God, flee from these things and pursue righteousness, godliness, faith, love, perseverance, and gentleness. Fight the good fight of the faith.” He charges Timothy “in the presence of God, who gives life to all things, and of Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate.”

John 18:33-37 gives the fullest account of Jesus’ answer to Pilate, and the Gospels place the trial in Jerusalem, so the pin stands there. “Man of God” was a name for Moses, Samuel, David and Elijah in the Old Testament. The “good confession” that Timothy made (6:12) may refer to his baptism, his ordination, or a public stand, and the letter does not say which. The doxology that follows calls God “the King of kings and Lord of lords” (6:15). “King of kings” was a title of Persian and Parthian monarchs, and Roman emperors were called “lord” and “savior,” so the words would have been heard against the claims of rulers.

e.n: “Guard what has been entrusted to you”
t: Paul writes, “Instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy.” He ends, “O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent, empty chatter and the opposing arguments of so-called ‘knowledge.’ “

The Greek for “what has been entrusted” (parathēkē) means a deposit left in someone’s care, and 2 Timothy 1:12 and 1:14 use the same word. The word “knowledge” is gnosis in Greek, and later Gnostic groups used it of their secret teaching, but the letter does not say which group it has in mind. The letter does not say where Timothy and the church were when it was read, but it places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), so the pin stands there.

Paul writes, “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus, To Timothy, my beloved child: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord.”

The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul’s chains, so the pin stands at Rome. Paul begins with “the promise of life” even as he faces death (4:6). The greeting is almost the same as 1 Timothy 1:2 (there it is “my true child in the faith”); here Timothy is “my beloved child,” a warmer note. Timothy had joined Paul at Lystra about AD 49-50 (Acts 16:1-3). The letter shows Paul in chains in Rome (1:8, 1:16-17, 2:9) and expecting death (4:6-8). If Paul wrote it, the usual view is that this is a second imprisonment after Acts ends, about AD 64-67, and that he was put to death under Nero; the letter itself does not tell us the end. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul’s name. Acts 28:30 describes a first imprisonment in rented lodgings; here the chains are heavier (“like a criminal,” 2:9) and friends have to search for him (1:17).

e.n: Tears, and the faith of Lois and Eunice
t: Paul writes, “I thank God, whom I serve with a clear conscience as did my forefathers, as I constantly remember you night and day in my prayers. Recalling your tears, I long to see you so that I may be filled with joy.” He is “reminded of your sincere faith, which first dwelt in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, and I am convinced is in you as well.”

Acts 16:1 says Timothy’s mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek, and it places the family at Lystra (or nearby Derbe), so the pin there is a judgment call. Lois and Eunice are named only here. The letter does not say what caused the tears; they may come from their last parting. Paul speaks of serving God “as did my forefathers,” so he sees his faith as growing out of Israel’s, and Timothy’s too (3:15). The grandmother, mother and son make three generations, a picture of what Paul asks Timothy to pass on in 2:2.

e.n: “Fan into flame the gift of God”
t: Paul writes, “For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control.”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The Greek verb (anazopyreo) means to stir up a fire again, as one blows on banked coals. The “laying on of my hands” is likely the same event as the laying on of hands “of the elders” in 1 Timothy 4:14, where Paul and the elders acted together; the letters do not explain further. The “spirit of fear” may hint that Timothy was timid, as 1 Corinthians 16:10-11 also suggests, but the letter does not say so directly.

e.n: “Do not be ashamed” of the testimony or of me
t: Paul writes, “So do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God.” He says, “I know whom I have believed, and I am convinced that He is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day.” Christ “has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel.”

The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul’s chains, so the pin stands at Rome. In the Roman world a prisoner in chains was shameful, and to be linked to one risked your own name. Paul answers with the same word he used in Romans 1:16: “I am not ashamed of the gospel.” The phrase “what I have entrusted to Him” can mean what Paul has put in God’s keeping (his life, his work) or what God has put in Paul’s keeping (the gospel); the Greek word is the same “deposit” found in 1:14 and 1 Timothy 6:20. The letter shows Paul in chains in Rome (1:8, 1:16-17, 2:9) and expecting death (4:6-8). If Paul wrote it, the usual view is that this is a second imprisonment after Acts ends, about AD 64-67, and that he was put to death under Nero; the letter itself does not tell us the end. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul’s name. Acts 28:30 describes a first imprisonment in rented lodgings; here the chains are heavier (“like a criminal,” 2:9) and friends have to search for him (1:17).

Paul writes, “Hold on to the pattern of sound teaching you have heard from me, with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus. Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us.”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The word for “pattern” (hypotyposis) means an outline or sketch that a writer or artist follows. The “treasure” is the deposit (parathēke) of 1 Timothy 6:20. A deposit in the ancient world was something valuable left with a trusted person, who had to hand it back unharmed. Timothy is asked to do this “with the help of the Holy Spirit,” not alone.

e.n: Deserted by Asia, refreshed by Onesiphorus
t: Paul writes, “You know that everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes. May the Lord grant mercy to the household of Onesiphorus, because he has often refreshed me and was unashamed of my chains. Indeed, when he arrived in Rome, he searched diligently until he found me.”

The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul’s chains, so the pin stands at Rome. Asia was the Roman province whose chief city was Ephesus, so “everyone in the Province of Asia” probably means that those from Asia who had been in Rome did not stand with Paul; the letter does not say how many or why. Phygelus and Hermogenes are named only here. Onesiphorus is also greeted in 4:19, where Paul greets “the household” and not the man himself, and some have thought he had died; that is a guess. He had also helped Paul “in Ephesus” (1:18). A man who “searched diligently” suggests that Paul was not easy to find in a large city.

Paul writes, “You therefore, my child, be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus. And the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well.” He gives three pictures: “a good soldier of Christ Jesus,” a competitor who “does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules,” and a farmer who “should be the first to partake of the crops.”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. Paul’s line has four links: Paul, Timothy, “faithful men,” and “others as well.” The soldier gives up civilian business to please his commander, the competitor keeps the rules, and the farmer works before he eats. Each picture asks for hard effort that will pay later. Paul uses the soldier and the athlete elsewhere (1 Corinthians 9:7, 9:24-27; Philippians 2:25).

e.n: “The word of God cannot be chained!”
t: Paul writes, “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel, for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained!” He gives a “trustworthy saying”: “If we died with Him, we will also live with Him; if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself.”

The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul’s chains, so the pin stands at Rome. The word for “criminal” (kakourgos) is the same one Luke uses for the two men crucified with Jesus (Luke 23:32-33). Most scholars think the “trustworthy saying” in 2:11-13 is an early hymn or creed that Paul quotes; it is one of five such sayings in the letters to Timothy and Titus (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). The line “If we deny Him, He will also deny us” echoes Jesus’ words in Matthew 10:33.

e.n: The approved workman; Hymenaeus and Philetus
t: Paul writes, “Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth.” The talk of the false teachers “will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some.”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The Greek for “accurately handles” (orthotomeo) literally means to cut straight, as a road is cut or a stone is squared; the word is rare and its first picture is debated. Hymenaeus was already named in 1 Timothy 1:20, where Paul said he had handed him over to Satan. Philetus appears only here. The claim that “the resurrection has already occurred” may mean a spiritual rising in baptism, with no future raising of the body; the letter does not explain it. The quotation “The Lord knows those who are His” (2:19) is close to Numbers 16:5, from the story of Korah’s revolt.

e.n: A large house: vessels for honor
t: Paul writes, “A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay.” He says, “if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a vessel for honor: sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work.” Then he writes, “Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace,” and says the Lord’s servant “must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing.”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. A wealthy Roman household kept fine vessels of silver for the table and plain clay ones for common use; the finds from Boscoreale near Pompeii show how much silver a rich house could hold. Paul uses a clay-pot picture elsewhere (Romans 9:21; 2 Corinthians 4:7). Here the “large house” is likely the church, which holds both honorable and common members. The “snare of the devil” (2:26) is a hunting picture of a trap, and the captives may “come to their senses” and be released.

Paul writes, “But understand this: In the last days terrible times will come. For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy.” The list goes on to people “having a form of godliness but denying its power. Turn away from such as these!”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The list has about eighteen terms, and similar lists appear in Romans 1:29-31 and Galatians 5:19-21. The Bible often calls the whole time since Christ’s first coming “the last days” (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and Paul says this is already the case, since he tells Timothy to turn away from such people now. The first term, “lovers of themselves” (philautoi), opens the list, and “lovers of pleasure” and “lovers of God” balance each other near its end.

Paul writes, “They are the kind who worm their way into households and captivate vulnerable women who are weighed down with sins and led astray by various passions, who are always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth. Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth.” He adds, “they will not advance much further.”

The Old Testament does not name Jannes and Jambres. Exodus 7:11 speaks of the wise men and sorcerers of Pharaoh without naming them. Jewish tradition did name them: the Damascus Document from Qumran mentions Jannes (and his brother) who opposed Moses, the Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus gives both names, and a damaged Greek papyrus of the third century AD preserves part of a “Book of Jannes and Jambres.” The pin at Egypt is a judgment call for the story Paul refers to. The “households” and the women (3:6) fit a picture of teachers who worked in private homes, where the early church met. The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call.

Paul writes, “You, however, have observed my teaching, my conduct, my purpose, my faith, my patience, my love, my perseverance, my persecutions, and the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. What persecutions I endured! Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them. Indeed, all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted.”

These three cities are the places of Paul’s first journey (Acts 13:14-14:23). At Pisidian Antioch Jews drove him out (Acts 13:50), at Iconium a plot to stone him forced him to leave (Acts 14:5-6), and at Lystra he was stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19). Timothy was from that region, so he would have known these stories, even if he did not join Paul until a later visit (Acts 16:1-3). The pin at Lystra stands for all three. The Greek word for “imposters” (goetes) can also mean magician or deceiver.

Paul writes, “But as for you, continue in the things you have learned and firmly believed, since you know from whom you have learned them. From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work.”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. The word “God-breathed” (theopneustos) is found only here in the New Testament. “The Holy Scriptures” Timothy knew from childhood were the Old Testament, which his mother and grandmother would have taught him (1:5); the writings of the apostles were not yet gathered. The line “All Scripture is God-breathed” can also be translated “Every God-breathed Scripture is useful,” and Christians have read the verse both ways. Scripture was kept on scrolls and read aloud in the assembly (1 Timothy 4:13).

Paul writes, “I charge you in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of His appearing and His kingdom: Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction.” He warns that “the time will come when men will not tolerate sound doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires.”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. A charge “in the presence of God” is solemn, formal language. The “itching ears” (knethomenoi) were ears that wanted to be tickled, and the picture is of people who want teachers to tell them what they like to hear. The noun “evangelist” (“do the work of an evangelist”) is rare: it occurs only here, in Acts 21:8 (of Philip) and in Ephesians 4:11.

Paul writes, “For I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing.”

The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul’s chains, so the pin stands at Rome. “Poured out like a drink offering” uses the same verb (spendomai) as Philippians 2:17, and “departure” (analysis) can mean loosening a ship’s ropes or striking a tent, a picture of leaving. The “crown” was a wreath of leaves given to the winner at games such as the Isthmian Games near Corinth (1 Corinthians 9:25). Paul says it will be given by the “righteous Judge,” the opposite of an unjust court. The letter shows Paul in chains in Rome (1:8, 1:16-17, 2:9) and expecting death (4:6-8). If Paul wrote it, the usual view is that this is a second imprisonment after Acts ends, about AD 64-67, and that he was put to death under Nero; the letter itself does not tell us the end. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul’s name. Acts 28:30 describes a first imprisonment in rented lodgings; here the chains are heavier (“like a criminal,” 2:9) and friends have to search for him (1:17).

e.n: Demas, Crescens, Titus, Luke, Mark, Tychicus
t: Paul writes, “Make every effort to come to me quickly, because Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica. Crescens has gone to Galatia, and Titus to Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Get Mark and bring him with you, because he is useful to me in the ministry. Tychicus, however, I have sent to Ephesus.”

The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul’s chains, so the pin stands at Rome. Demas was with Paul in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24; here he has left. Some early manuscripts read “Gaul” for “Galatia.” Dalmatia is on the Adriatic coast in what is now Croatia and Bosnia, near Illyricum (Romans 15:19). Luke is named as a companion in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24. Mark had been the cause of Paul and Barnabas parting (Acts 15:37-39), and Paul now calls him “useful.” Tychicus carried letters in Ephesians 6:21 and Colossians 4:7.
Paul writes, “When you come, bring the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments.”

Troas was the port on the northwest coast of Asia Minor where Paul had visited several times (Acts 16:8-11; 20:5-12; 2 Corinthians 2:12). Carpus is named only here. The Greek word for the “cloak” (phailones) is rare, and some ancient readers took it as a book-case. The “scrolls” were probably papyrus rolls and the “parchments” (membranai) were of animal skin, perhaps notebooks or copies of Scripture; the letter does not say what they held. The request shows Paul in a cold prison, wanting both warmth and something to read.
Paul writes, “Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me. The Lord will repay him according to his deeds. You too should beware of him, for he has vigorously opposed our message.”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. Acts 19:33 names an Alexander at the riot in the Ephesus theater, and 1 Timothy 1:20 names one whom Paul “handed over to Satan”; the letter does not say whether any of these is the same man, since Alexander was a common name. The words “The Lord will repay him according to his deeds” echo Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12, and they leave justice with God and not with Paul or Timothy.

e.n: The first defense: “the Lord stood by me”
t: Paul writes, “At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it. So I was delivered from the mouth of the lion. And the Lord will rescue me from every evil action and bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom.”

The letter names Rome as the place where Onesiphorus found Paul (1:17), and it speaks of Paul’s chains, so the pin stands at Rome. The “first defense” (apologia) seems to be a first hearing before the final verdict. A Roman defendant would normally have a patron or advocate to stand beside him, and none came. “The mouth of the lion” echoes Psalm 22:21 and Daniel 6:20-22; it may be a figure for danger or death, or for Nero, and the letter does not say. Paul says he was rescued yet he still expects to die (4:6), and he trusts the Lord to bring him into His heavenly kingdom. The prayer that it “not be charged against them” is close to Stephen’s in Acts 7:60.

e.n: Final greetings: Prisca, Aquila, Erastus, Trophimus
t: Paul writes, “Greet Prisca and Aquila, as well as the household of Onesiphorus. Erastus has remained at Corinth, and Trophimus I left sick in Miletus. Make every effort to come to me before winter. Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers. The Lord be with your spirit. Grace be with you all.”

The letter does not say where Timothy was, but 1:18 and 4:19 point to Ephesus, and 4:12 says Tychicus was sent there, so the pin stands at Ephesus as a judgment call. Prisca (Priscilla) and Aquila had lived at Corinth, Ephesus and Rome (Acts 18:2, 18:26; Romans 16:3-5); their greeting here is another sign that Timothy is at Ephesus. Erastus may be the city treasurer of Corinth in Romans 16:23. Trophimus was an Ephesian who came with Paul to Jerusalem (Acts 20:4; 21:29), so leaving him ill at Miletus must have happened on a later trip, which is one reason many place this letter after Acts ends. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3.3) names a Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles, but the letter does not say whether this is the same man. “Before winter” matters because sea travel stopped in winter. The letter shows Paul in chains in Rome (1:8, 1:16-17, 2:9) and expecting death (4:6-8). If Paul wrote it, the usual view is that this is a second imprisonment after Acts ends, about AD 64-67, and that he was put to death under Nero; the letter itself does not tell us the end. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul’s name. Acts 28:30 describes a first imprisonment in rented lodgings; here the chains are heavier (“like a criminal,” 2:9) and friends have to search for him (1:17).

Paul writes, “Paul, a servant of God and an apostle of Jesus Christ for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness, in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began.” He greets “Titus, my true child in our common faith: Grace and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Savior.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. The opening is long: four verses before the greeting itself. Paul calls himself “a servant of God,” which he does in no other opening; in Romans 1:1 he is “a servant of Christ Jesus.” The Greek word for “cannot lie” (apseudes) occurs only here in the New Testament, and Paul will soon quote a Cretan saying that Cretans are “always liars” (1:12). The word “Savior” is used three times of God and three times of Christ in this short letter (1:3-4; 2:10, 13; 3:4, 6). Titus does not say where Paul was when he wrote, but 3:12 says he plans to spend the winter at Nicopolis. If Paul wrote the letter, the usual view is that it comes after Acts ends, about AD 62-65, and that Paul and Titus had worked together on Crete (1:5); Acts does not tell that visit. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul’s name. Titus is known from other letters: a Greek who was not compelled to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1-3) and Paul’s trusted envoy to Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:6-7; 8:16-17).

e.n: Left in Crete to set things in order
t: Paul writes, “The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Acts 27:7-13 shows Paul sailing past Crete as a prisoner, but Acts does not say he taught there, so the work behind Titus 1:5 is usually placed after Acts. Cretans were among the listeners at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), and the Jewish writer Philo lists Crete among the places where Jews lived (Embassy to Gaius 282), so a first seed may have come through such travelers. The verb for “set in order” (epidiorthoo) occurs only here in the New Testament. Paul and Barnabas had likewise appointed elders in each church on the first journey (Acts 14:23). The letter says “in every town,” so the churches were probably small groups in many places across the island.

e.n: The elder: blameless, a steward of God
t: Paul writes, “An elder must be blameless, the husband of but one wife, having children who are believers and who are not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination. As God’s steward, an overseer must be above reproach.” He must be “hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined,” and “must hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. “Elder” and “overseer” name the same person here, as in Acts 20:17 and 20:28. The list is close to the one in 1 Timothy 3:1-7, but not identical: Titus has no ban on a recent convert, and it puts the weight on holding to the faithful word and answering opponents. “The husband of but one wife” is debated as it is in 1 Timothy 3:2: it may mean faithful to one wife, no polygamy, or not remarried after a divorce or a wife’s death. The Greek for “believers” in “children who are believers” can also mean “faithful,” and translators differ. A “steward” (oikonomos) managed a household for its owner, and Paul says the overseer manages God’s household.

Paul writes, “For many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision, who must be silenced. For the sake of dishonorable gain, they undermine entire households and teach things they should not.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. “Those of the circumcision” most likely means Jewish believers who pressed circumcision and the law on Gentile believers, as in Acts 11:2, Acts 15:1 and Galatians 2:12. The letter does not spell out what they taught; the clues are “Jewish myths” (1:14), questions about purity (1:15) and “quarrels about the law” (3:9). The Greek for “must be silenced” (epistomizo) is a rare word that means to stop the mouth, as one muzzles an animal. The harm is to “entire households,” and early churches met in homes (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19). Love of “dishonorable gain” is also charged against false teachers in 1 Timothy 6:5.

Paul writes, “As one of their own prophets has said, ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.’ This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith and will pay no attention to Jewish myths or to the commands of men who have rejected the truth.”

The pin stands at Knossos as a judgment call. The letter does not name the poet. Later Christian writers such as Clement of Alexandria and Jerome name Epimenides, a poet and seer traditionally from Knossos and placed by later writers about 600 BC. The first words of the line, “Cretans are always liars,” also open a verse of Callimachus’ Hymn to Zeus (3rd century BC), and Greek writers often joked about Cretan lying. Paul calls the poet “one of their own prophets,” which here means a seer or poet, not an Old Testament prophet. He says the saying is true of the people he has in mind, but the “rebuke” is aimed at the teachers of 1:10-11 and is meant to restore them to “sound” faith. The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there.

e.n: To the pure all things are pure
t: Paul writes, “To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled. They profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him. They are detestable, disobedient, and unfit for any good deed.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. The saying echoes teaching about clean and unclean food: Jesus said that what goes into a person does not defile him (Mark 7:14-23), and Paul wrote that nothing is unclean in itself (Romans 14:14, 20). It is not a claim that anything is allowed. The point is that the rules the teachers press (1:14) cannot cleanse a person whose mind and conscience are defiled, and the proof is how they live. The same contrast between profession and “actions” appears in 2 Timothy 3:5.

e.n: Sound teaching for older men and women
t: Paul writes, “But as for you, speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine. Older men are to be temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance. Older women, likewise, are to be reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good.” They can “train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. The Greek for “sound” (hygiaino) means healthy, the root of our word “hygiene,” and the pastoral letters use it again and again for teaching that is healthy (1 Timothy 1:10; 6:3; 2 Timothy 1:13; Titus 1:9, 13). The word for “teachers of good” (kalodidaskalos) occurs only here. Lists of duties for each group in a household, such as Colossians 3:18-4:1, Ephesians 5:22-6:9 and 1 Peter 2:18-3:7, were common in the ancient world, and Paul gives the reason as the reputation of the gospel: “so that the word of God will not be discredited.” Readers differ on how “submissive to their own husbands” applies today; the same word is used of all believers toward one another in Ephesians 5:21.

e.n: Younger men, and Titus as an example
t: Paul writes, “In the same way, urge the younger men to be self-controlled. In everything, show yourself to be an example by doing good works. In your teaching show integrity, dignity, and wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Younger men get only one request, to be self-controlled, a word that runs through the chapter (2:2, 5, 6, 12). Titus is told to be “an example,” as Timothy is told in 1 Timothy 4:12. The Greek word for “wholesome” (hygies) is the same “healthy” word used for sound teaching. The “opponents” are outsiders, and the aim is that they find nothing bad to say, which echoes the concern for reputation in 2:5 and 2:10.

Paul writes, “Slaves are to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not stealing from them, but showing all good faith, so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Slaves were part of most Roman households. The Greek verb for “stealing” (nosphizomai) means to keep something back for oneself, and it is the verb used in Acts 5:2-3 of Ananias and Sapphira. The word “adorn” (kosmeo) is the word for dressing or decorating, so even a slave’s honest conduct can make the gospel attractive. Paul does not say here whether slavery is right; 1 Timothy 1:10 lists slave traders among the lawless, and Philemon 15-16 asks Philemon to receive Onesimus as a brother. Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 4:1 give duties to masters, which Titus does not.

Paul writes, “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age, as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ. He gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. “Appeared” (epiphaino) and “appearance” (epiphaneia) are words for the arrival of a god or a ruler, and Paul uses the second word for both comings of Christ (2 Timothy 1:10; 4:1, 8). Grace here “instructs” (paideuo), the word for training a child, so grace teaches by discipline as well as by pardon. Most scholars read “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” as one person, so that Jesus is called God; others read two persons, the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. The Greek grammar allows both, and the debate is an old one (compare 2 Peter 1:1). The phrase “a people for His own possession” recalls Exodus 19:5 and Deuteronomy 14:2, and “redeem us from all lawlessness” echoes Psalm 130:8.

e.n: Speak with authority; submit to rulers
t: Paul writes, “Speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority. Let no one despise you.” He continues, “Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Crete was a Roman province, joined with Cyrene as one province, and Rome had taken the island only after a hard war in 69-67 BC, so a reminder about rulers was not empty. Paul gives the same advice in Romans 13:1-7 and 1 Timothy 2:1-2, as does Peter in 1 Peter 2:13-17. “Let no one despise you” is the same line given to Timothy in 1 Timothy 4:12. The aim is again outward: believers are to be “peaceable and gentle” to everyone, so that outsiders see good, not trouble.

e.n: Washed and renewed: the kindness of God appeared
t: Paul writes, “For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures—living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another. But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. The passage names God our Savior, the Holy Spirit and Jesus Christ our Savior, and some scholars think verses 4-7 are an early hymn or baptismal creed that Paul quotes. “His love for mankind” is one word (philanthropia), used of kind rulers in Greek writing and here of God. “Washing of new birth” is often read as baptism (compare Acts 22:16 and Ephesians 5:26), but whether baptism is meant, or only the cleansing work of the Spirit, is debated. The Greek for “new birth” (palingenesia) is used in Matthew 19:28 for the renewal of all things. “Poured out” recalls Joel 2:28-29 and Acts 2:17, 33, and salvation “not by the righteous deeds we had done” matches Ephesians 2:8-9.

e.n: Good deeds, foolish controversies and the divisive man
t: Paul writes, “This saying is trustworthy. And I want you to emphasize these things, so that those who have believed God will take care to devote themselves to good deeds. These things are excellent and profitable for the people. But avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless. Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. “This saying is trustworthy” is one of five such sayings in the letters to Timothy and Titus (1 Timothy 1:15; 3:1; 4:9; 2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8), and scholars debate whether it points back to 3:4-7 or forward to the call to good deeds. The “divisive man” is a hairetikos, the word that gave us “heretic,” but here it means someone who causes factions, and the later sense of a condemned heretic had not yet formed. The “first and second admonition” means two warnings, then he is to be left alone; compare Matthew 18:15-17. “Self-condemned” (autokatakritos) occurs only here, and it says that by refusing correction he has judged himself. The “genealogies” and “quarrels about the law” recall 1:14 and 1 Timothy 1:4.

e.n: Artemas or Tychicus; winter at Nicopolis
t: Paul writes, “As soon as I send Artemas or Tychicus to you, make every effort to come to me at Nicopolis, because I have decided to winter there.”

The pin is a judgment call. Several cities were named Nicopolis (the name means City of Victory), and the letter does not say which one Paul meant. Most scholars think of Nicopolis in Epirus, on the Ionian coast of Greece, which Augustus founded after his victory at Actium in 31 BC. Paul had preached as far as Illyricum (Romans 15:19), which lies north of Epirus, and 2 Timothy 4:10 says Titus later went to Dalmatia, part of Illyricum. Artemas is named only here. Tychicus appears in Acts 20:4, Ephesians 6:21-22, Colossians 4:7-8 and 2 Timothy 4:12. Whichever man came would take over on Crete. Winter is mentioned because sea travel was dangerous in that season, as Acts 27:9-12 shows off the coast of Crete itself. Titus does not say where Paul was when he wrote, but 3:12 says he plans to spend the winter at Nicopolis. If Paul wrote the letter, the usual view is that it comes after Acts ends, about AD 62-65, and that Paul and Titus had worked together on Crete (1:5); Acts does not tell that visit. Some scholars think a later writer used Paul’s name. Titus is known from other letters: a Greek who was not compelled to be circumcised (Galatians 2:1-3) and Paul’s trusted envoy to Corinth (2 Corinthians 7:6-7; 8:16-17).

Paul writes, “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need. And our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful. All who are with me send you greetings. Greet those who love us in the faith. Grace be with all of you.”

The letter places Titus on Crete (1:5), so the pin stands at Crete. It names no town. Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province, but the letter does not say Titus was there. Zenas is named only here. In the rest of the New Testament the word “lawyer” (nomikos) means an expert in the law of Moses (Luke 7:30; 10:25), so he may have been a Jewish believer trained in Scripture, but the letter does not say. Apollos was a Jew from Alexandria who taught at Ephesus and Corinth (Acts 18:24-28; 1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4-6; 16:12). The verb “equip” (propempo) means to send someone on his way with supplies and, often, an escort (Romans 15:24; 1 Corinthians 16:6; 3 John 6). The two men were probably passing through Crete, and some think they carried the letter, but that is a guess. The “pressing needs” are practical needs like these, and Paul wants believers to meet them so that they are not “unfruitful.” The greeting from “all who are with me” does not name anyone.

e.n: Paul and Timothy to Philemon, Apphia, Archippus and the house church
t: Paul writes, “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus, and Timothy our brother, To Philemon our beloved fellow worker, to Apphia our sister, to Archippus our fellow soldier, and to the church that meets at your house: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.”

The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called “one of you” in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. Paul does not call himself an apostle here, as he does in most letters; he calls himself a prisoner, which sets the tone of an appeal. Timothy joins him as sender, as in Colossians 1:1 and Philippians 1:1. “Fellow worker” is the word Paul uses for Titus, Timothy, Mark, Luke and others. Apphia is probably Philemon’s wife and Archippus perhaps his son, but the letter says only “sister” and “fellow soldier,” and Colossians 4:17 tells Archippus to complete the ministry he received. Churches met in houses (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; Colossians 4:15). Verses 4 to 21 say “you” in the singular, while verses 3, 22 and 25 use the plural, so the letter was meant to be read aloud to the whole church.

e.n: Thanks for Philemon’s faith and love
t: Paul writes, “I always thank my God, remembering you in my prayers, because I hear about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints.” He prays that Philemon’s “partnership in the faith may become effective” and says, “I take great joy and encouragement in your love, because you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints.”

The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called “one of you” in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. The thanks follows the pattern of Greek letters, which often began with a prayer or thanks to the gods for the person written to. The word for “partnership” (koinonia) can also mean sharing or fellowship, and it returns in verse 17 when Paul says, “if you consider me a partner.” The Greek word for “hearts” in verse 7 (splagchna) means the inner organs, the seat of feeling; Paul uses it again in verses 12 and 20. Philemon has already shown that he refreshes others, which is what Paul will soon ask him to do for Onesimus and for Paul himself.

e.n: I prefer to appeal on the basis of love
t: Paul writes, “So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, I prefer to appeal on the basis of love. For I, Paul, am now aged, and a prisoner of Christ Jesus as well.”

The letter does not name Paul’s prison. The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter does not say where Paul was. Rome is the traditional answer, with Paul’s two years under guard there about AD 60-62 (Acts 28:30). Paul’s hope to visit Philemon soon (verse 22) fits a prison nearer to Colossae better, so many scholars propose Ephesus (about AD 53-55, though Acts does not mention an imprisonment there) or Caesarea (AD 57-59, Acts 24:27). Colossians 4:7-9 sends Onesimus back with Tychicus, and Colossians 4:10-14 and Philemon 23-24 name nearly the same companions, so the two letters were probably written at the same time. Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, but almost everyone accepts Philemon as his. Paul says he could give an order but will not. The Greek word translated “aged” (presbytes) can also be read as the similar word presbeutes, “ambassador,” and Paul calls himself an ambassador in Ephesians 6:20 and 2 Corinthians 5:20; some scholars prefer that reading, but the manuscripts support “aged.” Paul calls himself a prisoner again, and the weight of his chains is part of the appeal.

Paul writes, “I appeal to you for my child Onesimus, whose father I became while I was in chains. Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me. I am sending back to you him who is my very heart.”

The letter does not name Paul’s prison. The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter does not say where Paul was. Rome is the traditional answer, with Paul’s two years under guard there about AD 60-62 (Acts 28:30). Paul’s hope to visit Philemon soon (verse 22) fits a prison nearer to Colossae better, so many scholars propose Ephesus (about AD 53-55, though Acts does not mention an imprisonment there) or Caesarea (AD 57-59, Acts 24:27). Colossians 4:7-9 sends Onesimus back with Tychicus, and Colossians 4:10-14 and Philemon 23-24 name nearly the same companions, so the two letters were probably written at the same time. Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, but almost everyone accepts Philemon as his. Onesimus is the first name in the request, held back until verse 10. The name means “useful” or “profitable” and was a common name for slaves. Paul plays on it: “useless” (achrestos) and “useful” (euchrestos) are close in sound to “Christ” (Christos), which some scholars think Greek speakers could hear as chrestos, “good.” Paul says he became Onesimus’s “father” in chains, so Onesimus met him in prison and believed there. The usual view is that Onesimus was a slave who had run away. Some scholars suggest he came to Paul as a slave in trouble who sought a friend of his master to speak for him, but the letter does not say how he reached Paul.

e.n: Sent back, not kept: nothing without your consent
t: Paul writes, “I would have liked to keep him with me, so that on your behalf he could minister to me in my chains for the gospel. But I did not want to do anything without your consent, so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will.”

The letter does not name Paul’s prison. The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter does not say where Paul was. Rome is the traditional answer, with Paul’s two years under guard there about AD 60-62 (Acts 28:30). Paul’s hope to visit Philemon soon (verse 22) fits a prison nearer to Colossae better, so many scholars propose Ephesus (about AD 53-55, though Acts does not mention an imprisonment there) or Caesarea (AD 57-59, Acts 24:27). Colossians 4:7-9 sends Onesimus back with Tychicus, and Colossians 4:10-14 and Philemon 23-24 name nearly the same companions, so the two letters were probably written at the same time. Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, but almost everyone accepts Philemon as his. Paul admits that he would have liked to keep Onesimus and says he will not do so without Philemon’s agreement. Under Roman law a slave belonged to his owner, and anyone who kept a runaway could be accused of theft. Paul stays on the right side of that law, yet leaves the real decision with Philemon. The “consent” (gnome) is Philemon’s own judgment, and the word “free will” (hekousion) is the opposite of being forced.

e.n: No longer a slave, but a beloved brother
t: Paul writes, “For perhaps this is why he was separated from you for a while, so that you might have him back for good—no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother. He is especially beloved to me, but even more so to you, both in person and in the Lord.”

The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called “one of you” in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. Paul says “perhaps” and uses a passive verb, “was separated,” which leaves God as the unnamed actor. “For good” translates a word that can mean forever. The letter does not say outright that Philemon should free Onesimus. Readers differ: some think Paul hints at freedom, some think he asks Philemon to accept Onesimus as a brother while he remains a slave, and others think he leaves it open. Paul says Onesimus is a brother “both in person and in the Lord,” which means both as a person in the household and as a believer.

e.n: Receive him as you would receive me
t: Paul writes, “So if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me. But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it—not to mention that you owe me your very self.”

The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called “one of you” in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. The language is that of business. “Charge it to my account” (ellogeo) is a ledger term. Paul writes the promise in his own hand, which made it a signed note; he usually dictated and then added a closing line himself (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18). “You owe me your very self” suggests that Paul had a part in Philemon’s own conversion, but the letter does not say where. Paul had not visited Colossae (Colossians 2:1). If Philemon met Paul at Ephesus, as some suggest, he would have been one of the many who heard the word there (Acts 19:10). Paul does not say what Onesimus had done wrong or owed, and “wronged” and “owes” are both stated as an “if.”

e.n: Refresh my heart: you will do even more
t: Paul writes, “Yes, brother, let me have some benefit from you in the Lord. Refresh my heart in Christ. Confident of your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I ask.”

The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called “one of you” in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. “Let me have some benefit” is the verb oninemi, from the same root as the name Onesimus, so Paul puns once more. “Refresh my heart” repeats the words of verse 7, where Philemon is said to have refreshed the hearts of the saints. “Even more than I ask” has led some readers to think Paul hopes for Onesimus’s freedom, while others think he means a warmer welcome than Philemon might have thought of. The letter does not say.

e.n: Prepare a guest room for me
t: Paul writes, “In the meantime, prepare a guest room for me, because I hope that through your prayers I will be restored to you.”

The pin stands at Colossae, where Philemon most likely lived. The letter itself does not name the town. Onesimus is called “one of you” in Colossians 4:9, and Archippus, who is greeted in verse 2, is greeted in Colossians 4:17 as well. Paul expects to be set free and to visit. The word “guest room” (xenia) means lodging for a guest. Paul tells the Philippians of a similar hope (Philippians 2:24), and in Romans 15:23-24 he looks toward Spain from Rome, so which hope applies depends on where he was imprisoned. A visit to Colossae would be a good fit if he were in Ephesus or Caesarea, and a harder one if he were in Rome. The “your” in “your prayers” is plural, so he is also speaking to the church.

e.n: Epaphras, Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke send greetings
t: Paul writes, “Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers. The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.”

The letter does not name Paul’s prison. The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter does not say where Paul was. Rome is the traditional answer, with Paul’s two years under guard there about AD 60-62 (Acts 28:30). Paul’s hope to visit Philemon soon (verse 22) fits a prison nearer to Colossae better, so many scholars propose Ephesus (about AD 53-55, though Acts does not mention an imprisonment there) or Caesarea (AD 57-59, Acts 24:27). Colossians 4:7-9 sends Onesimus back with Tychicus, and Colossians 4:10-14 and Philemon 23-24 name nearly the same companions, so the two letters were probably written at the same time. Some scholars doubt that Paul wrote Colossians, but almost everyone accepts Philemon as his. Epaphras is from Colossae (Colossians 4:12) and brought the report of the church to Paul (Colossians 1:7-8). Here he is called Paul’s “fellow prisoner”; in Colossians 4:10 that word is used for Aristarchus. Mark is the John Mark of Acts 12:12 and 15:37-39, who had left Paul on the first journey. Demas later left Paul (2 Timothy 4:10). Luke is Paul’s companion in the “we” sections of Acts. The last word of the letter, “your spirit,” is plural in Greek, so the whole church is blessed.

e.n: God has spoken to us by his Son
t: The writer says, “On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, whom He appointed heir of all things, and through whom He made the universe. The Son is the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature, upholding all things by His powerful word. After He had provided purification for sins, He sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high.”

The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer. It ends with “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The opening is one long Greek sentence. It sets the Son beside the prophets, who spoke “in many different ways,” and calls him heir of all things, the one through whom the universe was made, and the one who sits at the right hand after purifying sins. The letter does not open with a name or a greeting, unlike the letters of Paul, and it ends like a letter, so many call it a sermon with a letter’s ending.

e.n: The Son is greater than the angels
t: The writer says, “For to which of the angels did God ever say: “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father”? Or again: “I will be His Father, and He will be My Son”? And again, when God brings His firstborn into the world, He says: “Let all God’s angels worship Him.””

The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer. It ends with “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The writer strings together quotations from the Psalms, 2 Samuel and Deuteronomy to show that the Son is called Son in a way angels never are. The quotations follow the Greek Old Testament, which differs in some words from the Hebrew text, and the Dead Sea Scrolls show that Jews of the time thought a good deal about angels.

e.n: Pay closer attention: do not drift away
t: The writer says, “We must pay closer attention, therefore, to what we have heard, so that we do not drift away. For if the message spoken by angels was binding, and every transgression and disobedience received its just punishment, how shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation? This salvation was first announced by the Lord, was confirmed to us by those who heard Him,”

The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer. It ends with “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). This is the first of five warnings (2:1-4; 3:7-4:13; 5:11-6:12; 10:26-39; 12:25-29). The argument runs from lesser to greater: if the message spoken through angels (the law) had force, how much more the one spoken by the Lord. Jewish tradition said that angels were present when the law was given (Deuteronomy 33:2 in the Greek; Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19).

e.n: Made like us: crowned with glory through suffering
t: The writer says, “Now since the children have flesh and blood, He too shared in their humanity, so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death.”

The pin stands at Jerusalem, where the Gospels place Jesus’ suffering and death, though this passage names no place. The writer quotes Psalm 8 and says Jesus shared “flesh and blood” in order to free those held in slavery by the fear of death. Verse 17 introduces the word “high priest” for the first time, and the idea comes back in 4:14-5:10 and chapters 7-10.

e.n: Greater than Moses; Today, if you hear his voice
t: The writer says, “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts, as you did in the rebellion, in the day of testing in the wilderness,”

The pin stands at Kadesh-barnea, the oasis in the Negev where Israel refused to enter the land (Numbers 13-14), which is the best-known candidate for the rebellion the writer quotes from Psalm 95. The letter itself does not name the place. The identification of Kadesh with Ain el-Qudeirat is widely accepted but not certain. Moses is faithful as a servant in God’s house, the Son as the builder and the Son over the house (3:5-6). The “rest” the people failed to enter (3:11, 18; 4:1-11) is the central image of this section.

e.n: A great high priest who sympathizes
t: The writer says, “During the days of Jesus’ earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence. Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered.”

The pin stands at Gethsemane, the place the Gospels give for Jesus’ prayer with “loud cries and tears.” The letter does not name the garden, and the words may also gather up other moments of his prayer. Hebrews says the high priest must be taken from among men, must be called by God as Aaron was, and can “deal gently” with the ignorant because he is himself subject to weakness. The same verse (5:6) quotes Psalm 110:4 and calls Jesus a priest “in the order of Melchizedek.”

e.n: Press on to maturity: the anchor of the soul
t: The writer says, “We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.”

The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer. It ends with “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The section begins with a rebuke that the readers need milk and not solid food, and moves through the hardest passage in the letter (6:4-8) to the promise God made to Abraham with an oath (6:13-18). Readers differ widely on whether 6:4-6 describes believers who lose their salvation or people who only seemed to share in it; the letter itself says it is “convinced of better things” for its readers (6:9). The “anchor” is a harbor image; Hebrews 6:19 is the only place in the New Testament that uses an anchor as a picture of hope.

e.n: Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God Most High
t: The writer says, “This Melchizedek was king of Salem and priest of God Most High. He met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him, and Abraham apportioned to him a tenth of everything. First, his name means “king of righteousness.” Then also, “king of Salem” means “king of peace.” Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time.”

The pin stands at Jerusalem, which Psalm 76:2 and many readers identify with Salem; Genesis 14 does not say where Salem was. The writer draws on only two Old Testament passages, Genesis 14:17-20 and Psalm 110:4. The Dead Sea Scrolls (11Q13) also treat Melchizedek as a heavenly figure, but the writer of Hebrews calls him “like the Son of God” and not the same as him. Jesus is of Judah, not Levi, so the priesthood must change (7:11-14); the writer says the “order of Melchizedek” comes with an oath and lasts forever.

e.n: A better covenant: God will write his laws on their hearts
t: The writer says, “For this is the covenant I will make with the house of Israel after those days, declares the Lord. I will put My laws in their minds and inscribe them on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they will be My people.”

The pin stands at the Jerusalem Temple, which the letter does not name. The writer argues from the tabernacle of Moses and from the Scripture, not from the Temple of his own day, and scholars differ on whether the Temple was still standing when the letter was written. One of the longest Old Testament quotations in the New Testament (Jeremiah 31:31-34) is placed here. The writer says that the first covenant is “obsolete” and will “soon disappear” (8:13). Some scholars take that to mean the Temple still stood when the letter was written, and some think it was written after AD 70; the verses do not date the letter.

e.n: The earthly tabernacle and the Day of Atonement
t: The writer says, “When everything had been prepared in this way, the priests entered regularly into the first room to perform their sacred duties. But only the high priest entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood, which he offered for himself and for the sins the people had committed in ignorance.”

The pin stands at the Jerusalem Temple, which the letter does not name. The writer argues from the tabernacle of Moses and from the Scripture, not from the Temple of his own day, and scholars differ on whether the Temple was still standing when the letter was written. The writer describes the tent of Moses with a first room, the Holy Place, and an inner room, the Holy of Holies, entered only by the high priest once a year with blood (Leviticus 16). He lists the contents of the inner room in 9:4. Leviticus 16 and Exodus 25-30 do not say that the golden altar of incense stood in the inner room, and scholars discuss how verse 4 should be read.

e.n: Christ enters the heavenly sanctuary by his own blood
t: The writer says, “But when Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come, He went through the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands and is not a part of this creation. He did not enter by the blood of goats and calves, but He entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption.”

The pin stands at the traditional site of the crucifixion, though the passage speaks of a heavenly sanctuary and does not name Golgotha. The writer contrasts the blood of goats and bulls with the blood of Christ and says that “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (9:22). Verse 16 uses the word diatheke, which can mean both “covenant” and “will,” and the writer plays on both senses.

The writer says, “Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins. But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God.”

The pin stands at the Jerusalem Temple, which the letter does not name. The writer argues from the tabernacle of Moses and from the Scripture, not from the Temple of his own day, and scholars differ on whether the Temple was still standing when the letter was written. The priests stand daily and offer the same sacrifices, but Christ “sat down.” The writer says the law is a “shadow” of the good things to come, and he quotes Psalm 40 with the Greek reading “a body You prepared for Me,” which differs from the Hebrew, where the speaker says his ears were opened or dug out.

e.n: Draw near with a true heart; do not throw away your confidence
t: The writer says, “Remember the early days that you were in the light. In those days, you endured a great conflict in the face of suffering.
