Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution; at other times you were partners with those who were so treated. You sympathized with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property, knowing that you yourselves had a better and permanent possession.”

The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer. It ends with “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The writer recalls an earlier time when the readers were publicly exposed to abuse and sometimes shared the plight of others, and when they helped prisoners and accepted the loss of their goods. Some scholars connect this with the troubles of Jewish Christians in Rome about AD 49 under Claudius, others with other places and times. The letter does not say.

e.n: Faith defined: Abel, Enoch and Noah
t: The writer says, “Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see. This is why the ancients were commended. By faith we understand that the universe was formed at God’s command, so that what is seen was not made out of what was visible.”

The pin stands in the mountains of Ararat, where Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest, as a general marker; the passage names no place and tells of Abel, Enoch and Noah. The chapter opens with the nearest thing in the Bible to a definition of faith. It then names heroes one at a time, and the words “By faith” begin most of the sentences that follow. The list is told from Genesis, the Law and the histories.

e.n: Abraham and Sarah: strangers in tents, looking for a city
t: The writer says, “By faith Abraham, when called to go to a place he would later receive as his inheritance, obeyed and went, without knowing where he was going. By faith he dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob, who were heirs with him of the same promise. For he was looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God.”

The pin stands at Mamre near Hebron, where Genesis 13:18 and 18:1 place Abraham’s tents, though the passage speaks of him living “in tents” in the land generally. The writer says he went out “without knowing where he was going,” lived as a stranger, and looked forward to a city with foundations, “whose architect and builder is God.” Sarah is named as one who received power to conceive, and the offering of Isaac (verses 17-19) is told from Genesis 22.

e.n: By faith Moses, the Red Sea, Jericho and Rahab
t: The writer says, “By faith the walls of Jericho fell, after the people had marched around them for seven days. By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient.”

The pin stands at Jericho, where the walls fell and Rahab was spared, though the passage also tells of Moses’ parents in Egypt, the Passover and the crossing of the Red Sea. The writer says Moses chose “to suffer oppression with God’s people” and valued “disgrace for Christ” above the treasures of Egypt (11:25-26). Jericho’s walls and the date of their fall are debated by archaeologists.

e.n: The faithful who suffered: a list of names and nameless
t: The writer says, “Women received back their dead, raised to life again. Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection. Still others endured mocking and flogging, and even chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawed in two, they were put to death by the sword. They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated. The world was not worthy of them. They wandered in deserts and mountains, and hid in caves and holes in the ground.”

The pin stands at Jerusalem as a general marker; the passage names six judges and prophets (Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel) and then moves to unnamed people, some of whom were tortured, stoned or “sawed in two.” Verse 35 (“women received back their dead” and others were tortured) fits the story of the mother and her seven sons in 2 Maccabees 6-7, though the letter does not name them. The tradition that Isaiah was sawn in two comes from a later Jewish text, the Martyrdom of Isaiah. The chapter ends by saying that they did not receive what was promised, so that “together with us” they might be made perfect.

e.n: A great cloud of witnesses: run with endurance
t: The writer says, “Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us. Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.”

The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer. It ends with “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The race image would be familiar from the games at Isthmia, Corinth and elsewhere, and the writer speaks of throwing off “every encumbrance.” The “cloud of witnesses” are the people of chapter 11, seen as those who have already run and now look on, though the writer does not say that they can see the readers. Jesus is the “author and perfecter” of faith and endured the cross, “scorning its shame.”

e.n: The Lord disciplines the son he loves
t: The writer says, “And you have forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons: “My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives.””

The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer. It ends with “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The writer quotes Proverbs 3:11-12 as words addressed to his readers as sons. In a Greek and Roman household a father trained and corrected his sons, and the writer uses that picture, saying that discipline is painful at the time and yields “a harvest of righteousness and peace” later. He adds that “you have not yet resisted to the point of shedding your blood” (12:4).

e.n: Not Mount Sinai but Mount Zion
t: The writer says, “Instead, you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. You have come to myriads of angels in joyful assembly, to the congregation of the firstborn, enrolled in heaven. You have come to God the Judge of all, to the spirits of the righteous made perfect, to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, and to the sprinkled blood that speaks a better word than the blood of Abel.”

The pin stands at Mount Zion in Jerusalem, though the writer means the heavenly Zion, the city of the living God. Verses 18-21 recall Mount Sinai, with fire, darkness, a trumpet and a voice so frightening that the people begged it to stop; the traditional Sinai (Jebel Musa) is only one of several proposed. The writer sets the “sprinkled blood” of Jesus above the blood of Abel, and calls for gratitude since “we are receiving an unshakable kingdom.” Esau (12:16-17) is held up as a warning.

e.n: Let brotherly love continue: hospitality, prisoners, marriage, money
t: The writer says, “Continue in brotherly love. Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it.”

The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer. It ends with “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The last chapter turns to daily life. Inns of the Roman world were rough and often unsafe, so travelers, including traveling Christian teachers, depended on private homes, which makes hospitality a matter of real need. The saying that some “have entertained angels” echoes Abraham and Sarah at Mamre (Genesis 18) and perhaps Lot (Genesis 19).

e.n: Outside the camp: Jesus suffered outside the gate
t: The writer says, “And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood. Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore.”

The pin stands at the traditional site of the crucifixion, which the Gospels place outside the city (John 19:20). The writer says Jesus suffered “outside the city gate” to make the people holy through his own blood, as the bodies of the sin offering were burned outside the camp (Leviticus 16:27), and asks the readers to go to him “outside the camp.” Verse 15 offers “a sacrifice of praise” in place of animal sacrifice, and verse 17 asks the readers to obey their leaders.

e.n: Timothy is free; greetings from Italy
t: The writer says, “Be aware that our brother Timothy has been released. If he arrives soon, I will come with him to see you. Greet all your leaders and all the saints. Those from Italy send you greetings.”

The pin stands at Rome as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer. It ends with “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24), which can mean that the writer was in Italy and sent greetings home, or that Italians were with the writer away from Italy. The first readers are called Hebrews in the title, but that title was added later; the text says they were tested, had endured abuse and had once helped prisoners (10:32-34). The writer asks for prayer, hopes to be restored to the readers soon, and says that “our brother Timothy” has been released. This is likely Paul’s coworker, though the letter does not give his name more fully, and nothing else says when he was imprisoned. The closing blessing and personal notes lead many to think of Paul, but the writing style, the use of the Greek Old Testament and the absence of the writer’s name make the authorship an old question; Eusebius reports Origen as saying that only God knows who wrote it.

e.n: James greets the twelve tribes in the Dispersion
t: James writes, “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion: Greetings.”

The pin stands at Jerusalem, where the Book of Acts and Paul’s letter to the Galatians place James, the brother of the Lord, as a leader of the church (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9). The letter itself does not say where it was written. The writer calls himself “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” and does not say he is the Lord’s brother. The tradition that he is James the brother of Jesus is old and widely held; others have suggested a different James or a letter written in his name after his death. The Jewish historian Josephus tells of the stoning of James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, at the order of the high priest Ananus, about AD 62, so a letter from him would have to be earlier. The greeting uses the plain Greek word chairein, “Greetings,” which Paul does not use in his letter openings but which opens the letters quoted in Acts 15:23 and 23:26.

e.n: Consider it pure joy when you meet trials
t: James writes, “Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith develops perseverance. Allow perseverance to finish its work, so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. The Greek word for “trials” (peirasmos) means both an outside test and an inner temptation, and James uses it both ways in this chapter (1:2, 12-14). The call to be glad in testing has parallels in Jesus’ words in Matthew 5:11-12 and in Paul’s and Peter’s letters (Romans 5:3-4; 1 Peter 1:6-7). “Perseverance” (hypomone) is staying power under pressure, not a passive waiting.

e.n: Ask God for wisdom; the double-minded person
t: James writes, “Now if any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him. But he must ask in faith, without doubting, because he who doubts is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. Wisdom is the main theme of Israel’s wisdom books, and the story of Solomon asking for it is in 1 Kings 3. “Double-minded” translates dipsychos, literally two-souled. The word is not found in earlier Greek writing that survives, so James may have coined it or taken it from Jewish teaching; it returns in 4:8 and later fills the Shepherd of Hermas, a Christian writing of the 2nd century.

e.n: The lowly and the rich: the flower in the heat
t: James writes, “The brother in humble circumstances should exult in his high position. But the one who is rich should exult in his low position, because he will pass away like a flower of the field. For the sun rises with scorching heat and withers the plant; its flower falls and its beauty is lost. So too, the rich man will fade away in the midst of his pursuits.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. The picture of a plant withered by the sun is drawn from Isaiah 40:6-8 and Psalm 103:15-16. The Greek word for the “scorching heat” can mean the hot east wind of the land of Israel, which in summer can dry up the plants in a day. The same contrast between the poor who are lifted up and the rich who are brought down runs through the letter (2:5-6; 5:1-6) and echoes Mary’s song in Luke 1:52-53.

e.n: God tempts no one; every good gift is from above
t: James writes, “When tempted, no one should say, “God is tempting me.” For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone. But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed. Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. The “crown of life” is the victor’s wreath of the games (compare 1 Corinthians 9:25; Revelation 2:10). Verse 17 calls God “the Father of the heavenly lights,” probably a reference to the sun, moon and stars he made (Genesis 1:14-18; Psalm 136:7), with whom there is no change as there is in the sky from day to night. The last words of the verse are hard to translate and the manuscripts differ, so English versions vary. “A kind of firstfruits” borrows from Israel’s offering of the first of the harvest.

e.n: Quick to listen; be doers of the word; pure religion
t: James writes, “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves. For anyone who hears the word but does not carry it out is like a man who looks at his face in a mirror, and after observing himself goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like. But the one who looks intently into the perfect law of freedom, and continues to do so—not being a forgetful hearer, but an effective doer—he will be blessed in what he does.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. The mirror of the first century was a disk of polished metal, usually bronze, that gave a darker and less exact image than a modern mirror. “Religion” (threskeia) means outward worship, and James gives it a new content: caring for orphans and widows, the people the Law of Moses names again and again (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17-21). The “perfect law of freedom” (1:25; 2:12) may refer to the Law as Jesus taught it, but the letter does not define it.

e.n: Do not show favoritism: the gold ring in the assembly
t: James writes, “Suppose a man comes into your meeting wearing a gold ring and fine clothes, and a poor man in shabby clothes also comes in. If you lavish attention on the man in fine clothes and say, “Here is a seat of honor,” but say to the poor man, “You must stand” or “Sit at my feet,” have you not discriminated among yourselves and become judges with evil thoughts?”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. The Greek word for “your meeting” in 2:2 is synagoge, which can mean a gathering as well as a building. A gold ring was a mark of rank in the Roman world, and fine clothing a sign of wealth; a seat of honor at a banquet or assembly told everyone who stood where. James reminds his readers that it is the rich who drag them into court (2:6), and calls Leviticus 19:18, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” the “royal law” (2:8).

e.n: Faith without works: clothes and daily food
t: James writes, “What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him? Suppose a brother or sister is without clothes and daily food. If one of you tells him, “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed,” but does not provide for his physical needs, what good is that? So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. This is the passage that makes people compare James with Paul. Paul writes that “a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 2:16), and James writes that “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (2:24). Many readers hold that the two are answering different problems: Paul argues against requiring the works of the Law, such as circumcision, for acceptance with God, while James argues against a claim to faith that has no deeds of mercy. Martin Luther, in his preface to the New Testament of 1522, called James a letter of straw in comparison with John, Romans and 1 Peter, a verdict he did not repeat in later editions. In 2:19 even the demons “believe” and “shudder”; the Greek for “God is one” echoes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4.

e.n: Abraham offered Isaac: faith made complete by what he did
t: James writes, “Was not our father Abraham justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar? You see that his faith was working with his actions, and his faith was perfected by what he did. And the Scripture was fulfilled that says, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and he was called a friend of God.”

The pin stands on the Temple Mount, the place 2 Chronicles 3:1 names Mount Moriah; Genesis 22:2 says only that the place was in the region of Moriah, and the letter names no place. James and Paul both appeal to the same words about Abraham, “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (Romans 4:3), but Paul uses them to show that Abraham was accepted before he did anything, and James uses them to show the faith that was shown in what Abraham did. The phrase “friend of God” comes from Isaiah 41:8 and 2 Chronicles 20:7. The “justified” word in Greek (dikaioo) can mean “declared righteous” and also shown to be righteous, and which sense James has in view is part of the debate.

e.n: Rahab was justified by her actions
t: James writes, “In the same way, was not even Rahab the prostitute justified by her actions when she welcomed the spies and sent them off on another route? As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without deeds is dead.”

The pin stands at Jericho, where Joshua 2 puts the story of Rahab and the spies. James places Rahab, a foreign woman, after Abraham, the father of the nation, as a second example. Hebrews 11:31 also names her, and Matthew 1:5 lists her in the genealogy of Jesus. The “spirit” in 2:26 is the Greek pneuma, which also means breath, so the line can also be read as a body without breath being dead. The date of the fall of Jericho and the state of the city then are debated by archaeologists.

e.n: The tongue: bits, rudders and a spark
t: James writes, “In the same way, the tongue is a small part of the body, but it boasts of great things. Consider how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze. The tongue also is a fire, a world of wickedness among the parts of the body. It pollutes the whole person, sets the course of his life on fire, and is itself set on fire by hell.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. James begins with teachers, who “will be judged more strictly” (3:1), and moves to three pictures of small things that control large ones: a bit in a horse’s mouth, a rudder on a ship, and a spark in a forest. Verse 6 uses the word “hell” (Greek geenna, Gehenna), a word that appears elsewhere in the New Testament only in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke. The phrase rendered “sets the course of his life on fire” is literally a wheel of becoming in Greek, an expression whose exact sense is not agreed. Jewish wisdom writing, such as Sirach 28, also describes the harm of the tongue.

e.n: Two wisdoms: from below and from above
t: James writes, “But the wisdom from above is first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere. Peacemakers who sow in peace reap the fruit of righteousness.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. The question “Who is wise and understanding among you?” is the language of Israel’s wisdom teachers. James describes wisdom by its fruit and not by its learning. The wisdom “from above” echoes the request for wisdom in 1:5, and “peacemakers” echoes the beatitude of Jesus (Matthew 5:9). The jealousy and selfish ambition he names are what he says produce the quarrels of the next chapter.

e.n: Passions at war: submit to God, resist the devil
t: James writes, “Submit yourselves, then, to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and He will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. “You adulteresses” (4:4) uses the image of God’s people as his unfaithful bride, which runs through Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel. The saying about the Spirit that “yearns with envy” (4:5) is hard to translate, and it is not clear which Scripture James has in mind. The quotation “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” is from Proverbs 3:34, as in the Greek Old Testament, and 1 Peter 5:5 quotes it too. The commands that follow, to cleanse hands and purify hearts, borrow the language of the priests.

e.n: Do not slander one another: one Lawgiver and Judge
t: James writes, “Brothers, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against his brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it. And if you judge the law, you are not a practitioner of the law, but a judge of it. There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. In the Law, slander and grudges are placed beside the command to love one’s neighbor (Leviticus 19:16-18), which is why James says that a person who speaks against a brother “speaks against the law.” Jesus’ words in Matthew 7:1 are the nearest parallel. The “one Lawgiver and Judge” is God.

e.n: Today or tomorrow: you are a mist
t: James writes, “Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.” You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes. Instead, you ought to say, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that.””

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. James has in mind traders who plan a year in one city and a profit from it. Jews lived in trading cities all around the Mediterranean, and merchants moving from city to city were a feature of the Roman world. The “mist” echoes Psalm 144:4 and Proverbs 27:1. Verse 17, “Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin,” is often quoted by itself; in context it follows the warning against boasting.

e.n: A warning to the rich: wages that cry out
t: James writes, “Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you. Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes. Your gold and silver are corroded. Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire. You have hoarded treasure in the last days. Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. Wealth in the ancient world was stored as grain, clothes, gold and silver, and James says each has spoiled. He says the gold and silver are “corroded”; gold does not rust, so the word is generally taken as a figure of speech. The Law of Moses forbids holding back a hired worker’s pay overnight (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15). The “Lord of Hosts” is the Greek transliteration of the Hebrew Sabaoth, as in Romans 9:29. Verse 6 speaks of “the righteous” who “did not resist you”; it may mean the poor in general, or the Righteous One, that is, Jesus, and the letter does not say.

e.n: Be patient until the Lord comes; do not swear
t: James writes, “Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains. You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. The “fall and spring rains” are the early rain of autumn and the late rain of spring on which the farmers of the land of Israel depended (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24). “The Lord’s coming” is the Greek parousia, a word used for the arrival of a king. The prophets and Job are the two examples of endurance. Verse 12, about letting a yes be yes and a no be no, is very close to Jesus’ words in Matthew 5:37, and James gives it without saying where it comes from.

e.n: The prayer of faith; Elijah prayed for rain
t: James writes, “Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven. Therefore confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail.”

The pin stands at Mount Carmel, where 1 Kings 18 tells of Elijah’s contest with the prophets of Baal and his prayer for rain; the traditional site is Muhraqa on the southeastern end of the ridge. The letter itself names no place. The three and a half years of drought are in Luke 4:25 as well, while 1 Kings 18:1 says the rain came in the third year. Readers differ about the anointing with oil in 5:14: oil was used as medicine (Luke 10:34), the disciples anointed the sick in Mark 6:13, and some traditions treat this passage as the basis for a sacrament of anointing for the sick, while others read it as a sign of prayer for healing. The letter says that the elders are to pray “in the name of the Lord.”

e.n: Bring back the one who wanders
t: James writes, “My brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back, consider this: Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins.”

The pin stands at Antioch in Syria as a judgment call. The letter names neither its readers’ town nor its writer’s. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion,” which most readers take to mean Jewish believers living outside the land (the word is also used of believers in 1 Peter 1:1). Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and Acts 15:23 gives the same Greek greeting to a letter sent to believers in Antioch, Syria and Cilicia. That fits but does not prove the setting; other proposals range from Judea to Asia Minor and Rome. The letter ends here without a closing greeting or farewell, unlike most letters of the New Testament. “A multitude of sins” echoes Proverbs 10:12, which 1 Peter 4:8 also borrows. Whether the “soul” saved from death in 5:20 is the wanderer’s or the one who turns him back, and whether “death” means bodily or final death, are matters on which readers differ.

e.n: Peter writes to the exiles of the Dispersion
t: Peter writes, “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, chosen according to the foreknowledge of God the Father and sanctified by the Spirit for obedience to Jesus Christ and sprinkling by His blood: Grace and peace be yours in abundance.”

The pin stands at Rome, a judgment call. The letter says it was sent from “Babylon” (5:13). Early Christian writers took Babylon to mean Rome, and Eusebius reports that Papias and Clement of Alexandria said the letter was written there. Others have proposed the old city of Babylon on the Euphrates or the fortress town of Babylon in Egypt. The letter does not say. The writer calls himself “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ,” the name Jesus gave to Simon son of John, a fisherman of Bethsaida and Capernaum (John 1:42, 44; Matthew 16:18). Tradition says he died at Rome under the emperor Nero; Clement of Rome, writing about AD 96, says Peter suffered many hardships and then went to his place of glory (1 Clement 5). The letter gives its readers a name used by the Jews who lived outside the land, “exiles of the Dispersion,” but it uses the name for believers, and later calls them “foreigners” (2:11). Whether they were mostly Jewish or mostly Gentile is debated. The letter speaks of their “former ignorance” (1:14) and “the same desires as the Gentiles” (4:3), which fits Gentile converts, and also quotes the Old Testament a great deal. The opening has the three persons of the Trinity: the Father who foreknew, the Spirit who sanctifies, and Jesus Christ whose blood was sprinkled, language from the sealing of the covenant in Exodus 24:6-8.

e.n: A living hope: new birth and an inheritance that cannot fade
t: Peter writes, “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you,”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. “Born again” (anagennao) is used in the New Testament only here and in 1:23. The inheritance is described by three Greek words that all begin with the letter a, which in Greek means not (aphthartos, amiantos, amarantos): it cannot decay, be stained or fade. The Old Testament inheritance was the land (Deuteronomy 12:9-10; Joshua 1:15); Peter says the readers’ inheritance is kept in heaven and they are kept for it by the power of God. The word “shielded” (phroureo) is a military word for a garrison guarding a city.

e.n: More precious than gold: rejoicing in many trials
t: Peter writes, “In this you greatly rejoice, though now for a little while you may have had to suffer grief in various trials so that the proven character of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire—may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. “Various trials” translates the same two Greek words (poikilois peirasmois) that open the letter of James (James 1:2). Refining gold in a furnace to burn off the impurities is the picture in Proverbs 17:3, Zechariah 13:9 and Malachi 3:3. The letter does not say what the trials were. They seem to be insults and social pressure more than official punishment (2:12; 3:16; 4:4). Verse 8 speaks to people who had not seen Jesus, which fits readers far from Palestine, in a letter from an apostle who had.

e.n: The prophets searched; angels long to look
t: Peter writes, “Concerning this salvation, the prophets who foretold the grace to come to you searched and investigated carefully, trying to determine the time and setting to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing when He predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow. It was revealed to them that they were not serving themselves, but you, when they foretold the things now announced by those who preached the gospel to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven. Even angels long to look into these things.”

The pin stands at Jerusalem, where most of the prophets whose words Peter has in mind spoke. The letter does not name a place. The Greek for “searched and investigated” (exereunao and eraunao) is the language of careful study. “Even angels long to look” uses a verb (parakypto) meaning to stoop and peer in; it is the word for John looking into the empty tomb (John 20:5, 11) and for the man who looks into the mirror of the law in James 1:25. Peter’s point is that the prophets and the angels were looking for what the readers now hear: the sufferings of the Christ and the glories that follow (compare Isaiah 52:13-53:12; Luke 24:25-27).

e.n: Be holy: redeemed with the blood of a lamb
t: Peter writes, “For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. “Prepare your minds for action” is literally gird up the loins of your mind, the picture of tucking up a long robe to run or work (Exodus 12:11; Luke 12:35). “Be holy, because I am holy” is quoted from Leviticus, where it comes four times (11:44-45; 19:2; 20:7, 26). “Redeemed” is ransom language: a price paid to free a slave or a prisoner (Exodus 21:30; Isaiah 52:3). The “lamb without blemish or spot” recalls the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:5) and the suffering servant who is led like a lamb (Isaiah 53:7). The phrase “the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers” (patroparadotos) may point to Gentile readers, since a Jewish writer would hardly call Israel’s ancestral religion empty, though some take it as a comment on any inherited way of life.

e.n: Born again through the living word
t: Peter writes, “Since you have purified your souls by obedience to the truth so that you have a genuine love for your brothers, love one another deeply, from a pure heart. For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God. For, “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord stands forever.” And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. The quotation in 1:24-25 is from Isaiah 40:6-8, where the prophet comforts the exiles in Babylon with the promise that the word of God outlasts everything. Peter’s point is that this word is the gospel that was proclaimed to the readers. The letter of James uses the same picture of grass and flowers withered by the sun for the rich (James 1:10-11). The Greek word for brotherly love, philadelphia, is used in the New Testament of the love among believers (Romans 12:10; Hebrews 13:1).

e.n: Pure spiritual milk and the living stone
t: Peter writes, “As you come to Him, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ. For it stands in Scripture: “See, I lay in Zion a stone, a chosen and precious cornerstone; and the one who believes in Him will never be put to shame.””

The pin stands at Jerusalem, where Isaiah 28:16 puts the stone: “I lay in Zion a stone.” The letter does not name a place. Peter strings together three stone texts: Isaiah 28:16, Psalm 118:22 and Isaiah 8:14. Jesus himself quoted Psalm 118:22 against the leaders in Jerusalem (Mark 12:10-11), and Peter had used the same verse before the council in Acts 4:11. The picture of a stone laid as the first stone of a building fits the way a Herodian builder set the corner stones of the Temple. “Tasted that the Lord is good” is from Psalm 34:8 (the same psalm Peter quotes in 3:10-12). The “pure spiritual milk” (logikon adolon gala) is a milk of the word, and the babies of 2:2 are those just born again (1:23).

e.n: A chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation
t: Peter writes, “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.”

The pin stands at the traditional Mount Sinai (Jebel Musa) as a judgment call; the location of Sinai is debated and the letter names no place. The titles come from Exodus 19:5-6, where God tells Israel at Sinai that they will be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, and from Isaiah 43:20-21, where God calls Israel his chosen people who will declare his praise. “Once you were not a people” is from Hosea 1:9-10 and 2:23, where God says to those called Not My People, You are my people. Peter gives all four titles to the church. In the Old Testament the whole people were called to be priests, though only the family of Aaron served at the altar; Peter says every believer offers “spiritual sacrifices” (2:5).

e.n: Foreigners and exiles: honor everyone, even the king
t: Peter writes, “Submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, or to governors as those sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. The Greek for “foreigners and exiles” (paroikoi and parepidemoi) names resident aliens, people who lived in a place without the full rights of citizens. Peter uses it as a picture of the church’s place in the world (compare Genesis 23:4; Psalm 39:12; Hebrews 11:13). “The king” was the Roman emperor, who in the early 60s was Nero. The “governors” would be the Roman officials of provinces like Bithynia and Pontus, whose governor Pliny wrote to the emperor Trajan about Christians about AD 112. “Fear God, honor the king” echoes Proverbs 24:21. Paul gives similar teaching in Romans 13:1-7 and Titus 3:1.

e.n: Servants and the example of Christ who suffered
t: Peter writes, “For to this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth.” When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats, but entrusted Himself to Him who judges justly. He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness. “By His stripes you are healed.””

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. The word for “servants” here is oiketai, household slaves, not the more common douloi. Slaves made up a large share of the population of a Roman city, and a master could beat a slave with little hindrance. Peter does not argue about the system but tells slaves how to bear unjust suffering and points to Christ. He builds the passage on Isaiah 53: “no deceit was found in His mouth” (53:9), “by His stripes you are healed” (53:5), “like sheep going astray” (53:6). The word for “example” (hypogrammos) is a writing teacher’s copybook, the letters a child traces over. “The tree” (xylon) is the cross, as in Acts 5:30 and Galatians 3:13. “Shepherd and Overseer” (episkopos) is a title the elders of 5:1-4 are asked to imitate.

e.n: Wives and husbands: a gentle and quiet spirit
t: Peter writes, “Wives, in the same way, submit yourselves to your husbands, so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives when they see your pure and reverent demeanor.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. Peter writes of wives with husbands who “refuse to believe the word.” In the Roman world a wife was expected to share her husband’s religion; Plutarch, writing about AD 100, advised a wife to worship only the gods her husband believed in. A Christian wife who did otherwise could be seen as a threat to her household, and Peter tells her how to win her husband without words. The warning against braided hair and gold jewelry is also found in 1 Timothy 2:9. Sarah “called him lord” (Genesis 18:12). Readers differ widely on how to apply the call to submission today: some read it as a standing pattern for marriage, others as advice for a particular setting in which an early church was under suspicion. The instruction to husbands, to honor wives “as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life,” puts both partners on the same footing before God.

e.n: Do not repay evil with evil: blessing
t: Peter writes, “Finally, all of you, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. Peter ends the household teaching with a word for everyone, and backs it with a long quotation from Psalm 34:12-16. The same psalm gave him “tasted that the Lord is good” in 2:3. The command not to return evil for evil is in Romans 12:17 and in Jesus’ own teaching (Luke 6:27-28), and “inherit a blessing” is the reward of those who bless.

e.n: Suffering for what is right: be ready to give a reason for your hope
t: Peter writes, “But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. “Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken” quotes Isaiah 8:12-13, where the Lord tells Isaiah not to fear what the people fear but to regard the Lord of hosts as holy; Peter changes it to “sanctify Christ as Lord.” The word for “defense” (apologia) is the word for a speech made in court (Acts 22:1; 25:16; Philippians 1:7). It may mean a formal hearing, or any answer to a neighbor who asks why you live as you do. The gentleness and respect in the same verse show how the answer is to be given.

e.n: Christ suffered once; the spirits in prison; Noah and baptism
t: Peter writes, “For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit, in whom He also went and preached to the spirits in prison who disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water.”

The pin stands in the mountains of Ararat, where Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest; the region is ancient Urartu in eastern Turkey and the exact spot is unknown. This is one of the most disputed passages in the New Testament. Martin Luther said he did not know for certain what Peter meant. Three main readings are held. Some, like Augustine, think Christ preached through Noah to the people of his day, who are now “spirits in prison.” Many modern scholars think the “spirits” are the rebel angels of Genesis 6:1-4 as told in 1 Enoch 6-16 (compare 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6), and that Christ, raised and exalted (3:22), announced his victory to them. Others think Christ went to the realm of the dead to preach, a view that lies behind the line He descended into hell in later creeds. In verse 21, “pledge” or “appeal” (eperotema) is a rare word, and the sense of the phrase “a clear conscience” is also debated. Baptism is likened to the flood as water of judgment and salvation. Noah’s family was “saved through water” (Genesis 7:7; 2 Peter 2:5).

e.n: Armed with the same resolve: done with sin
t: Peter writes, “Therefore, since Christ suffered in His body, arm yourselves with the same resolve, because anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin. Consequently, he does not live out his remaining time on earth for human passions, but for the will of God. For you have spent enough time in the past carrying out the same desires as the Gentiles: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. The list in 4:3, “debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry,” describes common social life: feasts for the guilds and the gods were part of a town’s life. The Christians who would not “plunge with them into the same flood” were suspected and mocked. “The gospel was preached even to those who are now dead” (4:6) is another disputed line. Most readers take it to mean the gospel was preached to people who heard it when alive and have since died, and that Christians who died are not lost; others link it to 3:19.

e.n: Love covers sins; hospitality; stewards of God’s grace
t: Peter writes, “Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without complaining. As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. “Love covers over a multitude of sins” quotes Proverbs 10:12; James 5:20 uses it too. Travelers in the Roman world relied on the homes of friends, since inns were often rough, and hospitality (philoxenia) was a chief duty of early Christians (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2; 3 John 5-8). “Manifold” (poikiles) is the same Greek word as the “various” of the trials in 1:6, so grace comes in as many forms as trouble does. “Stewards” (oikonomoi) were managers of a household’s goods.

e.n: Do not be surprised at the fiery trial: suffer as a Christian
t: Peter writes, “Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed at the revelation of His glory. If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. “Fiery trial” (pyrosis) is built on the Greek for fire (pyr), which also stands in the “refined by fire” of 1:7. The name “Christian” occurs only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28; here). The earliest Roman references to it come from Tacitus, who tells how Nero punished “Christians” after the fire of Rome in AD 64, and Pliny’s letter to Trajan from Bithynia about AD 112 shows that being a Christian could be punished. The letter does not say whether the suffering it speaks of was official or the hostility of neighbors; scholars differ, and the date of the letter is part of the debate. “A meddler” (allotriepiskopos) occurs nowhere else. “Judgment to begin with the family of God” echoes Ezekiel 9:6 and Malachi 3:1-5, and 4:18 quotes Proverbs 11:31 in its Greek form.

e.n: Shepherd the flock: the Chief Shepherd
t: Peter writes, “Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but because it is God’s will; not out of greed, but out of eagerness; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. Peter calls himself a “fellow elder” and “a witness of Christ’s sufferings.” John 21:15-17 records Jesus telling him to feed and shepherd his sheep, and Ezekiel 34 is the Old Testament chapter about the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the sheep. “Chief Shepherd” (archipoimen) occurs only here. The crown is a wreath, such as the games gave a winner, and “will never fade away” (amarantinos) comes from the word for “unfading” in 1:4. Elders were the leaders of local churches (Acts 14:23; 20:17; Titus 1:5).

e.n: Humble yourselves; the roaring lion; the God of all grace
t: Peter writes, “Be sober-minded and alert. Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, standing firm in your faith and in the knowledge that your brothers throughout the world are undergoing the same kinds of suffering. And after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. The letter is addressed to believers in five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, “Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1), a region about 700 miles across, and no single town stands for all of them. Ancyra lies near the middle. The list may follow the route of the man who carried the letter, since it begins in the northeast and ends in the northwest. “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” is Proverbs 3:34, quoted in the same Greek form by James 4:6. “Cast all your anxiety on Him” echoes Psalm 55:22. The “adversary” (antidikos) was a legal opponent in court, and the lion that “prowls around” recalls Psalm 22:13 and Daniel 6. Peter closes the main body of the letter with a prayer that the God who called them will restore, secure, strengthen, and establish them after “a little while” of suffering, the same “little while” with which the letter began (1:6).

e.n: Silvanus, Babylon and Mark: closing greetings
t: Peter writes, “Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly, encouraging you and testifying that this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it. The church in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark.”

The pin stands at Rome, a judgment call. The letter says it was sent from “Babylon” (5:13). Early Christian writers took Babylon to mean Rome, and Eusebius reports that Papias and Clement of Alexandria said the letter was written there. Others have proposed the old city of Babylon on the Euphrates or the fortress town of Babylon in Egypt. The letter does not say. Silvanus is the Silas of Acts 15:22, 40 and 16:19, and the Silvanus Paul names with Timothy in 1 and 2 Thessalonians. “Through Silvanus” may mean he carried the letter, wrote it down as Peter’s secretary, or both; the polished Greek of the letter is one reason some think a secretary shaped it. Mark is probably John Mark, in whose mother’s house the church met in Acts 12:12; he is “my son” in the faith, and early writers such as Papias said Mark was Peter’s interpreter. The “kiss of love” is a greeting like the “holy kiss” of Romans 16:16. Scholars who place the letter after AD 70 take “Babylon” as a code word for Rome used the same way in Revelation 14:8 and 17-18, and some of them also think the letter was written in Peter’s name after his death; others hold it was written by Peter shortly before he died.

e.n: Simon Peter writes to those who share a faith as precious as his
t: Peter writes, “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours: Grace and peace be multiplied to you through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord.”

The pin stands at Rome, a judgment call. The letter names no place of writing. Church tradition says Peter died at Rome under Nero, and the writer says his death is near (1:14), so Rome is the usual guess. The writer calls himself “Simon Peter,” using the Greek form Symeon (Simeon) that Acts 15:14 also uses for him. Whether Peter himself wrote the letter is one of the most debated questions in New Testament study. Those who accept it point to the personal claims in 1:16-18 and 3:1, and say the different style from 1 Peter may come from another secretary (compare 1 Peter 5:12) or another time. Many scholars think it was written in Peter’s name after his death, some say between about AD 80 and 120, as a farewell testament, because its Greek is unlike 1 Peter, because it seems to use the letter of Jude, and because it was slow to be accepted: the church historian Eusebius, about AD 325, says it was not counted as part of the New Testament, though many found it useful (Church History 3.3.1-4). The earliest known copy is Papyrus 72, of the 3rd or 4th century. The greeting says the readers have “a faith as precious as ours,” and the Greek word (isotimon) means of equal standing, so their faith is not second-class beside the apostles’. It also names Jesus in one phrase as “our God and Savior Jesus Christ,” which most take as calling Jesus God.

e.n: His divine power has given us everything we need: partakers of the divine nature
t: Peter writes, “His divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence. Through these He has given us His precious and magnificent promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. “Knowledge” in the letter’s opening is epignosis, a full or personal knowing, and the word returns in 1:2, 1:8 and 2:20. “Glory and excellence” is doxa and arete; arete (virtue, excellence) is a word from Greek moral writing that the New Testament uses rarely (Philippians 4:8; 1 Peter 2:9; 2 Peter 1:3, 5). “Partakers of the divine nature” is the most famous phrase in the letter. The Eastern Orthodox churches have read it as sharing by grace in God’s own life (theosis, deification). Many Catholic and Protestant readers take it to mean sharing God’s moral character and the life of the age to come. The verse itself ties it to escaping “the corruption in the world caused by evil desires,” and it does not say that people become God.

e.n: Add to your faith: a ladder from virtue to love
t: Peter writes, “make every effort to add to your faith virtue; and to virtue, knowledge; and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness, love. For if you possess these qualities and continue to grow in them, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. But whoever lacks these traits is nearsighted to the point of blindness, having forgotten that he has been cleansed from his past sins. Therefore, brothers, strive to make your calling and election sure. For if you practice these things you will never stumble, and you will receive a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. The verb translated “add” (epichoregeo) comes from choregos, the wealthy citizen who paid for a chorus at a Greek festival, so it means to supply generously; the same verb gives the “lavish reception” of v.11. The seven qualities are faith, virtue, knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness and love, in a chain where each leads on to the next. Chains of this kind appear in Romans 5:3-5 and in Wisdom 6:17-20, and lists of virtues were common in Greek moral writing. “Nearsighted to the point of blindness” (v.9) renders the word muopazo, found only here in the New Testament. Being “cleansed from his past sins” may point to baptism, though the verse does not say so. “Calling and election” are God’s call and choice; the readers are told to make them sure by living them out.

e.n: The tent will soon be laid aside: Peter looks ahead to his departure
t: Peter writes, “I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of my body, because I know that this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me. And I will make every effort to ensure that after my departure, you will be able to recall these things at all times.”

The pin stands at Rome, a judgment call, because tradition says Peter died there under Nero. The writer pictures the body as a tent (skenoma, as in 2 Corinthians 5:1, 4) and his death as a “departure.” The Greek word is exodos, which is also the word for the Exodus, and in Luke 9:31 it is what Moses and Elijah discuss with Jesus on the mountain of the Transfiguration. “As our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me” may refer to Jesus’ words about Peter’s death in John 21:18-19; the letter does not say. Farewell speeches by people about to die were a familiar form in the Bible and in Jewish writing (Genesis 49, Deuteronomy 31-33, John 13-17, Acts 20, 2 Timothy 4), and many scholars see this letter as a “testament” of Peter. Those who think Peter wrote it take it as his own last words; others think a later writer used the form to carry Peter’s teaching forward. Early writers such as Clement of Rome (1 Clement 5) say Peter was put to death at Rome.

e.n: Eyewitnesses of His majesty on the holy mountain
t: Peter writes, “For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty. For He received honor and glory from God the Father when the voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory, saying, “This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain.”

The pin stands at Mount Tabor, a judgment call. The letter does not name the mountain. The Transfiguration is told in Matthew 17:1-8, Mark 9:2-8 and Luke 9:28-36, and Peter, James and John were the three with Jesus. From about the 4th century Christians have honored Mount Tabor in Galilee; others prefer Mount Hermon, nearer Caesarea Philippi, where the Gospels place Peter’s confession just before. The word for “eyewitnesses” (epoptai) is found only here in the New Testament; in Greek religion it named those admitted to the highest stage of the mystery rites, who had seen the sacred things themselves. The writer denies “cleverly devised fables” (muthoi, myths). The voice quotes words familiar from Psalm 2:7 and Isaiah 42:1, and the Gospel accounts give nearly the same words. Many readers see the scene as a preview of Christ’s “power and coming” (parousia), the same word the scoffers use in 3:4.

e.n: The word of the prophets: a lamp in a dark place
t: Peter writes, “We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt. And you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. The “morning star” (phosphoros, light-bearer) is found only here in the New Testament. It is the planet Venus rising before dawn. Numbers 24:17 speaks of a star from Jacob, and in Revelation 22:16 Jesus calls himself the bright morning star. “One’s own interpretation” (idias epiluseos) can mean that no prophet explained things from his own mind, which fits v.21, or that no reader should interpret a prophecy on private authority. Interpreters are divided, and the next verse favors the first reading. “Carried along” is the verb pheromai; the same verb describes a ship driven along by the wind in Acts 27:15, 17. It describes men moved by the Spirit and still speaking in their own voices.

e.n: False teachers among you: destructive heresies
t: Peter writes, “Now there were also false prophets among the people, just as there will be false teachers among you. They will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them—bringing swift destruction on themselves. Many will follow in their depravity, and because of them the way of truth will be defamed. In their greed, these false teachers will exploit you with deceptive words. The longstanding verdict against them remains in force, and their destruction does not sleep.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. Chapter 2 runs closely alongside the letter of Jude (compare Jude 4-18). Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude; a few reverse it, and some think both drew on a common source. The letter first says the false teachers “will” come (2:1; 3:3) and then describes them as already here (2:10-22), a shift that readers explain in different ways. “Heresies” (haireseis) first means parties or factions that choose their own line. The phrase “the Master who bought them” is debated: some read it as meaning that Christ’s death was for these people too, others as a description of what they claimed or a figure of speech. The Greek word for “Master” (despotes) is not the usual one for Christ. “Deceptive words” (plastois logois) means words that are molded or made up.
Peter writes, “For if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment;”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. The word translated “cast them deep into hell” is tartaroo, from Tartarus, a word used in Greek writing for the deep prison under the earth where rebel gods were held (for example in Homer and Hesiod). It occurs only here in the New Testament. The letter does not say what the angels did. Most readers link the verse to the story of the sons of God and the daughters of men in Genesis 6:1-4, which the Jewish Book of Enoch retells: the rebel angels are bound until the judgment (1 Enoch 10, 21). Fragments of Enoch in Aramaic were found in the Dead Sea Scrolls. Jude 6 says almost the same thing, and some think the writer means the fall of Satan and his angels instead. Compare the “spirits in prison” of 1 Peter 3:19-20.

e.n: Noah, a preacher of righteousness, and the flood
t: Peter writes, “if He did not spare the ancient world when He brought the flood on its ungodly people, but preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight;”

The pin stands in the mountains of Ararat, where Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest. Ararat is the ancient land of Urartu, in what is now eastern Turkey and Armenia, and the Bible names a range of mountains, not a single peak. Peter calls Noah “a preacher of righteousness” (kerux dikaiosynes). Genesis does not say that Noah preached, but Jewish writers did: Josephus says Noah urged people to change their ways (Antiquities 1.74), and 1 Clement 7 says Noah preached repentance. “Among the eight” counts Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives (Genesis 7:7, 13); 1 Peter 3:20 also counts eight in all. The flood is an example for the writer, as it is in 3:6.

e.n: Sodom and Gomorrah burned to ashes; Lot rescued
t: Peter writes, “if He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction, reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly; and if He rescued Lot, a righteous man distressed by the depraved conduct of the lawless (for that righteous man, living among them day after day, was tormented in his righteous soul by the lawless deeds he saw and heard)— if all this is so, then the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment.”

The pin stands at the east shore of the Dead Sea, a judgment call, because the site of Sodom is not known.
