The usual traditional guess puts it near the south end of the Dead Sea, and the Early Bronze Age town of Bab edh-Dhra on the east shore is one candidate; another proposal is Tall el-Hammam to the northeast, and neither is accepted by everyone. The story is in Genesis 18-19. Genesis never calls Lot righteous, but the Wisdom of Solomon does (Wisdom 10:6), and 2 Peter follows that view; he is shown as hospitable and as grieved by the town’s violence. Jude 7 uses Sodom as the example of the same kind of sin, and Jesus joined the days of Noah and the days of Lot in Luke 17:26-30. The letter says God “knows how to rescue the godly from trials” (2:9).
f: Sodom (traditional, east shore of the Dead Sea)

e.n: Bold and self-willed: they slander glorious beings
t: Peter writes, “Such punishment is specially reserved for those who indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh and despise authority. Bold and self-willed, they are unafraid to slander glorious beings. Yet not even angels, though greater in strength and power, dare to bring such slanderous charges against them before the Lord. These men are like irrational animals, creatures of instinct, born to be captured and destroyed. They blaspheme in matters they do not understand, and like such creatures, they too will be destroyed.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. “Glorious beings” (doxas) are probably angelic powers. Jude 8-10 has the same charge and adds the story of the archangel Michael and the devil over the body of Moses, which comes from a Jewish writing now lost in part (the Assumption of Moses, according to some early writers). 2 Peter leaves that story out and says only that angels do not bring slanderous charges “before the Lord.” The people described are “like irrational animals, creatures of instinct” (aloga zoa, phusika). The letter says they speak against things they do not understand, and it does not say which angels or which teaching.

e.n: The way of Balaam son of Beor
t: Peter writes, “The harm they will suffer is the wages of their wickedness. They consider it a pleasure to carouse in broad daylight. They are blots and blemishes, reveling in their deception as they feast with you. Their eyes are full of adultery; their desire for sin is never satisfied; they seduce the unstable. They are accursed children with hearts trained in greed. They have left the straight way and wandered off to follow the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness. But he was rebuked for his transgression by a donkey, otherwise without speech, that spoke with a man’s voice and restrained the prophet’s madness.”

The pin stands on the plains of Moab, east of the Jordan, where Numbers 22-24 sets the story; it is approximate. Balaam is said to have come from Pethor on the river Euphrates (Numbers 22:5), so he was a foreign seer hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel. The talking donkey is in Numbers 22:21-35. Numbers 31:16 says Balaam’s advice led Israel into sin at Peor, and Revelation 2:14 speaks of the teaching of Balaam. The Greek here reads “Bosor,” an unexplained form of Beor; the translation follows Numbers. A plaster inscription found at Tell Deir ’Alla in the Jordan valley, about 800 BC, mentions a seer named Balaam son of Beor, so he was remembered outside the Bible. The phrase “feast with you” points to the shared meals of the church (compare Jude 12), where these teachers sat at the table while they seduced the unstable.

e.n: Springs without water and mists driven by a storm
t: Peter writes, “These men are springs without water and mists driven by a storm. Blackest darkness is reserved for them. With lofty but empty words, they appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh and entice those who are just escaping from others who live in error. They promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. In a dry land a spring that fails is a bitter disappointment, and mists driven by a storm promise rain and give none. Jude 12-13 uses similar pictures (clouds without water, wild waves). The false teachers “promise them freedom” but are “slaves to depravity”; the saying that “a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him” echoes what Jesus says in John 8:34 and what Paul says in Romans 6:16. The “lofty but empty words” (huperogka mataiotetos) are boasts that swell and hold nothing.

e.n: Better never to have known the way: the dog and the sow
t: Peter writes, “If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first. It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them. Of them the proverbs are true: “A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud.””

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. The first proverb is Proverbs 26:11 in the Greek Old Testament. The second, about the washed sow, is not in the Old Testament; the writer calls both “true” proverbs. Dogs and pigs were unclean animals for Jews (Leviticus 11:7; Matthew 7:6). Jesus tells a similar story of a spirit that leaves a person and returns to find the house swept and empty, so that the last state is worse (Luke 11:24-26). Readers disagree about whether the people described had really been saved and lost it, or had only seemed to be; the text speaks of them as having “escaped the corruption of the world” and “known the way of righteousness.”

e.n: My second letter: remember the prophets and the apostles
t: Peter writes, “Beloved, this is now my second letter to you. Both of them are reminders to stir you to wholesome thinking by recalling what was foretold by the holy prophets and commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. The words “stir you to wholesome thinking” echo 1:12-13, where the writer also promises to stir up his readers by reminding them. The “commanded by our Lord and Savior through your apostles” puts the apostles beside the prophets as bearers of what God has said. Scholars who date the letter late take “your apostles” as a sign of a generation that looks back on them; others note that Peter could say it of the apostles who had founded these churches. Compare Jude 17.

e.n: Scoffers in the last days: Where is the promise of His coming?
t: Peter writes, “Most importantly, you must understand that in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires. “Where is the promise of His coming?” they will ask. “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation.” But they deliberately overlook the fact that long ago by God’s word the heavens existed and the earth was formed out of water and by water, through which the world of that time perished in the flood. And by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. “Scoffers” (empaiktai) is also the word in Jude 18. The scoffers say that nothing has changed “since our fathers fell asleep”: the “fathers” may be the first Christians who have died or the patriarchs of Israel, and readers differ. The reply goes back to creation (Genesis 1:6-10, earth “formed out of water and by water”) and to the flood (Genesis 6-8), and then looks ahead to fire. The idea of a final judgment by fire is also in Zephaniah 3:8 and Malachi 4:1. Some Greek philosophers, the Stoics, also taught that the world would end in a great fire and start again; the letter does not mention them, and its fire comes from God’s judgment and not from a natural cycle.

e.n: A day like a thousand years: the Lord is patient
t: Peter writes, “Beloved, do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance. But the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. The saying about a day and a thousand years comes from Psalm 90:4, where a thousand years in God’s sight are like yesterday. The “Day of the Lord” is a day of judgment in Amos 5:18-20, Joel 2 and Zephaniah 1; the New Testament says it “will come like a thief” (also 1 Thessalonians 5:2; Luke 12:39-40; Revelation 16:15). The Greek word translated “elements” (stoicheia) may mean the basic substances of the world (earth, water, air, fire), the sun, moon and stars, or spiritual powers (Galatians 4:3; Colossians 2:8). The last clause of v.10 is the best-known textual puzzle in the letter: the oldest manuscripts read “will be found” (or “found out”), and later ones read “burned up.” The BSB translates “laid bare.” Verse 9 is the heart of the answer: delay is patience, aimed at repentance. Compare Romans 2:4.

e.n: What kind of people ought you to be? A new heaven and a new earth
t: Peter writes, “Since everything will be destroyed in this way, what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness as you anticipate and hasten the coming of the day of God, when the heavens will be destroyed by fire and the elements will melt in the heat. But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. “Hasten the coming of the day of God” (speudo) can mean to wait eagerly or to bring it nearer by living holy lives and by the repentance for which God is waiting (3:9); readers differ. The promise of “a new heaven and a new earth” comes from Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22, and Revelation 21:1 uses the same words. The letter does not say the old creation is wiped out and a different one made; whether the fire cleanses and renews or destroys is a debated point, and the same verbs (melt, burn, laid bare) are used of both ideas. The emphasis is on “righteousness” at home in the new world, which is the reason for holy lives now.

e.n: Our beloved brother Paul and the rest of the Scriptures
t: Peter writes, “Therefore, beloved, as you anticipate these things, make every effort to be found at peace—spotless and blameless in His sight. Consider also that our Lord’s patience brings salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him. He writes this way in all his letters, speaking in them about such matters. Some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. The letter calls Paul “our beloved brother,” which suggests that the clash with Peter at Antioch (Galatians 2:11-14) did not end their friendship. It does not say which letter Paul “wrote you.” Some think of Romans 2:4, about God’s patience, and others of Galatians or Ephesians, since Galatia and Asia were among the provinces of 1 Peter. The phrase “the rest of the Scriptures” puts Paul’s letters beside the Old Testament, which is early evidence that his letters were collected and read as Scripture. If Peter wrote the letter, that was already so in the 60s; if not, it is later. The oldest surviving collection of his letters is Papyrus 46, from about AD 200. The word for “distort” (streblousin) is used for twisting on a rack. “Hard to understand” (dusnoeta) is found only here in the New Testament.

e.n: Be on your guard, and grow in grace and knowledge
t: Peter writes, “Therefore, beloved, since you already know these things, be on your guard so that you will not be carried away by the error of the lawless and fall from your secure standing. But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To Him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen.”

The pin stands at Ancyra (modern Ankara) in Galatia as a judgment call. 2 Peter names no town and no province. The writer says “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1), and many take that to mean 1 Peter, which was sent to five Roman provinces of Asia Minor; the pin follows 1 Peter. Others think the second letter was a different one, or that this letter was written for the church at large. The letter ends where it began: “grace” and “knowledge” of “our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:2-3). “Secure standing” (stērigmos) is a word that pictures a firm footing, matching the “unstable” people of 2:14 and 3:16. “To the day of eternity” (eis hemeran aionos) is an unusual phrase: the doxology looks to the day of God and of the new heaven and earth (3:12-13) and then to the age without end. The prayer is addressed to Christ; compare Revelation 1:5-6, Hebrews 13:21 and 2 Timothy 4:18.

e.n: What we have heard, seen and touched: the Word of life
t: The writer says, “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands—this is the Word of life. And this is the life that was revealed; we have seen it and testified to it, and we proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father and was revealed to us. We proclaim to you what we have seen and heard, so that you also may have fellowship with us. And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ. We write these things so that our joy may be complete.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The letter has no name, no greeting and no ending, and it begins like the opening of the Gospel of John: “from the beginning,” “the Word,” “life” (John 1:1-4, 14). The writer speaks as “we,” the group of eyewitnesses, and piles up verbs of the senses: heard, seen, gazed upon (the verb of John 1:14, “we have seen His glory”) and touched. The verb for “touched” (psēlaphaō) is the one Jesus uses in Luke 24:39, “Touch Me and see.” The writer is not named. Church writers from the 2nd century on, among them Irenaeus, quote the letter as the work of John the apostle; the Gospel and the letter share many words and phrases, and some scholars think one writer wrote both, others a school of John’s followers. Some manuscripts read “that your joy may be complete” in 1:4.

e.n: God is light: if we walk in the light
t: The writer says, “And this is the message we have heard from Him and announce to you: God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all. If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth. But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus His Son cleanses us from all sin.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. Light and darkness are old pictures of goodness and evil (Psalm 27:1; Isaiah 60:19-20), and Jesus says “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12). At Qumran the Community Rule speaks of the “sons of light” and the “sons of darkness” (1QS 3-4), so the pair was familiar in the Jewish world of the time. “Walk” is the Hebrew picture for how a person lives. “Do not practice the truth” (1:6) renders a phrase that treats truth as something done and not just believed (compare John 3:21). The blood of Jesus that “cleanses” echoes the sacrifices of Leviticus.

e.n: If we confess our sins: an advocate and the atoning sacrifice
t: The writer says, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. If we say we have not sinned, we make Him out to be a liar, and His word is not in us. My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. He Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.”

The pin stands at the Temple Mount, a judgment call. The letter names no place, but “atoning sacrifice” (hilasmos) draws on the Day of Atonement in Leviticus 16, which was held at the Temple. The same word appears again in 4:10. A related Greek word, hilastērion, is the lid of the ark, the “mercy seat,” in Exodus 25:17-22 in the Greek Old Testament and in Hebrews 9:5. The “advocate” (paraklētos) is the same word Jesus uses of the Holy Spirit in the Gospel of John (14:16, 26; 15:26; 16:7), usually “Helper” in the BSB. The word occurs five times in the New Testament: four in the Gospel of John and here. The three “if we say” statements in 1:6, 8 and 10 are read either as claims of the writer’s opponents or as general warnings; readers differ. “Faithful and just” echoes Deuteronomy 32:4.

e.n: How we know Him: keeping His commandments, and walking as He walked
t: The writer says, “By this we can be sure that we have come to know Him: if we keep His commandments. If anyone says, “I know Him,” but does not keep His commandments, he is a liar, and the truth is not in him. But if anyone keeps His word, the love of God has been truly perfected in him. By this we know that we are in Him: Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. Verbs of knowing and of abiding run through the whole letter. “Abide” or “remain” (menō) is one of the most frequent verbs, and “know” (ginōskō) another. The tests the writer gives, keeping the commandments, walking as Jesus walked, loving the brother, believing that Jesus is the Christ, come back again and again. Some readers think they answer teachers who claimed to know God without changing how they lived; the letter does not say so outright. “Walk” (peripateō) is the Hebrew picture for a way of life.

e.n: An old commandment that is new: love your brother
t: The writer says, “Beloved, I am not writing to you a new commandment, but an old one, which you have had from the beginning. This commandment is the message you have heard. Then again, I am also writing to you a new commandment, which is true in Him and also in you. For the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining. If anyone claims to be in the light but hates his brother, he is still in the darkness. Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no cause of stumbling in him. But whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness. He does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes.”

The pin stands at the traditional upper room in Jerusalem, a judgment call. In the Gospel of John, Jesus gives “a new commandment” to love one another on the night he is betrayed (John 13:34-35; 15:12), and the Gospel does not say where the room was. The letter calls the same command “old,” because the readers heard it “from the beginning,” and “new,” because “the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining.” “Brother” (adelphos) in this letter most often means a fellow believer; some readers think it can reach every person, and the letter does not settle the point. 2 John 5 repeats the phrase “from the beginning.”

The writer says, “I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven through His name. I am writing to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The writer addresses three groups, “children,” “fathers” and “young men,” each with a reason. Some read them as three ages in the church; others as all the readers addressed in three ways. The verb changes from “I am writing” (2:12-13) to “I have written” (2:13-14), and the reasons for the change are debated: it may be a style choice, or a reference to the Gospel written earlier. Teachers in the ancient world often called pupils “children” (teknia, paidia), and this letter calls its readers “little children” or “children” again at 2:1, 2:18, 2:28, 3:7, 3:18, 4:4 and 5:21.

e.n: Do not love the world: the desires of the flesh and the eyes, and the pride of life
t: The writer says, “Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life—is not from the Father but from the world. The world is passing away, along with its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. “The world” (kosmos) has more than one sense in John’s writings: the created world God loves (John 3:16), and the order of things set against God, which is meant here. The three phrases in 2:16, “the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life,” are often compared with the fruit in Genesis 3:6 and with the temptations of Jesus (Luke 4); the letter does not make either link. The Greek for “pride” (alazoneia), boasting about what one has, occurs in the New Testament only here and in James 4:16. Ephesus was a rich port city with a famous temple of Artemis and a growing cult of the emperors, which gave readers there plenty to love.

e.n: It is the last hour: many antichrists have appeared
t: The writer says, “Children, it is the last hour; and just as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. This is how we know it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us. But their departure made it clear that none of them belonged to us. You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth. I have not written to you because you lack knowledge of the truth, but because you have it, and because no lie comes from the truth. Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ? This is the antichrist, who denies the Father and the Son. Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The word “antichrist” is found only in 1 John (2:18, 22; 4:3) and 2 John 7; Paul’s “man of lawlessness” (2 Thessalonians 2) and the beast of Revelation are not called by that name. Here the writer says the antichrist was “coming,” and “many antichrists” are already here: people who left the community and deny that Jesus is the Christ and the Son. “They went out from us” tells of a split in the church. What the departed taught is debated. Early writers point to Cerinthus (a teacher of the late 1st century who, according to Irenaeus, taught that the Christ came upon Jesus at his baptism and left before the cross; Against Heresies 1.26.1) and to docetists, who said Christ only seemed to have a body (Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 4-6). Irenaeus (3.3.4) tells of John at Ephesus leaving a bathhouse when Cerinthus came in; he heard it from Polycarp’s circle, and it is a later story.

e.n: The anointing from the Holy One: remain in Him
t: The writer says, “As for you, let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you. If it does, you will also remain in the Son and in the Father. And this is the promise that He Himself made to us: eternal life. I have written these things to you about those who are trying to deceive you. And as for you, the anointing you received from Him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you. But just as His true and genuine anointing teaches you about all things, so remain in Him as you have been taught. And now, little children, remain in Christ, so that when He appears, we may be confident and unashamed before Him at His coming. If you know that He is righteous, you also know that everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. “Anointing” (chrisma) occurs in the New Testament only here (2:20, 27). It is related to “Christ,” the Anointed One. Readers take it as the Holy Spirit, as the word of the gospel, or as both. The sentence “you do not need anyone to teach you” (2:27) recalls Jeremiah 31:34; it is not an attack on teaching, since the writer is teaching them in the same breath. The phrase “born of Him” (2:29) is the first of seven in the letter (3:9; 4:7; 5:1, 4, 18).

e.n: Behold what manner of love: we are children of God
t: The writer says, “Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. And that is what we are! The reason the world does not know us is that it did not know Him. Beloved, we are now children of God, and what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is. And everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. “Children of God” (tekna theou) is a favorite phrase in John’s writings (John 1:12; 11:52). The writer separates “now” from “not yet”: children now, and what we will be “has not yet been revealed.” The subject of “when He appears” in 3:2 could be Christ or God, and “we will see Him as He is” has been read both ways. The verse promises likeness to Him, and the “hope” of 3:3 leads to purity, not idleness. “Purifies himself” (hagnizei) is the verb used of ritual preparation for the temple (John 11:55; Acts 21:24, 26).

e.n: Practicing righteousness, not sin: the works of the devil destroyed
t: The writer says, “Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well. Indeed, sin is lawlessness. But you know that Christ appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin. No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning. No one who continues to sin has seen Him or known Him. Little children, let no one deceive you: The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous. The one who practices sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the very start. This is why the Son of God was revealed, to destroy the works of the devil. Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin, because God’s seed abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God. By this the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil: Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. Verses 6 and 9 say that those who remain in Christ do not keep on sinning, and 1:8-10 says that anyone who claims to have no sin is deceived. Many readers see no contradiction because the Greek verb is in a tense that describes a continuing practice; others read it as a goal, or as the language of the writer’s opponents. “God’s seed” (sperma) in 3:9 is read as God’s word, God’s Spirit, or the new life he gives. “The devil has been sinning from the very start” echoes Jesus in John 8:44, where he is “a murderer from the beginning.” “Lawlessness” (anomia) in 3:4 is Paul’s word for the end-time rebellion (2 Thessalonians 2:3, 7), though the letter does not link them.

e.n: Do not be like Cain: love and hatred
t: The writer says, “This is the message you have heard from the beginning: We should love one another. Do not be like Cain, who belonged to the evil one and murdered his brother. And why did Cain slay him? Because his own deeds were evil, while those of his brother were righteous. So do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates you. We know that we have passed from death to life, because we love our brothers. The one who does not love remains in death. Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that eternal life does not reside in a murderer.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The story of Cain and Abel is in Genesis 4:1-16. Genesis gives no place that can be marked on a map, so the pin stays at Ephesus. The letter is the only place in the New Testament where Cain is explained as “belonged to the evil one,” although Hebrews 11:4, Matthew 23:35 and Jude 11 also mention him. The Greek for “murdered” (esphaxen) means to slaughter or cut the throat, and it is used again in the New Testament only in Revelation, of the slain Lamb and of the persecuted. Jesus said hatred is the root of murder (Matthew 5:21-22). “Passed from death to life” (3:14) repeats John 5:24.

e.n: Jesus laid down His life: let us love in action and truth
t: The writer says, “By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers. If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him? Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth.”

The pin stands at Golgotha, the traditional place of the cross, a judgment call, because the letter names no place. Jesus says in John 10:11, 15, 17-18 that the good shepherd lays down his life, and in John 15:13 that no one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends. The writer gives a plain example: “if anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need” (3:17). The wording “earthly possessions” is bios, a word for livelihood, and James 2:15-16 makes much the same point. “Compassion” is literally the “inner parts” (splanchna), the seat of feeling.
f: Golgotha (Church of the Holy Sepulchre, traditional)

e.n: God is greater than our hearts: confidence and the two commandments
t: The writer says, “And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence: Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things. Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and we will receive from Him whatever we ask, because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight. And this is His commandment: that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ, and we should love one another just as He commanded us. Whoever keeps His commandments remains in God, and God in him. And by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. Verse 20 is one of the hardest in the letter. Most read it as comfort: when our hearts condemn us, God is greater and knows all, including our sincere love. Some read it as a warning that God knows even what the heart will not admit. The Greek can be taken either way. “Whatever we ask” (3:22) is close to what Jesus says in John 14:13-14 and 15:7. Verse 23 sums up “His commandment” as one that has two parts: believe in the name of his Son, and love one another. The verse also first names the Spirit as the sign that God remains in us (3:24).

e.n: Test the spirits: the spirit of the antichrist and the Spirit of truth
t: The writer says, “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God. This is the spirit of the antichrist, which you have heard is coming and which is already in the world at this time. You, little children, are from God and have overcome them, because greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world. They are of the world. That is why they speak from the world’s perspective, and the world listens to them. We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. That is how we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. Testing prophets goes back to Deuteronomy 13:1-5 and 18:20-22, and Paul says “test everything” (1 Thessalonians 5:21). The Didache, a church manual from about the 90s to 120s, also gives rules for testing traveling prophets (Didache 11-12). The test in 4:2 is “that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.” The words may be aimed at those who said Christ only seemed to have a body, or that he left Jesus before the cross; the letter does not name them. Some manuscripts and early writers read “does not confess Jesus” in 4:3 as “dissolves Jesus.” The pair “the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception” is close to the spirits of truth and falsehood in the Qumran Community Rule (1QS 3:18-19).

e.n: God is love: He sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice
t: The writer says, “Beloved, let us love one another, because love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love. This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him. And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins. Beloved, if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another. No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. “God is love” appears in 4:8 and again in 4:16; only here in the Bible is love given as a description of what God is, although the letter has already said “God is light” (1:5). The love in view is agapē. “One and only Son” translates monogenēs, used of Jesus in John 1:14, 18 and 3:16, 18. “No one has ever seen God” (4:12) repeats John 1:18. The atoning sacrifice of 4:10 is the same word as in 2:2: the love of God shown in sending his Son, not in our loving him first.

e.n: We have seen and testify: the Father sent His Son as Savior of the world
t: The writer says, “By this we know that we remain in Him, and He in us: He has given us of His Spirit. And we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world. If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God. And we have come to know and believe the love that God has for us. God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. “Savior of the world” is found in the New Testament only here and in John 4:42, where the Samaritans say it. Roman rulers were also called savior, and Greek cities in Asia gave the title to Julius Caesar and later to emperors, so the phrase would have been heard against that background; the letter does not argue the point. Four times the letter says “God remains in us” and “we remain in Him” (3:24; 4:13, 15, 16), tying together Spirit, confession and love.

e.n: Perfect love drives out fear: whoever loves God must love his brother
t: The writer says, “In this way, love has been perfected among us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment; for in this world we are just like Him. There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment. The one who fears has not been perfected in love. We love because He first loved us. If anyone says, “I love God,” but hates his brother, he is a liar. For anyone who does not love his brother, whom he has seen, cannot love God, whom he has not seen. And we have this commandment from Him: Whoever loves God must love his brother as well.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. “Perfected” (teteleiōtai) runs through the letter: love perfected in us (2:5; 4:12, 17, 18). The “day of judgment” in 4:17 is the only use of that phrase in the letters of John; it is the same phrase as Matthew 10:15 and 2 Peter 3:7. “Fear involves punishment” (4:18) is not a warning against reverence for God, which the Bible praises elsewhere. Some manuscripts add “Him” or “God” after “We love” in 4:19.

e.n: Born of God: the victory that has overcome the world
t: The writer says, “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God, and everyone who loves the Father also loves those born of Him. By this we know that we love the children of God: when we love God and keep His commandments. For this is the love of God, that we keep His commandments. And His commandments are not burdensome, because everyone born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith. Who then overcomes the world? Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The writer ties belief, birth, love and keeping the commandments together. The verb “overcome” (nikaō) is used here and in 2:13-14 and 4:4. Jesus says in John 16:33, “I have overcome the world.” “His commandments are not burdensome” is close to Jesus’ words in Matthew 11:30, “My burden is light.” The claim of 5:1 that the Christ is Jesus is the first of the confessions that the letter sets against the departed teachers.

e.n: Water, blood and the Spirit: three that testify
t: The writer says, “This is the One who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ—not by water alone, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth. For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood—and these three are in agreement. Even if we accept human testimony, the testimony of God is greater. For this is the testimony that God has given about His Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has this testimony within him; whoever does not believe God has made Him out to be a liar, because he has not believed in the testimony that God has given about His Son. And this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son of God does not have life.”

The pin stands at the traditional baptism site on the Jordan, a judgment call, because the letter does not say where “water” refers. Four readings are common: the baptism and the cross; the birth and the death of Jesus; the water and blood that flowed from his side (John 19:34, in the other order); and baptism and the Lord’s Supper. The words “not by water alone” are often taken to answer teachers who said the Christ came at the baptism and left before the death (compare Irenaeus on Cerinthus, Against Heresies 1.26.1); the letter does not name them. Deuteronomy 19:15 requires two or three witnesses, and the “three” fit that rule. Later Latin manuscripts add words about the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit in 5:7-8; this addition is the Comma Johanneum. It is not in the early Greek manuscripts, and the BSB does not include it.
f: Jordan River: Qasr al-Yahud (traditional baptism site)

e.n: That you may know you have eternal life: ask according to His will
t: The writer says, “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life. And this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us. And if we know that He hears us in whatever we ask, we know that we already possess what we have asked of Him. If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he should ask God, who will give life to those who commit this kind of sin. There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin. All unrighteousness is sin, yet there is sin that does not lead to death.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 1 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5, 3.1.1 and 3.3.4; Eusebius, Church History 3.23), and the letter is usually read as meant for churches in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. Verse 13 is the writer’s purpose, much like the purpose given at the end of the Gospel (John 20:31). The sin that “leads to death” in 5:16 is not defined. Readers have linked it to Numbers 15:27-31, which separates unintentional sin from defiant sin; to a final turning away from Christ; or to the sin of the departed teachers. Others tie it to the warnings of Mark 3:29 and Hebrews 6:4-6. “He hears us” (5:14-15) joins the promise of John 14:13-14.

e.n: We know: keep yourselves from idols
t: The writer says, “We know that anyone born of God does not keep on sinning; the One who was born of God protects him, and the evil one cannot touch him. We know that we are of God, and that the whole world is under the power of the evil one. And we know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true; and we are in Him who is true—in His Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols.”

The pin stands at the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus, a judgment call, because the letter does not say which idols it means. The temple was among the most famous in the ancient world, and an imperial temple was built at Ephesus about AD 90. Some readers think the “idols” are false gods and images, others false pictures of God held by the teachers who left. The sentence “He is the true God and eternal life” can point to Jesus Christ, the nearest name, or to the Father; most readers take it of Jesus. The three “we know” statements (5:18, 19, 20) end a letter built on “we know” and “you know.”

e.n: The elder to the chosen lady and her children: truth and love
t: The writer says, “The elder, To the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in the truth—and not I alone, but also all who know the truth— because of the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever: Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, will be with us in truth and love.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 2 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5 and 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there, with the readers in a church somewhere in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The writer gives no name, only “the elder” (ho presbyteros), the same title 3 John opens with. Church writers from the 2nd century on, Irenaeus among them, quote 2 John as the work of John, the Lord’s disciple. A scholar named Papias, quoted by Eusebius, speaks of a “John the Elder” besides the apostle John, and some think this elder wrote the short letters; others hold that the apostle meant by “elder” simply an older man. The “chosen lady” (eklektē kyria) is most often read as a local church and her “children” as its members, since verse 13 sends greetings from the children of a “chosen sister,” meaning another church. Others take her as a real woman who led a house church, and a few as a name (Kyria or Electa). The letter does not say. The greeting is unusual: Paul’s letters wish “grace and peace,” while here “Grace, mercy, and peace ... will be with us,” stated as a promise. The word “truth” occurs five times in the first four verses.

e.n: Walking in the truth: the commandment we have had from the beginning
t: The writer says, “I was overjoyed to find some of your children walking in the truth, just as the Father has commanded us. And now I urge you, dear lady—not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning—that we love one another. And this is love, that we walk according to His commandments. This is the very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 2 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5 and 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there, with the readers in a church somewhere in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The writer has met “some of your children” and found them “walking in the truth,” which suggests travelers who had been with his own church. “Walk” (peripateō) is the old picture for a way of life. The command to love one another is “not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning,” the same idea 1 John 2:7 uses for the old commandment that is also new; see also John 13:34-35 and 15:12. “Love” is then defined as walking “according to His commandments” (verse 6), which matches 1 John 5:3. “Dear lady” (kyria) is the one place the letter calls her by this title after the opening. The Greek “you” is singular in verses 4, 5 and 13 and plural in verses 6, 8, 10 and 12.

e.n: Many deceivers: refusing to confess Jesus Christ in the flesh
t: The writer says, “For many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 2 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5 and 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there, with the readers in a church somewhere in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The word “antichrist” occurs in the New Testament only in 1 John (2:18, 22; 4:3) and here. The Greek of “the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh” uses a present participle (erchomenon, “coming”), where 1 John 4:2 says Jesus Christ “has come” (a perfect tense); readers disagree whether the change matters. “Deceiver” (planos) comes from the same root as “go astray.” The letter does not name the deceivers or spell out what they taught. Some scholars see the same group that left the church in 1 John 2:19; Irenaeus and others link them with Cerinthus or with docetists, who said Christ only seemed to have a body (Ignatius, Smyrnaeans 4-6). Polycarp of Smyrna, writing to the Philippians (chapter 7, probably in the first half of the 2nd century), uses nearly the same test.

e.n: Watch yourselves: do not lose what we have worked for
t: The writer says, “Watch yourselves, so that you do not lose what we have worked for, but that you may be fully rewarded.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 2 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5 and 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there, with the readers in a church somewhere in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The manuscripts disagree on the pronouns in this verse. Some read that you do not lose what you have worked for, others what we have worked for, and later copies put the whole verse in the “we” form, as the King James Version does (the Greek endings differ); the BSB follows the reading “what we have worked for.” The “full reward” (misthon plērē) is a picture from paid work, as in Ruth 2:12 in the Greek Old Testament, where Boaz prays that Ruth will have a full reward from the LORD. The letter does not say what the reward is. The warning matches Jesus’ words to be on guard against false prophets (Matthew 7:15) and 2 Peter 3:17.

e.n: Remaining in the teaching of Christ: the Father and the Son
t: The writer says, “Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ does not have God. Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 2 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5 and 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there, with the readers in a church somewhere in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. The verb “runs ahead” (proagōn) means to go beyond or lead on; some manuscripts read “transgresses” (parabainōn). The people described think they have advanced past the basic teaching. “The teaching of Christ” can mean the teaching Christ gave or the teaching about Christ; readers differ, and the surrounding verses (7, 9) point to what is taught about him. “Remains” (menō) is the verb of the Gospel of John and 1 John for abiding. Whoever remains has “both the Father and the Son,” which is close to 1 John 2:23: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father.”

e.n: Do not receive him into your home or even greet him
t: The writer says, “If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him. Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds.”

The pin stands at the terrace houses of Ephesus, a judgment call; the letter names no town, and the pin shows the sort of wealthy Roman house where a church could meet. Early Christians met in homes (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; Colossians 4:15; Philemon 2), and traveling teachers, prophets and workers depended on a Christian household for food and a bed. The Didache, an early church manual, gives rules for such guests: welcome a teacher who brings sound teaching, let a visitor stay two or three days, and treat one who asks for money or stays longer as a false prophet (Didache 11-12). To “greet” (chairein, a greeting that means “rejoice”) a person was to give blessing and support; “shares in his evil deeds” says that hospitality is a form of partnership. The verses are about teachers who bring a different teaching about Christ, not about every disagreement, and 3 John shows the opposite problem: Diotrephes refuses to receive the brothers (3 John 9-10). Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.16.3) quotes verse 11 against false teachers of his own day.
f: Ephesus: the terrace houses (wealthy homes of the Roman city)

e.n: Paper and ink: face to face, and greetings from the chosen sister
t: The writer says, “I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with paper and ink. Instead, I hope to come and speak with you face to face, so that our joy may be complete. The children of your elect sister send you greetings.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 2 John names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 2.22.5 and 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there, with the readers in a church somewhere in the province of Asia. Other places have been proposed. “Paper” (chartēs) is a sheet of papyrus and “ink” (melan) the black ink of the time, a mix of soot and gum. 3 John 13 has almost the same words, with “pen” in place of “paper.” A letter this short, about 245 Greek words, would fit on one sheet of papyrus. “Face to face” (literally “mouth to mouth”) is the way people spoke of a visit in the Greek of the time. The letter ends with greetings from “The children of your elect sister,” another church, where the writer probably is; it has no “farewell” or name of a scribe. 2 John was one of the books some churches were slow to accept. Eusebius (Church History 3.25.3) lists it among the “disputed” writings, and the early Syriac Bible left it out; it is in the 4th-century Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus.

e.n: The elder to the beloved Gaius: a prayer for health
t: The writer says, “The elder, To the beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth: Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 3 John names no place of writing. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there. The opening is very brief: the sender, the receiver, and no word of greeting; “Peace to you” comes at the very end (verse 14). Gaius was one of the most common Roman names. The New Testament knows a Gaius of Macedonia (Acts 19:29), a Gaius of Derbe (Acts 20:4) and a Gaius of Corinth who hosted Paul (Romans 16:23; 1 Corinthians 1:14), and nothing ties any of them to this Gaius. “Beloved” (agapētos) is used of him four times (verses 1, 2, 5 and 11). The wish of verse 2 follows the custom of Greek letters, which often opened with a prayer for the reader’s health; the papyrus letters from Egypt have many examples. The elder adds something of his own: he prays that Gaius will do as well in body and in his affairs as he is doing in soul. “Prosper” (euodoō) means literally to have a good journey. The verse is a friend’s prayer for one man. It is not a promise of wealth.

e.n: No greater joy: my children are walking in the truth
t: The writer says, “For I was overjoyed when the brothers came and testified about your devotion to the truth, in which you continue to walk. I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 3 John names no place of writing. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there. Brothers who had visited Gaius came back and spoke about him before the elder’s church (verses 3 and 6), so news moved between the two places with travelers. “Walk” is the old picture for a way of life, and “the truth” in these letters is the message about Jesus Christ and the life that fits it; the Greek word occurs six times in this short letter. “My children” may mean that Gaius came to faith through the elder, as Paul calls his converts his children (1 Corinthians 4:14-15), or it may be the way an old teacher speaks of those in his care, as 1 John does throughout. 2 John 4 has almost the same sentence about the children of the chosen lady.

e.n: Gaius and the strangers: fellow workers for the truth
t: The writer says, “Beloved, you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you. They have testified to the church about your love. You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God. For they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth.”

The pin stands at Pergamum, a judgment call that rests on a late and uncertain tradition. The letter does not say where Gaius lived. The Apostolic Constitutions (7.46), a church manual compiled about AD 380, lists a Gaius as bishop of Pergamum; nothing earlier supports it, and the list may have taken the name from this letter. Gaius was probably in a town within reach of the elder, perhaps in Roman Asia. The brothers were traveling Christian workers, and they were “strangers” to Gaius when he took them in. To “send them on their way” (propempō) was a set phrase for giving travelers what they needed for the next stage: food, money, sometimes companions (Acts 15:3; Romans 15:24; Titus 3:13). “The Name” is the name of Jesus (Acts 5:41). The letter never uses the words Jesus or Christ, the only New Testament book of which that is true. “Gentiles” here (ethnikoi) means pagans, people outside the faith: the workers took no support from those they preached to. Wandering philosophers and the begging servants of some cults did collect money on their travels, and the Christian workers did not want their message to look like that trade. So the churches had to supply them, and whoever does so becomes one of the “fellow workers for the truth.” The Didache (11-12) gives rules for receiving such travelers. 2 John 10-11 sets the limit on the other side: a teacher who does not bring the teaching of Christ is not to be received.
f: Pergamum (a late tradition for Gaius; the letter names no town)

e.n: Diotrephes, who loves to be first
t: The writer says, “I have written to the church about this, but Diotrephes, who loves to be first, will not accept our instruction. So if I come, I will call attention to his malicious slander against us. And unsatisfied with that, he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church.”

The pin stands at Pergamum, a judgment call that rests on a late and uncertain tradition. The letter does not say where Gaius lived. The Apostolic Constitutions (7.46), a church manual compiled about AD 380, lists a Gaius as bishop of Pergamum; nothing earlier supports it, and the list may have taken the name from this letter. Gaius was probably in a town within reach of the elder, perhaps in Roman Asia. “I have written to the church” points to an earlier letter. Most think it is lost, and some think it is 2 John. These verses and verse 6 are the only places in the Gospel and letters of John that use the word “church” (ekklēsia). “Who loves to be first” is one Greek word, philoprōteuōn, found nowhere else in the New Testament. The name Diotrephes means nourished by Zeus and is rare. The letter charges him with four things: he will not accept what the elder says, he spreads malicious talk against him, he refuses to welcome the brothers, and he stops others from doing so and puts them out of the church. It does not charge him with false teaching. Scholars read him in different ways: as the host of a house church who shut his door, as an early case of one leader taking control of a local church (the single bishop is known from the letters of Ignatius, about AD 110), or as a man guarding his church against outsiders he did not trust. Bede, in the 8th century, called him a heretic, but the letter does not say so. Jesus had said that whoever wants to be first must be the servant of all (Mark 9:35; 10:43-44).
f: Pergamum (a late tradition for Gaius; the letter names no town)

e.n: Do not imitate what is evil, but what is good
t: The writer says, “Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 3 John names no place of writing. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there. The verse turns from Diotrephes to Demetrius: one example to avoid and one to follow. “Imitate” (mimeomai) is the word from which English gets “mimic”; Paul and Hebrews use it for following the example of leaders (2 Thessalonians 3:7; Hebrews 13:7). “Of God” and “has not seen God” are phrases of 1 John (3:6, 10; 4:7-8): what a person does shows where he belongs. The Old Testament has the same call to turn from evil and do good (Psalm 34:14; 37:27). The sentence is a general one, and the letter does not say outright that Diotrephes has never seen God.

e.n: Demetrius: a good testimony from everyone
t: The writer says, “Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 3 John names no place of writing. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there. Demetrius is most likely the man who carried the letter, and perhaps one of the traveling brothers, so that verse 12 serves as a letter of recommendation for him, like Paul’s words for Phoebe in Romans 16:1-2. Such letters are common among the papyri from Egypt. Three witnesses speak for him: everyone who knows him, “the truth itself” (his life matches the message), and the elder with those around him. The Law asked for two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). “You know that our testimony is true” is close to the end of the Gospel of John (19:35; 21:24). Nothing connects him with the silversmith Demetrius of Ephesus (Acts 19:24), and Demetrius was a common name. The Apostolic Constitutions (7.46), about AD 380, make a Demetrius bishop of Philadelphia, a late tradition that cannot be checked.

e.n: Pen and ink: face to face, peace, and the friends by name
t: The writer says, “I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink. Instead, I hope to see you soon and speak with you face to face. Peace to you. The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name.”

The pin stands at Ephesus, a judgment call. 3 John names no place of writing. Church tradition puts the apostle John at Ephesus in his last years (Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.3.4), and “the elder” who writes 2 and 3 John is usually placed there. “Pen” (kalamos) is a reed cut to a point, and “ink” (melan) is the black ink of the time, made of soot and gum. 2 John 12 has almost the same words, with “paper” in place of “pen.” “Face to face” is literally “mouth to mouth.” “Peace to you” is the Jewish greeting, and the words of the risen Jesus in John 20:19, 21 and 26. “The friends” is a rare name for fellow believers; Jesus called his disciples his friends (John 15:14-15). To greet them “by name” recalls the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name (John 10:3). Many Bibles count the closing greetings as verse 15; the BSB keeps them in verse 14. At about 219 Greek words, 3 John is the shortest book in the New Testament. It was also one of the last to be widely received: no writer is known to quote it before the 3rd century, Eusebius (Church History 3.25.3) lists it among the disputed books, and the early Syriac Bible left it out. It is in the 4th-century Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus.

e.n: Jude, brother of James, to those who are called, loved and kept
t: Jude writes, “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James, To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ: Mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you.”

The pin stands at Nazareth, a judgment call. The letter names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Jude calls himself the brother of James, and the Gospels list a James and a Judas among the brothers of Jesus at Nazareth (Mark 6:3). Many scholars place the letter among Jewish Christians in the land of Israel or Syria, and others suggest Egypt or Asia Minor. Jude is the same name as Judas and Judah. He does not call himself an apostle, and in verse 17 he speaks of the apostles as others. Most readers take him to be the Judas of Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55, a brother of Jesus and of the James who led the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19). He calls himself a servant of Jesus Christ and not his brother, as James does (James 1:1). The brothers did not believe in Jesus during his ministry (John 7:5), were with the disciples after the resurrection (Acts 1:14), and later traveled as missionaries with their wives (1 Corinthians 9:5). Some scholars think a later writer used Jude’s name; others see no reason to doubt it, since Jude was too little known for his name to add weight. The date is put anywhere from the AD 50s to about AD 90. The readers are described with three words: called, loved and kept. The letter is fond of sets of three, and the greeting has another: mercy, peace and love.
f: Nazareth (home of the family of Jesus; the letter names no place)

e.n: Contend for the faith: certain men have crept in
t: Jude writes, “Beloved, although I made every effort to write to you about the salvation we share, I felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints. For certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.”

The pin stands at Nazareth, a judgment call. The letter names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Jude calls himself the brother of James, and the Gospels list a James and a Judas among the brothers of Jesus at Nazareth (Mark 6:3). Many scholars place the letter among Jewish Christians in the land of Israel or Syria, and others suggest Egypt or Asia Minor. Jude had planned a letter about the salvation he and his readers share, and news of trouble changed his subject. “Contend earnestly” (epagōnizomai) is a word from the athletic contest, found only here in the New Testament. “The faith” here means the message believed, and “once for all” (hapax) means it was handed over a single time and is not to be replaced. “Crept in” (pareisdynō), also found only here, is used of slipping in by a side door. The intruders are not named. Jude brings two charges: they turn the grace of God into a license for immorality, and by the way they live they deny Jesus Christ as Master and Lord. “Designated long ago” most likely points to the old examples and prophecies that follow in verses 5-16, which describe people like these and their end. Much of 2 Peter 2 runs alongside Jude 4-18, and most scholars think 2 Peter drew on Jude.
f: Nazareth (home of the family of Jesus; the letter names no place)

e.n: Three warnings: Israel in the wilderness, the angels, and Sodom
t: Jude writes, “Although you are fully aware of this, I want to remind you that after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe. And the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling—these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day. In like manner, Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them, who indulged in sexual immorality and pursued strange flesh, are on display as an example of those who sustain the punishment of eternal fire.”

The pin stands on the plain southeast of the Dead Sea, a judgment call. Genesis puts Sodom and Gomorrah near the Dead Sea but their sites are not known; the ruined Bronze Age towns of Bab edh-Dhra and Numeira are among the candidates. Jude gives three examples of judgment. The first is the generation that came out of Egypt and then refused to go into the land (Numbers 14:26-35). The BSB reads that Jesus delivered the people; this is the reading of several of the oldest copies. Many other copies read “the Lord” (as the Greek text in this app does), and the papyrus P72 reads “God Christ.” The second is the angels who left their proper place. Jude most likely has in mind Genesis 6:1-4 as it was retold in the Jewish Book of Enoch, where the angels called Watchers come down to take wives and are bound in darkness until the day of judgment (1 Enoch 6-10). Jude quotes that book by name in verse 14. The third is Sodom and Gomorrah (Genesis 19). “The cities around them” are Admah and Zeboiim (Deuteronomy 29:23). “Strange flesh” is literally “other flesh.” 2 Peter 2:4-9 uses the angels and Sodom in the same order and adds Noah and Lot, who were rescued.
f: The plain southeast of the Dead Sea (one proposed setting for Sodom)

e.n: Michael and the devil dispute over the body of Moses
t: Jude writes, “Yet in the same way these dreamers defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings.”

The pin stands at Mount Nebo, where Moses died (Deuteronomy 34:1-6). Deuteronomy says that he was buried in a valley in Moab and that no one knows his grave. Verses 8-10 charge the intruders with three things, on the strength of their dreams: they defile the body, reject authority, and speak abusively of “glorious beings,” most likely angels. Against this Jude sets Michael the archangel, who in a dispute with the devil over the body of Moses would not pronounce an abusive judgment himself but said, “The Lord rebuke you!” Those words are from Zechariah 3:2. The story is not in the Old Testament. Clement of Alexandria and Origen, about AD 200 to 230, say that Jude took it from a Jewish book they call the Assumption (or Ascension) of Moses. A work known as the Testament of Moses survives in one damaged Latin copy, and its ending, where the story would have stood, is lost. Michael is the guardian of Israel in Daniel 10:13, 10:21 and 12:1, and fights the dragon in Revelation 12:7. Jude’s point is plain: if the chief of the angels left the rebuke to God, these men should not speak with contempt about powers they do not understand. 2 Peter 2:10-11 makes the same point without the story.
f: Mount Nebo (traditional place of the death of Moses)

e.n: Woe to them: the path of Cain, the error of Balaam, the rebellion of Korah
t: Jude writes, “Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed headlong into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah’s rebellion.”

The pin stands at Deir ‘Alla in the Jordan valley, where a wall text of about 800 BC, found in 1967, tells of a seer named Balaam son of Beor. It is a judgment call, set there because the place gives the one name in this verse that is known outside the Bible. “Woe to them” is the cry of the prophets and of Jesus (Isaiah 5:8-23; Matthew 23:13-29). Three Old Testament names follow. Cain killed his brother (Genesis 4:1-16), and Jewish teachers also remembered him as a man who taught others to sin. Balaam was hired to curse Israel and could not (Numbers 22-24), and he is blamed for leading Israel into immorality and idolatry at Peor (Numbers 31:16; Revelation 2:14); “the error of Balaam” was to do it for pay. Korah led a revolt against Moses and Aaron, and the ground swallowed him and his company (Numbers 16:1-35). The three verbs grow stronger: they have traveled, they have rushed headlong, they have perished. Jude speaks of their ruin as already done. 2 Peter 2:15-16 keeps only Balaam.
f: Deir ‘Alla in the Jordan valley (where a wall text names Balaam son of Beor)

e.n: Hidden reefs at the love feasts: clouds, trees, waves and wandering stars
t: Jude writes, “These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves. They are clouds without water, carried along by the wind; fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted. They are wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame; wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever.”

The pin stands at Nazareth, a judgment call. The letter names no place of writing and no town for its readers. Jude calls himself the brother of James, and the Gospels list a James and a Judas among the brothers of Jesus at Nazareth (Mark 6:3). Many scholars place the letter among Jewish Christians in the land of Israel or Syria, and others suggest Egypt or Asia Minor. The “love feasts” (agapai) were the shared meals of the church, at which the Lord’s Supper was also held (1 Corinthians 11:20-22). This is the clearest use of the name in the New Testament; Ignatius, about AD 110, and Tertullian, about AD 197, describe the meal. The intruders sat at these meals. The Greek word spilades usually means rocks hidden under the sea, a danger to ships, and some translate it “blemishes,” as in 2 Peter 2:13. “Shepherding only themselves” echoes Ezekiel 34:2 and 34:8, on shepherds who feed themselves. Five pictures from nature follow: reefs in the sea, clouds that bring no rain (Proverbs 25:14), trees with no fruit at the end of the harvest season, pulled up by the roots, waves that throw up foam (Isaiah 57:20), and stars that leave their course. The last picture draws on the Book of Enoch, where stars that did not keep their appointed paths are bound in a dark prison (1 Enoch 18:13-16; 21:3-6). The Greek for “wandering” (planētai) gives English the word “planet.”
