In 1 Thessalonians: Apantesis, “meeting,” is used when people go out to meet an arriving person: the bridesmaids meeting the bridegroom (Matthew 25:6) and the believers meeting Paul on the road to Rome (Acts 28:15). In 4:17 believers are caught up “to meet the Lord in the air.”
The Greek πλάνη (planē) means “error.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Matthew (1).
In 1 Thessalonians: Plane, “error,” is a wandering from the path. In 2:3 Paul says his appeal does not arise from “deceit.” It is used of the “delusion” in 2 Thessalonians 2:11.
In 2 Thessalonians: Plane, “error” or “delusion,” is a wandering from the path. In 2:11 God sends “a powerful delusion.” In 1 Thessalonians 2:3 the same word is “deceit.”
In James: Plane, “error” or “wandering,” occurs in James 5:20, “the error of his way,” and the related verb planao in 5:19 (“wander from the truth”). A wanderer is one who has lost the road.
In Jude: Planē occurs once: “the error of Balaam” (11). The related word planētēs gives the “wandering stars” of verse 13.
The Greek πώρωσις (pōrōsis) means “hardening.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Mark (1).
In Ephesians: Porosis, “hardening,” was used of a callus on a bone or a stone-like heart. “The hardness of their hearts” (4:18) is the cause of ignorance; compare Mark 3:5 and Romans 11:25.
The Greek προσκαρτερέω (proskartereō) means “to continue in/with.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Mark (1).
In Acts: To stay with, to be devoted to. It describes the believers’ habits: teaching, fellowship, bread and prayers, and “with one accord in the temple.”
In Colossians: Proskartereo, “to devote oneself,” means to persist or stay near. “Devote yourselves to prayer” (4:2) is the same verb used for the first believers in Acts 2:42.
f: steadfastly continuing, may wait upon, will steadfastly continue, attending, being constant, attending continually

t: The Greek δαμάζω (damazō) means “to tame.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Mark (1).

In James: Damazo, “to tame,” occurs three times in James (3:7, 7, 8) and once in Mark 5:4, where nobody could subdue the man among the tombs. James says that animals have been tamed, but no one can tame the tongue.
f: to subdue, is subdued, he has been subdued

t: The Greek στενάζω (stenazō) means “to groan.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Mark (1).
In Romans: To groan. In Romans 8:22-26 the creation, believers and the Spirit all groan while they wait for the redemption of bodies.
f: he sighed deeply, groan, we groan, groaning, do grumble

t: The Greek ἀββά (abba) means “Father.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Mark (1).

In Galatians: Abba is Aramaic for “Father.” Paul gives it with its Greek translation: “crying out, ‘Abba, Father!’” (4:6). Jesus used it in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), and Paul uses it again in Romans 8:15.
The Greek πρεσβύτης (presbutēs) means “old man.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In Philemon: Presbytes is “an old man.” In verse 9 Paul calls himself “aged.” Some scholars think the original word was presbeutes, “ambassador” (compare Ephesians 6:20), but the manuscripts read “old man.”
f: an old man, aged men, aged

t: The Greek λειτουργία (leitourgia) means “ministry.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In Philippians: Leitourgia is “public service,” from laos (people) and ergon (work). Paul calls the church’s faith a “sacrifice and service” (2:17) and says Epaphroditus risked his life “to make up for your deficit of service to me” (2:30). The related leitourgos, “minister,” is in 2:25.
f: service, on the service, a ministry, ministry

t: The Greek σπλάγχνον (splanchnon) means “affection/entrails.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In Philippians: Splanchnon is the inner body, the seat of deep feeling. It is rendered “affection” in “the affection of Christ Jesus” (1:8) and “affection and compassion” (2:1).

In Philemon: Splagchnon is the plural for the “inner organs,” the seat of deep feeling. Paul uses it in verses 7, 12 and 20. In verse 12 Onesimus is “my very heart.” In English it is usually “heart”; older versions say “bowels.”
f: affections, hearts, intestines, affection, very heart —, heart

t: The Greek ἐπιφαίνω (epiphainō) means “to appear.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In Titus: Epiphaino is “to appear” or “to shine upon.” It is used in 2:11, “the grace of God has appeared,” and in 3:4 for the kindness of God. Elsewhere it describes light shining on those in darkness (Luke 1:79) and stars that cannot be seen in a storm (Acts 27:20).
f: to shine upon, appearing, has appeared, appeared

t: The Greek πατριά (patria) means “family line.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In Ephesians: Patria is a “family” or clan. In 3:14-15 there is a wordplay: the “Father” (pater) from whom every “family” (patria) in heaven and on earth is named.
The Greek πρωτότοκος (prōtotokos) means “firstborn.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In Colossians: Prototokos, “firstborn,” is used in 1:15 (“firstborn over all creation”) and 1:18 (“firstborn from among the dead”). In the Old Testament it describes rank and inheritance as well as birth order (Psalm 89:27).
The Greek ἀποκάλυψις (apokalupsis) means “revelation.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In Galatians: Apokalupsis, “revelation,” is how Paul received the gospel: “I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ” (1:12), God “was pleased to reveal His Son in me” (1:15-16), and he went up to Jerusalem “in response to a revelation” (2:2).
In Revelation: Apokalypsis is the first word of the Greek text, “the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1:1), and gives the book its Greek name and the English word apocalypse.
The Greek νηστεία (nēsteia) means “fasting.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
The Greek συνίστημι (sunistēmi) means “to commend.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In 2 Corinthians: To commend, introduce or recommend. “Are we beginning to commend ourselves again?” (3:1), and “we commend ourselves to every man’s conscience in the sight of God” (4:2). It is a main word of Paul’s defense.
f: already standing with, shows, demonstrates, i commend, to commend, commending

t: The Greek διακονία (diakonia) means “service.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In 2 Corinthians: Service or ministry. Paul speaks of the “ministry of death” (3:7), “the ministry of the Spirit” (3:8), “the ministry of righteousness” (3:9), “the ministry of reconciliation” (5:18), and the collection as “this ministry of service” (9:12).
The Greek πανοπλία (panoplia) means “complete armor.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In Ephesians: Panoplia is “full armor,” the whole kit of a heavy infantry soldier. It gives English “panoply.” Ephesians 6:11 and 6:13 are the only uses in Paul; Luke 11:22 has it too.
The Greek ἀναλύω (analuō) means “to depart.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In Philippians: Analyo, “to depart,” was used for loosing a ship’s moorings or striking a tent. “I desire to depart and be with Christ” (1:23) uses it of death as a departure.
The Greek καταργέω (katargeō) means “to abate.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In 2 Corinthians: To fade, abolish or make ineffective. The glory of Moses was “fleeting” or “fading away” (3:7, 11, 13), while the new covenant “endures.”
f: should it use up, will nullify, do we nullify, has been nullified, may be annulled, she has been cleared

t: The Greek οἰκέτης (oiketēs) means “slave.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In 1 Peter: Oiketes, “household slave,” occurs four times in the New Testament: Luke 16:13, Acts 10:7, Romans 14:4 and 1 Peter 2:18. It names a slave who belonged to a household, as distinct from the more common doulos.
The Greek ἐπισκοπή (episkopē) means “oversight.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In 1 Timothy: Episkope is “oversight” or “visitation.” In 3:1 it names the office of overseer, “he desires a noble task.” In Luke 19:44 it is the “visitation” of God, and in Acts 1:20 it is the office Judas left.
The Greek ὑστέρημα (husterēma) means “deficiency.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In 1 Thessalonians: Hysterema is “what is lacking.” In 3:10 Paul prays to “supply what is lacking from your faith.” The word is also used in Colossians 1:24 and Philippians 2:30.
f: need, poverty, deficiency, needs, deficit, is lacking

t: The Greek ἀπολύτρωσις (apolutrōsis) means “redemption.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In Romans: The price paid to free a slave or captive. Paul uses it for the redemption “that is in Christ Jesus” (3:24) and for “the redemption of our bodies” (8:23).

In Ephesians: Apolytrosis, “redemption,” is the language of buying back a person from slavery or captivity. It occurs three times: “redemption through His blood” (1:7), the Spirit is the pledge “until the redemption of those who are God’s possession” (1:14), and the “day of redemption” (4:30).
The Greek ἄνομος (anomos) means “lawless.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In 2 Thessalonians: Anomos, “lawless,” is the adjective form. “The lawless one” is named in 2:8 as the one the Lord Jesus will “slay with the breath of His mouth.”
f: outside the law, lawless, outside the law —, lawless one, for the lawless

t: The Greek πρεσβυτέριον (presbuterion) means “council of elders.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In 1 Timothy: Presbyterion is a “council of elders.” It occurs in Luke 22:66 and Acts 22:5 for the Jewish council, and in 4:14 for the elders who laid hands on Timothy.
The Greek λυτρόω (lutroō) means “to ransom.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In Titus: Lytroo is “to redeem” or “to ransom,” to set free by payment. It occurs only three times: Luke 24:21, here in 2:14 (“to redeem us from all lawlessness”) and 1 Peter 1:18.

In 1 Peter: Lytroo, “to ransom” or “to redeem,” occurs three times in the New Testament: Luke 24:21 (the disciples hoped Jesus was the one to redeem Israel), Titus 2:14 and 1 Peter 1:18. It is the word for paying the price that frees a slave or prisoner.
f: to redeem, he may redeem, you were redeemed

t: The Greek ἀνόητος (anoētos) means “foolish.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In Galatians: Anoetos means “without understanding,” not “wicked.” Paul uses it twice for the Galatians (3:1, 3), “O foolish Galatians!”
The Greek νοῦς (nous) means “mind.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).
In Romans: The mind. In Romans 12:2 believers are to be transformed by the renewing of the mind; in 7:23 Paul says the law of his mind is at war with another law.
In 1 Corinthians: Mind: “we have the mind of Christ” (2:16), and “I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind” (14:15).
f: mind, with mind, understanding, in mind

t: The Greek ἐπαγγελία (epangelia) means “promise.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in Luke (1).

In Galatians: Epangelia, “promise,” marks the argument of chapter 3. The inheritance “no longer depends on a promise” if it depends on the law, but “God freely granted it to Abraham through a promise” (3:18). Believers are “children of promise” (4:28).

In Hebrews: Epangelia is “promise.” It occurs 14 times in Hebrews, more than in any other New Testament book, and is tied to Abraham (6:12-17; 11:9-17) and to “the promised eternal inheritance” (9:15).
f: promise, promises, the promise, promises given, a promise

t: The Greek ἀνατρέπω (anatrepō) means “to overturn.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in John (1).

In Titus: Anatrepo is “to overturn.” It is used of Jesus overturning the tables in the temple (John 2:15), of teachers who “destroy the faith of some” (2 Timothy 2:18), and in 1:11 of men who “undermine entire households.”
f: he overthrew, they are overthrowing, overthrow

t: The Greek ζῆλος (zēlos) means “zeal.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in John (1).
In 2 Corinthians: Zeal or jealousy: the Corinthians show “zeal” (7:11), and Paul feels “a godly jealousy” for them (11:2).
f: zeal, jealousy, with jealousy, in jealousy, with the jealousy, fury

t: The Greek ἐπουράνιος (epouranios) means “heavenly.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in John (1).

In Ephesians: Epouranios, “heavenly,” is used five times in the phrase “in the heavenly realms” (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12). It names the unseen sphere where Christ reigns and where the powers still contend.
In Hebrews: Epouranios, “heavenly,” occurs 6 times in Hebrews: the calling (3:1), the gift (6:4), the heavenly things (8:5; 9:23), the country (11:16) and the Jerusalem (12:22).
f: heavenly, heavenly realms, heavenly one, heaven, in the heavens, heavenly things

t: The Greek γογγυσμός (gongusmos) means “murmuring.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in John (1).

In Philippians: Gongysmos, “complaining,” is a muttering sound. The Greek Old Testament uses it for Israel’s grumbling in the wilderness, so “without complaining or arguing” (2:14) recalls that story.
The Greek διασπορά (diaspora) means “dispersion.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in John (1).
In James: Diaspora, “scattering” or “dispersion,” occurs in John 7:35, James 1:1 and 1 Peter 1:1. It was the word for the Jews who lived outside the land of Israel.
The Greek ψεῦδος (pseudos) means “lie.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in John (1).
In 2 Thessalonians: Pseudos is “lie” or “falsehood.” It is part of “false wonder” in 2:9 and “the lie” in 2:11.
The Greek ὀσμή (osmē) means “aroma.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in John (1).
In Ephesians: Osme, “aroma,” combines with euodia in “a fragrant offering” (5:2), a phrase the Greek Old Testament uses for a sacrifice that pleases God (Genesis 8:21; Leviticus 1:9).
f: fragrance, an odor, a fragrance, an aroma

t: The Greek λατρεία (latreia) means “ministry.” It appears 1 time in the four Gospels, most in John (1).
In Romans: Service or worship offered to God. Paul says offering your body as a living sacrifice is your “spiritual service of worship” (12:1).
f: service, it is a service, worship, sacred services

t: The Greek ὁμοθυμαδόν (homothumadon) means “united.” It appears 10 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: Luke’s favorite word for the church’s unity. It means “with one mind” and is used in Acts more than anywhere else in the New Testament.
The Greek Κρής (Krēs) means “Cretan.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Titus: Kres is a “Cretan,” a person from Crete. It occurs only here in 1:12 and in Acts 2:11, where Cretans are among the people who hear the apostles at Pentecost.
The Greek ἀτμίς (atmis) means “vapor.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In James: Atmis, “mist” or “vapor,” occurs in Acts 2:19 (“billows of smoke”) and in James 4:14, where life is “a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes.”
The Greek ἐλπίς (elpis) means “hope.” It appears 8 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Romans: Hope is confident waiting for what God has promised. Paul says “suffering produces perseverance” and hope “does not disappoint us” (5:3-5).
In 1 Corinthians: Hope: one of the three that remain (13:13). Love “hopes all things” (13:7).

In 1 Peter: Elpis, “hope,” occurs three times in 1 Peter (1:3, 21; 3:15), and the related verb elpizo twice (1:13; 3:5). In 1:3 the hope is “living” because it rests on the resurrection of Jesus Christ, and in 3:15 it is the “hope that is in you” which the readers must be ready to explain.
f: hope, a hope, our hope, in hope

t: The Greek κοινωνία (koinōnia) means “participation.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: Luke uses it once, for the early church’s shared life: “they devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship.”
In 1 Corinthians: In 1 Corinthians it means a sharing in something: the cup is “a participation in the blood of Christ” and the bread “a participation in the body of Christ” (10:16).

In 2 Corinthians: Fellowship or sharing: “the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” (13:14), the sharing in “this service to the saints” (8:4), and the partnership that light cannot have with darkness (6:14).
In Galatians: Koinonia, “fellowship” or “sharing,” appears in the “right hand of fellowship” (2:9) given to Paul and Barnabas, a handshake of partnership.

In Philippians: Koinonia is “participation” or “partnership.” It appears in “your partnership in the gospel” (1:5), “fellowship with the Spirit” (2:1) and “the fellowship of His sufferings” (3:10). Related words are “partners in grace” (1:7), “share in my affliction” (4:14) and “partnered with me” (4:15).
In Philemon: Koinonia is “partnership,” “sharing” or “fellowship.” In verse 6 Philemon’s “partnership in the faith” is meant to be effective. A related word, koinonos, “partner,” is used in verse 17.
In 1 John: Koinonia, “fellowship,” occurs four times, all in chapter 1: “this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ” (1:3).
f: fellowship, a participation, in fellowship, a contribution, participation, partnership

t: The Greek εὐσέβεια (eusebeia) means “piety.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In 1 Timothy: Eusebeia, “godliness,” is the key word of the letter. It occurs eight times (2:2; 3:16; 4:7, 8; 6:3, 5, 6, 11), more than in any other book of the New Testament. It means reverence toward God shown in a way of life.
In 2 Peter: Eusebeia, “godliness,” occurs four times: “everything we need for life and godliness” (1:3), a link in the chain of qualities (1:6-7), and “holiness and godliness” (3:11).
The Greek ἀρχηγός (archēgos) means “founder.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: Used of Jesus as “Author” or “Leader” of life, and as “Leader and Savior.” It is a person who goes first so that others can follow.

In Hebrews: Archegos is “pioneer,” “founder,” “leader” or “author.” It occurs in Hebrews 2:10 (“the author of their salvation”) and 12:2 (“the author and perfecter of our faith”), and in Acts 3:15 and 5:31.
The Greek ἄγνοια (agnoia) means “ignorance.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: Ignorance. Peter says the people acted in ignorance, and Paul tells Athens that God overlooked the times of ignorance but now calls everyone to repent.
The Greek προορίζω (proorizō) means “to predestine.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Romans: To decide beforehand, predestine. In Romans only at 8:29-30, as part of the chain of foreknowing, predestining, calling, justifying and glorifying.
f: determined beforehand, he predestined to be, he predestined, foreordained, having predestined, having been predestined

t: The Greek Βαρνάβας (Barnabas) means “Barnabas.” It appears 23 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
The Greek νοσφίζω (nosphizō) means “to embezzle.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Titus: Nosphizo is “to set apart for oneself,” the word for “stealing” in 2:10. The only other use is in Acts 5:2-3, where Ananias “kept back” part of the money.
f: he kept back, to keep back, pilfering

t: The Greek πειθαρχέω (peitharcheō) means “to obey.” It appears 3 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Titus: Peitharcheo is “to obey one in authority.” It is used in 3:1 for submitting to rulers. The other uses are in Acts 5:29, 5:32 and 27:21.
f: to obey, obeying, having been obedient, to be obedient

t: The Greek Ἑλληνιστής (Hellēnistēs) means “Hellenist.” It appears 3 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: A Greek-speaking Jew. The Hellenists’ widows were overlooked in the daily food distribution, which led to the choice of the Seven.
The Greek πάροικος (paroikos) means “foreigner.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In 1 Peter: Paroikos, “resident alien,” occurs four times in the New Testament: Acts 7:6 and 7:29 (Abraham’s descendants and Moses in Midian), Ephesians 2:19 (the Gentiles are no longer foreigners) and 1 Peter 2:11. A paroikos lived in a place without the rights of a citizen.
The Greek κατάπαυσις (katapausis) means “rest.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In Hebrews: Katapausis is “rest,” “resting place.” It occurs 8 times, all in 3:7-4:11, and always of the “rest” of Psalm 95:11. The related verb katapauo (3 times) is used of God’s rest on the seventh day (4:4) and of Joshua’s failure to give rest (4:8).
The Greek ἐπίθεσις (epithesis) means “laying on.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In 1 Timothy: Epithesis is the “laying on” of hands. It occurs in 4:14, 2 Timothy 1:6, Acts 8:18 and Hebrews 6:2. The related verb epitithemi is in 5:22.
The Greek σύνδεσμος (sundesmos) means “bond(age).” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Colossians: Syndesmos, “bond,” can mean a ligament or a band. In 2:19 the body is “knit together by its joints and ligaments,” and in 3:14 love is “the bond of perfect unity.”
The Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolē) means “epistle.” It appears 5 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In 2 Corinthians: A letter. “You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone” (3:2). Critics said “His letters are weighty and forceful” (10:10).
The Greek ἐκλογή (eklogē) means “selecting.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Romans: Selecting or choosing, the noun behind “election.” Paul uses it of God’s choice of Jacob (9:11) and of the remnant “chosen by grace” (11:5).
The Greek παρρησιάζομαι (parrēsiazomai) means “to preach boldly.” It appears 7 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: The verb form of boldness. Paul and Barnabas and Apollos all “speak boldly” in the synagogues.
f: speaking boldly, he had spoken boldly, having spoken boldly, to speak boldly, he was speaking boldly, using boldness

t: The Greek καταδυναστεύω (katadunasteuō) means “to oppress.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In James: Katadynasteuo, “to oppress” or “to exploit,” is found in Acts 10:38 and James 2:6. In Acts it is what the devil did to those Jesus healed; in James it is what the rich do to the readers.
The Greek Χριστιανός (Christianos) means “Christian.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: A name formed with the Latin ending -ianos, meaning “followers of Christ.” It is used only twice in Acts, first in Antioch and then by King Agrippa.

In 1 Peter: Christianos, “Christian,” occurs three times in the New Testament: Acts 11:26 (the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch), Acts 26:28 (Agrippa), and 1 Peter 4:16. It is a Greek word with a Latin ending, meaning a follower or partisan of Christ.
The Greek Παῦλος (Paulos) means “Paul.” It appears 128 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
f: paul, to paul, after paul, paulus, by paul, with paul

t: The Greek ἀνάγνωσις (anagnōsis) means “reading.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In 1 Timothy: Anagnosis is a “public reading.” It is used of the reading of the Law and Prophets in the synagogue (Acts 13:15), of the reading of Moses (2 Corinthians 3:14) and, in 4:13, of the reading of Scripture in church.
The Greek δρόμος (dromos) means “racecourse.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In 2 Timothy: Dromos is a “course” or “race.” It is used in 4:7, “I have finished the race,” and in Acts 13:25 and 20:24.

e.u: προπέμπω · to help on the way
t: The Greek προπέμπω (propempō) means “to help on the way.” It appears 3 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Titus: Propempo is “to send forward” or “to help on the way” with supplies and company. In 3:13 Titus is to help Zenas and Apollos. It is used in Romans 15:24, 1 Corinthians 16:6 and 3 John 6.
In 3 John: Propempō occurs once: “You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God” (6). It means to equip travelers for the next stage of a journey.
f: having been sent forward, they were accompanying, while are accompanying, to be equipped, may equip, do equip

t: The Greek εἰδωλόθυτος (eidōlothutos) means “sacrificed to idols.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In 1 Corinthians: The word means “food sacrificed to idols.” It is found only nine times in the New Testament, five of them in 1 Corinthians (8:1, 4, 7, 10; 10:19).
The Greek πολιτάρχης (politarchēs) means “city authority.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: The Macedonian word for city magistrates. Luke is nearly the only literary source to use it, and inscriptions from Thessalonica confirm it.
The Greek Ἄρειος Πάγος (Areios pagos) means “Mars’ Hill.” It appears 4 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: The Areopagus, the hill in Athens (“hill of Ares”) and the council that met there. Paul addresses it in Acts 17.
The Greek ἄγνωστος (agnōstos) means “unknown.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: Paul reads the inscription “To an unknown god” on an altar in Athens and says, “What you worship as unknown, this I proclaim to you.”
The Greek ποιητής (poiētēs) means “doer.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In James: Poietes, “doer,” occurs four times in James (1:22, 23, 25; 4:11) and in Romans 2:13. In Acts 17:28 the same word means “poets.” In James 4:11 the one who judges the law is not a “doer” of it but a judge.
The Greek Τυχικός (Tuchikos) means “Tychicus.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Ephesians: Tychikos, Tychicus, is the carrier of the letter (6:21). The name means “fortunate.” He is called a “beloved brother and faithful servant in the Lord.”
The Greek ταπεινοφροσύνη (tapeinophrosunē) means “humility.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Philippians: Tapeinophrosyne is “humble-mindedness,” a word that was seldom a virtue in Greek moral writing. Paul asks the church to act “in humility” (2:3), with the humility modeled by Christ.
In Colossians: Tapeinophrosyne is “humility” or “lowliness of mind.” It is a virtue in 3:12, but in 2:18 and 2:23 Paul describes a “false humility” that he rejects.
The Greek ἐπίσκοπος (episkopos) means “overseer.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: Literally “overseer.” Paul uses it of the Ephesian elders whom the Holy Spirit has made “overseers” to shepherd the church.

In Philippians: Episkopos, “overseer,” is here in the greeting “together with the overseers and deacons” (1:1). The word means someone who looks over a household or group. It is the only time Paul’s opening mentions the office.
In 1 Timothy: Episkopos, “overseer,” is used in 3:2 for the office whose qualities Paul lists. It is used of the elders of Ephesus in Acts 20:28 and in Philippians 1:1 and Titus 1:7.
In Titus: Episkopos is “overseer,” one who watches over. In 1:7 it is used for the same man called “elder” in 1:5. It also occurs in Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:2 and 1 Peter 2:25.

In 1 Peter: Episkopos, “overseer,” occurs five times in the New Testament (Acts 20:28, Philippians 1:1, 1 Timothy 3:2, Titus 1:7 and 1 Peter 2:25). In 1 Peter 2:25 it is a title of Christ, the “Overseer of your souls.” The related episkope in 2:12 is the “day He visits us.”
The Greek εὐαγγελιστής (euangelistēs) means “evangelist.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In 2 Timothy: Euangelistes is an “evangelist,” a bringer of good news. It occurs only three times in the New Testament: Acts 21:8 (Philip), Ephesians 4:11 and 2 Timothy 4:5 (“do the work of an evangelist”).
The Greek ἀποστασία (apostasia) means “apostasy.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In 2 Thessalonians: Apostasia is a “rebellion” or “revolt.” The English word “apostasy” comes from it. It occurs in 2:3 and in Acts 21:21, where it means a turning away from Moses. Older English translations rendered 2:3 as “falling away.”
The Greek στοιχέω (stoicheō) means “to follow.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Galatians: Stoicheo, “to walk in line,” is related to stoicheion (4:3). Paul says “let us walk in step with the Spirit” (5:25) and speaks of “all who walk by this rule” (6:16).
f: you walk orderly, walking, we shall walk, will walk, we are to walk

t: The Greek ἀπολογία (apologia) means “defence.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Acts: A speech in defense. Paul gives apologies at Jerusalem, before Felix, Festus and Agrippa.

In Philippians: Apologia, “defense,” is the word for a legal defense in court. Paul uses it of “my defense and confirmation of the gospel” (1:7) and of being “appointed for the defense of the gospel” (1:16).

In 1 Peter: Apologia, “defense,” occurs eight times in the New Testament: Acts 22:1 and 25:16; 1 Corinthians 9:3; 2 Corinthians 7:11; Philippians 1:7 and 1:16; 2 Timothy 4:16; and 1 Peter 3:15. It is a speech in one’s own defense, such as before a court. The English word “apology” and the term “apologetics” come from it.
The Greek συνείδησις (suneidēsis) means “conscience.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In 1 Corinthians: Conscience: the inner sense of right and wrong. A “weak” conscience is “defiled” (8:7), and one should not eat for the sake of someone else’s conscience (10:28).

In Hebrews: Suneidesis, “conscience,” occurs 5 times in Hebrews (9:9, 14; 10:2, 22; 13:18). The writer says that the old sacrifices could not “cleanse the conscience of the worshiper,” and that Christ’s blood does.
f: conscience, a conscience, consciences, 16 a conscience

t: The Greek πολιτεύω (politeuō) means “be a citizen.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In Philippians: Politeuomai means to live as a citizen of a polis. “Conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel” (1:27) is literally to live as citizens. The only other New Testament use is Paul’s defense in Acts 23:1.
f: have lived as a citizen, do conduct yourselves

t: The Greek ἀνάθεμα (anathema) means “devoted.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In Galatians: Anathema is something set apart and handed over to God’s judgment. In 1:8-9 Paul says anyone who preaches another gospel is to “be under a curse.” The word also appears in Romans 9:3 and 1 Corinthians 16:22.
f: accursed, with an oath, a curse, accursed is

t: The Greek ἐγκόπτω (enkoptō) means “to impede.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In 1 Thessalonians: Enkopto means “to hinder” or “to block the way.” In 2:18 Satan “obstructed us.” The same verb is used in Romans 15:22 and Galatians 5:7.
f: i may be a hindrance, i was being hindered, impeded, hindered, cause to be impeded

t: The Greek θρησκεία (thrēskeia) means “religion.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Colossians: Threskeia, “worship” or religious practice, is used for the “worship of angels” (2:18). In James 1:26-27 it means religion in outward form.

In James: Threskeia, “religion” or outward worship, occurs only four times in the New Testament (Acts 26:5; Colossians 2:18; James 1:26, 27). James’s definition in 1:27 is the care of orphans and widows and a clean life.
The Greek ζημία (zēmia) means “damage/loss.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Philippians: Zemia, “loss,” is the opposite of kerdos, “gain.” In 3:7-8 Paul uses a ledger: what was gain he now counts as loss, “for the sake of Christ.”
The Greek παραχειμάζω (paracheimazō) means “to winter.” It appears 2 times in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In Titus: Paracheimazo is “to spend the winter.” In 3:12 Paul has “decided to winter” at Nicopolis. The other uses are in Acts 27:12 and 1 Corinthians 16:6.
f: to winter there —, having wintered, i will winter, to winter

t: The Greek πηδάλιον (pēdalion) means “rudder.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.
In James: Pedalion, “rudder,” occurs only in Acts 27:40 (plural, the steering oars of Paul’s ship) and in James 3:4.
The Greek φιλανθρωπία (philanthrōpia) means “benevolence.” It appears 1 time in Acts and not in the Gospels.

In Titus: Philanthropia is “love for mankind,” from the roots for “love” and “human being.” It occurs only here in 3:4 and in Acts 28:2, where the people of Malta show Paul and the others “extraordinary kindness.”
The Greek ὑπακοή (hupakoē) means “obedience.” It appears 7 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: Obedience. Paul opens and closes Romans with “the obedience that comes from faith” (1:5; 16:26) and sets Christ’s obedience against Adam’s disobedience (5:19).
The Greek ἐπιποθέω (epipotheō) means “to long for.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Philippians: Epipotheo, “to long for,” is a word for deep desire. Paul says, “I long for all of you with the affection of Christ Jesus” (1:8), and Epaphroditus “has been longing for all of you” (2:26). The related adjective appears in 4:1, “whom I love and long for.”
f: longing, i long, a longing, i long after, longing after, yearns

t: The Greek χάρισμα (charisma) means “gift.” It appears 6 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In 1 Corinthians: Charisma means a gift given freely by grace. Paul uses it for the gifts of the Spirit (12:4-31) and for the gift of marriage or singleness (7:7).
f: gifts, gift, grace bestowed, a gift

t: The Greek πνευματικός (pneumatikos) means “spiritual.” It appears 3 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In 1 Corinthians: The word used for “spiritual” gifts, people and bodies: “spiritual gifts” (12:1), “spiritual truths in spiritual words” (2:13), and the “spiritual body” of the resurrection (15:44).
f: spiritual, spiritual things, spiritual gifts, by spiritual means, to spiritual, spiritual ones

t: The Greek ποίημα (poiēma) means “workmanship.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Ephesians: Poiema, “workmanship,” is the word from which English gets “poem.” It means something made with skill, a work of art. “We are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (2:10); compare Romans 1:20.
The Greek ἄφθαρτος (aphthartos) means “incorruptible.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 1 Peter: Aphthartos, “imperishable,” occurs three times in 1 Peter: of the inheritance (1:4), the seed of the new birth (1:23), and the beauty of “a gentle and quiet spirit” (3:4). In all it occurs seven times in the New Testament, in 1 Corinthians, Romans, 1 Timothy and 1 Peter.
The Greek ἐπίγνωσις (epignōsis) means “knowledge.” It appears 3 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Colossians: Epignosis is “full knowledge,” a stronger form of gnosis. Paul prays for the “knowledge of His will” (1:9) and says the Colossians are “growing in the knowledge of God” (1:10). He uses it against teachers who offered other kinds of knowledge.

In 2 Peter: Epignosis, “knowledge,” occurs four times, always of knowing God or Christ: “through the knowledge of God and of Jesus our Lord” (1:2), “the knowledge of Him who called us” (1:3), “your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:8), and “the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (2:20).
f: knowledge, a knowledge, is knowledge, acknowledgment

t: The Greek χρηστότης (chrēstotēs) means “kindness.” It appears 5 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Titus: Chrestotes is “kindness” or “goodness.” In 3:4 it is the kindness of “God our Savior” that “appeared.” Paul also uses it in Romans 2:4, where God’s kindness leads to repentance, and in Galatians 5:22 as a fruit of the Spirit.
The Greek προσωποληψία (prosōpolēpsia) means “favoritism.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Ephesians: Prosopolempsia, “favoritism,” means literally to “receive the face,” to judge by outward position. “There is no favoritism with Him” (6:9); compare Romans 2:11.

In James: Prosopolempsia, “favoritism,” literally “receiving the face,” translates a Hebrew idiom for lifting a person’s face. It occurs in Romans 2:11, Ephesians 6:9, Colossians 3:25 and James 2:1. The verb prosopolepteo is found only in James 2:9.
The Greek ἀκροατής (akroatēs) means “hearer.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In James: Akroates, “hearer,” occurs three times in James (1:22, 23, 25) and in Romans 2:13. The same pairing of “hearers” and “doers” appears in both James and Paul.
The Greek καυχάομαι (kauchaomai) means “to boast.” It appears 5 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In 1 Corinthians: To boast: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (1:31). Boasting in men and in knowledge is what the Corinthians are told to give up (3:21; 4:7).

In 2 Corinthians: In 2 Corinthians boasting is the main issue between Paul and his critics. “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (10:17), and “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness” (11:30).
In Galatians: Kauchaomai, “to boast.” The agitators boast in the Galatians’ flesh (6:13). Paul says “may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).
f: boasting, to boast, you boast, should boast, may boast, boast

t: The Greek μόρφωσις (morphōsis) means “form.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In 2 Timothy: Morphosis is “outward form” or “appearance.” It occurs in 3:5, “a form of godliness but denying its power,” and in Romans 2:20.
The Greek ἱλαστήριος (hilastērios) means “propitiation.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: Used for the “atoning sacrifice” in Romans 3:25. The same word names the lid of the ark, the mercy seat, in the Greek Old Testament and in Hebrews 9:5.
The Greek κενόω (kenoō) means “to empty.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Philippians: Kenoo, “to empty,” appears here in the sense of Christ “emptied Himself” (2:7). Paul does not say what he emptied. The verse goes on to say how: “taking the form of a servant.” Elsewhere the verb means to make void (Romans 4:14; 1 Corinthians 1:17).
f: has been made void, may be emptied of power, will make void, may be made void, emptied

t: The Greek νεκρόω (nekroō) means “to put to death.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Colossians: Nekroo, “to put to death,” is a command in 3:5: “Put to death, therefore, the components of your earthly nature.” It is formed from nekros, “dead.”
f: expired, do put to death, as good as dead

t: The Greek δικαίωσις (dikaiōsis) means “justification.” It appears 2 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: A rare word in the New Testament, used for the verdict itself. In Romans 4:25 Jesus “was raised to life for our justification.”
The Greek προσαγωγή (prosagōgē) means “access.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Ephesians: Prosagoge is “access,” the right to be led into the presence of a ruler. Gentiles and Jews alike have “access to the Father by one Spirit” (2:18), and “in Him and through faith in Him we may enter God’s presence” (3:12); compare Romans 5:2.
The Greek καταλλάσσω (katallassō) means “to reconcile.” It appears 2 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 2 Corinthians: To reconcile means to change from enmity to friendship. God “reconciled us to Himself through Christ” (5:18) and “was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them” (5:19).
f: we were reconciled, having been reconciled, she should be reconciled, having reconciled, reconciling, do be reconciled

t: The Greek καταλλαγή (katallagē) means “reconciliation.” It appears 2 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: Reconciliation, a change from enmity to friendship. Romans 5:10-11 says believers were reconciled to God while they were still enemies.
In 2 Corinthians: Reconciliation: Paul says God “gave us the ministry of reconciliation” and “committed to us the message of reconciliation” (5:18-19).
The Greek ἐλλογέω (ellogeō) means “to charge.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Philemon: Ellogeo, “to charge to someone’s account,” is a bookkeeping word. In verse 18 Paul tells Philemon to put anything Onesimus owes on Paul’s account. The only other use in the New Testament is Romans 5:13.
The Greek ἐφάπαξ (ephapax) means “once/at once.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Hebrews: Ephapax, “once for all,” occurs in Hebrews 7:27, 9:12 and 10:10; elsewhere in the New Testament only in Romans 6:10 and 1 Corinthians 15:6. The related hapax, “once,” is used 8 times in Hebrews, including “once more” in 12:26-27.
The Greek ἁγιασμός (hagiasmos) means “holiness.” It appears 2 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: Holiness or sanctification. Paul says that those who were slaves to sin are now slaves to God, and “the fruit you reap leads to holiness” (6:22).
In 1 Thessalonians: Hagiasmos is “holiness” or “being made holy.” It is used in 4:3, 4, 7. It comes from hagios, “holy,” which means set apart for God.
The Greek πάθημα (pathēma) means “suffering.” It appears 2 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 1 Peter: Pathema, “suffering,” occurs four times in 1 Peter (1:11; 4:13; 5:1, 9), always in the plural. It speaks of “the sufferings of Christ” (1:11; 4:13; 5:1) and the same sufferings undergone by “your brothers throughout the world” (5:9).
The Greek ὑπερβολή (huperbolē) means “surpassing.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 2 Corinthians: Surpassing or beyond measure. The English word “hyperbole” comes from it. Paul speaks of “this surpassingly great power” (4:7), “far beyond comparison” (4:17), and “surpassingly great revelations” (12:7).
f: excess, a more surpassing, excessively, surpassingness, surpassing, excessiveness

t: The Greek ἐνοικέω (enoikeō) means “to dwell in/with.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Colossians: Enoikeo, “to dwell in,” is used of the word of Christ: “Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you” (3:16). It describes a guest who lives in a house.
f: dwelling, i will dwell, should dwell, dwelt, is dwelling

t: The Greek υἱοθεσία (huiothesia) means “adoption (as son).” It appears 3 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: Adoption as a son. In Roman law it gave a person the full rights of an heir. Paul says believers have the Spirit of sonship (8:15) and that the adoption belongs to Israel (9:4).

In Galatians: Huiothesia, “adoption as sons.” In Galatians 4:5 God sent his Son “to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons.” It also occurs in Romans 8:15, 8:23 and 9:4, and in Ephesians 1:5.
The Greek συγκληρονόμος (sunklēronomos) means “co-heir.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Ephesians: Synkleronomos is a “fellow heir” (3:6). Paul uses it also of believers who share Christ’s inheritance in Romans 8:17.
The Greek ἀποκαραδοκία (apokaradokia) means “eager expectation.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: A word for stretching out the neck to look ahead. Paul says the creation “waits in eager expectation” (8:19).
In Philippians: Apokaradokia, “eager expectation,” pictures a person stretching the neck to see. It occurs only here (1:20) and in Romans 8:19, where creation waits with the same longing.
The Greek ἀπεκδέχομαι (apekdechomai) means “to expect.” It appears 3 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Philippians: Apekdechomai, “to eagerly await,” pictures leaning forward to wait. “We eagerly await a Savior from there” (3:20). Paul uses it for the hope of the return of Christ and the redemption of the body (Romans 8:23, 25; 1 Corinthians 1:7).
f: awaits, awaiting, we await, eagerly awaiting, eagerly await, we are awaiting

t: The Greek ματαιότης (mataiotēs) means “futility.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Ephesians: Mataiotes, “futility,” is the emptiness of a life that misses its purpose; compare Romans 8:20. Gentiles walk “in the futility of their thinking” (4:17).
The Greek ἐλευθερία (eleutheria) means “freedom.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Galatians: Eleutheria, “freedom.” Paul says “It is for freedom that Christ has set us free” (5:1) and warns against using it “as an opportunity for the flesh” (5:13).
In James: Eleutheria, “freedom,” occurs in James twice, in the phrase “the perfect law of freedom” (1:25) and “the law that gives freedom” (2:12). James sees the law as liberating, not as a burden.
The Greek ἀπαρχή (aparchē) means “firstfruits.” It appears 3 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 1 Corinthians: The first part of a harvest, offered to God. Christ is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (15:20), and Stephanas’s household were the first converts in Achaia (16:15).
f: firstfruit, a firstfruit, from the beginning, firstfruits

t: The Greek κίνδυνος (kindunos) means “danger.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In 2 Corinthians: Danger. Paul lists “danger from rivers and from bandits” and other dangers (11:26).
The Greek σαβαώθ (sabaōth) means “of Hosts.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In James: Sabaoth, “of Hosts,” is a Greek spelling of a Hebrew word for armies. It occurs only in Romans 9:29 and James 5:4, both times in the title “Lord of Hosts.”
The Greek πρόσκομμα (proskomma) means “stumbling block.” It appears 4 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 1 Peter: Proskomma, “stumbling” or “obstacle,” occurs six times in the New Testament: Romans 9:32, 9:33, 14:13, 14:20, 1 Corinthians 8:9 and 1 Peter 2:8. Peter and Paul both apply Isaiah 8:14 to Christ as a stone that trips those who do not believe.
f: stumbling, any stumbling block, a stumbling block, an occasion of stumbling

t: The Greek πταίω (ptaiō) means “to stumble.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In James: Ptaio, “to stumble,” occurs three times in James (2:10; 3:2, twice), and in Romans 11:11 and 2 Peter 1:10. In James 3:2 it is the verb of “we all stumble in many ways.”
f: they did stumble, may stumble, we stumble, does stumble

t: The Greek συγκοινωνός (sunkoinōnos) means “sharer.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Philippians: Sygkoinonos, “fellow partaker,” is a double compound (syn + koinonos): “you are all partners in grace with me” (1:7). Paul uses the word of himself and the church together.
f: a fellow-partaker, a fellow partaker, fellow partakers

t: The Greek κλῆσις (klēsis) means “calling.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Ephesians: Klesis, “calling,” marks the three parts of the letter’s hope: “the hope of His calling” (1:18), “walk in a manner worthy of the calling” (4:1), and “called to one hope when you were called” (4:4).
f: calling, with a calling, the calling

t: The Greek ἀνεξιχνίαστος (anexichniastos) means “unsearchable.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Ephesians: Anexichniastos means “unsearchable” or “that cannot be traced out,” as when a trail cannot be followed. Paul speaks of “the unsearchable riches of Christ” (3:8); compare Romans 11:33.
The Greek λογικός (logikos) means “spiritual.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 1 Peter: Logikos, “spiritual” or “of the word,” is found in the New Testament only in Romans 12:1 (“your spiritual service of worship”) and 1 Peter 2:2 (“pure spiritual milk”). It is built on logos, “word,” and the exact sense in each place is debated.
The Greek συσχηματίζω (suschēmatizō) means “to conform to.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: To shape in the pattern of something else. Paul says, “Do not be conformed to this world” (12:2), and the world’s pattern is the one to resist.
The Greek ἀνακαίνωσις (anakainōsis) means “renewal.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Titus: Anakainosis is “renewal,” making new again. It occurs only here in 3:5 and in Romans 12:2, “the renewing of your mind.”
The Greek ἁπλότης (haplotēs) means “openness.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 2 Corinthians: Singleness or simplicity, and from that sincerity and generosity. Paul speaks of “sincerity” (1:12), “rich generosity” (8:2), “the generosity of your contribution” (9:13), and “simple and pure devotion to Christ” (11:3).
f: generosity, sincerity, openness, to the generosity, simplicity

t: The Greek προΐστημι (proistēmi) means “to set before.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 1 Timothy: Proistemi means “to stand before,” then “to lead,” “to manage” or “to care for.” It is used of the overseer who must “manage his own household well” (3:4, 5, 12) and of “elders who lead effectively” (5:17).

In Titus: Proistemi, “to stand before,” means to lead, manage or give oneself to. In 3:8 and 3:14 it is translated “devote themselves” to good works. In 1 Timothy 3:4-5 it is used of managing a household and caring for the church.
f: leading, taking the lead, managing, to manage, already ruling, to be devoted

t: The Greek φιλαδελφία (philadelphia) means “brotherly love.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 1 Peter: Philadelphia, “brotherly love,” is found six times in the New Testament: Romans 12:10, 1 Thessalonians 4:9, Hebrews 13:1, 1 Peter 1:22 and 2 Peter 1:7 (twice). In 1 Peter it is the fruit of obeying the truth: “Since you have purified your souls by obedience to the truth so that you have a genuine love for your brothers, love one another deeply, from a pure heart” (1:22).
In 2 Peter: Philadelphia, “brotherly kindness,” is the seventh link of the chain (1:7), set between godliness and love.
The Greek φιλοξενία (philoxenia) means “hospitality.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: Hospitality, literally love of strangers. Paul tells the Roman believers to practice it (12:13).
The Greek ἄνθραξ (anthrax) means “charcoal.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: Charcoal. In the New Testament it appears only in Romans 12:20, where Paul quotes Proverbs about heaping “burning coals” on an enemy’s head.
The Greek εἰκῇ (eikē) means “in vain.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Galatians: Eike, “for nothing” or “in vain,” appears in 3:4 (“for nothing” twice) and 4:11 (“in vain”), the fear that the Galatians’ experience and Paul’s work might come to nothing.
The Greek ἔκδικος (ekdikos) means “avenging.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In 1 Thessalonians: Ekdikos, “avenger,” is a person who sees that justice is done. In 4:6 “the Lord will avenge all such acts.” The word is also used of the government in Romans 13:4.
The Greek ἀνακεφαλαιόομαι (anakephalaioomai) means “to summarise.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In Ephesians: Anakephalaioo means to sum up or bring together under one head (kephale). “To bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ” (1:10) uses it; the only other use is Romans 13:9, where all the commandments are “summed up” in love.
f: it is summed up, to bring together

t: The Greek δόκιμος (dokimos) means “tested.” It appears 2 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.

In 2 Corinthians: Tested and approved: “it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends” (10:18). The word was used of coins and metals that passed the test.
The Greek εὐλογία (eulogia) means “praise.” It appears 2 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In 2 Corinthians: Blessing. In chapter 9 it also means a generous gift: “the bountiful gift you had promised” (9:5).
f: blessing, blessings, the blessing, flattery, a blessing

t: The Greek προστάτις (prostatis) means “patroness.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Romans: The only use in the New Testament is for Phoebe, a patron (a protector and benefactor) of many, including Paul.
The Greek συνεργός (sunergos) means “co-worker.” It appears 3 times in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Philippians: Synergos, “fellow worker,” is one of Paul’s favorite titles for partners in the gospel. He gives it to Epaphroditus (2:25) and to “the rest of my fellow workers” (4:3).
In Philemon: Synergos is “fellow worker,” one who works alongside. Paul uses it of Philemon (verse 1), and of Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke (verse 24).
In 3 John: Synergos occurs once: “so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (8). Paul uses the word of his co-workers; here it is given to those who support traveling workers from home.
f: fellow worker, fellow workers, a fellow worker, the fellow workers

t: The Greek συναιχμάλωτος (sunaichmalōtos) means “fellow prisoner.” It appears 1 time in Romans and not in the Gospels or Acts.
In Philemon: Synaichmalotos is “fellow prisoner,” a captive alongside another. It occurs in verse 23 for Epaphras, and in Romans 16:7 and Colossians 4:10 for others.
The Greek ἀνέγκλητος (anenklētos) means “irreproachable.” It appears 1 time in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.

In Titus: Anenkletos is “above reproach,” with no charge that can be brought against a person. In Titus it describes the elder in 1:6 and the overseer in 1:7. It is used in 1 Corinthians 1:8, Colossians 1:22 and 1 Timothy 3:10.
The Greek ψυχικός (psuchikos) means “natural.” It appears 4 times in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.

In James: Psychikos, “natural,” “of the soul,” and so “unspiritual,” occurs six times in the New Testament: four in 1 Corinthians, here in James 3:15, and in Jude 19. In James it is the wisdom that lacks the Spirit.
In Jude: Psychikos occurs once, in “worldly and devoid of the Spirit” (19): people who live by natural life alone.
The Greek μετασχηματίζω (metaschēmatizō) means “to transform.” It appears 1 time in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.
In Philippians: Metaschematizo, “to transform,” changes the outward form or fashion. The Savior “will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (3:21).
f: i have applied, disguising themselves, masquerades, masquerade, will transform

t: The Greek φυσιόω (phusioō) means “to inflate.” It appears 6 times in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.
In 1 Corinthians: To puff up or inflate, a word for pride. Paul uses it often in this letter: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (8:1), and love “is not proud” (13:4).
f: puffed up, you be puffed up, were puffed up, puffs up, is puffed up, being puffed up

t: The Greek παιδαγωγός (paidagōgos) means “guardian.” It appears 1 time in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.

In Galatians: Paidagogos, “guardian,” names the slave who led a boy to school and kept watch over him. It is not the word for “teacher.” In 3:24-25 the law is this kind of guardian “to lead us to Christ.” Paul uses the word once more in 1 Corinthians 4:15.
The Greek ὄλεθρος (olethros) means “destructive.” It appears 1 time in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.
In 1 Thessalonians: Olethros is “ruin” or “destruction.” In 5:3 it comes on those who say “Peace and security,” and it is used again in 2 Thessalonians 1:9 and 1 Corinthians 5:5.
In 2 Thessalonians: Olethros is “destruction.” In 1:9 it is “eternal destruction,” separated from “the presence of the Lord.”
The Greek κρείσσων (kreissōn) means “greater.” It appears 3 times in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.

In Hebrews: Kreitton, “better,” is the letter’s signature word. It occurs 13 times, as in “a better covenant” (7:22), “better promises” (8:6), “better sacrifices” (9:23) and “a better country” (11:16).
f: better, a better, superior, with better, to a better one, better thing

t: The Greek βραβεῖον (brabeion) means “prize.” It appears 1 time in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.
In Philippians: Brabeion, “prize,” is the award given to the winner of a contest. It is used in 3:14 and in 1 Corinthians 9:24.
The Greek εἰδωλολατρεία (eidōlolatreia) means “idolatry.” It appears 1 time in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.
In Colossians: Eidololatria, “idolatry,” is worship of an image. In 3:5 Paul writes that “greed, which is idolatry.”
The Greek μάκελλον (makellon) means “meat market.” It appears 1 time in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.
In 1 Corinthians: The meat market. This is the only place in the New Testament where the word appears: “Eat anything sold in the meat market” (10:25).
The Greek ἔσοπτρον (esoptron) means “mirror.” It appears 1 time in 1 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts or Romans.

In James: Esoptron, “mirror,” is used in the New Testament only in 1:23 and in 1 Corinthians 13:12. Ancient mirrors were polished metal and gave a dim image, so the man in James takes a quick look and forgets.
The Greek ἀρραβών (arrabōn) means “guarantee.” It appears 2 times in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In 2 Corinthians: A down payment that guarantees the rest. God gave the Spirit “as a pledge of what is to come” (1:22; 5:5). Modern Greek still uses the word for an engagement.
In Ephesians: Arrhabon is a “pledge” or first payment that guarantees the rest. The Spirit is “the pledge of our inheritance” (1:14).
The Greek πλεονεκτέω (pleonekteō) means “to exploit.” It appears 4 times in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In 2 Corinthians: To take advantage of. It is “outwit” in 2:11, “exploited” in 7:2, and “exploit” in 12:17-18.
f: we may be outwitted, we have exploited, did i exploit, did exploit, to overreach

t: The Greek νόημα (noēma) means “mind/thought.” It appears 5 times in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In 2 Corinthians: A thought, scheme or mind. Satan’s “schemes” (2:11), the “minds” that were closed (3:14) and blinded (4:4), and “every thought” taken captive (10:5).
The Greek θριαμβεύω (thriambeuō) means “to triumph.” It appears 1 time in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In 2 Corinthians: To lead in a triumph. It is found only here and in Colossians 2:15. God “always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ” (2:14).
In Colossians: Thriambeuo, “to lead in triumph,” is the language of a Roman triumph. In 2:15 God triumphs “over them by the cross.” Paul uses it also in 2 Corinthians 2:14.
The Greek ὑπερβάλλω (huperballō) means “to surpass.” It appears 2 times in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.

In Ephesians: Hyperballo, “to surpass,” shows up in Paul’s heaping of superlatives: “the surpassing greatness of His power” (1:19), “the surpassing riches of His grace” (2:7), and a love “that surpasses knowledge” (3:19).
The Greek κάλυμμα (kalumma) means “veil.” It appears 4 times in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.

In 2 Corinthians: A veil or covering. The Greek Old Testament uses the same word for the veil of Moses in Exodus 34. Paul says “the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant” (3:14), and “whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away” (3:16).
The Greek πρεσβεύω (presbeuō) means “be ambassador.” It appears 1 time in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In 2 Corinthians: To be an ambassador. The verb appears only here and in Ephesians 6:20: “we are ambassadors for Christ” (5:20).

In Ephesians: Presbeuo, “to be an ambassador,” is a word for a representative sent by a king or city. Paul is “an ambassador in chains” (6:20); compare 2 Corinthians 5:20. Chains (halysis) were what an ambassador was never supposed to wear.
f: we are ambassadors, i am an ambassador

t: The Greek γνήσιος (gnēsios) means “genuine.” It appears 1 time in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In 1 Timothy: Gnesios is “genuine” or “legitimate.” Paul calls Timothy “my true child in the faith” (1:2). The word is also used in 2 Corinthians 8:8, Philippians 4:3 and Titus 1:4.
The Greek ὑπόστασις (hupostasis) means “confidence/essence.” It appears 2 times in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.

In Hebrews: Hupostasis is literally “that which stands under.” It occurs in 1:3 (the Son is “the exact representation of His nature”), 3:14 (“the assurance we had at first”) and 11:1 (“faith is the assurance of what we hope for”). Translators vary between “substance,” “assurance,” “nature” and “being.”
The Greek αὐτάρκεια (autarkeia) means “self-sufficiency.” It appears 1 time in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In 1 Timothy: Autarkeia, “contentment” or “self-sufficiency,” occurs in 6:6 and 2 Corinthians 9:8. The related adjective autarkes is in Philippians 4:11.
The Greek ὁμολογία (homologia) means “confession.” It appears 1 time in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In 1 Timothy: Homologia is a “confession,” saying the same thing. It occurs in 6:12-13, 2 Corinthians 9:13 and Hebrews 3:1, 4:14 and 10:23.
The Greek καταδουλόω (katadouloō) means “to enslave.” It appears 1 time in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In Galatians: Katadouloo, “to enslave,” appears in 2:4, where false brothers wanted “to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us.”
The Greek ψευδάδελφος (pseudadelphos) means “false brother.” It appears 1 time in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In Galatians: Pseudadelphos, “false brother,” appears here (2:4) and in 2 Corinthians 11:26. It names people who claimed to be believers and were not.
The Greek φρουρέω (phroureō) means “to guard.” It appears 1 time in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.

In Philippians: Phroureo, “to guard,” is a military word for a garrison or sentry. “The peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds” (4:7). Paul uses it for a city under guard in 2 Corinthians 11:32 and for the law that held us “in custody” in Galatians 3:23.

In 1 Peter: Phroureo, “to guard” or “to garrison,” occurs four times in the New Testament: 2 Corinthians 11:32, Galatians 3:23, Philippians 4:7 and 1 Peter 1:5. It is a military word for a guard posted at a city gate. In 1 Peter the readers are “shielded by God’s power” (1:5).
f: was guarding, we were held in custody, will guard, are being guarded

t: The Greek σκόλοψ (skolops) means “thorn.” It appears 1 time in 2 Corinthians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or 1 Corinthians.
In 2 Corinthians: A thorn, stake or splinter: “a thorn in my flesh” (12:7). Paul does not say what it was.
The Greek κατασκοπέω (kataskopeō) means “to spy.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Galatians: Kataskopeo, “to spy out,” appears only in 2:4, for the false brothers who “had come in under false pretenses to spy on our freedom.”
The Greek στῦλος (stulos) means “pillar.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.

In Galatians: Stulos, “pillar,” in 2:9 names James, Cephas and John as “pillars” of the Jerusalem church. It is also used of the church in 1 Timothy 3:15 and of the one who overcomes in Revelation 3:12.
The Greek Ἰουδαΐζω (Ioudaizō) means “be Jewish.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Galatians: Ioudaizo, “to live like a Jew,” appears only in 2:14: “how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
The Greek βασκαίνω (baskainō) means “to bewitch.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.

In Galatians: Baskaino, “to bewitch,” appears only here in the New Testament (3:1). It was used of casting the evil eye on someone, and Paul uses the picture of a spell to describe how the Galatians have been led astray.
The Greek προευαγγελίζομαι (proeuangelizomai) means “to speak good news.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Galatians: Proeuangelizomai, “to announce the gospel beforehand,” appears only in 3:8, where Scripture “foretold the gospel to Abraham.”
The Greek κατάρα (katara) means “curse.” It appears 3 times in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Galatians: Katara, “curse.” Galatians 3:10 and 3:13 quote the law’s curses (Deuteronomy 27:26; 21:23) and say Christ “redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us.”
The Greek ἐξαγοράζω (exagorazō) means “to redeem.” It appears 2 times in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.

In Galatians: Exagorazo, “to redeem,” is built on agorazo, “to buy in the marketplace.” Paul says Christ “redeemed us from the curse of the law” (3:13) and came “to redeem those under the law” (4:5). The same root is behind “You were bought at a price” in 1 Corinthians 6:20.

In Ephesians: Exagorazo means “to buy out” or “redeem.” “Redeeming the time” (5:16) literally means buying up the opportunity (kairos) because “the days are evil.” Paul uses the verb for Christ’s redemption in Galatians 3:13 and 4:5.
In Colossians: Exagorazo, “to buy back” or “to make the most of,” is used for “redeeming the time” (4:5). The same verb is used for Christ redeeming us from the law in Galatians 3:13.
The Greek μεσίτης (mesitēs) means “mediator.” It appears 2 times in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Mesites is a “mediator,” one who stands between two parties. In 2:5 it is Christ Jesus. The word is used of Moses in Galatians 3:19-20 and of Christ in Hebrews 8:6, 9:15 and 12:24.

In Hebrews: Mesites, “mediator,” occurs three times in Hebrews, all of Jesus and a better covenant (8:6; 9:15; 12:24). In 1 Timothy 2:5 it is used for “one mediator between God and men” and in Galatians 3:19-20 for Moses.
The Greek στοιχεῖον (stoicheion) means “principle.” It appears 2 times in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.

In Galatians: Stoicheion, “basic principle” (4:3, 9). It means something in a row, like letters of the alphabet, and was used of the elements of the world. Paul may mean elementary teachings, the elements, or powers behind them, and scholars differ. It also occurs in Colossians 2:8, 2:20, Hebrews 5:12 and 2 Peter 3:10, 12.

In Colossians: Stoicheion is a basic element, a letter of the alphabet, or a first principle. In 2:8 and 2:20 Paul speaks of the “spiritual forces of the world,” and the same phrase is in Galatians 4:3, 9. It is debated whether he means the elements, elementary teachings or spirits.
The Greek ὠδίνω (ōdinō) means “be in labor.” It appears 2 times in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.

In Galatians: Odino, “to be in labor.” Paul calls the Galatians “My children, for whom I am again in the pains of childbirth until Christ is formed in you” (4:19), and quotes Isaiah 54:1, “you who have never travailed” (4:27).
The Greek μορφόω (morphoō) means “to form.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Galatians: Morphoo, “to form,” appears only in 4:19: “until Christ is formed in you.”
The Greek ἀλληγορέω (allēgoreō) means “to use an analogy.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Galatians: Allegoreo, “to speak figuratively,” is where we get “allegory.” It appears only in 4:24, where the Berean Standard Bible reads “these things serve as illustrations.”
The Greek πραΰτης (prautēs) means “gentleness.” It appears 2 times in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Galatians: Prautes, “gentleness,” appears in the fruit of the Spirit (5:23) and in the way to restore a fallen person, “with a spirit of gentleness” (6:1).
The Greek μυκτηρίζω (muktērizō) means “to mock.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Galatians: Mukterizo, “to mock,” appears only in 6:7. It literally means to turn up the nose at someone. “God is not to be mocked.”
The Greek οἰκεῖος (oikeios) means “of one’s household.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Ephesians: Oikeios means “belonging to the household,” so Gentiles become “members of God’s household” (2:19). Galatians 6:10 uses it for “the household of faith.”
The Greek στίγμα (stigma) means “mark.” It appears 1 time in Galatians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans or the Corinthian letters.
In Galatians: Stigma, “mark,” appears only in 6:17. It meant a mark burned or tattooed into the skin, as on slaves, animals or devotees of a god. Paul says “I bear on my body the marks of Jesus.”
The Greek ἄμωμος (amōmos) means “blameless.” It appears 2 times in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Amomos, “blameless,” frames the letter. God chose us “to be holy and blameless in His presence” (1:4), and Christ will present the church “holy and blameless” (5:27).
In Philippians: Amomos, “blameless,” was used of sacrificial animals without defect. The church is to be “blameless and pure, children of God without fault” (2:15).
In Jude: Amōmos occurs once: God is able “to present you unblemished in His glorious presence” (24).
The Greek κληρόω (klēroō) means “to obtain.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.

In Ephesians: Kleroo, in the form used in 1:11, means to be made a “portion” or heir, often rendered “chosen as God’s own.” It appears only here in the New Testament, and it ties the inheritance to God’s choice.
The Greek περιποίησις (peripoiēsis) means “acquiring.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Peripoiesis means something acquired, a “possession.” “God’s possession” (1:14) is Israel’s old title for God’s people (Malachi 3:17) now given to the church; see also 1 Peter 2:9.

In 1 Peter: Peripoiesis, “possession,” “acquiring,” occurs five times in the New Testament: Ephesians 1:14, 1 Thessalonians 5:9, 2 Thessalonians 2:14, Hebrews 10:39 and 1 Peter 2:9 (“a people for God’s own possession”). The phrase echoes Exodus 19:5, where Israel is God’s “treasured possession.”
The Greek ἐνέργεια (energeia) means “active energy.” It appears 3 times in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.

In Ephesians: Energeia is “working” or active power, the root of the English word energy. Paul speaks of “the working of His mighty strength” (1:19), the working of His power in him (3:7), and the working of each part of the body (4:16).

In 2 Thessalonians: Energeia, “working,” is the power of a force at work. It is used for the “working of Satan” (2:9) and for the “powerful delusion” God sends (2:11, literally a “working of error”). In Colossians 1:29 it is the power of Christ at work in Paul.
The Greek κυριότης (kuriotēs) means “lordship.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Colossians: Kyriotes, “dominion” or “lordship,” names a rank of power. It appears in 1:16 with three other terms for powers, and in Ephesians 1:21, 2 Peter 2:10 and Jude 8.
The Greek συζωοποιέω (suzōopoieō) means “to make alive with.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.

In Ephesians: Synzoopoieo, “to make alive together with,” is one of three “with” verbs in 2:5-6: made alive with Christ, raised with Him, and seated with Him. The prefix syn- (“with”) is the key: believers share in the resurrection and rule of Christ. Colossians 2:13 has a parallel.
f: made us alive with, he made alive together

t: The Greek ἀπαλλοτριόω (apallotrioō) means “to alienate.” It appears 2 times in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Apallotrioo means “to alienate” or make a stranger. It describes Gentiles “alienated from the commonwealth of Israel” (2:12) and “alienated from the life of God” (4:18).
The Greek ἄθεος (atheos) means “without God.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.

In Ephesians: Atheos, “without God,” appears only here in the New Testament (2:12). Paul does not mean that Gentiles denied that gods exist. He means that they had no covenant relationship with the one true God.
The Greek μεσότοιχος (mesotoichos) means “wall.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Mesotoichon, “the middle wall,” means a wall that stands between two spaces. It appears only here in the New Testament (2:14).
The Greek ἀποκαταλλάσσω (apokatallassō) means “to reconcile.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Apokatallasso means “to reconcile fully.” It is used only here (2:16) and twice in Colossians (1:20, 22). The prefix apo- suggests a complete change from enmity to peace.
In Colossians: Apokatallasso, “to reconcile fully,” is a stronger form of katallasso. It appears only in Colossians (1:20, 22) and Ephesians 2:16. It describes a full return to peace after enmity.
f: he may reconcile, to reconcile, he has reconciled you

t: The Greek συμπολίτης (sumpolitēs) means “fellow citizen.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Sympolites, “fellow citizen,” appears only here (2:19). It is one of several “fellow” words in Ephesians that stress the sharing of Jew and Gentile.
The Greek ἀκρογωνιαῖος (akrogōniaios) means “cornerstone.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.

In Ephesians: Akrogoniaios, “cornerstone,” appears in the New Testament only here (2:20) and in 1 Peter 2:6, where both quote Isaiah 28:16. It is the stone at the corner of the foundation that sets the line for the whole building.

In 1 Peter: Akrogoniaios, “cornerstone,” occurs twice in the New Testament: Ephesians 2:20 and 1 Peter 2:6, which quotes Isaiah 28:16. It names the stone set at the corner of a foundation, from which the walls were aligned.
The Greek συναρμολογέω (sunarmologeō) means “to join.” It appears 2 times in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Synarmologeo, “to fit together,” is used for the building (2:21) and the body (4:16). It paints a picture of joints or stones joined exactly.
f: being fitted together, being joined together

t: The Greek σύσσωμος (sussōmos) means “of the same body.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.

In Ephesians: Syssomos, “fellow member of the body,” appears only here (3:6). The verse has three “together” words in a row, fellow heirs, fellow members of the body and fellow partakers, to press the point that Gentiles share everything.
The Greek πολυποίκιλος (polupoikilos) means “manifold.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Polypoikilos, “manifold,” means many-colored or richly varied. “The manifold wisdom of God” (3:10) appears only here in the New Testament.
The Greek ἑνότης (henotēs) means “unity.” It appears 2 times in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Henotes, “unity,” appears only in Ephesians (4:3, 13). Believers are asked to “preserve the unity of the Spirit” (4:3) and to reach “unity in the faith” (4:13).
The Greek καταρτισμός (katartismos) means “preparation.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Katartismos, “equipping,” comes from a verb used of mending nets (Mark 1:19) and setting a bone. The leaders’ work is “to equip the saints for works of ministry” (4:12).
The Greek μεθοδεία (methodeia) means “scheme.” It appears 2 times in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Methodeia, “scheme,” is the root of English “method.” Wrong teachers use “deceitful scheming” (4:14), and the devil has “schemes” (6:11).
The Greek ἐπιχορηγία (epichorēgia) means “supply.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Philippians: Epichoregia, “provision” or “supply,” comes from the chorus-leader who paid for a drama chorus in Greek cities. Paul trusts in “the provision of the Spirit of Jesus Christ” (1:19).
The Greek εὔσπλαγχνος (eusplanchnos) means “compassionate.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Eusplanchnos, “tenderhearted,” is built from splanchna, the inner organs where the ancients located deep feeling. “Be kind and tenderhearted to one another” (4:32).
The Greek συγκοινωνέω (sunkoinōneō) means “to share with.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Philippians: Sygkoinoneo, “to share with,” is used for sharing in Paul’s trouble: “you have done well to share in my affliction” (4:14). The church became a partner in his chains.
f: do have fellowship with, having fellowship in

t: The Greek ὕμνος (humnos) means “hymn.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.

In Ephesians: Hymnos, “hymn,” is one of three terms in “psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” (5:19). Colossians 3:16 repeats the list. Scholars disagree whether they mean three kinds of songs or one flow of worship.
The Greek λουτρόν (loutron) means “washing.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Loutron, “washing,” is a bath. “The washing with water through the word” (5:26) has been read as baptism, and the only other use is Titus 3:5 (“the washing of rebirth”).

In Titus: Loutron is a “washing” or “bath.” It occurs only in 3:5 and in Ephesians 5:26, “the washing with water through the word.” The related verb louo is used of washing the body (Acts 9:37; Hebrews 10:22).
The Greek παιδεία (paideia) means “discipline.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Paideia is the training of a child (pais). Fathers are told to bring children up in “the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (6:4).

In Hebrews: Paideia, “discipline,” is the training of a child. It occurs 4 times, all in 12:5-11, and the related verb paideuo three times. It is the word for “discipline” in Proverbs 3:11-12, which the writer quotes.
The Greek πάλη (palē) means “struggle.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
