In Ephesians: Pale means “wrestling,” close hand-to-hand struggle. “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood” (6:12) uses it, and it appears only here in the New Testament.
The Greek κοσμοκράτωρ (kosmokratōr) means “world power.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Kosmokrator, “world ruler,” appears only here (6:12). Elsewhere in Greek it is used of gods and rulers. Paul puts it with “the powers of this world’s darkness.”
The Greek θώραξ (thōrax) means “breastplate.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In 1 Thessalonians: Thorax is a breastplate. In 5:8 it is made of “faith and love.” The pair of breastplate and helmet comes from Isaiah 59:17.
The Greek θυρεός (thureos) means “long shield.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Thyreos is a long shield shaped like a door (thyra), as big as a man and held to protect the whole body. It is the “shield of faith” (6:16).
The Greek περικεφαλαία (perikephalaia) means “helmet.” It appears 1 time in Ephesians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters or Galatians.
In Ephesians: Perikephalaia is a helmet, “around the head.” The “helmet of salvation” (6:17) is also found in Isaiah 59:17 and 1 Thessalonians 5:8.
In 1 Thessalonians: Perikephalaia, “helmet,” is something placed around the head. In 5:8 it is “the hope of salvation,” as in Isaiah 59:17 and Ephesians 6:17.
The Greek βεβαίωσις (bebaiōsis) means “confirmation.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.
In Philippians: Bebaiosis, “confirmation,” is a legal word for validation or guarantee. It is used only here in Paul (1:7), alongside “defense”: a case made and a case confirmed.
The Greek προκοπή (prokopē) means “progress.” It appears 2 times in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.
In Philippians: Prokope, “progress,” means moving ahead, as in cutting a path through a forest. “Advance the gospel” (1:12) and “your progress and joy in the faith” (1:25) use it.
The Greek κέρδος (kerdos) means “gain.” It appears 2 times in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Kerdos, “gain,” is a business word for profit. “To die is gain” (1:21), and what Paul counted as “gain” before Christ he now counts as loss (3:7). The profit-and-loss picture runs through chapters 1-4.
The Greek συναθλέω (sunathleō) means “to contend.” It appears 2 times in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Synathleo, “to contend side by side,” comes from athleo, to compete as an athlete, and the prefix syn-, “with.” The church is to be “contending side by side for the faith of the gospel” (1:27), and Euodia and Syntyche “labored with me for the gospel” (4:3) with the same word.
The Greek ἀγών (agōn) means “fight.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In 1 Timothy: Agon is a “contest” or “struggle,” and the English word “agony” comes from it. It is used in 6:12, “Fight the good fight,” and in 2 Timothy 4:7, Philippians 1:30, Colossians 2:1 and Hebrews 12:1.
The Greek μορφή (morphē) means “form.” It appears 2 times in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Morphe, “form,” means the outward shape that expresses what something is. Christ was “existing in the form of God” (2:6) and took “the form of a servant” (2:7). Scholars debate whether the word means nature, status or appearance.
The Greek ἁρπαγμός (harpagmos) means “something to grasp.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Harpagmos, “something to be grasped,” occurs only here in the New Testament (2:6). It can mean something stolen or held onto, or something to exploit. Translators differ on whether Christ refused to grasp something he lacked or refused to cling to what he had.
The Greek φωστήρ (phōstēr) means “light.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Phoster, “light” or “star,” means a luminary such as a star or the moon. “You shine as lights in the world” (2:15). The only other use is Revelation 21:11, where it describes the radiance of the new Jerusalem.
The Greek σπένδω (spendō) means “to pour a libation.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.
In 2 Timothy: Spendo is “to pour out as a drink offering.” It occurs only twice in the New Testament, here in 4:6, “I am already being poured out,” and in Philippians 2:17.
f: i am being poured out, am being poured out

t: The Greek συστρατιώτης (sustratiōtēs) means “fellow soldier.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.
In Philippians: Systratiotes, “fellow soldier,” is used of Epaphroditus (2:25) and of Archippus in Philemon 2. Paul uses military images for ministry throughout.
In Philemon: Systratiotes is “fellow soldier,” a comrade in arms. In Philemon it describes Archippus in verse 2. Paul uses it for Epaphroditus in Philippians 2:25.
The Greek σκύβαλον (skubalon) means “garbage.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.
In Philippians: Skybalon is a rare, crude word for rubbish, scraps or dung. Paul says “I consider them rubbish” (3:8). It appears only here in the New Testament.
The Greek συμμορφόομαι (summorphoomai) means “to make like.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Symmorphoo, “to be conformed,” means to take on the same form (morphe) as another. It occurs only here (3:10), “being conformed to Him in His death.” The adjective symmorphos is in 3:21 and Romans 8:29.
The Greek ἐξανάστασις (exanastasis) means “resurrection.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Exanastasis, resurrection from among the dead, appears only here in the New Testament (3:11). Paul uses a longer form than his usual word, and “somehow” suggests he does not claim to know the road.
The Greek σκοπός (skopos) means “goal.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.
In Philippians: Skopos, “goal” or “mark,” is the target a runner fixes his eyes on. It occurs only in 3:14. The English word “scope” comes from it.
The Greek πολίτευμα (politeuma) means “citizenship.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.
In Philippians: Politeuma, “citizenship,” can also mean a commonwealth or colony of citizens living abroad. It appears only in 3:20, “our citizenship is in heaven.”
The Greek σύζυγος (suzugos) means “yokefellow.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.
In Philippians: Syzygos, “yokefellow,” appears only in 4:3. The word may be a title (“loyal partner”) or a name (Syzygus), and Paul does not say.
The Greek ἐπιεικής (epieikēs) means “gentle.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.
In Philippians: Epieikes, “gentle” or “yielding,” describes someone who does not insist on every right. “Let your gentleness be apparent to all. The Lord is near” (4:5).
The Greek ἀρετή (aretē) means “virtue.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Arete, “excellence” or “virtue,” was a basic word in Greek moral writing. It occurs in 4:8, “if anything is excellent or praiseworthy,” and only a few times elsewhere in the New Testament.
In 2 Peter: Arete, “excellence” or “virtue,” is what God calls us by in “His own glory and excellence” (1:3), and the first quality to add to faith: “add to your faith virtue” (1:5).
The Greek αὐτάρκης (autarkēs) means “self-sufficient.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Autarkes, “content” or “self-sufficient,” was a Stoic ideal of needing nothing from outside. It appears only in 4:11. Paul uses it for contentment that rests on Christ, “who gives me strength” (4:13).
The Greek μυέω (mueō) means “to initiate.” It appears 1 time in Philippians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians or Ephesians.

In Philippians: Mueo, “to learn the secret,” was a word for being initiated into a mystery cult. It occurs only in 4:12, where Paul says he has been taught, as if initiated, how to live both “filled” and “hungry.”

e.u: ἀνταναπληρόω · to fill up in turn
t: The Greek ἀνταναπληρόω (antanaplēroō) means “to fill up in turn.” It appears 1 time in Colossians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians or Philippians.
In Colossians: Antanapleroo, “to fill up in turn,” occurs only in 1:24: “I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions.” The meaning of the verse is debated.
The Greek φιλοσοφία (philosophia) means “philosophy.” It appears 1 time in Colossians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians or Philippians.

In Colossians: Philosophia is “love of wisdom.” It appears only in 2:8 in the New Testament, in the warning against “philosophy and empty deception.” The word was also used by Jewish writers for their own schools.
The Greek σωματικῶς (sōmatikōs) means “bodily.” It appears 1 time in Colossians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians or Philippians.
In Colossians: Somatikos, “bodily,” appears only in 2:9 in the New Testament: “all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form.”
The Greek ἀπέκδυσις (apekdusis) means “removal.” It appears 1 time in Colossians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians or Philippians.
In Colossians: Apekdysis, “putting off,” is a noun from the same verb. It appears only in 2:11, “in the putting off of your sinful nature.”
The Greek χειρόγραφος (cheirographos) means “writen record.” It appears 1 time in Colossians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians or Philippians.

In Colossians: Cheirographon is a handwritten document, from cheir (hand) and grapho (write). It was the usual word for a signed note of debt. In 2:14 the “debt ascribed to us in the decrees” is canceled and nailed to the cross. It is the only New Testament use.
The Greek ἀπεκδύομαι (apekduomai) means “to take off.” It appears 2 times in Colossians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians or Philippians.

In Colossians: Apekdyomai means to strip off completely. It is used of Christ “having disarmed the powers and authorities” (2:15) and of believers having “taken off the old self” (3:9). Both uses are in Colossians and nowhere else in the New Testament.
The Greek δογματίζω (dogmatizō) means “to decree.” It appears 1 time in Colossians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians or Philippians.
In Colossians: Dogmatizo, “to submit to decrees,” comes from dogma, a decree. In 2:20 Paul asks why believers “submit to its regulations.” The word appears only here in the New Testament.
The Greek βραβεύω (brabeuō) means “to rule.” It appears 1 time in Colossians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians or Philippians.
In Colossians: Brabeuo, “to rule” or “to decide,” was the word for an umpire at the games. “Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts” (3:15). The word appears only here in the New Testament.
The Greek Ὀνήσιμος (Onēsimos) means “Onesimus.” It appears 1 time in Colossians and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians or Philippians.

In Philemon: Onesimos is “useful” or “profitable,” and was a common slave name. In verse 10 it is the name of the man Paul appeals for. The Greek word for “benefit” in verse 20 (oninemi) comes from the same root, so Paul plays on the name twice.

The Greek τροφός (trophos) means “nursing mother.” It appears 1 time in 1 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.
In 1 Thessalonians: Trophos, “nursing mother,” is the woman who feeds and cares for children, whether a nurse or the mother herself. It occurs only in 2:7 in the New Testament.

The Greek κέλευσμα (keleusma) means “command.” It appears 1 time in 1 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.
In 1 Thessalonians: Keleusma is a shouted command, as of a ship’s commander to rowers or an officer to soldiers. It occurs only in 4:16.

The Greek ἀρχάγγελος (archangelos) means “archangel.” It appears 1 time in 1 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.
In 1 Thessalonians: Archangelos, “archangel,” means a chief angel. It occurs only here and in Jude 9 in the New Testament.
In Jude: Archangelos occurs once: “the archangel Michael” (9). This is the only place in the Bible that names an archangel.

The Greek νήφω (nēphō) means “be sober.” It appears 2 times in 1 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.
In 1 Thessalonians: Nepho is “to be sober,” in the sense of clear-headed. It is used twice in this letter (5:6, 8) with “remain awake.”
f: we may be sober, may be sober, do be sober, being sober-minded, do sober, do be sober-minded

t: The Greek ἄτακτος (ataktos) means “disorderly.” It appears 1 time in 1 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.

In 1 Thessalonians: Ataktos means “out of order.” It was used of soldiers out of line, and in 5:14 Paul tells the church to “admonish the unruly.” The same family of words returns in 2 Thessalonians 3.

The Greek ὁλοτελής (holotelēs) means “wholly.” It appears 1 time in 1 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.
In 1 Thessalonians: Holoteles is “complete” or “through and through.” It is used only in 5:23: “sanctify you completely.”

The Greek ὁλόκληρος (holoklēros) means “whole.” It appears 1 time in 1 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.
In 1 Thessalonians: Holokleros is “whole,” with every part intact. In 5:23 Paul prays that “your entire spirit, soul, and body” be kept. It is used also in James 1:4.
In James: Holokleros, “complete in every part,” is found in 1:4 and in 1 Thessalonians 5:23. In James it is paired with teleios in the goal of “mature and complete, not lacking anything.”

The Greek ἐπιφάνεια (epiphaneia) means “appearing.” It appears 1 time in 2 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.

In 2 Thessalonians: Epiphaneia is a “shining forth” or “appearing.” In 2:8 Paul writes “the majesty of His arrival,” in which the word is joined with parousia. It is used for the appearing of Christ in 1 Timothy 6:14 and Titus 2:13.

The Greek ἀτάκτως (ataktōs) means “idly.” It appears 2 times in 2 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.
In 2 Thessalonians: Ataktos, “in disorder,” is an adverb that came to mean idle or undisciplined. It is used in 3:6 and 3:11, and in 3:7 the related verb says “we were not undisciplined among you.”

The Greek περιεργάζομαι (periergazomai) means “be a busybody.” It appears 1 time in 2 Thessalonians in the Thessalonian letters and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians or Colossians.

In 2 Thessalonians: Periergazomai, “to be a busybody,” is a play on ergazomai, “to work.” In 3:11 Paul says some are “accomplishing nothing but being busybodies,” or working at nothing and around everything. It occurs only here in the New Testament.

The Greek ἑτεροδιδασκαλέω (heterodidaskaleō) means “to teach heresy.” It appears 2 times in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Heterodidaskaleo is “to teach something different.” It is used only in 1:3 and 6:3 in the New Testament. It begins with heteros, “different,” as in the English word “heterodox.”
f: to teach other doctrines, teaches another doctrine

t: The Greek μῦθος (muthos) means “myth.” It appears 2 times in 1 Timothy and 1 in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Mythos is “myth” or “story.” In 1:4 and 4:7 it is a story that leads away from the truth. It is also used in 2 Timothy 4:4, Titus 1:14 and 2 Peter 1:16.

The Greek ἀποδοχή (apodochē) means “acceptance.” It appears 2 times in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Apodoche is “acceptance” or “welcome.” The phrase “worthy of full acceptance” is in 1:15 and 4:9. These are the only places in the New Testament where the word is used.

The Greek ὑποτύπωσις (hupotupōsis) means “example.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and 1 in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Hypotyposis is a “pattern” or “outline,” the first sketch that an artist or writer follows. It is used in 1:13, “the pattern of sound teaching,” and in 1 Timothy 1:16.

The Greek ἀντίλυτρον (antilutron) means “ransom.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Antilytron is “ransom” and occurs only in 2:6 in the New Testament. It comes from lytron (Mark 10:45) with the prefix anti, “in place of.”

The Greek αὐθεντέω (authenteō) means “to domineer.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.

In 1 Timothy: Authenteo occurs only in 2:12. Its meaning is debated: “to exercise authority,” “to domineer” and “to assume authority” have all been proposed. Outside the Bible the word is rare, and its sense there is also disputed.

The Greek τεκνογονία (teknogonia) means “childbearing.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Teknogonia, “childbearing,” occurs only in 2:15. The related verb teknogoneo, “to have children,” is in 5:14.

The Greek σώφρων (sōphrōn) means “self-controlled.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In Titus: Sophron is “self-controlled” or “of sound mind.” The word family (sophron, sophronizo, sophroneo, sophronos) is used six times in Titus (1:8; 2:2, 4, 5, 6, 12), mostly in chapter 2.

The Greek φιλόξενος (philoxenos) means “hospitable.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In Titus: Philoxenos is “hospitable,” literally “lover of strangers.” It is in 1:8, 1 Timothy 3:2 and 1 Peter 4:9.

In 1 Peter: Philoxenos, “hospitable,” literally loving strangers, occurs three times in the New Testament, in 1 Timothy 3:2, Titus 1:8 and 1 Peter 4:9. The first two list it among the qualifications of an overseer; in 1 Peter it is asked of all.

The Greek νεόφυτος (neophutos) means “new convert.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Neophytos means “newly planted.” It occurs only in 3:6, and the English word “neophyte” comes from it.

The Greek ἑδραίωμα (hedraiōma) means “foundation.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Hedraioma is a “support” or “foundation.” It occurs only in 3:15, where the church is “the pillar and foundation of the truth.”

The Greek ὁμολογουμένως (homologoumenōs) means “undeniably.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Homologoumenos, “by common confession” or “undeniably,” occurs only in 3:16, where it introduces the hymn about Christ.

The Greek καυτηριάζω (kautēriazō) means “to brand.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Kauteriazo means “to brand with a hot iron.” It occurs only in 4:2, where the consciences of liars are “seared.” Branding left a mark that did not heal.

The Greek γυμνάζω (gumnazō) means “to train.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.

In 1 Timothy: Gymnazo, “to train,” comes from gymnos, “naked,” because Greek athletes exercised without clothes. In 4:7 Paul tells Timothy to “train yourself for godliness.” It is also used in Hebrews 5:14 and 12:11 and 2 Peter 2:14.

The Greek ὠφέλιμος (ōphelimos) means “valuable.” It appears 2 times in 1 Timothy and 1 in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In Titus: Ophelimos is “useful” or “profitable.” It describes the good works in 3:8. It also describes godliness in 1 Timothy 4:8 and Scripture in 2 Timothy 3:16.

The Greek καταλέγω (katalegō) means “to enrol.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Katalego is “to enroll” in a list. It occurs only in 5:9, where a widow “should be enrolled” if she is at least sixty.

The Greek λογομαχία (logomachia) means “quarrel.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Logomachia is a “word-battle,” an argument about words. It occurs only in 6:4, with logomacheo, “to quarrel about words,” in 2 Timothy 2:14.

The Greek πορισμός (porismos) means “gain.” It appears 2 times in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.

In 1 Timothy: Porismos is “gain” or “means of profit.” It occurs only in 6:5-6, where the false teachers think godliness is “a means of gain” and Paul answers that “godliness with contentment is great gain.”

The Greek φιλαργυρία (philarguria) means “love of money.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Philargyria is “love of money,” literally “love of silver.” It occurs only in 6:10. The related adjective philargyros is used in Luke 16:14 and 2 Timothy 3:2.

The Greek παραθήκη (parathēkē) means “deposit.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and 2 in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Parathēkē is a “deposit,” something left with another to be kept safe. It occurs in 6:20, “guard what has been entrusted to you,” and in 2 Timothy 1:12, 14.
In 2 Timothy: Parathēkē is a “deposit.” Paul uses it twice in 1:12 and 1:14 for what has been entrusted. It is also used in 1 Timothy 6:20.
f: entrusted deposit, deposit committed to you

t: The Greek κενοφωνία (kenophōnia) means “empty talk.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and 1 in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Kenophonia is “empty talk,” literally “empty sound.” It occurs only in 2:16 and 1 Timothy 6:20.

The Greek ψευδώνυμος (pseudōnumos) means “falsely called.” It appears 1 time in 1 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 1 Timothy: Pseudonymos is “falsely named.” It occurs only in 6:20 in the New Testament, where “so-called knowledge” is named. The English word “pseudonym” comes from it.

The Greek ἀναζωπυρέω (anazōpureō) means “to rekindle.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Anazopyreo is “to rekindle” or “to fan into flame.” It occurs only in 1:6. It joins ana, “again,” with a word for kindling a fire.

The Greek συγκακοπαθέω (sunkakopatheō) means “to suffer with.” It appears 2 times in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Sygkakopatheo is “to suffer hardship together with.” It occurs only in 1:8 and 2:3, where Paul asks Timothy to “join me in suffering.”
f: do suffer together, do share in suffering

t: The Greek κακοπαθέω (kakopatheō) means “to endure.” It appears 2 times in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Kakopatheo is “to endure hardship” or “to suffer evil.” It is used of Paul in 2:9 (“I suffer”), of Timothy in 4:5 (“endure hardship”), and in James 5:13.
f: i suffer hardship, do endure afflictions, is suffering hardships

t: The Greek λογομαχέω (logomacheō) means “to quarrel.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Logomacheo is “to quarrel about words.” It occurs only in 2:14. The related noun logomachia is in 1 Timothy 6:4.

The Greek ὀρθοτομέω (orthotomeō) means “to cut straight.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Orthotomeo is “to cut straight.” It occurs only in 2:15, “accurately handles the word of truth.” In the Greek Old Testament it is used in Proverbs 3:6 and 11:5 of making paths straight.

The Greek γάγγραινα (gangraina) means “gangrene.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Gangraina is “gangrene,” a spreading rot of the flesh. It occurs only in 2:17, where the talk of false teachers “will spread like gangrene.”

The Greek εὔχρηστος (euchrēstos) means “helpful.” It appears 2 times in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.

In Philemon: Euchrestos is “useful,” “serviceable.” It occurs here in verse 11 and in 2 Timothy 2:21 and 4:11. It sounds close to achrestos, “useless,” in the same verse, which sets up Paul’s play on the name Onesimus.

The Greek φίλαυτος (philautos) means “selfish.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.

In 2 Timothy: Philautos is “lover of self.” It occurs only in 3:2, where it opens the list of the vices of the last days. The list continues with “lovers of money” and ends with “lovers of pleasure rather than lovers of God.”

The Greek γυναικάριον (gunaikarion) means “weak-willed woman.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.

In 2 Timothy: Gynaikarion is a diminutive of “woman.” It occurs only in 3:6. The form can be belittling, and translations vary (“weak women,” “silly women,” “vulnerable women”). The verse describes women led astray by false teachers and gives no general description of women.

The Greek γόης (goēs) means “imposter.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Goes is an “imposter” or “swindler.” In earlier Greek it meant a sorcerer who howled spells, and then a trickster. It occurs only in 3:13.

The Greek θεόπνευστος (theopneustos) means “God-breathed.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.

In 2 Timothy: Theopneustos, “God-breathed,” occurs only in 3:16 in the New Testament. It joins theos, “God,” with a word related to pneuma, “breath” or “spirit.” The usual sense is “breathed out by God.” The Latin Bible rendered the idea with a word that gives us “inspired.”

The Greek ἐπισωρεύω (episōreuō) means “to accumulate.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Episoreuo is “to heap up” or “to pile on.” It occurs only in 4:3, where people “gather around themselves teachers” in piles to suit their own desires.

The Greek κνήθω (knēthō) means “to itch.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Knetho is “to itch” or “to tickle.” It occurs only in 4:3, where people have “itching ears.” The related verb episoreuo, “to heap up,” is in the same verse.

The Greek φελόνης (phelonēs) means “cloak.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Phailones is a “cloak.” It occurs only in 4:13. It may come from the Latin paenula, a heavy traveling cloak, though a few ancient readers took the word as a book-case.

The Greek μεμβράνα (membrana) means “parchment.” It appears 1 time in 2 Timothy and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians or the Thessalonian letters.
In 2 Timothy: Membrana is “parchment,” a Latin loan word that occurs only in 4:13. Parchment was animal skin prepared for writing.

The Greek ἀψευδής (apseudēs) means “not a liar.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Apseudes is “not a liar,” “incapable of lying.” It occurs only in 1:2, where God “cannot lie.” The opposite idea is in 1:12, “Cretans are always liars.”

The Greek ἐπιδιορθόω (epidiorthoō) means “to straighten out.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.

In Titus: Epidiorthoo is “to put in order further” or “to straighten out in addition.” It occurs only in 1:5, where Titus is to “set in order what was unfinished.” It joins epi, “in addition,” with a verb for making straight.

The Greek φιλάγαθος (philagathos) means “lover of good.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Philagathos is “lover of good.” It occurs only in 1:8. Its opposite, aphilagathos, “haters of good,” is in 2 Timothy 3:3.

The Greek ματαιολόγος (mataiologos) means “babbler.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Mataiologos is an “empty talker,” someone whose words lead nowhere. It occurs only in 1:10. The related noun mataiologia is in 1 Timothy 1:6.

The Greek φρεναπάτης (phrenapatēs) means “deceiver.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Phrenapates is a “deceiver of minds,” from the roots for “mind” and “deceive.” It occurs only in 1:10.

The Greek ἐπιστομίζω (epistomizō) means “to silence.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Epistomizo is “to silence,” literally “to put a muzzle on the mouth.” It occurs only in 1:11, where the teachers “must be silenced.”

The Greek ἱεροπρεπής (hieroprepēs) means “reverent.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Hieroprepes is “reverent,” “fitting for a sacred person or place.” It occurs only in 2:3, of the behavior of older women.

The Greek καλοδιδάσκαλος (kalodidaskalos) means “teaching good.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Kalodidaskalos is “a teacher of what is good.” It occurs only in 2:3, where older women are “teachers of good.”

The Greek φίλανδρος (philandros) means “husband-loving.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Philandros, “husband-loving,” occurs only in 2:4. Its companion philoteknos, “child-loving,” is also found only there.

The Greek περιούσιος (periousios) means “special.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.

In Titus: Periousios is “special” or “treasured.” It occurs only in 2:14. In the Greek Old Testament it is the word for Israel as God’s “treasured possession” (Exodus 19:5; Deuteronomy 7:6; 14:2; 26:18).

The Greek περιφρονέω (periphroneō) means “to despise.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Periphroneo is “to think around,” so “to look down on.” It occurs only in 2:15, “Let no one despise you.” In 1 Timothy 4:12 a different verb, kataphroneo, is used for the same idea.

The Greek αἱρετικός (hairetikos) means “schismatic.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.

In Titus: Hairetikos is “factious” or “causing division.” It occurs only in 3:10. It comes from hairesis, “a choice” and then “a party” or “sect” (Acts 5:17; 1 Corinthians 11:19; Galatians 5:20). The English word “heretic” comes from this root.

The Greek αὐτοκατάκριτος (autokatakritos) means “self-condemned.” It appears 1 time in Titus and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Philemon.
In Titus: Autokatakritos is “self-condemned.” It occurs only in 3:11.

The Greek ἄχρηστος (achrēstos) means “useless.” It appears 1 time in Philemon and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Titus.
In Philemon: Achrestos is “useless,” “of no use.” It occurs only in verse 11. Its opposite, euchrestos, is in the same verse.

The Greek προσοφείλω (prosopheilō) means “to owe besides.” It appears 1 time in Philemon and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Titus.
In Philemon: Prosopheilo is “to owe in addition.” It occurs only in verse 19, where Paul reminds Philemon that he owes Paul “your very self.”

The Greek ὀνίνημι (oninēmi) means “to have joy.” It appears 1 time in Philemon and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters or Titus.
In Philemon: Oninemi is “to profit” or “to benefit.” It occurs only in verse 20, where Paul says “let me have some benefit from you.” It comes from the same root as the name Onesimus.

The Greek ἀπαύγασμα (apaugasma) means “radiance.” It appears 1 time in Hebrews and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus or Philemon.

In Hebrews: Apaugasma, “radiance” or “reflection,” occurs only in 1:3. The Son is “the radiance of God’s glory,” the light that shines out from a source. Wisdom of Solomon 7:26 uses the word of wisdom as the “reflection of eternal light.”

The Greek χαρακτήρ (charaktēr) means “reproduction.” It appears 1 time in Hebrews and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus or Philemon.
In Hebrews: Charakter is the mark struck by a die or seal, and so the “exact representation.” It occurs only in 1:3, where the Son is “the exact representation of His nature.”

The Greek παραρρέω (pararreō) means “to drift away.” It appears 1 time in Hebrews and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus or Philemon.

In Hebrews: Pararheo means “to drift” or “to flow past,” as of a boat that slips by its harbor. It occurs only in 2:1, where the writer says we must pay closer attention “so that we do not drift away.”

The Greek σαββατισμός (sabbatismos) means “Sabbath.” It appears 1 time in Hebrews and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus or Philemon.

In Hebrews: Sabbatismos is “a Sabbath rest,” or “keeping of the Sabbath.” It occurs only in 4:9, and not elsewhere in the New Testament or in the Septuagint. The writer may have coined it for the final rest of God’s people.

The Greek νωθρός (nōthros) means “dull.” It appears 2 times in Hebrews and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus or Philemon.

In Hebrews: Nothros means “sluggish,” “slow,” “dull.” It occurs in 5:11 (“you are dull of hearing”) and in 6:12 (“you will not be sluggish”), once as a diagnosis and once as the cure. The writer sets it opposite the diligence of 6:11.

The Greek ὁρκωμοσία (horkōmosia) means “oath.” It appears 4 times in Hebrews and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus or Philemon.
In Hebrews: Horkomosia is “oath-taking.” It occurs 4 times in Hebrews, all in 7:20-28, of the oath of Psalm 110:4 with which God appointed Jesus a priest. Nowhere else in the New Testament.

The Greek παρεπίδημος (parepidēmos) means “stranger.” It appears 1 time in Hebrews and 2 in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or James.

In 1 Peter: Parepidemos, “stranger” or “sojourner,” occurs three times in the New Testament: 1 Peter 1:1, 2:11 and Hebrews 11:13. It names a person who is staying in a place as a passing visitor. Peter’s readers are “exiles” (1:1) and “foreigners and exiles” (2:11).

The Greek τελειωτής (teleiōtēs) means “finisher.” It appears 1 time in Hebrews and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus or Philemon.
In Hebrews: Teleiotes, “perfecter,” is found only in Hebrews 12:2, where Jesus is “the author and perfecter of our faith.” It is not found elsewhere in the New Testament.

The Greek κάμνω (kamnō) means “be weary/sick.” It appears 1 time in Hebrews and 1 in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus or Philemon.
In James: Kamno, “to be weary” or “sick,” occurs in James 5:15, Hebrews 12:3 and Revelation 2:3. In James 5:14 the sick person is called by a different word, asthenei, “weak.”

The Greek ἐπισκοπέω (episkopeō) means “to oversee/care for.” It appears 1 time in Hebrews and 1 in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or James.

In 1 Peter: Episkopeo, to oversee or watch over, occurs twice in the New Testament, in Hebrews 12:15 and 1 Peter 5:2. In 1 Peter it describes what the elders do as shepherds: “watching over them not out of compulsion, but because it is God’s will.”

The Greek ῥαντισμός (rhantismos) means “sprinkling.” It appears 1 time in Hebrews and 1 in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or James.

In 1 Peter: Rhantismos, “sprinkling,” occurs twice in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 1:2 (“sprinkling by His blood”) and Hebrews 12:24 (“the sprinkled blood”). Both recall the blood that sealed the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:8).

The Greek δοκίμιον (dokimion) means “testing.” It appears 1 time in James and 1 in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.

In 1 Peter: Dokimion, “proving,” “testing” or “genuineness,” is found in the New Testament only in 1 Peter 1:7 and James 1:3. Both say that the testing of faith has a purpose. It is the word for the assay by which metal is proved to be genuine.

The Greek δίψυχος (dipsuchos) means “double-minded.” It appears 2 times in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.

In James: Dipsychos, “double-minded,” literally “two-souled,” is found in the New Testament only in James (1:8; 4:8) and not in earlier Greek writing that survives. It is the person who tries to hold on to God and something else at once.

The Greek ἀποκυέω (apokueō) means “to generate.” It appears 2 times in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.

In James: Apokyeo, “to give birth,” is a rare verb used of a mother. James uses it twice: sin “gives birth to death” (1:15), and God “chose to give us birth through the word of truth” (1:18). It appears in the New Testament only in these two verses.
f: it brings forth, he brought forth

t: The Greek ἔμφυτος (emphutos) means “implanted/ingrafted.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Emphytos, “implanted,” in 1:21 is found only here in the New Testament: the “word planted in you” is something that takes root, as seed does in a field.

The Greek χαλιναγωγέω (chalinagōgeō) means “to bridle.” It appears 2 times in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.

In James: Chalinagogeo, “to bridle,” occurs only in James, at 1:26 (“does not bridle his tongue”) and 3:2 (“able to control his whole body”). It is built from chalinos, “bit,” which is found in James 3:3 and Revelation 14:20.

The Greek χρυσοδακτύλιος (chrusodaktulios) means “gold-ringed.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Chrysodaktylios, “gold-ringed,” occurs only in James 2:2 in the New Testament. It describes the wealthy visitor in the story of favoritism.

The Greek φρίσσω (phrissō) means “to shudder.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Phrisso, “to shudder,” is found only in James 2:19. The demons believe, as the Shema says, that God is one, and “shudder” at it. It was a word for a person’s hair standing on end.

The Greek τροχός (trochos) means “course/wheel.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.

In James: Trochos, “wheel,” is found only in James 3:6, in the phrase usually translated “the course of his life,” where the Greek has a word for a wheel joined to a word for origin or becoming. Its exact sense is debated; it may refer to the cycle of a life or to something that spins out of control.

The Greek θανατήφορος (thanatēphoros) means “deadly.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Thanatephoros, “death-bringing” or “deadly,” is found only in James 3:8, of the tongue’s poison.

The Greek δαιμονιώδης (daimoniōdēs) means “demonic.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Daimoniodes, “demonic,” is found only in James 3:15, in the description of the earthly wisdom of jealousy and selfish ambition.

The Greek ἀδιάκριτος (adiakritos) means “impartial.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.

In James: Adiakritos, “impartial” (or “without wavering”), is found only in James 3:17. It is the opposite of the doubter who “wavers” in 1:6 and of the favoritism of chapter 2, which is why “impartial” is the usual translation.

The Greek φιλία (philia) means “friendship.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.

In James: Philia, “friendship,” occurs only in James 4:4, in the warning that friendship with the world is hostility toward God. The related word echthra, “hostility,” is in Romans 8:7 and Galatians 5:20.

The Greek καταλαλέω (katalaleō) means “to slander.” It appears 3 times in James and 2 in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Katalaleo, “to speak against” or “to slander,” occurs three times in James, all in 4:11, and twice in 1 Peter. James says that speaking against a brother is speaking against the law.
f: do speak against, speaking against, speaks against, they speak against, you are spoken against

t: The Greek νομοθέτης (nomothetēs) means “lawgiver.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Nomothetes, “lawgiver,” is found only in James 4:12: there is only one Lawgiver and Judge.

The Greek σήπω (sēpō) means “to rot.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.

In James: Sepo, “to rot,” is found only in James 5:2, of riches that have rotted. With setobrotos, “moth-eaten,” and katioomai, “to corrode” or “to rust,” in verses 2-3, James lists three kinds of spoilage.

The Greek βοή (boē) means “outcry.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Boe, “outcry,” is found only in James 5:4. The “cries of the harvesters” reach the “ears of the Lord of Hosts.”

The Greek πρώϊμος (prōimos) means “early rain.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.

In James: Proimos, “early,” and opsimos (G3797), “late,” are found only in James 5:7, of the early and late rains. The pair also stands in the Greek Old Testament for the rains of autumn and spring (Deuteronomy 11:14).

The Greek Ἰώβ (Iōb) means “Job.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Iob, “Job,” is named in the New Testament only in James 5:11. The writer points to Job’s endurance and to “the outcome from the Lord.”

The Greek πολύσπλαγχνος (polusplanchnos) means “very compassionate.” It appears 1 time in James and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon or Hebrews.
In James: Polysplanchnos, “very compassionate,” is found only in James 5:11. It is built on splanchna, the “inward parts” where compassion was thought to be felt.

The Greek ἀναγεννάω (anagennaō) means “to beget.” It appears 2 times in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Anagennao, to give new birth, occurs only twice in the New Testament, both times in 1 Peter (1:3, 23). In 1:3 God is the one who gives the new birth through the resurrection of Jesus; in 1:23 the means is the “living and enduring word of God.”

The Greek ἀμάραντος (amarantos) means “unfading.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Amarantos, “unfading,” is found only in 1 Peter 1:4, of the inheritance kept in heaven. It is built on the name of a flower, the amaranth, which was said never to wither. In 5:4 a different, related word (amarantinos, G262) describes the crown of glory “that will never fade away.”

The Greek ἄδολος (adolos) means “pure.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.
In 1 Peter: Adolos, “pure” or “unadulterated,” is found only in 1 Peter 2:2, of the “pure spiritual milk.” It describes something not watered down or mixed with anything else.

The Greek ἱεράτευμα (hierateuma) means “priesthood.” It appears 2 times in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Hierateuma, “priesthood,” occurs only in 1 Peter 2:5 and 2:9. In 2:5 the readers are a “holy priesthood” who offer spiritual sacrifices, and in 2:9 a “royal priesthood.” The Greek Old Testament uses the word in Exodus 19:6.

The Greek βασίλειος (basileios) means “kingly.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.
In 1 Peter: Basileios, “royal,” “kingly,” is found only in 1 Peter 2:9 (“a royal priesthood”). A related word, basilikos (G937), describes the “royal law” in James 2:8.

The Greek κακοποιός (kakopoios) means “wrongdoing.” It appears 3 times in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Kakopoios, “evildoer,” occurs three times in the New Testament, all in 1 Peter (2:12, 14; 4:15). In 2:12 the Gentiles “slander you as evildoers”; in 4:15 Peter lists what a Christian should not suffer as, such as a murderer or a thief.

The Greek ὑπογραμμός (hupogrammos) means “example.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Hypogrammos, “example,” is found only in 1 Peter 2:21. It is a writing teacher’s model of the letters of the alphabet, which a child traced over. Christ is the model, and the readers are to trace the same path “in His footsteps.”

The Greek φιλάδελφος (philadelphos) means “loving the brothers.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Philadelphos, loving the brothers, occurs only in 1 Peter 3:8, in the list “be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble.” It is related to the philadelphia of 1:22.

The Greek ἐπερώτημα (eperōtēma) means “pledge.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Eperotema, “pledge” or “appeal,” is found only in 1 Peter 3:21, in the phrase usually translated “the pledge of a clear conscience toward God.” Its exact sense is debated: it may mean a pledge made at baptism, a request or appeal to God for a clear conscience, or a response to a question.

The Greek πύρωσις (purōsis) means “burning.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Pyrosis, “burning,” “fiery ordeal,” is found in 1 Peter 4:12 (“the fiery trial”) and in Revelation 18:9, 18, where it is the burning of Babylon. In 1 Peter it is related to the “refined by fire” of 1:7.

The Greek ἀλλοτριεπίσκοπος (allotriepiskopos) means “meddler.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Allotriepiskopos, “meddler” or “busybody,” is found only in 1 Peter 4:15. It is built on allotrios, meaning belonging to another, and episkopos, “overseer,” and means one who oversees things that belong to other people. It may refer to someone who interferes in the affairs of others, or to a spy or informer, and the exact sense is debated.

The Greek συμπρεσβύτερος (sumpresbuteros) means “fellow elder.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.
In 1 Peter: Sympresbyteros, “fellow elder,” is found only in 1 Peter 5:1. Peter, an apostle, here puts himself alongside the elders he appeals to.

The Greek ἀρχιποίμην (archipoimēn) means “chief shepherd.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.
In 1 Peter: Archipoimen, “chief shepherd,” is found only in 1 Peter 5:4. It is a title of Christ, set over the elders who are under-shepherds.

The Greek ἀμαράντινος (amarantinos) means “unfading.” It appears 1 time in 1 Peter and not in the Gospels, Acts, Romans, the Corinthian letters, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, the Thessalonian letters, the Timothy letters, Titus, Philemon, Hebrews or James.

In 1 Peter: Amarantinos, “unfading,” describes the crown of glory in 1 Peter 5:4 and occurs nowhere else in the New Testament. It is related to amarantos (G263) in 1:4. The crown is a wreath of the kind given to winners in the games, but this wreath does not wither.
Aramaic for “Father,” an affectionate family word. Jesus using it in prayer to God was striking.
Daniel’s phrase for the temple being desecrated, recalling Antiochus IV setting up a pagan altar there in 167 BC. Jesus warns of a repeat.
Thlipsis literally means pressure, like grapes squeezed in a press, and was used for the hardship expected before the end.
Echoes Daniel 7, where a son of man receives all authority from God. Rome claimed that authority for Caesar.
Giving to the poor stood beside prayer and fasting as the three pillars of Jewish piety.
Agonia was used for an athlete’s tension before a contest; only Luke records Jesus’ sweat falling like drops of blood.
Kings and priests were anointed with oil. Reading Isaiah 61 in Nazareth, Jesus claims a Spirit anointing.
1 John 2:20 and 2:27 speak of the “anointing” (chrisma) that the readers have from “the Holy One,” which “remains in you.”
A sent envoy carried the full authority of the one who sent him. Twelve matched Israel’s twelve tribes.
Likely from Baal-zebub, a Philistine god (2 Kings 1); by Jesus’ day a name for the prince of demons.

e.n: Before abraham was born, i am
t: “I am” echoes God’s name in Exodus 3:14, and the crowd reaches for stones because they hear it as blasphemy.
Jews grouped their Scriptures as the Law (Moses), the Prophets and the Writings, so this means the whole Bible.
Jewish writers spoke of the “birth pains of the Messiah,” the suffering expected before the new age.
Insulting God. The penalty was stoning, which is why the Sanhedrin used the charge against Jesus.
Teachers saw themselves as guides to the blind (Romans 2:19), so Jesus turns the title upside down.
A nickname for James and John meaning “sons of thunder,” probably for their fiery temper (Luke 9:54).
Greek anothen means both “again” and “from above.” Nicodemus hears the first and Jesus means both.
1 John uses the same verb for “born of God” again and again (2:29; 3:9; 4:7; 5:1, 4, 18).
A desert picture of snakes fleeing a grass fire, used to say that running from judgment won’t save them.
Peter denied Jesus at a charcoal fire in the high priest’s courtyard, and John uses the same rare word for the fire where Jesus cooks breakfast.
Ekklesia was the citizen assembly of a Greek city, called together by a herald. The Greek Old Testament used it for Israel gathered.
“Clean” was ritual status. Skin diseases like those called leprosy meant exclusion until a priest declared you clean (Leviticus 13–14).
“Clean” was ritual status. Skin diseases like those called leprosy meant exclusion until a priest declared you clean (Leviticus 13–14).
Builders set a large foundation stone first and aligned the rest on it. Jesus applies Psalm 118:22 to himself.
An abandoned half-built tower was a public shame in an honor culture, so counting the cost first was common sense.
A covenant was a binding agreement sealed by sacrifice or a meal. Jeremiah 31 promised a new one, which Jesus announces at the Passover meal.
Epiousios barely appears outside the Lord’s Prayer, so whether it means “daily” or “for tomorrow” is debated.
Calling a woman a “daughter of Abraham” was rare and affirmed her full place in the covenant people.
Embrimaomai suggests a snort of indignation, like a horse. John uses it at Lazarus’ tomb.
Jeremiah 7 used the phrase of the temple, where people shelter after their crimes. Jesus quotes it while clearing the money changers.
To disown, as Peter later disowns Jesus. Taking up a cross, a Roman tool of execution, was a vivid picture of giving up your life.
To disown, as Peter later disowns Jesus. Taking up a cross, a Roman tool of execution, was a vivid picture of giving up your life.
Luke uses exodos: Jesus’ “departure” in Jerusalem echoes Israel’s Exodus, a deliverance accomplished through him.
Hosting a teacher and his disciples was a big job in a home-hospitality culture, which explains Martha’s pull.
Jews sometimes used “dogs” as a slur for Gentiles. Jesus’ word is the gentler “little dogs” of the household.
A swelling disease; the scene is a Sabbath meal at a Pharisee’s house.
Aramaic from Psalm 22:1. Some bystanders thought he called for Elijah because the sounds are close.
Malachi said Elijah would return before the day of the LORD, so many expected him. Jesus says John the Baptist is that figure.
Aramaic from Psalm 22:1. Some bystanders thought he called for Elijah because the sounds are close.
Aramaic for “be opened.” Mark keeps the foreign word as a memory of how Jesus really spoke.
“Eternal” means belonging to the age to come. Jews expected that age after the resurrection, and John says it starts now.
1 John uses “eternal life” six times (1:2; 2:25; 3:15; 5:11, 13, 20).
A proverb for the impossible: the camel was the largest animal people knew.
Jews counted days from the Sabbath, so this is Sunday, the day Christians later gathered.
Fishing was a major trade around the lake, and Jeremiah 16:16 uses fishing for gathering people. Jesus gives it a new purpose.
Genealogies proved belonging and inheritance. Matthew includes four women, which was unusual in Jewish family lists.
In Hebrew idiom an “evil eye” meant stinginess, so a “good eye” was generosity (Matthew 20:15).
To give weight and honor. In John, Jesus’ glory is paradoxically shown on the cross.
Shepherd was a title for kings and for God (Psalm 23, Ezekiel 34), and false shepherds were a prophet’s complaint, so Jesus’ claim is bold.
“Good news” was language for royal announcements, like an emperor’s accession or victory.
Pleonexia, the desire for more, was condemned by Greek moralists as the root of injustice.
Echoes Israel grumbling in the wilderness over manna, fitting a chapter about bread from heaven.
The Greek realm of the dead, like Hebrew sheol, a shadowy waiting place rather than the “hell” of later imagery.
A Hebrew idiom for stubborn refusal to listen, recalling Pharaoh.
“Have mercy” was the beggar’s cry for help, not only a religious phrase.
Parakletos: one called alongside to help, like an advocate in court.
Hebrew for “save now!” from Psalm 118, shouted by pilgrims at festivals and by crowds greeting a king.

e.n: House of prayer / den of robbers
t: Jeremiah 7 used the phrase of the temple, where people shelter after their crimes. Jesus quotes it while clearing the money changers.
In a culture ranked by honor, humility meant low status, so Jesus making it a virtue was a reversal.
A hypocrite was a Greek stage actor wearing a mask, so the word means playing a part.
“I am” echoes God’s own name, which is why the arresting soldiers draw back and fall.

e.n: I am the bread of life
t: The crowd had just asked for bread from heaven like Moses’ manna, and Jesus says he is it.

e.n: I am the light of the world
t: Said around the Feast of Tabernacles, which included a lamp-lighting ceremony in the temple, so the image would have been vivid.

e.n: I am the resurrection and the life
t: Martha believed in resurrection “at the last day.” Jesus makes it a person, present now.

e.n: I am the way, the truth, and the life
t: Said to disciples about to lose him. “The Way” later became one of the earliest names for Christians (Acts 9:2).

e.n: I and the father are one
t: Said at the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah). The crowd picks up stones because they hear a claim to deity.
From Isaiah 7:14, “God with us,” a sign to King Ahaz in a political crisis that Matthew applies to Jesus.
Mark’s favorite word (euthys), used dozens of times, gives his Gospel its breathless pace.
The Passover meal was itself a remembrance of the exodus, and Jesus gives the bread and cup a new one.
The road from Jerusalem to Jericho drops over 3,000 feet through desert hills known for robbers.
Tetelestai was used for completing a task and, on receipts, for a debt paid.
Literally “I am,” echoing God’s name, spoken as Jesus walks on a sea that Job 9:8 says only God treads.
The Greek is a quiet weeping, distinct from the loud wailing of the mourners.
A courtroom word: declared righteous. The tax collector goes home declared right with God.
Night was divided into watches, so this means staying awake at your post like servants waiting for their master.
Passover lambs, the daily temple lamb and Isaiah 53’s servant “like a lamb” all stand behind this title.
Leaven was a bit of old fermented dough. The woman’s three measures of flour is a large batch, enough for a feast.
A Roman legion was several thousand soldiers, so the name draws on the occupying army’s symbol of power.
Echoes Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses promises a prophet like himself whom Israel must hear.
Living water meant fresh, flowing spring water, prized over stored cistern water.
Magi were Persian-style priest-astronomers who studied the stars. Matthew never says there were three.
A disciple was an apprentice who learned by living with the teacher; here the call extends to all nations.
Mercy translates Hebrew chesed, faithful covenant love, not merely feeling sorry.
A mina was about a hundred denarii, roughly three months’ wages for a laborer.
Mammon is Aramaic for wealth, almost personified as a rival master.

e.n: My time has not yet come
t: Kairos means the appointed moment, which John ties to God’s timing rather than the calendar.
In Daniel a “mystery” is a hidden thing God reveals. The kingdom is hidden to outsiders and revealed to disciples.
In Daniel a “mystery” is a hidden thing God reveals. The kingdom is hidden to outsiders and revealed to disciples.
Nazareth was a tiny Galilean village, so “Nazarene” was a tag of obscurity.
For many Jews “neighbor” meant fellow Israelites. The Samaritan story stretches it to include an enemy.
The Law already said to love your neighbor; the new part is “as I have loved you.” Latin mandatum gives us “Maundy” Thursday.
1 John 2:7-8 calls it “an old one, which you have had from the beginning,” and also “a new commandment, which is true in Him and also in you.”
In 2 John, the writer asks that “we love one another,” but “not as a new commandment to you, but one we have had from the beginning” (5), the same point as 1 John 2:7.
A covenant was a binding agreement sealed by sacrifice or a meal. Jeremiah 31 promised a new one, which Jesus announces at the Passover meal.
From Genesis 2:24. In a world where a man could easily divorce, Jesus roots marriage in creation.
Ezekiel 34 promised God would gather scattered sheep. Here Jesus includes sheep beyond Israel.
Luke writes in the style of Greek historians who dedicated careful accounts to a patron.
Used for the cloud covering the tabernacle in Exodus, so God’s presence rests on Mary.
A Persian loan word for a walled royal garden, later used for the place of the blessed.
Teleios means whole or complete rather than flawless; the picture is maturity.
1 John uses the verb for love that is “perfected” (2:5; 4:12, 17, 18): “perfect love drives out fear” (4:18).
Anaideia means shameless boldness. In a hospitality culture a friend knocking at midnight shames the host into helping.
The widow’s two small copper coins were the smallest in circulation.
Same root as “clean”: vinedressers cleaned and trimmed branches so they would bear more fruit.
An Aramaic, more personal form of “rabbi”: “my teacher.”
Lytron was the price paid to free a slave or prisoner of war. Jesus says his life is that price.
Used for buying back slaves or prisoners, with Israel’s Exodus as the pattern.
A denarius carried Caesar’s face and title, so the coin was his; people bear God’s image, so they belong to God.
Literally “change your mind.” The prophets’ equivalent was “turn back,” a change of direction.
Literally “change your mind.” The prophets’ equivalent was “turn back,” a change of direction.
Literally “change your mind.” The prophets’ equivalent was “turn back,” a change of direction.
Simon’s new name, Cephas in Aramaic, means rock.
Salt preserved, seasoned and sealed covenants, and it was used in temple sacrifices.
To set apart for God, as the priests, temple and Sabbath were.
Used for gods and for emperors like Augustus. Luke gives the title to a baby in a manger; John has Samaritans say it.
Used for gods and for emperors like Augustus. Luke gives the title to a baby in a manger; John has Samaritans say it.
1 John 4:14 repeats the title: “we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world.”
John notes that Siloam means “sent,” the pool where the blind man was told to wash.
Diakonos meant waiting on tables, a low-status job, which Jesus takes on himself.
Echoes Lamech’s seventy-sevenfold vengeance in Genesis 4:24, reversed into forgiveness.
Shepherds were low in status, yet “shepherd” was also a title for kings and for God.
Wheat was shaken in a sieve to separate grain from chaff, and Satan asks to do that to Peter.
A messianic title; a blind man calling it out shows he sees who Jesus is.
“Son of” could mean sharing a character, and Rome styled Caesar Augustus a “son of god.”
From Daniel 7, a human figure given everlasting rule. In Aramaic it can also just mean “a human being.”
Its Aramaic name is Gabbatha, where Pilate sat in judgment; its exact location is debated.
A skandalon was the trigger of a trap, so to cause stumbling is to set a snare.
Aramaic for “little girl, get up.” Mark preserves the Aramaic words Jesus spoke.
Jewish law required two or three witnesses, which is why John lines up witnesses for Jesus.
1 John 5:9-11 says “the testimony of God is greater” and “this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.”
Both “test” and “tempt.” God tests to prove faith, Satan tempts to make it fail, and the wilderness echoes Israel’s forty years.
The bottomless deep, which Jewish writing treated as a prison for evil spirits.

In Revelation the Abyss is opened by a falling star and releases locusts whose king is Abaddon (9:1-11). The beast comes up out of it (11:7; 17:8), and Satan is shut up in it for a thousand years (20:1-3).
Greek for “Messiah,” the anointed one, a hoped-for king from David’s line.
In John “the hour” is the appointed time of Jesus’ death and glory, which he had said had not yet come.
Jerusalem was under Gentile rule, and Luke 21 uses the phrase for the period of Gentile domination.

e.n: The truth will set you free
t: Said to listeners who claimed never to have been enslaved, despite Egypt, Babylon and Rome.
A generation was about forty years in biblical thinking; “this generation” can recall the wilderness generation.

e.n: To the end of the age
t: Jews spoke of “this age” and “the age to come.”
The “traditions of the elders” were oral rules layered on the written Law, such as washing hands before meals.
Metamorphoo gives us “metamorphosis,” and Moses and Elijah, who also met God on mountains, appear with him.
With no banks, people buried valuables in the ground, so finding treasure in a field is believable.
Thlipsis literally means pressure, like grapes squeezed in a press, and was used for the hardship expected before the end.
A curtain screened the Holy of Holies, which only the high priest entered, once a year on the Day of Atonement.
Israel was often pictured as God’s vine or vineyard (Isaiah 5, Psalm 80), and Jesus claims to be the true one.
Isaiah 7:14 in Hebrew says “young woman”; the Greek translation Matthew quotes says parthenos, “virgin.”
Episkope means God coming to inspect or rescue; Luke says Jerusalem missed God’s coming.
Darnel looks like wheat until it heads out, and Roman law had penalties for sowing it in an enemy’s field.
Tithing herbs like mint and dill was careful law-keeping, and Jesus says the heavy matters are justice, mercy and faithfulness.
Combines Psalm 2:7 (the royal son) and Isaiah 42:1 (the servant).
Tombs were whitewashed so people could see them and avoid contact and uncleanness.
Farmers tossed grain in the air with a fork so the wind blew the chaff away, a ready picture of judgment.
Jewish law required two or three witnesses to establish a matter.
1 John uses the verb for witness six times, of the writer’s own testimony (1:2; 4:14) and of the testimony of God (5:6-10).
Mammon is Aramaic for wealth, almost personified as a rival master.
A yoke joins two animals to pull a load. Rabbis spoke of the “yoke of the Law” and the “yoke of the kingdom.”
“Zeal for your house” echoes Psalm 69, and “Zealot” later became a name for revolutionaries.
The Greek θεῖος (theios) means “divine,” belonging to God. It is a word of Greek religion and philosophy and is rare in the New Testament.
In 2 Peter: Theios occurs twice, in “His divine power” (1:3) and “partakers of the divine nature” (1:4).
The Greek φύσις (physis) means “nature,” the way a thing is by its own makeup. Greek thinkers used it for what a thing really is.
In 2 Peter: Physis occurs once, in “partakers of the divine nature” (1:4). This is the only place the New Testament speaks of a “divine nature.”
The Greek κοινωνός (koinōnos) means a partner or sharer in something. It belongs to the family of koinonia, “fellowship.”
In 2 Peter: Koinonos occurs once, in “partakers of the divine nature” (1:4).
The Greek ἐγκράτεια (enkrateia) means self-control, mastery of one’s desires. Greek moralists counted it among the chief virtues.
In 2 Peter: Enkrateia occurs twice in 1:6, the third link of the chain: “and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance.”
The Greek ἐπόπτης (epoptēs) means one who has watched something at first hand. In the Greek mystery religions it was the name of one who had been admitted to the highest rite and had seen it.
In 2 Peter: Epoptes occurs once, in “we were eyewitnesses of His majesty” (1:16). It is found only here in the New Testament.
The Greek ἔξοδος (exodos) means “way out,” a going out. It gives the book of Exodus its name in the Greek Old Testament, and can also mean death.
In 2 Peter: Exodos occurs once, in “after my departure” (1:15). Luke 9:31 uses the same word for the “departure” that Jesus would accomplish at Jerusalem.
The Greek σκήνωμα (skēnōma) means a tent or a dwelling. In the Greek Old Testament it can be used for the tabernacle.
In 2 Peter: Skenoma occurs twice, in “the tent of my body” and “this tent will soon be laid aside” (1:13-14). Paul uses the related word skenos for the body in 2 Corinthians 5:1.
The Greek ψευδοδιδάσκαλος (pseudodidaskalos) means a teacher of what is false. It is built from pseudo-, “false,” and didaskalos, “teacher.”
In 2 Peter: Pseudodidaskalos occurs once, in “there will be false teachers among you” (2:1), set against the “false prophets” of the past. It is found only here in the New Testament.
The Greek αἵρεσις (hairesis) comes from the verb “to choose.” It first meant a choice or a school of thought, and a party such as the Sadducees or the Pharisees, and only later a heresy.
In 2 Peter: Hairesis occurs once, in “destructive heresies” (2:1), which the false teachers “secretly introduce.”
The Greek ταρταρόω (tartaroō) means to send to Tartarus, the deep prison of the underworld in Greek myth.
In 2 Peter: Tartaroo occurs once, in “cast them deep into hell” (2:4). It is found only here in the New Testament, and it is not the word Gehenna.
The Greek μακροθυμία (makrothymia) means patience, “long-temperedness.” It is the word used of God’s patience with sinners.
In 2 Peter: Makrothymia occurs once, in “our Lord’s patience brings salvation” (3:15), and the verb makrothymeo in 3:9: the Lord “is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish.”
The Greek κλέπτης (kleptēs) means a thief. Jesus uses the thief who comes without warning as a picture of his coming (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39).
In 2 Peter: Kleptes occurs once, in “the Day of the Lord will come like a thief” (3:10).
The Greek στρεβλόω (strebloō) means to twist or wrench, and is used of torturing on the rack.
