In 2 Peter: Strebloo occurs once, in the “ignorant and unstable people” who “distort” Paul’s letters “as they do the rest of the Scriptures” (3:16).
The Greek ἐμπαίκτης (empaiktēs) means a mocker, one who makes sport of another.
In 2 Peter: Empaiktes occurs once, in “in the last days scoffers will come” (3:3). Jude 18 uses the same word.
In Jude: Empaiktēs occurs once: “In the last times there will be scoffers” (18). The only other use is 2 Peter 3:3.
The Greek ἀγοράζω (agorazō) means to buy in the market (agora). Paul and Peter use it for the price Christ paid for people.
In 2 Peter: Agorazo occurs once, in “even denying the Master who bought them” (2:1).
The Greek ἀρνέομαι (arneomai) means to deny, to disown. Jesus said whoever denies him before men he will deny before his Father, and the verb is the one used of Peter’s denials.
In 2 Peter: Arneomai occurs once, in “even denying the Master who bought them” (2:1).
In Jude: Arneomai occurs once: “they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (4), a denial made by the way they live.
The Greek ὑπόδειγμα (hypodeigma) means a pattern or example, something shown for others to follow or to take warning from.
In 2 Peter: Hypodeigma occurs once, in Sodom and Gomorrah “as an example of what is coming on the ungodly” (2:6).
The Greek δυσνόητος (dysnoētos) means hard to understand. It is built from dys-, “badly,” and the verb “to think.”
In 2 Peter: Dysnoetos occurs once, in “some parts of his letters are hard to understand” (3:16). It is found only here in the New Testament.
The Greek αὐξάνω (auxanō) means to grow or increase, and is used of plants and children and of the word of God spreading.
In 2 Peter: Auxano occurs once, in the letter’s last command: “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).
The Greek φωσφόρος (phōsphoros) means “light-bearer,” the morning star that comes before the sun.
In 2 Peter: Phosphoros occurs once, in “until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” (1:19). It is found only here in the New Testament.
The Greek ἐπίλυσις (epilysis) means a solution or an unraveling, an explanation.
In 2 Peter: Epilysis occurs once, in “no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation” (1:20). It is found only here in the New Testament.
The Greek ἐπιθυμία (epithymia) means strong desire. It can be good, but in the New Testament it usually means desire for what is wrong.

In 2 Peter: Epithymia occurs four times: believers have “escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires” (1:4); the false teachers “indulge the corrupt desires of the flesh” (2:10) and “appeal to the sensual passions” (2:18); the scoffers are “following their own evil desires” (3:3).
In Jude: Epithymia occurs twice: the intruders are “following after their own lusts” (16), and the scoffers “follow after their own ungodly desires” (18).
The Greek φθορά (phthora) means decay, ruin or corruption. It is the opposite of the imperishable.
In 2 Peter: Phthora occurs four times: “the corruption in the world” (1:4), the creatures “born to be captured and destroyed” (2:12, twice), and those who “are slaves to depravity” (2:19).
The Greek ἀσέλγεια (aselgeia) means shameless excess, a life without restraint, especially in sexual matters.

In 2 Peter: Aselgeia occurs three times, all of the false teachers: “Many will follow in their depravity” (2:2), Lot was distressed by “the depraved conduct of the lawless” (2:7), and they “appeal to the sensual passions of the flesh” (2:18).
In Jude: Aselgeia occurs once, in “a license for immorality” (4). 2 Peter uses it three times of the same kind of teacher.

e.u: σπουδάζω · to be eager, to make every effort
a: to be eager, to make every effort
t: The Greek σπουδάζω (spoudazō) means to hurry, to be eager, to make every effort.

In 2 Peter: Spoudazo occurs three times: “strive to make your calling and election sure” (1:10), “I will make every effort” (1:15), and “make every effort to be found at peace” (3:14). The noun spoude opens the chain of qualities in 1:5.
f: do be diligent, i will be diligent

t: The Greek τηρέω (tēreō) means to keep, to guard, to watch over, and also to hold in custody.

In 2 Peter: Tereo occurs four times, always of what God keeps for judgment: angels “held for judgment” (2:4), the unrighteous kept “for punishment” (2:9), “blackest darkness” reserved (2:17), and the heavens and earth “being kept for the day of judgment” (3:7).

In Jude: Tēreō, “to keep,” occurs five times and ties the letter together. The readers are “kept in Jesus Christ” (1); the angels did not keep their own domain, and God “has kept” them in chains (6); darkness “has been reserved” for the wandering stars (13); and the readers are to “keep yourselves in the love of God” (21).
f: being kept,, to keep,, has been reserved., being kept

t: The Greek ἱλασμός (hilasmos) means a means of atonement, the thing that makes forgiveness possible. It belongs to the family of words used for atonement in the Greek Old Testament.

In 1 John: Hilasmos occurs twice, in “He Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (2:2) and “sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (4:10). These are the only two uses in the New Testament.
The Greek χρῖσμα (chrisma) means an anointing, or the oil used for it. It comes from the same root as Christos, “the Anointed One.”
In 1 John: Chrisma occurs three times, in “an anointing from the Holy One” (2:20) and twice in 2:27. These are the only uses of the word in the New Testament.
The Greek ἀντίχριστος (antichristos) is built from anti-, which can mean “against” or “in place of,” and Christos, “the Anointed One.”
In 1 John: Antichristos occurs four times (2:18 twice, 2:22; 4:3). The fifth use in the New Testament is 2 John 7. The letter says “many antichrists have appeared.”
In 2 John: Antichristos occurs once, in 2 John 7: “Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist.” It is the last place in the New Testament where the word is found.
The Greek ψευδοπροφήτης (pseudoprophētēs) means a false prophet, one who speaks in God’s name without being sent.
In 1 John: Pseudoprophetes occurs once, in “many false prophets have gone out into the world” (4:1).
The Greek ὁμολογέω (homologeō) is built from homos, “same,” and logos, “word”: to say the same thing, to agree, to acknowledge.
In 1 John: Homologeo occurs five times, once of sins (“If we confess our sins,” 1:9) and four times of the Son (2:23; 4:2, 3, 15): “whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well.”
In 2 John: Homologeō occurs once, in a negative: “refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh” (7).
f: we shall confess, confessing, confesses, shall confess

t: The Greek ψεύστης (pseustēs) means a liar, one who speaks what is false.

In 1 John: Pseustes occurs five times (1:10; 2:4, 22; 4:20; 5:10): to deny sin, to break the commandments, to deny that Jesus is the Christ, to claim to love God while hating a brother, or not to believe God’s testimony makes one a liar.
The Greek ἀληθινός (alēthinos) means true in the sense of real, genuine, as opposed to a copy. It is a favorite word in John’s writings.
In 1 John: Alethinos occurs four times: “the true light is already shining” (2:8) and, in 5:20, three times of God: “Him who is true,” twice, and “the true God and eternal life.”
The Greek νικάω (nikaō) means to win, to conquer. The name Nike, the Greek goddess of victory, comes from the same root.
In 1 John: Nikao occurs six times (2:13, 14; 4:4; 5:4 twice; 5:5): “you have overcome the evil one” and “everyone born of God overcomes the world.” Jesus uses the verb in John 16:33.

In Revelation: Nikaō, “to overcome, to conquer,” is a key word of the book. Each of the seven letters ends with a promise to the one who overcomes (2:7-3:21); the Lion of Judah has triumphed (5:5); the beast is allowed to conquer the saints for a time (13:7); and the saints conquer the dragon by the blood of the Lamb (12:11).
f: you have overcome, have overcome, overcomes, having overcome, overcoming

t: The Greek νίκη (nikē) means victory. It is the name of the Greek goddess Nike.
In 1 John: Nike occurs once, in “this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith” (5:4). It is the only use of the noun in the New Testament.
The Greek τεκνίον (teknion) is a tender diminutive of teknon, “child,” a word a teacher or parent uses.

In 1 John: Teknion occurs seven times in this letter and only once in the Gospel of John (13:33): “my little children” (2:1), “little children” (2:12, 28; 3:7, 18; 4:4) and the last words of the letter (5:21).
The Greek ἀγαπητός (agapētos) means loved, beloved, and is formed from agapē.
In 1 John: Agapetos occurs six times (2:7; 3:2, 21; 4:1, 7, 11), always as a form of address to the readers: “Beloved, let us love one another” (4:7).
In 3 John: Agapētos, “beloved,” occurs four times, always of Gaius: “the beloved Gaius” (1) and the address “Beloved” in verses 2, 5 and 11.
In Jude: Agapētos, “beloved,” occurs three times as the address to the readers (3, 17, 20). The second and third begin with “But you,” setting them apart from the intruders.
The Greek μαρτυρία (martyria) means testimony, the witness given by someone who has seen. The English word “martyr” comes from the related martys, since early witnesses to Christ often died for it.
In 1 John: Martyria occurs six times, all in 5:9-11: “the testimony of God is greater” and “this is that testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son.”
In 3 John: Martyria, “testimony,” occurs once: “you know that our testimony is true” (12), close to John 21:24.

e.u: θεάομαι · to look at, to behold
t: The Greek θεάομαι (theaomai) means to gaze at, to look upon with attention. The English word “theater” comes from the same family.
In 1 John: Theaomai occurs three times: “which we have gazed upon” (1:1), “No one has ever seen God” (4:12), and “we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son” (4:14).
f: we have gazed upon, has seen;, have seen

t: The Greek ψηλαφάω (psēlaphaō) means to feel with the hands, to grope, and to touch.
In 1 John: Psēlaphaō occurs once, in “touched with our own hands” (1:1). Luke 24:39 uses it of the risen Jesus: “Touch Me and see.”

e.u: πλανάω · to lead astray, to deceive
t: The Greek πλανάω (planaō) means to lead astray, to make wander. The English word “planet” comes from the related word for a wanderer.
In 1 John: Planao occurs three times: “we deceive ourselves” (1:8), “those who are trying to deceive you” (2:26) and “let no one deceive you” (3:7).
f: we deceive, leading astray, should lead astray

t: The Greek ἁμαρτάνω (hamartanō) means to miss the mark, and so to sin. It is the verb that goes with the noun hamartia.

In 1 John: Hamartano occurs 10 times. Most are in the present tense in 3:6-9 and 5:18, where the BSB brings out the ongoing sense: “No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning” (3:6). In 1:10 and 2:1 it is a single act: “If we say we have not sinned” and “if anyone does sin.”
f: we have sinned,, you may sin;, shall sin,, sins;, is sinning, has been sinning., to continue sinning,, sinning, continues to sin;

t: The Greek ἀνθρωποκτόνος (anthrōpoktonos) means a man-killer, a murderer.

In 1 John: Anthropoktonos occurs twice, both in 3:15: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that eternal life does not reside in a murderer.” In John 8:44 Jesus uses it of the devil.
The Greek καταγινώσκω (kataginōskō) means to judge against, to find fault with.
In 1 John: Kataginosko occurs twice, in 3:20-21: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts,” and “if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God.”

e.u: παράγω · to pass away, to pass by
a: to pass away, to pass by
t: The Greek παράγω (paragō) means to go past, to pass by, and so to pass away.
In 1 John: Parago occurs twice, in the present tense: “the darkness is fading” (2:8) and “The world is passing away” (2:17).
The Greek κόλασις (kolasis) means punishment, and originally the pruning of a tree.
In 1 John: Kolasis occurs once, in “fear involves punishment” (4:18). The only other use is Matthew 25:46.
The Greek εἴδωλον (eidōlon) means an image, and so an idol; it comes from eidos, “form.”
In 1 John: Eidolon occurs once, in the last words of the letter: “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (5:21).
The Greek ἀλαζονεία (alazoneia) means boasting, empty pretension, the pride of someone who claims more than he has.
In 1 John: Alazoneia occurs once, in “the pride of life” (2:16). The only other use is James 4:16.
The Greek βίος (bios) means the course of life, and so a person’s livelihood and goods. The English word “biology” comes from it. It differs from zōē, the word for life in its fullness.
In 1 John: Bios occurs twice: “the pride of life” (2:16) and “earthly possessions” (3:17), where it means the means of living.
The Greek ἁγνίζω (hagnizō) means to make pure, to cleanse, especially for worship.
In 1 John: Hagnizo occurs once, in “everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure” (3:3).
The Greek διδαχή (didachē) means teaching, either the act of teaching or what is taught. It is the name of the Didache, an early church manual.
In 2 John: Didachē occurs three times, all in verses 9 and 10: “the teaching of Christ,” “His teaching” and “this teaching.” The phrase can mean what Christ taught or what is taught about him.
The Greek ἐκλεκτός (eklektos) means chosen, picked out. In the New Testament it is used of those whom God has chosen, and of Christ himself.
In 2 John: Eklektos occurs twice, in “the chosen lady” (1) and “your elect sister” (13). Both are most often read as churches.
The Greek κυρία (kyria) is the feminine of kyrios, “lord”: a lady, a woman of standing, the mistress of a house.
In 2 John: Kyria occurs twice, in “the chosen lady” (1) and “dear lady” (5), and nowhere else in the New Testament. Whether it is a title, a name or a picture of a church is argued.
The Greek πλάνος (planos) means leading astray, a deceiver. It comes from a root that means to wander, from which the English word “planet” also comes.

In 2 John: Planos occurs twice, both in verse 7: “many deceivers have gone out into the world,” and “Any such person is the deceiver.” Elsewhere it is found in Matthew 27:63, 2 Corinthians 6:8 and 1 Timothy 4:1.
The Greek μισθός (misthos) is what a worker is paid, his wages, and so a reward.
In 2 John: Misthos occurs once, in “that you may be fully rewarded” (8), literally “a full wage.” It is a picture from paid work; the letter does not say what the reward is.

e.u: προάγω · to go ahead, to lead forward
a: to go ahead, to lead forward
t: The Greek προάγω (proagō) means to lead forward or to go ahead. It can be a good thing, to go before others, or a bad one, to go too far.
In 2 John: Proagō occurs once, in “Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ” (9). Some manuscripts read parabainōn, “goes beyond,” “transgresses.”

e.u: κοινωνέω · to share, to take part
t: The Greek κοινωνέω (koinōneō) means to have a share with, to take part in. It belongs to the family of koinōnia, “fellowship.”
In 2 John: Koinōneō occurs once, in “Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds” (11). The word is the language of partnership.
The Greek χάρτης (chartēs) is a sheet of papyrus, the writing material of the day. The English word “chart” comes from it through Latin.
In 2 John: Chartēs occurs once, in “paper and ink” (12), and nowhere else in the New Testament. 3 John 13 has “pen and ink.”
The Greek μέλαν (melan) is ink; the word means “black.” It is the neuter of melas, “black.”
In 2 John: Melan occurs once, in “paper and ink” (12). It is used three times in the New Testament: 2 Corinthians 3:3, 2 John 12 and 3 John 13.
In 3 John: Melan occurs once, in “pen and ink” (13).
The Greek στόμα (stoma) means mouth, and so speech, edge or point.
In 2 John: Stoma occurs twice, both in verse 12: “speak with you face to face,” in Greek “mouth to mouth” (stoma pros stoma). 3 John 14 has the same phrase.
In 3 John: Stoma occurs twice in verse 14: “speak with you face to face,” in Greek mouth to mouth, the same phrase as 2 John 12.

e.u: ἀσπάζομαι · to greet, to send greetings
t: The Greek ἀσπάζομαι (aspazomai) means to greet, to welcome, to embrace. The closing of a letter often sends greetings in this word.
In 2 John: Aspazomai occurs once, in the last verse: “The children of your elect sister send you greetings” (13).
In 3 John: Aspazomai occurs twice in verse 14: the friends “send you greetings,” and Gaius is to “Greet each of our friends there by name.”

e.u: εὐοδόω · to prosper, to get along well
a: to prosper, to get along well
t: The Greek εὐοδόω (euodoō) is built from words for “good” and “road.” It means to have a good journey, and so to get along well or succeed.
In 3 John: Euodoō occurs twice, both in verse 2: “that in every way you may prosper” and “as your soul also prospers.” Elsewhere it is found only in Romans 1:10 and 1 Corinthians 16:2.
The Greek εὔχομαι (euchomai) means to pray or to wish. It is the usual verb for the health wish at the start of a Greek letter.
In 3 John: Euchomai occurs once: “I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health” (2).
The Greek ξένος (xenos) means a stranger or foreigner, and also a guest or host. The word for hospitality, philoxenia, means love of strangers.
In 3 John: Xenos occurs once: Gaius is faithful to the brothers, “and especially since they are strangers to you” (5).
The Greek ἐθνικός (ethnikos) comes from ethnos, “nation.” It describes a person of the nations, a pagan, someone outside the people of God.
In 3 John: Ethnikos occurs once: the brothers went out “accepting nothing from the Gentiles” (7), that is, from pagans. Elsewhere it is found only in Matthew 5:47, 6:7 and 18:17.

e.u: ὑπολαμβάνω · to take up, to support
t: The Greek ὑπολαμβάνω (hypolambanō) means to take up from below, and so to receive and support a person, or to take up a thought and suppose.
In 3 John: Hypolambanō occurs once: “we ought to support such men” (8). In Acts 1:9 it is the cloud that takes Jesus up, and in Luke 7:43 it means “I suppose.”
The Greek ἐπιδέχομαι (epidechomai) means to receive, to accept, to welcome a person or what he says.

In 3 John: Epidechomai occurs twice, both of Diotrephes, and nowhere else in the New Testament: he “will not accept our instruction” (9), and “he refuses to welcome the brothers” (10). In the Greek he does not receive the elder, and he does not receive the brothers.

e.u: φιλοπρωτεύω · to love to be first
t: The Greek φιλοπρωτεύω (philoprōteuō) joins the words for “love” and “first”: to be fond of first place.
In 3 John: Philoprōteuō occurs once, of Diotrephes, “who loves to be first” (9). It is found nowhere else in the New Testament.

e.u: φλυαρέω · to talk nonsense, to slander
t: The Greek φλυαρέω (phlyareō) means to babble, to talk nonsense, and so to bring empty charges against someone.

In 3 John: Phlyareō occurs once, in “his malicious slander against us” (10), literally talking nonsense about us with evil words. It is found nowhere else in the New Testament; a related word for gossips is in 1 Timothy 5:13.
The Greek μιμέομαι (mimeomai) means to imitate, to follow an example. The English words “mime” and “mimic” come from the same root.
In 3 John: Mimeomai occurs once: “do not imitate what is evil, but what is good” (11). Elsewhere it is found in 2 Thessalonians 3:7 and 3:9 and in Hebrews 13:7.

e.u: κακοποιέω · to do evil, to do harm
a: to do evil, to do harm
t: The Greek κακοποιέω (kakopoieō) means to do evil or to do harm, the opposite of agathopoieō, “to do good.”
In 3 John: Kakopoieō occurs once: “the one who does evil has not seen God” (11). Elsewhere it is found in Mark 3:4, Luke 6:9 and 1 Peter 3:17.
The Greek κάλαμος (kalamos) is a reed: the plant, a stalk or staff, a measuring rod, or a pen cut from a reed.
In 3 John: Kalamos occurs once, in “pen and ink” (13), the only place in the New Testament where it means a pen. In the Gospels it is the reed shaken by the wind and the staff put in Jesus’ hand.

e.u: ἐπαγωνίζομαι · to contend, to struggle for
t: The Greek ἐπαγωνίζομαι (epagōnizomai) is built on agōn, a contest in the games. It means to struggle hard on behalf of something.
In Jude: Epagōnizomai occurs once and nowhere else in the New Testament: “contend earnestly for the faith” (3).
The Greek ἅπαξ (hapax) means once, a single time, and so once for all. Hebrews uses it eight times, often of the one sacrifice of Christ.

In Jude: Hapax occurs twice: “the faith entrusted once for all to the saints” (3), and in verse 5, of the one great rescue from Egypt. Some copies place the word earlier in verse 5, with what the readers already know.
The Greek παρεισδύνω (pareisdynō) means to slip in by the side, to get in by stealth. Greek writers use it of a clever lawyer’s argument and of people who steal into a place.
In Jude: Pareisdynō occurs once and nowhere else in the New Testament: “certain men have crept in among you unnoticed” (4).
The Greek δεσπότης (despotēs) is the master of a household, with full rights over his slaves. English “despot” comes from it. It is used of God and, twice, of Christ.
In Jude: Despotēs occurs once: “they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (4). 2 Peter 2:1 has the same charge, of false teachers who deny the Master who bought them.
The Greek ἀσεβής (asebēs) means without reverence for God: a person who does not honor or fear him.

In Jude: Asebēs occurs twice: “ungodly ones” (4) and “ungodly sinners” (15). With the noun and the verb, the word group comes five times in the Greek text shown in this app, and the BSB has “ungodly” six times.
The Greek ἀσέβεια (asebeia) is ungodliness, the lack of reverence for God that shows in what a person does.
In Jude: Asebeia occurs twice: “every ungodly act of wickedness” (15, literally works of ungodliness) and “their own ungodly desires” (18, literally desires of ungodliness).
The Greek ζόφος (zophos) is thick darkness or gloom. In Homer it is the darkness of the world of the dead.

In Jude: Zophos occurs twice: the angels are kept “in eternal chains under darkness” (6), and for the wandering stars “blackest darkness has been reserved forever” (13). 2 Peter 2:4 and 2:17 use it in the same two settings.
The Greek σπιλάς (spilas) is a rock in or under the sea, a reef. A similar word, spilos, means a spot or stain, and some take that sense here.
In Jude: Spilas occurs once and nowhere else in the New Testament: “These men are hidden reefs in your love feasts” (12). 2 Peter 2:13 has the other word, for blots and blemishes.
The Greek πλανήτης (planētēs) means a wanderer. The Greeks called the planets wandering stars because they move against the fixed stars, and English “planet” comes from this word.

In Jude: Planētēs occurs once and nowhere else in the New Testament: “wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever” (13). In the Book of Enoch, stars that left their paths are bound in a dark prison.
The Greek Ἑνώχ (Henōch) is the name Enoch, from Hebrew Hanok. He is the father of Methuselah, and Genesis says God took him.
In Jude: The name occurs once: “Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them” (14). It is also in Luke 3:37 and Hebrews 11:5.
The Greek Μιχαήλ (Michaēl) is the Hebrew name Mikha’el, “Who is like God?” In Daniel he is the angel prince who guards Israel.
In Jude: The name occurs once: “the archangel Michael” (9). The only other New Testament use is Revelation 12:7.
The Greek Κόρε (Kore) is the Hebrew name Korah, the Levite who led a revolt against Moses and Aaron in Numbers 16.
In Jude: The name occurs once and nowhere else in the New Testament: “they have perished in Korah’s rebellion” (11).
The Greek ἄπταιστος (aptaistos) means not stumbling. Greek writers use it of a sure-footed horse and of a person who does not trip into wrong.
In Jude: Aptaistos occurs once and nowhere else in the New Testament: God “is able to keep you from stumbling” (24).
The Greek ἐποικοδομέω (epoikodomeō) means to build on a foundation already laid. Paul uses it of building on the foundation of Christ and the apostles.
In Jude: Epoikodomeō occurs once: “building yourselves up in your most holy faith” (20).
The Greek φυλάσσω (phylassō) means to guard, as a sentry guards a post or a shepherd a flock. It is stronger than the usual word for keeping.
In Jude: Phylassō occurs once: God “is able to keep you from stumbling” (24). Elsewhere in the letter “keep” is tēreō; here Jude changes to the word for standing guard.
The Greek μεγαλωσύνη (megalōsynē) means greatness or majesty. In Hebrews 1:3 and 8:1 “the Majesty” is a reverent name for God.
In Jude: Megalōsynē occurs once, in the doxology: “glory, majesty, dominion, and authority” (25).
The Greek γογγυστής (gongystēs) is a grumbler, one who mutters complaints. The related verb is used in the Greek Old Testament of Israel grumbling in the wilderness.
In Jude: Gongystēs occurs once and nowhere else in the New Testament: “These men are discontented grumblers” (16). The word recalls the wilderness generation of verse 5.

e.u: ἀποδιορίζω · to mark off, to cause divisions
a: to mark off, to cause divisions
t: The Greek ἀποδιορίζω (apodiorizō) means to mark off by a boundary, and so to separate people into parties.
In Jude: Apodiorizō occurs once and nowhere else in the New Testament: “These are the ones who cause divisions” (19).
The Greek διακρίνω (diakrinō) means to separate or judge between. In the middle voice it means to dispute with someone, or to be divided in oneself, to doubt.
In Jude: Diakrinō occurs twice with two senses: Michael “disputed with the devil” (9), and the readers are to “have mercy on those who doubt” (22).
The Greek ἀρνίον (arnion) is a lamb, in form a diminutive of arēn. Outside Revelation it occurs only in John 21:15, “Feed My lambs.”

In Revelation: Arnion is the main name for Christ, used 28 times of him, from the Lamb who appeared to have been slain (5:6) to the throne of God and of the Lamb (22:3). Once it is used of the beast from the earth, which had two horns “like a lamb” (13:11), a false copy of the true Lamb.
f: a lamb, lamb, lamb,, lamb!, lamb., as a lamb, lamb;

t: The Greek θηρίον (thērion) is a wild animal, especially a dangerous one. In Acts 28:4 it is the snake that bit Paul.

In Revelation: Thērion is the word for the beast from the sea (13:1) and the beast from the earth (13:11), and for the scarlet beast that carries Babylon (17:3). The picture comes from the four beasts of Daniel 7, and in Revelation the beast is set against the Lamb.
f: beasts, beast, a beast, beast., beast,, creature

t: The Greek δράκων (drakōn) is a dragon or great serpent. In the Greek Old Testament it is used for the sea monster and for Leviathan (Isaiah 27:1).

In Revelation: Drakōn occurs only in this book in the New Testament, always of Satan: the great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns (12:3), “that ancient serpent called the devil and Satan” (12:9), who is bound for a thousand years (20:2).
f: a dragon, dragon, dragon., a dragon., dragon,

t: The Greek ἑπτά (hepta) is the number seven, which in the Bible often stands for completeness, from the seven days of creation onward.

In Revelation: Hepta occurs more often than in any other book of the Bible: seven churches, spirits, lampstands, stars, seals, horns, eyes, trumpets, thunders, heads, plagues, bowls, mountains and kings.
f: seven, [the] seven, [there were] seven, seven., seven —

t: The Greek σφραγίς (sphragis) is a seal, the stamp pressed into clay or wax to close a document, mark ownership or guarantee a thing as genuine. Paul calls his converts the seal of his apostleship (1 Corinthians 9:2).
In Revelation: Sphragis is used of the seven seals on the scroll, which only the Lamb can open (5:1; 6:1-8:1), and of “the seal of the living God” put on the foreheads of his servants (7:2-3; 9:4).
f: with seals, seals, seal, seal,, [the] seal

t: The Greek φιάλη (phialē) is a wide, shallow bowl, used in temples for pouring offerings. In the Greek Old Testament it is used for the bowls of the tabernacle altar.

In Revelation: Phialē occurs only in this book in the New Testament. The elders hold golden bowls full of incense, “which are the prayers of the saints” (5:8), and seven angels pour out seven golden bowls of God’s wrath (15:7; 16:1-21).
The Greek παντοκράτωρ (pantokratōr) means the ruler of all. The Greek Old Testament uses it for the Lord of hosts. English Bibles translate it “the Almighty.”

In Revelation: Pantokratōr is a favorite title of God, beginning with “the Lord God, who is and was and is to come—the Almighty” (1:8) and ending with the city whose temple is “the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb” (21:22). Outside Revelation the New Testament uses it only in 2 Corinthians 6:18.
The Greek χάραγμα (charagma) is a mark engraved or stamped: the image on a coin, a seal on a document, a brand. In Acts 17:29 it means an image carved by human skill.
In Revelation: Charagma is always “the mark” of the beast, received on the right hand or the forehead (13:16-17; 14:9-11; 16:2; 19:20; 20:4). Those who refuse it reign with Christ.
The Greek μέτωπον (metōpon) is the forehead, the most visible place to bear a mark or a name.

In Revelation: Metōpon occurs only in this book in the New Testament. God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads (7:3) and bear his name there (14:1; 22:4); the followers of the beast take its mark there (13:16; 14:9); and Babylon’s name is written on hers (17:5).
The Greek ζῷον (zōon) is a living creature, an animal. Hebrews 13:11 and 2 Peter 2:12 use it of animals.

In Revelation: Zōon is the word for the four living creatures around the throne, like a lion, an ox, a man and a flying eagle, full of eyes and never resting from praise (4:6-9). They come from the creatures of Ezekiel 1 and the seraphim of Isaiah 6.
f: living creatures, living creature, living creatures,

t: The Greek χιλιάς (chilias) is a group of a thousand. With other numbers it makes the great counts of thousands.

In Revelation: Chilias is used for the 144,000, twelve thousand from each tribe (7:4-8; 14:1-3), for the thousands upon thousands of angels (5:11), and for the twelve thousand stadia of the city (21:16).
The Greek χίλιοι (chilioi) means a thousand. Peter writes that with the Lord a day is like a thousand years (2 Peter 3:8).
In Revelation: Chilioi is the word in “a thousand years,” repeated six times in Revelation 20:2-7, and in the 1,260 days of 11:3 and 12:6.
f: a thousand, one thousand, for a thousand, thousand

t: The Greek λυχνία (lychnia) is a lampstand, the stand on which a lamp is set to give light to the house (Matthew 5:15). In the Greek Old Testament it is the golden lampstand of the tabernacle.

In Revelation: Lychnia is the word for the seven golden lampstands among which Christ walks, which “are the seven churches” (1:12-20), the lampstand that may be removed from Ephesus (2:5), and the two witnesses (11:4).
The Greek letter Α (alpha) is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, and so the beginning of everything.
In Revelation: Alpha occurs only in the title “the Alpha and the Omega,” spoken by the Lord God (1:8; 21:6) and by Jesus (22:13).
The Greek letter Ω (omega, “big o”) is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, and so the end and goal of all things.
In Revelation: Omega occurs only in the title “the Alpha and the Omega” (1:8; 21:6; 22:13).
The Greek θυμός (thymos) is passion or fury, anger that boils up. Paul lists it among the works of the flesh (Galatians 5:20).

In Revelation: Thymos is used of God’s wrath, often with orgē: the winepress of God’s wrath (14:19), the seven golden bowls “full of the wrath of God” (15:1, 7), and the cup of the wine of his fury (16:19). It is also the devil’s great fury, because he knows his time is short (12:12).
The Greek πληγή (plēgē) is a blow or stroke, and so a wound or a plague. It is the word for the beatings Paul received (2 Corinthians 6:5) and for the plagues of Egypt in the Greek Old Testament.
In Revelation: Plēgē is the word for the plagues of the trumpets and bowls, the seven last plagues (15:1, 6), and the fatal wound of the beast that was healed (13:3, 12).
The Greek σφάζω (sphazō) means to slaughter, as an animal is slaughtered for sacrifice, or to kill violently. 1 John 3:12 uses it of Cain.

In Revelation: Sphazō is used of the Lamb “who appeared to have been slain” (5:6, 9, 12; 13:8), of the souls of those slain for the word of God (6:9; 18:24), and of the beast’s head that seemed slain (13:3), a copy of the Lamb.
f: slain, you were slain, they will slay.

t: The Greek λίμνη (limnē) is a lake. Luke uses it for the Sea of Galilee, the lake of Gennesaret (Luke 5:1).
In Revelation: Limnē is always “the lake of fire,” into which the beast, the false prophet, the devil, Death and Hades are thrown (19:20; 20:10, 14-15; 21:8).
The Greek Βαβυλών (Babylōn) is Babylon, the city on the Euphrates that destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC and carried its people into exile.
In Revelation: Babylōn is “Babylon the great” (14:8; 16:19; 17:5; 18:2, 10, 21), the great city of luxury and persecution whose fall the book announces. Most readers see Rome behind the name.
The Greek ᾠδή (ōdē) is a song, the root of the English word ode. Paul uses it in “psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs” (Ephesians 5:19).
In Revelation: Ōdē is used of the “new song” of the elders and of the 144,000 (5:9; 14:3) and of “the song of God’s servant Moses and of the Lamb” (15:3).
The Greek κέρας (keras) is a horn, and in the Bible a picture of strength. Zechariah praises God for raising up “a horn of salvation” (Luke 1:69).

In Revelation: Keras is used of the Lamb’s seven horns (5:6), of the ten horns of the dragon and the beast (12:3; 13:1), which are ten kings (17:12), and of the two lamb-like horns of the false prophet (13:11).
The Greek ἀριθμός (arithmos) is a number or count, the root of the English word arithmetic.
In Revelation: Arithmos is used of the counts of the angels and the army (5:11; 9:16), of the 144,000 (7:4), and above all of “the number of the beast,” 666 (13:17-18; 15:2).
The Greek βύσσινος (byssinos) means made of fine linen, a costly cloth from Egypt worn by priests and the rich.

In Revelation: Byssinos is the dress of Babylon and part of her cargo (18:12, 16), the clothing of the armies of heaven (19:14), and the bright, clean linen of the bride, which is “the righteous acts of the saints” (19:8).
f: of fine linen [things], fine linen, the fine linen

t: The Greek χλιαρός (chliaros) means warm or tepid, neither hot nor cold.
In Revelation: Chliaros occurs once, in the letter to Laodicea: “So because you are lukewarm—neither hot nor cold—I am about to vomit you out of My mouth” (3:16).
The Greek Νικολαΐτης (Nikolaitēs) is a follower of a man named Nicolaus. Some early writers linked the group with Nicolas of Antioch, one of the seven in Acts 6:5, but this is uncertain.

In Revelation: Nikolaitēs occurs twice: Ephesus hates the works of the Nicolaitans (2:6), and some in Pergamum hold their teaching (2:15). The name may mean “conqueror of the people,” and some think it is a Greek form of the Balaam named alongside them.
The Greek σαλπίζω (salpizō) means to blow a trumpet. Paul says the trumpet will sound and the dead will be raised (1 Corinthians 15:52).
In Revelation: Salpizō is used for the seven angels who sound their trumpets one after another (8:6-11:15).
f: they may sound the trumpets., sounded [his] trumpet,, to sound [their] trumpets!, to sound [the] trumpet,

t: The Greek κατοικέω (katoikeō) means to live in a place, to settle down there.

In Revelation: Katoikeō is used most often in the phrase “those who dwell on the earth,” the book’s name for people who belong to this world and worship the beast (3:10; 6:10; 13:8, 14; 17:8). It is also used of the church at Pergamum, which lives where Satan’s throne is (2:13).

Missing the mark: failing to be what God made us to be and to do what he asks. The Gospels describe it as acts (stealing, lying, lust) and as something deeper in the heart, which is why Jesus says defilement comes from within. Jesus is called Savior because he will save his people from their sins.

In Romans Paul says “all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God” (3:23) and treats sin as a power that “reigned in death” (5:21) and a master (6:14). He says “the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (6:23).

Paul says “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (15:3), and “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law” (15:56). In Corinth he deals with particular sins: divisions, sexual immorality, lawsuits, drunkenness at the Lord’s Supper.
In 2 Corinthians Paul says Christ “knew no sin” but was made “sin on our behalf” (5:21).

In Ephesians Paul says “you were dead in your trespasses and sins” (2:1), and lists sins of speech, anger, stealing and sexual impurity (4:25-5:5). Believers are told “Be angry, yet do not sin” (4:26).

James traces sin to desire: “after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death” (1:15). He also says that “anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin” (4:17) and that favoritism is sin (2:9).

In 1 John, “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1:8), “sin is lawlessness” (3:4), and “All unrighteousness is sin, yet there is sin that does not lead to death” (5:17). Jesus “appeared to take away sins” (3:5).

Set apart, belonging to God and different from the ordinary. God is holy in a way no one else is, and people and places become holy by being set apart for him. In the Gospels, spirits cry out to Jesus as “the Holy One of God,” and Jesus teaches that holiness is about the heart as much as about ritual purity.

Paul writes “to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy” (1:2), and tells the Corinthians “you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of our God” (6:11). Holiness is God’s gift first, and a calling to live out second.
In 2 Corinthians Paul concludes his call to separation with “let us cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit, perfecting holiness in the fear of God” (7:1).

In Ephesians God chose believers “to be holy and blameless in His presence” (1:4), the new self is “created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness” (4:24), and Christ means to present the church “holy and blameless” (5:27).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians Paul writes, “it is God’s will that you should be holy” (1 Thessalonians 4:3), prays that God would “establish your hearts in blamelessness and holiness” (3:13) and says God chose them for “the sanctification of the Spirit” (2 Thessalonians 2:13).
In 1 Timothy Paul asks that women continue “in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control” (2:15) and Timothy is told to keep himself “pure” (5:22).

In Hebrews God disciplines his children “so that we may share in His holiness” (12:10), and readers are told to “Pursue peace with everyone, as well as holiness, without which no one will see the Lord” (12:14). Jesus “sanctifies” believers by his offering (2:11; 10:10).
1 Peter 1:15-16 quotes Leviticus: “Be holy, because I am holy.” The church is a “holy nation” and a “holy priesthood” (2:5, 9).

2 Peter 3:11 asks, “what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness” as the Day of God is awaited, and 1:21 calls the prophets’ message the work of “the Holy Spirit.”

The Gospels use several Greek words for love, and the most important is agape: a self-giving, chosen love that wants the good of the other. Jesus says the greatest commandment is to love God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength, and the second is to love your neighbor as yourself. He tells his disciples to love one another as he has loved them, and to love even their enemies.

In Romans Paul says “God has poured out His love into our hearts through the Holy Spirit” (5:5), that nothing can separate believers from the love of God in Christ (8:35-39), and that “love is the fulfillment of the law” (13:10).

In 1 Corinthians love is called “the most excellent way” (12:31): without it tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith and even giving everything away count for nothing (13:1-3). “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (8:1), and Paul closes the letter with “Do everything in love” (16:14).

In 2 Corinthians “Christ’s love compels us” (5:14), love is among the marks of a minister (“in sincere love,” 6:6), and Paul asks the church to “reaffirm your love” for the offender (2:8). He tests their love by their giving (8:8, 24) and ends with “the God of love and peace will be with you” (13:11) and “the love of God” (13:14).

In Ephesians love is the thread: God “in love” chose us (1:4-5), “because of His great love for us” made us alive (2:4), believers are “rooted and grounded in love” (3:17), speak “the truth in love” (4:15), and “walk in love, just as Christ loved us” (5:2).
In Philippians Paul prays that the church’s “love may abound more and more in knowledge and depth of insight” (1:9), and asks them to have “the same love” (2:2).
In Colossians Paul thanks God for “your love for all the saints” (1:4) and tells the church, “over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity” (3:14).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians Paul speaks of their “labor of love” (1 Thessalonians 1:3) and prays that “the Lord cause you to increase and overflow with love for one another and for everyone else” (3:12). They “have been taught by God to love one another” (4:9), and “your love for one another is increasing” (2 Thessalonians 1:3).
1 Peter 1:22 calls for “a genuine love for your brothers,” and 4:8 says, “Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins.”
In 2 Peter love is the last link in the chain of qualities that begins with faith: “and to brotherly kindness, love” (1:7).

In 1 John, “God is love” (4:8, 16), and the proof is that “God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him” (4:9). The word occurs 18 times in the letter, and “We love because He first loved us” (4:19). It is shown in deed: “let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth” (3:18).
In 2 John, the writer loves the readers “in the truth” (1) and asks that “we love one another” (5). The letter says what love is: “this is love, that we walk according to His commandments” (6).
In 3 John, Gaius is called beloved four times, and the brothers “testified to the church about your love” (6), which they had seen in his open house.

Unearned favor: God’s generosity toward people who cannot deserve it. John says grace and truth came through Jesus Christ. Jesus’ parables of the workers in the vineyard and the prodigal son show a God who gives more than people have earned.
In Acts Barnabas sees “the grace of God” in Antioch, and the Jerusalem Council affirms that Jews and Gentiles are saved by the grace of the Lord Jesus.
In Romans grace is God’s free gift: “where sin increased, grace increased all the more” (5:20), and “sin shall not be your master, because you are not under law, but under grace” (6:14).
Paul says “by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace to me was not in vain” (15:10), and ends the letter with “The grace of the Lord Jesus be with you” (16:23).

In 2 Corinthians grace is God’s gift (“My grace is sufficient for you,” 12:9), the pattern of Christ’s giving (8:9), and the word for the collection itself (“this grace of giving,” 8:7). The letter ends with “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ” (13:14).

Galatians begins and ends with grace (1:3; 6:18). Paul says God “called me by His grace” (1:15), and “I do not set aside the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, Christ died for nothing” (2:21). Those who try to be justified by the law “have fallen away from grace” (5:4).
In Ephesians grace begins and ends the letter (1:2; 6:24). “It is by grace you have been saved through faith” (2:8), and Paul calls his own work “the stewardship of God’s grace” (3:2).
In 1 Timothy Paul writes, “the grace of our Lord overflowed to me, along with the faith and love that are in Christ Jesus” (1:14).
In 2 Timothy Timothy is told to “be strong in the grace that is in Christ Jesus” (2:1), and God saved us “by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began” (1:9).

In Titus “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone” (2:11), and the letter ends, “Grace be with all of you” (3:15). Having been “justified by His grace,” believers become “heirs with the hope of eternal life” (3:7).
2 Peter opens with “Grace and peace be multiplied to you” (1:2) and closes with “grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (3:18).
In 2 John, the greeting is a promise: “Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father, will be with us in truth and love” (3).
Jude warns of people who “turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality” (Jude 4): grace treated as permission to sin.

Trust and faithfulness. The Greek word pistis covers both believing something is true and trusting someone. Jesus often responds to faith with healing, marvels at it in a Roman soldier, and rebukes his disciples for “little faith.” The father of the boy with a spirit says, “I believe; help my unbelief.”
In Acts faith is the response to the apostles’ preaching, and God “made no distinction” between Jew and Gentile “having cleansed their hearts by faith.”
In Romans Paul says people are “justified by faith apart from works of the law” (3:28), points to Abraham as the pattern, and says “faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” (10:17).

In 1 Corinthians faith is one of the gifts (12:9), and “faith, hope, and love” remain (13:13). “If Christ has not been raised,” Paul says, “your faith is futile” (15:17). He closes with “Stand firm in the faith” (16:13).

In 2 Corinthians “we walk by faith, not by sight” (5:7), and Paul tells the Corinthians “it is by faith that you stand firm” (1:24) and to “examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith” (13:5).

In Galatians faith is how the promise comes: “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness” (3:6), “those who have faith are sons of Abraham” (3:7), and “All that matters is faith, expressed through love” (5:6).

In Ephesians faith is the way salvation is received (“through faith,” 2:8), the way believers come to God with “boldness and confidence” (3:12), and the way Christ dwells in the heart (3:17). The “shield of faith” puts out the flaming arrows of the evil one (6:16).

In Hebrews “faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see” (11:1), and chapter 11 tells the story of the faithful from Abel to the martyrs. “Without faith it is impossible to please God, because anyone who approaches Him must believe that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him” (11:6). Jesus is “the author and perfecter of our faith” (12:2).

In James faith is tested and shown by action. “The testing of your faith develops perseverance” (1:3), a doubter should not expect to receive anything (1:6-7), and “faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead” (2:17). See “Faith and works in James.”
In Jude, “the faith” means the message believed, “entrusted once for all to the saints” (3), and the readers are to build themselves up “in your most holy faith” (20).

Letting go of a debt or offense. Jesus teaches people to ask God for forgiveness and to forgive others, forgiving “seventy times seven.” He claims the authority to forgive sins, which makes his opponents ask who can forgive sins but God alone.
In Acts forgiveness of sins is offered in Jesus’ name to Jews and Gentiles alike.
In 2 Corinthians Paul asks the church to forgive the one who caused grief: “you ought to forgive and comfort him” (2:7), and says “If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him” (2:10).
In Ephesians “In Him we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (1:7), and believers are to be “forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you” (4:32).
In Colossians God “forgave us all our trespasses” (2:13), and believers are told, “Forgive as the Lord forgave you” (3:13).

In Philemon Paul asks a master to take back a slave who “has wronged you in any way or owes you anything” (18), and offers to pay the debt himself. The letter does not use the word “forgive,” but the request is for mercy in place of punishment.

In Hebrews the new covenant promise of Jeremiah 31 is quoted twice: “I will forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more” (8:12; 10:17), and the writer concludes, “where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed” (10:18).

A change of mind and direction, turning back to God. John the Baptist and Jesus both start by calling people to repent because the kingdom of heaven is near. The Greek word metanoia means a changed mind, and the Hebrew idea is turning around, shuv.
In Acts the first sermons end with the call to repent: “Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins.”
In Romans Paul asks, “do you disregard the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness leads you to repentance?” (2:4).
In 2 Corinthians 7:9-10 Paul rejoices that the Corinthians’ “sorrow led you to repentance,” because “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret.”

God’s reign and rule, already present in Jesus but not yet complete. It is Jesus’ main theme: he announces it, teaches about it in parables, and shows it with healings and exorcisms. Matthew usually says “kingdom of heaven,” which means the same thing.
In Acts the risen Jesus speaks of the kingdom for forty days, and Luke ends the book with Paul “proclaiming the kingdom of God and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ.”

In 1 Corinthians the kingdom is something to be inherited: “the wicked will not inherit the kingdom of God” (6:9), and “flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God” (15:50). At the end Christ “hands over the kingdom to God the Father” (15:24).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians God “calls you into His own kingdom and glory” (1 Thessalonians 2:12), and the church will “be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are suffering” (2 Thessalonians 1:5).

Rescue and wholeness. In the Gospels the verb “to save” can mean rescued from drowning, healed of illness, or saved from sin and death. Jesus’ name means “the Lord saves.” John 3:16 says God so loved the world that he gave his Son so that everyone who believes would have eternal life.
In Acts Peter tells the council that salvation is found in no one else, and the jailer asks, “What must I do to be saved?”
In Romans Paul says the gospel “is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (1:16), and “Everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved” (10:13).

In 1 Corinthians the message of the cross is “the power of God” to “us who are being saved” (1:18). Believers are saved through the gospel “if you hold firmly to the word I preached” (15:2), and a person can be saved “only as if through the flames” when his work is burned (3:15).
In 2 Corinthians Paul says “now is the day of salvation!” (6:2) and that “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret” (7:10).
In Ephesians salvation is a past gift (“you have been saved,” 2:5, 8), “the gospel of your salvation” (1:13), and “the helmet of salvation” (6:17).
In Philippians the believers are told to “continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling” because God “works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose” (2:12-13).
In Colossians the language is of rescue, reconciliation and being made alive: God “rescued us from the dominion of darkness” (1:13) and “made you alive with Christ” (2:13).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians salvation is both present and future: “God has not appointed us to suffer wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:9), and God chose them “to be saved” (2 Thessalonians 2:13).

In 1 Timothy Christ Jesus “came into the world to save sinners” (1:15), God “wants everyone to be saved” (2:4), and Timothy will “save both yourself and those who hear you” by watching his life and teaching (4:16).
In 2 Timothy God “has saved us and called us to a holy calling” (1:9), and the Holy Scriptures are “able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus” (3:15).
In Titus God “saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy” (3:5), and “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone” (2:11).

In Hebrews salvation is “such a great salvation” which, if neglected, cannot be escaped (2:3). Jesus is “the author of their salvation” (2:10) and “the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him” (5:9), and he “is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him” (7:25). He will appear a second time “to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him” (9:28).
1 Peter 1:5, 9-10 calls salvation the readers’ coming goal, “ready to be revealed in the last time,” and the “salvation of your souls,” about which the prophets “searched and investigated carefully.”
2 Peter says “our Lord’s patience brings salvation” (3:15), and wants no one to perish “but everyone to come to repentance” (3:9). Jesus is called “Savior” five times in the letter.

Being in right standing with God, and living the way God desires. Jesus says that unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees you will not enter the kingdom, and tells people to seek first God’s kingdom and his righteousness.
In Romans “the righteousness of God” is revealed in the gospel (1:17), and righteousness is “credited” to those who believe (4:5), as it was for Abraham.

In Galatians righteousness is credited to those who believe, as to Abraham (3:6), and “we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness” (5:5). Paul says “if righteousness comes through the law, Christ died for nothing” (2:21).
In Ephesians the new self is created in “true righteousness and holiness” (4:24), the fruit of the light includes “righteousness” (5:9), and the breastplate of the armor is righteousness (6:14).

In 1 John, “everyone who practices righteousness has been born of Him” (2:29), and “The one who practices righteousness is righteous, just as Christ is righteous” (3:7). Jesus is “the Righteous One” (2:1).

Making things right between God and humanity at the cost of a sacrifice. In the Gospels, Jesus says the Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many, and at the Last Supper calls the cup his blood poured out for the forgiveness of sins. How the cross accomplishes this has been described in several ways in Christian history.
In Romans Paul says God presented Christ “as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood” (3:25), and that believers are “reconciled to Him through the death of His Son” (5:10).

In Hebrews Jesus is the high priest who makes “atonement for the sins of the people” (2:17), and the Day of Atonement is the model for his work: he enters the heavenly sanctuary “by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption” (9:12), and “without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (9:22). The writer insists on one offering: “by a single offering He has made perfect for all time those who are being sanctified” (10:14).
1 John 2:2 and 4:10 call Jesus “the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (hilasmos), the only places in the New Testament where that Greek word is used.

Rising bodily from death. Pharisees believed in it, Sadducees did not. Jesus teaches that he is “the resurrection and the life” and that he would be killed and rise on the third day, and all four Gospels report the empty tomb and his appearances afterward.
In Acts the resurrection is the heart of apostolic preaching. Peter says the apostles are witnesses to it, and in Athens Paul’s mention of it divides his audience.

In Romans Paul says Jesus “was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (1:4), was “raised to life for our justification” (4:25), and that the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus will “give life to your mortal bodies” (8:11).

In 1 Corinthians 15 Paul says Christ’s resurrection is “of first importance,” and that without it “your faith is futile” (15:17). Christ is “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (15:20), and believers will be raised “imperishable” (15:52).
In 2 Corinthians Paul says “the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence” (4:14), and that God “raises the dead” (1:9).

In Philippians Paul wants “to know Christ and the power of His resurrection” and “to attain to the resurrection from the dead” (3:10-11). Christ “will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (3:21).
In Colossians Christ is the “firstborn from among the dead” (1:18), and believers are “raised with Him through your faith in the power of God” (2:12; 3:1).

In 1 Thessalonians the resurrection of Jesus is the ground of hope for believers who have died: “since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, we also believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him,” and “the dead in Christ will be the first to rise” (4:14, 16).
In 2 Timothy Paul tells Timothy to “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead” (2:8) and names Hymenaeus and Philetus, who say “the resurrection has already occurred” (2:18).

In Hebrews the resurrection of the dead is one of the “elementary teachings” (6:1-2). Abraham “reasoned that God could raise the dead” (11:19), and some of the faithful endured torture “so that they might gain a better resurrection” (11:35). God “brought back from the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep” (13:20).
1 Peter 1:3 says the readers were born again “to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead,” and 3:21 says baptism saves “through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.”
Life of the age to come, beginning now in knowing God. In John it means above all knowing the Father and Jesus Christ. In the other Gospels, people ask Jesus what they must do to inherit it.
In 2 Timothy Paul begins “according to the promise of life in Christ Jesus” (1:1) and says Christ “has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel” (1:10).
In Titus Paul writes of “the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began” (1:2), and believers are “heirs with the hope of eternal life” (3:7).

1 John 5:11-13 says “God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son,” and “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life.” The letter ends, “He is the true God and eternal life” (5:20).

God’s final putting right of all things, when everyone answers for how they lived. Jesus speaks of a day of judgment, of separating sheep and goats, and also says he did not come to judge the world but to save it. He also commands his followers not to judge hypocritically.
In Acts, Paul tells the Athenians that God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world by a man he has appointed, and speaks to Felix of “righteousness and self-control and the coming judgment.”
In Romans Paul says “we will all stand before God’s judgment seat” (14:10) and that God’s “righteous judgment will be revealed” (2:5).

In 1 Corinthians the Day “will bring it to light” and test each person’s work by fire (3:13). Paul says “judge nothing before the appointed time; wait until the Lord comes” (4:5). Believers “will judge the world” and even angels (6:2-3), and when the Lord disciplines, it is “so that we will not be condemned with the world” (11:32).
In 2 Corinthians 5:10 Paul says “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad.”

In 2 Thessalonians the church’s endurance is “clear evidence of God’s righteous judgment” (1:5), and the Lord Jesus is “revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in blazing fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel” (1:7-8).
In 2 Timothy Christ Jesus “will judge the living and the dead” (4:1), and Paul looks for “the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day” (4:8).

In Hebrews “man is appointed to die once, and after that to face judgment” (9:27). Those who reject the Son face “a fearful expectation of judgment” (10:27), and “It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God” (10:31).

James says that “judgment without mercy will be shown to anyone who has not been merciful. Mercy triumphs over judgment” (2:13), warns teachers of stricter judgment (3:1), and tells his readers not to complain, since “the Judge is standing at the door” (5:9).
1 Peter 4:17 says that “it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God,” and 1:17 reminds the readers that they call on a Father “who judges each one’s work impartially.”

2 Peter says “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from trials and to hold the unrighteous for punishment on the day of judgment” (2:9), and that “the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men” (3:7). The examples are the angels, the flood and Sodom and Gomorrah (2:4-8).
Jude gives three past judgments as warnings (5-7) and quotes Enoch on the Lord’s coming “to execute judgment on everyone” (15). The fallen angels are “bound for judgment on that great day” (6).
Revelation ends with the great white throne, where the dead, great and small, are judged according to their deeds (20:11-13).

Jesus uses two different words usually translated hell. Gehenna, from the Valley of Hinnom just south of Jerusalem, was once a place of child sacrifice and later a rubbish dump, and became a picture of final judgment. Hades is the realm of the dead. Christians have understood what Jesus teaches about final punishment in different ways.
James 3:6 says the tongue “is itself set on fire by hell” (Gehenna). It is the only use of the word in the New Testament outside Matthew, Mark and Luke.
2 Peter 2:4 uses the Greek verb tartaroo, “cast them deep into hell,” of the angels who sinned. It comes from Tartarus, the prison of the Greek underworld, and is not the word Gehenna.

In the Gospels, “heaven” can mean the sky, God’s dwelling place, or a way of speaking about God himself (“kingdom of heaven”). Jesus speaks of treasure in heaven, angels in heaven, and the Father in heaven.
In 2 Corinthians Paul speaks of “an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands” (5:1) and of one “caught up to the third heaven” and to “Paradise” (12:2-4).
In Ephesians Christ is seated “at His right hand in the heavenly realms” (1:20), and believers are seated “with Him” there (2:6).

In Hebrews Jesus “passed through the heavens” (4:14) and has entered “heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God” (9:24). The readers have come to “the heavenly Jerusalem” (12:22), and the faithful long for “a better country, a heavenly one” (11:16).
2 Peter 3:13 looks forward to “a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells,” after the present heavens “will disappear with a roar” (3:10).

Speaking with God. Jesus prays alone, often early in the morning or at night, and teaches his disciples to pray simply, persistently and without showing off. He gives them the Lord’s Prayer, and in John 17 prays at length for himself, his disciples and all who will believe.
In Acts the church prays at every turning point: choosing Matthias, after the council’s threats, when Peter is in prison, and when Barnabas and Saul are sent out.

In Corinth Paul says “I will pray with my spirit, but I will also pray with my mind” (14:15), and that the person who speaks in a tongue “should pray that he may interpret” (14:13). He also speaks of men and women who pray or prophesy in the meeting (11:4-5).
In 2 Corinthians Paul asks the Corinthians for prayer (“as you help us by your prayers,” 1:11) and tells how he prayed three times about his thorn in the flesh (12:8).
In Ephesians the letter is full of prayer: a thanksgiving and prayer for wisdom (1:15-19), a prayer for strength and love (3:14-21), and an instruction to “pray in the Spirit at all times” (6:18-20).

In Philippians Paul prays “with joy” for the church (1:4), asks that “your love may abound more and more” (1:9), and tells them to bring “everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving” to God (4:6).

In Colossians Paul prays “since the day we heard about you” (1:9), asks them to “devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful” (4:2), and tells of Epaphras “always wrestling in prayer for you” (4:12).
In 1 and 2 Thessalonians Paul prays for the church “in our prayers” (1 Thessalonians 1:2), says “Pray without ceasing” (5:17), and asks, “Brothers, pray for us as well” (5:25; 2 Thessalonians 3:1).
In 1 Timothy Paul urges “petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving” for everyone (2:1), and the widow “who is truly in need” continues “night and day in her petitions and prayers” (5:5).

James tells the lacking to ask God for wisdom (1:5-6), says that the readers do not receive because they “ask with wrong motives” (4:3), and gives instructions for the sick to call the elders (5:14-15). “The prayer of a righteous man has great power to prevail,” and Elijah is his example (5:16-18).

1 John 5:14-15 says, “this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us,” and 5:16 tells a believer to ask God for a brother who sins a sin not leading to death.

The prayer Jesus taught his disciples. Matthew gives a longer form, in the Sermon on the Mount, and Luke a shorter one when the disciples ask him to teach them to pray. It begins “Our Father in heaven” and asks for God’s name to be honored, his kingdom to come, daily bread, forgiveness and rescue from the evil one.

Going without food, usually for a spiritual purpose. Jesus fasts forty days in the wilderness, teaches that fasting should be private, and says his disciples will fast when the bridegroom is taken from them.

Immersion in water as a sign of repentance and cleansing. John the Baptist baptized for repentance, and Jesus was baptized by him in the Jordan. Jesus’ followers are told to baptize in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Christians have understood and practiced baptism in different ways.
In Acts people are baptized after they believe: at Pentecost, in Samaria, the Ethiopian on the road, Cornelius’s household, Lydia, the jailer and the disciples at Ephesus.
In Romans Paul says all who were baptized into Christ Jesus “were baptized into His death” and were “buried with Him through baptism into death” so as to “walk in newness of life” (6:3-4).

Paul says “in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (12:13), recalls that Israel was “baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (10:2), and says he baptized few in Corinth because “Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel” (1:17).
Paul says “all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ” (Galatians 3:27), the picture of putting on a new garment.

In Ephesians there is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (4:5), and Christ cleanses the church “by the washing with water through the word” (5:26). Some scholars see baptism in both places; the text does not say so directly.
In Colossians believers are “buried with Him in baptism” and “raised with Him through your faith in the power of God” (2:12).

In Titus Paul speaks of “the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit” (3:5). Some readers see baptism in this phrase, others the cleansing work of the Spirit. The text does not say water, so the question is open.

1 Peter 3:21 compares the flood waters with baptism, “the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ.” See the entry on the spirits in prison.

The meal Jesus shared with his disciples the night he was betrayed, when he gave them bread and wine as his body and his blood of the new covenant. Different Christian traditions call it Communion, the Eucharist or the Mass, and understand it in different ways.

Paul has the oldest written account of the Supper. He says the bread and cup are “a participation in the blood of Christ” and “in the body of Christ” (10:16), and recalls what he received: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me” (11:25). The Corinthians are shamed for dividing at the meal, and told to “wait for one another” (11:33).

Compassion in action toward people in need or in the wrong. The Gospels often say Jesus was moved with compassion. He says, “Blessed are the merciful,” and tells the religious leaders to learn what Hosea meant: “I desire mercy, not sacrifice.”

In Romans Paul says God “has mercy on whom He wants to have mercy” (9:18) and “consigned everyone to disobedience so that He may have mercy on everyone” (11:32). He urges the believers to offer themselves “on account of God’s mercy” (12:1).
In 1 Timothy “mercy” is added to the greeting “grace, mercy, and peace” (1:2), and Paul says, “I was shown mercy” because he “had acted in ignorance and unbelief” (1:13, 16).
In 2 Timothy “mercy” is again part of the greeting (1:2), and Paul prays that the Lord grant mercy to Onesiphorus “on that day” (1:16, 18).
In Titus God saved us “according to His mercy” (3:5), and the letter’s greeting, “Grace and peace” (1:4), omits the word “mercy” that the Timothy letters add.
In James, “Mercy triumphs over judgment” (2:13), the wisdom from above is “full of mercy and good fruit” (3:17), and “the Lord is full of compassion and mercy” (5:11).
In 2 John 3, mercy stands between grace and peace in the opening wish. The same three words appear in the greetings of 1 and 2 Timothy.

In Jude, mercy frames the letter: the greeting wishes the readers “Mercy, peace, and love” (2), they wait for “the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ” (21), and they are told to “have mercy on those who doubt” (22).
Not thinking of oneself too highly, and taking the lowest place. Jesus says he is “gentle and lowly in heart,” washes his disciples’ feet, and says that whoever humbles himself will be exalted.
In 2 Corinthians Paul calls Christ’s “mildness and gentleness” the model for his own appeal (10:1). He shows humility by working with his hands (11:7) and by letting his weakness show (12:9).
In Ephesians believers are to walk “with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love” (4:2), and to “submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” (5:21).
In Philippians the model is Christ, who “humbled Himself and became obedient to death” (2:8). Paul asks the church to “in humility consider others more important than yourselves” (2:3).

James quotes Proverbs 3:34, “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble,” and says, “Humble yourselves before the Lord, and He will exalt you” (4:6, 10). The lowly brother is to “exult in his high position” (1:9), and wisdom shows itself in “the humility that comes from wisdom” (3:13).

1 Peter 5:5-6 quotes Proverbs 3:34 and says, “Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you.” All of the readers are to “clothe yourselves with humility toward one another.”

Following Jesus as a learner and apprentice. He calls people to follow him, and to take up their cross and lose their lives for his sake. The Twelve are the closest disciples, but many others follow, including women.
In Ephesians discipleship is a walk: “walk in a manner worthy of the calling” (4:1), “walk in love” (5:2), “walk as children of light” (5:8), and “pay careful attention … to how you walk” (5:15).

Jesus is blunt about money. He says, “You cannot serve God and money,” tells a rich man to sell what he has and give to the poor, blesses the poor in spirit and warns that the rich will find it hard to enter the kingdom. Luke gives special attention to the poor and the outcast.

In Acts the first believers share property so that “there was not a needy person among them,” Ananias and Sapphira lie about their gift, and Paul reminds the Ephesian elders of Jesus’ words, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.”

In 2 Corinthians Paul says of himself and his team “poor, yet making many rich” (6:10), of the Macedonians that “deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity” (8:2), and of Christ that “though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor” (8:9).

In 1 Timothy Paul says “godliness with contentment is great gain” (6:6), warns that “the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (6:10) and tells the rich to be “generous and ready to share” (6:18).
In 2 Timothy the list of the last days begins with “lovers of themselves, lovers of money” (3:2).

In the Sermon on the Mount, Jesus tells his followers not to be anxious about food, drink and clothing, because the Father knows what they need. He points to the birds and the lilies and says, “Seek first the kingdom of God.”
In Philippians Paul writes, “Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God” (4:6).
1 Peter 5:7 says, “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you,” echoing Psalm 55:22.

Wholeness and well-being, not only the absence of conflict. The angels announce peace on earth at his birth, Jesus tells people to “go in peace,” and before his death he says, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.” After the resurrection, the first thing he says to the disciples is, “Peace be with you.”
In Romans Paul says “since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ” (5:1), and urges, “live at peace with everyone” (12:18).
Paul says “God has called you to live in peace” (7:15), and “God is not a God of disorder, but of peace” (14:33). He begins the letter with “Grace and peace to you” (1:3).
Paul ends 2 Corinthians with “Aim for perfect harmony, encourage one another, be of one mind, live in peace. And the God of love and peace will be with you” (13:11).

In Ephesians Christ “Himself is our peace” (2:14), preached peace to the far and the near (2:17), and the church is to keep “the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace” (4:3). The shoes of the armor are “the readiness of the gospel of peace” (6:15).
In Philippians “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (4:7), and “the God of peace will be with you” (4:9).
In Colossians Christ makes “peace through the blood of His cross” (1:20), and “the peace of Christ” is to rule in their hearts (3:15).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians the Day of the Lord comes on those who are saying, “Peace and security” (1 Thessalonians 5:3), and Paul prays that “the God of peace Himself” and “the Lord of peace Himself” will give them peace (5:23; 2 Thessalonians 3:16).
In 2 John 3, peace is part of a promise that “will be with us in truth and love,” not only a wish.
In 3 John 14 the letter ends with the greeting “Peace to you,” where 2 John put peace in its opening (2 John 3).

In John, truth is not just a set of correct statements but something found in a person. Jesus says, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life,” and that the truth will set people free. Pilate asks, “What is truth?”

In Ephesians believers hear “the word of truth” (1:13), speak truth in love (4:15, 25), and fasten on “the belt of truth” (6:14). The “fruit of the light” is “all goodness, righteousness, and truth” (5:9).

In 2 Thessalonians those who are perishing “refused the love of the truth that would have saved them” (2:10), and God chose the church “by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth” (2:13).
In 1 Timothy God “wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2:4), and the church is “the pillar and foundation of the truth” (3:15).

In 2 Timothy Paul tells Timothy to handle “the word of truth” accurately (2:15), says opponents are “always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth” (3:7), and warns that people will “turn their ears away from the truth” (4:4).
In Titus Paul writes for “their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness” (1:1), and calls the false teachers men “who have rejected the truth” (1:14).
In 1 John, those who claim fellowship with God while walking in darkness “do not practice the truth” (1:6). The readers “know the truth” (2:20-21), and “the Spirit is the truth” (5:6).

In 2 John, the word occurs five times in the first four verses: the writer loves “in the truth,” the truth “abides in us and will be with us forever,” and he is glad to find the children “walking in the truth” (1-4).

In 3 John, the Greek word occurs six times in fourteen verses: Gaius is loved “in the truth” (1), his children are “walking in the truth” (4), supporters become “fellow workers for the truth” (8), and Demetrius has a good word “from the truth itself” (12).

A word picture running through the Bible for God’s presence, truth and goodness, in contrast with darkness. John opens with the Word as the light shining in the darkness, and Jesus says, “I am the light of the world.” He also tells his followers, “You are the light of the world.”
In 2 Corinthians Paul says “God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ made His light shine in our hearts” (4:6). He also warns that “Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light” (11:14).

In Ephesians Paul says “you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light” (5:8). Everything exposed by the light “becomes visible” (5:13), and the one asleep is told, “Christ will shine on you” (5:14).
In 1 Thessalonians believers are “sons of the light and sons of the day” and “we do not belong to the night or to the darkness” (5:5).

In 1 John, “God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (1:5). Believers “walk in the light as He is in the light” (1:7), and “the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining” (2:8).

The weighty, shining presence of God. In the Old Testament it fills the tabernacle and temple. John says the Word became flesh and “we have seen his glory.” In John, the cross is the hour when Jesus is glorified.

In 2 Corinthians the glory of the old covenant was “fading away,” while the glory of the new “endures” (3:7-11). Believers “are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory” (3:18), and present affliction is “producing for us an eternal weight of glory” (4:17).
1 Peter speaks of “the glories to follow” the sufferings of Christ (1:11), of the “Spirit of glory” resting on those insulted for Christ (4:14), and of the “crown of glory” for faithful elders (5:4).

Honoring and adoring God. Jesus tells the Samaritan woman that the hour is coming when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, and he accepts worship himself from the Magi, the man born blind and Thomas.
In Acts Paul tells the Athenians that God “does not live in temples made by man” and is not served by human hands.
