Paul pictures an outsider who comes in and hears prophecy: “he will fall facedown and worship God, proclaiming, ‘God is truly among you!’” (14:25).
In Ephesians believers are to speak “with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs,” making music in their hearts to the Lord, and “always giving thanks to God the Father” (5:19-20).

In Hebrews the first covenant had “regulations for worship and also an earthly sanctuary” (9:1), and the readers are told to “worship God acceptably with reverence and awe” (12:28). “Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name” (13:15).

Revelation is the New Testament’s great book of worship. The word for worship (proskyneō) comes about twenty-four times, and the whole book turns on one question: whether people will worship God and the Lamb or the beast and its image (14:7, 9-11).

A testing or enticement to sin. After his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus into the wilderness, where he fasts forty days and is tempted by Satan. Each time he answers with Scripture from Deuteronomy. In the Lord’s Prayer, his followers ask not to be led into temptation.
In Ephesians believers are told not to give “the devil a foothold” (4:27) and to “make your stand against the devil’s schemes” (6:11).
In 1 Thessalonians Paul fears “that the tempter had somehow tempted you and caused our labor to be in vain” (3:5).
In 1 Timothy those who want to be rich “fall into temptation” (6:9), and a recent convert may fall “into the snare of the devil” (3:6-7).

In Hebrews, “Because He Himself suffered when He was tempted, He is able to help those who are being tempted” (2:18), and the high priest “was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (4:15).

James separates trials from temptation: “God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone. But each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed” (1:13-14). The blessing is for the one “who perseveres under trial” (1:12).

Acting a part. The Greek word was used for a stage actor. Jesus warns about it in prayer, giving and fasting, and in Matthew 23 pronounces seven woes on scribes and Pharisees who do not practice what they teach.

Paul uses the word in Galatians 2:13 for what he saw at Antioch, when Peter, “the other Jews,” and even Barnabas drew back from the Gentiles. The Greek word is the one used for acting a part on stage.

Messengers of God. Gabriel announces the births of John and Jesus, an angel appears to Joseph, and angels announce the birth to the shepherds. Angels minister to Jesus after the temptation and in Gethsemane, and they are at the empty tomb.
In Acts an angel frees the apostles and Peter from prison, sends Philip to the Ethiopian road, appears to Cornelius, and stands beside Paul in the storm.

In 1 Corinthians the angels are watchers: “We have become a spectacle to the whole world, to angels as well as to men” (4:9). Believers “will judge angels” (6:3), and Paul speaks of “the tongues of men and of angels” (13:1).
In 2 Corinthians Paul warns that “Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light” (11:14).
In Ephesians Paul speaks of “rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms” who learn God’s wisdom through the church (3:10). Whether these are good or bad powers, or both, is debated.
In Colossians Paul warns against “the worship of angels” (2:18) and says that “thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities” were created in Christ and for Him (1:16).
In 1 and 2 Thessalonians the Lord descends with “the voice of an archangel” (1 Thessalonians 4:16) and is revealed “with His mighty angels” (2 Thessalonians 1:7).
In 1 Timothy the Christ of the hymn “was seen by angels” (3:16), and Paul charges Timothy “before God and Christ Jesus and the elect angels” (5:21).

Hebrews 1-2 sets the Son above the angels. Seven Old Testament passages are strung together to show that he is greater: “Are not the angels ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation?” (1:14). The law was “spoken by angels” (2:2), but “it is not to angels that He has subjected the world to come” (2:5). Jesus did not come to help angels but “the descendants of Abraham” (2:16). The readers are told, “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it” (13:2), and they have come to “myriads of angels in joyful assembly” (12:22).
1 Peter 1:12 says that “even angels long to look into” the things announced by the gospel, and 3:22 says Christ is at God’s right hand “with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him.”

2 Peter 2:4 says “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment,” and 2:10-11 says that “not even angels, though greater in strength and power,” bring slanderous charges against glorious beings before the Lord.

In Jude, angels appear three ways: those who left their place and are held for judgment (6), the “glorious beings” whom the intruders slander (8), and Michael the archangel, who would not pronounce judgment even on the devil (9). The “holy ones” who come with the Lord in verse 14 are angels too.

Angels fill Revelation: they stand at the throne, blow the trumpets, pour out the bowls, explain the visions and fight the dragon. When John falls down to worship an angel he is told, “Do not do that! I am a fellow servant with you” (19:10; 22:9).

Evil spirits that afflict people. Jesus casts them out with a word, and they recognize who he is. The Gospels distinguish demon possession from ordinary illness, though modern readers understand the conditions described in different ways. Jesus says the exorcisms show that the kingdom of God has come.
In Acts evil spirits come out of many in Samaria, a slave girl at Philippi is freed, and at Ephesus a group of exorcists fail to use the name of Jesus.

Paul says “the sacrifices of pagans are offered to demons, not to God,” and does not want the Corinthians to be “participants with demons” (10:20). “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons too” (10:21).

In Ephesians the unseen enemy is “the ruler of the power of the air” (2:2), the devil with his “schemes” (6:11), and “the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms” (6:12). Paul never describes them in detail.
In 1 Timothy Paul says that “in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons” (4:1).

Good news. The Greek word euangelion was used for the announcement of a king’s victory or birth. Mark opens, “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ,” and Jesus preaches “the gospel of the kingdom.” Matthew, Mark, Luke and John are each called a Gospel because each tells the good news about Jesus.
In Acts Paul says his one aim is to “testify to the gospel of the grace of God.”
In Romans Paul calls himself “set apart for the gospel of God” (1:1) and says “I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (1:16).

In 1 Corinthians the gospel is the message “I preached to you, which you received, and in which you stand firm” (15:1): Christ died for our sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to many witnesses (15:3-8). Paul says “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!” (9:16).

In 2 Corinthians Paul says the gospel is “veiled to those who are perishing” (4:3), warns against “a different gospel” (11:4), and describes the church’s “obedient confession of the gospel of Christ” (9:13).

In Galatians Paul uses the word for the message he received “by revelation from Jesus Christ” (1:12) and says that anyone who preaches another, “even if we or an angel from heaven,” is under a curse (1:8-9).

In Ephesians the gospel is “the word of truth—the gospel of your salvation” (1:13), the message that the Gentiles are “fellow heirs” (3:6), “the gospel of peace” (6:15) and “the mystery of the gospel” (6:19).

In Philippians the word “gospel” appears nine times. The church has a “partnership in the gospel” (1:5), Paul is “appointed for the defense of the gospel” (1:16), and believers are to live “in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ” (1:27).
In Colossians the gospel “is bearing fruit and growing” “all over the world” (1:6), and Paul has “become a servant” of it (1:23).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians the gospel came to the church “not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction” (1 Thessalonians 1:5). Paul and his coworkers share it along with “our own lives as well” (2:8), and those who “do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus” will face judgment (2 Thessalonians 1:8).
In 2 Timothy Paul says, “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel” (2:8).

The community of Jesus’ followers. Jesus uses the word ekklesia only twice in the Gospels, both in Matthew, when he says to Peter, “On this rock I will build my church,” and when he teaches how to deal with a brother who sins. The word means an assembly or gathering.

In Acts the church is first mentioned at the death of Ananias and Sapphira, then spreads from Jerusalem to Judea, Samaria, Antioch and Asia Minor. Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in every church, and Paul tells the Ephesian elders to care for “the church of God” which he bought with his own blood.

Paul writes to “the church of God in Corinth” (1:2). In 1 Corinthians it is God’s field, building and temple (3:9, 16), the body of Christ (12:27), and the household that meets “at their house” (16:19). He urges unity, order and love in its meetings.

In Ephesians the church is Christ’s body (1:22-23), the household and holy temple of God (2:19-22), the place where “the manifold wisdom of God” is displayed (3:10), and the bride Christ loves (5:25-27). The word always means the whole church, not one local congregation.
In 1 Timothy the church is “God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (3:15).

In 3 John, the word comes three times (6, 9, 10): the brothers “testified to the church” about Gaius, the elder has “written to the church,” and Diotrephes is “putting them out of the church.” These are the only uses of the word in the Gospel and letters of John.

God’s instruction given through Moses, first the five books of the Torah and then, in a wider sense, the whole Hebrew Scriptures. Jesus says he has come to fulfill it, summarizes it as love of God and neighbor, and argues with others over how to keep it.
In Acts the question is whether Gentile believers must keep the law of Moses; the Council says they should avoid idols, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood.

In Romans Paul says the law is “holy” (7:12) but “merely brings awareness of sin” (3:20), and that believers “died to the law through the body of Christ” (7:4). He also says faith does not nullify the law but upholds it (3:31).

Paul quotes “the Law of Moses” about the ox (9:9) and the Law on tongues (14:21). He also says “the power of sin is the law” (15:56), and says that to those under the law he became “like one under the law” (9:20).

Galatians asks “Why then was the law given?” (3:19). It “was added because of transgressions,” did not cancel the earlier promise (3:17-19), and “became our guardian to lead us to Christ” (3:24). The whole law is “fulfilled in a single decree” of love (5:14), and believers fulfill “the law of Christ” (6:2).
In Ephesians Christ “abolished in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees” in order to make one new people out of Jew and Gentile (2:15). Paul still cites a commandment in 6:2.
In 1 Timothy Paul writes, “the law is good, if one uses it legitimately,” and says it is for “the lawless and rebellious” (1:8-9).

James speaks of “the perfect law of freedom” (1:25), “the royal law” of love for one’s neighbor (2:8), and warns that breaking one command breaks the whole law (2:10). He says that a person who slanders a brother “speaks against the law” (4:11).

Asked which commandment is greatest, Jesus quotes Deuteronomy 6:4-5, loving the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, mind and strength, and Leviticus 19:18, loving your neighbor as yourself, and says all the Law and Prophets depend on these two.

1 John 3:23 gathers the commandments into two parts: “that we should believe in the name of His Son, Jesus Christ, and we should love one another just as He commanded us.” 4:21 adds, “Whoever loves God must love his brother as well.”

Jesus’ longest block of teaching, in Matthew 5 to 7, given on a hillside near Capernaum. It includes the Beatitudes, teaching on anger, lust, oaths and enemies, the Lord’s Prayer, the warning about worry and the call to build on the rock. Luke has a shorter parallel, often called the Sermon on the Plain.

To witness is to say what you have seen and heard. Jesus tells the apostles that the Holy Spirit will make them his witnesses “in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth,” and the book of Acts follows that outline. The Greek word martys later came to mean someone who died for the faith.

1 John speaks of what the writer and others “have seen and testify” (4:14) and of the testimony of the Spirit, the water and the blood (5:6-8): “the testimony of God is greater. For this is the testimony that God has given about His Son” (5:9).

Luke says the first believers “devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and the fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.” The word means sharing a common life, not just meeting. It showed in meals, prayers and giving.

Paul asks whether the cup and the bread are “a participation” in the blood and body of Christ (10:16), using the same Greek word. “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body; for we all partake of the one loaf” (10:17).

In 2 Corinthians the word covers the gift for the poor in Jerusalem (8:4; 9:13), the partnership of believers and unbelievers that Paul questions (6:14), and “the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” (13:14).
In Philippians Paul speaks of “your partnership in the gospel” (1:5), “fellowship with the Spirit” (2:1), and “the fellowship of His sufferings” (3:10).
In Philemon Paul prays that Philemon’s “partnership in the faith may become effective” (6), and calls him a “partner” (17).

1 John opens with the purpose of fellowship: “so that you also may have fellowship with us. And this fellowship of ours is with the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ” (1:3). The word occurs four times in the letter, all in chapter 1.

Parresia is speaking plainly and without fear. The council notices that Peter and John are bold even though they are ordinary men, and the believers pray for more of it. It is Luke’s mark of a Spirit-filled witness.
In 2 Corinthians Paul says “since we have such a hope, we are very bold” (3:12). Hope in the new covenant allows him to speak openly, without the veil.
In Ephesians believers “enter God’s presence with boldness and confidence” (3:12), and Paul asks for prayer to “boldly make known the mystery of the gospel” (6:19).

Hebrews uses parresia four times: believers hold fast “our confidence” (3:6), approach “the throne of grace with confidence” (4:16), have “confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus” (10:19), and are told, “do not throw away your confidence” (10:35).

The most surprising turn in Acts. Peter sees a vision of unclean animals and goes to Cornelius, the Spirit falls on Gentiles, and the Jerusalem Council agrees that Gentiles are saved by grace without circumcision. Luke tells the story in three stages: Samaritans, an Ethiopian and Cornelius, then the Gentile mission.

In Romans Paul says there is “no distinction” between Jew and Gentile in need or in God’s grace (3:22), and that Christ became a servant of the circumcised “so that the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy” (15:8-9).

Galatians says “The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham: ‘All nations will be blessed through you’” (3:8), and that the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles in Christ (3:14).

In Ephesians the mystery is that “through the gospel the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus” (3:6), and that Christ has broken down “the dividing wall of hostility” (2:14).

In Acts the apostles are flogged and rejoice that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name. Paul is told at his call how much he must suffer for the name of Jesus. Stephen’s death shows that witness may cost a life.

2 Corinthians has the most personal account of Paul’s sufferings: “the sufferings of Christ overflow to us” (1:5), “struck down, but not destroyed” (4:9), and the long list in 11:23-29. He accepts them as part of his work: “death is at work in us, but life is at work in you” (4:12).
In Ephesians Paul writes in chains and asks his readers “not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory” (3:13).
In Philippians Paul says, “it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him” (1:29), and that he wants “the fellowship of His sufferings” (3:10).
In Colossians Paul says, “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you” (1:24), and he asks them to “remember my chains” (4:18).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians the church received the message “in spite of your great suffering” (1 Thessalonians 1:6), “suffered from your own countrymen” (2:14), and is told that the endurance of “all the persecution and affliction” is a sign that they will “be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are suffering” (2 Thessalonians 1:4-5).
In 2 Timothy Paul asks Timothy to “join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God” (1:8) and says that “all who desire to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted” (3:12).

In Hebrews the readers recall an earlier time of ridicule, imprisonment and loss of property (10:32-34), and are told that Jesus “learned obedience from what He suffered” (5:8). “Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart” (12:3).

1 Peter 4:14-16 says, “If you are insulted for the name of Christ, you are blessed,” and “if you suffer as a Christian, do not be ashamed, but glorify God that you bear that name.” This is one of three places where the New Testament uses the name “Christian.”

In Acts people are baptized, healed and saved in the name of Jesus. Peter tells the council that “there is no other name under heaven given among men by which we must be saved.” A name carries a person’s authority and presence.

The question at the Jerusalem Council. Some from Judea teach that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Peter says, “We believe that we will be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they will.”

Galatians gives Paul’s own account of the same dispute. Titus “was not compelled to be circumcised” (2:3), and Paul told the Galatians that if they let themselves be circumcised, “Christ will be of no value to you at all” (5:2).

At Pentecost, in Samaria, at Cornelius’s house and at Ephesus the Spirit’s coming is marked by speaking in tongues, praise or prophecy. At Pentecost the languages are known ones, and the crowd understands.

To justify is to declare someone righteous, the way a judge acquits. Paul says no one “will be justified in His sight by works of the law” (3:20), and that people “are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (3:24). Faith is the way a person receives it, not a work that earns it. Churches have long disagreed about whether justification is only a declaration or also makes a person righteous; Paul’s words in Romans are the main text in that debate.

Galatians gives a short, sharp account: “a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16). “Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because, ‘The righteous will live by faith’” (3:11).

Ephesians does not use the word “justify,” but it states the same gospel: “It is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works” (2:8-9).
In Philippians Paul wants “the righteousness from God on the basis of faith” and not “my own righteousness from the law” (3:9).
In Titus believers are “justified by His grace” so that they “become heirs with the hope of eternal life” (3:7).

James 2:21-25 uses the verb “justified” of Abraham and Rahab, and concludes that “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (2:24). How this relates to Paul’s teaching is discussed in “Faith and works in James.”

Paul says the gospel “reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish” (1:17). The phrase can mean God’s own right dealing, the right standing he gives to people, or both. Paul says God shows it in Christ so that he can “be just and ... justify the one who has faith in Jesus” (3:26).
The phrase ends the great statement of 2 Corinthians 5:21: “so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.”

In Philippians Paul wants to be found in Christ, with “the righteousness from God on the basis of faith” (3:9), and prays that the church be “filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ” (1:11).

In Romans 3:25 Paul says “God presented Him as the atoning sacrifice through faith in His blood.” The Greek word hilasterion is also used in the Greek Old Testament for the lid of the ark, the mercy seat, which was sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement. Translators render it “atoning sacrifice,” “propitiation,” “expiation” or “mercy seat” and debate whether it means turning away God’s anger, removing sin, or both.

Redemption is buying back: the price paid to free a slave or prisoner. Paul says believers “are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus” (3:24) and speaks of waiting for “the redemption of our bodies” (8:23).
Galatians uses a different Greek word that means to buy out of slavery: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (3:13), and “to redeem those under the law” (4:5).

In Ephesians “we have redemption through His blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses” (1:7). The Spirit is the pledge “until the redemption of those who are God’s possession” (1:14), and believers are sealed “for the day of redemption” (4:30).
In Colossians “we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” in the Son (1:14).
Hebrews speaks of “eternal redemption” (9:12), which Christ secured by his own blood, and says his death was “to redeem them from the transgressions committed under the first covenant” (9:15).

1 Peter 1:18-19 uses a different Greek verb, lytroo, “ransom”: the readers were redeemed “not with perishable things such as silver or gold” but “with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot.”

To reconcile is to turn enemies into friends. Paul says “when we were enemies of God, we were reconciled to Him through the death of His Son” (5:10), and that Israel’s rejection has become “the reconciliation of the world” (11:15).

The fullest teaching on reconciliation is in 2 Corinthians 5:18-21, where God “reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation,” and Paul appeals, “Be reconciled to God.”
In Ephesians Christ reconciles “both of them to God in one body through the cross” (2:16), joining Jew and Gentile and making peace with God.

In Colossians God reconciles “all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through the blood of His cross” (1:20), and the Colossians, once “alienated from God,” are now reconciled “by Christ’s physical body through death” (1:21-22).
In Philemon Paul asks for two people, a master and a slave, to be reconciled, so that Philemon will have Onesimus back “as a beloved brother” (16).

Paul says “The wrath of God is being revealed from heaven against all the godlessness and wickedness of men” (1:18). He warns that stubborn hearts are “storing up wrath” for the day of judgment (2:5), says believers are saved from wrath through Christ (5:9), and tells them not to avenge themselves but to “leave room for God’s wrath” (12:19).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians Jesus is “our deliverer from the coming wrath” (1 Thessalonians 1:10), and “God has not appointed us to suffer wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ” (5:9).

Revelation speaks of “the great day of Their wrath” (6:17), the winepress of God’s wrath (14:19) and seven golden bowls “full of the wrath of God” (15:7). The wrath is God’s judgment on what destroys the earth (11:18).

In Roman law an adopted son received the full standing and inheritance of a natural son. Paul says believers “received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (8:15) and are “heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ” (8:17). He says Israel also has “the adoption as sons” (9:4).

Galatians 4 says “God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law, to redeem those under the law, that we might receive our adoption as sons” (4:4-5). “So you are no longer a slave, but a son; and since you are a son, you are also an heir through God” (4:7).
In Ephesians God “predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ” (1:5), and believers are called “beloved children” who are to imitate their Father (5:1).
In Hebrews God is “bringing many sons to glory” (2:10), and treats his people as sons when he disciplines them: “God is treating you as sons. For what son is not disciplined by his father?” (12:7).

Paul writes that “those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son” (8:29), and in chapters 9-11 speaks of God’s choice of Isaac and Jacob, and of a remnant “chosen by grace” (11:5). Christians read these chapters differently: some see God choosing individuals for salvation, others see him choosing a people or a way of salvation. All agree Paul ends the argument in praise: “O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (11:33).

In Ephesians the choosing is “in Him before the foundation of the world” (1:4), and it is for adoption “according to the good pleasure of His will” (1:5). It serves holiness, love and “the praise of His glorious grace” (1:6).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians Paul says, “we know that He has chosen you” (1 Thessalonians 1:4), and “God has chosen you from the beginning to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth” (2 Thessalonians 2:13).

In 2 Timothy God “has saved us and called us to a holy calling, not because of our works, but by His own purpose and by the grace He granted us in Christ Jesus before time began” (1:9), and Paul endures “for the sake of the elect” (2:10).
In Titus Paul writes “for the faith of God’s elect and their knowledge of the truth that leads to godliness” (1:1).
1 Peter 1:1-2 is addressed “to the elect... according to the foreknowledge of God the Father,” and 2:9 calls the church “a chosen people.”

Paul asks, “Aren’t you aware that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death?” (6:3). Baptism pictures dying with Christ and rising to “walk in newness of life” (6:4). Paul uses it to answer the question whether grace gives license to sin.

e.n: Dead to sin, alive to God
t: Paul tells the believers in Rome, “you too must count yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus” (6:11). He says sin once ruled them like a slave owner, and now they have “been set free from sin” and “become slaves to righteousness” (6:18).

In Romans “flesh” can mean the physical body, but in chapters 7-8 it usually means human life ruled by sin, set against life led by God’s Spirit. Paul says “You, however, are controlled not by the flesh, but by the Spirit, if the Spirit of God lives in you” (8:9).

Galatians 5 sets them in conflict: “the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh” (5:17). The acts of the flesh are listed in 5:19-21, and the fruit of the Spirit in 5:22-23. Paul says “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (5:24).

In Ephesians the old life was “fulfilling the cravings of our flesh” (2:3). Believers are “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (1:13), are told to be “filled with the Spirit” (5:18), and wield “the sword of the Spirit” (6:17).
1 John 2:16 speaks of “the desires of the flesh” as part of the world that is “not from the Father,” and 4:2 asks for the confession that Jesus Christ “has come in the flesh.”

In Romans 7:15 the speaker says, “I do not understand what I do. For what I want to do, I do not do. But what I hate, I do.” Readers have long debated whether Paul is describing his life before Christ, his present life as a believer, or Israel under the law. All agree the passage shows that the law is “holy” (7:12) but cannot free a person from sin.

Paul sets two men side by side: “just as sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin,” so “the many will be made righteous” through “the obedience of the one man” (5:12, 19). He calls Adam “a pattern of the One to come” (5:14). Where sin increased, “grace increased all the more” (5:20).

Paul says “the creation waits in eager expectation for the revelation of the sons of God” and “has been groaning together in the pains of childbirth until the present time” (8:19, 22). The creation, believers and the Spirit all groan, and all wait for freedom from decay.

e.n: Nothing can separate us from God’s love
t: Paul ends the great chapter 8 with questions: “Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?” and answers that nothing, “neither death nor life ... nor anything else in all creation” can do it (8:35-39). He lists trouble, danger and the sword among the things that cannot.

e.n: Christ is the end of the law
t: Paul writes, “Christ is the end of the law, to bring righteousness to everyone who believes” (10:4). The Greek word for “end” (telos) can mean goal, culmination or termination, and readers argue which Paul means. Earlier he asks whether faith nullifies the law and answers, “Certainly not! Instead, we uphold the law” (3:31).
Galatians reaches the same conclusion by another road: “the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ... Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian” (3:24-25).

Paul writes, “if you confess with your mouth, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved” (10:9). In the Roman world Caesar was also given the title “lord,” so the confession was a public claim. He adds that “faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of Christ” (10:17).
In Philippians every tongue will “confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (2:11).

1 John 4:2-3 sets the test for every spirit: “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God.” 4:15 adds, “If anyone confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God abides in him, and he in God.”

Paul pictures Israel as a cultivated olive tree from which some branches were broken, and Gentile believers as “a wild olive shoot” grafted in. He warns, “You do not support the root, but the root supports you” (11:18), and says “all Israel will be saved” (11:26).

After eleven chapters of teaching, Paul urges the Romans “on account of God’s mercy, to offer your bodies as living sacrifices, holy and pleasing to God, which is your spiritual service of worship” (12:1). He adds, “Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (12:2).

Paul tells the Roman believers, “Do not repay anyone evil for evil,” “live at peace with everyone,” and “overcome evil with good” (12:17-21). He quotes Proverbs 25:21-22 about feeding an enemy, which will “heap burning coals on his head.”

Paul writes, “Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except that which is from God” (13:1). He tells the believers in Rome to pay taxes and to give respect and honor to whom they are due. The letter was written under the young Nero; Revelation 13 later shows another view of an empire that demands worship. Christians have long debated where obedience ends.
1 Peter 2:13-17 tells the readers to submit “to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, or to governors,” and ends, “fear God, honor the king.”

Paul says “Be indebted to no one, except to one another in love. For he who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law” (13:8), and “love is the fulfillment of the law” (13:10). It echoes Jesus’ teaching on the greatest commandment.
Galatians 5:14 says the same: “The entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself.’” Paul also speaks of “the law of Christ” (6:2).
James calls Leviticus 19:18 “the royal law”: “If you really fulfill the royal law stated in Scripture, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself,’ you are doing well” (2:8).

In Romans 14 Paul says believers should not “pass judgment” on each other over food and holy days. “Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind” (14:5). He gives the reason: “whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord” (14:8), and “the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking, but of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit” (14:17).

James tells his readers, “Brothers, do not slander one another. Anyone who speaks against his brother or judges him speaks against the law and judges it” (4:11), and reminds them that there is only one Lawgiver and Judge (4:12).

Paul tells the Roman believers to “Share with the saints who are in need. Practice hospitality” (12:13). The Greek word means love of strangers, and in a world with few inns it often meant opening a home to traveling believers. Romans 16 names Prisca and Aquila and Gaius as hosts of the church.
In Titus an elder must be “hospitable” (1:8), and Titus is to “equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos” for their journey (3:13).
In Philemon Paul asks, “prepare a guest room for me” (22), expecting to be released and to visit.

In Hebrews, “Do not neglect to show hospitality to strangers, for by so doing some people have entertained angels without knowing it” (13:2), an echo of Abraham and Sarah’s guests in Genesis 18. The Greek word is philoxenia, “love of strangers.”
1 Peter 4:9 says, “Show hospitality to one another without complaining,” in a letter to people who were themselves “foreigners and exiles” (2:11).

In 2 John, hospitality has a limit: “If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him” (10). The limit applies to a teacher who denies the teaching of Christ, not to the stranger in general.

In 3 John, hospitality is the main subject. Gaius is praised because “you are faithful in what you are doing for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you” (5), and the elder says “we ought to support such men” (8). Diotrephes is blamed because “he refuses to welcome the brothers” (10).

Paul opens and closes Romans with the aim of calling the nations “to the obedience that comes from faith” (1:5; 16:26). The phrase joins faith and obedience: trust in Christ shows itself in a changed life.

e.n: The gift for the saints in Jerusalem
t: Paul tells the Romans that Macedonia and Achaia “were pleased to make a contribution for the poor among the saints in Jerusalem” (15:26), and he is about to deliver it. He argues that the Gentiles “have shared in their spiritual blessings” and owe material help in return (15:27). The collection also appears in 1 Corinthians 16 and 2 Corinthians 8-9.

Paul gave the Corinthians the same instructions he gave “the churches of Galatia”: “On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income, saving it up, so that when I come no collections will be needed” (16:1-2). Their chosen messengers would carry the gift to Jerusalem (16:3).

Paul spends two chapters on the collection in 2 Corinthians 8-9. He holds up the Macedonians, sends Titus and two brothers ahead, and says the aim is fairness: “there may be equality” (8:14). The gift brings “many expressions of thanksgiving to God” (9:12).

e.n: The wisdom of God and the message of the cross
t: Corinth admired polished speakers and clever arguments. Paul says “the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God” (1:18). Jews “demand signs and Greeks search for wisdom, but we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (1:22-23). Christ is the wisdom of God, and has “become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption” (1:30). Real wisdom is a gift of the Spirit, “the mysterious and hidden wisdom of God” (2:7).

Paul says God chose the weak “so that no one may boast in His presence” (1:29), and quotes Jeremiah: “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (1:31). He asks the Corinthians, “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” (4:7). Boasting in a favorite teacher is one more way of boasting in oneself: “stop boasting in men” (3:21).

In 2 Corinthians Paul boasts “only within the field of influence that God has assigned” (10:13), quotes “Let him who boasts boast in the Lord” (10:17), and plays the fool by boasting of “the things that show my weakness” (11:30).
In Galatians he says “may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (6:14).

News reaches Paul that the Corinthians are saying “I follow Paul,” “I follow Apollos,” “I follow Cephas,” or “I follow Christ” (1:12). He asks, “Is Christ divided?” and traces the quarrels to pride (3:3-4). Divisions also show up at the Lord’s Supper (11:18-19). His answer is that all the leaders are servants and all believers belong to the one Lord.

In Titus Paul tells the church to “avoid foolish controversies, genealogies, arguments, and quarrels about the law, because these things are pointless and worthless” (3:9), and to reject a “divisive man” after two warnings (3:10).

Paul and Apollos are “servants through whom you believed, as the Lord has assigned to each his role” (3:5). He pictures the work as a farm (“I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow,” 3:6) and as a household in which workers are “stewards of the mysteries of God.” “Now it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (4:1-2).

In 2 Corinthians Paul describes himself and his team as “servants” and “ministers of a new covenant” (3:6), and says “we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake” (4:5).
In Ephesians Paul describes “the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you” (3:2) and “the stewardship of this mystery” (3:9).

Paul tells the Corinthians “you are God’s field, God’s building” and that he laid a foundation, “which is Jesus Christ” (3:9-11). Builders may use “gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw,” and the Day will test each one’s work by fire (3:12-15). Then: “Do you not know that you yourselves are God’s temple, and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (3:16). In Greek the “you” is plural, so the whole church is the temple.
In 2 Corinthians 6:16 Paul says “we are the temple of the living God,” and quotes the promise “I will dwell with them and walk among them.”
In Ephesians the whole church “grows into a holy temple in the Lord” and is “a dwelling place for God in His Spirit” (2:21-22).

A man in the church “has his father’s wife” (5:1). Paul tells them to act: “hand this man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that his spirit may be saved on the Day of the Lord” (5:5). The aim is rescue as well as protection, and “a little leaven works through the whole batch of dough” (5:6). Paul limits the rule to those inside the church: “God will judge those outside” (5:13). Scholars differ on what “destruction of the flesh” means, and on whether this man is the offender Paul later asks the church to forgive (2 Corinthians 2:5-8).

In 2 Corinthians the aim is restoration: after the majority had punished the offender, Paul says “you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow” (2:7). For the third visit he cites the rule of two or three witnesses (13:1).

In Titus the rule is gradual. Paul says, “Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned” (3:10-11). The warnings come first and the rejection only after they are refused. The letter does not say what rejection involved, or whether it was meant to end in restoration.

Paul answers the slogan “Everything is permissible for me” with “not everything is beneficial” (6:12). He says the body “is not intended for sexual immorality, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body” (6:13), asks “Shall I then take the members of Christ and unite them with a prostitute? Never!” (6:15), and says “Flee from sexual immorality” (6:18). Sexual sin is a matter of the whole body, which belongs to Christ. His list in 6:9-10 ends with “And that is what some of you were. But you were washed, you were sanctified, you were justified” (6:11).

Paul tells the Corinthians that “your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have received from God. You are not your own; you were bought at a price. Therefore glorify God with your body” (6:19-20). Believers are the dwelling of God’s Spirit, one by one and together.

Paul is shocked that believers “go to law before the unrighteous instead of before the saints” (6:1). He argues that “the saints will judge the world,” so they can settle small matters among themselves (6:2-3), and says “Why not rather be wronged? Why not rather be cheated?” (6:7). Lawsuits showed how far the church had slipped from its own life together.

Paul answers questions the Corinthians wrote to him (7:1). He says each person has “his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that” (7:7), and that husband and wife owe each other (7:3-5). He separates what he says “not I, but the Lord” (7:10, the word of Jesus on divorce) from what he says “I, not the Lord” (7:12). A believer is not bound when an unbelieving partner leaves (7:15). He advises most people to “remain in the situation he was in” (7:20) because “the time is short” (7:29) and “the present crisis” (7:26) is pressing.
In Ephesians Paul compares marriage to Christ and the church, and quotes Genesis 2:24 before saying, “This mystery is profound” (5:31-32).
In 1 Timothy the teachers who “prohibit marriage” are rejected (4:3), and younger widows are advised to “marry, have children, and manage their households” (5:14).

Paul twice says to the Corinthians “you were bought at a price” (6:20; 7:23). It is the language of buying a slave out of slavery, as when a slave was freed by being sold to a god in a temple. A slave called by the Lord is “the Lord’s freedman,” and a free man called by Christ is “Christ’s slave” (7:22). Belonging to Christ frees believers from other masters.

Meat in Corinth often came from temple sacrifices, and feasts were held in the temples. Paul agrees that “an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one” (8:4). But “not everyone has this knowledge” (8:7). A believer who eats in an idol’s temple may lead a person with a weak conscience to do the same (8:10). Paul tells them to “flee from idolatry” (10:14), says “you cannot partake in the table of the Lord and the table of demons too” (10:21), but allows “anything sold in the meat market” (10:25).

Paul treats conscience as a sense of right and wrong that can be trained and can be hurt. A conscience that is “weak” is “defiled” when a person acts against it (8:7). Paul says to eat what is sold in the market “without raising questions of conscience” (10:25), and not to eat if someone points out that the food was offered to idols, “for the sake of the one who told you and for the sake of conscience” (10:28). The conscience he means is the other person’s as much as the believer’s own.

In 1 Timothy the goal of instruction is “a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith” (1:5). Some “have rejected” a good conscience and shipwrecked their faith (1:19), and the consciences of the liars are “seared with a hot iron” (4:2).
In Titus the minds and consciences of the false teachers are “defiled” (1:15), so that they “profess to know God, but by their actions they deny Him” (1:16).

In Hebrews the old sacrifices “were unable to cleanse the conscience of the worshiper” (9:9). The blood of Christ will “purify our consciences from works of death” (9:14), and believers draw near “having our hearts sprinkled to cleanse us from a guilty conscience” (10:22). The writer also asks for prayer, being “convinced that we have a clear conscience” (13:18).
1 Peter 3:16 and 3:21 speak of “a clear conscience,” and 2:19 of one who “endures the pain of unjust suffering because he is conscious of God.”

Paul claims freedom (“Am I not free?” 9:1) and refuses to use it when it would hurt someone: “Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak” (8:9). “Everything is permissible, but not everything is beneficial” (10:23). The rule is “No one should seek his own good, but the good of others” (10:24), and “do it all to the glory of God” (10:31).

Paul says he has the right to be supported: “the Lord has prescribed that those who preach the gospel should receive their living from the gospel” (9:14). He backs it with the law about the ox: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (9:9). But he chose to work for his living: “we put up with anything rather than hinder the gospel of Christ” (9:12). He adds that he is under obligation to preach: “Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!” (9:16).

Paul says he is “free of obligation to anyone,” yet makes himself “a slave to everyone, to win as many as possible” (9:19). He lives like a Jew among Jews and like one outside the law among those outside it, “To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some” (9:22). The goal is always the gospel, not his own freedom or comfort.

Paul uses the picture of an athlete: “in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize. Run in such a way as to take the prize” (9:24). Athletes train with strict discipline for “a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable” (9:25). He ends: “I discipline my body and make it my slave, so that after I have preached to others, I myself will not be disqualified” (9:27).
In Philippians Paul presses “toward the goal to win the prize of God’s heavenly calling” (3:14), and calls the church “my joy and crown” (4:1).
In 2 Timothy a competitor “does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules” (2:5), and Paul says, “I have finished the race” and looks for “the crown of righteousness” (4:7-8).
In Hebrews the picture of a race returns: “let us run with endurance the race set out for us. Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith” (12:1-2).

Paul recalls that “our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea,” ate the same spiritual food, and drank from “the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ” (10:1-4). Yet most of them fell. “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come” (10:11). He ends with a promise: “God is faithful; He will not let you be tempted beyond what you can bear” (10:13).

Hebrews 3-4 builds a long warning on the same story. Psalm 95 is read as God’s word to the readers: “Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts” (3:7-8, 15). The generation that left Egypt did not enter God’s rest “because of their unbelief” (3:19).

In 11:2-16 Paul says men and women who pray or prophesy in the meeting should do so with their heads covered or uncovered in a way that is fitting (11:4-5). Both men and women pray and prophesy aloud. The passage is among the hardest in the letter. Scholars differ on whether it concerns veils or hairstyle (11:15 says “long hair is given to her as a covering”), whether “head” means source or authority (11:3), and what “a sign of authority on her head” means (11:10). Paul ends by saying “we have no other practice, nor do the churches of God” (11:16).

Paul says “There are different gifts, but the same Spirit” (12:4), and “to each one the manifestation of the Spirit is given for the common good” (12:7). He lists the message of wisdom, knowledge, faith, healing, miracles, prophecy, distinguishing between spirits, tongues and interpretation (12:8-10). All are “the work of one and the same Spirit, who apportions them to each one as He determines” (12:11). Gifts are for building up the church, not for status.
In Ephesians the gifts are people given to the church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, pastors and teachers (4:11), who “equip the saints for works of ministry” (4:12).
In 1 Thessalonians Paul says, “Do not extinguish the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things” (5:19-21).

Paul writes, “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, slave or free” (12:13), and “Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it” (12:27). Every member is needed: “The eye cannot say to the hand, ‘I do not need you’” (12:21). “If one part suffers, every part suffers with it; if one part is honored, every part rejoices with it” (12:26).

In Ephesians the church is “His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all” (1:23), the “one body” for Jew and Gentile (2:16; 4:4), and a body that “grows and builds itself up in love” as each part works (4:16).

In Colossians Christ “is the head of the body, the church” (1:18). The body “supported and knit together by its joints and ligaments, grows as God causes it to grow” (2:19), and believers “were called as members of one body” (3:15).

Tongues were one of the gifts the Corinthians prized (12:10, 28). Paul says “he who speaks in a tongue does not speak to men, but to God” (14:2), and that the church needs it to be interpreted, “so that the church may be edified” (14:5). He wishes that all could speak in tongues but would rather they prophesy, and says “in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue” (14:19). In the meeting, “two, or at most three, should speak in turn, and someone must interpret” (14:27).

Paul pictures the Corinthian meeting: “everyone has a psalm or a teaching, a revelation, a tongue, or an interpretation. All of these must be done to build up the church” (14:26). Prophets speak in turn, and “the others should weigh carefully what is said” (14:29). “God is not a God of disorder, but of peace” (14:33), and “everything must be done in a proper and orderly manner” (14:40). Verses 34-35 on women being silent are debated: some manuscripts put them after verse 40, and scholars differ on whether Paul is limiting disorder, quoting a Corinthian view, or whether the lines were added later.

Chapter 13 sits in the middle of Paul’s teaching on gifts. Without love, even tongues “of men and of angels” are “only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal” (13:1). “Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud” (13:4). It “bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things” (13:7). “Love never fails” (13:8), while prophecies, tongues and knowledge pass away. “Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face” (13:12).

“And now these three remain: faith, hope, and love; but the greatest of these is love” (13:13). The three appear together elsewhere in Paul, but here love is placed first because it is the way the others are lived and because it will outlast the gifts. The chapter ends with “Earnestly pursue love” (14:1).
In Colossians Paul thanks God for “your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints,” both coming from “the hope stored up for you in heaven” (1:4-5).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians Paul remembers their “work of faith, your labor of love, and your enduring hope” (1 Thessalonians 1:3) and tells them to put on “the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation” (5:8). Their “faith is growing more and more, and your love for one another is increasing” (2 Thessalonians 1:3).

In 1 Timothy “the love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith” is the goal of instruction (1:5), and Timothy is told to “set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity” (4:12).
1 Peter 1:3 speaks of “a living hope,” 1:21 says that “your faith and hope are in God,” and 1:22 calls for “a genuine love for your brothers.”

Paul reminds the church of the gospel “which you received, and in which you stand firm” (15:1), what he “received” and “passed on” as “of first importance”: “that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures, that He was buried, that He was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, and that He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve” (15:3-5). Scholars generally think the wording goes back to within a few years of the crucifixion. Paul lists the witnesses, ending with himself, “as to one of untimely birth” (15:8).

e.n: If Christ has not been raised
t: Some in Corinth said “there is no resurrection of the dead” (15:12). Paul answers: “if Christ has not been raised, our preaching is worthless, and so is your faith” (15:14), and “you are still in your sins” (15:17). But “Christ has indeed been raised from the dead, the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (15:20). The resurrection of Christ is the pledge of the resurrection of believers.

In arguing for the resurrection Paul asks, “what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are people baptized for them?” (15:29). No other passage in the New Testament mentions the practice. Scholars have proposed many explanations, and Paul does not say whether he approves of it. He uses it only to show that even the Corinthians’ own practice assumes the dead rise.

To the question “With what kind of body will they come?” (15:35) Paul answers with a seed: “What you sow does not come to life unless it dies” (15:36). God gives each seed “its own body” (15:38). “It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body” (15:44). The body is raised “imperishable,” in “glory” and in “power” (15:42-43). “Just as we have borne the likeness of the earthly man, so also shall we bear the likeness of the heavenly man” (15:49).
In Philippians the Savior “will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (3:21).

Paul says Christ must reign “until He has put all His enemies under His feet. The last enemy to be destroyed is death” (15:25-26). Then Christ hands the kingdom to God the Father “so that God may be all in all” (15:28). He ends with a song of victory: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O Death, is your victory? Where, O Death, is your sting?” (15:54-55) and “thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ!” (15:57).

Paul tells “a mystery”: “We will not all sleep, but we will all be changed—in an instant, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, the dead will be raised imperishable, and we will be changed” (15:51-52). “Flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom of God, nor does the perishable inherit the imperishable” (15:50). Those who are alive and those who have died are given the same new body.

Several of the sentences in 1 Corinthians look like sayings of the Corinthians that Paul repeats before he answers them: “Everything is permissible for me” (6:12; 10:23), “Food for the stomach and the stomach for food” (6:13), “We know that we all have knowledge” (8:1), and “an idol is nothing at all in the world” (8:4). He often agrees in part and then limits the claim. Scholars still debate exactly which lines are slogans.

Paul opens with a blessing: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles, so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves have received from God” (1:3-4). The words for comfort (and for urging and encouraging) appear nearly thirty times in the letter. Comfort here is not only a feeling. It is God’s help in trouble, passed on to others. When Titus arrives with good news, Paul says “God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus” (7:6).

Paul does not say believers escape trouble. “Just as the sufferings of Christ overflow to us, so also through Christ our comfort overflows” (1:5). His troubles and his comfort are both for the church: “If we are afflicted, it is for your comfort and salvation” (1:6). He tells how in Asia “We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life” (1:8), so that “we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead” (1:9).

e.n: All the promises are “Yes” in Christ
t: Some in Corinth said Paul could not be trusted because he changed his travel plans. He answers that his message was not “Yes” and “No,” because “the Son of God, Jesus Christ, who was proclaimed among you by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not ‘Yes’ and ‘No,’ but in Him it has always been ‘Yes’” (1:19). “All the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ. And so through Him, our ‘Amen’ is spoken to the glory of God” (1:20).

e.n: The seal and the pledge of the Spirit
t: Paul says God “anointed us, placed His seal on us, and put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come” (1:21-22). A seal marked who owned something, and a pledge (a deposit) was a first payment that guaranteed the rest. He uses the pledge again in 5:5, “God has prepared us for this very purpose and has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come.”

In Ephesians believers “were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our inheritance until the redemption of those who are God’s possession” (1:13-14), and are warned not to grieve the Spirit “in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (4:30).

A man in the church had caused grief, and the majority had punished him. Paul says “The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him. So instead, you ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow. Therefore I urge you to reaffirm your love for him” (2:6-8). He adds “If you forgive anyone, I also forgive him” (2:10), so “that Satan should not outwit us” (2:11). Discipline is meant to restore.

Paul uses the picture of a victory parade: “thanks be to God, who always leads us triumphantly as captives in Christ and through us spreads everywhere the fragrance of the knowledge of Him” (2:14). He adds that “we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing. To the one, we are an odor of death and demise; to the other, a fragrance that brings life” (2:15-16). The same message has two effects. Paul then asks, “who is qualified for such a task?” (2:16).

e.n: Not peddling the word of God
t: Paul says “we are not like so many others, who peddle the word of God for profit. On the contrary, in Christ we speak before God with sincerity, as men sent from God” (2:17). He makes the same point when he says he preached to the Corinthians “free of charge” and accepted help from Macedonia (11:7-9), and when he says “I am not seeking your possessions, but you” (12:14).

e.n: A letter from Christ written on hearts
t: Some teachers came to Corinth carrying letters of recommendation. Paul asks, “do we need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you?” and answers: “You yourselves are our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone” (3:1-2). The Corinthians are “a letter from Christ, the result of our ministry, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (3:3).

e.n: The ministry of the Spirit and of the new covenant
t: Paul says God “has qualified us as ministers of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (3:6). He compares the “ministry of death, which was engraved in letters on stone” with “the ministry of the Spirit” (3:7-8) and “the ministry of righteousness” (3:9). The old came with glory, but it was “fading away”; the new “endures” (3:11). Paul is not rejecting the law but pointing to what the Spirit does that the written code alone could not.

e.n: The veil over the reading of Moses
t: When Moses came down from Sinai his face shone, and he put a veil over it (Exodus 34:29-35). Paul says “We are not like Moses, who would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away” (3:13). He then says “to this day the same veil remains at the reading of the old covenant. It has not been lifted, because only in Christ can it be removed” (3:14). “But whenever anyone turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away” (3:16).

“Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (3:17). Paul does not describe the freedom as doing anything one pleases, but as being no longer veiled, able to see the glory of the Lord, and being changed by the Spirit. Scholars differ on whether “the Lord” in 3:17 is the Lord of Exodus 34:34 or Christ, but the point is that the Spirit brings the Lord’s presence to his people.
“It is for freedom that Christ has set us free” (Galatians 5:1), and freedom is for loving service: “serve one another in love” (5:13).

Paul says “we, who with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory, which comes from the Lord, who is the Spirit” (3:18). Christ “is the image of God” (4:4), and God has “made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:6). Believers are changed by looking at Christ.
In Colossians the new self is “being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (3:10), and Christ is “the image of the invisible God” (1:15).

Paul says “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ” (4:4). He warns the church to watch for Satan’s schemes (2:11), and says “Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light” (11:14). He also speaks of his own “messenger of Satan” (12:7). Satan is real and active in Paul’s account, but he is never shown as equal to God.

Paul says “we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us” (4:7). The apostles are fragile and ordinary containers. He lists the strain: “hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed” (4:8-9). We “always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body” (4:10).

e.n: Our outer self is wasting away
t: Paul says “we do not lose heart. Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day” (4:16). He calls the trouble “light and momentary affliction” that “is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison” (4:17). He asks believers to “fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen. For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal” (4:18).

e.n: The earthly tent and the heavenly house
t: Paul says “if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands” (5:1). Paul, who made tents himself (Acts 18:3), uses the tent as a picture of the body. He groans, not wanting to be “unclothed but clothed, so that our mortality may be swallowed up by life” (5:4). He says “we walk by faith, not by sight” (5:7), and would “prefer to be away from the body and at home with the Lord” (5:8). Scholars differ on how this fits with the resurrection in 1 Corinthians 15.
2 Peter 1:13-14 uses the same picture: “the tent of my body,” soon to “be laid aside.”

Paul says “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, that each one may receive his due for the things done in the body, whether good or bad” (5:10). The word is bema, the raised platform where a Roman official sat, like the one in Corinth’s forum. Paul says this is why “we try to persuade men” (5:11), and why believers aim “to please Him” (5:9).

Paul says “Christ’s love compels us, because we are convinced that One died for all, therefore all died” (5:14). Because of that, “from now on we regard no one according to the flesh” (5:16). “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away. Behold, the new has come!” (5:17). The change is more than moral improvement: the whole person belongs to a new order that began with Christ’s resurrection.
Paul uses the phrase again at the end of Galatians: “neither circumcision nor uncircumcision means anything. What counts is a new creation” (6:15).
2 Peter 3:13 speaks of “a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells.”

Paul says “All this is from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation: that God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men’s trespasses against them. And He has committed to us the message of reconciliation” (5:18-19). God took the first step. Paul’s part is the appeal: “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us. We implore you on behalf of Christ: Be reconciled to God” (5:20).

An ambassador spoke for a ruler who was not present. Paul says “we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making His appeal through us” (5:20). In the Roman empire, ambassadors from kings and cities came to the emperor’s court. Paul’s words mean that the message comes with God’s authority, and also that the messenger has no standing apart from the one who sent him.

Paul says “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God” (5:21). It is one of his shortest statements of the exchange at the cross: Christ, who had no sin, was treated as sin, and those in him are given the standing that belongs to God’s own righteousness. Scholars differ on how best to describe the exchange, but it is one of Paul’s clearest statements of what happens at the cross.

e.n: Now is the day of salvation
t: Paul urges the Corinthians “not to receive God’s grace in vain,” and quotes Isaiah 49:8: “In the time of favor I heard you, and in the day of salvation I helped you.” Then he adds: “Behold, now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!” (6:1-2). In Isaiah the words are spoken to God’s servant. Paul says the time has now come.

Paul lists what he does and what he endures: “in great endurance; in troubles, hardships, and calamities; in beatings, imprisonments, and riots; in labor, sleepless nights, and hunger” (6:4-5), then in “purity, knowledge, patience, and kindness” (6:6). He ends with a string of contrasts, such as “dying, and yet we live on,” “sorrowful, yet always rejoicing,” “poor, yet making many rich” (6:9-10). In chapter 11 the list is longer: five times the forty lashes minus one, three beatings with rods, one stoning, three shipwrecks (11:23-28).

Paul tells the Corinthians “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers. For what partnership can righteousness have with wickedness? Or what fellowship does light have with darkness?” (6:14). The picture is of two animals of different kinds tied under one yoke, as Deuteronomy 22:10 forbids. He asks “What agreement can exist between the temple of God and idols? For we are the temple of the living God” (6:16). The passage is about close partnership in worship and life, and its exact reach is debated.

Paul says his earlier letter hurt the Corinthians, and that he first regretted it, but now rejoices “not because you were made sorrowful, but because your sorrow led you to repentance” (7:9). He separates two kinds: “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death” (7:10). Real sorrow over wrongdoing produces “earnestness,” “eagerness to clear yourselves,” “indignation,” “alarm,” “longing,” “zeal” and “vindication” (7:11).

Paul holds up the churches of Macedonia, whose “abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity” (8:2). They gave “according to their ability and even beyond it,” pleading “for the privilege of sharing in this service to the saints” (8:3-4). Paul asks Corinth to finish what it began: “see that you also excel in this grace of giving” (8:7). He calls the offering a “grace,” not a tax, and tests “the sincerity of your love” (8:8).

In Philippians the church’s gift is “a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God,” and God “will supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus” (4:18-19).

e.n: He became poor for your sakes
t: The reason for generosity is Christ: “you know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich” (8:9). Paul uses Christ’s own giving as the pattern for the collection. Scholars debate whether “rich” and “poor” refer to Christ’s heavenly state and incarnation or to his earthly life, and many see both.

Paul explains that the aim is fairness, not hardship for Corinth: “It is not our intention that others may be relieved while you are burdened, but that there may be equality. At the present time, your surplus will meet their need, so that in turn their surplus will meet your need” (8:13-14). He quotes Exodus 16:18: “He who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall” (8:15).

Paul gives a principle for giving. “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously. Each one should give what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (9:6-7). God “is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work” (9:8). The gift is also a service that leads to thanksgiving to God (9:12).

e.n: Paul’s authority is for building up
t: Paul says the authority the Lord gave him is “for building you up rather than tearing you down” (10:8; 13:10). His enemies said “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account” (10:10). He answers that “the weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds” (10:4), and that he will not “boast beyond our limits,” only within “the field of influence that God has assigned to us” (10:13).

Paul says “We tear down arguments and every presumption set up against the knowledge of God; and we take captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ” (10:5). The battle he describes is over ideas and loyalties, not armies. The weapons are “divine power” (10:4), not the tools of persuasion and show that his critics prized.

Paul fears that “just as Eve was deceived by the serpent’s cunning, your minds may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ” (11:3). Visitors preach “a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed,” “a different spirit,” or “a different gospel,” and the church “put up with it way too easily” (11:4). He calls them “false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ” (11:13). Their teaching, not their style, is the issue.

Paul is forced to boast because the Corinthians were impressed by those who did. He calls it foolishness: “I am not speaking as the Lord would, but as a fool” (11:17). He lists his credentials (“Are they Hebrews? So am I,” 11:22), then his sufferings, then his visions (12:1-4). He ends by boasting only in weakness: “If I must boast, I will boast of the things that show my weakness” (11:30). The speech is irony: he shows his critics’ standards and turns them upside down.

e.n: The visions of the third heaven
t: Paul speaks of “a man in Christ who fourteen years ago was caught up to the third heaven. Whether it was in the body or out of it I do not know, but God knows” (12:2). He was “caught up to Paradise. The things he heard were too sacred for words, things that man is not permitted to tell” (12:4). Most readers think he means himself, since he goes on to say “I will boast about such a man, but I will not boast about myself, except in my weaknesses” (12:5). He keeps the revelation private.

To keep him humble, Paul says “I was given a thorn in my flesh, a messenger of Satan, to torment me” (12:7). He does not name it. Guesses have included an illness, poor eyesight, or opposition from people, but nothing in the letter settles it. He asked three times for it to be removed (12:8). The answer was no, and a promise: “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness” (12:9).

Paul answers the thorn with a rule that runs through the letter: “Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me. That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses, in insults, in hardships, in persecutions, in difficulties. For when I am weak, then I am strong” (12:9-10). The cross is the pattern: “He was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God’s power” (13:4).

Since the Corinthians demanded “proof that Christ is speaking through me” (13:3), Paul turns the test around: “Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith; test yourselves. Can’t you see for yourselves that Jesus Christ is in you—unless you actually fail the test?” (13:5). He prays “that you will not do anything wrong—not that we will appear to have stood the test, but that you will do what is right” (13:7).

Paul ends with “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with all of you” (13:14). It names Christ, God and the Spirit together, a pattern that later Christians used in discussing the Trinity. Paul writes it as a blessing for a church that is still in conflict.

e.n: Paul’s visits and letters to Corinth
t: The Corinthian story is longer than Acts shows. Paul founded the church (about AD 50-52), then wrote an earlier letter (1 Corinthians 5:9), then 1 Corinthians. He seems to have made a short, painful second visit (2 Corinthians 2:1; 13:2), wrote a sharp letter “through many tears” (2:4), waited anxiously for Titus (2:12-13), and received good news in Macedonia (7:5-7). He then wrote 2 Corinthians and made a third visit (12:14; 13:1; Acts 20:2-3). Scholars differ on where the sharp letter went, and many think chapters 10-13 come from it or from a later letter.

Paul has no greeting of thanks. He is “amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ and are turning to a different gospel,” and he adds that it “is not even a gospel” (1:6-7). He says even “we or an angel from heaven” should be under a curse if they preach another (1:8-9). In Antioch he says Peter and the others “were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel” (2:14). For Paul the gospel is not one opinion among several. It is the message of Christ crucified, and adding to it changes it.

The letter opens with a claim: Paul is “an apostle—sent not from men nor by man, but by Jesus Christ and God the Father” (1:1). He says the gospel he preached “was not devised by man” and “I received it by revelation from Jesus Christ” (1:11-12). God “was pleased to reveal His Son in me so that I might preach Him among the Gentiles” (1:15-16). Later he says the leaders in Jerusalem “added nothing” to him (2:6) and recognized that he had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised (2:7).

Paul tells his own story to show that the gospel did not come from Jerusalem. After his call he went to Arabia and back to Damascus (1:17), and “only after three years” went up to Jerusalem to “confer with Cephas” for fifteen days, seeing no other apostle except James (1:18-19). “Fourteen years later” he went again with Barnabas and Titus and set the gospel he preached before them (2:1-2). The leaders gave him and Barnabas “the right hand of fellowship,” asking only that they “remember the poor” (2:9-10). How this visit fits with Acts is debated: many match it with the visit of Acts 15, others with the famine visit of Acts 11:30.

Paul says that when Cephas came to Antioch, “I opposed him to his face, because he stood to be condemned” (2:11). Before certain men came from James, Peter ate with Gentile believers, but then “began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group,” and the other Jews, even Barnabas, followed (2:12-13). Paul’s question to Peter is “If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?” (2:14). Galatians does not report how Peter answered. Many think the incident came after the Jerusalem meeting, but some place it before.

Paul says “a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (2:16), and asks the Galatians whether they received the Spirit “by works of the law, or by hearing with faith” (3:2; see also 3:5). He adds that “All who rely on works of the law are under a curse” (3:10). Scholars differ on what the phrase covers. Some take it to mean any attempt to earn God’s favor by obedience, and others stress the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision and food laws. The argument of the letter touches both.
In Philippians Paul says that “as to righteousness in the law,” he was “faultless” (3:6), but he does not want “my own righteousness from the law” (3:9).

e.n: Faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ?
t: Several verses can be read two ways in Greek. In 2:16 Paul writes of being justified “by faith in Jesus Christ,” but the Greek can also mean “through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.” The same question arises in 2:20 (“faith in the Son of God”) and 3:22. Translators and scholars are divided. Either way, the verses say that being counted righteous rests on what Christ has done, and that people receive it by trusting him.

Paul writes, “I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me” (2:20). He says believers “have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (5:24), and that through the cross “the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (6:14). The cross is both what Christ did for him and the end of his old way of living.

e.n: Christ became a curse for us
t: Paul says “All who rely on works of the law are under a curse,” quoting “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law” (3:10; Deuteronomy 27:26).
