Then: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: ‘Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree’” (3:13; Deuteronomy 21:23). The purpose was “that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit” (3:14).

e.n: The promise to Abraham and his seed
t: Paul argues from Genesis that God made a promise to Abraham long before the law. “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed,” and Paul reads “seed” as “One, who is Christ” (3:16). “The law that came 430 years later does not revoke the covenant previously established by God” (3:17), and “if the inheritance depends on the law, then it no longer depends on a promise; but God freely granted it to Abraham through a promise” (3:18). All who belong to Christ are “Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (3:29).

Paul asks, “Why then was the law given?” and answers, “It was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed” (3:19). He says “the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ, that we might be justified by faith. Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian” (3:24-25). The Greek word was used for the slave who watched over a child until he was grown. Scholars differ on how positive or negative Paul’s picture is, but he says the law’s role lasted until Christ came.

e.n: One in Christ: neither Jew nor Greek
t: Paul writes, “You are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus” (3:26-28). The three pairs name the great divisions of his world, and he says they no longer decide who belongs. This is why the table at Antioch (2:11-14) mattered to him.

e.n: The basic principles of the world
t: Paul says “when we were children, we were enslaved under the basic principles of the world” (4:3), and tells the Gentile believers they were once “slaves to those who by nature are not gods” and asks why they turn back to “those weak and worthless principles” (4:8-9). The Greek word, stoicheia, has several possible meanings: elementary teachings (like the ABCs), the elements of the world, or spiritual powers behind them. Scholars debate which Paul has in mind, and some think he means more than one at once.

Paul corrects himself in the middle of a sentence: “now that you know God, or rather are known by God” (4:9). The order matters to him. Knowing God begins with God knowing his people and calling them (see also 1:6, 15), and that is why turning back to old slaveries makes no sense.

e.n: Special days, months, seasons and years
t: Paul is dismayed that the Galatians are “observing special days and months and seasons and years” (4:10). The letter does not say which days he means. Some think of the Jewish Sabbath and feast calendar, others of pagan festivals and astrological days, and some think of both. He treats the practice as part of turning back to “weak and worthless principles” (4:9), and fears that “my efforts for you may have been in vain” (4:11).

Paul says “it was because of an illness that I first preached the gospel to you. And although my illness was a trial to you, you did not despise or reject me. Instead, you welcomed me as if I were an angel of God, as if I were Christ Jesus Himself” (4:13-14). He adds that “if it were possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me” (4:15). The letter does not name the illness, and guesses range from eye trouble to malaria to the “thorn in the flesh” of 2 Corinthians 12.

Paul tells the story of Abraham’s two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman, and says “these things serve as illustrations, for the women represent two covenants. One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery: This is Hagar” (4:24). Hagar “corresponds to the present-day Jerusalem,” while “the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother” (4:25-26). He quotes Isaiah 54:1 about the barren woman (4:27) and Genesis 21 to say “Expel the slave woman and her son” (4:30). Believers are “children of promise” like Isaac (4:28). His reading is a picture drawn from the story, not a claim that Genesis was only about this.

Paul sets “the present-day Jerusalem” against “the Jerusalem above,” which “is free, and she is our mother” (4:25-26). The phrase points to a heavenly city that already exists and to which believers belong. Hebrews 12:22 and Revelation 21:2 use similar ideas.

In Hebrews, “you have come to Mount Zion, to the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem” (12:22), and “here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come” (13:14).

God gave circumcision to Abraham as the sign of the covenant (Genesis 17). It becomes the main issue in Galatians. The agitators want the Gentile believers circumcised (6:12), and Paul refuses to have Titus compelled (2:3). He warns, “if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no value to you at all” (5:2), and that such a person “is obligated to obey the whole law” (5:3). He says “in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any value. All that matters is faith, expressed through love” (5:6), and “What counts is a new creation” (6:15).
In Philippians Paul says “it is we who are the circumcision, we who worship by the Spirit of God” (3:3), and lists himself as “circumcised on the eighth day” (3:5).

In Colossians the Gentile believers are “circumcised, in the putting off of your sinful nature, with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands” (2:11), and in the new life “there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised” (3:11).

In Titus the troublemakers are “especially those of the circumcision” (1:10), men who are “rebellious and full of empty talk and deception.” The letter does not say whether they were Jewish believers or others who held that Gentiles must keep the law.

Paul says “All that matters is faith, expressed through love” (5:6). Faith is not set against action. It “works” through love, and love is how freedom is lived: “serve one another in love. For the entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’” (5:13-14).

e.n: It is for freedom that Christ has set us free
t: Freedom is Paul’s word for what the gospel gives. “It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery” (5:1). The “false brothers” had come to “spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us” (2:4). Yet “you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh. Rather, serve one another in love” (5:13).

Paul uses a common saying: “A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough” (5:9). He uses it here about the false teaching. Leaven could stand for something small that spreads, and he uses a similar line in 1 Corinthians 5:6 about sin in the church.

Paul says, “walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (5:16), and “if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the law” (5:18). He ends the section with “Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit” (5:25). The Spirit is not only the gift received at the start (3:2) but the power for the whole way of life.

Paul says “The acts of the flesh are obvious” and lists “sexual immorality, impurity, and debauchery; idolatry and sorcery; hatred, discord, jealousy, and rage; rivalries, divisions, factions, and envy; drunkenness, orgies, and the like” (5:19-21). The list mixes sins of the body, of worship and of community. He warns “those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God” (5:21).

After the list of the flesh’s acts, Paul writes, “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law” (5:22-23). In Greek “fruit” is singular, as if the nine are one growth. Paul calls them the Spirit’s work, not something believers produce alone.

Paul says “Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ” (6:2). Earlier he said “the entire law is fulfilled in a single decree: ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’” (5:14). Scholars debate exactly what the phrase means, but the context points to Christ’s own pattern of love and self-giving (2:20) and to bearing one another’s weight.

Paul asks the “spiritual” to “restore him with a spirit of gentleness” when someone “is caught in a trespass,” and to “watch yourself, or you also may be tempted” (6:1). Then: “Carry one another’s burdens” (6:2), but also “each one should carry his own load” (6:5). The two Greek words differ, and the first is often explained as a heavy weight that needs help, the second as a personal pack that each must carry.

Paul writes, “Do not be deceived: God is not to be mocked. Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return. The one who sows to please his flesh, from the flesh will reap destruction; but the one who sows to please the Spirit, from the Spirit will reap eternal life” (6:7-8). He then encourages, “Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up” (6:9), and “as we have opportunity, let us do good to everyone, and especially to the family of faith” (6:10).

The agitators “want you to be circumcised that they may boast in your flesh” (6:13). Paul says, “may I never boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (6:14).

Paul closes with “Peace and mercy to all who walk by this rule, even to the Israel of God” (6:16). Who is meant is debated. Some read it as all believers, Jew and Gentile together. Others read it as believing Jews, or as the people of Israel who will yet believe. Nothing else in Galatians uses the phrase.

Paul ends with “From now on let no one cause me trouble, for I bear on my body the marks of Jesus” (6:17). The word for “marks” was used of brands or tattoos. Paul probably means the scars of floggings and stoning that came from serving Christ (compare 2 Corinthians 11:23-25). Some compare slave brands, and the phrase can mean that he belongs to Jesus.

The letter opens with a single long burst of praise. In the Greek, 1:3-14 is one sentence: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us in Christ with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly realms” (1:3). Paul then lists the blessings one after another: chosen before the world began, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, shown the mystery of God’s plan, given an inheritance, and sealed with the Holy Spirit. Three refrains mark its sections: “to the praise of His glorious grace” (1:6), “for the praise of His glory” (1:12) and “to the praise of His glory” (1:14).

e.n: Chosen before the foundation of the world
t: Paul writes, “He chose us in Him before the foundation of the world to be holy and blameless in His presence” (1:4), and “He predestined us for adoption as His sons through Jesus Christ, according to the good pleasure of His will” (1:5). The choosing is “in Him,” that is, in Christ, and its purpose is holiness and love. Christians disagree about whether the choosing is of individuals or of the people gathered in Christ, and about how it fits with human faith, which Paul also mentions in 1:13.

The little phrase “in Christ” or “in Him” runs through the letter like a thread. God blessed us “in Christ” (1:3), chose us “in Him” (1:4), gave grace “in the Beloved One” (1:6), and made “all things in heaven and on earth” one “in Christ” (1:10). Believers are seated “in Christ Jesus” (2:6), “created in Christ Jesus” (2:10) and “brought near” in Him (2:13). For Paul, being a Christian is more than agreeing with a teaching; it is being joined to a person.

In the New Testament a “mystery” is not a puzzle but a secret that God has now made known. Ephesians uses the word six times. God “has made known to us the mystery of His will” (1:9), the mystery was “made known to me by revelation” (3:3), and it is that “the Gentiles are fellow heirs, fellow members of the body, and fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus” (3:6). It had “for ages past” been “kept hidden in God” (3:9). Marriage points to a “profound” mystery of Christ and the church (5:32), and Paul asks for prayer to make known “the mystery of the gospel” (6:19).
In Colossians the “mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints” is “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:26-27).

God’s plan, Paul says, is “a plan for the fullness of time, to bring all things in heaven and on earth together in Christ” (1:10). The Greek verb, anakephalaioo, pictures gathering up a whole under a single head (kephale). The same Christ who is “head over everything for the church” (1:22) is the one under whom God means to unite heaven and earth. Colossians 1:15-20 sings a similar song.

e.n: Paul’s prayer for wisdom and revelation
t: After the praise, Paul prays for his readers. He asks God to give “a spirit of wisdom and revelation in your knowledge of Him” (1:17), that “the eyes of your heart may be enlightened” to know “the hope of His calling, the riches of His glorious inheritance in the saints, and the surpassing greatness of His power to us who believe” (1:18-19). The measure of that power, he says, is the power that raised Christ from the dead and seated Him at God’s right hand (1:20).

e.n: Seated with Christ in the heavenly realms
t: God “raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus” (2:6). The same verse follows 2:5, “made us alive with Christ even when we were dead in our trespasses.” Paul uses three “with Christ” verbs, made alive, raised and seated, for what God has already done for believers, so that “in the coming ages” He may “display the surpassing riches of His grace” (2:7). Paul speaks of all three in the past tense, as things God has already done.

e.n: Dead in trespasses, alive with Christ
t: Ephesians 2:1-3 describes life before Christ in three parts. “You were dead in your trespasses and sins,” conformed “to the ways of this world,” following “the ruler of the power of the air,” and “fulfilling the cravings of our flesh” (2:1-3). Paul then includes himself: “all of us” lived that way, and “we were by nature children of wrath.” The next words turn the whole passage: “But because of His great love for us, God, who is rich in mercy, made us alive with Christ” (2:4-5).

“For it is by grace you have been saved through faith, and this not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not by works, so that no one can boast” (2:8-9). Paul does not stop there. He adds, “For we are God’s workmanship, created in Christ Jesus to do good works, which God prepared in advance as our way of life” (2:10). Good works are the result of salvation, not the way to it. Where Galatians argues against works of the law, Ephesians states the same gospel as a gift.

Paul reminds Gentiles that they were “separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world” (2:12). Now, “He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility” (2:14). Many scholars think Paul has in mind the stone barrier in the Jerusalem Temple that kept non-Jews out of the inner courts, though he may also mean the law that divided Jew from Gentile. Both pictures fit “abolishing in His flesh the law of commandments and decrees” (2:15).

e.n: One new man out of the two
t: Christ’s purpose, Paul says, was “to create in Himself one new man out of the two, thus making peace, and reconciling both of them to God in one body through the cross, by which He extinguished their hostility” (2:15-16). Jew and Gentile are not made into copies of each other. They become something new. The next verses add that through Him “we both have access to the Father by one Spirit” (2:18).

e.n: Fellow citizens and the household of God
t: Gentile believers are “no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (2:19). Paul changes the picture at once, from a city to a house to a temple: “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone. In Him the whole building is fitted together and grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (2:20-21). The church is God’s “dwelling place” in the Spirit (2:22).

Paul calls himself a steward of the mystery: “the stewardship of God’s grace that was given to me for you” (3:2). He is “less than the least of all the saints” yet is given “this grace” to preach “the unsearchable riches of Christ” to the Gentiles (3:8). A steward manages a household for its owner, and Paul sees his work among the nations the same way. He is writing, he says, as “the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles” (3:1).

e.n: The church shows God’s wisdom to the powers
t: God’s purpose was “that now, through the church, the manifold wisdom of God should be made known to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms, according to the eternal purpose that He accomplished in Christ Jesus our Lord” (3:10-11). The church is not only a community on earth. Its unity of Jew and Gentile is a sign to unseen powers of what God is doing. Paul does not say what those powers think of it, or how they learn from it.

Paul uses the phrase “in the heavenly realms” five times: believers are blessed there (1:3), Christ is seated there (1:20), believers are seated with Him there (2:6), the powers learn God’s wisdom there (3:10), and the struggle against “spiritual forces of evil” happens there (6:12). It is not the sky and it is not only the future. It is the unseen side of life where Christ already rules and where the struggle still goes on.

e.n: Access to the Father with boldness
t: “Through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit” (2:18), and “In Him and through faith in Him we may enter God’s presence with boldness and confidence” (3:12). Access (prosagoge) is a word for being led into the presence of a king. Gentiles who once stood outside the Temple barrier now have the same way in as Jews, and it is open every day.

e.n: The length and width and height and depth
t: Paul’s second prayer asks that Christ “may dwell in your hearts through faith,” that the readers be “rooted and grounded in love,” and that they “comprehend the length and width and height and depth of the love of Christ, and to know this love that surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled with all the fullness of God” (3:17-19). The prayer ends with praise to the One “who is able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine” (3:20).

The letter turns here from what God has done to how to live. “As a prisoner in the Lord, then, I urge you to walk in a manner worthy of the calling you have received: with all humility and gentleness, with patience, bearing with one another in love, and with diligence to preserve the unity of the Spirit through the bond of peace” (4:1-3). “Walk” is Paul’s word for the whole way of life, and it appears again at 4:17, 5:2, 5:8 and 5:15.
In 1 Thessalonians Paul urges them “to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory” (2:12).

e.n: One body, one Spirit, one Lord
t: Paul gives seven “ones”: “There is one body and one Spirit, just as you were called to one hope when you were called; one Lord, one faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all” (4:4-6). The list moves from the Spirit to the Lord to the Father, and it grounds the call to unity in who God is. Unity is something the Spirit has made, which believers are asked to “preserve” (4:3).

Paul quotes a psalm, “When He ascended on high, He led captives away, and gave gifts to men” (4:8), and says that the One who descended is the One who “ascended above all the heavens, in order to fill all things” (4:10). Psalm 68:18 in the Hebrew says the conqueror “received” gifts. Some scholars point out that an old Aramaic rendering of the psalm reads “gave,” which may be what Paul had in mind. The gifts that follow are people: “some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers” (4:11).

e.n: Equipping the saints and growing up
t: The leaders are given “to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ” (4:12). Most readers take this to mean that ministry belongs to the whole church, and its leaders prepare the rest. The goal is “unity in the faith” and maturity “to the full measure of the stature of Christ” (4:13). Then believers will no longer be “tossed about by the waves and carried around by every wind of teaching” (4:14). Instead they will be “speaking the truth in love” and growing “into Christ Himself, who is the head” (4:15).

e.n: Put off the old self, put on the new
t: Paul first describes the Gentile way of life as “the futility of their thinking,” with the mind “darkened” and “alienated from the life of God” (4:17-18). Then he says, “this is not the way you came to know Christ” (4:20). Believers were taught “to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires; to be renewed in the spirit of your minds; and to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness” (4:22-24). The image is of changing clothes.
In Colossians the Colossians “have taken off the old self with its practices, and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (3:9-10).

e.n: Do not let the sun set upon your anger
t: Having said “put off,” Paul gives examples. Speak truth, “for we are all members of one another” (4:25). “Be angry, yet do not sin. Do not let the sun set upon your anger, and do not give the devil a foothold” (4:26-27). The thief should work and “have something to share with the one in need” (4:28). Speech should be “helpful for building up” (4:29). And “Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander,” and “Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you” (4:31-32).

e.n: Do not grieve the Holy Spirit
t: “And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (4:30). The verse sits in the middle of a list about speech and anger, so the grief it speaks of comes from the way believers treat each other. It also shows that the Spirit is a person who can be grieved, and that the seal on believers (1:13) is meant to last until “the day of redemption.”

e.n: Imitators of God, walking in love
t: “Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God” (5:1-2). The pattern for a Christian life is God’s own forgiving love (4:32), seen most clearly in the cross. Paul uses the Old Testament language of a sacrifice that pleases God (“a fragrant offering”), but here the offering is Christ’s gift of himself.

“For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light, for the fruit of the light consists in all goodness, righteousness, and truth” (5:8-9). Paul asks readers to “test and prove what pleases the Lord” (5:10), to avoid “the fruitless deeds of darkness” and expose them (5:11). He ends with a saying that begins “So it is said”: “Wake up, O sleeper, rise up from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” (5:14). The words are not found exactly in the Old Testament, and scholars suggest an early hymn or a blend of passages such as Isaiah 60:1.

“Pay careful attention, then, to how you walk, not as unwise but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (5:15-16). Then: “Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit” (5:18). In the Greek, “be filled” is a command in the present tense, which suggests going on being filled. The results follow in a list: speaking to one another with “psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs,” making music in the heart, “always giving thanks,” and submitting “to one another out of reverence for Christ” (5:19-21).

“Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” (5:21) opens the household section. In the Greek the verb “submit” in 5:21 carries on into 5:22, and in the best manuscripts 5:22 has no verb of its own. So the instruction to wives is part of a call to the whole church. Submission here is willing and rests on the reverence for Christ, not on fear. Readers differ on how far the instruction to submit shapes the church and home today.

e.n: Christ and the church: husbands and wives
t: Paul speaks to wives in three verses (5:22-24) and to husbands in nine (5:25-33), so most of the passage is addressed to husbands. “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, and to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless” (5:25-27). A husband’s pattern is Christ’s self-giving love. Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says “This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church” (5:31-32). He ends, “each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband” (5:33). Christians differ over how the headship in 5:23 applies today.

“Children, obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (6:1). Paul quotes the fifth commandment, “Honor your father and mother,” and calls it “the first commandment with a promise” (6:2). Fathers get a brief command: “do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (6:4). In a world where the father held great power over his household, Paul speaks to the children directly as members of the church, and limits what the father may do.

Paul tells slaves to obey “with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ,” not “to please them while they are watching, but as servants of Christ” (6:5-6). Then he turns to masters: “do the same for your slaves. Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him” (6:9). The passage does not end slavery, and it has been misused to defend it. Yet it treats slaves as people who answer to Christ and masters as people who answer to the same Lord.

In Colossians slaves are told to work “for the Lord and not for men” (3:23), and masters are told to give their slaves “what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven” (4:1). Onesimus, a slave, goes with the letter (4:9).

In 1 Timothy “all who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited” (6:1). Slaves with believing masters are not to “show disrespect because they are brothers” (6:2). The letter lists “slave traders” among the lawless (1:10).

In Titus slaves are told “to submit to their own masters in everything, to be well-pleasing, not argumentative, not stealing from them, but showing all good faith” (2:9-10). The reason is that “in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior.” The letter does not say whether slavery should end. The word for “stealing” (nosphizo) is the one used in Acts 5:2-3 of Ananias, who “kept back” part of the money.

In Philemon the question becomes personal. Paul asks a master to receive his slave Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (16), and the letter gives no duties or rules for the slave or the master.
1 Peter 2:18-25 is addressed to household slaves, who are told to submit “even to those who are unreasonable” and are given Christ’s suffering as their example.

“For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms” (6:12). The words echo the list of powers Christ is seated “far above” (1:21). The word for struggle, pale, is a wrestling match, a fight at close quarters. Paul wants his readers to know that their trouble with other people also has an unseen side, and he names the devil’s “schemes” (6:11).
In Colossians Christ is “the head over every ruler and authority” (2:10), and on the cross, “having disarmed the powers and authorities,” He triumphed over them (2:15).

“Put on the full armor of God, so that you can make your stand against the devil’s schemes” (6:11). The pieces are the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, feet “fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace,” the shield of faith “with which you can extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one,” the helmet of salvation, and “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (6:14-17). Paul never says “fight.” The word he keeps using is “stand” (6:11, 13, 14). Parts of the picture are close to Isaiah’s description of God as a warrior (Isaiah 11:5; 59:17).
In 1 Thessalonians believers are told to put on “the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation” (5:8), an earlier and shorter form of the armor in Ephesians 6.

e.n: Pray in the Spirit at all times
t: The armor ends with prayer: “Pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition. To this end, stay alert with all perseverance in your prayers for all the saints” (6:18). Paul then asks the readers to pray for him: “that whenever I open my mouth, words may be given me so that I will boldly make known the mystery of the gospel, for which I am an ambassador in chains. Pray that I may proclaim it fearlessly, as I should” (6:19-20).
Jude 20 has the same phrase: the readers build themselves up by “praying in the Holy Spirit.”

Ephesians calls Paul “the prisoner of Christ Jesus for the sake of you Gentiles” (3:1), “a prisoner in the Lord” (4:1), and “an ambassador in chains” (6:20). An ambassador was a high official who spoke for a king, and Paul uses the word for himself while wearing a chain. He asks his readers “not to be discouraged because of my sufferings for you, which are your glory” (3:13). Acts 28:16-31 shows Paul under guard in Rome, which is the traditional place of writing, though Caesarea and Ephesus have also been suggested.
In 2 Timothy Paul is “His prisoner” (1:8), “chained like a criminal” (2:9), and a man whose friend “searched diligently until he found me” (1:17).
In Philemon he calls himself “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” twice (1, 9) and says that Onesimus became his child “while I was in chains” (10). He does not name the place where he is held.

The oldest copies of Ephesians, including the papyrus known as P46, do not have the words “in Ephesus” in 1:1. The letter also has none of the personal greetings found in Paul’s letters to churches he knew well, such as Corinth. Many scholars have concluded that Ephesians was a circular letter meant for several churches in Asia, with Tychicus carrying copies. Others think “in Ephesus” was original and was left out by some copyists. Colossians 4:16 mentions “the letter from Laodicea,” and a few have wondered if that is this one; the text does not say.

The Greek word koinonia, “fellowship” or “partnership,” and its family run through the letter. Paul thanks God for “your partnership in the gospel from the first day until now” (1:5), says they are “partners in grace with me” (1:7), speaks of “fellowship with the Spirit” (2:1) and “the fellowship of His sufferings” (3:10), and recalls that “no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving” (4:15). The church had shared money, prayer, a messenger and its own suffering. This is what Paul means by partnership: it is shared work, not only shared belief.
In Philemon the word koinonia, “partnership,” is used of Philemon’s share in the faith (6), and then Paul says, “if you consider me a partner, receive him as you would receive me” (17).

e.n: He who began a good work
t: Paul writes, “being confident of this, that He who began a good work in you will carry it on to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (1:6). The one who starts the work is God, and he is the one who finishes it. The same thought returns in 2:13, “it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose,” and in the prayer that they be “filled with the fruit of righteousness that comes through Jesus Christ” (1:11). “The day of Christ” (1:6, 10; 2:16) is the horizon for the whole letter.

Paul is a prisoner, yet writes, “my circumstances have actually served to advance the gospel” (1:12). The guard has heard why he is in chains (1:13), and “most of the brothers, confident in the Lord by my chains, now dare more greatly to speak the word without fear” (1:14). Some preach “out of envy and rivalry” and hope to add to his distress, but Paul says, “in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice” (1:18). He measures his own situation by what happens to the gospel, not by what happens to him.
In Philemon Paul is again “in my chains for the gospel” (13). He uses his chains as a reason to appeal for Onesimus and says that Onesimus could serve him there.

e.n: To live is Christ, to die is gain
t: Paul does not know whether his trial will end in release or in death. He writes, “For to me, to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (1:21). He is “torn between the two”: “I desire to depart and be with Christ, which is far better indeed. But it is more necessary for you that I remain in the body” (1:23-24). He ends convinced that he will stay and see them again (1:25). The passage shows that Paul expected to be “with Christ” at death, and that he chose to value his life by the good he could do for others.

e.n: Live as citizens of the gospel
t: The Greek verb in 1:27, politeuesthe, is usually translated “conduct yourselves,” but it comes from polis, “city,” and means to live as a citizen. “Conduct yourselves in a manner worthy of the gospel of Christ,” Paul says, and then describes citizen duties: stand “firm in one spirit,” “contending side by side for the faith of the gospel,” and not “frightened in any way by those who oppose you” (1:27-28). Philippi was a Roman colony whose people were proud of their citizenship, so Paul’s language suited them. In 3:20 he returns to the idea: “our citizenship is in heaven.”

Paul tells the church that “it has been granted to you on behalf of Christ not only to believe in Him, but also to suffer for Him” (1:29). The verb translated “granted” comes from charis, grace. Suffering and belief are both described as gifts. He adds that they face “the same struggle you saw I had, and now hear that I still have” (1:30), which points back to his beating and jailing in Philippi (Acts 16:19-24). The letter does not say what the Philippians’ own trouble was.

Paul asks for “like-minded” people “having the same love” and “united in spirit and purpose” (2:2). He then names the enemies of unity: “selfish ambition or empty pride.” The remedy is to “in humility consider others more important than yourselves” and to look “not only to your own interests, but also to the interests of others” (2:3-4). The appeal is made concrete in 4:2, where two women who “labored with me for the gospel” are asked to “agree with each other in the Lord.”

Philippians 2:6-11 is written in a rising and falling pattern that many scholars take to be an early hymn or poem. In the first half Christ, “existing in the form of God,” does not treat “equality with God” as “something to be grasped,” but “emptied Himself, taking the form of a servant,” and was “obedient to death, even death on a cross.” In the second half “God exalted Him to the highest place,” gives Him “the name above all names,” and every knee bows and every tongue confesses “that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” Scholars debate whether Paul quotes it or wrote it, what “grasped” means, and whether Adam is in the background. All agree that the hymn is a model of humility: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus” (2:5).

God gives Jesus “the name above all names,” so that “at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord” (2:9-11). The words come from Isaiah 45:22-23, where it is the LORD who says that every knee will bow to him and every tongue swear by him. Paul applies those words to Jesus and says the result is “the glory of God the Father.” The Greek Old Testament uses kyrios, “Lord,” to translate God’s name, and Greek cities also gave the title to emperors.

“Continue to work out your salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you to will and to act on behalf of His good purpose” (2:12-13). The verb means to work something out to its conclusion, as a field is worked or a mine is worked, and it does not mean to earn it. The “you” is plural, so Paul is speaking to the church together. The reason for the working is that God is already working in them, both in the wanting and in the doing. The verse comes right after the hymn about Christ, and it follows the hymn’s pattern of obedience.

e.n: Shine like stars in a crooked generation
t: Paul says, “Do everything without complaining or arguing, so that you may be blameless and pure, children of God without fault in a crooked and perverse generation, in which you shine as lights in the world as you hold forth the word of life” (2:14-16). “Complaining” recalls Israel’s grumbling in the wilderness, and “crooked and perverse generation” is from Moses’ song (Deuteronomy 32:5). The word for “lights” (phosteres) means a heavenly body such as a star, and Daniel 12:3 says that those who lead many to righteousness will shine like the stars. The church is called to be to its city what the stars are to the night.

e.n: Poured out like a drink offering
t: Paul compares his possible death to a libation: “even if I am being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad and rejoice with all of you” (2:17). The Philippians’ faith is the sacrifice, and Paul’s life is the wine poured over it. In 4:18 he turns the picture around and calls the church’s gift “a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God.” Both sides of the partnership are described in the language of the altar.
In 2 Timothy 4:6 Paul writes again, “I am already being poured out like a drink offering, and the time of my departure is at hand,” this time looking toward death.

Paul recommends two men to the church. Of Timothy he says, “I have nobody else like him who will genuinely care for your needs” (2:20), and “as a child with his father he has served with me to advance the gospel” (2:22). Epaphroditus is “my brother, fellow worker, and fellow soldier, who is also your messenger and minister to my needs” (2:25), who “nearly died for the work of Christ” (2:30). The pair shows what the hymn’s humility looks like in daily life: “all the others look after their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (2:21), but these two do not.
In 2 Timothy Paul calls Timothy “my beloved child” (1:2), recalls his tears and his sincere faith (1:4-5) and asks him to “come to me quickly” (4:9).

Paul warns against those who put weight on outward marks. “It is we who are the circumcision,” he says, “who worship by the Spirit of God, who glory in Christ Jesus, and who put no confidence in the flesh” (3:3). He could claim much more: “circumcised on the eighth day, of the people of Israel, of the tribe of Benjamin; a Hebrew of Hebrews; as to the law, a Pharisee; as to zeal, persecuting the church; as to righteousness in the law, faultless” (3:5-6). Paul does not say these things were bad. He says that Christ is better, and counts them “as loss for the sake of Christ” (3:7).

Paul wants to “be found in Him, not having my own righteousness from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God on the basis of faith” (3:9). The Greek behind “through faith in Christ” can also be read as through the faithfulness of Christ, and scholars discuss which Paul means. Either way, the righteousness is God’s gift and not Paul’s own achievement. The word “rubbish” in 3:8 (skybalon) is chosen to be rough.

e.n: Knowing Christ and the power of His resurrection
t: Paul wants “to know Christ and the power of His resurrection and the fellowship of His sufferings, being conformed to Him in His death, and so, somehow, to attain to the resurrection from the dead” (3:10-11). To “know” here means more than knowing facts. The resurrection and the sufferings are joined, as they were for Christ. “Somehow” is not doubt that he will be saved but a sign that he does not know the road, since it may lead through death.

Paul says, “Not that I have already obtained all this, or have already been made perfect, but I press on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me” (3:12). The picture is a runner: “Forgetting what is behind and straining toward what is ahead, I press on toward the goal to win the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus” (3:13-14). Just after saying he is not “made perfect,” Paul says, “All of us who are mature should embrace this point of view” (3:15). The words for “perfect” and “mature” come from the same Greek root, so the “mature” are those who know they are still running.

e.n: Citizens of heaven, waiting for a Savior
t: “Our citizenship is in heaven, and we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ, who, by the power that enables Him to subject all things to Himself, will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (3:20-21). The Greek for “citizenship,” politeuma, can mean a commonwealth or colony of citizens living in a foreign place. Philippians belonged to a Roman colony, and Paul describes the church as a colony of heaven. The hope is bodily: the “lowly body” will be made like Christ’s “glorious body.”

Joy is the letter’s note. The verb “rejoice,” its partner “rejoice with,” and the noun “joy” together appear sixteen times in four short chapters. Paul prays “with joy” (1:4), rejoices that Christ is preached (1:18), asks the church to “make my joy complete” (2:2), and tells them to “rejoice with me” (2:18). The call is repeated at the center of the final chapter: “Rejoice in the Lord always. I will say it again: Rejoice!” (4:4). He writes from chains. The joy is “in the Lord,” not in circumstances.
In 1 Thessalonians the command is shorter: “Rejoice at all times” (5:16), and Paul says the Thessalonians welcomed the message “with the joy of the Holy Spirit” (1:6).

e.n: Do not be anxious; pray with thanksgiving
t: “Be anxious for nothing, but in everything, by prayer and petition, with thanksgiving, present your requests to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (4:6-7). The verb for “be anxious” is the one Jesus uses in Matthew 6:25. The verb “guard” is a military word for a sentry or a garrison. The command is just before and after “The Lord is near” (4:5) and “the God of peace will be with you” (4:9).

Paul gives a list: “whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is right, whatever is pure, whatever is lovely, whatever is admirable” and “if anything is excellent or praiseworthy” (4:8). Several of these words, such as “excellent” (arete) and “praiseworthy,” were the common currency of Greek moral writing, and Paul uses them without apology. He then adds a rule: “Whatever you have learned or received or heard from me, or seen in me, put it into practice” (4:9). Thinking and doing belong together.

Paul says, “I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances. I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound” (4:11-12). He has learned the secret, a word from the mystery religions, of being “filled” and “hungry,” of having “plenty” and “need.” The word for “content” (autarkes) was a favorite in Stoic writing, where it meant self-sufficient. Paul uses it for a different source of strength: “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength” (4:13). The verse is about enduring hunger and plenty, not about winning at everything.
In 1 Timothy “godliness with contentment is great gain” and “if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these” (6:6, 8).

The church’s gift to Paul is described in the language of accounts. “No church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving” (4:15), and Paul says, “I am looking for the fruit that may be credited to your account” (4:17). He has “all I need and more” (4:18). The gift is also an act of worship, “a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God,” and God will “supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus” (4:19). Paul delays his thanks until the end, perhaps because he did not want to make the gift sound like a payment.

e.n: Names in the Book of Life
t: Paul calls his fellow workers those “whose names are in the Book of Life” (4:3). The picture comes from the Old Testament, where Moses asks to be blotted out of God’s book (Exodus 32:32-33), the psalmist asks that his enemies be (Psalm 69:28), and Daniel says that everyone whose name is written will be delivered (Daniel 12:1). Revelation uses the image several times. Here Paul uses it to say that Euodia, Syntyche, Clement and the others belong to God, whatever their disagreements.

At the great white throne “the dead were judged according to their deeds, as recorded in the books,” and anyone whose name was not found written in the book of life was thrown into the lake of fire (Revelation 20:12-15).

Colossians 1:15-20 is built in two matching halves, and many scholars take it to be an early hymn or poem that Paul quotes or shapes. Each half begins in Greek with “who is.” The first half is about creation: the Son is “the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation,” and “all things were created through Him and for Him.” The second half is about new creation: He is “the beginning and firstborn from among the dead,” and through Him God reconciles “all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through the blood of His cross.” Others think Paul wrote the passage for this letter. Either way it is one of the fullest statements in the New Testament about who Christ is.

e.n: In Him all things hold together
t: Paul writes, “He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together” (1:17). The Greek verb (synesteken) means to stand together or be held in place. The Son is not only the one through whom the world began but also the one who keeps it from falling apart. Hebrews 1:3 says something close, that the Son is “sustaining all things by His powerful word.” Colossians 1:16 adds that this includes “thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities,” so none of the powers stands outside His rule.

e.n: Rescued from the dominion of darkness
t: Paul thanks the Father, “who has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light” (1:12). God “has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” (1:13-14). The two verbs, “rescued” and “brought into,” are the language of deliverance and of moving a people to a new homeland. Paul says this has already happened to the Colossians, though “the hope stored up for you in heaven” (1:5) is still ahead.

Paul prays that God would “fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding” (1:9). The aim is practical: “so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way: bearing fruit in every good work, growing in the knowledge of God” (1:10). The Greek word for “knowledge” here (epignosis) is a stronger form that means full or true knowledge, and the letter sets it against teachers who offer hidden knowledge of another kind (2:2-4, 18). Knowing the will of God leads to fruit, endurance and thanks (1:10-12).

e.n: What is lacking in Christ’s afflictions
t: Paul writes, “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church” (1:24). The verse is hard, because the same letter says that Christ’s death was complete: God reconciled “by making peace through the blood of His cross” (1:20) and “canceled the debt” (2:14). Most readers therefore take it to mean the suffering that comes to the church as the gospel goes into a hostile world, which Paul takes up as Christ’s servant. Others point to a Jewish idea of a set measure of suffering before the end. It is debated, and the letter itself does not explain.

e.n: Christ in you, the hope of glory
t: Paul speaks of “the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints” (1:26). It is “Christ in you, the hope of glory,” made known “among the Gentiles” (1:27). In this letter the mystery is Christ Himself (2:2; 4:3). Paul says, “We proclaim Him, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ” (1:28), and he works “striving with all His energy working powerfully within me” (1:29).

Paul wants the Colossians to know “the mystery of God, namely Christ, in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (2:2-3). Proverbs 2:4 speaks of searching for wisdom as one would search for hidden treasure. Paul says the search ends in Christ, so there is no need for further secrets. He adds, “I say this so that no one will deceive you by smooth rhetoric” (2:4).

e.n: Philosophy and the spiritual forces of the world
t: Paul warns, “See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception, which are based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world rather than on Christ” (2:8). This is the only place Paul uses the word “philosophy,” and it need not mean the Greek schools, since Jewish writers such as Josephus also called their groups philosophies. The Greek behind “spiritual forces of the world” is stoicheia tou kosmou. The word can mean the basic elements of the world (earth, air, fire and water), the ABCs of teaching, or the spirits tied to them, and scholars disagree about which Paul means. Galatians 4:3, 9 uses the same phrase. Colossians 2:20 says that believers “died with Christ to the spiritual forces of the world.”

Paul says, “In Him you were also circumcised, in the putting off of your sinful nature, with the circumcision performed by Christ and not by human hands. And having been buried with Him in baptism, you were raised with Him through your faith in the power of God, who raised Him from the dead” (2:11-12). Circumcision and baptism are joined as two pictures of the same change, which does not need a mark on the body. Paul says the Colossians were “dead in your trespasses” and “God made you alive with Christ” (2:13). Romans 6:3-4 uses the same picture of baptism as a burial.

Paul says that God “forgave us all our trespasses, having canceled the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us. He took it away, nailing it to the cross!” (2:13-14). The Greek word (cheirographon) means a handwritten note of debt, like an IOU. The picture is of a signed bill that could not be paid, now destroyed. Some readers also see the written charge fixed above a crucified man (Mark 15:26). Either way, the debt is gone, and nobody may bring it back.

Paul writes, “And having disarmed the powers and authorities, He made a public spectacle of them, triumphing over them by the cross” (2:15). The picture is a Roman triumph, in which a victorious general led his captives and spoils through the streets. The surprise is that the cross, a shameful form of execution, is the place of victory. Scholars still debate who the “powers and authorities” are and who is leading the procession, God or Christ, and the Greek can be read either way.

e.n: A shadow of the things to come
t: Paul writes, “let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ” (2:16-17). He does not call the festivals evil. He says the Colossians are not to let others judge them by these, because the reality has come. The letter to the Hebrews uses the same picture of the law as a shadow of what was to come (Hebrews 8:5; 10:1).
Hebrews 8:5 and 10:1 say the same of the law. The sanctuary is “a copy and shadow of what is in heaven,” and “the law is only a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves.”

Paul warns, “Do not let anyone who delights in false humility and the worship of angels disqualify you with speculation about what he has seen” (2:18). The Greek can mean worship given to angels or worship that angels offer to God, and scholars are divided. Some Jews of the time wrote of visions of the heavenly temple and its angelic praise, as in the Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice. Later writers say that Christians in this region called on angels, and a church council at Laodicea in the 4th century forbade it. The letter does not name the teachers, so this is debated.

e.n: Rules with an appearance of wisdom
t: Paul asks, “If you have died with Christ to the spiritual forces of the world, why, as though you still belonged to the world, do you submit to its regulations: ‘Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!’?” (2:20-21). He says such rules “have an appearance of wisdom, with their self-prescribed worship, their false humility, and their harsh treatment of the body; but they are of no value against the indulgence of the flesh” (2:23). The target is the idea that holiness can be gained by avoiding things. The cure, he says next, is to set the mind “on things above” (3:2).

Paul turns from warning to practice with the words, “Therefore, since you have been raised with Christ, strive for the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on things above, not on earthly things. For you died, and your life is now hidden with Christ in God” (3:1-3). The verb “strive” means to seek actively. “Above” does not mean escape from the world, because the next verses go straight to anger, lies and how to treat a neighbor. The reason is that “Christ, who is your life, appears,” and then “you also will appear with Him in glory” (3:4).

e.n: Christ is all and is in all
t: Paul says the new self is renewed “in the image of its Creator,” and that “here there is no Greek or Jew, circumcised or uncircumcised, barbarian, Scythian, slave, or free, but Christ is all and is in all” (3:10-11). Greeks called all non-Greeks barbarians, and Scythians, from the lands north of the Black Sea, were the standard example of wild people. Galatians 3:28 makes a similar list. Paul names the groups that most divided his world and says that none of them is the thing that makes a person belong.

Paul writes, “as the elect of God, holy and beloved, clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience. Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else. Forgive as the Lord forgave you. And over all these virtues put on love, which is the bond of perfect unity” (3:12-14). The terms “elect of God, holy and beloved” were used of Israel, and here they describe a mostly Gentile church. The picture of clothing is the same as for the old and new self (3:9-10). Love is the garment that holds the others together.

Paul writes, “Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, for to this you were called as members of one body. And be thankful. Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you as you teach and admonish one another with all wisdom, and as you sing psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs with gratitude in your hearts to God” (3:15-16). The Greek verb for “rule” (brabeuo) is the word for an umpire who decides a contest. Singing is described as teaching and correction as well as praise. Ephesians 5:19 has almost the same line. The letter itself may quote an early hymn (1:15-20).

Colossians 3:18 to 4:1 speaks to wives, husbands, children, fathers, slaves and masters, in that order. Greek and Roman writers also wrote about how to run a household (Aristotle’s Politics begins with it), but they spoke to the master of the house. Paul speaks to each member directly, and every instruction is tied to the Lord: “as is fitting in the Lord” (3:18), “pleasing to the Lord” (3:20), “the Lord Christ you are serving” (3:24). Each side also has a duty to the other, and the masters are told that “you also have a Master in heaven” (4:1). How the instructions apply today has been debated for centuries.

In Titus Paul gives household instruction to older men, older women, younger women, younger men and slaves (2:1-10). Masters are not addressed, and the stated goal is that the teaching “about God our Savior” will be made attractive.
1 Peter 2:18-3:7 covers slaves, wives and husbands, and in each case points the reader to the example of Christ or to hope in God. See the entry on wives and husbands in 1 Peter 3.

e.n: Whatever you do, work for the Lord
t: To slaves Paul writes, “obey your earthly masters in everything, not only to please them while they are watching, but with sincerity of heart and fear of the Lord. Whatever you do, work at it with your whole being, for the Lord and not for men, because you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as your reward. It is the Lord Christ you are serving” (3:22-24). Slaves had no legal right to an inheritance in a master’s house, so the promise of an “inheritance from the Lord” would be notable. The passage does not praise slavery. It speaks to people who were slaves, and Paul’s letter to Philemon asks that Onesimus be received “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 1:16).

e.n: An open door and speech seasoned with salt
t: Paul asks the Colossians to “devote yourselves to prayer, being watchful and thankful, as you pray also for us, that God may open to us a door for the word” (4:2-3). He asks not for release but for the chance to speak, “so that we may proclaim the mystery of Christ, for which I am in chains.” To outsiders they are to “act wisely” and to let their “speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how to answer everyone” (4:5-6). Salt both flavored and preserved food, so the picture is of speech that is pleasant and also sound.

Paul writes of Epaphras, “He is always wrestling in prayer for you, so that you may stand mature and fully assured in the full will of God” (4:12). The Greek verb (agonizomai) comes from agon, a contest, and Paul uses the same family of words of his own labor: “striving with all His energy working powerfully within me” (1:29) and “how much I am struggling for you” (2:1). Epaphras is far from home and in prison with Paul (Philemon 23), and his work for the churches is done through prayer.

Paul tells the Colossians, “After this letter has been read among you, make sure that it is also read in the church of the Laodiceans, and that you in turn read the letter from Laodicea” (4:16). Letters were read aloud and passed from church to church, and this is how Paul’s letters began to be collected. The “letter from Laodicea” is not known. Some think it is lost, and some think it is Ephesians, since some early copies of that letter leave out the name of the city. Others say it was a letter that Laodicea had sent on to them. Paul does not say.

e.n: Work of faith, labor of love, enduring hope
t: Paul remembers the Thessalonians’ “work of faith, your labor of love, and your enduring hope in our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 1:3). Each of the three is joined to something that shows: faith that works, love that labors, and hope that endures. The Greek word for labor (kopos) means toil that wears a person out, and the word for enduring (hypomone) means staying under a load. Paul says these three show that God “has chosen you” (1:4). He uses the same three again in 5:8, where faith and love are a breastplate and hope is a helmet.

e.n: Turned from idols to serve the living God
t: Paul says other churches report “how you turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God and to await His Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead—Jesus our deliverer from the coming wrath” (1 Thessalonians 1:9-10). The sentence has three parts: turn, serve and wait. Thessalonica was a port city with many temples, and the Thessalonians had given up worship that was part of public life. Acts 17:4 says some Jews, a large number of God-fearing Greeks and several leading women joined Paul, so the church was not drawn from one group.

e.n: The word of God at work in you
t: Paul thanks God because, “when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of men, but as the true word of God—the word which is now at work in you who believe” (1 Thessalonians 2:13). He says in 1:5 that the gospel came “not only in word, but also in power, in the Holy Spirit, and with great conviction.” For Paul the message is not only information. The Greek verb for “at work” (energeo) is the same word used for God’s power in other places, and it is what the Thessalonians had seen in their own lives.

e.n: Like a nursing mother, like a father
t: Paul describes how he and his coworkers treated the Thessalonians: “we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother caring for her children” (1 Thessalonians 2:7), and “we treated each of you as a father treats his own children—encouraging you, comforting you, and urging you to walk in a manner worthy of God” (2:11-12). Both pictures are of close care in a family. He also says, “we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel of God, but our own lives as well” (2:8). He sets this beside the claim that he did not use flattery or look for praise (2:5-6), which marks him off from speakers who sought pay or praise.

Paul reminds the church, “We worked night and day so that we would not be a burden to anyone while we proclaimed to you the gospel of God” (1 Thessalonians 2:9). He says almost the same thing in 2 Thessalonians 3:8, where he adds that he and his companions “did not eat anyone’s food without paying for it.” In Acts 18:3 Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla as a tentmaker at Corinth, where he most likely wrote these letters. Work was an ordinary part of the way he shared the gospel, and the second letter uses his example against those who would not work (3:7-9).

e.n: Imitators of us and of the Lord
t: Paul tells the Thessalonians, “you became imitators of us and of the Lord when you welcomed the message with the joy of the Holy Spirit, in spite of your great suffering” (1 Thessalonians 1:6). Later he says they “became imitators of the churches of God in Judea” (2:14). In the second letter he asks them to imitate him in his work: “we wanted to offer ourselves as an example for you to imitate” (2 Thessalonians 3:9). The Greek word (mimetes) is the root of the English “mimic.” Paul asks his readers to imitate because they can see a person’s life.
In 3 John 11 the same word is used: “do not imitate what is evil, but what is good.”

Paul says that he tried “again and again” to return to Thessalonica, “but Satan obstructed us” (1 Thessalonians 2:18). The Greek verb (enkopto) means to hinder or block the way. He does not say how Satan did it, and the book of Acts does not mention it. In 3:5 he fears “the tempter had somehow tempted you and caused our labor to be in vain.” In both places Paul writes as someone who has a real opponent and who still sends Timothy and writes a letter.

e.n: The will of God: your holiness
t: Paul writes, “it is God’s will that you should be holy” (1 Thessalonians 4:3). The Greek word (hagiasmos) means being set apart for God. He then speaks about sexual morality, about not wronging a brother and about love, and says that “God has not called us to impurity, but to holiness” (4:7). The phrase in 4:4, to “control his own body,” is debated: the Greek word for “body” (skeuos) is literally a vessel, and some take it to mean one’s own wife. Paul says that whoever rejects the command “does not reject man but God, the very One who gives you His Holy Spirit” (4:8).

e.n: Quiet work with your own hands
t: Paul tells the church “to aspire to live quietly, to attend to your own matters, and to work with your own hands, as we instructed you” (1 Thessalonians 4:11). The reason he gives is how it looks to others: “Then you will behave properly toward outsiders, without being dependent on anyone” (4:12). The word “aspire” in Greek (philotimeomai) means to make something a point of honor, so quiet work is treated as an ambition and not a second best. The second letter returns to the same command for those who had stopped working (2 Thessalonians 3:11-12).

e.n: Hope for those who sleep in death
t: Some Thessalonians had died, and the church was grieving. Paul writes, “we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). The ground for hope is the resurrection of Jesus: “since we believe that Jesus died and rose again, we also believe that God will bring with Jesus those who have fallen asleep in Him” (4:14). “Sleep” was an ordinary way to speak of death, and for believers it also suggests waking. Paul does not say that grief is wrong. He says that it should not be “like the rest,” who have no hope. He finishes, “encourage one another with these words” (4:18).

e.n: Caught up to meet the Lord
t: Paul writes, “the Lord Himself will descend from heaven with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God, and the dead in Christ will be the first to rise. After that, we who are alive and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air. And so we will always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). The Greek word for “meeting” (apantesis) is used in Matthew 25:6 for going out to meet the bridegroom and in Acts 28:15 for the believers who came out to meet Paul on the road to Rome. Some scholars think it describes a city going out to welcome a visiting official and then coming back with him. This is debated. The Latin Bible rendered “caught up” as rapiemur, and from it English gets the word “rapture.” Christians disagree about when this happens in relation to other events, and Paul’s point in the passage is that those who died will not miss it.

e.n: The coming of the Lord Jesus
t: The Greek word parousia means “presence” or “arrival.” Paul uses it for the coming of the Lord Jesus in 1 Thessalonians 2:19, 3:13, 4:15 and 5:23, and in 2 Thessalonians 2:1 and 2:8. In Greek writing it could describe the arrival of a ruler or official. In the two letters the coming is set before the church as hope (“who is our hope, our joy, our crown of boasting, if it is not you yourselves in the presence of our Lord Jesus at His coming?”, 1 Thessalonians 2:19), as a reason to live in holiness (3:13; 5:23), as comfort for those who grieve (4:15) and as an end to the evil that the lawless one brings (2 Thessalonians 2:8). Paul uses the same word for the arrival of the lawless one (2:9).

e.n: The Day of the Lord like a thief
t: Paul says, “you are fully aware that the Day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5:2). The prophets spoke of a day when God would act in judgment (Amos 5:18-20; Zephaniah 1:14-15), and Jesus used the picture of a thief, saying that if the owner had known when the thief was coming, he would have stayed awake (Matthew 24:43). Paul adds that destruction will come “suddenly, like labor pains on a pregnant woman,” but that believers “are not in the darkness so that this day should overtake you like a thief” (5:3-4). The aim of the passage is to call the church to watchfulness, and he gives no dates (5:1).

2 Peter 3:10 says, “the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare.” The delay is God’s patience (3:9).
Revelation uses the same picture twice: “I will come like a thief” (3:3) and “Behold, I am coming like a thief” (16:15).

Paul says that the Day will come “while people are saying, ‘Peace and security’” (1 Thessalonians 5:3). Roman rulers spoke of peace and safety as the gift of the empire, and some think Thessalonian readers would hear that claim in the words. The prophets had also condemned leaders who said “Peace, peace” when there was no peace (Jeremiah 6:14; Ezekiel 13:10). Paul does not name a target. The words describe a settled and confident attitude that does not expect any change, which he sets against the watchful attitude of the church.

e.n: Sons of light and the armor of hope
t: Paul tells the Thessalonians, “you are all sons of the light and sons of the day; we do not belong to the night or to the darkness” (1 Thessalonians 5:5). He then contrasts sleep and drunkenness, which belong to the night, with staying awake and sober, and adds, “let us be sober, putting on the breastplate of faith and love, and the helmet of our hope of salvation” (5:8). The picture of a breastplate and helmet comes from Isaiah 59:17, where God puts on righteousness and a helmet of salvation. Here the believers wear what God wears. Faith, love and hope are the same three Paul named in 1:3.

In three short sentences Paul writes, “Rejoice at all times. Pray without ceasing. Give thanks in every circumstance, for this is God’s will for you in Christ Jesus” (1 Thessalonians 5:16-18). The three commands are placed together in the middle of a list of quick instructions, and “this is God’s will” may refer to all three. Paul says he does this himself: he prays “night and day” (3:10) and gives thanks “continually” (2:13).

After the short commands Paul writes, “Do not extinguish the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt, but test all things. Hold fast to what is good. Abstain from every form of evil” (1 Thessalonians 5:19-22). The verb “extinguish” (sbennymi) is used of putting out a fire or a lamp. The church is not to shut down the gifts of the Spirit, and it is not to accept every word either: “test all things.” The same Greek verb for “test” (dokimazo) is used of God testing Paul’s heart (2:4), so the church tests prophecy as God tests people.

Paul prays, “may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely, and may your entire spirit, soul, and body be kept blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Readers disagree about whether Paul is describing three parts of a person or using three words for the whole person. The two words for “completely” and “entire” stress that nothing is left out. The verse does not ask the Thessalonians to make themselves blameless. God does it, and in the next verse Paul says “The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it” (5:24).

e.n: The One who calls you is faithful
t: Paul ends the first letter with a promise: “The One who calls you is faithful, and He will do it” (1 Thessalonians 5:24). The second letter adds, “the Lord is faithful, and He will strengthen you and guard you from the evil one” (2 Thessalonians 3:3). In both places Paul has just told the church what to do, and then he points to God as the reason it can be done. The call is the one in 1 Thessalonians 2:12, to “walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into His own kingdom and glory.”

Paul says, “Brothers who are beloved by God, we know that He has chosen you” (1 Thessalonians 1:4), and in the second letter, “God has chosen you from the beginning to be saved by the sanctification of the Spirit and by faith in the truth” (2 Thessalonians 2:13). Some manuscripts read “as firstfruits” instead of “from the beginning.” In both places the knowledge of being chosen comes from what he has seen: the gospel came with power, they received it with joy and they “turned to God from idols” (1 Thessalonians 1:5-9). Election is placed beside faith, and Paul writes of it with thanks.

Paul describes Jesus as “our deliverer from the coming wrath” (1 Thessalonians 1:10) and says, “God has not appointed us to suffer wrath, but to obtain salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ. He died for us so that, whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him” (5:9-10). The wrath is seen as future, and it falls on those who say “Peace and security” (5:3). Paul’s statement in 2:16 that “the utmost wrath has come upon” those who hindered the preaching to the Gentiles is debated, and some think it refers to a judgment already under way. The point for the church is that salvation is a gift through Jesus.

Paul tells the suffering church that its endurance “is clear evidence of God’s righteous judgment” (2 Thessalonians 1:5). He says that “it is only right for God to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are oppressed and to us as well” (1:6-7). The same Greek root is used for “affliction” and “afflict,” so the repayment fits the act. This will take place when “the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in blazing fire” (1:7-8). The passage does not call the church to take revenge. It asks the church to wait for God to act, and Paul prays that God will make them worthy of His calling (1:11).

e.n: A letter seeming to be from us
t: Some in Thessalonica claimed the Day of the Lord “has already come,” and Paul warns them not to be “easily disconcerted or alarmed by any spirit or message or letter seeming to be from us” (2 Thessalonians 2:2). So he ends the second letter with a mark: “This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. This is my mark in every letter; it is the way I write” (3:17). Paul usually used a secretary and added a line in his own hand (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11). The warning has led some scholars to ask whether 2 Thessalonians itself was written by Paul, and others hold that it was. The letter claims to be Paul’s, and this is how the church received it.

e.n: The rebellion and the man of lawlessness
t: Paul says that the Day of the Lord “will not come until the rebellion occurs and the man of lawlessness—the son of destruction—is revealed” (2 Thessalonians 2:3). This figure “will oppose and exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship. So he will seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God” (2:4). The language recalls Daniel’s king who “will exalt and magnify himself above every god” (Daniel 11:36) and the king of Tyre who said, “I am a god” (Ezekiel 28:2). In 167 BC Antiochus IV set up an altar to Zeus in the Jerusalem Temple, and in AD 40 the emperor Caligula tried to have his statue set there. Readers disagree whether Paul means one person, a series of rulers or a power in history, and whether “the temple of God” is the Jerusalem Temple or the church. Paul says the Lord Jesus “will slay him with the breath of His mouth” (2:8), echoing Isaiah 11:4.
1 John 2:18-19 says “it is the last hour” and that many antichrists have appeared, and that “They went out from us, but they did not belong to us.”
Many readers set this passage beside the beast of Revelation 13, who speaks proud and blasphemous words and makes war on the saints.

Paul writes, “you know what is now restraining him, so that he may be revealed at the proper time. For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work, but the one who now restrains it will continue until he is taken out of the way” (2 Thessalonians 2:6-7). The Greek says “what restrains” in verse 6 and “the one who restrains” in verse 7, one neuter and one masculine. Paul reminds them “that I told you these things while I was still with you” (2:5), and the letter does not say who or what the restrainer is. Suggestions include the Roman order, the preaching of the gospel and an angel, and none is certain. Early readers already knew of several guesses.

Paul says the coming of the lawless one “will be accompanied by the working of Satan, with every kind of power, sign, and false wonder, and with every wicked deception directed against those who are perishing, because they refused the love of the truth that would have saved them” (2 Thessalonians 2:9-10). He then says, “God will send them a powerful delusion so that they believe the lie, in order that judgment may come upon all who have disbelieved the truth and delighted in wickedness” (2:11-12). The explanation Paul gives is that people first refused the truth. Readers differ on how to understand God’s part in the delusion, and some compare Exodus 8:15 and 1 Kings 22:22.

e.n: Stand firm and hold the traditions
t: Paul ends the long passage with a command: “stand firm and cling to the traditions we taught you, whether by speech or by letter” (2 Thessalonians 2:15). The word “traditions” (paradosis) means what is handed on. Earlier in the passage he had to correct a false letter, so he points to what the church had been taught from him in person and in writing. The same word appears in 3:6, in “the tradition you received from us.” In Paul’s use, tradition is not the same as human custom. In Mark 7:8 Jesus criticizes the elders’ tradition, and in 1 Corinthians 11:2 and 15:3 Paul uses the word for the gospel he received and passed on.

e.n: If anyone is unwilling to work
t: Paul reminds the church of a rule he gave when he was with them: “If anyone is unwilling to work, he shall not eat” (2 Thessalonians 3:10). He had heard that “some of you are leading undisciplined lives and accomplishing nothing but being busybodies” (3:11). In Greek the last two words are a play on words, ergazomai (to work) and periergazomai (to work around), so these people were busy about everything but their own work. Paul commands them “to begin working quietly to earn their own living” (3:12). The rule is aimed at those who will not work, not at those who cannot, and it comes with Paul’s own example of working “night and day” (3:8).

Paul tells the church to “keep away from any brother who leads an undisciplined life” (2 Thessalonians 3:6) and to “take note of anyone who does not obey the instructions we have given in this letter. Do not associate with him, so that he may be ashamed. Yet do not regard him as an enemy, but warn him as a brother” (3:14-15). The aim is repentance, and the person remains a brother. The first letter had already said to “admonish the unruly, encourage the fainthearted, help the weak, and be patient with everyone” (1 Thessalonians 5:14). Then Paul adds, “do not grow weary in well-doing” (2 Thessalonians 3:13).

e.n: My true child in the faith
t: Paul addresses the letter “To Timothy, my true child in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2) and later calls him “Timothy, my child” (1:18). The Greek word for “true” (gnesios) means genuine, as in a legitimate child. Paul does not say he was Timothy’s father by birth.
