Acts 16:1-3 shows Timothy as a young disciple from Lystra whom Paul took along, and in Philippians 2:22 Paul says that Timothy “served with me in the work of the gospel like a son with his father.” The picture is of faith passed on from one person to the next.

e.n: Paul, or a follower of Paul?
t: The letter begins “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 1:1), and for most of church history it was read as Paul’s own. Many scholars today think a follower of Paul wrote 1 Timothy, 2 Timothy and Titus (the “pastoral letters”) after his death, and they point to the vocabulary, the interest in church offices and the difficulty of fitting the letters into Acts. Others hold that Paul wrote them, perhaps with a secretary’s help, after the period covered by Acts, about AD 62-65. Both sides agree that the letter is meant to be read as Paul’s voice to Timothy, and the debate is not settled by the text itself.

In 2 Timothy the question is sharpest because of the setting: Paul writes in chains, expects death and names many friends and places. Those who accept Paul as author place it in a second Roman imprisonment after Acts. Others see a later writer shaping a last testament in Paul’s name. The letter itself does not settle it.

In Titus the letter is addressed to a man Paul names elsewhere: Titus went up to Jerusalem with him (Galatians 2:1-3) and helped with the collection in Corinth (2 Corinthians 8:6, 16-17, 23). Acts never mentions him, and the Crete mission in the letter has no place in Acts, so those who accept Paul as author place it after the period Acts covers. Others see the letter as written in Paul’s name by a later follower who used these facts. The text does not settle the question.

Paul writes, “As I urged you on my departure to Macedonia, you should stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines” (1 Timothy 1:3). Ephesus is the city where Paul had spent more than two years (Acts 19:8-10). At Miletus he had warned the elders of Ephesus that “savage wolves” would come and that men would “rise up and distort the truth” from their own number (Acts 20:29-30). The letter shows Timothy set to deal with that danger, and it gives him a charge, a church order and a personal word.

Paul tells Timothy to ask certain men not to “devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies, which promote speculation rather than the stewardship of God’s work, which is by faith” (1 Timothy 1:4). In 4:7 he says “reject irreverent, silly myths.” Titus 3:9 also warns against genealogies and foolish controversies. The letter does not say what the myths were. Suggestions include Jewish stories built on the family lists of Genesis, early forms of what later became Gnostic teaching, or a mixture, and none is certain.

In Titus the “Jewish myths” and “the commands of men who have rejected the truth” (1:14) are linked to “genealogies” and “quarrels about the law” (3:9). The letter gives no detail of the teaching, only its effect, that these teachers “undermine entire households” (1:11).

e.n: The law is good, if used legitimately
t: Paul writes, “Now we know that the law is good, if one uses it legitimately” (1 Timothy 1:8). The men he opposes “want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying” (1:7). He says that “law is not enacted for the righteous, but for the lawless and rebellious” and gives a list of wrongdoing (1:9-10). Many readers note that the list follows the order of the Ten Commandments, from offenses against God to offenses against parents, life and truth. The law is not discarded, and it is not made the way to be right with God.

Paul uses the phrase “This is a trustworthy saying” three times in 1 Timothy (1:15; 3:1; 4:9) and twice more in the other pastoral letters (2 Timothy 2:11; Titus 3:8). In 1:15 and 4:9 he adds “worthy of full acceptance.” The phrase marks a line that Paul wants Timothy to remember, and some think it was a saying already known in the churches. The sayings cover the gospel (“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners”), the work of an overseer and the hope of godliness.

Paul writes, “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the worst” (1 Timothy 1:15). He remembers that he was “formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man; yet because I had acted in ignorance and unbelief, I was shown mercy” (1:13). He says that God showed him mercy “so that in me, the worst of sinners, Christ Jesus might display His perfect patience as an example to those who would believe in Him for eternal life” (1:16). Acts 9:1-19 tells how Paul was stopped on the road to Damascus.

Paul charges Timothy that by the earlier prophecies he “may fight the good fight, holding on to faith and a good conscience” (1 Timothy 1:18-19) and later writes, “Fight the good fight of the faith. Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called” (6:12). The Greek word for fight (agon) means a contest, and it is the source of the English word “agony.” It was used of athletic games and of battle. In 2 Timothy 4:7 Paul uses the same picture of his own life. The goal is to keep faith, not to defeat opponents.

Paul says that some “have rejected” a good conscience “and thereby shipwrecked their faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:19-20). The picture is of a ship wrecked on rocks. “Handed over to Satan” is the same wording Paul uses for the man at Corinth (1 Corinthians 5:5) and may mean putting a person out of the church so that the church is protected and the person is led to turn back. The purpose given here is that they be “taught,” and the letter does not say whether it worked.

e.n: Pray for kings and all in authority
t: Paul begins the instructions on worship with prayer: “I urge that petitions, prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone—for kings and all those in authority—so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all godliness and dignity” (1 Timothy 2:1-2). Jeremiah had told the exiles in Babylon to seek the peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:7). Early Christians prayed for rulers who did not share their faith. The reason given is a quiet life, and the letter does not mention any particular emperor.
In Titus believers are told “to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work” (3:1).

e.n: God our Savior, who wants everyone to be saved
t: First Timothy calls God “our Savior” three times (1:1; 2:3; 4:10). Paul says that God “wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (2:4) and that He is “the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe” (4:10). The statements about “everyone” and “especially” have been read in different ways. Some take them to mean that the offer of the gospel is for all, and others take them to mean that God cares for all while saving believers in a special way. In Asia, emperors were also called “savior,” and a reader would hear the claim in that setting.
In Titus the Father is “God our Savior” three times (1:3; 2:10; 3:4), and “the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone” (2:11).

e.n: Teaching and authority in the assembly
t: Paul tells the women to “adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, but with good deeds” (1 Timothy 2:9-10). He then writes, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet” (2:12) and gives reasons from Adam and Eve (2:13-14). The Greek word for “exercise authority” (authenteo) occurs only here in the New Testament, and its meaning is debated. Some read the passage as a rule for all churches, some as a rule for a particular situation at Ephesus, and the reasons given are weighed differently.

Paul writes, “Women, however, will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with self-control” (1 Timothy 2:15). Readers differ on what this means. Suggestions include that women will be kept safe through childbirth, that the childbearing is the birth of the Messiah to a woman, that a woman finds her place in God’s purpose through ordinary family life, or that “saved” refers to being preserved in faithfulness. All of them read the verse as a sentence about women who remain “in faith, love, and holiness,” not about earning salvation by having children, which would contradict Ephesians 2:8-9.

e.n: If anyone aspires to be an overseer
t: Paul writes, “If anyone aspires to be an overseer, he desires a noble task” (1 Timothy 3:1) and gives a list: “above reproach, the husband of but one wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach” (3:2). Most of the list is about character. “The husband of but one wife” is read as faithfulness in marriage, as a ban on remarrying after a death or divorce, or as a ban on having more than one wife, and readers disagree. The overseer must also not be “a recent convert” (3:6) and must have “a good reputation with outsiders” (3:7). Overseer, elder and shepherd may be names for the same work in these letters (Titus 1:5-7; Acts 20:17, 28).
In Titus 1:5-9 the same list appears for “elders,” and verse 7 switches to “overseer” for the same man. See the entry on what an elder must be in Titus.

Paul says that deacons “must be dignified, not double-tongued or given to much wine or greedy for money” and “must first be tested” (1 Timothy 3:8-10). Then he writes, “In the same way, the women must be dignified, not slanderers, but temperate and faithful in all things” (3:11). The Greek says “women” with no word for “their,” and readers disagree on whether it refers to the wives of deacons or to women who were deacons themselves. Phoebe is called a deacon of the church at Cenchrea in Romans 16:1. The deacon “must be the husband of but one wife” (3:12).

e.n: The pillar and foundation of the truth
t: Paul writes so that Timothy “will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). The church is a household (compare Ephesians 2:19-22) and also a structure that holds the truth up where others can see it. Ephesus was a city with a famous temple whose columns stood among the wonders of the world, and some readers hear the picture against that background. Most readers take the picture to mean that the church holds the truth up for all to see and does not create it.

Paul quotes a short poem: “By common confession, the mystery of godliness is great: He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, was taken up in glory” (1 Timothy 3:16). The six lines come in pairs and move between earth and heaven. Most scholars think Paul is using a hymn the churches already sang. The “mystery” is not a secret but Christ Himself, now made known. Other early Christians are known to have sung to Christ, for example in the letter of Pliny to the emperor Trajan, about AD 110.

Paul says that “in later times some will abandon the faith to follow deceitful spirits and the teachings of demons” and “will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods that God has created to be received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:1-3). His answer is that “every creation of God is good, and nothing that is received with thanksgiving should be rejected, because it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer” (4:4-5). The letter does not name the teachers. Some think of a Jewish form of asceticism and others of a mixture of Jewish and Greek ideas, and both fit what Paul says at Colossae (Colossians 2:16-23).

Paul writes, “reject irreverent, silly myths. Instead, train yourself for godliness. For physical exercise is of limited value, but godliness is valuable in every way, holding promise for the present life and for the one to come” (1 Timothy 4:7-8). The Greek word for “train” (gymnazo) comes from the gymnasium, where men exercised. Godliness (eusebeia) is the word that runs through the letter, and means devotion to God shown in life. Paul does not dismiss the body, and he says exercise has some value.

e.n: Let no one despise your youth
t: Paul tells Timothy, “Let no one despise your youth, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity” (1 Timothy 4:12). The Greek word for youth (neotes) did not have a fixed age, and the letter does not say how old Timothy was. The way to answer contempt is to be an example in five things. Paul then tells him to “devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching” (4:13).

In Titus the same charge is given to Titus, “Let no one despise you” (2:15), after he is told to “speak these things as you encourage and rebuke with all authority.” The Greek verb (periphroneo) means to look down on, and occurs only here in the New Testament. The letter does not say how old Titus was. The answer is to be “an example by doing good works” (2:7).

Paul tells Timothy, “devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching” (1 Timothy 4:13). The order is reading, then exhortation (encouragement), then teaching, as in the synagogue, where the Law and Prophets were read aloud and then explained (Luke 4:16-21; Acts 13:15). Scrolls were costly and many people could not read, so the church depended on hearing. Paul asks that his own letters be read to the whole church (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27).

In 2 Timothy Paul says that “All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness” (3:16), and asks for his “scrolls, especially the parchments” (4:13).

e.n: The gift and the laying on of hands
t: Paul writes, “Do not neglect the gift that is in you, which was given you through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders” (1 Timothy 4:14). Earlier he spoke of “the previous prophecies about you” (1:18). Hands were laid on people to commission them in Acts 6:6 and 13:3. Paul also warns, “Do not be too quick in the laying on of hands and thereby share in the sins of others” (5:22). The letter does not say where the event took place, and 2 Timothy 1:6 adds that Paul’s own hands were laid on Timothy.

e.n: Honor the widows who are truly widows
t: Paul writes, “Honor the widows who are truly widows” (1 Timothy 5:3). If a widow has children or grandchildren, they should “show godliness to their own family and repay their parents” (5:4). A widow “who is truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God” (5:5), and “a widow should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, the wife of one man, and well known for good deeds” (5:9-10). Paul asks the church not to enroll younger widows and advises them to “marry, have children, and manage their households” (5:11-14). “Enrolled” may mean a list of those supported or a group who served the church, and readers disagree.

Paul says, “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). The letter treats care for family as part of faith. Children and grandchildren are to “repay their parents” (5:4), and a believing woman with widows in her household is to “assist them and not allow the church to be burdened” (5:16). The church was to care for those who had no one else.

Paul writes, “Elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching” (1 Timothy 5:17). He gives two sayings as support: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” (Deuteronomy 25:4) and “The worker is worthy of his wages” (5:18; compare Luke 10:7). “Honor” may include payment, and “double” may mean twice the honor or a generous share. He then says an accusation against an elder needs “two or three witnesses” (5:19) and that sin must be corrected publicly (5:20).

e.n: A little wine for your stomach
t: Paul tells Timothy, “Stop drinking only water and use a little wine instead, because of your stomach and your frequent ailments” (1 Timothy 5:23). It comes in the middle of a passage on purity and responsibility (5:22, 24-25). It shows that Timothy had frequent ailments. Wine was also used on wounds, as in the story of the good Samaritan (Luke 10:34), but the letter gives no more detail. The letter also says overseers and deacons are not to be “dependent on wine” or “given to much wine” (3:3, 8).

Paul contrasts teachers who “regard godliness as a means of gain” with the truth that “godliness with contentment is great gain” (1 Timothy 6:5-6). The Greek word for contentment (autarkeia) means having enough, and Greek thinkers used it for self-sufficiency. Paul gives it a different base: “we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it. But if we have food and clothing, we will be content with these” (6:7-8). The word is related to the one Paul uses of himself in Philippians 4:11.

Paul warns, “Those who want to be rich, however, fall into temptation and become ensnared by many foolish and harmful desires that plunge them into ruin and destruction. For the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil. By craving it, some have wandered away from the faith and pierced themselves with many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6:9-10). The Greek word (philargyria) occurs only here in the New Testament. The Greek has no word “the” before “root,” and some translations read “a root of all kinds of evil.” The warning is against the love of money, not against money.

Paul tells Timothy to “instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy” (1 Timothy 6:17). They are to “do good, to be rich in good works, and to be generous and ready to share, treasuring up for themselves a firm foundation for the future” (6:18-19). He does not tell them to give up what they have. Jesus had said something close in Matthew 6:19-21.

In Titus good works are in every chapter. Titus himself is to be “an example by doing good works” (2:7), and believers are to be “ready for every good work” (3:1) and to “devote themselves to good works” so that they “will not be unfruitful” (3:14).

Paul tells Timothy, “Take hold of the eternal life to which you were called when you made the good confession before many witnesses” (1 Timothy 6:12). He then points to Jesus: “Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate” (6:13). The first confession was probably made at baptism or when Timothy was commissioned, and readers disagree. The second refers to Jesus’ answer to Pilate in John 18:33-37 and the naming of Pontius Pilate fixes the confession in history.

Paul ends with “O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you. Avoid irreverent, empty chatter and the opposing arguments of so-called ‘knowledge,’ which some have professed and thus swerved away from the faith” (1 Timothy 6:20-21). The Greek word for “what has been entrusted” (parathēkē) means a deposit, something left in another’s care to be returned unharmed. The same word appears in 2 Timothy 1:12, 14. The deposit is the gospel as it was handed down. The word “knowledge” is gnosis, and some think Paul has an early form of what was later called Gnosticism in mind, though the letter does not say so.

In 2 Timothy the same word (parathēkē) is used twice. Paul is sure that God “is able to guard what I have entrusted to Him for that day” (1:12), and Timothy is to “Guard the treasure entrusted to you, with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us” (1:14).

e.n: An appeal rather than an order
t: Paul writes, “So although in Christ I am bold enough to order you to do what is proper, I prefer to appeal on the basis of love” (Philemon 8-9). He has the standing of an apostle and could give a command. Instead he asks, and he says why he asks: “so that your goodness will not be out of compulsion, but by your own free will” (14). The same habit appears elsewhere. In 2 Corinthians 8:8 he says he is not giving a command, and in 1 Corinthians 7:6 he separates his advice from a command. The letter treats the decision as Philemon’s own, and puts the weight on love and on Paul’s own chains.

e.n: Useless and useful: the name Onesimus
t: Paul writes, “Formerly he was useless to you, but now he has become useful both to you and to me” (Philemon 11). The name Onesimus means “useful” or “profitable” and was often given to slaves. The Greek has two near-matching words: achrestos, “useless,” and euchrestos, “useful.” Paul plays on the name again in verse 20, “let me have some benefit from you,” where the verb (oninemi) comes from the same root. The same word “useful” is used of Mark in 2 Timothy 4:11 and of a vessel “useful to the Master” in 2 Timothy 2:21. Some scholars think the wordplay also echoes “Christ” (Christos), which sounded like chrestos, “good,” but that is debated.

Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother” (Philemon 16). “In person and in the Lord” (16) means both in the household and in the church. Elsewhere Paul says that in Christ there is no “slave nor free” (Galatians 3:28; Colossians 3:11) and that a slave called in the Lord is the Lord’s freedman (1 Corinthians 7:22). The letter never says “free him.” Readers have long disagreed on whether Paul hints at it (verses 16 and 21), asks only for a brotherly welcome, or leaves the question open on purpose. What is clear is that Onesimus is no longer to be seen as only a slave.

Paul writes, “But if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything, charge it to my account. I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it” (Philemon 18-19). The language is that of a ledger. Paul takes on whatever Onesimus owes, though he also reminds Philemon that “you owe me your very self” (19). Judah makes a similar pledge for Benjamin in Genesis 43:9 and 44:32-33. Many readers since Martin Luther (in his preface to the letter, 1522) have heard in Paul’s offer a picture of Christ taking on another’s debt. The letter itself does not make that comparison, so it is a reader’s application and not Paul’s own statement.

Paul thanks Philemon because “you, brother, have refreshed the hearts of the saints” (Philemon 7) and then asks, “Refresh my heart in Christ” (20). The Greek verb (anapauo) means to give rest, as in Jesus’ words “I will give you rest” (Matthew 11:28). The word for “heart” (splagchna) means the inner organs and was used for deep feeling; Paul uses it three times in the letter (7, 12, 20), and says Onesimus is “my very heart” (12). Elsewhere Paul says friends “refreshed my spirit” (1 Corinthians 16:18), and Onesiphorus “often refreshed me” (2 Timothy 1:16). The letter asks Philemon to give Onesimus the same kind of rest.

The usual reading is that Onesimus was Philemon’s slave and had run away, perhaps taking money, since Paul says “if he has wronged you in any way or owes you anything” (Philemon 18). He met Paul in prison and became a believer, and Paul sends him back (10-12). Other readings exist. Some scholars suggest he went to Paul on purpose, as a friend of his master, to ask Paul to speak for him, which Roman jurists did not count as running away. A few suggest the church at Colossae had sent him to help Paul. John Knox proposed in 1935 that Archippus was the owner and that Colossians 4:17 hints at his giving Onesimus up for Paul’s work. The letter does not say, and these are all debated.

e.n: Where was Paul when he wrote Philemon?
t: Paul writes as “a prisoner of Christ Jesus” and says he is “in chains” (Philemon 1, 9, 10, 13). The letter does not name the place. Rome is the traditional answer, since Acts 28:16-31 ends with Paul under guard there for two years. Ephesus is proposed because Colossae is only about 105 miles (170 km) away and Paul asks for a guest room, which suggests he expects to visit soon (22). Caesarea is a third option (Acts 24:27). Philemon and Colossians share many names, and Tychicus and Onesimus carried Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9), so they were probably written at the same time. The dates range from about AD 53 to 62, depending on the place.

e.n: The letter of James: who wrote it and to whom
t:
The letter opens, “James, a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, To the twelve tribes of the Dispersion: Greetings” (James 1:1). It does not say which James. Early Christian tradition took him to be James the brother of Jesus, the leader of the Jerusalem church (Acts 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 1:19; 2:9), whom Josephus says was stoned in Jerusalem about AD 62. Some scholars think the letter was written in his name after his death, others that it is his, perhaps with a secretary’s help, since the Greek is polished. The “twelve tribes of the Dispersion” are most likely Jewish believers living outside the land, though some take the phrase more widely for the whole church. The letter does not say where it was written or where its readers lived.
The first writer to cite it by name is Origen, in the early 200s, and Eusebius reports that some doubted it, though most churches read it. Martin Luther compared it unfavorably with John, Romans and 1 Peter in his preface of 1522. The book is a string of short, direct commands, with images from farming, sailing and the home, and many echoes of the teaching of Jesus, especially the Sermon on the Mount (compare 1:5 with Matthew 7:7, 1:22 with Matthew 7:24-26, 5:2-3 with Matthew 6:19-20, and 5:12 with Matthew 5:34-37).

e.n: Count it all joy: trials and endurance
t: James begins with a command that surprises: “Consider it pure joy, my brothers, when you encounter trials of many kinds, because you know that the testing of your faith develops perseverance” (1:2-3). The reason for the joy is what the trial produces, not that it is pleasant. The Greek word hypomone, “perseverance,” is staying power under weight, and James wants it to “finish its work, so that you may be mature and complete, not lacking anything” (1:4). He returns to it at the end of the letter, where the farmer, the prophets and Job are examples of those who waited (5:7-11), and he promises a blessing to the one who “perseveres under trial,” who “will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him” (1:12). The thought is close to Paul’s in Romans 5:3-4, where suffering produces perseverance, and Peter’s in his first letter.

“If any of you lacks wisdom, he should ask God, who gives generously to all without finding fault, and it will be given to him” (1:5). Wisdom in Israel’s tradition is skill in living in the fear of God, the subject of Proverbs, and Solomon’s request for it is the model (1 Kings 3). James’s version is simple: ask, and expect God to give. The condition is faith without doubt: the person who doubts “is like a wave of the sea, blown and tossed by the wind” (1:6). Wisdom comes up again in chapter 3, where James contrasts wisdom that shows itself in good conduct and gentleness with a “wisdom” of jealousy and selfish ambition (3:13-18). The word sophia occurs four times in the letter, all in these two places.

The doubter of 1:6-8 is “a double-minded man, unstable in all his ways.” The Greek word dipsychos, literally “two-souled,” occurs in the New Testament only in James (1:8; 4:8) and is not known from earlier Greek writing that survives, so James may have coined it or taken it from Jewish teaching. A double-minded person is divided between trusting God and trusting something else, so that the prayer for wisdom is made with one eye on other options. In 4:8 the double-minded are told to purify their hearts, in the same breath as the call to draw near to God. The word became a favorite of early Christian writers, in the Didache, in a saying quoted by 1 and 2 Clement, and many times in the Shepherd of Hermas.

e.n: The rich and the poor in James
t: James takes the side of the poor throughout. The brother “in humble circumstances” is told to exult in his high position, and the rich to exult in his low position, “because he will pass away like a flower of the field” (1:9-10). In the assembly the rich man in a gold ring is given the seat of honor and the poor man is told to stand (2:2-3), though James asks whether God has not “chosen the poor of this world to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom” (2:5) and it is the rich who drag the readers into court (2:6). The last strong passage turns on the rich directly: “Come now, you who are rich, weep and wail over the misery to come upon you” (5:1). The tone echoes the blessings and woes of Luke 6:20-25. James does not say that wealth is wrong in itself; he condemns pride in it, favoritism for it, and gaining it by withholding wages.

The same Greek word, peirasmos, means a “trial” in 1:2 and 1:12 and “tempting” in 1:13-14, and translators choose by context. James makes sure his readers do not blame God for the second kind: “When tempted, no one should say, ‘God is tempting me.’ For God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone” (1:13). The source is desire. “Each one is tempted when by his own evil desires he is lured away and enticed. Then after desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it is full-grown, gives birth to death” (1:14-15). The picture is of pregnancy, and James uses the same rare Greek verb for giving birth of God’s action in verse 18, where “He chose to give us birth through the word of truth.” The line between the two is “Every good and perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow” (1:17).

e.n: Quick to listen, slow to speak
t: “My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires” (1:19-20). The command sums up the letter’s concern with speech, which returns in the warnings about the tongue (1:26; 3:1-12), slander (4:11), complaining (5:9) and oaths (5:12). Jewish wisdom writing, such as Sirach, says similar things about listening and speaking. James adds a link to the next verses: the “word planted in you, which can save your souls” (1:21) is received by listening and shown by doing.

e.n: Doers of the word, not hearers only
t: “Be doers of the word, and not hearers only. Otherwise, you are deceiving yourselves” (1:22). James illustrates with a man who looks at his face in a mirror and, after observing himself, “goes away and immediately forgets what he looks like” (1:23-24). The hearer who looks “intently into the perfect law of freedom, and continues to do so,” will be “blessed in what he does” (1:25). The Greek has two matching words, akroates (“hearer”) and poietes (“doer”), and Paul uses the same pair in Romans 2:13. The idea is also Jesus’ at the end of the Sermon on the Mount, where the one who hears and acts on his words builds on rock (Matthew 7:24-27). James returns to the point in chapter 2, where faith that does nothing is “dead.”

“Pure and undefiled religion before our God and Father is this: to care for orphans and widows in their distress, and to keep oneself from being polluted by the world” (1:27). The Greek word for “religion,” threskeia, means outward worship and its observances; it occurs only four times in the New Testament (Acts 26:5; Colossians 2:18; James 1:26-27). James does not abolish ritual, but he says that what God looks for in worship is care for the helpless and a clean life. Orphans and widows are the people the Law of Moses returns to again and again as having no one to provide for them (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17-21). The verb for “care for” is the one used for visiting the sick in Matthew 25:36.

“My brothers, as you hold out your faith in our glorious Lord Jesus Christ, do not show favoritism” (2:1). The Greek word prosopolempsia, literally “receiving the face,” comes from a Hebrew idiom for lifting someone’s face, that is, showing partiality. It appears in Romans 2:11, Ephesians 6:9 and Colossians 3:25, always of God, who shows none. James gives a scene: a man in a gold ring and fine clothes comes into the meeting and is offered a seat of honor, while the poor man is told to stand or sit at someone’s feet (2:2-3). That, he says, is to become “judges with evil thoughts” (2:4). He backs the point with the “royal law” of Leviticus 19:18, saying that favoritism is sin and the one who shows no mercy will get none: “Mercy triumphs over judgment” (2:13).

e.n: The royal law and the law of freedom
t: James speaks of “the perfect law of freedom” (1:25), “the royal law stated in Scripture, ‘Love your neighbor as yourself’” (2:8) and “the law that gives freedom” (2:12). These probably name one thing, the Law of Moses as Jesus taught it, summed up in love of neighbor (Matthew 22:39-40; Galatians 5:14). James adds that “whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles at just one point is guilty of breaking all of it” (2:10), since the same God gave all of the commands. The Greek word for “royal,” basilikos, probably means the law that belongs to the King. Nomos, “law,” occurs ten times in James, all in 1:25, chapter 2 and 4:11. In 4:11-12 he adds that to slander or judge a brother is to set oneself above the law, and over it stands “only one Lawgiver and Judge.”

“What good is it, my brothers, if someone claims to have faith, but has no deeds? Can such faith save him?” (2:14). The question opens the best-known and most debated passage of the letter. James gives the example of a brother or sister without clothes or food who is told “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed” and given nothing, and concludes, “So too, faith by itself, if it does not result in action, is dead” (2:15-17). Even the demons believe that God is one “and shudder” (2:19). He appeals to Abraham, who was “justified by what he did when he offered his son Isaac on the altar” (2:21), and to Rahab (2:25), and concludes: “a man is justified by his deeds and not by faith alone” (2:24). The Greek words are used as heavily here as anywhere: pistis, “faith,” occurs sixteen times in James, thirteen of them in chapter 2, and ergon, “work” or “deed,” fifteen times, twelve in chapter 2.
Paul says, “a man is not justified by works of the law, but by faith in Jesus Christ” (Galatians 2:16), and cites the same verse about Abraham (Romans 4:3). Readers have taken the two in several ways. Many hold that they answer different problems and mean different things: Paul argues that people are accepted by God through faith and not by keeping the works that marked out Israel, such as circumcision, while James argues against a bare assent that has no deeds of mercy; they use “justify” differently, as “declare righteous” and as “show to be righteous.” Others see a real difference of emphasis that cannot be fully smoothed out, as Luther did. Most agree that James does not teach that deeds earn salvation, and that Paul does not teach that faith can do without deeds (Galatians 5:6; Ephesians 2:8-10).

James opens chapter 3 with a warning to teachers, who “will be judged more strictly” (3:1), and goes straight to the tongue. A bit controls a horse and a small rudder a large ship; “how small a spark sets a great forest ablaze” (3:3-5). The tongue is “a fire, a world of wickedness among the parts of the body. It pollutes the whole person... and is itself set on fire by hell” (3:6). The word for “hell” is Gehenna, which in the New Testament appears outside the Gospels of Matthew, Mark and Luke only here. All kinds of animals have been tamed, “but no man can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison” (3:7-8). The sharpest charge is the double use: “With the tongue we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in God’s likeness” (3:9). Spring, fig tree and vine each produce only their own kind (3:11-12). The theme of speech runs through the letter (1:19, 26; 4:11; 5:9, 12).

James asks, “Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show it by his good conduct, by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom” (3:13). Wisdom is shown by life, not by learning. He names a false wisdom of “bitter jealousy and selfish ambition” and says it “does not come from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic” (3:14-15); the Greek for “demonic,” daimoniodes, is found only here in the New Testament. Where it rules, “there will be disorder and every evil practice” (3:16). The other kind is described by a list of seven: “first of all pure, then peace-loving, gentle, accommodating, full of mercy and good fruit, impartial, and sincere” (3:17). The result is “the fruit of righteousness” sown in peace by peacemakers (3:18), a thought close to Jesus’ blessing on peacemakers (Matthew 5:9) and Paul’s list of the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22-23).

“What causes conflicts and quarrels among you? Don’t they come from the passions at war within you?” (4:1). James traces fights to unmet desire (4:2-3) and then turns to the readers’ loyalty: “You adulteresses! Do you not know that friendship with the world is hostility toward God?” (4:4). The image of God’s people as an unfaithful bride is the prophets’ (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). Verse 5 is hard to translate and it is not clear which Scripture James has in mind. Then comes a run of commands: submit to God, resist the devil, draw near to God, cleanse your hands, purify your hearts, grieve, and humble yourselves (4:7-10). The reason for each is the quotation from Proverbs 3:34: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (4:6). The Greek for “friendship,” philia, is found only here in the New Testament. A related command is in 1 John 2:15: do not love the world or the things in the world.
1 John 2:15 says, “Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”

“Come now, you who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit.’ You do not even know what will happen tomorrow! What is your life? You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes” (4:13-14). James does not forbid trade or planning but the boast that leaves God out. The right way is to say, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that” (4:15). The Greek for “mist,” atmis, occurs only here and in Acts 2:19, where it is the “billows of smoke” in Peter’s quotation of Joel. The passage ends with a sentence about sin that applies beyond business: “Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin” (4:17). The thought is close to Jesus’ story of the rich fool (Luke 12:16-21).

“Look, the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields are crying out against you. The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts” (5:4). The Law forbade keeping back a hired worker’s pay overnight (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14-15), and the picture of an unpaid wage crying out to God recalls Abel’s blood crying from the ground (Genesis 4:10). James adds that the riches have rotted, the clothes are moth-eaten, and the gold and silver are corroded, so the very wealth they have stored will testify against them (5:2-3). Gold does not rust, so the language is generally taken as a figure of speech. The charge that the rich have “fattened your hearts in the day of slaughter” and “condemned and murdered the righteous, who did not resist you” (5:5-6) may speak of the poor generally, or of the Righteous One, Jesus; the letter does not say.

“Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains” (5:7). The farmer of the land of Israel sowed after the early rain of autumn and waited for the late rain of spring (Deuteronomy 11:14). “You, too, be patient and strengthen your hearts, because the Lord’s coming is near” (5:8). The word for “coming,” parousia, was used for the arrival of a king and is the New Testament’s word for the return of Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:15; Matthew 24:3). James adds: “Do not complain about one another, brothers, so that you will not be judged. Look, the Judge is standing at the door!” (5:9). The examples are the prophets and Job, “See how blessed we consider those who have persevered. You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy” (5:10-11).
2 Peter 3:9 says the Lord “is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance,” and 3:15 adds “our Lord’s patience brings salvation.”

“Above all, my brothers, do not swear, not by heaven or earth or by any other oath. Simply let your ‘Yes’ be yes, and your ‘No,’ no, so that you will not fall under judgment” (5:12). It is very close to Jesus’ saying in the Sermon on the Mount, “But I tell you not to swear at all... Simply let your ‘Yes’ be ‘Yes,’ and your ‘No,’ ‘No.’ Anything more comes from the evil one” (Matthew 5:34-37). James gives the saying without saying where it comes from. People in the ancient world used oaths freely to make a statement believed, and some oaths, by heaven or by the Temple, were considered less binding than others (Matthew 23:16-22).

e.n: The prayer of faith and anointing the sick
t: James gives three situations and a response to each: “Is any one of you suffering? He should pray. Is anyone cheerful? He should sing praises. Is any one of you sick? He should call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord” (5:13-14). “The prayer offered in faith will restore the one who is sick. The Lord will raise him up. If he has sinned, he will be forgiven” (5:15). Readers differ on the oil. Some take it as medicine used together with prayer, since oil was used on wounds (Luke 10:34); others as a sign of setting the person apart for God; the Catholic and Orthodox churches treat the anointing of the sick as a sacrament, while many Protestant churches practice it as a prayer for healing without that name. The disciples had anointed the sick with oil in Mark 6:13. James adds that people should “confess your sins to each other and pray for each other so that you may be healed” (5:16), and holds up Elijah, “a man just like us,” who prayed that it would not rain, and it did not for three and a half years, and then prayed again and the heavens gave rain (5:17-18; Luke 4:25).

The letter ends without a farewell: “My brothers, if one of you should wander from the truth and someone should bring him back, consider this: Whoever turns a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death and cover over a multitude of sins” (5:19-20). The phrase “cover over a multitude of sins” echoes Proverbs 10:12, which 1 Peter 4:8 also borrows. Readers differ on whether the “soul” saved is the wanderer’s or the rescuer’s, and whether “death” means bodily death or final separation from God. The thought is of the community as a place where a brother who strays is sought and not left. Jesus’ teaching on a brother who sins (Matthew 18:15) and Paul’s on restoring a person “gently” (Galatians 6:1) are the nearest parallels.

e.n: The first letter of Peter: who wrote it and to whom
t: The letter opens, “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, To the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Peter 1:1). The writer is Simon, the fisherman from Bethsaida whom Jesus named Peter (John 1:42; Matthew 16:18). The five provinces are in what is now Turkey, a region about 700 miles across, so the letter was a circular meant to go round several churches. Whether the readers were mostly Jews or mostly Gentiles is debated. The letter speaks of their “empty way of life” (1:18) and of “the same desires as the Gentiles” (4:3), which points to Gentile converts, but it also calls them “exiles of the Dispersion” and quotes the Old Testament on almost every page.

The letter was known and used very early. Clement of Rome, Polycarp and Papias seem to echo or use it, and Irenaeus and Tertullian quote it as Peter’s. The question is whether the apostle wrote it himself. In favor are the opening words, the many echoes of the sayings and acts of Jesus, and “Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly” (5:12). Against, some scholars point to the polished Greek, close to the Greek Old Testament, which they find hard to expect from a Galilean fisherman, and to a lack of personal memories of Jesus. Many who accept Peter as the author think Silvanus (the Silas of Acts) helped with the wording, which “through Silvanus” would allow. Others think a follower of Peter wrote in his name after his death, in Rome, where tradition says he died under Nero. If Peter wrote it, the date falls in the early to mid 60s; if not, it may be later, anywhere to about AD 90. The letter does not give a date.

The main themes are a living hope grounded in the resurrection (1:3), the call to be holy (1:15-16), the church as God’s people, priests and building (2:4-10), submission and good conduct before a watching world (2:11-3:12), readiness to suffer for doing good (3:13-4:19), and the care of the flock by its elders (5:1-4). The hardest passage is 3:18-22; see the entry on the spirits in prison.

The letter closes, “The church in Babylon, chosen together with you, sends you greetings, as does my son Mark” (5:13). Three places have been proposed. The oldest and most common view takes “Babylon” as a name for Rome, as Revelation 17-18 does. Eusebius (about AD 325) reports that Papias and Clement of Alexandria held that Peter wrote from Rome and called it Babylon in a figure, and the tradition that Peter died in Rome is strong from about AD 96 on. Another view points to the real city of Babylon on the Euphrates, where there was a large Jewish community, though by the first century it was largely deserted. A third view points to a Roman fort called Babylon in Egypt, near modern Cairo, where Coptic Christians say Mark taught. The letter does not say.

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ! By His great mercy He has given us new birth into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, and into an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled, and unfading, reserved in heaven for you,” (1:3-4). Peter’s hope is a person and an event, not a wish. It is “living” because the Christ it rests on is alive, and the inheritance is reserved in heaven while the readers are “shielded by God’s power” (1:5). In the Old Testament the inheritance was the land (Deuteronomy 12:9-10); Peter says the readers’ inheritance cannot be taken, spoiled or faded. Hope is mentioned again in 1:13, 1:21 and 3:5, and in 3:15 the readers are to be ready to give an answer for “the reason for the hope that is in you.”

e.n: Proven faith, more precious than gold
t: Peter tells readers who are grieved by “various trials” that these have come “so that the proven character of your faith—more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire—may result in praise, glory, and honor at the revelation of Jesus Christ” (1:6-7). A goldsmith put raw ore into a furnace to burn away the impurities, and the Old Testament uses the picture for God’s testing of his people (Proverbs 17:3; Zechariah 13:9; Malachi 3:3). Peter’s claim is that faith is worth more than the gold, because gold perishes. He does not say what the trials were. They seem to have been insults, slander and exclusion (2:12; 3:16; 4:4) more than any official action. The same words for “various trials” open the letter of James (1:2). In 4:12 he comes back to the picture: “do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you.”

e.n: Ransomed from an empty way of life
t: “For you know that it was not with perishable things such as silver or gold that you were redeemed from the empty way of life you inherited from your forefathers, but with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot” (1:18-19). The Greek lytroo, “to ransom,” is the word of the slave market and the prison: the price paid to free someone. The Law required the Passover lamb to be “without blemish” (Exodus 12:5), and Isaiah 53:7 pictures the servant as a lamb led to the slaughter. Peter adds that this plan was settled before the creation of the world (1:20). The “empty way of life” suggests that most of his readers were Gentile in background, though a Jewish writer could also speak of a tradition that has lost its power.

e.n: Born again through the living word
t: “For you have been born again, not of perishable seed, but of imperishable, through the living and enduring word of God.” Peter has already said that God “has given us new birth” (1:3). The Greek anagennao is found in the New Testament only in these two verses. Peter quotes Isaiah 40:6-8: “All flesh is like grass... but the word of the Lord stands forever,” and adds, “And this is the word that was proclaimed to you” (1:24-25). A person’s life is as fragile as grass, but the word that gave the readers a new birth does not wither. The new birth is the root of the brotherly love of 1:22 and of the milk of 2:2. Jesus spoke of being “born again” to Nicodemus (John 3:3-7).

e.n: A spiritual house of living stones
t: “As you come to Him, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight, you also, like living stones, are being built into a spiritual house to be a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.” (2:4-5). Peter weaves three Old Testament stone texts together: Isaiah 28:16 (“I lay in Zion a stone”), Psalm 118:22 (“the stone the builders rejected”) and Isaiah 8:14 (“A stone of stumbling and a rock of offense,” 2:8). Jesus had applied Psalm 118:22 to himself against the Jerusalem leaders (Mark 12:10-11), and Peter had used it before the council (Acts 4:11). The church is a temple made of people, as Paul also says (Ephesians 2:19-22; 1 Corinthians 3:16). Jesus’ own word to Simon was that he would be the rock on which he would build his church (Matthew 16:18), and Peter here gives the title to Christ and the believers.

“But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, to proclaim the virtues of Him who called you out of darkness into His marvelous light. Once you were not a people, but now you are the people of God; once you had not received mercy, but now you have received mercy.” (2:9-10). Each title comes from Israel’s Old Testament: a kingdom of priests and a holy nation in Exodus 19:5-6, the chosen people of Isaiah 43:20-21, and “Not My People” in Hosea 1:9-10 and 2:23. Peter gives them to a church that is mostly Gentile. In Israel the whole nation was called to be a priestly people, though only Aaron’s family served at the altar. Peter says every believer is part of the “holy priesthood” and offers “spiritual sacrifices” (2:5): praise (Hebrews 13:15), good works (Hebrews 13:16) and lives given to God (Romans 12:1). The Greek hierateuma, “priesthood,” is found only in 1 Peter 2:5 and 2:9.

e.n: Honor everyone, fear God, honor the king
t: “Submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, or to governors as those sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right.... Treat everyone with high regard: Love the brotherhood of believers, fear God, honor the king.” (2:13-14, 17). The king was the Roman emperor, who in the early 60s was Nero, and the governors were officials like the ones in Bithynia and Pontus (1:1). Peter tells the readers that “it is God’s will that by doing good you should silence the ignorance of foolish men” (2:15) and to “live in freedom, but do not use your freedom as a cover-up for evil; live as servants of God” (2:16). His four commands are carefully balanced: “honor everyone,” “love the brotherhood,” “fear God,” “honor the king.” The verb “fear” is kept for God. Paul teaches similarly in Romans 13:1-7 and Titus 3:1. A generation later, in the book of Revelation, Rome appears as a beast (Revelation 13).

e.n: Servants and the example of Christ
t: “Servants, submit yourselves to your masters with all respect, not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable.” (2:18). The word is oiketai, household slaves, who made up a large part of every Roman town and who were open to beating with little recourse. Peter does not argue for or against slavery as an institution in this letter. He addresses slaves as moral agents who have a standing before God, and he tells them how to bear unjust suffering by looking at Christ: “To this you were called, because Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps” (2:21). The next verses follow Isaiah 53 closely: “He committed no sin, and no deceit was found in His mouth” (2:22), and “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree, so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness” (2:24). The Greek hypogrammos, “example,” was a writing teacher’s model of letters that a child traced over. It is found only here in the New Testament. Many readers today feel the discomfort of a passage that does not tell slaves to leave their masters. Paul tells Philemon that Onesimus is now more than a slave, a beloved brother (Philemon 1:16).

“Wives, in the same way, submit yourselves to your husbands, so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives” (3:1). Peter has in mind a wife whose husband does not share her new faith. In the Roman world a wife was expected to follow her husband’s gods, and a wife who took up a new religion could be seen as a threat to the household. Peter tells her to win him by conduct. Her beauty is to come “from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious in God’s sight” (3:4), not from “outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes” (3:3), a warning also in 1 Timothy 2:9. Sarah is the example (3:5-6). Husbands are to “treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered” (3:7). Readers differ on how to apply the call to submission today. Some read it as a standing pattern for marriage, others as advice for a particular setting where a small church was under suspicion. All agree that Peter puts husband and wife on the same footing before God as “fellow heirs.”

e.n: Do not repay evil with evil
t: “Finally, all of you, be like-minded and sympathetic, love as brothers, be tenderhearted and humble. Do not repay evil with evil or insult with insult, but with blessing, because to this you were called so that you may inherit a blessing.” (3:8-9). Peter backs it with a long quotation from Psalm 34:12-16 (3:10-12), the same psalm he drew on in 2:3 (“you have tasted that the Lord is good”). The command goes back to Jesus’ teaching to bless those who curse (Luke 6:27-28) and appears in Paul (Romans 12:17-21). Peter says that Jesus himself did it: “When they heaped abuse on Him, He did not retaliate; when He suffered, He made no threats” (2:23).

e.n: Ready to give a reason for your hope
t: “But even if you should suffer for what is right, you are blessed. ‘Do not fear what they fear; do not be shaken.’ But in your hearts sanctify Christ as Lord. Always be prepared to give a defense to everyone who asks you the reason for the hope that is in you. But respond with gentleness and respect, keeping a clear conscience, so that those who slander you may be put to shame by your good behavior in Christ.” (3:14-16). “Do not fear what they fear” quotes Isaiah 8:12-13, where the Lord tells Isaiah not to fear what the people fear but to treat the Lord of hosts as holy; Peter changes the last words to “sanctify Christ as Lord.” The Greek apologia, “defense,” is the word for a speech made in court (Acts 22:1; 25:16; 2 Timothy 4:16), but Peter may mean any answer to a neighbor who asks why you live as you do. The tone he asks for is “gentleness and respect.” The word has given its name to Christian apologetics.

e.n: Christ and the spirits in prison
t: “For Christ also suffered for sins once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God. He was put to death in the body but made alive in the Spirit, in whom He also went and preached to the spirits in prison who disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built. In the ark a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water.” (3:18-20). This is one of the most disputed passages in the New Testament. Martin Luther wrote that he did not know for certain what Peter meant. Three main readings are held. First, Augustine and many others thought Christ preached through Noah to the people of Noah’s day, who are now the “spirits in prison.” Second, many modern scholars think the “spirits” are the rebel angels of Genesis 6:1-4 as told in 1 Enoch 6-16 (compare 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6), and that Christ, raised and exalted (3:22), announced his victory to them. Third, others think Christ went to the realm of the dead to preach, a view that lies behind the line about descending into hell in later creeds. The Greek for “prison” is phylake, and the exact sense of the word translated “pledge” in verse 21 (eperotema) is also debated.

Two things are plain. The passage ends with Christ risen and exalted “at the right hand of God, with angels, authorities, and powers subject to Him” (3:22), so the point is Christ’s triumph. Peter also ties the flood to baptism: “And this water symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ,” See also 4:6, “the gospel was preached even to those who are now dead,” which is a separate disputed line.

e.n: Love covers a multitude of sins
t: “Above all, love one another deeply, because love covers over a multitude of sins. Show hospitality to one another without complaining. As good stewards of the manifold grace of God, each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another.” (4:8-10). “Love covers over a multitude of sins” is from Proverbs 10:12 and is used again in James 5:20. It means that love does not keep a list of faults and is quick to forgive. It does not mean that love can pay for sins; Peter has already said who did that (2:24). Hospitality (philoxenia, literally love of strangers) mattered a great deal to the early churches, because travelers from other towns relied on the homes of believers, and inns were poor places (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2; 3 John 5-8). “Manifold” is the Greek poikile, the same word as the “various” of the trials in 1:6, so that grace comes in as many forms as trouble does.

“Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery trial that has come upon you, as though something strange were happening to you. But rejoice that you share in the sufferings of Christ, so that you may be overjoyed at the revelation of His glory.” (4:12-13). Peter distinguishes suffering for wrongdoing (murderer, thief, wrongdoer, meddler, 4:15) from suffering “as a Christian” (4:16). The name “Christian” occurs only three times in the New Testament (Acts 11:26; 26:28; 1 Peter 4:16). The Roman historian Tacitus says that Nero punished the “Christians” at Rome after the fire of AD 64, and Pliny, governor of Bithynia, wrote to the emperor Trajan about AD 112 asking how to handle them, so the name could bring a person before the authorities. The letter does not say whether its readers faced official action or the hostility of neighbors, and the answer depends partly on its date. Peter writes that “it is time for judgment to begin with the family of God” (4:17), and ends the chapter, “those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good” (4:19).

“As a fellow elder, a witness of Christ’s sufferings, and a partaker of the glory to be revealed, I appeal to the elders among you: Be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you, watching over them not out of compulsion, but because it is God’s will; not out of greed, but out of eagerness; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away.” (5:1-4). The elders are given three warnings, each with a contrast: not by compulsion but willingly, not for shameful gain but eagerly, not as rulers but as examples. Peter speaks as an apostle who calls himself a “fellow elder,” and he has in mind Jesus’ own words to him to “feed My sheep” (John 21:15-17) and the Old Testament chapter on the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and not the flock (Ezekiel 34). Paul uses the same picture for the Ephesian elders (Acts 20:28). Elders and overseers are the same leaders in the Pastoral Letters (Titus 1:5-7).

e.n: Humble yourselves, and cast your anxiety on Him
t: “Young men, in the same way, submit yourselves to your elders. And all of you, clothe yourselves with humility toward one another, because, ‘God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves, therefore, under God’s mighty hand, so that in due time He may exalt you. Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you.” (5:5-7). The quotation is Proverbs 3:34, which James 4:6 quotes in the same Greek form. “Clothe yourselves” refers to a garment put on, and some think it recalls the towel Jesus tied around himself when he washed the disciples’ feet (John 13:4-5). “Cast all your anxiety on Him” echoes Psalm 55:22. Peter follows at once with a warning: “Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour. Resist him, standing firm in your faith” (5:8-9). He closes with a prayer that “the God of all grace, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you” (5:10).

e.n: The Son, greater than the prophets
t: Hebrews opens without a greeting: “On many past occasions and in many different ways, God spoke to our fathers through the prophets. But in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son” (Hebrews 1:1-2). The writer piles up seven claims about the Son in a few lines: heir of all things, the one through whom God made the universe, “the radiance of God’s glory and the exact representation of His nature,” the one who upholds “all things by His powerful word,” who provided “purification for sins,” and who “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (1:2-3). The rest of the letter works out the claim “So He became as far superior to the angels as the name He has inherited is excellent beyond theirs” (1:4). The two Greek words in verse 3, apaugasma (“radiance”) and character (“exact representation”), are rare. The first is like light from a flame and the second is like the impression made by a seal. Both are pictures of one who is distinct from God and yet fully shows him.

e.n: Better than: the argument of Hebrews
t: The Greek word kreitton, “better,” runs through the letter thirteen times. Jesus is “far superior to the angels” (1:4). He brings “a better hope” (7:19), is the guarantee of “a better covenant” (7:22), and mediates it on “better promises” (8:6). He offers “better sacrifices” (9:23). Believers have “a better and permanent possession” (10:34), look for “a better country, a heavenly one” (11:16), and hope for “a better resurrection” (11:35). The sprinkled blood “speaks a better word than the blood of Abel” (12:24). The point is not that the old things were bad. The writer says the law was given by angels (2:2), that Moses was “faithful in all God’s house” (3:5), and that the Levitical priests and sacrifices were God’s own pattern (8:5). The point is that they were “a shadow of the good things to come, not the realities themselves” (10:1), so that to go back to them would be to leave the thing for its outline.

Genesis 14 gives Melchizedek only three verses: he is king of Salem and priest of God Most High, he blesses Abraham and receives a tenth. Psalm 110:4 then says of the king David calls his Lord, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.” Hebrews puts the two texts together. The writer reads Melchizedek’s name (“king of righteousness”) and his city (“king of peace”), and notes that Genesis gives him no father, mother or genealogy and records no birth or death: “Without father or mother or genealogy, without beginning of days or end of life, like the Son of God, he remains a priest for all time” (7:2-3). The writer argues from what Scripture does not say. Because Abraham, and through him Levi, gave Melchizedek a tenth and received his blessing, and “the lesser is blessed by the greater” (7:7), the priesthood of Melchizedek ranks above the Levitical priesthood. Since Jesus is from Judah, a tribe about which “Moses said nothing about priests” (7:14), his priesthood rests “not by a law of succession, but by the power of an indestructible life” (7:16). A scroll from Qumran (11Q13) shows that some Jews of the period also pictured Melchizedek as a heavenly figure of judgment and rescue, but Hebrews makes no use of that picture and uses only the text of Genesis and the Psalm.

Two Greek words carry the idea: hapax, “once,” and ephapax, “once for all.” They are the writer’s answer to the repeated rituals of the tabernacle. The high priest “entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood” (9:7), and priests “day after day” stand to offer “again and again the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins” (10:11). Christ, by contrast, “sacrificed for sin once for all when He offered up Himself” (7:27), “entered the Most Holy Place once for all by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption” (9:12), and by that will “we have been sanctified through the sacrifice of the body of Jesus Christ once for all” (10:10). The proof the writer offers is that the offering stopped: “when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down” (10:12). The contrast is between priests who stand and keep working (10:11) and a priest who has sat down (10:12). The writer adds, “where these have been forgiven, an offering for sin is no longer needed” (10:18). Hebrews 9:27-28 sets the pattern: people die once and face judgment, Christ was “offered once to bear the sins of many,” and will appear a second time “not to bear sin, but to bring salvation to those who eagerly await Him.”
Jude uses the shorter word, hapax, of the faith “entrusted once for all to the saints” (Jude 3).

e.n: The heavenly sanctuary: copy and shadow
t: Hebrews says that the tabernacle was built on a pattern: “The place where they serve is a copy and shadow of what is in heaven. This is why Moses was warned when he was about to build the tabernacle: ‘See to it that you make everything according to the pattern shown you on the mountain’” (8:5; compare Exodus 25:40). So there is “the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands” (9:11), and “Christ did not enter a man-made copy of the true sanctuary, but He entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God” (9:24). Scholars have asked where the writer found this picture of a heavenly original and an earthly copy. Plato’s world of forms, the writings of Philo of Alexandria, and the Jewish apocalyptic idea of a heavenly temple have all been proposed. The writer’s own source is the verse in Exodus, and the contrast he draws is not between the physical and the spiritual so much as between the first covenant and the age that follows its fulfillment, “the time of reform” (9:10). A “copy” is a pointer to something real and not an illusion.

Hebrews 3:7-4:13 is a sermon on Psalm 95:7-11 (“Today, if you hear His voice, do not harden your hearts”), read as a warning from the wilderness generation. The people Moses led out of Egypt heard the good news and did not enter “because of their unbelief” (3:19). The writer then argues that the rest was not finished with Joshua: “if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later about another day” (4:8). Psalm 95 was written centuries later, through David, and still says “Today.” So “There remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God” (4:9). The word for “Sabbath rest” is sabbatismos, found nowhere else in the New Testament. The writer pictures three layers: God’s own rest on the seventh day when “His works have been finished since the foundation of the world” (4:3-4), the land of Canaan, and the final rest that those who believe enter. Scholars differ on whether that rest is already present (“we who have believed enter that rest,” 4:3), still future, or both, and Hebrews seems to hold both. “Let us, therefore, make every effort to enter that rest” (4:11).

Hebrews alternates between teaching about Christ and sharp warnings to the readers. Scholars usually count five: against drifting away from “such a great salvation” (2:1-4); against hardening the heart as Israel did in the wilderness (3:7-4:13); against falling away after being enlightened (5:11-6:12); against deliberately going on sinning “after we have received the knowledge of the truth” (10:26-31); and against refusing the God who speaks from heaven (12:25-29). The most debated is 6:4-6, where it is “impossible” for those who have “once been enlightened” and “have fallen away” to be restored to repentance. Christians have read it in four main ways. Some say it describes true believers who can lose their salvation. Some say it describes people who shared the community’s blessings and never truly believed. Some read it as a hypothetical warning that makes the point by showing what would be at stake. Some read it as a loss of reward and not of salvation. The text itself softens the warning at once: “we are convinced of better things in your case—things that accompany salvation” (6:9). The warnings are written to keep people from drifting, and the readers are urged to endure and not to despair.

e.n: Faith defined: the hall of faith
t: “Now faith is the assurance of what we hope for and the certainty of what we do not see” (11:1). The Greek hupostasis, here “assurance,” is literally “what stands under.” In the everyday papyri it is also found in documents that establish ownership, and the writer uses it in 1:3 for God’s “nature.” The writer then tells the story of Israel by naming people who acted on what God had said before they could see it: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses and his parents, Rahab, and then a quick list of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets (11:32). The writer insists on two points. Faith believes “that He exists and that He rewards those who earnestly seek Him” (11:6). And many of these people “died in faith, without having received the things they were promised” (11:13); “These were all commended for their faith, yet they did not receive what was promised” (11:39). They are included in the same promise, “so that together with us they would be made perfect” (11:40). Faith here is trust that lasts through delay.

“Therefore, since we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off every encumbrance and the sin that so easily entangles, and let us run with endurance the race set out for us” (12:1). The Greek for “witnesses,” martyres, is the word that later came to mean “martyrs.” Here it most naturally means those just listed in chapter 11, who bear witness by their lives to what faith looks like. It does not necessarily say that they are watching from the stands. The picture of a stadium may be intended, since the next verse is about running with the eyes fixed on one person: “Let us fix our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith, who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God” (12:2). The word “endurance” (hupomone) is a word of staying power under pressure. Jesus is both the pioneer who goes ahead (archegos, as in 2:10) and the one who brings faith to its goal (teleiotes).

Hebrews 12 applies Proverbs 3:11-12 to the readers’ suffering: “My son, do not take lightly the discipline of the Lord, and do not lose heart when He rebukes you. For the Lord disciplines the one He loves, and He chastises every son He receives” (12:5-6). The Greek paideia means the whole upbringing of a child, including training and correction, not just punishment. The writer says, “Endure suffering as discipline; God is treating you as sons” (12:7), and admits plainly, “No discipline seems enjoyable at the time, but painful. Later on, however, it yields a harvest of righteousness and peace to those who have been trained by it” (12:11). The point is not that every hardship is a punishment for sin. The readers have been persecuted for their faith (10:32-34), and the writer reads their trouble as the training of a father who wants his children to “share in His holiness” (12:10).

e.n: Strangers and exiles: the city to come
t: The people of faith in chapter 11 live as outsiders. Abraham “dwelt in the promised land as a stranger in a foreign country. He lived in tents, as did Isaac and Jacob” (11:9), “looking forward to the city with foundations, whose architect and builder is God” (11:10). At the end the writer says they “acknowledged that they were strangers and exiles on the earth” and were “longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them” (11:13, 16). The close of the letter says the same to the readers: “For here we do not have a permanent city, but we are looking for the city that is to come” (13:14). The heavenly Jerusalem is also described in 12:22-24. The theme is not escape from the world. The last chapter sends the readers “outside the camp” (13:13) and tells them to do good and to share (13:16).
1 Peter calls its readers “exiles of the Dispersion” (1:1) and urges them, “as foreigners and exiles, to abstain from the desires of the flesh, which war against your soul” (2:11).

After the picture of Mount Zion, the writer warns that the God who spoke at Sinai now speaks from heaven. “At that time His voice shook the earth, but now He has promised, ‘Once more I will shake not only the earth, but heaven as well’” (12:26, quoting Haggai 2:6). He explains the words “Once more”: they “signify the removal of what can be shaken—that is, created things—so that the unshakable may remain” (12:27). The answer is gratitude and worship: “since we are receiving an unshakable kingdom, let us be filled with gratitude, and so worship God acceptably with reverence and awe. For our God is a consuming fire” (12:28-29, quoting Deuteronomy 4:24). The fire that frightened Israel at Sinai is not removed. The point of the contrast is that the readers have a better access, and so a heavier responsibility.

e.n: He learned obedience from what He suffered
t: Hebrews gives a strong picture of Jesus’ humanity. He shared “flesh and blood” (2:14), was “made like His brothers in every way” (2:17), and “suffered when He was tempted” (2:18). “During the days of Jesus’ earthly life, He offered up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and He was heard because of His reverence” (5:7). Many take this as a reference to Gethsemane. “Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered. And having been made perfect, He became the source of eternal salvation to all who obey Him” (5:8-9). The text does not say that Jesus was disobedient; it says that in the school of suffering he carried obedience through to its end. “Made perfect” (teleioo) means brought to the goal, completed for his work as high priest. As a result, “we do not have a high priest who is unable to sympathize with our weaknesses, but we have one who was tempted in every way that we are, yet was without sin” (4:15).

When God made a promise to Abraham, “since He had no one greater to swear by, He swore by Himself” (6:13). The writer says why: “So when God wanted to make the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise, He guaranteed it with an oath. Thus by two unchangeable things in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged” (6:17-18). The two unchangeable things are the promise and the oath. The same idea is applied to Jesus’ priesthood, which came “with an oath by the One who said to Him: ‘The Lord has sworn and will not change His mind: You are a priest forever’” (7:21). The Levitical priests had no oath. The hope the oath secures is “an anchor for the soul, firm and secure. It enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain” (6:19).

The last chapter returns to the sacrifices. “Although the high priest brings the blood of animals into the Holy Place as a sacrifice for sin, the bodies are burned outside the camp. And so Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood” (13:11-12; compare Leviticus 16:27). Then comes the call: “Therefore let us go to Him outside the camp, bearing the disgrace He bore” (13:13). “The camp” may mean Judaism and its worship, or may be a way of saying the world’s approval and security; scholars differ. The altar of verse 10 is also debated: it may be the cross, the heavenly sanctuary, or the Lord’s Supper. What the writer then says is clear: “Through Jesus, therefore, let us continually offer to God a sacrifice of praise, the fruit of lips that confess His name. And do not neglect to do good and to share with others, for with such sacrifices God is pleased” (13:15-16).

e.n: The word of God is living and active
t: “For the word of God is living and active. Sharper than any double-edged sword, it pierces even to dividing soul and spirit, joints and marrow. It judges the thoughts and intentions of the heart. Nothing in all creation is hidden from God’s sight; everything is uncovered and exposed before the eyes of Him to whom we must give account” (4:12-13). The sentence closes the sermon on Psalm 95. “Word” here is logos, and it may mean God’s spoken message (compare 1:1-2) more than the whole Bible, although both fit the context. The sword is the machaira, the short sword or knife. The images of the sword and of the open, bared body suggest an examination from which nothing is hidden. The writer turns at once to a priest who can “sympathize with our weaknesses” (4:15), as comfort for those who stand exposed.

Hebrews does not give the name of its author. The title “To the Hebrews” is not part of the letter itself but appears in the earliest manuscripts, such as Papyrus 46 (about AD 200), which places it directly after Romans. The writer uses “we” and “I” (11:32; 13:19, 22-23), is a skilled Greek stylist who quotes the Old Testament from the Septuagint, and knows Timothy (13:23). In the East, Hebrews was widely received as Paul’s, or as based on Paul’s teaching: Clement of Alexandria thought Paul wrote it in Hebrew and Luke put it into Greek. In the West it was doubted until the fourth century.
