Origen, in the third century, said that the thoughts were Paul’s but the style and wording were someone else’s, and that only God knew who actually wrote it. Tertullian suggested Barnabas, Martin Luther suggested Apollos, and Adolf von Harnack suggested Priscilla; none of these can be shown. The letter has been valued for what it says, and the church accepted it because of its content, whoever wrote it. The male participle in 11:32 (“to tell”) is the only grammatical clue, and some scholars read it as pointing to a man.

The letter gives hints but no address. The readers are believers (“holy brothers, who share in the heavenly calling,” 3:1) who have been through hard times: “you endured a great conflict in the face of suffering. Sometimes you were publicly exposed to ridicule and persecution; at other times you were partners with those who were so treated. You sympathized with those in prison and joyfully accepted the confiscation of your property” (10:32-34). They have not yet been persecuted to death (12:4), they have leaders (13:7, 17), and they are tempted to drift (2:1) and to stop meeting (10:25). The final greeting “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24) can mean that the writer is in Italy and writing to a church elsewhere, or that Italians away from Italy are sending greetings home to Rome; scholars are divided. Most readers have assumed a mainly Jewish Christian audience because of the constant use of Israel’s Scriptures and rituals. Others point out that the argument also makes sense for anyone tempted to return to a familiar religion. The letter calls itself “a word of exhortation” (13:22), which is the phrase Acts 13:15 uses for a synagogue sermon.

Two facts frame the date. By about AD 96 the letter was known in Rome: 1 Clement uses its language about the Son in chapter 36. And Timothy is still alive and free (13:23). Beyond that, scholars disagree. Some argue for a date in the 60s, before the Romans destroyed the Temple in AD 70, because the writer speaks of the priests and sacrifices in the present tense (for example, “Day after day every priest stands to minister,” 10:11) and does not mention the Temple’s fall as an argument. Others reply that the writer is describing the tabernacle of the Scriptures, never the Temple (he does not mention the Temple at all), and that after AD 70 the argument that the sacrifices had ended would have been even stronger. The same question applies to the persecution of 10:32-34, which some link to Claudius’ expulsion of Jews from Rome (about AD 49) and others to Nero’s later cruelty. The dating chosen in the app’s timeline, “c. AD 60-95,” reflects this uncertainty.

e.n: Left in Crete to set things in order
t: Paul writes, “The reason I left you in Crete was that you would set in order what was unfinished and appoint elders in every town, as I directed you” (Titus 1:5). The Greek verb for “set in order” (epidiorthoo) means to straighten out further, and it occurs only here in the New Testament. Titus is a trusted helper with a task left half done, and the letter is his written authority for it. Paul and Barnabas had earlier “appointed elders for them in each church” (Acts 14:23), so the pattern is an old one. The letter does not say how Paul came to be on Crete, or how long he stayed. The ship that carried Paul as a prisoner stopped at Crete (Acts 27:7-13), but that call was brief, so if Paul wrote the letter the visit it describes is a separate one after the end of Acts.

e.n: What an elder must be in Titus
t: Titus 1:6-9 lists what an elder must be. He is “blameless, the husband of but one wife,” with “children who are believers and who are not open to accusation of indiscretion or insubordination” (1:6). Verse 7 calls the same man an “overseer” and adds that he is “God’s steward,” so he must be “above reproach,” not self-absorbed, quick-tempered, drunken, violent or greedy for money. He must be “hospitable, a lover of good, self-controlled, upright, holy, and disciplined” (1:8). He must also “hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught, so that he can encourage others by sound teaching and refute those who contradict it” (1:9). Most of the list is about character, with one item about teaching. Parts of it overlap with 1 Timothy 3:1-7. “Husband of but one wife” has been read as faithfulness in marriage, as a ban on remarriage, and as a ban on having more than one wife, and readers disagree. “Children who are believers” can also be read “faithful children,” and the letter does not say what happens when a grown child leaves the faith.

Paul quotes “one of their own prophets”: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons.” He then says, “This testimony is true. Therefore rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith” (Titus 1:12-13). The line is a known saying, and Clement of Alexandria and Jerome name the Cretan poet Epimenides as its source. A very similar phrase is in the Hymn to Zeus by the poet Callimachus, who explains it by the Cretan claim that Zeus had a tomb on the island. A Greek verb meaning “to play the Cretan” came to mean to lie. Paul does not turn the line into a logic puzzle. He uses a stinging remark from their own side to say that Titus will meet resistance and must not be gentle with the teachers who exploit it. The saying is a verdict on a reputation, and the letter does not say that every Cretan was this way. Chapter 3 tells believers to “malign no one” and to show “full consideration to everyone” (3:2), so the sharpness is aimed at the false teaching.

e.n: To the pure, all things are pure
t: Paul writes, “To the pure, all things are pure; but to the defiled and unbelieving, nothing is pure. Indeed, both their minds and their consciences are defiled” (Titus 1:15). He has just warned against “Jewish myths” and “the commands of men who have rejected the truth” (1:14). The letter does not list the rules, but they are often taken to be rules about food and ritual cleanness. Jesus taught that what comes out of a person defiles, not what goes in (Mark 7:14-23), and Paul says “nothing is unclean in itself” (Romans 14:14) and that everything God created is good when received with thanks (1 Timothy 4:3-5). The saying is not a license. The next verse says that those who “profess to know God” can “deny Him” by their actions (1:16), so purity is judged at the level of mind and conscience, and then by conduct.

Titus uses the language of health for teaching. An elder must encourage others “by sound teaching” (1:9), believers are to be “sound in the faith” (1:13), and Titus is told, “speak the things that are consistent with sound doctrine” (2:1). Older men are to be “sound in faith, love, and perseverance” (2:2), and Titus’s own speech is to be “wholesome” (2:8). The Greek root (hygiaino) gives us the word “hygiene.” The picture is of teaching that keeps a community alive and well, in contrast to the “empty talk” of the teachers in chapter 1. What follows 2:1 is a list of ordinary conduct for older men, older women, younger people and slaves, so “sound doctrine” in this letter is taught and then shown in daily life. The same word is used in 1 Timothy 1:10 and 2 Timothy 4:3.
In 2 John, the standard is “the teaching of Christ” (9), a phrase that sets the limit of what a church can welcome from its visitors.

e.n: So that the word of God will not be discredited
t: Three times in chapter 2 Paul gives the same kind of reason for how believers should live. Younger women are to live well “so that the word of God will not be discredited” (2:5). Titus must show “wholesome speech that is above reproach, so that anyone who opposes us will be ashamed, having nothing bad to say about us” (2:8). Slaves are to be honest and well-pleasing “so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior” (2:10). The concern is how outsiders see the gospel. The Greek word for “adorn” (kosmeo) is the root of “cosmetics,” and means to arrange something so that its beauty shows. Other New Testament letters make the same point about outsiders (1 Timothy 3:7; 6:1; 1 Peter 2:12; 3:16). Paul does not say that conduct earns salvation, which he denies in 3:5. He says conduct can make the message look attractive or hollow.

Paul asks that older women be “reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good.” In this way, he says, “they can train the young women to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited” (Titus 2:3-5). The first requirement is the older women’s own conduct. Their teaching is passed on person to person, from older to younger, and the setting is the household, not a lecture hall. The matching charge for men is shorter: older men are to be “temperate, dignified, self-controlled” (2:2), and younger men are to be “self-controlled” (2:6). Readers differ on how far the list reflects the culture of the first century and how far it is meant for every age. Most agree that the passage takes for granted that women are teachers of the church’s next generation.

e.n: The grace of God has appeared
t: Paul writes, “For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation to everyone. It instructs us to renounce ungodliness and worldly passions, and to live sensible, upright, and godly lives in the present age, as we await the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:11-13). Grace here is something that “has appeared,” a word used of a light shining out, and it acts as a teacher. The Greek for “instructs” (paideuo) is the word for training a child. The sentence has two appearances: grace has already appeared, and the glory of Christ is still awaited. In between, believers live “in the present age” with self-control and good works. Chapter 3 returns to the same movement: “when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared, He saved us” (3:4-5). The weight falls on God’s initiative, and the life of the believer follows from it.

e.n: A people for His own possession
t: Paul writes that Jesus “gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds” (Titus 2:14). The phrase “a people for His own possession” comes from the language used of Israel. God told Moses that Israel would be His “treasured possession” among all peoples (Exodus 19:5-6), and Moses said the Lord had chosen them “to be a people for His own possession” (Deuteronomy 7:6; 14:2). The word for “possession” (periousios) occurs only here in the New Testament. The verse also echoes Psalm 130:8, which says the Lord will redeem Israel from all their iniquities. Paul says the redeemed people is gathered by what Christ gave, and it is marked by zeal for good deeds. Peter takes up the same picture in 1 Peter 2:9.
1 Peter 2:9 uses the same phrase: “a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession.” See the entry on the royal priesthood.

e.n: Submit to rulers and be ready for every good work
t: Paul tells Titus, “Remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to be obedient and ready for every good work, to malign no one, and to be peaceable and gentle, showing full consideration to everyone” (Titus 3:1-2). The reminder is about public life. Believers are to obey authorities, work for the good of others, and speak and act without insult or quarrel. Romans 13:1-7, 1 Peter 2:13-17 and 1 Timothy 2:1-2 give related instructions. The New Testament also shows limits to obedience: when the council forbade the apostles to speak, Peter answered, “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Titus 3:3-7 then gives the reason for gentleness: the believers were once as difficult as anyone, and God was kind to them.

Paul writes, “For at one time we too were foolish, disobedient, misled, and enslaved to all sorts of desires and pleasures--living in malice and envy, being hated and hating one another” (Titus 3:3). He includes himself with the word “we.” The picture is of people who were led, as slaves are led, by their desires. The next verse turns on the words “But when the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared” (3:4). Paul gives similar lists in Ephesians 2:1-3 and 1 Corinthians 6:9-11, where he says, “And that is what some of you were.” The purpose is humility toward others, and 3:2 makes the link: believers are to show “full consideration to everyone” because they remember what they were.

e.n: The washing of new birth and renewal
t: Paul writes, “He saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done, but according to His mercy, through the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. This is the Spirit He poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by His grace, we would become heirs with the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:5-7). The sentence names the Father, the Son and the Spirit, and gathers many words for salvation: mercy, washing, new birth, renewal, pouring out, justification, heirs and hope. The word for “washing” (loutron) is the one used of the church’s cleansing in Ephesians 5:26, and “new birth” (palingenesia) is used only once more in the New Testament, in Matthew 19:28 for the renewal of all things. Readers disagree about whether the “washing” refers to baptism, to an inner cleansing by the Spirit, or to both together. Either way, the verse says the washing comes from God’s mercy and not from human deeds, and that the Spirit is the one who renews.

e.n: Saved not by works, and devoted to good works
t: Titus holds two statements side by side. God “saved us, not by the righteous deeds we had done” (3:5). Yet Christ gave Himself to purify “a people for His own possession, zealous for good deeds” (2:14), and Titus is to urge believers “to devote themselves to good deeds” (3:8) and to learn “to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others, so that they will not be unfruitful” (3:14). The phrase “good works” or “good deeds” appears in every chapter (1:16; 2:7, 14; 3:1, 8, 14). Ephesians 2:8-10 puts the same order: saved by grace through faith, “created in Christ Jesus to do good works.” The order matters. Good deeds are the result of the new birth and not its price. The “pressing needs of others” show what the works are for.

Paul asks Titus, “Do your best to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos, so that they will have everything they need” (Titus 3:13). The Greek verb (propempo) means to send someone on a journey with supplies and company. It was an expected duty toward traveling teachers and workers (Romans 15:24; 1 Corinthians 16:6, 11; 3 John 5-8). In 3 John 6 the elder says, “You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God.” The next verse of Titus applies the same principle to the whole church: “our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works in order to meet the pressing needs of others” (3:14). The letter ends with ordinary hospitality and travel plans, and treats them as part of the church’s good works.

Paul opens with “the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, promised before time began. In His own time He has made His word evident in the proclamation entrusted to me by the command of God our Savior” (Titus 1:2-3). The Greek word for “cannot lie” (apseudes) occurs only here in the New Testament. Numbers 23:19 says, “God is not a man, that He should lie,” and Hebrews 6:17-18 says it is “impossible for God to lie.” The opening sets God’s truthfulness over a letter that soon meets “liars” (1:12) and “deception” (1:10). Paul does not draw the contrast himself. The promise was made “before time began” and God kept it “in His own time,” through the preaching entrusted to Paul. The same thought is in 2 Timothy 1:9.

e.n: Paul in chains: the setting of 2 Timothy
t: In 2 Timothy Paul calls himself the Lord’s “prisoner” (1:8), says he is “chained like a criminal” (2:9) and speaks of “the time of my departure” (4:6). Acts ends with Paul under guard in his own rented house in Rome, free to receive visitors and to preach (Acts 28:30-31). The chains here are heavier: a friend had to search for him, and at his first defense “no one stood with me” (4:16). Readers who accept Paul as the author usually place the letter in a second Roman imprisonment after the end of Acts, about AD 64-67. Early writers such as the author of 1 Clement (chapter 5) and Eusebius say Paul was put to death at Rome under Nero. Others think a follower of Paul wrote the letter after his death as a last testament in his name. The letter itself does not say how things ended.

e.n: Fan into flame the gift of God
t: Paul writes, “I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands. For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:6-7). The Greek verb (anazopyreo) means to stir a fire back to life, as one blows on glowing coals. The letter does not say what the gift was; 1 Timothy 4:14 speaks of a gift given “through the prophecy spoken over you at the laying on of the hands of the elders.” Paul’s reminder follows his memory of Timothy’s tears and sincere faith (1:4-5), and may point to a young man who needed encouragement, as 1 Corinthians 16:10-11 also hints.

Paul asks Timothy, “do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, or of me, His prisoner. Instead, join me in suffering for the gospel by the power of God” (2 Timothy 1:8). To be linked to a man in chains could cost a person his name and his safety, and Paul admits that all in Asia had left him (1:15). He says of himself, “I am not ashamed; for I know whom I have believed” (1:12), and he praises Onesiphorus, who “was unashamed of my chains” (1:16). The same word echoes Romans 1:16, “I am not ashamed of the gospel,” and Jesus’ warning in Mark 8:38.

Paul writes, “the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). The line has four links: Paul, Timothy, “faithful men,” and “others as well.” It follows his call to “hold on to the pattern of sound teaching” and to “guard the treasure entrusted to you” (1:13-14). The letter does not say who the “faithful men” were or how they were chosen. Titus 1:5 shows Paul asking Titus to appoint elders in Crete, and 1 Timothy 3:1-7 lists what to look for in an overseer.
In Titus the same work is given to Titus on Crete: “appoint elders in every town” (1:5) who “hold firmly to the faithful word as it was taught” (1:9).

Paul gives Timothy three pictures of work that takes effort and pays later. A soldier “refrains from entangling himself in civilian affairs, in order to please the one who enlisted him.” A competitor “does not receive the crown unless he competes according to the rules.” And “the hardworking farmer should be the first to partake of the crops” (2 Timothy 2:4-6). The three jobs were everyday in the Roman world. Paul uses the soldier and the athlete in other letters (1 Corinthians 9:7, 24-27; Philippians 2:25). He adds, “Consider what I am saying, for the Lord will give you insight into all things” (2:7), which suggests that Timothy is to think about how each picture applies to him.

e.n: The word of God is not chained
t: Paul tells Timothy to “Remember Jesus Christ, raised from the dead, descended from David, as proclaimed by my gospel, for which I suffer to the extent of being chained like a criminal. But the word of God cannot be chained!” (2 Timothy 2:8-9). He adds, “I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus” (2:10). Earlier, from another imprisonment, he had written that his chains had “actually served to advance the gospel” (Philippians 1:12-14). The point is that the message can move even when its messenger cannot.

e.n: If we are faithless, He remains faithful
t: Paul gives a “trustworthy saying” in four lines: “If we died with Him, we will also live with Him; if we endure, we will also reign with Him; if we deny Him, He will also deny us; if we are faithless, He remains faithful, for He cannot deny Himself” (2 Timothy 2:11-13). Most scholars think this is a hymn or creed that Paul quotes. The first lines echo Romans 6:8 and 8:17, and the third echoes Jesus’ words in Matthew 10:33. The last line is read in different ways: some take it as a promise that God stays faithful to his own people, and others as a statement that God stays true to himself, including in judgment. The letter does not explain further.

Paul writes, “Make every effort to present yourself approved to God, an unashamed workman who accurately handles the word of truth” (2 Timothy 2:15). The Greek word for “accurately handles” (orthotomeo) literally means to cut straight. It is used in the Greek of Proverbs 3:6 for making paths straight, and the picture may be of a road builder, a stonecutter or a farmer plowing a straight furrow; the sense is debated. The surrounding verses set the workman against those who are drawn to “quarreling over words” and whose talk “will spread like gangrene” (2:14-17).

e.n: A large house, vessels for honor
t: Paul writes, “A large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay. Some indeed are for honorable use, but others are for common use. So if anyone cleanses himself of what is unfit, he will be a vessel for honor: sanctified, useful to the Master, and prepared for every good work” (2 Timothy 2:20-21). The “large house” is most likely the church, which holds both honorable and common members. Paul uses a similar picture of vessels in Romans 9:21-23 and 2 Corinthians 4:7. The call that follows is to “Flee from youthful passions and pursue righteousness, faith, love, and peace” (2:22).

e.n: Terrible times in the last days
t: Paul writes, “In the last days terrible times will come. For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy” (2 Timothy 3:1-2). The list has about eighteen terms and ends with people “having a form of godliness but denying its power” (3:5). The New Testament often calls the whole time since Christ’s first coming “the last days” (Acts 2:17; Hebrews 1:2), and Paul tells Timothy to “turn away” from such people now. Peter and Jude warn of mockers in similar words (2 Peter 3:3; Jude 17-19).

Paul writes, “Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth” (2 Timothy 3:8). The Old Testament does not name the magicians who copied Moses’ signs before Pharaoh (Exodus 7:11-12), but Jewish tradition did. The Damascus Document from Qumran names Jannes and his brother, a Targum of Exodus names Jannes and Jambres as Pharaoh’s chief magicians, and a damaged 3rd-century papyrus preserves part of a book about them. Paul assumes his readers know the names. He adds that “their folly will be plain to everyone” (3:9).

Paul writes, “From infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures, which are able to make you wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. All Scripture is God-breathed and is useful for instruction, for conviction, for correction, and for training in righteousness, so that the man of God may be complete, fully equipped for every good work” (2 Timothy 3:15-17). The Greek word theopneustos, “God-breathed,” is found only here in the New Testament. The “Holy Scriptures” Timothy knew from childhood were the Old Testament. Peter also speaks of men “carried along by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter 1:21). Christians differ on what “God-breathed” implies for how Scripture is to be read, and the verse can also be translated “Every God-breathed Scripture is useful.”
2 Peter 1:21 says that “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit,” and 3:16 puts Paul’s letters beside “the rest of the Scriptures.”

Paul gives Timothy a solemn charge “in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead”: “Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; reprove, rebuke, and encourage with every form of patient instruction” (2 Timothy 4:1-2). He tells him to “be sober in all things, endure hardship, do the work of an evangelist, fulfill your ministry” (4:5). The word “evangelist” occurs only three times in the New Testament (Acts 21:8; Ephesians 4:11; 2 Timothy 4:5). Paul had said to the Ephesian elders that he had not shrunk from declaring “the whole will of God” (Acts 20:27).

Paul writes, “the time will come when men will not tolerate sound doctrine, but with itching ears they will gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires. So they will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths” (2 Timothy 4:3-4). The Greek verb for “itching” (knetho) means to tickle or scratch, and “gather around” (episoreuo) means to heap up. The picture is of people who pile up teachers who tell them what they like to hear. The letter does not name a group, and Paul says similar things are already happening (3:5-9).

e.n: I have fought the good fight
t: Paul writes, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the race, I have kept the faith. From now on there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day—and not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing” (2 Timothy 4:7-8). He had told Timothy to “Fight the good fight of the faith” (1 Timothy 6:12). The three lines use the pictures of the arena, the racecourse and a trust kept. At Miletus he had said he wanted to “finish my course” (Acts 20:24). The crown is given by the Lord, and not only to Paul.

Paul’s last letter names the friends who left and the few who stayed. “Everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me” (2 Timothy 1:15). “Demas, in his love of this world, has deserted me” (4:10). Crescens and Titus have gone elsewhere (4:10), and Tychicus has been sent to Ephesus (4:12). “Only Luke is with me” (4:11). At the first defense “everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them” (4:16). Mark, once the cause of a quarrel (Acts 15:37-39), is now “useful to me in the ministry” (4:11). The same Greek verb, egkataleipo, “to leave behind,” is used in Mark 15:34 for Jesus’ cry on the cross.

Paul writes, “At my first defense, no one stood with me, but everyone deserted me. May it not be charged against them. But the Lord stood by me and strengthened me, so that through me the message would be fully proclaimed, and all the Gentiles would hear it. So I was delivered from the mouth of the lion” (2 Timothy 4:16-17). A Roman defendant would normally have a patron or advocate to stand beside him. “The mouth of the lion” echoes Psalm 22:21 and Daniel 6:20-22, and may mean danger or death, or perhaps Nero himself; the letter does not say. Paul still expects to die (4:6), and trusts that the Lord “will rescue me from every evil action and bring me safely into His heavenly kingdom” (4:18).

e.n: 2 Peter: who wrote it and to whom
t: The letter opens, “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ, To those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours” (2 Peter 1:1). The writer says he was with Jesus “on the holy mountain” (1:18), that the Lord “has made clear to me” that his death is near (1:14), and that “this is now my second letter to you” (3:1). He calls Paul “our beloved brother” (3:15). The readers are not named and no place is given. If the first letter of 3:1 is 1 Peter, the readers are the same churches of Asia Minor, but the letter does not say so.

Whether Peter wrote it is one of the most debated questions in New Testament study. Those who accept it point to the personal claims of 1:14-18 and 3:1, and say the different Greek could come from another secretary (compare 1 Peter 5:12). Many scholars think someone wrote it in Peter’s name after his death, as a farewell testament, some say between about AD 80 and 120. They point to the Greek, which is very unlike 1 Peter, to the way chapter 2 follows Jude, to its mention of Paul’s letters as already a collection (3:15-16), and to its slow acceptance: Origen, Eusebius and Jerome all record that some doubted it. Athanasius lists it among the books of the New Testament in AD 367. Neither side can prove its case, so this app says “the writer” where the question matters and “Peter” where the letter does.
f: If Peter, the mid-60s; if not, perhaps about AD 80-120

t: “His divine power has given us everything we need for life and godliness through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and excellence. Through these He has given us His precious and magnificent promises, so that through them you may become partakers of the divine nature, now that you have escaped the corruption in the world caused by evil desires” (1:3-4). The word for “partakers” (koinonoi) means those who share in something, and “divine nature” (theia physis) is a phrase from Greek philosophy that the Bible does not use anywhere else.

The verse is read in more than one way. The Eastern church fathers, among them Athanasius, took it to mean that believers are brought into a share of God’s life, and the Orthodox idea of deification (theosis) leans on it. Protestant readers usually take it to mean sharing in God’s moral character and eternal life through the promises, with the stress on “escaped the corruption.” Nearly all agree that it does not mean that people become God. The next verses show what sharing looks like: the readers are to “make every effort” to grow in goodness (1:5-7).

e.n: Add to your faith: the chain of qualities
t: “For this very reason, make every effort to add to your faith virtue; and to virtue, knowledge; and to knowledge, self-control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, brotherly kindness; and to brotherly kindness, love” (1:5-7). The eight qualities are faith, virtue (or excellence), knowledge, self-control, perseverance, godliness, brotherly kindness and love. Each is joined to the next, and the chain ends in love. Lists of virtues were common in Greek moral writing, and the New Testament has others, such as the fruit of the Spirit in Galatians 5:22-23 and Paul’s chain from suffering to hope in Romans 5:3-5.

Peter says that if you have these qualities “and continue to grow in them, they will keep you from being ineffective and unproductive in your knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:8). Whoever lacks them is “nearsighted to the point of blindness” (1:9). He then tells the readers to “strive to make your calling and election sure” (1:10), and promises “a lavish reception into the eternal kingdom of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:11).

The writer says, “I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of my body, because I know that this tent will soon be laid aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me. And I will make every effort to ensure that after my departure, you will be able to recall these things at all times” (1:13-15). The tent is a picture of the body as a temporary home, the picture Paul uses in 2 Corinthians 5:1. The word for “departure” is exodos, the same word Luke uses in 9:31 for the “exodus” that Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about on the mountain, and the letter goes on at once to tell of that mountain.

John 21:18-19 records that Jesus told Peter he would be led where he did not want to go, and John says this showed by what kind of death Peter would glorify God. Early Christian writers say Peter died at Rome under Nero (1 Clement 5 mentions his many hardships and his place of glory). If the letter is by Peter, it is his farewell. If it was written in his name later, it is a farewell testament in the way of such writings, and the scene is part of the form.

“For we did not follow cleverly devised fables when we made known to you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but we were eyewitnesses of His majesty” (1:16). The writer sets what he tells against “fables” (muthoi, myths), stories made up to sound clever. He says he and others saw the majesty of Jesus: “He received honor and glory from God the Father when the voice came to Him from the Majestic Glory, saying, ‘This is My beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.’ And we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain” (1:17-18).

The Gospels tell of the Transfiguration and name Peter, James and John as the three who went up (Matthew 17:1-8; Mark 9:2-8; Luke 9:28-36). The letter does not name the mountain, and it does not name the event, though nearly all readers think this is the Transfiguration. The claim of being an eyewitness is one reason some accept Peter as the author; others think a later writer put the claim in Peter’s mouth. Either way, the letter rests its case on what the apostles saw and heard, and then adds the written word of the prophets (1:19-21).

e.n: No prophecy by the will of man
t: “We also have the word of the prophets as confirmed beyond doubt. And you will do well to pay attention to it, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts. Above all, you must understand that no prophecy of Scripture comes from one’s own interpretation. For no such prophecy was ever brought forth by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit” (1:19-21).

Verse 20 can be read two ways. Many take “one’s own interpretation” to mean that the prophet did not make up the message, which fits verse 21, where the reason given is that no prophecy came “by the will of man.” Others take it to mean that no reader may interpret Scripture on his own, apart from the church or the Spirit; the chapters that follow, about those who distort the Scriptures (3:16), are sometimes used for this. The verb for “carried along” (pheromenoi) is the one Acts 27 uses of a ship driven by the wind; it does not say how the Spirit worked on the human writers. See also 2 Timothy 3:16 and the entry on all Scripture being God-breathed.

Most of 2 Peter 2 runs alongside Jude 4-18. Both speak of ungodly teachers who slipped in, of angels who sinned and were held in darkness (2 Peter 2:4; Jude 6), of Sodom and Gomorrah as an example (2 Peter 2:6; Jude 7), of people who slander glorious beings (2 Peter 2:10-11; Jude 8-10), of the way of Balaam (2 Peter 2:15; Jude 11), of waterless springs and mists or clouds driven by wind (2 Peter 2:17; Jude 12), and of scoffers in the last days (2 Peter 3:3; Jude 18).

Most scholars think 2 Peter used Jude: Jude is shorter, and 2 Peter smooths over its use of Jewish books outside the Old Testament, such as the quotation from Enoch (Jude 14-15) and the dispute over the body of Moses (Jude 9), which 2 Peter leaves out. Some think Jude used 2 Peter, and a few think both used an older source. 2 Peter also adds things Jude lacks, the stories of Noah and Lot. Jude says the false teachers have slipped in; 2 Peter speaks of them as a future danger (“there will be false teachers among you,” 2:1) and then, in the verses that follow, as already present.

Read from Jude’s side, the overlap looks like this: Jude 4 (intruders), 6 (angels), 7 (Sodom), 8-10 (slander of glorious beings), 11 (Balaam), 12-13 (waterless clouds and darkness reserved), 16 (boastful words) and 17-18 (scoffers) all have partners in 2 Peter 2:1-3:3, in the same order. Jude alone has the wilderness generation, Michael and the body of Moses, Cain and Korah, and the quotation from Enoch.

e.n: A day like a thousand years
t: The scoffers ask, “Where is the promise of His coming?” and say, “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation” (3:4). Peter answers, “do not let this one thing escape your notice: With the Lord a day is like a thousand years, and a thousand years are like a day. The Lord is not slow in keeping His promise as some understand slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish but everyone to come to repentance” (3:8-9). He ends the point with “our Lord’s patience brings salvation” (3:15).

The saying echoes Psalm 90:4, where a thousand years are like yesterday in God’s sight. It is an answer to the delay, not a timetable. Some early writers, Irenaeus among them, took “a day is like a thousand years” as a way of counting the ages of the world, but the verse says only that God does not measure time as people do and that the delay has a purpose: repentance. The Day will still come “like a thief” (3:10).
Revelation 20:1-6 is the only passage that speaks of a reign of a thousand years, and readers who take that number as a symbol often point to this verse.

e.n: The heavens and earth reserved for fire
t: Peter says the world of Noah’s time “perished in the flood” (3:6), and that “by that same word, the present heavens and earth are reserved for fire, being kept for the day of judgment and destruction of ungodly men” (3:7). Then, “the Day of the Lord will come like a thief. The heavens will disappear with a roar, the elements will be destroyed by fire, and the earth and its works will be laid bare” (3:10). He adds, “But in keeping with God’s promise, we are looking forward to a new heaven and a new earth, where righteousness dwells” (3:13), the promise of Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22.

The picture is hard to read. The oldest manuscripts have the earth’s works “will be found” (which the BSB renders “laid bare”), while later manuscripts have “will be burned up.” The “elements” (stoicheia) may be the basic parts of the world or the heavenly bodies. Some readers take the fire to be a cleansing that renews the creation, others a replacement of it; the letter does not settle which. Its stress falls on the question that follows: “what kind of people ought you to be? You ought to conduct yourselves in holiness and godliness” (3:11). Compare Hebrews 12:26-29 and Revelation 21:1.

e.n: Paul and “the rest of the Scriptures”
t: The letter ends by pointing to Paul: “our Lord’s patience brings salvation, just as our beloved brother Paul also wrote you with the wisdom God gave him. He writes this way in all his letters, speaking in them about such matters. Some parts of his letters are hard to understand, which ignorant and unstable people distort, as they do the rest of the Scriptures, to their own destruction” (3:15-16).

Three things stand out. Peter calls Paul “our beloved brother,” though Galatians 2:11-14 tells of a sharp disagreement between them at Antioch. He admits that Paul is hard to follow at times. And he puts Paul’s letters beside “the rest of the Scriptures,” which suggests that by the time of the letter Paul’s writings were gathered and read in church as Scripture. Those who put 2 Peter in the 60s say several letters were already in circulation; those who put it later say the whole collection was known. The papyrus P46 shows Paul’s letters bound together by about AD 200.

e.n: Escaped the corruption, then entangled again
t: “If indeed they have escaped the corruption of the world through the knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, only to be entangled and overcome by it again, their final condition is worse than it was at first. It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than to have known it and then to turn away from the holy commandment passed on to them” (2:20-21). The false teachers promise “freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity. For a man is a slave to whatever has mastered him” (2:19).

Readers differ on what this says about those who fall away. Some take it that real believers can turn back and be lost, as the warnings in Hebrews 6 and 10 are read. Others hold that such people only seemed to be believers, since the letter speaks of “knowing” the way and not of being born again. The letter itself gives the two proverbs of 2:22 and goes on to its call to “make every effort” (1:10; 3:14).

e.n: 1 John: who wrote it and to whom
t: The letter has no greeting, no name and no closing. It begins with the Word of life, which “we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands” (1:1), and ends with “Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (5:21). The writer says why he writes: “so that our joy may be complete” (1:4), “so that you will not sin” (2:1), and “so that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). He speaks to his readers as “little children” and “beloved,” and he is dealing with teachers who “went out from us” (2:19).

From the second century the church ascribed the letter to John the apostle. Irenaeus, who grew up in Asia Minor and knew Polycarp, says John lived at Ephesus until the time of Trajan, and Eusebius reports that Papias used 1 John. The Second and Third Letters name “the elder” as their writer, and a few scholars think the Ephesian John was this Elder and not the apostle; most who accept the tradition place the letter late in the first century, between about AD 85 and 100. The readers are not named, but Ephesus and the churches of the province of Asia are the usual guess. The letter does not follow a plain outline. It circles three themes again and again: walking in the light, keeping the commandments and loving the brothers, and believing that Jesus is the Christ come in the flesh.

The Second Letter is a short companion of this one. It uses the same words (commandment, truth, abide, antichrist, “from the beginning”) and the same test of the coming in the flesh, but it is a real letter with a sender, receivers and a greeting. See “2 John: who wrote it and to whom.”

The Third Letter is a private note from the same circle. It has the same “walking in the truth” and the same test of conduct (“The one who does good is of God”), but it deals with hospitality and leadership, not with false teaching.
f: Not named; early tradition says John

e.n: The Gospel of John and the letters of John
t: The first letter of John and the Gospel of John share so many words and turns of phrase that nearly all readers think they come from the same circle, and many from the same hand. Both speak of what was “from the beginning,” of the Word and of life, of light and darkness, of truth, of the world, of abiding, of being born of God, and of a commandment to love one another. Both call Jesus the “only” Son (1 John 4:9; John 1:14, 18; 3:16) and speak of “eternal life.” The Gospel was written “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in His name” (John 20:31), and the letter says “I have written these things to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13).

The two also differ. The letter has no Old Testament quotation, tells no story of Jesus, and names Cain as its one Old Testament figure; it uses the word “antichrist,” which the Gospel never does; and it speaks of Jesus as the “advocate” (2:1) where the Gospel gives that word to the Spirit. Which came first is debated. Some think the letter was written first and the Gospel grew out of the same preaching; others think the letter was written to people who knew the Gospel and were reading it in the wrong way, perhaps the teachers of 2:19. Either way, the letter reads best beside the Gospel.

2 John and 3 John are two short notes from the same circle, with the same title “the elder,” the same walking “in the truth,” and the same commandment “from the beginning” as in 1 John and the Gospel. 2 John 5 is close to 1 John 2:7, and 2 John 7 to 1 John 4:2-3.

3 John shares the Gospel’s words too: testimony that “is true” (12; John 21:24), the greeting of peace (14; John 20:19), believers as friends (14; John 15:15), and each one known by name (14; John 10:3).

e.n: The Word of life: heard, seen and touched
t: The letter opens with a long sentence that waits until its last words to name its subject: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands—this is the Word of life” (1:1). Four verbs build up: heard, seen, gazed upon, touched. The last is the strongest; the Greek verb (psēlaphaō) is used of feeling for something in the dark and, in Luke 24:39, of the risen Jesus telling his disciples to touch him and see that he is not a spirit. The writer then says that the life “was revealed; we have seen it and testified to it” (1:2), and that he writes so that readers “may have fellowship with us” and with “the Father and with His Son, Jesus Christ” (1:3).

The sentence is the first answer to those who denied that Jesus came in the flesh. The Word “from the beginning” (compare John 1:1) can be heard, seen and handled, and the eyewitnesses are the ones who can say so. “Word of life” can mean Christ himself or the message about him; the sentence allows both, and John 1:14 says the Word became flesh.

The message of the letter is stated plainly: “This is the message we have heard from Him and announce to you: God is light, and in Him there is no darkness at all” (1:5). Light in the Bible stands for God’s holiness, truth and presence: the psalmist says the LORD is his light and salvation, and Isaiah promises that the LORD will be an everlasting light. In the Gospel, Jesus says, “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12), and the letter turns the idea toward life: “If we say we have fellowship with Him yet walk in the darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth” (1:6).

The next verses set three false claims, each opened with “If we say,” against their answers. To claim fellowship while walking in darkness is a lie (1:6). To say “we have no sin” is to deceive ourselves (1:8). To say “we have not sinned” is to make God “out to be a liar” (1:10). The answer to the first is to “walk in the light as He is in the light,” which brings fellowship with one another and the cleansing “blood of Jesus His Son” (1:7). Light and darkness set against each other were also at home in the Dead Sea Scrolls, where the Community Rule speaks of sons of light and sons of darkness; the letter uses the same pair for a different purpose.

“If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1:9). To “confess” (homologeō) is to say the same thing, to agree with God about what we have done. The promise rests on God’s own character: He is “faithful,” because He keeps His word, and “just,” because the debt has been paid by “the blood of Jesus His Son” (1:7). The psalmist gave the same pattern long before: when he stopped hiding his sin and acknowledged it, the LORD forgave (Psalm 32:5), and on the Day of Atonement the priest confessed the people’s sins over the goat (Leviticus 16:21).

The verses on each side (1:8 and 1:10) are aimed at the claim to be without sin. Read together with 2:1, “I am writing these things to you so that you will not sin. But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate,” the picture is of a believer who aims at not sinning, who admits it when he fails, and who is forgiven by an advocate and not by his own efforts. The verb for “confess” is the same one used of confessing the Son (2:23; 4:2-3, 15), so honesty about one’s sin and honesty about Christ go together in the letter.

e.n: An advocate and the atoning sacrifice
t: “But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One. He Himself is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world” (2:1-2). The Greek word for advocate, paraklētos, means one called alongside, as a friend or a lawyer. The Gospel of John uses it of the Holy Spirit, who is “another Helper” (John 14:16), The word occurs only five times in the New Testament, four in the Gospel of John and here. In 1 John it is Jesus who pleads before the Father, and Hebrews 7:25 and Romans 8:34 say the same of his intercession.

The other word, hilasmos (“atoning sacrifice,” the KJV’s “propitiation”), occurs only here and in 4:10. It belongs to the language of the Day of Atonement, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for forgiveness and atonement (Psalm 130:4). Readers differ on its force: some say it means turning aside God’s anger, others that it means removing sin, and many hold that both are in it. John adds that the sacrifice is “not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world.” Some take “the whole world” to mean people of every nation and not only the Jewish believers; others take it more widely. Either way, the rest of the letter says that God “sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice” out of love (4:10).

The verb “to abide” (menō) occurs 24 times in the letter, and the Gospel of John uses it 40. The BSB renders it “abide” in some verses and “remain” in others. The letter uses it of the believer in Christ (“Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked,” 2:6), of what the readers heard from the beginning (“let what you have heard from the beginning remain in you,” 2:24), of God’s word and anointing (2:14, 27), and of love (“whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him,” 4:16).

Abiding is also the test that separates true from false. Those who left “would have remained with us” if they had belonged to us (2:19), and “No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning” (3:6). The sign that it is real is the Spirit: “by this we know that He remains in us: by the Spirit He has given us” (3:24). The picture is that of John 15, where Jesus speaks of the vine and the branches, and tells the disciples to abide in him and in his love.
In 2 John, the truth “abides in us” (2), and whoever is not “remaining in the teaching of Christ” does not have God, while “Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son” (9).

e.n: An old commandment that is new
t: “Beloved, I am not writing to you a new commandment, but an old one, which you have had from the beginning. This commandment is the message you have heard. Then again, I am also writing to you a new commandment, which is true in Him and also in you. For the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining” (2:7-8). The commandment is old because the readers have had it since they first heard the gospel, and because the law already said to love one’s neighbor (Leviticus 19:18). It is new because Jesus gave it a new measure on the night before his death, that his disciples love one another as he had loved them (John 13:34), and because the new age has begun.

The test of whether someone is in the light is how he treats his brother: “Whoever loves his brother remains in the light” and “whoever hates his brother is in the darkness and walks in the darkness” (2:10-11). “Brother” here and in the rest of the letter most naturally means a fellow believer; Jesus’ saying about loving enemies and the Good Samaritan show that love goes beyond that, though the letter itself speaks of the family of faith. The command comes back in 3:11, 3:23 and 4:21, and 2 John 5 repeats it.
In 2 John, the commandment is again “one we have had from the beginning” (5) and “the very commandment you have heard from the beginning, that you must walk in love” (6).

“Do not love the world or anything in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world—the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life—is not from the Father but from the world. The world is passing away, along with its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever” (2:15-17). The word “world” (kosmos) has more than one sense in John’s writings. It can be the created order or the human race that God loves and sent His Son to save (John 3:16; 1 John 4:9, 14), and it can be the order of life that stands against God. Here it is the second: the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life (alazoneia, boasting about what one has).

The three desires have been compared to the first temptation in Eden (the fruit was good for food, a delight to the eyes and desirable for wisdom, Genesis 3:6) and to the temptations of Jesus in the wilderness, but the letter does not make the link itself. In the city of Ephesus, with its temple of Artemis, its imperial shrines and its wealth, the readers lived close to such a world. The verb for “passing away” is present tense, and its opposite is “whoever does the will of God remains forever.”

e.n: The last hour and many antichrists
t: “Children, it is the last hour; and just as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared. This is how we know it is the last hour” (2:18). The word antichristos occurs in the New Testament only in 1 John (2:18, 22; 4:3) and 2 John 7, and the letter does not describe a single ruler: the antichrist is the one “who denies the Father and the Son” (2:22), and the spirit of the antichrist is “already in the world at this time” (4:3). The readers had “heard” that he was coming, a teaching they had from the church, likely drawing on Jesus’ warning of false christs (Matthew 24:24) and on Paul’s “man of lawlessness” (2 Thessalonians 2:3-4).

“The last hour” does not set a date. The writer says the last period of history has begun, since the Son has come, and sees it confirmed by the departure of the teachers. Later Christian writers joined the antichrist to the beast of Revelation 13 and the man of lawlessness, but Revelation does not use the word. In 1 John the test is the confession of Jesus as the Christ, the Son (2:22-23; 4:2-3).

e.n: The anointing from the Holy One
t: “You, however, have an anointing from the Holy One, and all of you know the truth” (2:20). Later the writer says, “the anointing you received from Him remains in you, and you do not need anyone to teach you. But just as His true and genuine anointing teaches you about all things, so remain in Him as you have been taught” (2:27). The Greek word chrisma, “anointing,” occurs in the New Testament only here, and it is built on the same root as Christos, “the Anointed One.” Readers differ on what is meant. Most take the anointing to be the Holy Spirit, who was given to every believer; some take it to be the message they first heard, which “remains in you” (2:24).

The verse does not mean that the readers have no use for teaching. The letter itself is teaching, and the writer says “as you have been taught.” The point is that the readers have what they need to recognize the lie, because they have the truth already. The promise recalls Jeremiah 31:34, that all will know the LORD, and Jesus’ saying that the Spirit “will teach you all things” (John 14:26).

e.n: Children of God, born of God
t: “Behold what manner of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God. And that is what we are!” (3:1). The letter returns again and again to being “born of God”: those who practice righteousness have been “born of Him” (2:29), the one born of God “refuses to practice sin” (3:9), whoever loves has “been born of God and knows God” (4:7), whoever believes that Jesus is the Christ “has been born of God” (5:1), and everyone born of God “overcomes the world” (5:4). The verb (gennaō) is the one John 3 uses when Jesus tells Nicodemus that one must be born again, and John 1:12-13 says those who received Him were given “the right to become children of God.”

The writer calls his readers “children” (teknia, “little children,” and tekna) and holds the word “Son” (huios) for Jesus alone. The present gift is real, and the future is open: “what we will be has not yet been revealed. We know that when Christ appears, we will be like Him, for we will see Him as He is” (3:2). “Everyone who has this hope in Him purifies himself, just as Christ is pure” (3:3).

The letter seems to say two things about sin. On one hand: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1:8), and “if anyone does sin, we have an advocate” (2:1). On the other: “No one who remains in Him keeps on sinning” (3:6), “Anyone born of God refuses to practice sin, because God’s seed abides in him; he cannot go on sinning, because he has been born of God” (3:9), and “anyone born of God does not keep on sinning” (5:18). The BSB brings out that most of the verbs in the second group are in the present tense, which describes an ongoing practice. In the first group the verbs refer to individual acts.

Readers explain the difference in several ways: the second group speaks of habitual sin, or of what a believer is in his new birth, or of the ideal, or of the opponents’ claim that they were above sin and did not need forgiveness, which the writer turns back on them. All agree that the letter gives no license to sin. It defines the matter: “Everyone who practices sin practices lawlessness as well. Indeed, sin is lawlessness” (3:4), and Christ “appeared to take away sins, and in Him there is no sin” (3:5).

“By this we know what love is: Jesus laid down His life for us, and we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers. If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him? Little children, let us love not in word and speech, but in action and truth” (3:16-18). The standard is the cross, and the first step is small: sharing what one has. James puts the same point in terms of faith without works (James 2:15-16).

The contrast with Cain in 3:12 sets the choice out in full: he murdered his brother, while the one who has life gives up his own. “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer” (3:15), because hatred is the root of killing, as Jesus taught in the Sermon on the Mount. Christian care for the needy was noticed by outsiders in the next century; a satirist and a defender both describe the churches helping those in need (see the entry on early Christian care for the needy).

e.n: God is greater than our hearts
t: “And by this we will know that we belong to the truth, and will assure our hearts in His presence: Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things. Beloved, if our hearts do not condemn us, we have confidence before God, and we will receive from Him whatever we ask, because we keep His commandments and do what is pleasing in His sight” (3:19-22). The verse is read in two ways. Some take “God is greater” as comfort: when a believer’s conscience accuses him, God, who knows all, is more merciful than his heart. Others take it as a warning that God sees more than the heart does. The comfort reading fits the context, which is about reassuring the heart.

The word for confidence, parrēsia, means freedom to speak. It describes the believer’s standing before God now in prayer (3:21; 5:14) and at Christ’s coming (2:28; 4:17). The condition in verse 22 does not mean prayer is a reward for good conduct. The writer says an obedient life and trust in Christ’s name go together (3:23).

“Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world. By this you will know the Spirit of God: Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God, and every spirit that does not confess Jesus is not from God” (4:1-3). “Spirits” stands for those who claim to speak by the Spirit. The Old Testament set tests for prophets: Deuteronomy 13:1-5 says a prophet whose sign comes true but who leads people to other gods is to be refused, and Deuteronomy 18:20-22 says a prophet whose word does not come true has not spoken for the LORD. Paul gave a similar test in 1 Corinthians 12:3: “no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except by the Holy Spirit.”

John’s test is about Christ, and then about hearing: “We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. That is how we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception” (4:6). The early church manual called the Didache gave rules for testing traveling prophets by their teaching and by how they lived, as John does by confession and by love.
In 2 John, the test of 1 John 4 is turned into a rule for the door: look at what a visitor teaches about Jesus Christ before you open your home.

e.n: Jesus Christ has come in the flesh
t: The confession that the letter requires is “Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (4:2), and the opposite is “the spirit of the antichrist” (4:3). It matches the earlier test: “Who is the liar, if it is not the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ?” (2:22), and the Son is the one who “came by water and blood” (5:6). The verb “has come” is in the perfect tense: he came, and the result stands. 2 John 7 speaks of deceivers who have gone out into the world and refuse to confess Jesus Christ as coming in the flesh.

The letter does not say what the teachers claimed. Irenaeus says that Cerinthus, a teacher in Asia, held that “the Christ” came on Jesus at his baptism and left before the cross. Ignatius, writing to churches of Asia about AD 110, argues against those who said that Christ only seemed to suffer, a view later called docetism (from the Greek dokeō, “to seem”). Polycarp wrote that everyone who does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is an antichrist. Scholars debate how closely any of these matches the opponents of 1 John.

In 2 John, the same test is put as the refusal “to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh” (7). The Greek here is a present participle, erchomenon, “coming,” where 1 John 4:2 uses a perfect, “has come.” Scholars differ over whether the change matters; most hold that both mean the same confession, that Jesus Christ is the one who came as a man.

“Beloved, let us love one another, because love comes from God. Everyone who loves has been born of God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God, because God is love” (4:7-8). The sentence “God is love” is repeated in 4:16. It is a statement about who God is, not a definition of love, and the letter says at once where love is seen: “This is how God’s love was revealed among us: God sent His one and only Son into the world, so that we might live through Him. And love consists in this: not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (4:9-10).

The word is agapē, which occurs 18 times in 1 John. It is used of God’s love for us, of the love in us, and of our love for one another; it ends in a loop: “We love because He first loved us” (4:19). “No one has ever seen God; but if we love one another, God remains in us, and His love is perfected in us” (4:12), which takes the line of John 1:18 and says that although God is unseen, His love can be seen in the community. Paul had said the same of the cross: God shows His love for us in that Christ died for us while we were still sinners (Romans 5:8).

“In this way, love has been perfected among us, so that we may have confidence on the day of judgment; for in this world we are just like Him. There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, because fear involves punishment. The one who fears has not been perfected in love” (4:17-18). The verb “perfected” (teleioō) means brought to its goal, completed. Love is “perfected” by being lived out (2:5; 4:12), and when it is, it gives “confidence” (parrēsia) at the judgment. The word for punishment (kolasis) is used in Matthew 25:46 for the punishment of the unrighteous, but here it describes the fear that has no place in love.

The fear in question is dread of God’s judgment, not reverence. The letter says that the believer’s standing at the judgment is settled by Jesus’ atoning sacrifice and by the love that has begun in him: “We love because He first loved us” (4:19). Paul describes the same change when he says believers did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear but the Spirit of adoption (Romans 8:15).

e.n: The victory that overcomes the world
t: “Everyone born of God overcomes the world. And this is the victory that has overcome the world: our faith. Who then overcomes the world? Only he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God” (5:4-5). The verb “overcome” (nikaō) comes six times in 1 John: the young men “have overcome the evil one” (2:13-14), the readers “have overcome” the false prophets “because greater is He who is in you than he who is in the world” (4:4), and here. Jesus used the same verb in John 16:33: “I have overcome the world.” Revelation uses it more than any other book, of the one who conquers.

The “victory” (nikē) here is faith, and its object is the Son of God. Faith is not described as a strong feeling but as the confession that Jesus is the Son. The same verse says that God’s commands “are not burdensome” (5:3), since everyone born of God has been given strength to keep them. The “evil one” is beaten by the One “who is in you,” not by the readers’ own strength.

“This is the One who came by water and blood, Jesus Christ—not by water alone, but by water and blood. And it is the Spirit who testifies to this, because the Spirit is the truth. For there are three that testify: the Spirit, the water, and the blood—and these three are in agreement” (5:6-8). What “water” and “blood” mean is one of the most debated questions in the letter. Many early readers took them as Jesus’ baptism and his death, and the words “not by water alone” as aimed at teachers who said the Christ came on Jesus at his baptism and left before the cross. Others take the water to be his birth, and a third group takes them to be the water and blood that flowed from his pierced side in John 19:34-35, which Augustine and others also tied to baptism and the Lord’s Supper.

The “three that testify” follow the Old Testament rule that a matter is settled by two or three witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). The testimony is about the Son: “God has given us eternal life, and this life is in His Son” (5:11). The King James Version adds words in 5:7-8 about “three that bear record in heaven.” They are missing in the early Greek manuscripts and in nearly all Greek copies (see the entry on the added words in 1 John 5:7-8).

e.n: The sin that leads to death
t: “If anyone sees his brother committing a sin not leading to death, he should ask God, who will give life to those who commit this kind of sin. There is a sin that leads to death; I am not saying he should ask regarding that sin. All unrighteousness is sin, yet there is sin that does not lead to death” (5:16-17). The letter does not say what the sin is. The main answers are these. Some take it to be a sin of the kind that cuts a person off from Christ, which the Catholic tradition has called mortal sin; many take it to be the denial of the Son by the teachers who left (2:19, 22), which is the one sin that no prayer can mend. Others take “death” to be physical death sent as discipline on a believer, as at Corinth (1 Corinthians 11:30).

The Old Testament gave a distinction between sins done unintentionally, which could be forgiven, and sins done defiantly, for which there was no sacrifice (Numbers 15:27-31), and Hebrews 6:4-6 and 10:26 speak of willful turning away. The point of the passage as given is a kindness: pray for a brother who sins. The sentence “I am not saying he should ask” is a caution and not a ban, and the writer follows it at once with “yet there is sin that does not lead to death.”

The letter ends without a farewell: “We know that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, so that we may know Him who is true; and we are in Him who is true—in His Son Jesus Christ. He is the true God and eternal life. Little children, keep yourselves from idols” (5:20-21). The Greek word for idol, eidōlon, is used here alone in the letter. The warning can be read in two ways. Taken literally, it fits Ephesus, where the great temple of Artemis, the shrines of the emperors and many other gods stood, and where believers were asked to take part in civic worship. Taken more widely, as some commentators, Calvin among them, have taken it, it warns against any false picture of God set up in place of “Him who is true.”

The previous verses call Jesus “true” three times, and the readers have just been told that the teachers deny the Father and the Son (2:22), as the antichrist does,. An idol is whatever claims the place of the true God. The verb “keep” (phylassō) is not the same as the verb in 5:18 (tēreō, “protects”), where the Son who was born of God protects the believer; it is a command to guard oneself.

e.n: 2 John: who wrote it and to whom
t: Second John and 3 John are the two shortest books of the New Testament. Unlike 1 John, this one is a real letter, with a sender, a receiver, a greeting and a close. It opens “The elder, To the chosen lady and her children, whom I love in the truth” (1) and ends “The children of your elect sister send you greetings” (13). In between, the writer is glad that some of her children are “walking in the truth” (4), urges love (5-6), warns against “many deceivers” who refuse “to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh” (7), and tells his readers what to do about a teacher who does not bring the teaching of Christ (10-11).

The writer does not give his name. Church writers from the second century on, Irenaeus among them, quote the letter as the work of John, the Lord’s disciple. Eusebius lists 2 and 3 John among the “disputed” books, and the early Syriac Bible left them out. Papias spoke of an elder named John besides the apostle, and a number of scholars think this elder wrote the two short letters; others hold that the apostle called himself “the elder” as an older man with standing among the churches. The letter has so much in common with 1 John (the commandment “from the beginning,” “walking” in truth and love, the deceivers who deny that Christ came in the flesh) that the two are almost always read together. The date is put late in the first century, about AD 85 to 100, and the place is not named; Ephesus and the churches of Asia are the usual guess. The readers are most likely a church and its sister church, not named, and the letter says it is written in place of a visit.
The Third Letter is its companion: the same elder, the same closing lines, and the same concern for travelers, seen from the other side. See the overview of 3 John.
f: Not named; calls himself “the elder”; early tradition says John

e.n: 2 John and 3 John: two short letters of the elder
t: The Second and Third Letters of John are the same size, open with the same title (“the elder”), speak of walking in the truth, and close with almost the same words about paper or pen and ink and a hope to come and talk face to face (2 John 12; 3 John 13-14). Each deals with the same hard question from the other side. In 2 John the danger is welcoming a traveling teacher who brings a different teaching about Christ: “do not receive him into your home or even greet him” (10). In 3 John a man named Diotrephes, who likes to be first, will not receive the brothers the elder sent, and the elder asks his friend Gaius to support them (3 John 5-10).

Read together they show a church network along which letters, travelers and teachers moved, and a writer who feels responsible for the guests and the hosts both. They also show why the two letters are best read in pairs: the first sets a limit to hospitality for the sake of the truth, the second says that closing the door to the sent brothers is a wrong of its own. Both were slow to be widely accepted; see the notes on Eusebius and on the Syriac Bible.
In 3 John the same elder writes to one man, Gaius. He thanks him for receiving the brothers, names Diotrephes as the one who refuses them, and commends Demetrius (3 John 5-12).

The first four verses use the word “truth” five times: “whom I love in the truth,” “all who know the truth,” “the truth that abides in us and will be with us forever,” “in truth and love,” and “walking in the truth.” In the letter truth is the message about Jesus Christ and the life it shapes, and it is something that “abides” in the believers and that they “know.” Love is the other half: the writer loves the lady and her children in the truth, hopes that grace, mercy and peace “will be with us in truth and love” (3), and asks that “we love one another” (5).

The letter defines love in a way that may surprise a reader: “this is love, that we walk according to His commandments” (6). Love is a way of walking, and it has a shape that the commandments give it. This is why the same short letter that speaks of love so warmly can say, a few lines later, that a teacher who does not bring the teaching of Christ is not to be received (10). The writer does not set truth against love; in 1 John he wrote that we are to love “in action and truth” (3:18). Where the two seem to pull apart, as at verses 10-11, the letter’s view seems to be that a person who has left the truth has also left the love that goes with it.

The Greek word is didachē, “teaching,” and 2 John uses it three times in verses 9 and 10: “remaining in the teaching of Christ,” “Whoever remains in His teaching has both the Father and the Son,” and “does not bring this teaching.” The phrase can mean what Christ taught or what is taught about Christ. The verses around it point to the second: the deceivers refuse “to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh” (7), and what the teacher believes about the Son decides whether he has the Father. The letter says that “Anyone who runs ahead without remaining in the teaching of Christ does not have God.” The teachers it warns against think of themselves as going forward; the writer calls it running ahead and leaving the ground.

The thought is the same as 1 John 2:23: “Whoever denies the Son does not have the Father, but whoever confesses the Son has the Father as well.” In the Gospel of John “remaining” is the word for staying in Jesus and in his word. The early church saw the same test as the one John gives: Polycarp of Smyrna, writing to the Philippians, and Ignatius, writing to Smyrna, name the denial that Christ came in the flesh as the mark of a false teacher. The letter does not list the whole teaching; it names what is at stake, the Father and the Son, the coming in the flesh, and the commandment to love.

e.n: Hospitality and its limits in 2 John
t: The first Christians relied on hospitality. A traveling teacher, prophet or worker had no inn to turn to and was taken in by the believers of the next town, who gave him food and a bed and sent him on his way. 2 John puts a limit on this: “If anyone comes to you but does not bring this teaching, do not receive him into your home or even greet him. Whoever greets such a person shares in his evil deeds” (10-11). The reason given is that to receive a teacher was to back his work. The Greek for “greet” is chairein, which means “rejoice” and was the usual word of greeting in a letter or on the road; to say it to someone was to wish him well, and “shares” (koinōnei) is the word for partnership.

The verses are about teachers who bring a different teaching about Christ (7, 9), not about people the readers disagree with or dislike. The Didache, an early church manual, treats visiting teachers in much the same way: receive a visitor who comes in the name of the Lord, let him stay a day or two, and count one who asks for money or stays on as a false prophet. The letter does not say how far “receive” reaches, whether to lodging, to a hearing, or to a place in the church’s meeting, and the first readers would have known. The same hospitality is commanded elsewhere without limit for the stranger and the needy (Romans 12:13; Hebrews 13:2), and 3 John shows the opposite fault in a church leader who will not receive the brothers at all.

e.n: The chosen lady: a church or a woman?
t: The letter is addressed “To the chosen lady and her children” (1), and sends greetings from “The children of your elect sister” (13). Three readings are held. Most commentators take the lady to be a local church and her children its members. They point to the plural “you” that takes over in verses 6, 8, 10 and 12, to the way the letter speaks to a body of people about a visitor, and to other places where a church is spoken of as a woman, as in the “she” of 1 Peter 5:13. A sister church, with its own “children,” would then be sending greetings in verse 13.

Others think a real woman is meant, the leader of a church that met in her home, in which case verse 10 would mean her own house. A third view reads the Greek as a proper name, Kyria (“Lady”) or Electa (“Chosen”); the name Kyria is known from other writings, but the letter gives no sign that it is a name here. The Greek word kyria is the feminine of kyrios, “lord,” and appears nowhere else in the New Testament. The letter does not settle it, and what it says about truth, love, the teaching of Christ and the guest is much the same whichever reading is taken.

e.n: 3 John: who wrote it and to whom
t: Third John is the shortest book in the New Testament, about 219 Greek words, and the most personal of the three letters of John. It is a private note from “The elder” to a man named Gaius (1). The elder thanks Gaius for taking in traveling brothers (5-8), reports that Diotrephes, “who loves to be first,” has refused them and is putting their hosts “out of the church” (9-10), commends a man named Demetrius (12), and says he hopes to come soon (13-14). Unlike 1 and 2 John, it says nothing about false teaching. The trouble here is about hospitality and about who leads.

The writer gives no name. He uses the same title as 2 John, the same phrases (“whom I love in the truth,” “walking in the truth”), and nearly the same closing lines, so the two letters are taken to be from one hand. Early tradition names John the apostle, at Ephesus; Papias spoke of an elder named John besides the apostle, and some scholars think this elder wrote both notes. The date is usually put late in the first century, about AD 85 to 100. No town is named for Gaius. The letter was slow to be known: Origen, in the 3rd century, is the first writer known to mention it, Eusebius lists it among the disputed books, and the early Syriac Bible left it out. It never uses the names Jesus or Christ, and speaks only of “the Name” (7).
f: Not named; calls himself “the elder”; early tradition says John
Gaius, in a church that is not named
14 verses in the BSB (15 in many Bibles); about 219 Greek words

e.n: The prayer for health in 3 John 2
t: “Beloved, I pray that in every way you may prosper and enjoy good health, as your soul also prospers” (2). A wish for the reader’s health was a standard line near the start of a Greek letter, and the papyrus letters from Egypt are full of them: a young recruit named Apion begins a letter to his father with a prayer that he is well and will go on in good health. The elder keeps the custom and deepens it. He takes it for granted that Gaius is doing well in soul, and he prays that the rest of his life will match.

The word for “prosper” (euodoō) means to have a good road, to get along well; Paul uses it of a hoped-for journey in Romans 1:10 and of a person’s earnings in 1 Corinthians 16:2. The verse has sometimes been read as a promise that God wills health and wealth for every believer. It is a personal prayer for a friend, in the ordinary form of a letter, and the measure it uses is the health of the soul.
