The New Testament elsewhere expects believers to know sickness and need as well as plenty (Philippians 4:12; 2 Timothy 4:20).

e.n: For the sake of the Name
t: “For they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles” (7). “The Name” stands by itself, with no “of Jesus” added, much as Jews spoke of God as the Name. In Acts the apostles rejoice at being counted worthy to suffer for the Name (Acts 5:41), and the Lord says of Paul that he will show him how much he must suffer for his name (Acts 9:16). 3 John never writes Jesus or Christ; this one word carries all it says of him.

The brothers “went out,” the same verb 2 John 7 uses of the deceivers who “have gone out into the world.” Two kinds of travelers were on the road, and a church had to tell them apart. These took nothing from “the Gentiles,” meaning the pagans they preached to; the Greek word, ethnikos, is used the same way in Matthew 5:47 and 18:17. Jesus had sent the Twelve out to give freely and to stay with a worthy host (Matthew 10:8-11), and Paul refused pay at Corinth so as to put no obstacle in the way of the gospel (1 Corinthians 9:12). Because they would not ask outsiders for money, the workers depended on believers like Gaius.

“Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (8). The elder includes himself in “we.” The Greek word for “support” means to take up or take in, to get under a load with someone. The thought is that the one who gives a bed, a meal and travel money shares the work of the one who preaches. Jesus said that whoever receives a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward (Matthew 10:41), and Paul calls the Philippians partners in the gospel because of their gifts (Philippians 1:5; 4:15).

“Fellow worker” (synergos) is one of Paul’s words for his team, used of Timothy, Titus, Priscilla and Aquila and others. Here it is given to people who never leave home. It is the positive side of the warning in 2 John 11, where the person who welcomes a deceiver “shares in his evil deeds.” Hospitality in both letters is a kind of partnership, and so it matters whom one welcomes.

Diotrephes is described in one Greek word, philoprōteuōn, “who loves to be first” (9). It is found nowhere else in the New Testament. What it leads to is spelled out: he “will not accept our instruction,” he uses “malicious slander against us,” and “he refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church” (9-10). The letter gives his conduct and not his reasons, and it does not say that he taught anything false.

The Gospels set the standard he fails. When the disciples argued about who was greatest, Jesus said that anyone who wants to be first must be last of all and servant of all (Mark 9:35), and that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, but it is not to be so among his followers (Mark 10:42-45). Peter tells elders not to lord it over the flock (1 Peter 5:3). The elder’s own way is different: he writes, he sends people, he plans to come and speak openly, and he asks Gaius to imitate what is good. Some readers see in Diotrephes the first sign of a single leader ruling a church, a pattern that the letters of Ignatius show in Asia about AD 110. That may be so, but the fault the letter names is the love of first place, which can go with any office or with none.

“Beloved, do not imitate what is evil, but what is good. The one who does good is of God; the one who does evil has not seen God” (11). The verse stands between a bad example, Diotrephes, and a good one, Demetrius, and tells Gaius which to copy. People learn a way of life by watching someone live it, and the New Testament says so often: Paul asks his churches to imitate him as he imitates Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1), and Hebrews tells its readers to imitate the faith of their leaders (Hebrews 13:7).

The second half is in the language of 1 John. There, the one who does what is right is righteous, and no one who keeps on sinning has seen God or known him (1 John 3:6-7). Doing good does not earn a place with God; it shows where a person already belongs. In 3 John the good in view is plain: taking in strangers, supporting those who work for the truth, and refusing to push oneself forward.

Gaius was one of the commonest first names in the Roman world, and Acts and Paul mention a Gaius in three settings. Gaius of Macedonia was seized with Aristarchus in the riot at Ephesus (Acts 19:29). Gaius of Derbe traveled with Paul toward Jerusalem (Acts 20:4). Gaius of Corinth was baptized by Paul and later hosted him and the whole church (1 Corinthians 1:14; Romans 16:23). Then there is the Gaius of 3 John.

Because the Gaius of Corinth was known for his hospitality, some early readers, Bede among them, took him to be the same man as the Gaius of 3 John. Nothing in the letter supports it, and some thirty or forty years lie between Romans and 3 John. A church manual of the late 4th century, the Apostolic Constitutions, names a Gaius as bishop of Pergamum, which is the reason for the pin on the map. The safest statement is that the Gaius of 3 John is otherwise unknown: a believer of some means, loved by the elder, with a home open to travelers.

e.n: Jude: who wrote it and to whom
t: Jude is a letter of 25 verses, about 460 Greek words, set just before Revelation. The writer calls himself “Jude, a servant of Jesus Christ and a brother of James” (1). Jude is the same name as Judas. Most readers take him to be the Judas whom Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55 list among the brothers of Jesus, and “James” to be the brother who led the church in Jerusalem. He does not call himself an apostle, and he speaks of “the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ” as others (17). Some scholars think a later Christian wrote in his name. Others answer that Jude was too little known for anyone to borrow his name, and that the letter’s Jewish learning fits a member of that family.

The readers are not named. They are “called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ” (1). Jude expects them to know the Old Testament and the Jewish books that grew up around it, which suggests Jewish Christians, perhaps in the land of Israel or Syria; Egypt and Asia Minor have also been proposed. The date is uncertain: anywhere from the AD 50s to about AD 90. Jude had planned to write about “the salvation we share,” but “certain men have crept in among you unnoticed” (3-4), and the letter became a call to “contend earnestly for the faith.”

The plan is simple. A greeting (1-2) and the reason for writing (3-4) are followed by a long middle section that sets the intruders beside old examples of judgment (5-19). Then the readers are told what to do (20-23), and the letter closes with a hymn of praise (24-25). Most of verses 4-18 has a parallel in 2 Peter 2.
f: Jude (Judas), brother of James; by the usual reading a brother of Jesus
A church or churches not named, probably with Jewish roots

t: Jude says he “felt it necessary to write and urge you to contend earnestly for the faith entrusted once for all to the saints” (3). The verb (epagōnizomai) comes from the games: it is the effort of an athlete in a contest, and English “agony” comes from the same root. It is found only here in the New Testament. Paul uses the simpler verb for his own work and for the fight of faith (1 Timothy 6:12).

The letter shows what Jude means by contending. He does not tell his readers to attack the intruders or to throw them out. He tells them to remember what they were taught (5, 17), to build themselves up in the faith, to pray, to keep themselves in the love of God (20-21), and to show mercy to those who have been shaken (22-23). The contest is fought mostly by holding to the truth and living by it.

e.n: The faith entrusted once for all
t: In “the faith entrusted once for all to the saints” (3), “the faith” means what is believed: the message about Jesus Christ that the apostles taught. “Entrusted” is the word for handing on a tradition, the same word Paul uses when he says he passed on what he had received (1 Corinthians 15:3). “Once for all” (hapax) means it was given a single time and is complete. Hebrews uses the same word for the one sacrifice of Christ.

Jude’s point is that the gospel is not open to revision by teachers who claim new visions (8). “The saints” are simply God’s people, all believers. In verse 20 he calls it “your most holy faith,” the foundation on which the readers are to build themselves up.

Jude’s first charge against the intruders is that “They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality” (4). The Greek word behind “license for immorality” (aselgeia) means conduct with no restraint and no shame, often sexual. The intruders seem to have argued that because God forgives freely, what a believer does with the body does not matter. Paul met the same idea and rejected it (Romans 6:1-2; Galatians 5:13).

The second charge follows from the first: “they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ.” Jude does not say they taught false things about who Jesus is. They denied him as Master by refusing to obey him. Scholars use the word antinomian, “against law,” for teaching of this kind.

The letter is addressed “To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ” (1). The three words say that God took the first step, that he loves them, and that he is guarding them. The words echo what the prophet Isaiah says of Israel, the people God called, loved and kept.

“Keep” is one of Jude’s chosen words. The rebel angels did not keep their own domain, and God has kept them for judgment (6); darkness is “reserved” for the wandering stars (13), the same Greek verb. The readers are “kept in Jesus Christ” (1), are told to “keep yourselves in the love of God” (21), and are given over at the end to the God “who is able to keep you from stumbling” (24), where a second verb means to guard. Jude holds both sides together: God keeps his people, and they are to stay where his love keeps them.

Jude arranges nearly everything in threes. The writer is Jude, servant, brother (1). The readers are called, loved and kept (1), and are wished mercy, peace and love (2). There are three examples of judgment: the wilderness generation, the angels and Sodom (5-7). The intruders defile, reject and slander (8). They follow Cain, Balaam and Korah (11). They are grumblers, boasters and flatterers (16), and they cause divisions, are worldly, and lack the Spirit (19). Mercy is shown to three kinds of people (22-23), and the praise at the end covers three times: before all time, now, and for all eternity (25).

The habit helps a listener follow and remember a letter that was read aloud. It also suggests a careful writer: the Greek of Jude is polished, with a large vocabulary and more than a dozen words found nowhere else in the New Testament.

Verses 5-7 remind the readers of three judgments. The people who were “delivered” “out of the land of Egypt” later refused to trust God at the edge of the promised land, and that generation died in the wilderness (Numbers 14). Angels “who did not stay within their own domain” are held “in eternal chains under darkness.” And “Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them” are “on display as an example.”

Each group had a high standing and lost it: a rescued people, angels, and cities in a rich plain. That is the warning for a church in which some have begun to presume on grace. The same three examples appear together in older Jewish writings, such as Sirach 16:7-10, so Jude is using a known list. 2 Peter 2:4-9 has the angels, the flood and Sodom, in the order of Genesis, and adds that God rescued Noah and Lot.

e.n: Jesus or the Lord in Jude 5
t: The BSB reads, “after Jesus had delivered His people out of the land of Egypt, He destroyed those who did not believe” (5). The Greek copies differ at this point. Codex Vaticanus, Codex Alexandrinus and the old Latin and Coptic versions read “Jesus.” Codex Sinaiticus and most later copies read “the Lord,” which is what the King James Version has. The papyrus P72, the oldest copy, reads “God Christ.” The Greek text shown word by word in this app has “the Lord,” so the Greek and the English differ at this verse.

Many recent editions of the Greek text choose “Jesus” because it is found in early and widespread copies and is the harder reading, the one a scribe would be more likely to change. If it is right, Jude says that Jesus was at work in the Exodus, as Paul says that the rock that followed Israel was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). The Greek name is also the name Joshua, and a few have thought Jude meant him, but Joshua did not bring the people out of Egypt. Either way the warning is the same: being rescued once is no shield for those who then refuse to believe.

e.n: Michael and the body of Moses
t: Jude writes that “even the archangel Michael, when he disputed with the devil over the body of Moses, did not presume to bring a slanderous charge against him, but said, ‘The Lord rebuke you!’” (9). The Old Testament says only that Moses died on Mount Nebo, that the Lord buried him, and that no one knows the grave (Deuteronomy 34:5-6). Jewish storytellers filled in the scene: the devil claimed the body, and Michael, sent to bury it, answered him with the words God speaks to Satan in Zechariah 3:2.

Clement of Alexandria and Origen say Jude found the story in a book called the Assumption (or Ascension) of Moses. The surviving Testament of Moses breaks off before the end, so the story itself is known only from Jude and from later Christian writers who summarize it.

Jude uses it for one lesson. The intruders “slander glorious beings” (8). Michael, the highest of the angels, did not take it on himself to condemn even the devil, and left the judgment to God. How much less should these men speak with contempt of what they do not understand (10).

“Woe to them! They have traveled the path of Cain; they have rushed headlong into the error of Balaam; they have perished in Korah’s rebellion” (11). Jude names three men of the Old Testament in one sentence. Cain murdered his brother (Genesis 4), and later Jewish teaching made him the first to lead others into wrongdoing. Balaam was the seer who would say anything for a fee and who showed Moab how to draw Israel into sin (Numbers 22-24; 31:16). Korah raised a revolt against the leaders God had appointed (Numbers 16).

Put together, the three describe the intruders: no love for their brothers, teaching for gain, and contempt for authority. The verbs climb from walking to rushing to perishing, and the last is in the past tense, as if the sentence had already been carried out.

Verses 12-13 describe the intruders with five pictures, one after another. They are “hidden reefs in your love feasts”: rocks under the water that wreck a ship. They are “clouds without water, carried along by the wind,” which promise rain to a dry land and give none. They are “fruitless trees in autumn, twice dead after being uprooted”: no fruit at the end of the season, and no root. They are “wild waves of the sea, foaming up their own shame,” all noise and what they leave on the shore is dirt. And they are “wandering stars, for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever,” lights that cannot be steered by.

The pictures take in sea, sky, land, sea again and the heavens. A passage near the start of the Book of Enoch (chapters 2-5) points to the clouds, the trees, the seas and the stars as works of God that keep to their order, and then blames sinners who do not. Jude turns the same works of nature into pictures of people who have left their order. Each picture shows something that looks useful and fails those who rely on it.

“Enoch, the seventh from Adam, also prophesied about them: ‘Behold, the Lord is coming with myriads of His holy ones to execute judgment on everyone, and to convict all the ungodly’” (14-15). The words are from 1 Enoch 1:9, the opening vision of a Jewish book that was widely read in the time of Jesus. The vision itself draws on Deuteronomy 33:2 and Zechariah 14:5, where the Lord comes with his holy ones. In Enoch the one who comes is God; Jude writes “the Lord,” and his readers would think of the coming of Jesus (see Matthew 25:31).

Christians have read Jude’s use of the book in several ways. Some hold that this one saying truly goes back to Enoch and was kept in the book. Some hold that Jude quotes a book that he, his readers and their opponents all respected, in order to make his point from it, as Paul quotes a Cretan poet in Titus 1:12. Some hold that Jude counted the book among the prophets. The letter says that Enoch “prophesied” and does not use the formula “it is written.”

The quotation caused Jude trouble later. Tertullian defended the Book of Enoch by pointing to Jude. Jerome says many rejected Jude because of it. The church kept the letter and, outside Ethiopia, did not keep the book.

e.n: Jude and the books outside the Old Testament
t: Jude draws on Jewish books that are not in the Hebrew Bible. Verses 14-15 quote the Book of Enoch, and verse 6 (the angels) and verse 13 (the wandering stars) use its stories. Verse 9 uses a story about the burial of Moses that early writers trace to the Assumption of Moses. These books are often called the Pseudepigrapha, writings set under the names of ancient figures. They were popular among Jews in the last centuries before Christ, and the Dead Sea Scrolls include many copies of Enoch.

Jude uses these books the way a preacher uses stories his hearers already know. He also uses the Old Testament itself throughout: Egypt, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, Korah, Zechariah 3. 2 Peter, which runs alongside Jude, keeps the Old Testament examples and leaves out the quotation from Enoch and the story of Michael.

The question this raised is old. Some early Christians valued Enoch because Jude quoted it; others doubted Jude for the same reason. Most churches have concluded that an inspired writer can quote a true or useful saying from a book without the whole book being Scripture.

In the BSB the word “ungodly” comes six times in Jude’s 25 verses, more thickly than anywhere else in the New Testament. The intruders are “ungodly ones” (4). In the quotation from Enoch the Lord comes “to convict all the ungodly of every ungodly act of wickedness and every harsh word spoken against Him by ungodly sinners” (15). The apostles warned of scoffers who “follow after their own ungodly desires” (18).

The Greek word (asebēs) means without reverence: living as though God were not to be honored or feared. Jude’s complaint is about that attitude more than any one doctrine. It shows in what the intruders do with their bodies, in how they talk about authority, and in their grumbling and boasting (16).

e.n: Keep yourselves in the love of God
t: “But you, beloved, by building yourselves up in your most holy faith and praying in the Holy Spirit, keep yourselves in the love of God as you await the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ to bring you eternal life” (20-21). There is one command, “keep yourselves,” with three actions around it: building, praying and waiting. The building is done together, on the faith they were taught. Praying “in the Holy Spirit” is prayer led and helped by the Spirit, whom the intruders lack (19); Paul uses the same phrase in Ephesians 6:18.

“The love of God” here is God’s love for them. To keep oneself in it is to stay where that love is known, as Jesus told his disciples to remain in his love by keeping his commands (John 15:9-10). The sentence names the Holy Spirit, God and the Lord Jesus Christ together, and joins faith, love and hope: the waiting looks ahead to mercy at the coming of Christ.

“And indeed, have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh” (22-23). After hard words for the intruders, Jude is gentle with the people they have unsettled. Those who waver are to be treated with mercy and not scolded. Those already in danger are to be pulled out quickly, like a stick from a fire. Those deep in the wrong are still to be shown mercy, by helpers who watch themselves.

The pictures come from Zechariah 3:2-4, where the high priest Joshua stands accused by Satan, is called a burning stick snatched from the fire, and has his filthy clothes taken off and clean ones put on. The clothing in Jude is the inner garment worn against the skin. The Greek copies of these two verses differ more than any others in the letter: some have two groups, some three, and the verbs vary. The BSB follows the form with three groups, which suits Jude’s habit of threes.

“Now to Him who is able to keep you from stumbling and to present you unblemished in His glorious presence, with great joy—to the only God our Savior be glory, majesty, dominion, and authority through Jesus Christ our Lord before all time, and now, and for all eternity. Amen” (24-25). A doxology is a short form of praise that gives glory to God. Jude ends with one in place of greetings and names, and it has been used to close services of worship ever since.

It answers the fear the letter might leave behind. The readers have been warned about people who fell: a rescued nation, angels, whole cities. Now they are told that God is able to guard them from falling and to bring them before him without fault and glad. “Unblemished” is the word for a sacrifice with no defect. “The only God” is the confession of Israel, and “our Savior” is here said of God the Father, who saves “through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Four things are given to God: glory, majesty, dominion and authority. Three times are named: before all time, now, and forever. The closest parallels are Romans 16:25-27 and Ephesians 3:20-21, which also begin with the one who is able.

e.n: Revelation: who wrote it and when
t: The writer calls himself John four times (1:1, 4, 9; 22:8). He says he “was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (1:9), and he writes to seven churches in the Roman province of Asia, in what is now western Turkey. He calls the book a prophecy and himself a brother and fellow servant. He never claims to be an apostle.

Justin Martyr, about AD 155, and Irenaeus, about AD 180, say the writer was John the apostle, and most of the early church agreed. About AD 250 Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, argued from the Greek style that a different John wrote it, though he accepted the book as inspired. Modern scholars are divided: some hold to the apostle, and others think of another John, perhaps the elder John known to Papias.

Irenaeus says the vision was seen near the end of the reign of Domitian, who ruled from AD 81 to 96, and most scholars date the book about AD 95. A smaller group dates it to the late 60s, after Nero’s persecution and before the temple fell in AD 70, pointing to the measuring of the temple (11:1-2) and the count of kings (17:9-11). The date matters for some ways of reading the book.
f: John, on Patmos; by early tradition the apostle
Most often about AD 95 (Domitian); some say the late 60s
Seven churches in the Roman province of Asia

t: Christians have read Revelation in four main ways, and many readers combine them. The preterist reading (from a Latin word for “past”) holds that most of the visions were about John’s own time: the persecution of the churches, the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, or the fall of pagan Rome, with the last chapters still to come. The historicist reading sees the book as a map of church history from John’s day to the end, and was common among Protestant writers from the Reformation to the 1800s.

The futurist reading holds that most of chapters 4-22 describe events still in the future, in the last years before Christ returns. Many futurists are premillennial, and one form, dispensationalism, expects the church to be taken up before a seven-year tribulation; it spread through J. N. Darby in the 1830s and the Scofield Reference Bible of 1909. The idealist or symbolic reading sees the visions as pictures of the struggle between God and evil in every age, not tied to particular dates.

Each reading has strengths. The preterist reading takes seriously that the book was written to real churches who were told the time is near (1:3). The futurist reading takes seriously that the book ends with a return of Christ and a new creation that have not yet come. The idealist reading explains why the book has spoken to Christians in every century. The app’s notes describe what the text says and name the main readings where they differ.

Revelation opens with the Greek word apokalypsis, “unveiling” (1:1), and has given its name to a kind of writing. Jewish apocalypses such as Daniel 7-12, the Book of Enoch, 4 Ezra and 2 Baruch share a style: a seer receives visions, often explained by an angel; beasts, numbers and colors stand for powers and periods; heaven and earth are shown as one great conflict; and the visions end with God’s judgment and the rescue of his people.

Revelation uses all of this but is different in three ways. Its writer gives his own name instead of borrowing one from the distant past. It calls itself a prophecy (1:3; 22:7, 18-19). And it is framed as a letter, with a greeting (1:4-5) and a closing blessing (22:21). Reading it as an apocalypse means expecting pictures, not photographs: John tells his readers more than once that what he sees is a sign (12:1, 3; 15:1) and explains some of his symbols himself (1:20; 17:9-18).

Numbers carry meaning in Revelation. Seven, the number of days in the week of creation, stands for completeness: seven churches, spirits, seals, trumpets and bowls. Twelve stands for the people of God: twelve tribes and twelve apostles, and twelve times twelve thousand in the 144,000 (7:4-8; 14:1). The new Jerusalem has twelve gates, twelve foundations and a wall of 144 cubits (21:12-17). Four is the number of the world: four corners, four winds, four living creatures.

A short, limited time of trouble is given in three matching ways: forty-two months (11:2; 13:5), 1,260 days (11:3; 12:6), and “a time, and times, and half a time” (12:14), all three and a half years, half of seven. The figure comes from Daniel 7:25 and 12:7. A thousand is a very large round number, as in the thousand years of chapter 20. Six, one short of seven, is often taken as the mark of falling short, as in 666.

Readers disagree about how far to take the numbers literally. Some read the 144,000, the 1,260 days and the thousand years as exact counts; others read them as symbols of a complete people, a limited time and a long age. Even readers who take the numbers literally recognize that John himself gives some of them symbolic meanings.

e.n: The pattern of the seven letters
t: Chapters 2 and 3 hold seven short messages, one to each church, and all follow one pattern. Each opens “To the angel of the church in” a city. Each opens with a title of Christ taken from the vision in chapter 1. Each says “I know,” followed by what Christ sees in the church; then comes praise, or rebuke, or both, and a call to repent or hold on. Each has the line “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches,” and each ends with a promise to the one who overcomes.

Smyrna and Philadelphia, the two poorest and weakest churches, receive no rebuke. Laodicea, the richest, receives no praise. Details in several letters fit what is known of each city: the earthquakes at Philadelphia, the banks and eye salve of Laodicea, the throne-like altar and the emperor’s temple at Pergamum, the trade guilds of Thyatira. Because there are seven, and every letter ends by speaking to “the churches,” all seven were meant to be read by all. The historicist reading also sees in them seven ages of church history; most readers take them as messages to real churches that speak to churches in every age.

e.n: The promises to the one who overcomes
t: Each of the seven letters ends with a promise “to the one who overcomes” (Greek nikaō, “to win, to conquer”). The one who overcomes will eat from the tree of life (2:7), will not be harmed by the second death (2:11), will receive hidden manna and a white stone with a new name (2:17), authority over the nations and the morning star (2:26-28), white garments and a name kept in the book of life (3:5), a place as a pillar in God’s temple (3:12), and a seat with Christ on his throne (3:21).

Almost every promise comes true in the last chapters: the tree of life (22:2), freedom from the second death (21:7-8; 20:6), the names of God and the Lamb (22:4), the book of life (21:27), the throne (22:5). The letters show what overcoming means. It is not winning a battle with weapons but holding on to Christ under pressure, as he himself overcame (3:21; 5:5) and as the martyrs overcame “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (12:11).

Three series of seven judgments fill chapters 6-16. The Lamb opens seven seals on a scroll (6:1-8:1). Seven angels blow seven trumpets (8:6-11:19). Seven angels pour out seven bowls of God’s wrath (16:1-21). In each series the first four go together, there is a pause before the seventh (chapters 7 and 10-11), and the seventh brings thunder, lightning and an earthquake (8:5; 11:19; 16:18).

The judgments grow. The fourth seal touches a fourth of the earth (6:8), the trumpets strike a third (8:7-12), and the bowls strike everything (16:3). Many of them echo the plagues of Egypt: hail and fire, water turned to blood, darkness, sores, frogs and locusts. Readers disagree about how the three series fit together. Some read them as one sequence, each series following the last. Others, from Victorinus of Pettau about AD 260 onward, read them as the same span of time seen three times with growing force, which is called recapitulation.

In chapter 4 John goes through an open door into heaven and sees a throne with one seated on it, shining like jasper and carnelian, with a rainbow like an emerald around it. Around the throne are twenty-four elders on thrones and four living creatures, full of eyes, who never stop saying, “Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!” (4:8). The scene draws on the visions of Isaiah 6 and Ezekiel 1.

The throne is the center of the whole book: the word appears about forty times in Revelation, more than in all the rest of the New Testament. Before any judgment falls, the reader is shown that God is on the throne. Chapter 5 adds the Lamb, standing at the center of the throne, and from then on the worship is given to God and to the Lamb together (5:13; 7:10). For churches under the power of Rome, the vision answered the question of who really rules.

In chapter 5 no one is found worthy to open the sealed scroll, and John weeps. An elder tells him, “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed to open the scroll and its seven seals” (5:5). John turns and sees not a lion but “a Lamb who appeared to have been slain” (5:6), standing at the center of the throne. The Lion has conquered by being slain.

From then on “the Lamb” is the book’s main name for Christ, used about twenty-eight times. The Lamb has seven horns and seven eyes, full power and full sight (5:6). The Lamb is worshiped with God (5:13), opens the seals (6:1), shepherds the great multitude (7:17), conquers the beast and its allies (17:14), marries his bride (19:7), and shares God’s throne in the new Jerusalem (22:1). Revelation uses a different Greek word (arnion) from John 1:29, but the picture is the same: the sacrificed Passover lamb.

Revelation is full of worship. The living creatures and elders sing at the throne (4:8, 11); a new song is sung to the Lamb (5:9-10); thousands upon thousands of angels and then every creature join in (5:11-14). There are songs at the sealing of the multitude (7:10-12), at the seventh trumpet (11:15-18), at the casting down of the dragon (12:10-12), by the sea of glass (15:3-4) and at the fall of Babylon (19:1-8). The word “Hallelujah” occurs in the New Testament only in Revelation 19, four times.

The songs often explain the visions around them: they say why God’s judgments are just and what the victory means. Many have passed into Christian worship, and some may echo hymns already sung in the churches. They also carry a challenge. In the cities of Asia crowds hailed the emperor as worthy and as lord; in Revelation that praise belongs to God and to the Lamb alone.

Revelation never says “it is written” and quotes no passage in full, yet it is soaked in the Old Testament. Scholars count several hundred allusions, more than in any other New Testament book. Daniel gives the beasts from the sea, the one like a son of man and the three and a half times. Ezekiel gives the living creatures, the eaten scroll, the measured temple, Gog and Magog, and the river from the temple. Exodus gives the plagues, the song of Moses and a kingdom of priests. Zechariah gives the horses, the lampstands and the olive trees. Isaiah and Jeremiah give the fall of Babylon and the new heavens and new earth.

John does not simply repeat these passages. He combines them and points them to Christ: the four creatures of Ezekiel take the faces of Ezekiel and the six wings of Isaiah’s seraphim, and the Babylon of the prophets becomes the great city of his own day. Knowing the Old Testament background is one of the surest guides to what the symbols meant to John’s first readers.

“Here is a call for wisdom: Let the one who has insight calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man, and that number is 666” (13:18). In Greek and Hebrew, letters also served as numbers, so every name had a number value; the practice is called gematria. A graffito at Pompeii says, “I love her whose number is 545.” John invites his readers to count.

The best-known answer is Nero. The Greek “Nero Caesar” written in Hebrew letters adds up to 666, and spelled the Latin way, without the final n, it adds up to 616. That would explain why some early copies, including Papyrus 115 and Codex Ephraemi, read 616, a reading Irenaeus already knew about AD 180. Irenaeus himself would not name anyone; he suggested several names and warned against guessing.

Other readers take 666 as a symbol: six, one short of the perfect seven, three times over, the mark of a power that imitates God and always falls short. Futurist readers expect a ruler still to come whose name or number will fit. Through history the number has been applied to many people, and every such guess has passed with its time.

e.n: The mark of the beast and the seal of God
t: Revelation sets two marks side by side. God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads before the winds of judgment are released (7:3), and later the 144,000 have the name of the Lamb and his Father written there (14:1); in the new Jerusalem his servants “will see His face, and His name will be on their foreheads” (22:4). The picture comes from Ezekiel 9:4, where a mark is put on the foreheads of those who grieve over the city’s sins.

The second beast forces everyone to receive a mark (charagma) on the right hand or forehead, “so that no one could buy or sell” without it (13:16-17). Charagma was the word for an official stamp on documents and the image on coins. Readers take the mark in different ways: as a future visible sign or technology; as a symbol of allegiance, like the commands Israel was to bind on hand and forehead (Deuteronomy 6:8); or as the pressure on Christians in Asia to take part in the emperor’s worship and the trade guilds tied to it. All agree on the book’s point: everyone carries one name or the other, and the choice is between God and the beast (14:9-11).

At the sixth bowl, demonic spirits gather the kings of the whole world “for battle on the great day of God the Almighty” (16:14), “in the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon” (16:16). The name is usually taken as Har Megiddo, “the mountain of Megiddo.” Megiddo was a fortress city above the plain of Jezreel, where many battles were fought: Deborah’s victory (Judges 5:19) and the death of King Josiah (2 Kings 23:29) among them.

There is no mountain called Megiddo, only the mound of the ancient city, so the name may be a symbol: the classic battlefield made into the place of the last battle. Some readers expect a literal gathering of armies in that valley. Others note that no battle is described there; when the armies meet the rider on the white horse in chapter 19, they are simply defeated by the sword from his mouth.

Revelation 20:1-6 is the only passage in the Bible that speaks of a thousand-year reign. An angel binds Satan and throws him into the Abyss for a thousand years; John sees thrones and the souls of those beheaded for their testimony, who “came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years” (20:4); this is “the first resurrection” (20:5). Afterward Satan is released, gathers Gog and Magog, and is thrown into the lake of fire (20:7-10). The Latin word for a thousand years gives the name millennium.

Premillennial readers expect Christ to return before a reign of a thousand years on earth; Papias, Justin Martyr and Irenaeus held an early form of this view. Amillennial readers, following Augustine (City of God, book 20), take the thousand years as the present age, in which Christ reigns and Satan is restrained, with the saints reigning with him now in heaven. Postmillennial readers expect the gospel to spread until a long age of righteousness comes before Christ returns. Each view is held by faithful Christians, and the passage is one of the hardest in the book.

e.n: The great tribulation and the rapture question
t: John writes as “your brother and partner in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance that are in Jesus” (1:9). The great multitude in white robes are “the ones who have come out of the great tribulation” (7:14). The word thlipsis means pressure or affliction, and Revelation uses it both for the suffering all believers share and for a time of great trouble before the end (compare Daniel 12:1; Matthew 24:21).

The word rapture, from the Latin for being “caught up” (1 Thessalonians 4:17), does not appear in Revelation, but the book is central to the debate about it. Pretribulation readers expect the church to be taken up before the last seven years of trouble, and some see the call to John, “Come up here” (4:1), as a picture of that event. Midtribulation and prewrath readers place the rapture partway through. Posttribulation readers, and amillennial and postmillennial readers, see the church in the tribulation and its gathering at the one return of Christ (19:11-16). Revelation itself names no secret coming and no rapture; each view draws on other passages as well.

e.n: The lake of fire and the second death
t: The beast and the false prophet are thrown alive into “the fiery lake of burning sulfur” (19:20); the devil follows (20:10); then Death and Hades are thrown in: “This is the second death—the lake of fire” (20:14), with anyone whose name was not found in the book of life (20:15; 21:8). The first death is the death of the body; the second is final judgment. The one who overcomes will not be harmed by it (2:11), and those in the first resurrection are free of it (20:6).

Christians read the passage in different ways. The traditional view, held by most of the church, takes it as unending conscious punishment (14:11; 20:10). Others hold that the lost are finally destroyed, since death itself is thrown into the lake and ends there. Many stress that the fire and sulfur are images, as much of Revelation is, for complete exclusion from God’s presence. All agree that the lake of fire is the end of everything that opposes God, so that the new creation can come without death, mourning or pain (21:4).

e.n: A new heaven and a new earth
t: “Then I saw a new heaven and a new earth, for the first heaven and earth had passed away, and the sea was no more” (21:1). The words take up Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22. A loud voice from the throne announces, “Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man, and He will dwell with them” (21:3): the promise of the tabernacle and the temple fulfilled at last. God will wipe away every tear, and death, mourning, crying and pain will be no more (21:4). The one on the throne says, “Behold, I make all things new” (21:5).

Much of the last two chapters reverses the opening chapters of Genesis. The tree of life returns (22:2), the curse is gone (22:3), and God’s people see his face (22:4). The sea, which in Revelation is the home of the beast and a picture of chaos, is no more. Christians differ on whether the new creation is the old world renewed or a wholly new one; the text speaks of the first earth passing away and of all things being made new.

An angel carries John to a high mountain and shows him “the holy city of Jerusalem coming down out of heaven from God” (21:10), the bride of the Lamb. The city has a great high wall with twelve gates named for the twelve tribes and twelve foundations named for the twelve apostles (21:12-14). It is laid out as a cube, 12,000 stadia (about 1,400 miles or 2,200 kilometers) in length, width and height (21:16), the shape of the Most Holy Place in Solomon’s temple (1 Kings 6:20). Its foundations are twelve precious stones, like the twelve stones on the high priest’s breastpiece (Exodus 28:17-21), and each gate is a single pearl.

John sees no temple in the city, “because the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are its temple” (21:22), and no sun or moon, because God’s glory is its light (21:23). Nothing unclean enters; the gates are never shut, and the nations bring their glory into it (21:24-27). Some readers expect a literal city of these measurements; many take the measurements as symbols of a people complete and holy, in whom God dwells. The city is both a place and a people: the bride is the city.

Jesus says “I am coming soon” three times in the last chapter (22:7, 12, 20), and the book opens with “Behold, He is coming with the clouds” (1:7). The church answers, “Amen. Come, Lord Jesus!” (22:20), the same prayer as the Aramaic Maranatha of 1 Corinthians 16:22. The book is framed by the hope of Christ’s return.

Readers have long asked what “soon” means after so many centuries. Some take it as soon from God’s side, where a thousand years are like a day (2 Peter 3:8); some as sudden rather than near; some, in the preterist way, as a coming in judgment within John’s generation, with the final coming still ahead. Whatever the reading, the book uses the nearness of the end to call its readers to stay awake, keep their garments clean and hold on (16:15; 22:7, 11-12).

In the West Revelation was accepted early. Justin Martyr and Irenaeus quote it as the work of the apostle John, and the Muratorian list includes it. In the East it was questioned for a long time, partly because some groups used the thousand years to teach an earthly kingdom of feasting. Dionysius of Alexandria accepted the book but doubted that the apostle wrote it. Eusebius, about AD 325, could not decide where to place it, and the early Syriac Bible did not include it. Athanasius listed it among the New Testament books in AD 367, and in time the whole church received it.

Doubts continued. Martin Luther wrote in 1522 that he could not see the Holy Spirit in the book, though he later spoke of it more warmly. John Calvin wrote commentaries on every New Testament book except 2 John, 3 John and Revelation. The Orthodox churches still do not read Revelation in their Sunday services. Yet the book has shaped Christian worship, art and hope as few others have, from the hymns of heaven to the paintings of the Last Judgment.

The Bible begins and ends with the tree of life. In Eden it stands in the middle of the garden (Genesis 2:9), and after the fall the way to it is guarded so that the man will not eat and live forever (Genesis 3:22-24). In Proverbs wisdom is “a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Proverbs 3:18).

Revelation gives the tree back. Christ promises the church in Ephesus, “To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to eat from the tree of life in the Paradise of God” (2:7). In the new Jerusalem the tree stands on both banks of the river, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, a crop for each month, and “the leaves of the tree are for the healing of the nations” (22:2). The last blessing of the book is for those who wash their robes, “so that they may have the right to the tree of life” (22:14), and the last warning speaks of losing a share in it (22:19).

e.n: The seven spirits before the throne
t: John’s greeting comes from God, “from the seven Spirits before His throne,” and from Jesus Christ (1:4-5). Christ “holds the seven Spirits of God” (3:1); seven lamps of fire before the throne “are the seven Spirits of God” (4:5); and the Lamb’s seven eyes “represent the seven Spirits of God sent out into all the earth” (5:6).

Because the greeting sets the seven Spirits between the Father and Jesus Christ, many readers take them as the Holy Spirit in his fullness, seven being the number of completeness; the picture draws on the seven lamps and seven eyes of Zechariah 4:2-10 and the sevenfold Spirit of Isaiah 11:2 in its Greek form. Others take them as seven chief angels who stand before God (compare 8:2).
The ordinary word for God. In Hebrew, Elohim (a plural form used with singular verbs); in Greek, theos. The Gospels use it constantly, and John 1:1 says the Word was God.

God’s personal name, revealed to Moses at the burning bush. It was considered too holy to speak, so Jews said Adonai (“Lord”) instead, and most English Bibles print LORD in capitals. In the Greek Old Testament it became kyrios, the same word applied to Jesus.

A title of honor meaning master or lord. For God it is Adonai in Hebrew. In the Gospels, kyrios is used as a polite “sir” and also as a title of divinity. Thomas’s confession, “My Lord and my God,” is the climax of John.
In Romans “Jesus is Lord” is the confession that saves (10:9), and Paul applies Joel’s “the name of the Lord” to Jesus (10:13).

In 1 Corinthians “no one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except by the Holy Spirit” (12:3). Paul says there is “one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came” (8:6), applying the name for God to Jesus.
In 2 Corinthians Paul writes “we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord” (4:5), and speaks of “the Lord” who commends (10:18) and who answers his prayer (12:8-9).
In Philippians the hymn ends with every tongue confessing “that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father” (2:11), using the title that the Greek Old Testament gives to God.
In Colossians believers are told to “walk in” Christ Jesus “as Lord” (2:6) and to do everything “in the name of the Lord Jesus” (3:17).

In 1 and 2 Thessalonians “the Lord Jesus Christ” appears in the first line of each letter, and Paul applies Old Testament language about “the Day of the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 5:2; 2 Thessalonians 2:2) to Him.
In 1 Timothy “Christ Jesus our Lord” is the one who strengthened Paul and appointed him to service (1:12), and he is “our Lord Jesus Christ” in the charge at the end (6:14).
In 2 Peter Jesus is “our Lord and Savior” (3:2, 18), and “the Day of the Lord will come like a thief” (3:10).
Jesus consistently speaks of God as Father, and prays to him as Abba, the Aramaic family word for father. It was unusual to address God so directly. He teaches the disciples to pray, “Our Father.”
In Romans Paul says believers “received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (8:15).
In 2 Corinthians God is “the Father of compassion” (1:3) and promises “I will be a Father to you” (6:18).
Galatians 4:6 says “God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, ‘Abba, Father!’” (compare Romans 8:15).
In Ephesians believers have “access to the Father by one Spirit” (2:18), and the Father is the one “from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name” (3:15).
In Philippians “every tongue” will confess Jesus as Lord “to the glory of God the Father” (2:11), and the letter ends “To our God and Father be glory forever and ever” (4:20).

At the burning bush, God told Moses his name was “I AM WHO I AM.” In John, Jesus uses “I am” in the absolute sense, as in “Before Abraham was, I am,” and the crowd picks up stones. He also makes seven “I am” statements with a picture word.
A title for God as above all other powers. It is used by Gabriel when speaking of Jesus, and by demons who recognize him.

A name God used with Abraham and the patriarchs, usually translated “God Almighty.” It stresses his power and sufficiency. The Gospels use the idea when Mary sings that “the Mighty One has done great things for me.”
Literally “LORD of armies,” a title that describes God as commander of heavenly and earthly forces. Common in the prophets, it appears in the Gospels mostly in Old Testament quotations.
James 5:4 says that the cries of the harvesters whose wages were withheld “have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts.” The Greek transliterates the Hebrew word Sabaoth, as in Romans 9:29.

Jesus is the Greek form of the Hebrew Yeshua, a short form of Yehoshua (Joshua), meaning “the LORD saves.” The angel tells Joseph to give the child this name “because he will save his people from their sins.”

Christ is Greek (Christos) for the Hebrew Mashiach, Messiah, meaning “anointed one.” Kings, priests and prophets were anointed with oil. Peter confesses, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” and Matthew opens, “the genealogy of Jesus Christ.”
In 1 Corinthians “Christ” is almost a second name, but Paul also uses it as the title for the crucified and risen Messiah: “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (15:3).
In 2 Corinthians “Christ” is the center of the message: “God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ” (5:19), and Paul fears the church will be led from “devotion to Christ” (11:3).
In Ephesians “Christ” is both a title and a name, and the letter uses it constantly, as in “Christ Jesus” (1:1; 2:6-7, 10, 13) and “the mystery of Christ” (3:4).
In Philippians “Christ” appears 37 times in four short chapters. “To me, to live is Christ” (1:21).
In Colossians “Christ” is the center of the letter. Paul speaks of the mystery as “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (1:27) and says “Christ is all and is in all” (3:11).

Hebrews uses “Christ” in contexts of priesthood, as in “when Christ came as high priest of the good things that have come” (9:11), and of faithfulness: “Christ is faithful as the Son over God’s house” (3:6).

In Israel, “son of God” could mean the king or the nation. In the Gospels, the heavenly voice at Jesus’ baptism and transfiguration calls him “my beloved Son,” demons call him Son of God, and John says he is the only Son who is himself God.
In Romans Paul says Jesus “was declared with power to be the Son of God by His resurrection from the dead” (1:4).
In 2 Corinthians Paul says “the Son of God, Jesus Christ” was proclaimed among the Corinthians, and “in Him it has always been ‘Yes’” (1:19).
Paul says “I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20), and “God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (4:4).
In 1 Thessalonians the church waits “to await His Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead” (1:10).

In Hebrews the Son is the one through whom God made the universe and who “is the radiance of God’s glory” (1:2-3). The writer quotes “You are My Son; today I have become Your Father” (1:5; 5:5). “Jesus the Son of God” is the great high priest (4:14). “Although He was a Son, He learned obedience from what He suffered” (5:8). Those who turn away have “trampled on the Son of God” (10:29).

Jesus’ favorite title for himself, used about eighty times in the Gospels and almost never by anyone else. In Aramaic it can simply mean “a human being,” but Daniel 7 uses it for a figure who comes on the clouds and receives everlasting dominion. Jesus uses it for his earthly work, his suffering and his return in glory.
In Revelation John sees “One like the Son of Man” among the lampstands (1:13) and seated on a white cloud with a sickle (14:14), in words taken from Daniel 7:13.
f: ὁ υἱὸς τοῦ ἀνθρώπου (ho huios tou anthrōpou)

t: A title for the promised king from David’s line. The blind men of Jericho and the crowds at the triumphal entry call Jesus by it, and Matthew begins by calling him son of David.

John the Baptist sees Jesus coming and says, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!” The title draws on the Passover lamb and on Isaiah’s suffering servant, who was led like a lamb to the slaughter.
Paul writes “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (5:7).
Hebrews does not call Jesus a lamb, but it applies sacrificial language to him: he “offered Himself unblemished to God” (9:14) and was “offered once to bear the sins of many” (9:28).
1 Peter 1:19 calls Christ “a lamb without blemish or spot,” whose precious blood paid the price of redemption.
In Revelation “the Lamb” is the main name for Christ, about twenty-eight times, beginning with “a Lamb who appeared to have been slain” (5:6). The Greek word is arnion, not the amnos of John 1:29.

John opens, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God... and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Logos means word, reason or message, and it carried weight in both Jewish and Greek thought.
Hebrews does not call Jesus the Word, but its first lines make the same claim: God “has spoken to us by His Son” (1:2), the Son upholds “all things by His powerful word” (1:3).

1 John begins with “the Word of life” (1:1), echoing the Gospel’s “In the beginning was the Word.” It uses the same Greek word, logos, for “the word of God” that “abides in you” (2:14) and for what the readers heard from the beginning.
Isaiah’s name for the promised child, meaning “God with us.” Matthew applies it to Jesus at his birth, and ends his Gospel with Jesus’ promise, “I am with you always.”

“I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger, and whoever believes in me shall never thirst.” Said in Capernaum after the feeding of the five thousand, in contrast with the manna Israel ate in the wilderness.

“I am the light of the world. Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness but will have the light of life.” Said in the temple at the Feast of Tabernacles, when great lamps were lit, and again before healing the man born blind.
1 John does not use the title, but it carries the idea: “the darkness is fading and the true light is already shining” (2:8).
“I am the door of the sheep... If anyone enters by me, he will be saved.” A shepherd sometimes slept across the opening of the sheepfold so that he was the door.
“I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” The picture of God as shepherd runs through Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34.
1 Peter 2:25 calls Christ “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” and 5:4 “the Chief Shepherd.”
“I am the resurrection and the life. Whoever believes in me, though he die, yet shall he live.” Said to Martha at the tomb of Lazarus just before he raises him.

e.n: The Way, the Truth and the Life
t: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me.” Jesus says this to Thomas in the upper room, when the disciples ask where he is going.
“I am the true vine, and my Father is the vinedresser.” Israel was often pictured as God’s vine, and Jesus says his disciples must abide in him to bear fruit.
Jesus calls himself the bridegroom when asked why his disciples do not fast, and tells parables about waiting for the bridegroom. John the Baptist calls himself the friend of the bridegroom.
In Revelation the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his bride has made herself ready (19:7). The bride is the holy city, the new Jerusalem (21:2, 9-10).

Rabbi, “my great one,” was a respectful address for a teacher. Disciples and others call Jesus Rabbi or Teacher, and Mary Magdalene calls him Rabboni. Jesus tells his followers not to seek the title for themselves.
Demons recognize Jesus with this title. Peter, speaking for the Twelve in John 6, also calls him “the Holy One of God.”
The Magi ask where the king of the Jews has been born, and Pilate asks Jesus whether he is. The sign above the cross reads, “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews,” in three languages.
After the feeding of the five thousand, the crowd says, “This is indeed the Prophet who is to come into the world,” thinking of the prophet like Moses. Jesus calls himself a prophet in Nazareth.
Jesus says, “The Son of Man came not to be served but to serve,” and Matthew sees him as Isaiah’s servant. He washes his disciples’ feet.
In Acts the early believers call Jesus God’s Servant (pais), a title taken from Isaiah.
In Philippians Christ takes “the form of a servant” (2:7). The Greek word is doulos, a slave, and the passage echoes the servant of Isaiah 52-53 in its movement from humbling to exaltation.
From Nazareth, where Jesus grew up. It is also a title used on the cross. Nathanael asked, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”

God’s Spirit, who fills John the Baptist, Elizabeth, Zechariah, Mary and Simeon in Luke, descends on Jesus at his baptism and is promised to the disciples. John gives the Spirit several titles: Helper (Paraclete), Spirit of truth.
In Acts he is also called “the Spirit of Jesus” and “the Spirit of the Lord.”
2 Corinthians has the “Spirit of the living God” (3:3), the “pledge” of the Spirit (1:22; 5:5), and “the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” (13:14).
In Ephesians the Spirit is “the promised Holy Spirit” (1:13), “the Holy Spirit of God” (4:30) and the “Spirit of wisdom and revelation” (1:17).
In Titus the Spirit brings “renewal” and is “poured out on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior” (3:5-6).
Peter calls Jesus “the Author of life,” using a Greek word that also means pioneer, leader or founder. He is the one who goes first and opens the way for others.
Hebrews uses the same Greek word, archegos, in 2:10 (“the author of their salvation”) and 12:2 (“the author and perfecter of our faith”).
In Acts Peter, Stephen and Paul call Jesus “the Holy and Righteous One” or “the Righteous One” to say that an innocent man was rejected and God raised him.
1 John 2:1 names Jesus Christ “the Righteous One,” and 2:20 speaks of “the Holy One” (most take this as Christ).
At Cornelius’s house Peter says Jesus Christ is “Lord of all,” which means he is Lord of Gentiles as well as Jews.

e.n: Judge of the living and the dead
t: Peter and Paul both say God has appointed Jesus as judge of the living and the dead.
In 2 Timothy 4:1 Paul charges Timothy “in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead.”
James says “the Judge is standing at the door” (5:9) and that there is “only one Lawgiver and Judge” (4:12); he does not say whether he means the Father or the Lord Jesus.
Peter tells the council that God exalted Jesus “as Leader and Savior,” and Paul says God has brought to Israel a Savior, Jesus, as he promised.
In Philippians “we eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ” (3:20).
In 1 Thessalonians Jesus is “our deliverer from the coming wrath” (1:10).
In 1 Timothy God is called “our Savior” (1:1; 2:3; 4:10) and “Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1:15).
In 2 Timothy Paul speaks of “the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death” (1:10).
In Titus Jesus is “Christ Jesus our Savior” (1:4), “our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (2:13) and “Jesus Christ our Savior” (3:6), while God the Father is also “our Savior” (1:3; 2:10; 3:4).

Paul says God predestined believers “to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers” (8:29). Firstborn here means the first and the head of a family, and it ties Christ’s resurrection to the future of those who belong to him.
In Colossians the Son is “the firstborn over all creation” (1:15) and “firstborn from among the dead” (1:18).

e.n: The one to come (the second Adam)
t: Paul calls Adam “a pattern of the One to come” (5:14) and sets the disobedience of the one man against “the obedience of the one man” through whom “the many will be made righteous” (5:19). Later writers called Christ the second or last Adam.
Paul’s regular greeting and closing name for Jesus in Romans. He gives him all three names together, “Jesus Christ our Lord,” when he says the Son was “declared with power” by his resurrection (1:4).
In 2 Corinthians Paul ends the letter with “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ” (13:14), and says the day of “our Lord Jesus” will be the day of boasting (1:14).
Ephesians begins and ends with “the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:2) and “our Lord Jesus Christ with an undying love” (6:24).
Philippians begins with “the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:2) and ends with “the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ” (4:23).

Paul says “we preach Christ crucified, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Gentiles” (1:23), and that he “resolved to know nothing while I was with you except Jesus Christ and Him crucified” (2:2). The cross is the center of his preaching, not a detail.
Paul reminds the Galatians that “Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified” before their eyes (Galatians 3:1), and speaks of “the offense of the cross” (5:11).

e.n: The power of God and the wisdom of God
t: To “those who are called, both Jews and Greeks,” Paul says Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1:24). Later he says Christ “has become for us wisdom from God: our righteousness, holiness, and redemption” (1:30).
Paul says that “None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (2:8). The title joins the cross and the glory of God in one phrase.
Paul tells the church to clear out the old leaven because “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (5:7). The picture links Christ’s death with the lamb of the Exodus.
1 Peter 1:18-19 does not use the word Passover, but describes Christ as “a lamb without blemish or spot,” as the Law required of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:5).

Paul says Israel in the wilderness “drank from the spiritual rock that accompanied them, and that rock was Christ” (10:4). He reads the water from the rock (Exodus 17; Numbers 20) as a sign of Christ’s presence with his people.

Paul quotes “The first man Adam became a living being” and adds “the last Adam a life-giving spirit” (15:45). Adam brought death to all, and Christ brings life to all who are in him: “as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (15:22).

e.n: Firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep
t: Paul calls the risen Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (15:20, 23). The firstfruits were the first part of the harvest, offered to God as a pledge of the rest.

e.n: The God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ
t: Paul begins “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort” (1:3). Near the end of his boasting he swears by the same title: “The God and Father of the Lord Jesus, who is forever worthy of praise, knows that I am not lying” (11:31). God is known in relation to Jesus.
Ephesians opens with the same blessing: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1:3), and calls him “the glorious Father” (1:17).
Philippians ends, “To our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen” (4:20).
1 Peter 1:3 opens its praise with nearly the same words as 2 Corinthians 1:3 and Ephesians 1:3: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ!”

Paul says “Now the Lord is the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (3:17), and ends the chapter with “the Lord, who is the Spirit” (3:18). He also calls the Spirit “the Spirit of the living God” (3:3). Scholars differ on how to read “the Lord” here, but Paul clearly joins the Spirit with the Lord’s presence and glory.

Paul says Satan blinds unbelievers “so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God” (4:4). The word is eikon, an exact likeness, as on a coin. To see Christ is to see God: “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ” (4:6).
In Colossians “the Son is the image of the invisible God” (1:15), and the new self is renewed “in the image of its Creator” (3:10).

Paul says “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God” (5:21). The title shows Jesus as sinless, which is why his death can stand in for others.

e.n: Rich and poor: the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ
t: Paul asks the Corinthians to “know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though He was rich, yet for your sakes He became poor, so that you through His poverty might become rich” (8:9). The letter closes with the same words: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ” (13:14).

Paul says “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. The Scripture does not say, ‘and to seeds,’ meaning many, but ‘and to your seed,’ meaning One, who is Christ” (3:16). Because “you are all one in Christ Jesus,” believers are also “Abraham’s seed and heirs according to the promise” (3:28-29).

Paul writes, “because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of His Son into our hearts, crying out, ‘Abba, Father!’” (4:6). The Spirit is named by his relation to Jesus, as he is in Romans 8:9 (“the Spirit of Christ”). The Spirit lets believers address God as Jesus did.

Ephesians 1:6 says God’s grace “He has freely given us in the Beloved One.” The title echoes the voice at Jesus’ baptism, “This is My beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17). Believers are called “beloved children” in 5:1, and they are loved because they are in the One whom the Father loves.
In Colossians God “brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son” (1:13).

God “made Him head over everything for the church, which is His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all” (1:22-23). Believers are to “grow up into Christ Himself, who is the head” (4:15), and “the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior” (5:23). The Greek word kephale means head, and scholars debate whether it carries the sense of authority, source, or both.
In Colossians “He is the head of the body, the church” (1:18), and “the head over every ruler and authority” (2:10).

“For He Himself is our peace, who has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility” (2:14). Paul does not say that Christ brings peace, but that he is peace. Gentiles who were far away and Jews who were near (2:17) are both reconciled to God “in one body through the cross” (2:16).

e.n: The Father from whom every family is named
t: Paul bows “before the Father, from whom every family in heaven and on earth derives its name” (3:14-15). In Greek there is a wordplay: pater (father) and patria (family). Every family on earth takes its meaning from the Father of all. In 4:6 he is “one God and Father of all, who is over all and through all and in all.”

Philippians 2:6 says Christ was “existing in the form of God” and “did not consider equality with God something to be grasped.” The Greek word morphe, “form,” points to the real nature that shows itself, not a mask. The same word is used in “the form of a servant” (2:7). In the passage Christ shows his equality with God by giving himself up, not by holding on to it. Christians have read this verse as one of the clearest statements of Christ’s deity and preexistence, and scholars debate the meaning of “grasped.”

“We eagerly await a Savior from there, the Lord Jesus Christ” (3:20). Paul gives Jesus two titles that the Roman world also gave its emperors, “Savior” and “Lord.” Philippi was a colony that looked to Rome. Paul tells the church to look to heaven. The Savior’s work is bodily: he “will transform our lowly bodies to be like His glorious body” (3:21).

Paul prays that “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (4:7), and promises that “the God of peace will be with you” (4:9). He speaks of “my God” at the start (1:3) and the end (4:19), the God who will “supply all your needs according to His glorious riches in Christ Jesus.” The letter closes, “To our God and Father be glory forever and ever. Amen” (4:20).
In 1 Thessalonians Paul prays, “may the God of peace Himself sanctify you completely” (5:23).

Colossians 1:15 calls the Son “the firstborn over all creation” and 1:18 calls Him “the beginning and firstborn from among the dead.” In the Old Testament “firstborn” (prototokos) is a rank as well as an order of birth. God calls Israel “my firstborn” (Exodus 4:22), and God promises to make the king of David’s line his firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth (Psalm 89:27). “Over” means He holds the rank of heir and ruler, and the second use shows that He is the first of many who rise from the dead. Some in the early church argued that “firstborn” meant that the Son was created, but the next verse says that “in Him all things were created,” so He is not one of them.

e.n: All the fullness of the Deity
t: Paul says that “God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him” (1:19), and “in Christ all the fullness of the Deity dwells in bodily form” (2:9). The Greek word pleroma, “fullness,” is used for the whole of something. Paul adds that the Colossians “have been made complete in Christ” (2:10), using the same root. The word “bodily” is stressed, so God’s fullness is not a spirit far away but is in a body. The same letter says that reconciliation comes “by Christ’s physical body through death” (1:22).

Paul tells the Colossians that “your life is now hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, who is your life, appears, then you also will appear with Him in glory” (3:3-4). The title says that Christ is not only the giver of life but the content of it. It stands beside “to me, to live is Christ” (Philippians 1:21) and “Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). Hidden now, the life will be seen at His appearing.

e.n: Jesus our deliverer from the coming wrath
t: Paul says the Thessalonians await God’s Son from heaven, “whom He raised from the dead—Jesus our deliverer from the coming wrath” (1 Thessalonians 1:10). The Greek verb (rhyomai) means to rescue or pull out of danger. The Son who is coming is the one who rescues from judgment. The statement stands at the end of a sentence that begins with turning from idols, so it sums up the gospel in one line: turn to God, serve Him and wait for His Son.

Paul closes the second letter with a prayer: “Now may the Lord of peace Himself give you peace at all times and in every way. The Lord be with all of you” (2 Thessalonians 3:16). In the first letter the same kind of prayer is addressed to “the God of peace” (1 Thessalonians 5:23). Here the title is given to the Lord, who is Jesus in the letter’s usage (see 3:12, 18). The prayer follows a chapter about discipline and conflict in the church.

e.n: The one mediator between God and men
t: Paul writes, “there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all” (1 Timothy 2:5-6). A mediator (mesites) stands between two parties. The word is used of Moses in Galatians 3:19-20 and of Jesus in Hebrews 8:6, 9:15 and 12:24. “Ransom” is antilytron, which occurs only here, and goes with Jesus’ words in Mark 10:45. Paul stresses both His humanity (“the man”) and His offering of Himself.
Hebrews uses mesites for Jesus three times: “the covenant He mediates is better” (8:6), “Christ is the mediator of a new covenant” (9:15), and “Jesus the mediator of a new covenant” (12:24).

The letter opens with “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the command of God our Savior and of Christ Jesus our hope” (1 Timothy 1:1). Hope here is a person, not an event. Paul can say “we have set our hope on the living God” (4:10), and rich people are told to put their hope “in God” (6:17). The greeting asks for “grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Christ Jesus our Lord” (1:2). In Paul’s letters, “mercy” is added to the usual “grace and peace” only in 1 and 2 Timothy.

Two outbursts of praise frame the letter. The first is “Now to the King eternal, immortal, and invisible, the only God, be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen” (1 Timothy 1:17). The second names God as “the blessed and only Sovereign One—the King of kings and Lord of lords” who “alone is immortal and dwells in unapproachable light. No one has ever seen Him, nor can anyone see Him” (6:15-16). Rulers of the time took such titles for themselves, and the praise gives them to God alone.

James calls God “the Father of the heavenly lights, with whom there is no change or shifting shadow” (1:17). The “lights” are probably the sun, moon and stars that God made on the fourth day (Genesis 1:14-18; Psalm 136:7). They rise and set and change, but their maker does not. The Greek has two rare words, parallage (“variation”) and aposkiasma (“shadow”), and the manuscripts differ at the end of the verse, so translations vary. The point is the contrast with 1:13-15: God is the source of every good gift, never of temptation.

“There is only one Lawgiver and Judge, the One who is able to save and destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?” (4:12). The Greek nomothetes, “lawgiver,” is found only here in the New Testament. In the context James has been warning against slandering a brother (4:11), and he says that to judge a brother is to take the place of the lawgiver. Only God, who made the law and can save or destroy, has that place. The same thought appears at the end of the letter, where the Judge “is standing at the door” (5:9).

Peter promises that “when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away” (5:4). The Greek archipoimen is found only here in the New Testament. Earlier in the letter Peter calls Jesus “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (2:25), using a title for a person who watches over a flock, from episkopos, the word translated “overseer” in other letters. The picture goes back to Ezekiel 34, where God promises to be the shepherd of his scattered flock, and to Jesus’ words, “I am the good shepherd” (John 10:11). Hebrews 13:20 calls him “that great Shepherd of the sheep.” Peter was himself told by the risen Jesus to “feed My sheep” (John 21:17).

“As you come to Him, the living stone, rejected by men but chosen and precious in God’s sight” (1 Peter 2:4). Peter takes a title from three Old Testament texts: the stone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16), the stone the builders rejected that became the cornerstone (Psalm 118:22), and the stone of stumbling (Isaiah 8:14). “Living” is Peter’s own addition, and it makes the stone a person who is alive by his resurrection. “To you who believe, then, this stone is precious. But to those who do not believe,” he becomes a stone of stumbling (2:7-8). The Greek akrogoniaios, “cornerstone,” is found only here and in Ephesians 2:20.

“So then, those who suffer according to God’s will should entrust their souls to their faithful Creator and continue to do good” (1 Peter 4:19). It is the only place in the New Testament where God is called ktistes, “creator,” in this way. For Peter, the God who made the world and the readers’ bodies is faithful to look after the souls of those who suffer for doing good. The title joins the faithful God of the Old Testament (Deuteronomy 7:9) to Jesus’ words on the cross, “Father, into Your hands I commit My spirit” (Luke 23:46).

“And after you have suffered for a little while, the God of all grace, who has called you to His eternal glory in Christ, will Himself restore you, secure you, strengthen you, and establish you” (1 Peter 5:10). The title occurs only here. Peter ends the main part of his letter with a prayer in which four verbs describe what God does after a time of suffering: restore, secure, strengthen, establish. “A little while” is the same phrase that began the letter (1:6). The letter ends by telling the readers that “this is the true grace of God. Stand firm in it” (5:12).

Hebrews is the only New Testament book that calls Jesus a high priest. He is “a merciful and faithful high priest in service to God, in order to make atonement for the sins of the people” (2:17), “the apostle and high priest whom we confess” (3:1), and “a great high priest who has passed through the heavens” (4:14). The Greek word archiereus occurs seventeen times in the letter. The writer builds the case in three steps. A high priest must be appointed from among people and able to “deal gently” with the ignorant, and he must be called by God, “just as Aaron was” (5:1-4); Jesus was called, “You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek” (5:6). He has shared human life and was tempted (4:15). And he is “holy, innocent, undefiled, set apart from sinners, and exalted above the heavens,” so he does not need to offer sacrifice for himself (7:26-27). Because he lives forever, “He is able to save completely those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them” (7:25).

e.n: Author and perfecter of our faith
t: Two titles in Hebrews use the Greek idea of one who goes ahead and leads others to a goal. In 2:10 God makes “the author of their salvation perfect through suffering,” and in 12:2 Jesus is “the author and perfecter of our faith.” The first word, archegos, is also used in Acts 3:15 and 5:31 and can be translated “pioneer,” “founder,” “leader” or “author.” The second, teleiotes, occurs only here. Together they present Jesus as the first runner who has completed the course (compare “forerunner” in 6:20) and as the one who makes it possible for others to finish. In Hebrews 12 this is set at the end of the list of the faithful in chapter 11, where the writer says they did not receive what was promised “so that together with us they would be made perfect” (11:40).

e.n: Our great God and Savior Jesus Christ
t: Paul writes that believers await “the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:13). Many translators and scholars read this as one person, Jesus, who is called both “God” and “Savior,” because a single article governs both titles in the Greek. Others read two persons, “the great God and our Savior, Jesus Christ,” and place the Father in the first title. The question is a grammatical one, and 2 Peter 1:1 raises the same issue. In either reading, Titus uses “Savior” six times in 46 verses, of God the Father (1:3; 2:10; 3:4) and of Christ Jesus (1:4; 2:13; 3:6), as if the two share the work of saving.

Paul looks for “the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous Judge, will award to me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:8). Earlier he charges Timothy “in the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and the dead, and in view of His appearing and His kingdom” (4:1). Paul’s own case was judged by Roman courts. He looks past them to a Judge who will be just and who will give the crown “not only to me, but to all who crave His appearing.” Acts 10:42 and 17:31 also describe Jesus as the one appointed to judge.

Paul says God “has revealed this grace through the appearing of our Savior, Christ Jesus, who has abolished death and illuminated the way to life and immortality through the gospel” (2 Timothy 1:10).
