The Greek word for “appearing” (epiphaneia) is used here for his first coming, and in 4:1 and 4:8 for his return. The word was also used of the appearance of a god or the arrival of a ruler. Titus 2:11-14 uses the word for both the first and the second appearing.

In Titus the first appearance is “the grace of God has appeared” (2:11) and “the kindness of God our Savior and His love for mankind appeared” (3:4). The second is “the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ” (2:13).

e.n: Our God and Savior Jesus Christ
t: The letter opens by writing “to those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours” (1:1). In the Greek, one article stands before both “God” and “Savior,” which is why most translators and many scholars take both titles to describe Jesus Christ, and so to call him God. A few translators read it as two persons, “our God and the Savior, Jesus Christ.” The same sort of phrase appears in Titus 2:13.

“Savior” is a favorite title in 2 Peter and is always used of Jesus: “our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ” (1:11; 2:20; 3:18), and “our Lord and Savior” (3:2). The Greek word soter occurs five times in the short letter.

“I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is and was and is to come—the Almighty” (1:8). Alpha and omega are the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, so the title means the beginning and the end of everything. God says it again from the throne (21:6). In the last chapter Jesus says it of himself: “I am the Alpha and the Omega, the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End” (22:13).

The title echoes Isaiah, where the Lord says, “I am the first and I am the last” (Isaiah 44:6; 48:12). That Revelation gives the same title to God and to Jesus is one of the clearest ways the book shows who Jesus is. Christ also calls himself “the First and the Last” in the vision of chapter 1 (1:17) and in the letter to Smyrna (2:8).

e.n: The Lion of the tribe of Judah
t: An elder tells John, “Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed to open the scroll and its seven seals” (5:5). The titles come from Jacob’s blessing of Judah as a lion’s cub, from whom the scepter would not depart (Genesis 49:9-10), and from Isaiah’s shoot from the stump of Jesse, the root of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1, 10).

Both titles mark Jesus as the promised king from David’s line. Jesus calls himself “the Root and the Offspring of David” in 22:16. Yet when John turns to see the Lion he sees a slain Lamb (5:6). The book never pictures Christ as a lion again; it shows his power through the Lamb.

e.n: King of kings and Lord of lords
t: The rider on the white horse has a name written on his robe and on his thigh: “KING OF KINGS AND LORD OF LORDS” (19:16). The Lamb is given the same title when the ten kings make war on him (17:14). In Daniel the king of Babylon is called “king of kings” (Daniel 2:37), and in Deuteronomy the Lord is “God of gods and Lord of lords” (Deuteronomy 10:17).

Paul uses a form of the title for God in 1 Timothy 6:15. In a world where the emperor claimed to rule the kings of the earth, Revelation gives the title to Jesus and shows the kings of the earth either making war on him or bringing their glory into his city (21:24).

e.n: Faithful and True, the Word of God
t: Heaven opens and a white horse appears. “its rider is called Faithful and True” (19:11). His eyes are like a blazing fire, on his head are many crowns, and he has a name written that only he knows. He is dressed in a robe dipped in blood, “and His name is The Word of God” (19:13). A sharp sword comes from his mouth (19:15).

Christ calls himself “the faithful and true Witness” in the letter to Laodicea (3:14), and John’s Gospel begins with the Word who was with God (John 1:1). The robe is dipped in blood before the battle begins, which many take as his own blood; the sword from his mouth is his word. The rider defeats the armies of the beast with no battle described at all (19:19-21).

In the last chapter Jesus says, “I am the Root and the Offspring of David, the bright Morning Star” (22:16). The morning star, the planet Venus seen before dawn, announces that the night is almost over. Balaam foresaw “a star will come forth from Jacob” (Numbers 24:17), and 2 Peter 1:19 speaks of the morning star rising in believers’ hearts.

To the church in Thyatira Christ promises, “I will give him the morning star” (2:28): the one who overcomes will receive Christ himself. Roman emperors were sometimes compared to the star of dawn; Revelation gives the title to Jesus.

The seventh day, a day of rest from work, kept from Friday sundown to Saturday sundown. It recalls God’s rest after creation and Israel’s rescue from slavery. In the Gospels, many conflicts with Jesus are about what is lawful on the Sabbath, and he says, “The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.”

In Galatians 4:10 Paul criticizes “observing special days and months and seasons and years.” The letter does not list the days, and scholars differ on whether he means Jewish days such as the Sabbath, pagan festivals, or both.

In Colossians Paul says, “let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the body that casts it belongs to Christ” (2:16-17).
Hebrews 4 calls the final rest of God’s people a “Sabbath rest” (4:9) and ties it to God’s own rest on the seventh day (4:4, quoting Genesis 2:2).

The yearly feast recalling the night God passed over Israelite homes in Egypt and freed his people. A lamb was sacrificed and eaten with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. Pilgrims filled Jerusalem. All four Gospels place the death of Jesus at Passover, and the Last Supper is a Passover meal in Matthew, Mark and Luke.
Paul writes to the Corinthians, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (5:7), and tells them to keep “the feast” with sincerity and truth.
1 Peter 1:18-19 describes Christ as “a lamb without blemish or spot,” in the language of the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:5).
A seven-day feast right after Passover, when no leaven (yeast) was eaten, recalling the haste of leaving Egypt. By Jesus’ day the two were treated almost as one eight-day festival.

Paul uses the removal of leaven as a picture: “Get rid of the old leaven, that you may be a new unleavened batch” (5:7), and “let us keep the feast, not with the old bread, leavened with malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and of truth” (5:8).

A feast during the week of Unleavened Bread when the first sheaf of the barley harvest was brought to the priest. The Gospels place the resurrection on “the first day of the week” after Passover, and Paul later calls Christ the firstfruits of those who have died.
Paul calls Christ “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep” (15:20, 23) and Stephanas and his household “the first converts in Achaia” (16:15).

James 1:18 says that God “chose to give us birth through the word of truth, that we would be a kind of firstfruits of His creation,” using Israel’s offering of the first of the harvest as a picture of believers.

Fifty days after Passover, Israel celebrated the wheat harvest and (in later Jewish tradition) the giving of the law at Sinai. In Acts, the Spirit comes on the disciples on this day. Jesus does not mention it by name in the Gospels, but he promises the Spirit.
Paul writes from Ephesus, “I will stay in Ephesus until Pentecost, because a great door for effective work has opened to me” (16:8-9).

A day marked by trumpet blasts at the start of the seventh month, opening the autumn feast season and calling Israel to prepare for the Day of Atonement. Later Jewish tradition calls it Rosh Hashanah.

The holiest day of the year, when the high priest entered the Most Holy Place to make atonement for himself and the nation, and the scapegoat carried sins into the wilderness. The Gospels do not describe it, but the temple curtain torn at Jesus’ death and the book of Hebrews connect it to his sacrifice.

Hebrews builds its picture of Jesus’ work on this day. The high priest “entered the second room, and then only once a year, and never without blood” (9:7), and Christ entered “once for all by His own blood” (9:12). Hebrews 13:11 recalls that the bodies of the sin offering were “burned outside the camp.”
1 John 2:2 and 4:10 call Jesus “the atoning sacrifice for our sins,” using a word (hilasmos) that belongs to the vocabulary of atonement.

A week-long autumn harvest feast when people lived in leafy booths to remember the wilderness years. Each day water was carried from the pool of Siloam to the altar and the temple courts were lit with great lamps. John 7 and 8 set Jesus’ teaching on living water and “the light of the world” in this feast.

An eight-day winter feast of lights commemorating the rededication of the temple in 164 BC after the Maccabean revolt. It is not in the Old Testament. John says Jesus was in Jerusalem at the Feast of Dedication, walking in Solomon’s Colonnade, when he said, “I and the Father are one.”

A joyful feast recalling how Esther and Mordecai saved the Jews from Haman’s plot. Some scholars think “a feast of the Jews” in John 5:1 could be Purim, but the Gospel does not say which feast it was.

Every seventh year the land was to rest and debts were released. Every fiftieth year, the Jubilee, slaves were freed and land returned to its family. Jesus’ first sermon at Nazareth uses Isaiah’s language of “proclaiming the year of the Lord’s favor.”
The day before the Sabbath (Friday), when food was prepared and work finished. The Gospels use it to date the crucifixion and burial, which had to be done before sundown when the Sabbath began.

e.n: The first day of the week
t: The day after the Sabbath. All four Gospels place the discovery of the empty tomb on this day, and Christians came to gather on it, calling it the Lord’s Day.
Paul tells the Corinthians “On the first day of every week, each of you should set aside a portion of his income” (16:2). It is one of the earliest hints that Christians were meeting on that day.
Revelation 1:10 speaks of “the Lord’s day,” the first use of that name for the day of the resurrection. John was in the Spirit on that day when he heard the voice behind him.
Many pious Jews fasted on Mondays and Thursdays. The Pharisee in Jesus’ parable says, “I fast twice a week.” Jesus teaches that fasting should be private and sincere, not for show.

A covenant is a solemn, binding agreement, often sealed with a sacrifice or a meal, between two parties. The Bible tells the story of God’s relationship with his people through a series of covenants, each building on the one before. The Greek word is diatheke, and the Latin word for it is testamentum, which is where “Testament” in Old and New Testament comes from.
Paul links the “Yes” of God’s promises in Christ to the new covenant: “all the promises of God are ‘Yes’ in Christ” (1:20).

Hebrews uses the word diatheke (“covenant”) seventeen times, more than any other New Testament book. In 9:15-17 it plays on the double sense of the word, which can also mean “will”: “a will does not take effect until the one who made it has died.”
After the flood, God promised never again to destroy the earth by flood and set the rainbow in the clouds as the sign. It was made with Noah, his descendants and every living creature.
1 Peter 3:20-21 recalls the flood and says that “only eight souls were saved through water,” and compares the water to baptism. Peter does not mention the rainbow.
2 Peter 2:5 and 3:5-6 recall the flood and Noah, “a preacher of righteousness.”

God promised Abraham land, countless descendants and that all nations would be blessed through him. Circumcision was the sign. Luke has Mary and Zechariah both celebrate God remembering this covenant, and John the Baptist warns that being Abraham’s children is not enough.
In Romans Paul says the promise to Abraham “was not given through the law, but through the righteousness that comes by faith,” so that Abraham is “the father of us all” (4:13, 16).

Galatians 3 argues that the promise to Abraham stands: “Even a human covenant, once it is ratified, cannot be canceled or amended” (3:15), and the law “does not revoke the covenant previously established by God” (3:17). Believers are “heirs according to the promise” (3:29).
In Ephesians Gentiles were once “strangers to the covenants of the promise” (2:12), and are now “fellow partakers of the promise in Christ Jesus” (3:6).
Hebrews recalls that God “swore by Himself” in confirming the promise to Abraham (6:13-18), and that Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek (7:1-10).
James 2:21-23 recalls Abraham’s offering of Isaac and the verse “Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness,” and says that he was called a friend of God.

At Mount Sinai, God gave Israel the law through Moses, beginning with the Ten Commandments, and the people agreed to obey. Moses sealed it with blood. Jesus says he has not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it.
Paul calls the ministry of Sinai the “ministry of death, which was engraved in letters on stone,” which came with such glory that “the Israelites could not gaze at the face of Moses” (3:7).
In Galatians 4 Paul says “One covenant is from Mount Sinai and bears children into slavery: This is Hagar” (4:24). In chapter 3 he says the law came 430 years after the promise (3:17).

Hebrews compares the first covenant, sealed by blood in Exodus 24, to the new: “That is why even the first covenant was not put into effect without blood” (9:18). At Sinai the people saw a mountain “burning with fire” (12:18); the readers have come to Mount Zion instead.
1 Peter 1:2 speaks of the “sprinkling by His blood” in language from the sealing of the covenant at Sinai (Exodus 24:6-8), and 2:9 gives the church the titles God gave Israel there.
God promised David that his house, throne and kingdom would last forever and that his descendant would be God’s son. The Gospels open by tracing Jesus to David, and crowds greet him as Son of David.
Hebrews reads 2 Samuel 7:14 (“I will be His Father, and He will be My Son”) of Jesus in 1:5 and applies royal psalms to him in 1:8-13.

Jeremiah promised a new covenant in which God would put his law in people’s hearts and forgive their sin. At the Last Supper, Jesus passes the cup and says it is the new covenant in his blood, poured out for many.
In Romans Paul ties Israel’s future to the promise, “The Deliverer will come from Zion; He will remove godlessness from Jacob,” and calls God’s gifts and call “irrevocable” (11:26, 29).
Paul gives the oldest written account of the words of Jesus over the cup: “This cup is the new covenant in My blood; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of Me” (11:25).

2 Corinthians 3 is Paul’s fullest comparison of the two covenants. He is a minister of “a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (3:6), and its ministry “endures” (3:11). He ties it to the Spirit who writes on the heart.

Hebrews quotes the whole promise of Jeremiah 31:31-34 in 8:8-12, the longest Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, and the key lines again in 10:16-17. The writer concludes that “By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete” (8:13). Jesus is “the mediator of a new covenant” (9:15; 12:24), with a “guarantee of a better covenant” (7:22). The “blood of the eternal covenant” brought Jesus back from the dead (13:20).

Priests descended from Aaron and offered sacrifices at the temple, and Levites assisted them with music, guarding and teaching. Zechariah was a priest. In the good Samaritan parable a priest and a Levite pass by the man on the road.

Hebrews contrasts the Levitical priests with Jesus. Priests “collect a tenth from the people” (7:5), are “mortal men” and “death prevented them from continuing in office” (7:8, 23), and they “serve at the tabernacle” (13:10). Jesus is a priest from Judah “in the order of Melchizedek.”

The chief priest of Israel, who alone entered the Most Holy Place on the Day of Atonement. In Jesus’ time the Romans appointed the office. Annas had held it earlier, and Caiaphas was high priest the year Jesus died.
Hebrews gives the fullest New Testament account of the Jewish high priest’s duties and calls Jesus the “great high priest” (4:14). See “Great high priest.”

The supreme Jewish council in Jerusalem, made up of about seventy elders, priests and scribes, with the high priest presiding. It tried Jesus and sent him to Pilate. Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea were members.

Respected leaders from leading families who sat with the chief priests and scribes in the council, and who also led local communities. Together these three groups question Jesus’ authority and condemn him.
James 5:14 asks the sick person to “call the elders of the church to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord.”
1 Peter 5:1-4 asks the elders to “be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you,” not for gain but eagerly, and promises “the crown of glory” when the Chief Shepherd appears.

In 2 John, the writer gives no name but “The elder” (1), the title also used in 3 John. It may be the title of a leader known to the churches, or the word of an older man, and early writers took it to be John.

In 3 John, the writer again calls himself only “The elder” (1). He has enough standing to write to a church, to send workers and to plan a visit, and yet a local leader, Diotrephes, can refuse him (9-10).
Revelation shows twenty-four elders seated on thrones around God’s throne, dressed in white with golden crowns (4:4).
Another word for scribes: experts in the Law of Moses who copied, taught and applied it. A lawyer tests Jesus with the question about eternal life that leads to the good Samaritan parable.
A movement of Jewish nationalists who wanted to drive out the Romans by force. One of the Twelve, Simon, is called the Zealot.

A strict Jewish community with members living by the Dead Sea at Qumran, who produced the Dead Sea Scrolls. They are not named in the Gospels, but they help show the variety of Jewish life in Jesus’ day.
Luke records that Jesus sent out seventy (or seventy-two, depending on the manuscript) of his followers in pairs to the towns he was going to visit, to announce that the kingdom of God had come near.

Large groups of ordinary people who follow Jesus for healing and teaching. Their reactions swing from amazement to confusion, and Jesus has compassion on them because they are like sheep without a shepherd.
Everyone who was not Jewish. Jesus’ ministry is mostly to Jews, but he helps a Roman centurion, a Syrophoenician woman and others, and sends his followers to all nations.

In 3 John 7 the traveling brothers went out “accepting nothing from the Gentiles.” The Greek word here is ethnikos, and it means pagans, people outside the faith, whether or not the workers themselves were Jews.

In the Gospels, “sinners” often means people living outside what the religious leaders thought acceptable, such as tax collectors and prostitutes, rather than only people who had committed obvious wrongs. Jesus eats with them, and says he came to call sinners.

In the Bible, leprosy covers a range of serious skin diseases that made people ritually unclean and forced them to live apart. Jesus touches and heals lepers and sends them to the priests for confirmation.

Roman army officers commanding about a hundred soldiers. The Gospels show them in a good light: the centurion of Capernaum has great faith, and the centurion at the cross says, “Truly this man was the Son of God.”

The largest unit of the Roman army, about six thousand men. When Jesus asks the possessed man his name, he answers, “Legion, for we are many.” Jesus tells Peter that he could call twelve legions of angels.

The Roman official who ruled Judea. In Jesus’ time it was Pontius Pilate (AD 26-36). He lived in Caesarea on the coast but came to Jerusalem for the feasts, to keep order. Only he could order an execution.
The official who organized worship in a local synagogue. Jairus is one, and another is indignant when Jesus heals a woman on the Sabbath.
A local meeting place for prayer, Scripture reading and teaching, found in nearly every town. Jesus regularly taught in synagogues in Galilee, and he was rejected in the one in Nazareth.
James 2:2 calls the readers’ meeting a synagogue (the Greek synagoge), in the passage about the rich man and the poor man.

In the ancient world, widows were among the most vulnerable people. Jesus shows special concern for them: he raises the widow of Nain’s son, praises the widow’s two small coins, and condemns those who devour widows’ houses.
In 1 Timothy the church lists widows over sixty who are “well known for good deeds” and cares for those “truly in need,” while younger widows are advised to marry (5:3-16).
James 1:27 names orphans and widows “in their distress” as the people pure religion cares for.

The early believers’ own name for themselves was “the Way.” Outsiders in Antioch first called them Christians, and officials spoke of them as “the sect of the Nazarenes.” By the end of Acts all three names are in use.

A proselyte was a Gentile who had fully converted to Judaism, including circumcision. A God-fearer, by contrast, attended the synagogue and honored Israel’s God without converting. Both groups are often the first to respond to Paul in a new city.
The governor of a senatorial province, chosen by the Senate for a year. In Acts the proconsuls are Sergius Paulus of Cyprus and Gallio of Achaia. Luke uses the correct title for both.
The governor of a smaller province governed for the emperor, such as Judea. Felix and Festus are called governors in Acts. Both lived at Caesarea and judged Paul there.
The commander of a cohort of about 1,000 men. Claudius Lysias, the tribune of the Jerusalem garrison, saves Paul from the mob, learns that he is a Roman citizen, and sends him to Felix.
Citizens had legal rights across the empire: a fair hearing, freedom from flogging, and the right to appeal to Caesar. Paul uses this status at Philippi, in Jerusalem, and before Festus.
Philippians 3:20 says “our citizenship is in heaven,” and 1:27 tells the church to “conduct yourselves” as citizens (politeuesthe). Philippi was a Roman colony.
City officials in Greek and Roman towns. Thessalonica had politarchs, Philippi had praetors with lictors (officers with rods), and Ephesus had a town clerk who calmed the crowd.
The emperor’s own soldiers. When Paul reaches Rome he is allowed to live in his own rented house with a soldier guarding him, so the guard would hear what Paul said.

In Philippians Paul says, “it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ” (1:13). The Greek word (praitorion) can mean the emperor’s guard, a governor’s headquarters or the palace staff.

The first Christians met in homes, not in church buildings. Paul greets “the church that meets at their house” of Prisca and Aquila (16:5), and the groups around Aristobulus, Narcissus, Asyncritus and others in Romans 16 may have been separate house gatherings in Rome. Gaius also hosted “all the church” in Corinth (16:23).
In Philemon Paul greets “the church that meets at your house” (2), the house of Philemon, probably at Colossae.

In 2 John, the readers are told not to receive a false teacher “into your home” (10). If the “chosen lady” was the head of a house church, the home was the church’s meeting place and the lodging of its guests.

In 3 John, one man can refuse visitors and put people “out of the church” (10), and another, Gaius, can take the same visitors in (5-6). Both are easiest to picture as householders in whose homes believers met.

Slaves and freed people made up a large share of the population of Rome; some scholars estimate about a third. Paul calls himself a servant (doulos, literally a slave) of Christ Jesus (1:1), says believers have “become slaves to righteousness” (6:18), and greets a number of people in Romans 16 whose names were common among slaves and freed people.

In Philippians Paul and Timothy are “servants of Christ Jesus” (1:1), literally slaves, and Christ takes “the form of a servant” (2:7). The letter ends with greetings from “the household of Caesar” (4:22), the emperor’s slaves and freed people.

Paul opens “called to be an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God” (1:1) and defends his place: “Am I not an apostle? Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?” (9:1). He lists apostles first among the gifts God has set in the church (12:28), and says Christ appeared “to James, then to all the apostles,” and last of all to himself, “the least of the apostles” (15:7-9). The word means someone sent, and covers more than the Twelve.
Jude 17 tells its readers to “remember what was foretold by the apostles of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Jude speaks of the apostles as a group he does not belong to.

e.n: Prophets and teachers in the church
t: Paul ranks them after apostles: “first of all apostles, second prophets, third teachers” (12:28). A prophet “speaks to men for their edification, encouragement, and comfort” (14:3). Prophets speak in turn and “the others should weigh carefully what is said” (14:29).

Paul sarcastically calls the visiting teachers who impressed the Corinthians the “super-apostles” (11:5; 12:11). They preached “a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed” (11:4), boasted of being Hebrews, Israelites and descendants of Abraham (11:22), and took advantage of the church (11:20). Paul says they are “false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ” (11:13). Who they were is debated.

The churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. Paul tells the Corinthians how they gave to the poor in Jerusalem out of “deep poverty” (8:2), and how they were glad to help (8:4). Paul had boasted to them about the Corinthians (9:2), and some would travel with him to Corinth (9:4).
In 1 Thessalonians the church at Thessalonica is an example to “all the believers in Macedonia and Achaia” (1:7), and shows love “to all the brothers throughout Macedonia” (4:10).

Titus and two brothers are sent to Corinth ahead of Paul to prepare the collection. One is “praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel” and “was chosen by the churches to accompany us with the offering” (8:18-19). Paul says the purpose is “to avoid any criticism of the way we administer this generous gift” (8:20). He calls them “messengers of the churches, to the glory of Christ” (8:23).

Paul does not name the teachers who troubled the churches. He says “some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ” (1:7), “Those people are zealous for you, but not in a good way” (4:17), “the one who is troubling you will bear the judgment” (5:10), and calls them “those who are agitating you” (5:12). They pressed the Gentile believers to be circumcised (6:12). Scholars rebuild their message only from what Paul says against it.

In Jerusalem, “some false brothers had come in under false pretenses to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us.” Paul says “We did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you” (2:4-5). The letter does not say who they were or how they connect to the teachers in Galatia.

Paul names “James, Cephas, and John—those reputed to be pillars” in Jerusalem (2:9). He says they “added nothing” to him (2:6), saw that he had been entrusted with the gospel to the uncircumcised (2:7), and “gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship” (2:9). The word fits a household or a temple, where pillars bear the weight.

Paul says that “before certain men came from James,” Peter ate with the Gentiles, but when they arrived he withdrew “for fear of those in the circumcision group” (2:12). The letter does not say what message they carried, and Paul never says that James himself held the view of the men who came.

Paul writes “to the churches of Galatia” (1:2), in the plural. They had “received the Spirit” (3:2) and welcomed Paul warmly (4:14-15). The letter does not say which cities they were in. Scholars hold either that they were in the old Celtic territory around Ankara (the north) or in the southern cities of the Roman province, such as Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (the south).

Paul uses this phrase twice. In 2:2 “the spirit who is now at work in the sons of disobedience” is behind the old way of life his readers once followed. In 5:6 “because of such things the wrath of God is coming on the sons of disobedience,” and he adds, “do not be partakers with them” (5:7). It is a Hebrew way of speaking: sons of something share its character. Paul is not drawing a line between types of people but between ways of living, since he says “all of us” once lived that way (2:3).

e.n: Those far away and those near
t: Paul says Gentiles “who once were far away have been brought near through the blood of Christ” (2:13), and that Christ “preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near” (2:17). “Far away” means the nations outside Israel’s covenants, and “near” means Israel. The words echo Isaiah 57:19, which speaks of peace for those far and near.

Philemon ends with greetings from five men. “Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, sends you greetings, as do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke, my fellow workers” (Philemon 23-24). Epaphras is from Colossae (Colossians 4:12) and brought the news of the church to Paul (Colossians 1:7-8). Mark is the cousin of Barnabas and the John Mark of Acts. Aristarchus came from Thessalonica and was with Paul on the voyage to Rome (Acts 27:2). Demas later left Paul (2 Timothy 4:10), and Luke stayed with him to the end (2 Timothy 4:11). The same names, with Jesus called Justus, appear in Colossians 4:10-14.

The Greek word diaspora, “scattering,” was used for the Jews who lived outside the land of Israel: in Babylon after the exile and, by New Testament times, in cities all around the Mediterranean. Jesus’ opponents in John 7:35 wonder whether he will go “where the Jews are dispersed among the Greeks, and teach the Greeks.” Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered by the persecution after Stephen. James is written “to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion” (1:1), and Peter’s first letter has the same word. Whether James means Jewish believers or the church as a whole is debated. The writer Philo of Alexandria says that Jewish colonies stretched from Egypt and Syria to Asia, Greece and beyond the Euphrates.

James writes to believers who are poor and under pressure, and some of whom are fighting among themselves. The letter names no town. The readers face “trials of many kinds” (1:2), are dragged into court by the rich (2:6), have a meeting, literally a synagogue, where seats are given out by rank (2:2-3), and include traders who plan journeys for profit (4:13) and some workers whose wages are withheld (5:4). They have elders to whom the sick are to go (5:14). Many readers place them in Syria, near Antioch, because Acts 15:23 sends a letter with the same Greek greeting to believers there, but the letter does not say.

James says that “not many of you should become teachers... because you know that we who teach will be judged more strictly” (3:1). Teaching was a respected role in the early church (Acts 13:1; 1 Corinthians 12:28; Ephesians 4:11), and a teacher’s words would be heard by many, which is why James warns that a mistake in speech weighs more. By saying “we who teach,” he includes himself.

Peter calls his readers “exiles of the Dispersion” (1:1) and later “foreigners and exiles” (2:11), using two Greek words, parepidemoi and paroikoi, that name people living in a place without the full rights of citizens. Greek inscriptions from the cities of Asia Minor use the word paroikos for people who lived in a city or on its land without being citizens and who could be taxed and could not hold office. Some scholars think many of Peter’s readers were literally in this position, and that the letter tells them that God has given them a place and a house (2:5, 10). Others read the words as a picture of the church’s life in the world, as in Hebrews 11:13 (“strangers and exiles on the earth”). The Old Testament uses the same picture for Abraham (Genesis 23:4) and for Israel in Egypt.

The letter is addressed to a community of believers whom the writer knows well but does not name. They have shown “work and the love” for “the saints” (6:10), endured a painful early period of public abuse and loss (10:32-34), and have leaders who “spoke the word of God” to them (13:7). Now they are tired. The writer says they have become “dull of hearing” (5:11), need milk and not solid food (5:12), are in danger of drifting (2:1), and some have stopped meeting together (10:25). The writer does not accuse them of abandoning the faith but fears that they may. “Even though we speak like this, beloved, we are convinced of better things in your case” (6:9). Where they lived is not stated; see “To whom was Hebrews written?”

Chapter 11 is a gallery of Old Testament figures named for their faith: Abel, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph, Moses and his parents, and Rahab, then Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets (11:4-32). The writer then speaks of unnamed people: some “conquered kingdoms” and “shut the mouths of lions”; others “were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection,” were “stoned,” “sawed in two,” or “went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated” (11:33-37). Their choices are mixed with failures; Samson and Jephthah are included alongside the others, which shows that the list does not claim these people were perfect. The sawing in two may reflect later Jewish tradition about the prophet Isaiah, and the torture that refused release recalls the Maccabean martyrs (2 Maccabees 6-7). The writer says only: “The world was not worthy of them” (11:38).

Hebrews mentions the readers’ leaders three times in chapter 13: “Remember your leaders who spoke the word of God to you. Consider the outcome of their way of life and imitate their faith” (13:7); “Obey your leaders and submit to them, for they watch over your souls as those who must give an account” (13:17); and in the closing greetings, “Greet all your leaders and all the saints” (13:24). The Greek word, hegoumenoi, means “those who lead” and is not an office title. The first group may be earlier leaders who had died, since the writer asks the readers to consider “the outcome of their way of life,” and the others are living leaders who “watch over your souls.” Acts 15:22 uses the same word for Judas and Silas as “leading men” among the brothers.

Twelve men appointed to be with Jesus and to be sent out, matching the twelve tribes of Israel. The four lists in the New Testament differ slightly in the order and minor names. In Acts the eleven choose Matthias, then stand with Peter at Pentecost and lead the church until the Seven are chosen.

e.u: Teachers who stressed the oral tradition
t: A lay movement that stressed purity, tithing, Sabbath-keeping and the “tradition of the elders”. They were respected among ordinary people and clashed with Jesus over Sabbath, table fellowship and authority. In Acts Gamaliel, a Pharisee, advises caution; some Pharisees join the church and argue for circumcision (15:5); Paul says he is a Pharisee (23:6; 26:5). In Philippians 3:5-6 Paul says he was “as to the law, a Pharisee,” “as to zeal, persecuting the church,” and “as to righteousness in the law, faultless.”

A group of wealthy priestly families that controlled the Temple and accepted only the written Torah. They denied the resurrection and the existence of angels. In Acts they arrest Peter and John because they teach the resurrection (4:1-2), and they divide from the Pharisees at Paul’s hearing.
Professional teachers and copyists of Scripture, also called lawyers or teachers of the law. Many belonged to the Pharisees.

The ruling body in Jerusalem, made up of the high priest, senior priests, elders and scribes. It could try cases but needed Rome’s approval to carry out an execution. In Acts the council arrests the apostles, tries Stephen, and hears Paul. Saul carries letters from the chief priest to Damascus.
Political backers of the Herod family. They are named only twice together with the Pharisees, plotting against Jesus.
Local men who bid for the right to collect tolls and customs, often for a share of the money. Hated as collaborators and extortioners, they are often grouped with “sinners” in the Gospels.

e.u: Neighbors of the Jews, kin of Israel
t: Descendants of the northern kingdom’s people, with their own temple on Mount Gerizim and their own Torah. Jews and Samaritans were bitter rivals, which is why Jesus’ parable of the Good Samaritan startled his listeners. In Acts Philip preaches in Samaria and many believe; Peter and John come down and the Spirit is given.

Rome ruled Judea through a prefect and auxiliary troops stationed in Caesarea and in Jerusalem’s Antonia fortress. Soldiers appear as the centurion, the Gethsemane arrest party, the mocking guard and those who cast lots for the clothing. In Acts, Roman officers include the centurion Cornelius, the tribune Lysias, the governors Felix and Festus, and the centurion Julius. In Ephesians 6:10-17 Paul describes God’s armor in terms of a Roman soldier’s gear. He was under their guard when he wrote (Acts 28:16, 20).
Hired and family shepherds who lived outdoors near Bethlehem and across Judea and Galilee. In Luke, they are the first to hear the birth announcement.

Learned men from the east, likely astrologers from Persia or Babylon, who followed a star to Jerusalem and then to Bethlehem with gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh. Matthew does not give a number.

Luke names Mary Magdalene, Joanna and Susanna among the women who funded Jesus’ ministry. They were present at the crucifixion and discovered the empty tomb. In Acts 1:14 the women are with the eleven in the upper room.

The Spirit descends on Jesus at his baptism and leads him into the wilderness. In John, Jesus promises the Spirit as a Helper who will teach the disciples and remind them of all he has said. In Acts the Spirit comes at Pentecost, fills the believers, falls on Samaritans and Gentiles, sends Barnabas and Saul, and guides the mission step by step. Romans 8 is the fullest teaching on the Spirit in Paul: the Spirit gives life, leads God’s children and prays for believers. In 1 Corinthians the Spirit searches all things, “even the deep things of God” (2:10), dwells in the believer’s body as in a temple (6:19), and gives gifts to each “for the common good” (12:7). In 2 Corinthians the Spirit is the “pledge of what is to come” (1:22), writes on hearts “not with ink” (3:3), and “gives life” (3:6). “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (3:17), and the letter ends with “the fellowship of the Holy Spirit” (13:14). In Galatians the Spirit is received “by hearing with faith” (3:2), sent into hearts crying “Abba, Father” (4:6), and produces fruit: “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control” (5:22-23). Paul says “Since we live by the Spirit, let us walk in step with the Spirit” (5:25). In Ephesians believers are “sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (1:13) and have access to the Father “by one Spirit” (2:18). Paul prays that they be strengthened “with power through His Spirit” (3:16), urges them to keep “the unity of the Spirit” (4:3), warns “do not grieve the Holy Spirit” (4:30), says “be filled with the Spirit” (5:18), and calls the Word “the sword of the Spirit” (6:17). Second Timothy 1:14 says to guard the treasure “with the help of the Holy Spirit who dwells in us,” and 1:7 says God has given “a spirit of fear” no place but “of power, love, and self-control.” Titus 3:5-6 speaks of “renewal by the Holy Spirit” and says God “poured out” the Spirit “abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior.”

In 1 John the Spirit is the proof that God remains in the believer: “by the Spirit He has given us” (3:24; 4:13). The letter names “the Spirit of truth” (4:6) and says the Spirit testifies, with the water and the blood (5:6-8).
Jude tells his readers to keep on “praying in the Holy Spirit” (Jude 20), and says the intruders are “devoid of the Spirit” (Jude 19).

Mark and Matthew name four brothers and mention sisters. The Gospels say they did not believe in him during his ministry. James later led the Jerusalem church. In Acts 1:14 they are with the believers, and James leads the Jerusalem church.
The letter of James is traditionally the work of James, the brother of Jesus (1:1), though it does not say so. The letter itself calls its writer “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ.”

The letter of Jude is written by “a brother of James” (Jude 1), by the usual reading the Judas of Mark 6:3. Hegesippus tells of grandsons of Jude who farmed in the land of Israel late in the first century.

Jews who spoke Greek and often came from the Diaspora. Their widows are overlooked in the daily food, which leads to the choice of the Seven. Persecution after Stephen falls most on them, and they carry the message to Antioch.

Seven men of good repute, full of the Spirit and wisdom, chosen by the church and set apart by the apostles’ prayer: Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolaus of Antioch. All have Greek names.

About 120 gather in Acts 1, and about three thousand are added at Pentecost. They meet in the temple and in homes, share possessions, and are known as followers of “the Way” before they are called Christians at Antioch. In Romans the believers are those who are justified by faith, not by works of the law. In 1 Corinthians Paul calls them “the saints” and says they “will judge the world.” In 2 Corinthians they are “a letter from Christ” (3:3), “must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (5:10), and are “a new creation” (5:17). In Galatians they are “sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus” (3:26), “all one in Christ Jesus” (3:28), heirs “according to the promise” (3:29), and called to bear one another’s burdens (6:2). In Ephesians they are chosen “before the foundation of the world” (1:4), saved “by grace” through faith (2:8), “created in Christ Jesus to do good works” (2:10), and “fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (2:19). In Colossians believers are “the elect of God, holy and beloved” (3:12), who have been “raised with Christ” (3:1). In 1 Thessalonians believers are those who “believe that Jesus died and rose again” (4:14), and the Thessalonians are told to “encourage one another” with these words (4:18). First Timothy 4:12 tells Timothy to “set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct, in love, in faith, in purity.” Titus 3:1 asks Titus to “remind the believers” of their duties, and 3:14 says “our people must also learn to devote themselves to good works.”
Non-Jews who attended synagogue and kept parts of the law but were not full converts. Cornelius is one. Luke notes them often as the first Gentiles to listen to Paul in each city.

The two schools that meet Paul in the marketplace. Epicureans taught that the gods do not interfere in human life; Stoics taught that the universe is ordered by a divine reason. Both call Paul a “babbler” and invite him to explain.

Paul and Barnabas appoint elders in each church with prayer and fasting. The elders of Jerusalem join the apostles at the council, and the elders of Ephesus are told by Paul at Miletus to “care for the church of God.” The Ephesian elders came to Paul at Miletus. He told them, “Be shepherds of the church of God,” and warned that “savage wolves will come in among you” (Acts 20:28-29). Ephesians 4:11-16 describes shepherds and teachers whose work is to equip the saints. In 1 Timothy the elders laid their hands on Timothy (4:14), and “elders who lead effectively are worthy of double honor, especially those who work hard at preaching and teaching” (5:17). Timothy is not to be “too quick in the laying on of hands” (5:22). Titus 1:5-9 tells Titus to “appoint elders in every town” and lists what an elder must be. In 1:7 the same man is called an overseer. James 5:14 tells the sick person to call “the elders of the church” to pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord. The Greek word is presbyteroi, and James does not say how many there were or how they were chosen. In 1 Peter 5:1-4 Peter, “a fellow elder,” appeals to the elders to be shepherds of God’s flock “not out of compulsion, but because it is God’s will; not out of greed, but out of eagerness.” He promises that when “the Chief Shepherd appears,” they will receive “the crown of glory that will never fade away.”
Hebrews calls the leaders of its readers hegoumenoi, “those who lead” (13:7, 17, 24).

Paul calls the leaders together on the third day after he arrives. Some are persuaded by what he says from morning to evening, and some do not believe. They tell him they have received no letters about him, but know that this sect is spoken against everywhere. Romans speaks to a church in which Jewish and Gentile believers are learning to live together.

Paul addresses “all in Rome who are loved by God and called to be saints,” a group he has not yet met. The church probably met in several households and began with Jews and converts to Judaism, then grew among Gentiles. Paul says “your faith is being proclaimed all over the world” (1:8) and later greets many of them by name.
If Hebrews was addressed to Rome, the greeting “Those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24) would come from Italians away from home. See “To whom was Hebrews written?”

Paul speaks to a Jewish reader who relies on the law and boasts in God (2:17), and asks what advantage the Jew has (3:1). In chapters 9-11 he grieves over Israel’s unbelief, insists that God has not rejected his people, and says “all Israel will be saved” (11:26).

In Romans 1 Paul describes the Gentile world that turned from God to idols. In Romans 15 he says Christ became “a servant of the circumcised” so that “the Gentiles may glorify God for His mercy,” and describes himself as “a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles.”
Paul warns the Gentile believers in Rome not to boast over the Jewish branches that were broken off, because “You do not support the root, but the root supports you” (11:18).

In Romans 14-15 some believers eat anything and others eat only vegetables, and some keep certain days and others treat all days alike. Paul tells both sides to welcome each other: “Accept him whose faith is weak, without passing judgment on his opinions.” In 1 Corinthians 8 the “strong” know an idol is nothing, and the “weak” are still accustomed to idols and have a weak conscience.
Paul says that “at the present time there is a remnant chosen by grace” (11:5), as in Elijah’s day when God kept seven thousand who had not bowed to Baal.

Paul tells the believers in Rome to “Everyone must submit himself to the governing authorities” (13:1), to pay taxes and revenue, and to give respect and honor to those who are owed them. Romans was written in the early years of Nero’s rule. Titus 3:1 tells Titus to remind believers “to submit to rulers and authorities.”
Quoting Isaiah 52:7, Paul asks, “And how can they preach unless they are sent?” and says “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news.”
Timothy, Lucius, Jason and Sosipater send greetings to Rome, along with Quartus, Gaius and Erastus. Paul calls Lucius, Jason and Sosipater “my fellow countrymen,” which probably means fellow Jews.

Paul greets Prisca and Aquila, Epenetus, Mary, Andronicus and Junia, Ampliatus, Urbanus, Stachys, Apelles, Herodion, Tryphena and Tryphosa, Persis, Rufus, Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, Philologus, Julia, Nereus and Olympas, along with the households of Aristobulus and Narcissus. Many of the names were common among slaves and freed people.

e.u: Those who crucified the Lord of glory
t: Paul says, “None of the rulers of this age understood it. For if they had, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory.” Some take the “rulers” as the human officials who put Jesus to death, others also include the unseen powers behind them.

Paul writes “To the church of God in Corinth, to those sanctified in Christ Jesus and called to be holy.” Most were Gentiles who had worshiped idols (12:2), with some Jews (Acts 18:4-8), and a mix of rich and poor. They were gifted, divided, proud, and loved by Paul, who calls them “my beloved children” (4:14). In 2 Corinthians Paul calls them “our letter, inscribed on our hearts” (3:2), says “Our hearts are open wide” (6:11), asks them to finish their gift for Jerusalem (chapters 8-9), and grieves over the quarreling and sin that remain (12:20-21).

e.u: The church as one body with many parts
t: Paul writes, “Now you are the body of Christ, and each of you is a member of it.” He also says “your bodies are members of Christ” (6:15). The body is made up of Jews and Greeks, slaves and free, with different gifts, and “if one part suffers, every part suffers with it.” In Ephesians the church is “His body, the fullness of Him who fills all in all” (1:23), the “one body” in which Jews and Gentiles are reconciled (2:16), and the body that “grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part” (4:16). Christ is “the head of the church, His body” (5:23). In Colossians Christ “is the head of the body, the church” (1:18). The body “supported and knit together by its joints and ligaments, grows as God causes it to grow” (2:19), and believers are “called as members of one body” (3:15).

In chapter 7 Paul says each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband, and that the husband and wife owe each other their duty. He tells the married, “(not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband,” and gives his own view on mixed marriages with an unbelieving partner.

Paul says “It is good to abstain from sexual relations,” that he wishes all were as he is, and that those who cannot control themselves should marry. He advises the unmarried and widows to remain as they are “because of the present crisis.”

Paul tells slaves, “Do not let it concern you—but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity.” He adds that “he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman,” and that “he who was a free man when he was called is Christ’s slave.”
Paul writes, “in a race all the runners run, but only one receives the prize.” He applies the picture to himself: “I do not run aimlessly; I do not fight like I am beating the air.”

e.u: Apostles who took their wives along
t: Paul asks, “Have we no right to take along a believing wife, as do the other apostles and the Lord’s brothers and Cephas?” Peter (Cephas) and the brothers of Jesus were known to the Corinthians, and the passage suggests they traveled with their wives.

Paul says that “our forefathers were all under the cloud, and that they all passed through the sea.” Yet most of them fell: “Now these things happened to them as examples and were written down as warnings for us, on whom the fulfillment of the ages has come.” Hebrews 3:7-4:13 draws a warning from Israel’s time in the wilderness: the generation that heard God’s voice hardened their hearts at Kadesh and did not enter his rest, and the readers are told not to follow their example of unbelief.
In Hebrews the wilderness generation is a warning: “who were the ones who heard and rebelled? Were they not all those Moses led out of Egypt?” (3:16).
Jude 5 uses the same warning: after the people were brought out of Egypt, “He destroyed those who did not believe.”

e.n: The rich and the poor in Corinth
e.u: Those who ate at the Lord’s Supper
t: Paul says that each one “goes ahead without sharing his meal” at the Lord’s Supper: “While one remains hungry, another gets drunk.” He asks those with homes to eat there, and says some “humiliate those who have nothing.”

e.u: Those who speak for God in the church
t: Paul ranks prophets second after apostles (12:28) and says “he who prophesies is greater than one who speaks in tongues, unless he interprets so that the church may be edified.” He wants prophets to speak in turn, and their words to be weighed.
James holds up the prophets as an example of patience: “Brothers, as an example of patience in affliction, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord” (5:10).

Paul does not forbid speaking in tongues, and says “I wish that all of you could speak in tongues, but I would rather have you prophesy.” He wants tongues to be interpreted, so that the whole church can understand, and says “in the church, I would rather speak five coherent words to instruct others than ten thousand words in a tongue.”

Paul pictures “some who are uninstructed or some unbelievers” coming into the meeting and asks what they would think if everyone spoke in tongues: “will they not say that you are out of your minds?” Prophecy instead convicts the outsider and leads him to worship.

In the creed Paul lists those to whom the risen Christ appeared: “He appeared to Cephas and then to the Twelve,” “more than five hundred brothers at once,” then James, “all the apostles,” and “last of all He appeared to me also, as to one of untimely birth.”

Paul quotes what they say: “His letters are weighty and forceful, but his physical presence is unimpressive, and his speaking is of no account” (10:10). They look at “outward appearances” and “compare themselves with themselves” (10:7, 12). Paul answers that he will be the same in person as in his letters. He does not say whether they are the same people as the “super-apostles.”

Visitors who came to Corinth boasting of their credentials and preaching “a Jesus other than the One we proclaimed.” Paul calls them “false apostles, deceitful workers, masquerading as apostles of Christ,” and says he is “in no way inferior to those ’super-apostles’” (11:5, 13; 12:11). They claimed to be Hebrews, Israelites and descendants of Abraham (11:22), and the church put up with anyone who “enslaves you or exploits you or takes advantage of you” (11:20). Paul does not name them, and scholars still debate who they were.

e.u: Poor churches that gave beyond their means
t: The churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Berea. Paul holds them up as an example: “In the terrible ordeal they suffered, their abundant joy and deep poverty overflowed into rich generosity” (8:2). They “gave according to their ability and even beyond it,” and Paul had boasted to them of the Corinthians’ eagerness (9:2). Some Macedonians were to come with Paul to Corinth (9:4).

Titus is sent ahead with two brothers Paul does not name. One is “praised by all the churches for his work in the gospel” and was “chosen by the churches to accompany us with the offering” (8:18-19). The other has an “earnestness” that “has been proven many times and in many ways” (8:22). Paul calls them “messengers of the churches, to the glory of Christ” (8:23). Acts 20:4 names seven men who later went with the gift.

e.u: How Paul asks the Corinthians to give
t: Paul pictures giving as sowing: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously.” Each one gives “what he has decided in his heart to give, not out of regret or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver” (9:6-7). God “supplies seed to the sower and bread for food” (9:10), and Paul ends, “Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!”

e.u: The poor believers the gift was for
t: The believers in Jerusalem, many of them poor, for whom the collection is taken. Paul calls it “this service to the saints” (8:4) and says it overflows in “many expressions of thanksgiving to God” (9:12). Their prayers for the Corinthians will “express their affection for you” (9:14). Romans 15:25-27 says Macedonia and Achaia both gave.

Paul says the gospel is veiled to “those who are perishing,” because “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers” (4:3-4). He then tells the believers, “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers,” and asks what a believer has “in common with an unbeliever” (6:14-15).

Paul writes “to the churches of Galatia” (1:2) and is “amazed how quickly you are deserting the One who called you by the grace of Christ” (1:6). He calls them “foolish Galatians” (3:1), reminds them that they received the Spirit by hearing with faith (3:2), and recalls how they once welcomed him “as if I were an angel of God” (4:14). Scholars disagree whether they lived in the old Celtic north of the region or in the southern cities of the Roman province.

Paul says “some people are troubling you and trying to distort the gospel of Christ” (1:7). They press the Gentile believers to be circumcised (6:12), and Paul says they want to “make a good impression outwardly” and “avoid persecution for the cross of Christ.” He says they are “zealous for you, but not in a good way,” because they “want to isolate you from us” (4:17). Their names are not given, and scholars reconstruct their message only from what Paul says against it.

e.u: Those who spied on freedom in Jerusalem
t: Paul says “some false brothers had come in under false pretenses to spy on our freedom in Christ Jesus, in order to enslave us” (2:4). He says, “We did not give in to them for a moment, so that the truth of the gospel would remain with you” (2:5). Some link them to the teachers who came to Galatia, but the letter does not say so.

Paul calls “James, Cephas, and John” those “reputed to be pillars” (2:9). He reports that they added nothing to his message, recognized the grace given to him, and gave him and Barnabas “the right hand of fellowship,” agreeing that Paul and Barnabas would go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised (2:6-9).

e.u: Those whose arrival changed Peter’s table
t: Paul says that before “certain men came from James,” Peter ate with the Gentiles, but “when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group” (2:12). The letter does not say what message they carried or whether James sent them to say it.

Paul writes, “if someone is caught in a trespass, you who are spiritual should restore him with a spirit of gentleness. But watch yourself, or you also may be tempted” (6:1). The word describes believers who live by the Spirit, as in 5:25, not a special class.

e.u: Paul’s word for life without the Spirit
t: In Galatians “flesh” often means human nature on its own, as opposed to the Spirit. Paul says “the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh” (5:17), lists “the acts of the flesh” (5:19-21), and says “those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (5:24).

Paul asks, “Why then was the law given?” and answers that “it was added because of transgressions, until the arrival of the seed” (3:19). He says it was “our guardian to lead us to Christ” (3:24), that it cannot give life (3:21), and that Christ “redeemed us from the curse of the law” (3:13). He also says the whole law is fulfilled in one command: “Love your neighbor as yourself” (5:14).

Paul writes “To the saints in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus” (1:1). Some of the oldest copies leave out “in Ephesus,” so the letter may have been meant for several churches in Asia. Paul says he has “heard about your faith in the Lord Jesus and your love for all the saints” (1:15). Most of them were Gentiles who had once lived “fulfilling the cravings of our flesh” (2:3) and “without hope and without God in the world” (2:12). Paul had spent about three years in the city (Acts 20:31).

e.u: The unseen forces Ephesians speaks of
t: Paul says Christ is seated “far above all rule and authority, power and dominion” (1:21), and God’s wisdom is made known “to the rulers and authorities in the heavenly realms” through the church (3:10). He also says “our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the powers of this world’s darkness, and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms” (6:12). The letter gives no names and no lists. Colossians names “thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities” among the things created in Christ (1:16). Christ is “the head over every ruler and authority” (2:10), and on the cross He disarmed “the powers and authorities” (2:15).

Paul tells Gentile readers to remember that they were “separate from Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel, and strangers to the covenants of the promise, without hope and without God in the world” (2:12). Now they are “no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household” (2:19), and “fellow heirs” (3:6). He also tells them that they “must no longer walk as the Gentiles do, in the futility of their thinking” (4:17).

e.u: The nearer ones and the first to hope
t: Paul speaks of those “called uncircumcised by the so-called circumcision” (2:11), of “the commonwealth of Israel” (2:12), and of “we, who were the first to hope in Christ” (1:12), meaning Jewish believers. He says Christ “has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility” (2:14), and that the Gentiles are “fellow heirs” with them (3:6).

e.u: The life put on in Christ
t: Paul tells his readers “to put off your former way of life, your old self, which is being corrupted by its deceitful desires,” and “to put on the new self, created to be like God in true righteousness and holiness” (4:22-24). He then spells out what that looks like: truth, honest anger, honest work, gracious speech, kindness and forgiveness (4:25-32).

e.u: Called to love as Christ loved
t: Paul writes, “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her” (5:25). He says husbands “ought to love their wives as their own bodies” (5:28) and that “each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself” (5:33). The command to submit that comes first (5:21) is addressed to everyone, and the weight in this section falls on the husband’s costly love.
1 Peter 3:7 tells husbands to “treat your wives with consideration... with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life.”

Paul writes, “Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord” (5:22), after saying all believers should “submit to one another out of reverence for Christ” (5:21). He compares the husband’s headship to Christ’s as head of the church (5:23) and ends, “the wife must respect her husband” (5:33). Scholars disagree about how far the instruction reaches today.
1 Peter 3:1-6 tells wives to win unbelieving husbands “without words by the behavior of their wives.”

e.u: The household’s young and the head
t: Paul tells children, “Obey your parents in the Lord, for this is right” (6:1), and quotes the commandment “Honor your father and mother” with its promise (6:2-3). He tells fathers, “do not provoke your children to wrath; instead, bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord” (6:4).

e.u: The most unequal pair in the household
t: Paul tells slaves to obey their earthly masters “with respect and fear and sincerity of heart, just as you would obey Christ” (6:5), as “servants of Christ” (6:6). He tells masters to “do the same for your slaves” and to “give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him” (6:9). Some Christian readers have used the passage to defend slavery, and others to show that its foundation was undone. Colossians gives the same pair in a short form: “Slaves, obey your earthly masters in everything” (3:22), and “Masters, supply your slaves with what is right and fair, since you know that you also have a Master in heaven” (4:1).

e.u: The foundation of the household of God
t: Paul says God’s household is “built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the cornerstone” (2:20). He says the mystery of Christ “has now been revealed by the Spirit to God’s holy apostles and prophets” (3:5). In 4:11 apostles and prophets are listed among Christ’s gifts to the church. Scholars disagree whether the prophets are New Testament or Old Testament figures.

e.u: Apostles, prophets, evangelists, shepherds and teachers
t: Paul quotes Psalm 68 and says that when Christ ascended he “gave gifts to men” (4:8). He lists them: “it was He who gave some to be apostles, some to be prophets, some to be evangelists, and some to be pastors and teachers, to equip the saints for works of ministry and to build up the body of Christ” (4:11-12). The goal is that “we all reach unity in the faith” and “grow up into Christ Himself, who is the head” (4:13-15).

Paul writes “To all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons” (1:1). Their “partnership in the gospel from the first day until now” (1:5) shows in the gift they sent him by Epaphroditus (4:18). Acts 16 begins the church with Lydia and the jailer and their households. Paul says they are “encountering the same struggle you saw I had” (1:30), tells them to “shine as lights in the world” (2:15), and calls them “my joy and crown” (4:1). He also hears of a quarrel between two women (4:2).

e.u: The leaders Paul greets by title
t: The greeting reads “together with the overseers and deacons” (1:1). No names are given and no duties are listed. This is the only one of Paul’s letters whose opening mentions these two groups. First Timothy 3:1-13 lists what is needed in an overseer (“above reproach, the husband of but one wife,” “able to teach”) and in deacons (“dignified, not double-tongued”). Whether the overseer and the elders are the same office is debated.

e.u: Those who heard that Paul was in chains for Christ
t: Paul writes, “it has become clear throughout the whole palace guard and to everyone else that I am in chains for Christ” (1:13). The Greek word (praitorion) can mean the emperor’s guard, a governor’s headquarters, or the staff of a palace, and scholars disagree about which Paul means. Acts 28:16 says that in Rome he was allowed to live with a soldier guarding him.

e.u: Rivals who preach Christ from bad motives
a: Some preach Christ out of envy
t: Paul writes, “some preach Christ out of envy and rivalry, but others out of goodwill” (1:15). The former “preach Christ out of selfish ambition, not sincerely, supposing that they can add to the distress of my chains” (1:17). Paul says, “in every way, whether by false motives or true, Christ is preached. And in this I rejoice” (1:18). He does not name them.

e.u: People Paul warns the church to watch out for
t: Paul writes, “Watch out for those dogs, those workers of evil, those mutilators of the flesh!” (3:2). He contrasts them with “we who are the circumcision,” who “worship by the Spirit of God” and “put no confidence in the flesh” (3:3). The letter does not name them. Many scholars think they were teachers who insisted that Gentile believers be circumcised.
2 Peter 2:22 quotes the proverb about the dog that returns to its vomit.

e.u: Those whose minds are set on earthly things
a: Enemies of the cross of Christ
t: Paul says, with tears, “Many live as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction, their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame. Their minds are set on earthly things” (3:18-19). He sets them against those whose “citizenship is in heaven” (3:20). The letter does not name them, and scholars disagree about whether they are the same people as in 3:2.

e.u: Two women who worked beside Paul
t: Paul writes, “I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord” (4:2). He asks his “true yokefellow” to “help these women who have labored with me for the gospel” (4:3). Nothing else is known about them. Acts 16:13-15 tells of women who gathered to pray at Philippi.

e.u: The emperor’s slaves and freed people
t: Paul ends, “All the saints send you greetings, especially those from the household of Caesar” (4:22). The phrase meant the emperor’s staff of slaves and freed people, not his family. They worked in Rome and in cities across the empire.

Paul writes “To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae” (1:2). He has “heard about your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints” (1:4), and he delights in their “orderly condition and firm faith in Christ” (2:5). He has not met them (2:1). They learned the gospel from Epaphras (1:7), and he warns them against being “taken captive” by teaching that adds rules and powers to Christ (2:8). Several of them were slaves, and at least one house church met in the valley (4:15).

e.u: Those who offered a “philosophy” in addition to Christ
t: Paul writes, “See to it that no one takes you captive through philosophy and empty deception, which are based on human tradition and the spiritual forces of the world rather than on Christ” (2:8). He mentions rules about “what you eat or drink,” feasts, New Moons and Sabbaths (2:16), “false humility and the worship of angels” (2:18), and slogans such as “Do not handle, do not taste, do not touch!” (2:21). The letter never names them or says how many there were, and scholars still debate whether they were Jewish, pagan, or a mixture.

e.n: The old self and the new self
e.u: Paul’s picture of the life the Colossians left behind and the life they have put on
t: Paul says, “you have taken off the old self with its practices, and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge in the image of its Creator” (3:9-10). The old self shows itself in “sexual immorality, impurity, lust, evil desires, and greed” (3:5) and in “anger, rage, malice, slander, and filthy language” (3:8). The new self wears “compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience” (3:12), with love as “the bond of perfect unity” (3:14). In this life, “Christ is all and is in all” (3:11).

e.u: The church Paul writes to twice
t: Paul writes “To the church of the Thessalonians in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thessalonians 1:1). Most had “turned to God from idols” (1:9). They welcomed the message “in spite of your great suffering” (1:6), and their faith became known across Macedonia and Achaia (1:7-8). Acts 17:4 says Jews, God-fearing Greeks and leading women joined Paul. Paul had to leave them soon, and he writes to answer their questions about those who have died, the Day of the Lord and those who would not work.

e.u: The three who send both letters
t: Both letters open with the same three names: “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy” (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Silvanus is the Silas of Acts. Paul, Silas and Timothy had all been in Thessalonica (Acts 17:1-10) and Paul says “we” through the letters. Paul writes “I, Paul” in a few places (1 Thessalonians 2:18; 2 Thessalonians 3:17).

e.u: Believers who had died, and the church’s grief for them
t: Paul writes, “we do not want you to be uninformed about those who sleep in death, so that you will not grieve like the rest, who are without hope” (1 Thessalonians 4:13). He says that “the dead in Christ will be the first to rise” (4:16) and that “we will always be with the Lord” (4:17). “Sleep” was a common way to speak of death, and Paul uses it for believers who have died. He adds, “whether we are awake or asleep, we may live together with Him” (5:10).

e.u: The workers Paul asks the church to respect
t: Paul writes, “we ask you, brothers, to acknowledge those who work diligently among you, who preside over you in the Lord and give you instruction” and tells them to “hold them in highest regard because of their work” (1 Thessalonians 5:12-13). They are not named and no office is given. Paul calls them to “live in peace with one another” (5:13).

Paul tells the church “to admonish the unruly” (1 Thessalonians 5:14) and to “work with your own hands, as we instructed you” (4:11). In the second letter he commands them to “keep away from any brother who leads an undisciplined life” (2 Thessalonians 3:6) and says, “we hear that some of you are leading undisciplined lives and accomplishing nothing but being busybodies” (3:11). He asks them to “begin working quietly to earn their own living” (3:12). He does not say why they had stopped, and some think they expected the Lord to come very soon.

e.u: The opponents behind the pressure on the church
t: Paul says the church suffered “from your own countrymen the very things they suffered from the Jews” (1 Thessalonians 2:14). In the second letter he says that “it is only right for God to repay with affliction those who afflict you” (2 Thessalonians 1:6) and that they endure “all the persecution and affliction” (1:4). The letters do not name the persecutors, and they give no details of what was done.

e.u: The members of the church who were doing what Paul asked
t: Paul says, “we have confidence in the Lord that you are doing and will continue to do what we command” (2 Thessalonians 3:4), and tells them, “do not grow weary in well-doing” (3:13). He sets them apart from the idle but asks that even the disobedient be treated “as a brother” (3:15).

e.u: Two men Paul says have shipwrecked their faith
t: Paul says some have “rejected” a good conscience and “thereby shipwrecked their faith. Among them are Hymenaeus and Alexander, whom I have handed over to Satan to be taught not to blaspheme” (1 Timothy 1:19-20). The letter gives no further account of what they did. Names like these appear again in 2 Timothy: a Hymenaeus in 2:17 and an Alexander the coppersmith in 4:14, and the letters do not say whether they are the same men. In 2 Timothy Hymenaeus is named again, with Philetus (2:17-18), and Paul says, “Alexander the coppersmith did great harm to me” (4:14). The letters do not say whether the Alexanders are one man.

e.u: The men Timothy is to instruct and correct
t: Paul asks Timothy to “stay on at Ephesus to instruct certain men not to teach false doctrines or devote themselves to myths and endless genealogies” (1 Timothy 1:3-4). Some “want to be teachers of the law, but they do not understand what they are saying” (1:7). Later Paul says some “will prohibit marriage and require abstinence from certain foods” (4:3), and describes those who “regard godliness as a means of gain” (6:5). The letter does not name a school or a movement, and the readers disagree about who these men were. In 2 Timothy the same kind of teaching appears: Paul says to avoid “quarreling over words” (2:14) and warns that people “with itching ears” will “gather around themselves teachers to suit their own desires” (4:3).

In 1 John: Later tradition places the readers of 1 John in the same region. The letter speaks of teachers who “went out from us” (2:19) and of “many false prophets” (4:1), and ends with “keep yourselves from idols” (5:21).

e.u: The church as Paul describes it to Timothy
t: Paul writes so “you will know how each one must conduct himself in God’s household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Timothy 3:15). The letter speaks to how it prays (2:1-8), who leads it (3:1-13), how it cares for widows (5:3-16) and how its members treat one another, including masters and slaves (6:1-2).

e.u: Women the church was to honor and support
t: Paul says, “Honor the widows who are truly widows” (1 Timothy 5:3). A widow who is “truly in need and left all alone puts her hope in God” (5:5). One “should be enrolled if she is at least sixty years old, the wife of one man, and well known for good deeds” (5:9-10). Younger widows are not to be enrolled, and Paul advises them “to marry, have children, and manage their households” (5:11, 14). If “any believing woman has dependent widows, she must assist them and not allow the church to be burdened” (5:16). What “enrolled” means, whether a list for support or an order of service, is debated.

e.u: The relatives Paul says must care for their own
t: Paul says that if a widow “has children or grandchildren, they must first learn to show godliness to their own family and repay their parents” (1 Timothy 5:4), and “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially his own household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (5:8). The household was the first place of care, and the church was to help those who had no family (5:5, 16).

Paul warns that “those who want to be rich” fall “into temptation” and that “the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil” (1 Timothy 6:9-10). He tells Timothy to “instruct those who are rich in the present age not to be conceited and not to put their hope in the uncertainty of wealth, but in God,” and to “be generous and ready to share” (6:17-18). The letter does not say they must give up what they have.

James warns the rich three times: in 1:10-11, where wealth fades like a flower; in 2:2-6, where the rich are favored in the assembly and drag the poor into court; and in 5:1-6, where rotted riches and unpaid wages testify against them.

e.u: Those under the yoke and those they served
a: Those under the yoke of slavery
t: Paul says that “all who are under the yoke of slavery should regard their masters as fully worthy of honor, so that God’s name and our teaching will not be discredited,” and that those with “believing masters” are not to “show disrespect because they are brothers” (1 Timothy 6:1-2). The letter gives no instruction about freeing slaves. Many slaves were members of the early churches. Titus 2:9-10 asks slaves to submit, to be honest and well-pleasing, “so that in every respect they will adorn the teaching about God our Savior.”

e.u: The women Paul addresses in the instructions on prayer
t: Paul says, “I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God” (1 Timothy 2:9-10). He then says, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to exercise authority over a man; she is to remain quiet” (2:12). Readers differ on what these verses meant in Ephesus and how they apply now, and on the meaning of “saved through childbearing” in 2:15. In 3:11 “the women” may be deacons’ wives or women deacons.

e.u: Two men from Asia who left Paul
t: Paul says, “You know that everyone in the Province of Asia has deserted me, including Phygelus and Hermogenes” (2 Timothy 1:15). They are named only here, and the letter does not say what they did or why. Paul sets them beside Onesiphorus, who was “unashamed” of his chains (1:16).

e.u: The next link in the chain of teaching
t: Paul says, “the things that you have heard me say among many witnesses, entrust these to faithful men who will be qualified to teach others as well” (2 Timothy 2:2). The line has four links: Paul, Timothy, faithful men, and “others.” The letter does not name the faithful men, and it does not say whether they were elders (compare 1 Timothy 3:1-7; Titus 1:5-9).

e.u: Two teachers whose talk spread “like gangrene”
t: Paul says the talk of such men “will spread like gangrene. Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have deviated from the truth. They say that the resurrection has already occurred, and they undermine the faith of some” (2 Timothy 2:17-18). Hymenaeus was named in 1 Timothy 1:20. Philetus appears only here. The letter does not explain what they meant by saying the resurrection had already occurred.
