e.u: The kind of teacher Timothy is to be
t: Paul says that “a servant of the Lord must not be quarrelsome, but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, and forbearing. He must gently reprove those who oppose him, in the hope that God may grant them repentance leading to a knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 2:24-25). The aim is that opponents “will come to their senses and escape the snare of the devil” (2:26).

Paul says, “I endure all things for the sake of the elect, so that they too may obtain the salvation that is in Christ Jesus, with eternal glory” (2 Timothy 2:10). “The elect” means those whom God has chosen. The letter does not say who is meant in particular.

e.u: Men Paul says will be “lovers of themselves”
t: Paul says, “In the last days terrible times will come. For men will be lovers of themselves, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, abusive, disobedient to their parents, ungrateful, unholy” (2 Timothy 3:1-2). They have “a form of godliness but denying its power,” and Timothy is to “turn away from such as these” (3:5). Later he writes that “evil men and imposters go from bad to worse, deceiving and being deceived” (3:13).
1 John 2:18 says, “Children, it is the last hour,” and finds the sign in the many antichrists who have appeared.

e.u: Magicians who opposed Moses in Jewish tradition
t: Paul says, “Just as Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth” (2 Timothy 3:8). The Old Testament does not name them, but Jewish tradition gave these names to the magicians of Pharaoh (Exodus 7:11). Paul adds that “their folly will be plain to everyone” (3:9).

Paul ends, “Eubulus sends you greetings, as do Pudens, Linus, Claudia, and all the brothers” (2 Timothy 4:21). These four are named only here. Irenaeus (Against Heresies 3.3.3) names a Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the apostles, but the letter does not say whether this is the same man.

e.u: The people of the island and their reputation
t: Paul quotes a saying about the people of the island: “Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons” (Titus 1:12). He says, “This testimony is true,” and tells Titus to “rebuke them sternly.” Cretans were among those who heard the apostles at Pentecost (Acts 2:11), and a ship carrying Paul put in at Fair Havens on Crete (Acts 27:7-12). Crete was a Roman province in Paul’s day. The letter tells Titus to appoint elders “in every town,” which suggests small groups of believers in several towns.

Paul says “many are rebellious and full of empty talk and deception, especially those of the circumcision,” who “undermine entire households” for “dishonorable gain” (Titus 1:10-11). Their teaching included “Jewish myths” and “commands of men who have rejected the truth” (1:14). Titus is to silence them and rebuke them sternly. The letter does not say how many they were, or whether they were believers.

e.u: Models for the rest of the church
t: Paul tells Titus to teach “older men” to be “temperate, dignified, self-controlled, and sound in faith, love, and perseverance” (Titus 2:2). “Older women” are to be “reverent in their behavior, not slanderers or addicted to much wine, but teachers of good” (2:3), and they can “train the young women” (2:4). Their teaching role grows out of their own conduct.

e.u: Taught by their elders and by Titus
t: Younger women are trained “to love their husbands and children, to be self-controlled, pure, managers of their households, kind, and submissive to their own husbands, so that the word of God will not be discredited” (Titus 2:4-5). Younger men are urged “to be self-controlled” (2:6). Paul’s stated aim is the reputation of the gospel among outsiders, and Titus himself is to be “an example by doing good works” (2:7).

e.u: The person who is to be rejected after two warnings
t: Paul writes, “Reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition, knowing that such a man is corrupt and sinful; he is self-condemned” (Titus 3:10-11). He is not named, and the letter does not say what he taught beyond the “foolish controversies” and “quarrels about the law” of 3:9.

e.u: The congregation the letter is read to
t: Paul writes “to the church that meets at your house” (Philemon 2). Most of the letter says “you” in the singular to Philemon, but verses 3, 22 and 25 use the plural, so the whole church heard it read. Churches in homes are also found in Romans 16:5, 1 Corinthians 16:19 and Colossians 4:15. The letter does not say how large the group was.

e.u: The first three in the list of the faithful
t: The list in chapter 11 begins with three men from Genesis. Abel offered “a better sacrifice than Cain” (11:4). Enoch “was taken up so that he did not see death” (11:5), and Noah, “in godly fear,” built an ark to save his family (11:7). The writer sets each beside the great pattern of faith: they acted on what God said before they saw it.
2 Peter 2:5 names Noah only: “a preacher of righteousness,” one of “the eight” preserved from the flood.

e.u: The faithful of chapter 11, seen as onlookers
t: Hebrews 12:1 says “we are surrounded by such a great cloud of witnesses.” The witnesses are the people just named in chapter 11, who testify by their lives to what faith is. The writer does not say that they can see the readers, only that their example surrounds them, and that the readers should look to Jesus, who “endured the cross, scorning its shame” (12:2).

e.n: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David and Samuel
e.u: Six names in the second half of the list of the faithful
a: Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel
t: Hebrews 11:32 says there is not time to tell of “Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah, David, Samuel and the prophets.” The four judges came first in Israel’s history, and the list is not in order of time. The writer then speaks in general of what faith achieved and what the faithful suffered (11:33-38). The list does not mention failures, though the stories in Judges and Samuel record them.

e.n: The priests and the high priest
e.u: The Levitical priests Hebrews compares with Christ
t: Hebrews speaks of the priests who served under the law: the high priest taken from among men (5:1), the priests who went into the first room “continually” (9:6), and the great number of them, since death kept them from continuing (7:23). The writer says they served at a copy and shadow of heavenly things (8:4-5) and had to offer sacrifices again and again, and compares their service with Christ, who offered one sacrifice for sins for all time (10:11-12).

e.u: The community the letter is written to
t: The letter does not say where its readers lived or who they were. It says they had been enlightened and had endured a hard struggle with sufferings, publicly exposed to abuse, and they had shared the lot of prisoners and accepted the loss of their possessions (10:32-34). They had shown love to the saints (6:10), but had grown “dull of hearing” (5:11), and some had stopped meeting together (10:25). The writer thinks better of them (6:9) and tells them to hold on. The title was added later, and most scholars take the readers to be Christians from a Jewish background, though some think the community included others.

e.u: Those who spoke the word of God to them and keep watch over them
t: Hebrews 13:7 asks the readers to remember their leaders, who spoke the word of God to them, and to imitate their faith. Verse 17 asks them to obey and submit, since the leaders keep watch over their souls and will give an account. Verse 24 asks the readers to greet all of them. The letter does not name any of them.

e.u: Heavenly beings the Son is set above
t: The first two chapters set the Son above the angels. They are “ministering spirits sent to serve those who will inherit salvation” (1:14), they were present when the law was given (2:2), and the Son was made for a little while lower than they (2:7). The writer also says that some have entertained angels without knowing it (13:2), and that at Mount Zion the readers have come to “myriads of angels” (12:22).

e.n: The twelve tribes of the Dispersion
e.u: The scattered believers James writes to
t: James is addressed “to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion” (1:1). Dispersion (diaspora) was the word for Jews living outside the land, and the letter also says “your meeting” (2:2, a synagogue) and speaks of the Law and of Abraham, which fits readers from a Jewish background. Some take the phrase more widely, as a title for the whole church, like the “exiles of the Dispersion” in 1 Peter 1:1. The letter names no town. Acts 11:19 tells of believers scattered after the death of Stephen who reached Phoenicia, Cyprus and Antioch, and many readers think James has such people in mind.

James 1:27 says that pure religion before God is to care for orphans and widows in their distress. They are the people the Law of Moses names again and again as needing protection, since they had no man of the household to speak for them or to provide (Deuteronomy 10:18; 24:17-21). The Greek verb translated “care for” is the word used for visiting the sick or the prisoner in Matthew 25.

e.u: Rich people in the assembly and outside it
t: James speaks of the rich three times. The rich believer is told to take pride in his low position, because he will pass away like a flower (1:10-11). In the assembly the rich man in a gold ring is given the seat of honor, while the poor man is told to stand (2:2-3); James says it is the rich who drag the readers into court (2:6). At the end he calls on “you who are rich” to weep over the misery to come, since their wealth has rotted and the wages they held back are crying out (5:1-6). It is not clear whether the rich of chapter 5 are believers; the letter addresses them with the voice of a prophet and does not call them brothers.

e.n: The poor and the lowly in James
t: James says the brother “in humble circumstances” should be glad of his high position (1:9). The poor man in shabby clothes who is told to stand or to sit on the floor (2:2-3) is one of those God has chosen to be rich in faith and to inherit the kingdom (2:5), which echoes Jesus’ words “Blessed are you who are poor” (Luke 6:20). James also says that to say “Go in peace; stay warm and well fed” to a person in need, without giving what the body needs, is worthless (2:15-16).

e.u: Those who teach in the assembly
t: James begins chapter 3 by saying that not many should become teachers, since “we who teach will be judged more strictly” (3:1). He includes himself with “we,” so the writer is a teacher. A teacher had a place of honor among the early believers, and the tongue was his tool, which is why the rest of the chapter is about its power.

James asks, “Who is wise and understanding among you?” and answers that such a person shows it by good conduct and by deeds done in the humility that comes from wisdom (3:13). He says that jealousy and selfish ambition are not wisdom, and that the wisdom from above is pure, peace-loving, gentle, full of mercy and good fruit (3:14-17).

e.u: Those God opposes and those he lifts up
t: Quoting Proverbs 3:34, James says “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (4:6). He asks the double-minded to cleanse their hands and purify their hearts, to grieve and mourn, and to humble themselves before the Lord, who “will exalt you” (4:8-10). Jesus says nearly the same thing in Matthew 23:12.

e.u: Traders who plan a year ahead
t: James addresses those who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business, and make a profit” (4:13). He does not condemn trade but the boast that leaves God out. Life is “a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes” (4:14), and they ought to say, “If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that” (4:15).

James tells his readers to be patient “until the Lord’s coming,” and “See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains” (5:7). The farmer sows after the early rain of autumn and waits for the late rain of spring before the harvest, and cannot hurry either.

e.n: The believers of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia
t: The letter is addressed “to the elect who are exiles of the Dispersion throughout Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1:1). These were five Roman provinces of Asia Minor, today most of Turkey. Peter calls them “foreigners and exiles” (2:11), a “chosen people, a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (2:9), and “God’s flock” (5:2). They were being slandered as evildoers (2:12) and were put to shame for no longer joining in the life of their neighbors (4:4). Whether they were mostly Jewish or mostly Gentile in background is debated; the letter reminds them of their “empty way of life” (1:18) and of “the same desires as the Gentiles” (4:3), which points to Gentile converts.

In 2 Peter: The second letter is addressed “to those who through the righteousness of our God and Savior Jesus Christ have received a faith as precious as ours” (2 Peter 1:1) and calls itself “my second letter to you” (3:1). Many take the readers to be the same churches as in 1 Peter; the letter does not name them.

e.n: The prophets of the old covenant
e.u: Those who searched for the salvation Peter proclaims
t: Peter says the prophets “searched and investigated carefully” about this salvation, “trying to determine the time and setting to which the Spirit of Christ in them was pointing when He predicted the sufferings of Christ and the glories to follow” (1:10-11). They were “not serving themselves, but you” (1:12). The letter quotes Isaiah, Psalms, Proverbs, Hosea, Leviticus and Exodus, and the picture of the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 shapes chapter 2.

2 Peter 1:19-21 says “the word of the prophets” is “a lamp shining in a dark place,” and that “men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.” 3:2 speaks of what was foretold “by the holy prophets.”

Peter tells “servants” (the Greek oiketai, household slaves) to “submit yourselves to your masters with all respect, not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable” (2:18). He says the pain of unjust suffering is “to be commended” when borne by one who is conscious of God (2:19), and points them to Christ, who suffered and left an example. Slaves were a large part of any Roman city. Peter does not tell them to seek freedom, and he does not argue about slavery as an institution; he speaks as well of the dignity of the believing slave, who is a “servant of God” (2:16).

e.u: The non-Christian neighbors who watched and spoke against the readers
t: Peter tells his readers to “conduct yourselves with such honor among the Gentiles that, though they slander you as evildoers, they may see your good deeds and glorify God on the day He visits us” (2:12). The same neighbors “consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you” (4:4). They are not named, and the letter does not describe any trial before a court; the pressure is social, with ridicule, exclusion and insult.

e.u: The old companions who now heap abuse
t: In chapter 4 Peter says that the readers “have spent enough time in the past carrying out the same desires as the Gentiles: living in debauchery, lust, drunkenness, orgies, carousing, and detestable idolatry” (4:3). Their old friends are surprised that they no longer join in and “heap abuse on you” (4:4). The letter says they “will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead” (4:5).

Peter writes to wives first, “so that even if they refuse to believe the word, they will be won over without words by the behavior of their wives” (3:1), and says that their beauty should come not from “braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes” but “from the inner disposition of your heart, the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit” (3:3-4). He holds up the holy women of the past who “put their hope in God” (3:5), among them Sarah. To husbands he says, “treat your wives with consideration as a delicate vessel, and with honor as fellow heirs of the gracious gift of life, so that your prayers will not be hindered” (3:7).

e.u: The two who share the closing greeting
t: Peter writes “through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother” (5:12) and sends greetings from the church in Babylon and from “my son Mark” (5:13). Silvanus is the Silas of Acts, Paul’s companion, named with Timothy in the greetings of 1 and 2 Thessalonians. Mark is almost certainly John Mark, the cousin of Barnabas, who first went with Paul and then with Barnabas, and who was later with Paul in Rome (Colossians 4:10; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11). Early writers said that Mark was Peter’s interpreter, and that his Gospel keeps Peter’s preaching.

Peter tells his readers to “submit yourselves for the Lord’s sake to every human institution, whether to the king as the supreme authority, or to governors as those sent by him to punish those who do wrong and to praise those who do right” (2:13-14). He ends with “Fear God, honor the king” (2:17). The king meant the Roman emperor, who in the early 60s was Nero. The governors were the officials he sent to the provinces. Peter does not name either.

e.u: The people the elders are to shepherd
t: Peter tells the elders to “be shepherds of God’s flock that is among you” (5:2). They are not to be “lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock” (5:3). The picture is that of Ezekiel 34 and of John 21:15-17, where the risen Jesus tells Peter to feed his sheep. The “Chief Shepherd” is Christ, who is also “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (2:25).

The letter says “there will be false teachers among you,” who “will secretly introduce destructive heresies, even denying the Master who bought them” (2:1). It says they are driven by greed and exploit the readers “with deceptive words” (2:3), that they “despise authority” and “slander glorious beings” (2:10), that they carouse and are “reveling in their deception as they feast with you” (2:13), and that they “promise them freedom, while they themselves are slaves to depravity” (2:19). The letter does not name them or their teaching. Much of the chapter follows the letter of Jude, which speaks of ungodly people who have slipped in. Scholars have suggested early forms of Gnostic or libertine teaching, or teachers who denied the coming judgment, and the scoffers of 3:3-4 may be the same people.

e.u: Those who ask where the promise is
t: Peter says that “in the last days scoffers will come, scoffing and following their own evil desires” (3:3). They ask, “Where is the promise of His coming?” and say, “Ever since our fathers fell asleep, everything continues as it has from the beginning of creation” (3:4). The letter answers that they “deliberately overlook” creation and the flood (3:5-6), and that the delay is God’s patience (3:9). Jude 18 uses the same word for mockers. The letter does not say who they were or whether they were inside or outside the church.
Jude 18 gives the apostles’ warning in nearly the same words: “In the last times there will be scoffers who will follow after their own ungodly desires.”

e.u: Those who heard the voice on the holy mountain
t: The writer says “we were eyewitnesses of His majesty” and “we ourselves heard this voice from heaven when we were with Him on the holy mountain” (1:16-18). The Gospels name Peter, James and John as the three disciples Jesus took up the mountain (Matthew 17:1; Mark 9:2; Luke 9:28). The letter does not name the mountain.

The letter says “God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment” (2:4). It does not say what they did. Most readers link the verse to Genesis 6:1-4 and the Jewish Book of Enoch, where rebel angels are bound until the judgment; Jude 6 says almost the same. Some take it to mean the fall of Satan and his angels. The Greek verb is from Tartarus, the prison of the underworld in Greek writing.
Jude 6 reads, “the angels who did not stay within their own domain but abandoned their proper dwelling—these He has kept in eternal chains under darkness, bound for judgment on that great day.”

e.u: Those who heard, saw and touched
a: The eyewitnesses of the Word of life
t: The letter opens with “we”: “which we have heard, which we have seen with our own eyes, which we have gazed upon and touched with our own hands—this is the Word of life” (1:1). They “testified to it” and “proclaim to you the eternal life that was with the Father” (1:2). Most readers take this to be the apostles, or the apostolic circle, who knew Jesus in his earthly life. In 4:14 the same voice says “we have seen and testify that the Father has sent His Son to be the Savior of the world.”

The letter does not name a church or a city. It speaks to its readers as “my little children” (2:1), “beloved” (2:7; 3:2; 4:1), and “brothers” (3:13), and says it writes “to you who believe in the name of the Son of God, so that you may know that you have eternal life” (5:13). Since the second century, readers have placed them in the churches around Ephesus in the province of Asia. They have been shaken by teachers who left their fellowship.
If the “chosen lady” of 2 John is a church, as most think, she and her “elect sister” (13) may belong to the same circle of churches that 1 John is written to.

a: Little children, fathers and young men
t: In a pair of three-line verses the writer says: “I am writing to you, little children, because your sins have been forgiven through His name. I am writing to you, fathers, because you know Him who is from the beginning. I am writing to you, young men, because you have overcome the evil one” (2:12-13). He repeats them with “I have written” in 2:14. Some take the three words to mean ages of life; others take them to mean three stages of Christian growth, or the whole church under three names.

e.n: Those who went out from us
e.u: The teachers who left the fellowship
a: Those who went out from us
t: The letter says “They went out from us, but they did not belong to us. For if they had belonged to us, they would have remained with us” (2:19). It calls them liars who deny “that Jesus is the Christ” (2:22) and “those who are trying to deceive you” (2:26), and says they do not confess “that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (4:2). It does not give their names or spell out their teaching. Some scholars think of Cerinthus, others of an early form of docetism, which held that Christ only seemed to have a body; the evidence is debated.
In 2 John, “many deceivers have gone out into the world” (7). The words are close to 1 John 2:19 and 4:1, and many readers think the same teachers are meant, now moving from church to church.

e.n: The antichrist and the many antichrists
t: The word “antichrist” appears in the New Testament only in 1 John (2:18, 22; 4:3) and 2 John 7. The letter says, “just as you have heard that the antichrist is coming, so now many antichrists have appeared” (2:18), and defines the antichrist as the one “who denies the Father and the Son” (2:22). In 4:3 “the spirit of the antichrist” is “already in the world at this time.” The writer sees the mark of the antichrist in a present denial, not in a single figure in the future.

In 2 John 7 the word occurs for the last time in the New Testament: “Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist.” Here it is applied to anyone who is a deceiver and denies that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, which agrees with 1 John’s “many antichrists.”
Revelation never uses the word antichrist. Many readers identify the antichrist with the beast from the sea (13:1-10); others see the beast as a power or empire rather than one person.

e.n: The false prophets and the spirits
t: The letter tells its readers, “do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God. For many false prophets have gone out into the world” (4:1). The test is whether the spirit “confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh” (4:2). The writer adds, “We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. That is how we know the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception” (4:6).
In 2 John, the “many deceivers” (7) are the same kind of travelers, and the test is the same: whether they confess Jesus Christ come in the flesh.

e.n: The children of God and the children of the devil
e.u: Two families, told apart by what they do
t: The letter says, “By this the children of God are distinguished from the children of the devil: Anyone who does not practice righteousness is not of God, nor is anyone who does not love his brother” (3:10). It opens the chapter with “we should be called children of God. And that is what we are!” (3:1), and in 3:8 says “The one who practices sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the very start.”

e.n: The chosen lady and her children
a: The elect lady and her children
t: The letter is addressed to “the chosen lady and her children” (1:1). Most readers take the lady to be a local church and her children its members, because verse 13 sends greetings from “the children of your elect sister,” and because the letter turns to a plural “you” in verses 6, 8, 10 and 12. Others think a real woman who led a church in her home is meant, and a few take Kyria or Electa as her name. The letter does not say where she lived. The writer loves her “in the truth,” urges her to love one another (1:5), and tells her not to “receive him into your home” if he does not bring the teaching of Christ (1:10).

e.n: The children of the chosen sister
a: The children of your elect sister
t: The letter ends, “The children of your elect sister send you greetings” (1:13). The sister is usually read as the church where the writer is, and her children as its members. The letter does not say where it is. The word for “elect” (eklektē) is the same one used for the lady in verse 1.

e.u: Those who refuse to confess Jesus Christ in the flesh
t: The letter says, “many deceivers have gone out into the world, refusing to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh. Any such person is the deceiver and the antichrist” (1:7). It also describes people who run ahead “without remaining in the teaching of Christ” (1:9) and who bring a different teaching to a house (1:10). The writer does not name them or describe what they taught beyond this. Many readers link them with the teachers who “went out from us” in 1 John 2:19, and early writers such as Irenaeus and Ignatius point to those who said Christ only seemed to have a body, or who separated the man Jesus from the Christ.

e.u: The guests who needed a home
t: Early Christian teachers, prophets and workers moved from church to church and depended on Christian households for food and a bed. The Third Letter praises those who welcomed such brothers, and the Didache gives rules for receiving them. 2 John uses this setting: a visitor who “does not bring this teaching” is not to be received “into your home or even greet him” (1:10). The letter does not tell the readers to refuse everyone who disagrees with them; its test is what a visitor teaches about Christ.

3 John shows the custom from the other side. Gaius is praised for what he does “for the brothers, and especially since they are strangers to you” (3 John 5), and the elder says, “we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (3 John 8).

e.u: Workers who went out for the Name
t: Christian workers who traveled from church to church. They were “strangers” to Gaius when he took them in (1:5), and afterward “They have testified to the church about your love” (1:6). The elder says, “they went out on behalf of the Name, accepting nothing from the Gentiles. Therefore we ought to support such men, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth” (1:7-8). Diotrephes “refuses to welcome the brothers” (1:10). They are not named, unless Demetrius is one of them, and the letter does not say where they were going.

e.u: Believers with the elder and with Gaius
t: The letter ends, “The friends here send you greetings. Greet each of our friends there by name” (1:14). “The friends” are the believers around the elder and those around Gaius. It is a rare name for Christians in the New Testament; in the Gospel of John Jesus tells his disciples that he calls them friends. Greeting each one by name fits a small circle in which everyone was known.

a: Those who are called, loved and kept
t: The letter is written “To those who are called, loved by God the Father, and kept in Jesus Christ” (1:1). No town or region is named. They are “Beloved” three times (1:3, 17, 20), they share a common salvation with Jude, they hold love feasts (1:12), and apostles had taught them (1:17-18). They know the stories of the Old Testament well enough to need only a reminder (1:5), which points to a church with deep Jewish roots. Jude tells them to keep themselves “in the love of God” (1:21) and to “have mercy on those who doubt” (1:22), and he ends with praise to the God “who is able to keep you from stumbling” (1:24).

e.n: The ungodly men who crept in
t: Jude writes, “certain men have crept in among you unnoticed—ungodly ones who were designated long ago for condemnation. They turn the grace of our God into a license for immorality, and they deny our only Master and Lord, Jesus Christ” (1:4). He calls them “these dreamers” who “defile their bodies, reject authority, and slander glorious beings” (1:8). They are “hidden reefs in your love feasts” (1:12), “discontented grumblers” who “flatter others for their own advantage” (1:16), and people “who cause divisions, who are worldly and devoid of the Spirit” (1:19). Jude never names them or sets out their teaching. They seem to have been traveling teachers who claimed visions and taught that grace set believers free from moral rules. Later writers linked them with Gnostic groups, but the letter itself shows only their way of life. 2 Peter 2 describes its false teachers in much the same words.

e.n: Those who doubt and those in the fire
t: Near its end the letter turns to members of the church who have been unsettled: “have mercy on those who doubt; save others by snatching them from the fire; and to still others show mercy tempered with fear, hating even the clothing stained by the flesh” (1:22-23). The first group wavers, the second has gone further and needs quick rescue, and the third is to be helped with care so that the helper is not drawn in. The Greek copies differ in these verses, and some have only two groups. The pictures of fire and stained clothing come from Zechariah 3:2-4. Jude is hard on the intruders and gentle with those they have misled.

John is told, “Write on a scroll what you see and send it to the seven churches: to Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea” (1:11). The seven cities lay on a loop of road in the Roman province of Asia, in the order a messenger from Patmos would reach them. There were other churches in the province, such as Colossae and Troas, so the seven stand for the whole church; seven is the number of completeness in this book. Each is pictured as a golden lampstand with Christ walking among them (1:20; 2:1). Their conditions differ. Smyrna and Philadelphia are poor, pressed and praised. Ephesus is sound and loveless. Pergamum and Thyatira are faithful but put up with false teaching. Sardis is nearly dead, and Laodicea is rich and self-satisfied. Every letter ends, “He who has an ear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”

e.n: The angels of the seven churches
e.u: The seven stars in Christ’s hand
t: Each of the seven letters is addressed “To the angel of the church” in a city, and Christ explains that “The seven stars are the angels of the seven churches” (1:20). Who they are is debated. They may be heavenly angels who represent or guard each church, as nations have angels in Daniel 10. They may be human messengers or leaders, since the Greek word also means messenger. Or the angel may be a way of speaking of the church itself, its spirit or character, which would explain why the angel is praised and blamed for what the church does. Everywhere else in Revelation the word means a heavenly being.

e.u: A group in the churches of Asia
a: Those who hold the teaching of Balaam
t: The church at Ephesus is praised: “You hate the works of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate” (2:6). At Pergamum some hold their teaching, which is set beside “the teaching of Balaam,” who led Israel to “eat food sacrificed to idols and commit sexual immorality” (2:14-15). The prophetess at Thyatira taught the same (2:20). They seem to have been Christians who argued that believers could take part in the feasts of the trade guilds and the city, where the meat came from the temples and the emperor and the gods were honored. Paul dealt with a similar question at Corinth (1 Corinthians 8-10). Irenaeus and later writers traced the group to Nicolas of Antioch, one of the seven in Acts 6:5, but they may only have been guessing from the name.

e.u: Those who stay faithful to the end
t: Each of the seven letters ends with a promise “To the one who overcomes.” The Greek verb is nikaō, to conquer or win, from the word for victory. The promises are the tree of life, safety from the second death, hidden manna and a white stone, authority over the nations and the morning star, white clothing and a name kept in the Book of Life, a place as a pillar in God’s temple, and a seat on Christ’s throne: “just as I overcame and sat down with My Father on His throne” (3:21). All of them return in chapters 20-22. The book shows how the victory is won. The Lamb conquered by being slain (5:5-6), and his people conquer the dragon “by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony” (12:11). In Revelation to overcome is to stay faithful, if need be to death.

e.u: Enthroned around the throne of God
t: John sees that “Surrounding the throne were twenty-four other thrones, and on these thrones sat twenty-four elders dressed in white, with golden crowns on their heads” (4:4). They fall down before God, lay their crowns before the throne, hold harps and bowls of incense, sing the new song to the Lamb, and one of them twice explains to John what he sees (5:5; 7:13-14). Their number has been explained as twelve tribes and twelve apostles, the whole people of God in both covenants, whose names are on the gates and foundations of the new Jerusalem (21:12-14). Others see the twenty-four orders of priests and singers in 1 Chronicles 24-25, and others an order of angels, a heavenly council like that of Isaiah 24:23.

e.u: Around the throne, never ceasing to praise
t: Around the throne are four living creatures, covered with eyes, the first like a lion, the second like an ox, the third with a face like a man, the fourth like a flying eagle. “Day and night they never stop saying: ‘Holy, Holy, Holy, is the Lord God Almighty, who was and is and is to come!’” (4:8). They combine the four-faced cherubim of Ezekiel 1 and 10 with the six-winged seraphim of Isaiah 6. They lead the worship of heaven, call out the four horsemen (6:1-7), and hand the seven bowls to the angels (15:7). They are usually taken to stand for the whole living creation praising its Maker. From the 2nd century Christians also used them as signs of the four Gospels: in the best-known scheme the man is Matthew, the lion Mark, the ox Luke and the eagle John.

e.u: Riders of the first four seals
a: The four horsemen of the Apocalypse
t: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, four riders are called out. The first rides a white horse, holds a bow and is given a crown, “and he rode out to overcome and conquer” (6:2). The second, on a red horse, takes peace from the earth. The third, on a black horse, holds scales, and a voice names famine prices for wheat and barley. The fourth is on a pale green horse: “Its rider’s name was Death, and Hades followed close behind” (6:8). They are given authority over a quarter of the earth. The horses come from Zechariah 1 and 6. The riders are conquest, war, famine and death, the troubles Jesus called “the beginning of birth pains.” Some readers take the first rider as Christ or the gospel going out, since Christ rides a white horse in 19:11; most take him as conquest, like the other three.

e.u: Those slain for the word of God
t: At the fifth seal John sees “under the altar the souls of those who had been slain for the word of God and for the testimony they had upheld. And they cried out in a loud voice, ‘How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood and judge those who dwell upon the earth?’” (6:9-10). Each is given a white robe and told to rest a little longer. They appear again as those who conquered the beast (15:2), as the blood found in Babylon (17:6; 18:24), and as the souls who come to life and reign with Christ (20:4). Revelation treats their deaths as victories and their prayer for justice as one God will answer.

a: The servants of God sealed on their foreheads
t: John hears “the number of those who were sealed, 144,000 from all the tribes of Israel” (7:4), twelve thousand from each of twelve tribes. They are marked on the forehead as God’s own before the judgments fall. They appear again on Mount Zion with the Lamb, with his name and his Father’s name on their foreheads: “They follow the Lamb wherever He goes. They have been redeemed from among men as firstfruits to God and to the Lamb” (14:4). Some readers take them as Jewish believers. Others take the number as a picture of the whole church as God’s army, counted like the tribes in the book of Numbers, and identify them with the countless multitude that John sees straight afterward. The group known as Jehovah’s Witnesses takes the number literally, as those who will reign in heaven.

e.u: From every nation, before the throne
a: The multitude no one could count
Those who come out of the great tribulation
t: After the 144,000 are numbered, John sees “a multitude too large to count, from every nation and tribe and people and tongue, standing before the throne and before the Lamb. They were wearing white robes and holding palm branches in their hands” (7:9). An elder explains: “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb” (7:14). They serve God day and night, and the Lamb is their shepherd. A great multitude is heard again in 19:1-6, shouting “Hallelujah!” at the fall of Babylon and the wedding of the Lamb.

A voice says, “I will empower my two witnesses, and they will prophesy for 1,260 days, clothed in sackcloth” (11:3). “These witnesses are the two olive trees and the two lampstands that stand before the Lord of the earth” (11:4), a picture from Zechariah 4. Fire comes from their mouths, they can shut the sky and turn water to blood, as Elijah and Moses did. When they finish, the beast from the Abyss kills them; their bodies lie in the street of the great city for three and a half days while the world celebrates; then God raises them and calls them up to heaven. Readers have taken them as Moses and Elijah, as Enoch and Elijah (who did not die), as two prophets of the last days, as the Law and the Prophets, or as the church bearing witness, since two is the number of witnesses the law requires (Deuteronomy 19:15).

e.u: The great city, pictured as a prostitute
a: The woman on the scarlet beast
t: John sees a woman dressed in purple and scarlet, seated on a scarlet beast, drunk with the blood of the saints. “And on her forehead a mysterious name was written: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF PROSTITUTES AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH” (17:5). An angel explains that she sits on seven mountains and that she “is the great city that rules over the kings of the earth” (17:18). Chapter 18 is a funeral song over her: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” (18:2). Kings, merchants and sailors mourn the loss of her trade, and God’s people are told to come out of her. Babylon was the empire that destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC. For John’s first readers the name pointed to Rome, the city on seven hills, which destroyed Jerusalem again in AD 70. Other readings take her as unfaithful Jerusalem, as a world power still to come, or as human society organized without God in any age. She is the opposite of the bride, the new Jerusalem.

e.u: Those who grew rich from Babylon
a: Those who make their living from the sea
t: Three groups stand at a distance and lament the burning of Babylon. The kings of the earth, who shared her luxury, weep first. Then “the merchants of the earth will weep and mourn over her, because there is no one left to buy their cargo” (18:11), and John lists the cargo, from gold to slaves. Last come the shipmasters and sailors, throwing dust on their heads. Each group cries “Woe, woe” and marvels that she fell in a single hour. None of them mourns for her people; they mourn their own losses. The passage follows Ezekiel 26-27, the lament for the trading city of Tyre.

e.n: The bride, the wife of the Lamb
e.u: The people of God as a city
t: Heaven announces, “the marriage of the Lamb has come, and His bride has made herself ready” (19:7). Her fine linen “is the righteous acts of the saints” (19:8). When an angel says, “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb” (21:9), John is shown a city: “the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband” (21:2). The bride is the whole people of God, joined to Christ forever, and the city is where God lives with them. The picture comes from the prophets, who call God the husband of Israel (Isaiah 54:5; 62:5; Hosea 2:19), and from Paul (Ephesians 5:25-32). At the end “The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’” (22:17).

e.u: The nations gathered for the last battle
t: After the thousand years Satan goes out “to deceive the nations in the four corners of the earth—Gog and Magog—to assemble them for battle. Their number is like the sand of the seashore” (20:8). They surround the camp of the saints, and fire from heaven consumes them. In Ezekiel 38-39 Gog is a prince of the land of Magog who leads a great army from the far north against Israel and is destroyed by God. Magog is a grandson of Noah in Genesis 10:2. In Revelation the two names together stand for all the hostile nations of the world. Attempts to identify them with particular modern countries have changed with every generation and have no basis in the text.

e.n: Those who dwell on the earth
e.u: Revelation’s name for a world against God
a: Those who dwell upon the earth
t: The phrase “those who dwell on the earth” comes about ten times in Revelation and always means people who side with the beast against God. The souls under the altar ask God to “judge those who dwell upon the earth” (6:10); they gloat over the death of the two witnesses (11:10); and “all who dwell on the earth will worship the beast—all whose names have not been written from the foundation of the world in the Book of Life belonging to the Lamb who was slain” (13:8). They are deceived by the false prophet and made drunk by Babylon. Set against them are those whose home is in heaven. Yet the judgments are meant to bring them to repentance, and an angel still carries an eternal gospel “to those who dwell on the earth” (14:6).

Leaven is yeast, a small piece of fermented dough that makes a whole batch rise. Jesus uses it twice: as a warning, “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees,” meaning their hypocrisy and teaching, and as a picture of the kingdom of God spreading quietly through the world. The disciples at first thought he was talking about bread.
A Roman silver coin, about a day’s wage for a laborer or soldier. It is the pay in the workers in the vineyard parable, and Jesus asks to see one when asked about taxes to Caesar.
The smallest Greek bronze coin, worth a fraction of a denarius. The widow in the temple gives two of them, and Jesus says she has given more than all the rest.

A very large unit of weight, about 75 pounds (34 kg), used for silver and gold. A single talent was worth about fifteen years of a laborer’s wages. In the parable of the talents, the servants receive five, two and one.
A Greek unit worth about a hundred denarii, or about three months’ wages. In Luke’s parable of the minas, the servants each receive one.

A silver shekel was the Jewish temple coin. The stater was a Greek silver coin worth four drachmas, the exact temple tax for two people. Jesus tells Peter that the coin in the fish’s mouth will be enough for both of them.

The price Judas was paid to betray Jesus. It was also the compensation for a slave gored by an ox in the law of Moses. Judas threw the coins into the temple and the priests used them to buy the potter’s field.
The staple food, usually barley or wheat flatbread baked daily. Jesus feeds crowds with it, calls himself the bread of life, and breaks it at the Last Supper and on the road to Emmaus.

Paul says “the bread that we break” is a participation in the body of Christ, and “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body” (10:16-17). At the Supper “the Lord Jesus, on the night He was betrayed, took bread” (11:23).
A main source of protein in Galilee, usually dried or pickled. Several of the disciples were fishermen. Fish appear in the feedings, the miraculous catches and the breakfast on the beach.
The ordinary drink at meals, usually mixed with water. Jesus makes water into wine at Cana, is accused of being “a drunkard,” and uses the cup of wine at the Last Supper.
In Ephesians Paul says, “Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to reckless indiscretion. Instead, be filled with the Spirit” (5:18).
In Philippians Paul says he may be “poured out like a drink offering” (2:17).
In 1 Timothy overseers are not to be “dependent on wine” and Timothy is told to “use a little wine” for his stomach (3:3; 5:23).
A bag made from animal skin that held wine. New wine ferments and expands, so it needs flexible new skins. Old, stiff skins would burst.
The cup of wine at the Passover meal, which Jesus calls the new covenant in his blood. It also stands for suffering: in Gethsemane he prays, “Let this cup pass from me.”
Paul uses the cup for the Lord’s Supper: “the cup of blessing that we bless” and “the cup of the Lord” against “the cup of demons” (10:16, 21), and “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (11:25).

Six large stone jars, each holding twenty to thirty gallons, used for Jewish rites of purification. Stone did not become ceremonially unclean like pottery. Jesus has them filled with water, which becomes wine.

A small clay lamp burning olive oil, which gave a dim light. It was put on a stand, not under a basket. Jesus says, “You are the light of the world,” and lamps feature in the parable of the ten virgins.

A tiny seed, proverbially the smallest a farmer sowed, that grows into a bush two to three meters tall. Jesus compares the kingdom of God to it, and says faith as small as a mustard seed can move mountains.

A heavy grinding stone. A large one turned by a donkey was far heavier than the small hand mills women used each morning. Jesus says it would be better to be thrown into the sea with a millstone around the neck than to cause a little one to stumble.

A wooden beam that joined two animals for plowing. Rabbis spoke of the “yoke of the law” and a teacher’s yoke. Jesus invites the weary, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me... for my yoke is easy.”
Paul writes “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14).

Paul writes “do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery” (Galatians 5:1), pointing to the burden of the law that some wanted Gentile believers to take on. In Acts 15:10 Peter uses the same picture.

Leather soles tied to the foot with straps. Taking off or carrying another’s sandals was a servant’s task. John the Baptist says he is not worthy to untie the thong of the coming one’s sandals. Disciples are told to take no extra pair.

The tunic was the basic undergarment, and the cloak a heavier outer garment that also served as a blanket. The law forbade keeping a poor person’s cloak overnight. Jesus says that if someone takes your tunic, give your cloak as well.
In 2 Timothy 4:13 Paul asks Timothy to bring “the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas.” The Greek word, phailones, occurs only here in the New Testament.
In Hebrews the prophets and others who suffered “went around in sheepskins and goatskins” (11:37).

Jewish men wore tassels on the corners of their cloaks to remember God’s commandments. The woman with a hemorrhage touches Jesus’ tassel, and Jesus criticizes the scribes who lengthen theirs for show.
Small leather boxes containing Scripture verses, strapped to the forehead and arm during prayer. Jesus criticizes those who make their phylacteries broad to be noticed.

A small flask carved from soft stone, used for expensive perfume. A woman breaks one and pours nard on Jesus’ head or feet. John names her as Mary of Bethany and says the perfume was worth about a year’s wages.

The gifts of the Magi. Gold was for kings, frankincense was incense used in temple worship, and myrrh was a fragrant resin used in burial. Matthew does not say there were three Magi, only three gifts.
Strips of cloth wrapped around a newborn to keep it warm and still. Luke gives them as a sign to the shepherds.
A feeding trough for animals, where Mary laid Jesus. Houses in Judea often kept animals in a lower room or a nearby cave. Luke does not say “stable” or “innkeeper.” The “inn” may be a guest room.
A cast net was thrown by hand and a dragnet was pulled between boats. Peter, Andrew, James and John mended and cast nets, and Jesus calls them to “fish for people.”

A wooden fishing boat. In 1986, a first-century boat was found in the mud of the Sea of Galilee, about 27 feet long, large enough for a crew of five. Jesus often teaches from a boat and crosses the lake in one.
Paul says “three times I was shipwrecked. I spent a night and a day in the open sea” (2 Corinthians 11:25).
Salt was used to season and to preserve food and it was valuable. Jesus says, “You are the salt of the earth,” and warns that salt which has lost its taste is good for nothing.
In Colossians speech is to be “gracious, seasoned with salt” (4:6).
Grapevines grew throughout Judea and Galilee. Israel is called God’s vine in the prophets, and Jesus says, “I am the true vine.”
A common tree whose fruit was eaten fresh, dried or pressed into cakes. Jesus uses it in parables about fruitfulness and readiness, and Nathanael was under a fig tree when Jesus saw him.

The most important animal in Israel’s economy and a constant image in the Gospels, for people in need, followers of Jesus and God’s flock. Shepherds lived with their flocks, so the title “shepherd” was personal.
1 Peter 2:25 says “you were like sheep going astray, but now you have returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls,” and 5:2 tells the elders to be “shepherds of God’s flock.”
A bird of the poor. Mary and Joseph offered two doves at the presentation of Jesus, and doves were sold in the temple courts. The Spirit descends “like a dove” at Jesus’ baptism.
Guests in a house had their dusty feet washed by a servant. At the Last Supper, Jesus takes off his outer garment, wraps a towel around his waist and washes his disciples’ feet.

A fire of burning charcoal appears twice in John: in the high priest’s courtyard where Peter warms himself and denies Jesus, and on the beach where the risen Jesus cooks fish for breakfast and later restores Peter.
A wreath of thorny branches that Roman soldiers pressed on Jesus’ head to mock him as a king, together with a purple robe and a reed for a scepter.

A Roman method of execution for slaves, rebels and non-citizens, designed to be slow and humiliating. The condemned usually carried the crossbeam to the place of execution. Jesus tells his followers to take up their own cross.

Galatians returns to the cross at each turning point: Christ “clearly portrayed as crucified” (3:1), “the offense of the cross” (5:11), and “the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me” (6:14).
A sign (titulus) stating the charge. John says Pilate had it written in Hebrew, Latin and Greek: “Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews.” The chief priests asked him to change it, and he refused.
A Roman soldier pierced Jesus’ side with a spear to confirm that he was dead, and blood and water came out. John sees this as fulfilling Scripture.

A small bushy herb used to sprinkle blood and water in purification rituals, and at the first Passover to apply lamb’s blood to doorposts. John says a sponge of sour wine was lifted to Jesus’ lips on a hyssop branch.
In Hebrews, Moses sprinkles “the scroll and all the people” with blood, “water, scarlet wool, and hyssop” (9:19).

Jews wrapped bodies in linen strips with spices such as myrrh and aloes. Nicodemus brought about seventy-five pounds of them for Jesus’ burial. Peter and John later see the empty linen cloths and the face cloth folded separately.

Rock tombs were sealed with a large stone, which was either wedged in place or rolled in a groove across the entrance. Joseph of Arimathea laid Jesus in his own new tomb, cut from rock, and the women find the stone rolled away.
Books were scrolls of parchment or papyrus. In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus is handed the scroll of Isaiah, finds the place and reads.
Paul speaks of “the reading of the old covenant,” meaning the public reading of the scrolls of the law in the synagogue (2 Corinthians 3:14-15).
Paul quotes “the Book of the Law” (Galatians 3:10) and says “the Scripture” announced the gospel to Abraham (3:8).
In 2 Timothy Paul asks for “my scrolls, especially the parchments” (4:13).

Roman soldiers and the temple guard were armed. In Gethsemane, a disciple draws a sword and cuts off a servant’s ear, and Jesus says, “Put your sword back... for all who take the sword will perish by the sword.”
In Ephesians the one weapon of attack is “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (6:17).

In Hebrews, “the word of God” is “sharper than any double-edged sword” (4:12), and some of the faithful “escaped the edge of the sword” while others “were put to death by the sword” (11:34, 37). The word is machaira, the short sword.

A rule of later Jewish tradition limiting how far one could walk on the Sabbath, about 2,000 cubits (about three-quarters of a mile). Luke mentions it when describing the distance from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem.
Small stones or marked objects drawn or thrown to learn God’s choice, a custom behind Proverbs 16:33. The eleven cast lots to choose Matthias to replace Judas.
The Greek word spyris means a large woven basket, big enough for a man. The disciples lower Saul over the wall of Damascus in one.
Paul says he escaped Damascus when “I was lowered in a basket through a window in the wall” (2 Corinthians 11:33).
A large linen sheet let down from heaven with all kinds of animals, reptiles and birds. Peter is told, “What God has made clean, do not call common.”
Prisoners were chained to guards or fastened in wooden stocks. Peter sleeps between two soldiers in chains, Paul and Silas are fastened in stocks, and Paul is chained at Caesarea and in Rome.
Paul lists “imprisonments” among his hardships (2 Corinthians 6:5; 11:23).
In Ephesians Paul says “I am an ambassador in chains” (6:20).
In Philippians Paul writes that “my chains” are known “throughout the whole palace guard” (1:13), and that the brothers are more confident “by my chains” (1:14).
In Colossians Paul says the mystery of Christ is “for which I am in chains” (4:3), and ends, “Remember my chains” (4:18). Aristarchus is “my fellow prisoner” (4:10).
In 2 Timothy Paul is “chained like a criminal” (2:9) and speaks of Onesiphorus as “unashamed of my chains” (1:16).
Cloth dyed with an expensive dye taken from sea snails. A seller of purple was a trader to the wealthy. Lydia is one.
Paul and Aquila were skenopoioi, which means tentmakers or leatherworkers. They would have sewn goatskin and canvas, and the trade let Paul pay his own way.
Paul says he worked for his living in Corinth and other cities (9:6, 12; compare Acts 18:3), though he had the right to be supported.
In 2 Corinthians Paul calls the body “the earthly tent we live in” (5:1) and says he supported himself in Corinth and was “not a burden” (11:7-9; 12:13).
In 1 and 2 Thessalonians Paul reminds the church that he worked “night and day” so as not to be a burden (1 Thessalonians 2:9; 2 Thessalonians 3:8).
Small silver models of Artemis’ temple that the silversmiths of Ephesus sold to pilgrims and visitors. The trade collapses if people stop worshiping her, so Demetrius leads the riot.
Books of spells, charms and magic formulas. New believers at Ephesus burn their scrolls in public, worth 50,000 pieces of silver.
Small cloths worn by a worker at his trade. Luke says cloths touched by Paul were carried to the sick, who were healed.
A large ship dropped four anchors from the stern in the storm to keep from running aground. The sailors tried to escape in the skiff (small boat), but Paul tells the centurion they must stay.

In Hebrews the hope set before believers is “an anchor for the soul, firm and secure” (6:19), the only use of the picture in the New Testament, which goes with the idea of a ship holding firm in the harbor.
A large freighter from Egypt carrying wheat to Rome. The ship in Acts holds 276 people and has the Twin Brothers (Castor and Pollux) as its figurehead.

An olive tree gives fruit for oil and may live for hundreds of years. Farmers could graft a branch from one tree into another. Paul pictures Israel as a cultivated olive and the Gentiles as a wild olive shoot grafted in “contrary to nature” (11:24), and tells them not to boast over the branches that were broken off.

A potter shaped each jar on a wheel from a lump of clay. Isaiah and Jeremiah both use the picture of God as potter and his people as clay. Paul asks, “Does not the potter have the right to make from the same lump of clay one vessel for special occasions and another for common use?” (9:21).

Charcoal fires cooked food and warmed houses. Paul quotes Proverbs 25:21-22: feed your hungry enemy, “for in so doing, you will heap burning coals on his head” (12:20). Scholars read the picture as shame leading to repentance.
The gold lid of the ark of the covenant, sprinkled with blood on the Day of Atonement. The Greek word hilasterion, used for it, is the word Paul uses in Romans 3:25 for the “atoning sacrifice.”
In Hebrews, “Above the ark were the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat” (9:5). The Greek word is hilasterion, the same word Paul uses in Romans 3:25.
A kiss of greeting among family and close friends. Paul closes with “Greet one another with a holy kiss” (16:16), which shows that the Roman believers treated each other as family.
Paul ends 1 Corinthians with “Greet one another with a holy kiss” (16:20).
Paul ends 2 Corinthians with “Greet one another with a holy kiss” (13:12).
In 1 Thessalonians Paul ends with “Greet all the brothers with a holy kiss” (5:26).
1 Peter 5:14 says “Greet one another with a kiss of love.”

Mirrors were disks of polished metal, usually bronze, with a handle. They gave a darker and less exact image than a modern mirror, and Corinth was known for its bronze work. Paul writes, “Now we see but a dim reflection as in a mirror; then we shall see face to face” (13:12).
In 2 Corinthians 3:18 the verb can mean to look as in a mirror or to reflect: believers “with unveiled faces all reflect the glory of the Lord.”

James 1:23-24 compares the one who hears the word and does not do it to a man who looks at his face in a mirror and forgets what he looks like. The Greek word for mirror, esoptron, occurs in the New Testament only here and in 1 Corinthians 13:12.

Paul uses instruments to make a point about clear speech. Without love a person is “only a ringing gong or a clanging cymbal” (13:1). A flute or harp must give distinct notes, and “if the trumpet sounds a muffled call, who will prepare for battle?” (14:8). In the same way, speech in the meeting must be understood.

Paul tells the church that each builder on the foundation of Christ must be careful what he uses: “gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or straw.” The Day will test the work: what is made of gold, silver or stone survives fire, and what is made of wood, hay or straw burns (3:12-15).
In Ephesians the church is built on a foundation with Christ as the “cornerstone,” and “the whole building is fitted together” (2:20-21).

A farmer sowed a bare seed and God gave the plant. Paul uses the picture twice: “I planted the seed and Apollos watered it, but God made it grow” (3:6), and in the resurrection: “What you sow does not come to life unless it dies” (15:36). The seed and the plant are the same plant in two forms, as the natural body and the spiritual body are.
In 2 Corinthians Paul says “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly” (9:6) and that God “supplies seed to the sower and bread for food” (9:10).
Paul uses the farmer’s rule in Galatians 6:7-9: “Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return,” and “in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.”

On the threshing floor an ox walked over the cut grain to loosen the kernels. The law said not to muzzle it while it worked. Paul applies the rule to preachers: “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain.” “Is it about oxen that God is concerned?” (9:9). The workman deserves a share of the harvest.
In 1 Timothy Paul quotes “Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain” as a reason to give elders “double honor” (5:17-18).

The Greek word is makellon, from the Latin macellum, a building of shops where butchers and food sellers worked. Much of the meat for sale had come from temple sacrifices. Paul tells believers, “Eat anything sold in the meat market without raising questions of conscience” (10:25).

Winners in the great Greek games received a wreath of leaves, such as pine or celery at the Isthmian Games near Corinth. It withered within days. Paul says athletes train “for a crown that is perishable, but we do it for a crown that is imperishable” (9:25).
In Philippians Paul calls the church “my joy and crown” (4:1), using the word for a victor’s wreath, and presses “toward the goal to win the prize” (3:14).
In 1 Thessalonians Paul calls the church “our hope, our joy, our crown of boasting” (2:19).
In 1 Timothy “train yourself for godliness” and “fight the good fight of the faith” use the language of the athlete (4:7-8; 6:12).
In 2 Timothy “the crown of righteousness” waits for Paul and for “all who crave His appearing” (4:8).
1 Peter 5:4 promises the faithful elder “the crown of glory that will never fade away,” a wreath that does not wither as a victor’s wreath did.

In Paul’s world women often wore a veil or a fold of the cloak over the head in public, and men commonly prayed with the head covered at Roman sacrifices. Paul speaks of heads covered and uncovered in the meeting (11:4-7), and of hair as “a covering” (11:15). What he meant is debated.

Clay jars were the ordinary containers of the ancient world, used for water, oil, grain and wine. They were cheap and easy to break. Some of the Dead Sea Scrolls were found stored in such jars. Paul writes, “we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us” (4:7).

A seal was a small stamp, often cut in stone, pressed into soft clay or wax to close a letter, a door or a jar and show who owned it. Paul says God “placed His seal on us” (1:22). It marks God’s ownership, along with the Spirit given as a pledge.
In Ephesians believers “were sealed with the promised Holy Spirit” (1:13) and are told not to grieve him, “in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (4:30).
In Revelation God’s servants are sealed on their foreheads (7:3), and the locusts may harm only those without the seal of God (9:4).

A veil was a cloth worn over the head or face. Paul recalls the veil of Moses, who “would put a veil over his face to keep the Israelites from gazing at the end of what was fading away” (3:13). He uses it as a picture of a mind that cannot yet see: “only in Christ can it be removed” (3:14).
Hebrews uses the word katapetasma for the temple or tabernacle curtain, not a head covering. See “The curtain (katapetasma).”

Travelers who were strangers carried a letter from someone known in the place they were going. Many such letters survive on papyrus. Paul asks, “do we need, like some people, letters of recommendation to you or from you?” (3:1), and says “it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends” (10:18).
2 John does not mention a letter of recommendation, but it gives the test a church applied to a visitor: what he teaches about Jesus Christ (7-11).

In 3 John 12 the elder vouches for Demetrius, who probably carried the letter: “We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true.” The verse works as a short letter of recommendation inside the letter.

Incense and perfume were part of festivals, banquets and temple worship. Paul says “we are to God the sweet aroma of Christ among those who are being saved and those who are perishing” (2:15). The Old Testament uses the same words for a pleasing sacrifice.
In Philippians the church’s gift is “a fragrant offering, an acceptable sacrifice, well-pleasing to God” (4:18).

Two kinds of beating are on Paul’s list. Roman magistrates had officers carry rods bound in a bundle (Acts 16:22). The Jewish punishment was a flogging limited by Deuteronomy 25:3 to forty strokes, and later Jewish practice gave thirty-nine to stay under the limit. Paul says, “Five times I received from the Jews the forty lashes minus one. Three times I was beaten with rods” (11:24-25).

Soldiers carried swords, shields and spears, and armies used siege engines and ramps to break strongholds. Paul uses both pictures: “with the weapons of righteousness in the right hand and in the left” (6:7), and “The weapons of our warfare are not the weapons of the world. Instead, they have divine power to demolish strongholds” (10:4).
In Ephesians 6:10-17 the weapons are those of a Roman soldier, but they are spiritual: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation and the word of God.

In wealthy Greek and Roman homes a trusted slave called a paidagogos led a boy to school and back, watched his conduct and kept him out of trouble. He did not teach the lessons, and his job ended when the boy grew up. Paul uses the word in “the law became our guardian to lead us to Christ” and “Now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian” (3:24-25). He also says an heir who is a child is “subject to guardians and trustees until the date set by his father” (4:2).

Leaven was a piece of fermented dough kept from the last baking to start the next batch, and a little spread through all of it. Paul says “A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough” (5:9) about the false teaching. In 1 Corinthians 5:6 he uses the same saying about sin in the church.

e.n: Large letters, in his own hand
t: Paul usually dictated to a scribe (Romans 16:22). In Galatians he takes the pen: “See what large letters I am using to write to you with my own hand!” (6:11). Papyrus letters often show the same change, as the sender added a closing line in his own writing. Whether the large letters were for emphasis or because of his eyesight is a guess.
In 2 Thessalonians Paul writes, “This greeting is in my own hand—Paul. This is my mark in every letter” (3:17).
In Philemon he says, “I, Paul, write this with my own hand” (19) in the middle of the letter, as he promises to repay what Onesimus owes.

A Roman legionary carried a large curved shield (the scutum), a helmet, a breastplate of mail or plates, a belt that held his sword, and hobnailed sandals for marching. Paul was under guard from such men (Acts 28:16) and uses their gear to describe God’s armor: “the belt of truth,” “the breastplate of righteousness,” feet “fitted with the readiness of the gospel of peace,” “the shield of faith,” “the helmet of salvation” and “the sword of the Spirit” (6:14-17). The Greek word for the shield (thyreos) is a long door-shaped shield.
In 1 Thessalonians the breastplate and helmet stand for “faith and love” and “the hope of salvation” (5:8).
In 2 Timothy the soldier is “a good soldier of Christ Jesus” who “refrains from entangling himself in civilian affairs” (2:3-4).

e.n: Cornerstone and ligaments: the building and body images
t: Ephesians pictures the church as a building and as a body. The building has a foundation of “the apostles and prophets,” with Christ as the “cornerstone,” and the “whole building is fitted together” (2:20-21). The body is “fitted and held together by every supporting ligament” and “grows and builds itself up in love through the work of each individual part” (4:16). The same Greek verb, “to fit together,” is used for both.
1 Peter 2:4-8 calls Christ the “living stone” and believers “living stones” built into a “spiritual house.”

A drink offering, or libation, was wine poured out beside or over a sacrifice. The law of Moses required it with the burnt offering (Numbers 15:1-10), and Greeks and Romans poured wine to their gods at meals and at altars. Paul says, “even if I am being poured out like a drink offering on the sacrifice and service of your faith, I am glad and rejoice” (Philippians 2:17).
In 2 Timothy 4:6 Paul says, “I am already being poured out like a drink offering.”

Ancient letters and papyri show how people recorded payments. The word “receipt” is often a form of the Greek verb apecho, meaning I have received in full. Paul uses the same verb in Philippians 4:18, “I have all I need and more, now that I have received your gifts,” and speaks of “giving and receiving” (4:15) and of “fruit that may be credited to your account” (4:17). The language is that of bookkeeping, used for a gift of love.
In Colossians the “debt ascribed to us in the decrees” (2:14) is a handwritten note of debt (cheirographon), the kind of document recorded on papyrus.

The Lycus Valley was known for its wool and its dyes. The Greek geographer Strabo writes that the sheep of Laodicea gave a very fine wool, and Hierapolis had guilds of dyers and weavers, as its tombstones show. Paul uses the picture of clothing for the new life: “you have taken off the old self with its practices, and have put on the new self” (3:9-10), and “clothe yourselves with hearts of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience” (3:12). The readers made their living in cloth and would know what a garment is.

Paul’s letters were carried by trusted friends, who also gave the news and could answer questions. In Colossians, Tychicus and Onesimus bring the letter and “will tell you about everything here” (4:7-9). Letters were read aloud to a group, and then copied and passed on, as 4:16 describes. A scribe often wrote the body of a letter, and Paul adds, “This greeting is in my own hand” (4:18).
In 1 Thessalonians Paul charges the church “before the Lord to have this letter read to all the brothers” (5:27), and in 2 Thessalonians he warns against a “letter seeming to be from us” (2:2).
In Philemon the letter may have gone with Onesimus himself when he went back to Colossae with Tychicus, who carried Colossians (Colossians 4:7-9).
1 Peter 5:12 says, “Through Silvanus, whom I regard as a faithful brother, I have written to you briefly,” which may mean that Silvanus wrote the letter down, carried it, or both.

In 2 John, the writer would “prefer not to do so with paper and ink” (12) but come in person, and the letter closes with greetings from the children of “your elect sister” (13), a church that is also sending its regards. The letter was probably carried by a trusted friend.
In 3 John, brothers carry news of Gaius to the elder (3, 6), and Demetrius probably carries the letter back (12). The elder also mentions an earlier letter: “I have written to the church” (9).

Paul says the Lord will descend “with a loud command, with the voice of an archangel, and with the trumpet of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). In the Old Testament a trumpet (shofar) was blown to call the people together, to announce a festival or to warn of war, and a great trumpet sounded at Sinai (Exodus 19:16). Jesus says the angels will gather the elect “with a great trumpet call” (Matthew 24:31), and Paul says “the trumpet will sound” at the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:52). In all of them the trumpet is a signal that God is acting.
In Revelation seven angels are given seven trumpets (8:2), and the seventh trumpet announces that the kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ (11:15).

Paul says the women should adorn themselves “with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes, but with good deeds” (1 Timothy 2:9-10). Pearls were costly, and the verse puts braids with gold and pearls among the marks of wealth. Peter gives a similar warning about braids and gold in 1 Peter 3:3-4. The point is where the adornment comes from, and Paul does not forbid every style.
1 Peter 3:3 says that a wife’s beauty “should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes,” but from “the unfading beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit.”

Paul writes, “I, Paul, write this with my own hand. I will repay it” (Philemon 19). In the Roman world a debt could be recorded in a note signed by the debtor in his own hand, called a cheirographon in Greek. Colossians 2:14 uses that word for the record of debt that was canceled at the cross. Paul normally dictated his letters and added a closing line himself (1 Corinthians 16:21; Galatians 6:11; Colossians 4:18), but here he says he wrote the promise, which gives it the force of a signed note. Whether he meant the whole letter or just this part is debated.

James pictures a man who comes into the meeting “wearing a gold ring and fine clothes” (2:2). The Greek word for “gold-ringed,” chrysodaktylios, is found only here in the New Testament. In Rome a gold ring marked rank, as the writer Pliny the Elder explains: first reserved for senators, then for the order of knights, and later granted by emperors to favored freedmen. In the story of the prodigal son the father puts a ring on his returning son’s finger (Luke 15:22), a mark of honor. James’s story is of a visitor who looks important, and the point is how the assembly treats him.

“Consider ships as well. Although they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are steered by a very small rudder wherever the pilot is inclined” (3:4). Large ancient ships were steered by one or two broad steering oars at the stern, and Acts 27:40 speaks of the “rudders” (the same Greek word, pedalion, plural) that were lashed up in the storm. The word occurs in the New Testament only in these two places. In James the rudder is the picture of the tongue: small, yet it turns the whole.

“When we put bits into the mouths of horses to make them obey us, we can guide the whole animal” (3:3). The Greek word chalinos, “bit,” occurs here and in Revelation 14:20, where it is the horses’ “bridle.” James uses the verb “to bridle” (chalinagogeo) twice: of the tongue in 1:26 and of the whole body in 3:2. Both words are found only in James in the New Testament. The picture is of a small piece of metal that decides where a large animal goes.

Olive oil was used for cooking, lamps, skin care and wounds. In the parable of the good Samaritan he pours oil and wine on the wounds (Luke 10:34), and Mark 6:13 says the disciples “anointing them with oil” healed the sick. In James 5:14 the elders of the church “anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord” and pray over him. The Greek words are elaion, “olive oil,” and aleipho, “to anoint.” The oil may have been used as medicine, or as a sign, or both, and churches have read it in different ways.

A goldsmith heated raw gold in a small clay furnace until the impurities rose to the top and could be skimmed off, leaving pure gold. Excavators at Sardis, one of the cities of the Roman province of Asia named in 1 Peter 1:1, found workshops of the sixth century BC where gold and silver were separated from each other. Proverbs 17:3 says that the crucible tests silver and the furnace gold, but the LORD tests hearts. Peter says that “the proven character of your faith” is “more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire” (1:7). The “fiery trial” of 4:12 uses a Greek word related to fire.

“Like newborn babies, crave pure spiritual milk, so that by it you may grow up in your salvation, now that you have tasted that the Lord is good” (2:2-3). The Greek logikon, “spiritual” or “of the word,” is a rare word found elsewhere only in Romans 12:1, and adolon, “pure,” is found only here. Peter has just said that his readers have been “born again” through the word (1:23), so the babies of 2:2 are those new to the faith. Hebrews 5:12-14 and 1 Corinthians 3:2 also use the picture of milk, but there it stands for what a person ought to have outgrown. Peter’s use is positive: milk is the food of the newly born, and the readers should long for it.

Genesis 6-9 tells how Noah built a large boat of “gopher wood” at God’s command and was saved with his family and the animals when the flood came, and how the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat (8:4). 1 Peter 3:20 recalls “the days of Noah while the ark was being built” and says that in the ark “a few people, only eight souls, were saved through water.” Peter then compares the water with baptism (3:21). Babylonian flood stories on clay tablets, such as Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, also tell of a boat built to survive a flood, with a dove and other birds sent out to find land. Scholars debate how the accounts are related. The ark’s resting place is not known; the Bible names a region, and the name Ararat is the same as Urartu, a kingdom around Lake Van.
2 Peter 2:5 says God “preserved Noah, a preacher of righteousness, among the eight,” and does not mention the ark.

“Your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Lions lived in Israel in biblical times and were a threat to flocks (1 Samuel 17:34-35; Amos 3:12). The Psalms use the lion for enemies who attack the righteous (Psalm 22:13, 21), and Daniel was kept safe in the den of lions (Daniel 6). In the Roman world lions were also killed or used to kill people in the arena. Peter’s readers would know both. The “adversary” (antidikos) is a legal opponent in court. Peter tells them to be “sober-minded and alert” and to “resist him, standing firm in your faith.”
In Revelation 5:5 Christ is “the Lion of the tribe of Judah,” and the first living creature is like a lion (4:7).

“For, ‘All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field; the grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of the Lord stands forever.’ And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.” The words are from Isaiah 40:6-8, a promise to the exiles in Babylon. In Israel grass and wildflowers grew in the winter rains and were scorched when the hot east wind blew in late spring (Psalm 103:15-16). James uses the same picture for the rich man (James 1:10-11).
