For Peter the contrast is between the short life of any human glory and the word that gave his readers new birth.

e.n: The ark of the covenant and what was in it
t: Hebrews describes the tabernacle’s furniture in the Most Holy Place: “the golden altar of incense and the gold-covered ark of the covenant. Inside the ark were the gold jar of manna, Aaron’s staff that had budded, and the stone tablets of the covenant. Above the ark were the cherubim of glory, overshadowing the mercy seat” (9:4-5). The ark is a point of difficulty. In Exodus 16:33-34 and Numbers 17:10 the jar of manna and Aaron’s staff were set “before the testimony,” and 1 Kings 8:9 says that when Solomon brought the ark into the temple there was nothing in it except the two stone tablets. The writer may be describing the whole arrangement or following a Jewish tradition that placed all three inside. The “altar of incense” raises a second question: in Exodus 30:6 it stood in front of the curtain. The Greek word thumiaterion can also mean “censer,” the pan of incense the high priest carried on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:12-13), and scholars think this may be the writer’s meaning. The writer does not stop to explain: “we cannot discuss these things in detail now” (9:5).

The “curtain” of Hebrews is the veil that hung between the Holy Place and the Most Holy Place (“Behind the second curtain was a room called the Most Holy Place,” 9:3). It is the barrier the high priest could pass only once a year. The writer uses it three times. Hope “enters the inner sanctuary behind the curtain, where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf” (6:19-20). And believers have “confidence to enter the Most Holy Place by the blood of Jesus, by the new and living way opened for us through the curtain of His body” (10:19-20). In the Gospels, the curtain of the temple was torn in two at Jesus’ death (Mark 15:38). The phrase “the curtain of His body” is explained in different ways: the curtain was his flesh, which was torn in death, or the way in was opened through his body in the sense of his life given.

e.n: Scarlet wool, hyssop and the ashes of a heifer
t: Hebrews mentions two kinds of purification. The first is the covenant ceremony at Sinai: Moses “took the blood of calves and goats, along with water, scarlet wool, and hyssop, and sprinkled the scroll and all the people, saying, ‘This is the blood of the covenant, which God has commanded you to keep’” (9:19-20; compare Exodus 24:6-8). Exodus does not mention scarlet wool or hyssop in that scene, which come from other purification rites, such as Leviticus 14 and Numbers 19. The second is “the ashes of a heifer sprinkled on those who are ceremonially unclean” (9:13), the red heifer of Numbers 19, which made a person clean after touching a dead body. The writer’s point is a contrast of effect: such rites “sanctify them so that their bodies are clean,” but the blood of Christ will “purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God” (9:13-14). “Without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness” (9:22).

Of the unnamed faithful, Hebrews says that “They went around in sheepskins and goatskins, destitute, oppressed, and mistreated” (11:37). A skin garment was the clothing of the poor and of the prophets; Elijah is described in 2 Kings 1:8 as wearing a garment of hair and a leather belt, and the cloak passed to Elisha is a prophet’s mantle (1 Kings 19:19). Zechariah 13:4 mentions a hairy cloak worn by prophets. The writer joins the picture of poverty with that of exile: “They wandered in deserts and mountains, and hid in caves and holes in the ground” (11:38), as Elijah did and as faithful Jews did during the Maccabean revolt (1 Maccabees 2:28-38).

Paul asks Timothy to bring “my scrolls, especially the parchments” (2 Timothy 4:13). Parchment is animal skin prepared for writing, and ancient writers said it was developed at Pergamon, which gave the word its name. Most books in Paul’s day were papyrus rolls, and the Roman poet Martial describes small parchment notebooks. The Greek word for the “parchments” (membranai) is a Latin loan word, and the letter does not say what was written on them. The request comes from a man in chains who expects to die and still wants to read.

e.n: Vessels of gold, silver, wood and clay
t: Paul writes of “a large house” with “vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay,” some “for honorable use” and others “for common use” (2 Timothy 2:20). A wealthy Roman household kept fine silver for the table, as the silver set found at Boscoreale shows, and plain clay and wooden vessels for everyday work. Paul turns the picture into a call to “cleanse” oneself and become “a vessel for honor” (2:21). In Romans 9:21-23 and 2 Corinthians 4:7 he uses clay vessels in other ways.

Franciscan archaeologists (from 1968) dug under an octagonal church and found a cluster of small basalt houses around shared courtyards. One room was plastered and used for gatherings from the 1st century on, and later got a church of its own.

The Gospels place Jesus’ base, and Simon Peter’s home, in Capernaum. The early veneration of this one house, and the way it changed from a home into a meeting place, makes it a strong candidate. The Peter of the Capernaum house is the apostle who calls himself “Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ” at the head of this letter. The fisherman from Bethsaida became the leader of the church in Jerusalem and then travelled.
Caution: No inscription names Peter. The link rests on early veneration, not on a signed doorway.
f: Capernaum, north shore of the Sea of Galilee
1st century AD, with a church built over it in the 5th

e.n: Capernaum: the white synagogue and the black one beneath
t: The striking white limestone synagogue visible today is later than Jesus. Beneath it, excavators found black basalt walls and a pavement that many think belonged to a 1st-century synagogue.
Luke says a Roman centurion helped build the town’s synagogue, and Mark and Luke show Jesus teaching and healing there on the Sabbath. The basalt layer is the likeliest remnant of that building.
Caution: The white building you see is 300+ years after Jesus; scholars still argue about its exact date and about the basalt layer.
f: White building 4th–5th century AD; basalt foundations below are earlier

t: In the drought of 1986 two brothers spotted the outline of a wooden hull in the exposed mud. It is about 27 ft (8.2 m) long and 7.5 ft (2.3 m) wide, patched with at least a dozen kinds of wood, and could hold around 15 people. Radiocarbon and pottery date it to Jesus’ time.

It shows the kind of working fishing boat the Gospels describe: a vessel big enough to carry a teacher and a few disciples, to be rowed or sailed across the lake, or to serve as a floating platform near the shore.
Caution: The nickname is modern. Nothing links this boat to Jesus or his disciples; it is evidence of the same world.

e.n: Fishing on the lake: hooks, weights and salted fish
t: Lead weights for casting nets, stone anchors and bronze fishhooks turn up at lakeshore sites such as Magdala and Bethsaida. Magdala’s Greek name, Taricheae, means “salted fish”, and it was a processing center for the catch.
It was a real trade with owners, hired men and partners, as Zebedee and his sons show. Fishing also fed the economy that taxes and tolls were collected from along the shore.

e.n: Magdala: a synagogue with a carved stone
t: Excavations since 2009 uncovered a 1st-century synagogue, a market, harbor installations and ritual baths. In the synagogue hall lay the Magdala Stone, carved with a seven-branched menorah and other Temple symbols.
Magdala was the home of Mary Magdalene. The synagogue is one of the very few from Jesus’ lifetime, and the stone suggests how closely Galilean Jews felt tied to the Jerusalem Temple.
Caution: The Gospels never say Jesus taught in Magdala’s synagogue; it shows the setting, not a recorded event.
f: Magdala (Migdal), west shore of the lake
1st century BC – AD 67 (the town was destroyed in the revolt)

t: A Byzantine church floor in front of the altar shows a basket of loaves flanked by two fish. Nearby springs flowed into the lake, the “seven springs” (Heptapegon) that gave the place its Arabic name.
Pilgrims since the 4th century have remembered the feeding of the crowd here, and the nearby shoreline chapel recalls the breakfast on the beach after the resurrection.
Caution: The Gospels do not name the exact spot, and John places the feeding near Bethsaida; Tabgha is the traditional site.
f: Mosaic about AD 450–480 (church tradition from the 4th century)

e.n: Chorazin: a town of black basalt
t: Excavations show a basalt town with houses, olive presses and ritual baths. Its later synagogue is richly carved and held a basalt “Seat of Moses” for the one reading the Law.

Jesus names Chorazin with Bethsaida and Capernaum as towns that saw his miracles and did not repent, yet the Gospels record none of those miracles. The town shows how much of his work we do not read about.
Caution: The impressive synagogue is later than Jesus, though a 1st-century settlement lay beneath it.
f: Town of Jesus’ day; ornate synagogue 3rd–4th century AD

e.n: Bethsaida: et-Tell and a rival site
t: At et-Tell, excavators found an Iron Age city gate, and Hellenistic and Roman houses, including a so-called fisherman’s house with hooks and net weights. A second candidate, el-Araj, nearer the shore, has been dug since 2015.
Bethsaida was the hometown of Peter, Andrew and Philip, and the place where Jesus healed a blind man by stages and (by Luke) fed the five thousand nearby.
Caution: Which mound is the true Bethsaida is still debated.
f: North shore of the lake, east of the Jordan
1st century AD (city of Philip the tetrarch)

t: A large cave and a strong spring pour out at the foot of Mount Hermon. Beside them are niches carved for the god Pan and the nymphs, and the footings of a temple Herod built for Augustus. Philip the tetrarch renamed the city Caesarea.

Jesus asks his disciples “Who do people say that I am?” in the district around this pagan city. Some scholars suggest the cave, regarded as a gate to the underworld, forms the backdrop for “the gates of Hades.”
Caution: The Gospels never describe the shrine; the connection to “gates of Hades” is a suggestion, not a statement.
f: Shrine of Pan from the 3rd century BC; Philip’s city from 2 BC

e.n: The east shore: Kursi, Gadara and Hippos
t: Kursi, on the steep eastern shore, has a large Byzantine monastery and church that, by tradition, mark the healing of the demoniac. Gadara (Umm Qais) kept a theater and colonnaded street, and Hippos (Sussita) a hilltop forum and church.

This was Gentile country, the Decapolis, where pigs were raised. Matthew, Mark and Luke use different names for the district (Gadarenes, Gerasenes), which tells us the story’s location was already being remembered in several ways.
Caution: Kursi is the traditional site only; Gadara and Gerasa are inland, and the Gospels’ own names differ.
f: Sea of Galilee’s east shore and the Decapolis
Roman Decapolis cities; Byzantine monastery at Kursi

e.n: Tiberias and Sepphoris: Herod Antipas’s new cities
t: Antipas rebuilt Sepphoris, about 6 km (under 4 miles) from Nazareth, as a showpiece capital with a theater, and founded Tiberias on the lake. Excavations show Roman-style streets, public baths and prosperous houses.

Jesus grew up between these projects. The Gospels never say he entered either city, though the lake bears the name “Sea of Tiberias” in John, and Antipas, the city’s founder, appears in the story of John the Baptist.
Caution: The Gospels do not mention a visit to either city; the possibility that Jesus worked there as a builder is a scholar’s guess.
f: Sepphoris rebuilt after 4 BC; Tiberias founded AD 18–20

t: Digs under and around modern Nazareth reveal a small farming village: cisterns, grain silos, wine and olive presses and rock-cut tombs. A 1st-century house was found beside the Church of the Annunciation, and “Nazareth Village” is a modern reconstruction on an excavated farm.

This is the setting of Jesus’ childhood and the synagogue scene in Luke 4. The finds confirm a modest place with a few dozen households, matching Nathanael’s question, “Can anything good come out of Nazareth?”
Caution: Nazareth Village is a reconstruction, and the grotto under the Church of the Annunciation is venerated, not proved.
f: Village of the 1st century BC – 1st century AD

t: Khirbet Qana, a ruin about 14 km north of Nazareth, has Roman-era houses, tombs, and later pilgrim sites. Kafr Kanna, the modern village nearer to Nazareth, hosts the traditional Wedding Church.
Two signs happen at Cana in John’s Gospel: the water into wine and the healing of an official’s son. Which village it was affects the route Jesus took.
Caution: Some scholars prefer Khirbet Qana (older name, early pilgrim reports); Kafr Kanna has the longer pilgrim tradition. No inscription settles it.

A rounded mountain rising out of the Jezreel Valley, crowned by a Franciscan basilica (1924) and a Greek Orthodox church. Josephus says he fortified the summit in AD 66, so it was a military site in the lifetime of the first Christians.
Christians from the 4th century on have honored Tabor as the mountain of the Transfiguration, though the Gospels simply say “a high mountain”.
Caution: An alternate site is Mount Hermon, nearer to Caesarea Philippi. The Gospels give no name.
2 Peter 1:16-18 does not name the mountain either; it says only “the holy mountain.”
f: Fortified in the 1st century; churches from the 4th–6th centuries

t: A hill above the lake with a small octagonal church (1938) and a broad natural slope that works like an amphitheater. The pilgrim Egeria in the 4th century mentions a cave and a hillside nearby that were honored in memory of the sermon.
Matthew places Jesus’ great sermon “on the mountain”; Luke says “on a level place.” Neither names the spot, but the lakeshore slopes make it easy to see how a large crowd could hear one voice.
Caution: The site is traditional. The Gospels don’t say where the sermon was given.
f: Church built 1938; tradition from the 4th century

e.n: Synagogues of Jesus’ day: Gamla, Magdala and the Theodotus stone
t: Gamla, a town on the Golan destroyed by Rome in AD 67, preserved a basalt synagogue with stone benches around the walls. In Jerusalem, a Greek inscription (the Theodotus stone) records a synagogue built “for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments,” with a guesthouse for travelers.

The Gospels picture Jesus reading and teaching in synagogues. These buildings show they were community halls as much as places of worship: meeting rooms, schools and hostels. Paul says he received “the forty lashes minus one” from the Jews five times (2 Corinthians 11:24), a punishment carried out in synagogues (Matthew 10:17). James 2:2 calls the readers’ meeting a synagogue (the Greek synagoge, which can mean a gathering as well as a building). In a hall like the one at Gamla, with stepped stone benches along the walls, where a person sat could be seen by everyone, which is the situation James has in mind when a rich man is offered a good seat and a poor man is told to stand (2:3).
Caution: Few synagogues from before AD 70 survive, so scholars debate exactly how they were used.

e.n: Qumran and the Dead Sea Scrolls
t: Between 1947 and 1956 shepherds and archaeologists found hundreds of scrolls in eleven caves above a desert settlement. The settlement has stepped, plastered pools used for ritual washing and a long communal dining room.

The community saw itself as the voice “crying in the wilderness” of Isaiah 40:3, the same verse the Gospels apply to John the Baptist. It shows that waiting for God’s coming in the Judean desert and ritual immersion were part of Jewish life in Jesus’ day. Many of the scrolls found in the caves had been stored in clay jars, an everyday container like the “jars of clay” in 2 Corinthians 4:7. The phrase “works of the law” in Galatians 2:16 and 3:2, 5, 10 has a Hebrew counterpart in a Qumran text known as 4QMMT, which lists rulings its authors thought essential. Scholars discuss how closely it matches Paul’s use. The Qumran community called its members “sons of light” and its opponents “sons of darkness,” and the scrolls often use the word “mystery” for the hidden plans of God. Ephesians 5:8 says, “you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light,” and uses the word mystery six times. The Dead Sea Scrolls include the Melchizedek text (11Q13) and works about angels and a heavenly temple, which show that readers like those of Hebrews were also thinking about Melchizedek, angels and a sanctuary above.
Caution: There is no evidence that John or Jesus visited Qumran. The scrolls are background, not a record of the Gospel events.
f: Northwest shore of the Dead Sea
Settlement 2nd century BC – AD 68; scrolls about 250 BC – AD 68

t: A nearly complete scroll of Isaiah, about 7.3 m (24 ft) long, sewn from 17 sheets of parchment. It was found in 1947 and is the oldest copy of the whole book of Isaiah by over a thousand years.

In the Nazareth synagogue Jesus is handed the scroll of Isaiah and finds the passage about the Lord’s anointed. This is what such a scroll looked like and how it was unrolled. Second Timothy 3:15 reminds Timothy that “from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures.” Scripture was copied by hand on scrolls like this one, and read aloud in the assembly. 1 Peter draws on Isaiah more than on any other prophet: “All flesh is like grass” (Isaiah 40:6-8) in 1:24-25, the stone laid in Zion (Isaiah 28:16) in 2:6, and the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 in 2:22-25. The Isaiah scroll found at Qumran is a copy of this book a century or two before Peter.
Caution: It is a Dead Sea scroll, not the one Jesus held, but a copy of the same text from his world.
f: Found in Qumran Cave 1; kept at the Israel Museum, Jerusalem

e.n: Al-Maghtas and Qasr al-Yahud: where John baptized
t: On the east bank (Jordan), a UNESCO site has pools, baptism steps and several churches, with “Elijah’s Hill” nearby. On the west bank, across the river, Qasr al-Yahud has its own monasteries. Pilgrims from the 4th century, and the 6th-century Madaba mosaic map, mark this stretch.
John 1:28 says John baptized at “Bethany beyond the Jordan,” which fits the east bank. The two sites stand opposite each other.
Caution: Both banks honor the baptism; no inscription names the spot.
1 John 5:6 says Jesus “came by water and blood,” which many take to mean his baptism and his death.
f: Lower Jordan River, east and west banks
Byzantine churches 5th–6th century; tradition from the 4th century

t: A steep desert cliff above Jericho with caves where hermits lived from the early Byzantine period. A Greek Orthodox monastery clings to the rock face.
Christians have long linked this wilderness to the forty days Jesus fasted. The name Quarantal comes from the Latin for “forty”.
Caution: The Gospels say only “the wilderness”. The identification is traditional.
f: Hermits from the 4th century; Orthodox monastery 1895

t: A fortress-palace on a lonely ridge, with a bath, a dining hall and cells cut in the rock. Italian and Hungarian digs have exposed its rooms and the Roman siege ramp from AD 72.
The Jewish historian Josephus says John the Baptist was imprisoned and killed here by Herod Antipas. The Gospels give the banquet and the beheading but never name the place.
Caution: The location comes from Josephus, not the Gospels.
f: Rebuilt by Herod the Great, in use in Jesus’ day

e.n: Herodium: the fortress-palace of Herod the Great
t: An artificial cone-shaped hill with a circular palace, a theater with a royal box and, in 2007, the discovery of what its excavator, Ehud Netzer, believed was Herod’s tomb. Floors with mosaics and wall plaster survive in the palace.

Herod’s paranoid rule frames the birth narrative: Matthew pictures him searching for the child king. The Herodium shows the wealth and defensive mindset of the ruler who died here in 4 BC (his burial there is described by Josephus).
Caution: The Gospels never mention Herodium; it illustrates the world around the story.

e.n: Jericho: three cities in one valley
t: Tell es-Sultan, Old Testament Jericho, is among the oldest cities known. The New Testament city lay a mile or two south, where Hasmonean and Herodian kings built winter palaces with pools, gardens and diamond-patterned stonework. Herod died here in 4 BC.

Jesus passes through the oasis on his last journey up to Jerusalem, healing blind Bartimaeus on the way out and dining with Zacchaeus the chief tax collector, a man whose wealth fits the toll-rich palace town. Hebrews 11:30-31 names the fall of Jericho’s walls and Rahab’s welcome of the spies as acts of faith. Excavators have found the Bronze Age walls of Jericho collapsed, but they disagree about the date (about 1550 BC or about 1400 BC) and about whether any city stood there when Israel arrived. James 2:25 names Rahab, who welcomed the spies at Jericho and sent them away by another route, as his second example of faith shown by action, after Abraham.
Caution: The Gospels’ Jericho is the Herodian oasis, not the mound of Joshua.
f: Herod’s palaces 1st century BC–AD 1; Old Testament Jericho thousands of years earlier

t: About 27 km (17 miles) of road drops from Jerusalem at roughly 750 m above sea level to Jericho more than 250 m below it. Parts of the Roman road, milestones and a ruined inn (Khan al-Hatrura, later Ottoman) survive in the Wadi Qelt.
The Good Samaritan is set on this road: steep, remote, ideal for ambush. Jesus’ audience would have known exactly how dangerous it was.
Caution: The “Inn of the Good Samaritan” is a later building on the traditional site; the parable is a story, not a place report.
f: Wadi Qelt and the desert descent

e.n: The Church of the Nativity, Bethlehem
t: Constantine’s basilica was built over a cave honored as the birthplace, then rebuilt in the 6th century. In 1934 excavators uncovered a beautiful mosaic floor under the nave from the original church. Justin Martyr, around AD 160, already speaks of a cave in Bethlehem.
Luke 2 and Matthew 2 place Jesus’ birth in Bethlehem. The unbroken veneration of this one cave from the 2nd century is among the oldest Christian site traditions.
Caution: The Gospels do not mention a cave; some homes then used caves for animals, which is how the tradition took shape.
f: Built about AD 327–339; rebuilt in the 6th century

t: East of Bethlehem, Byzantine ruins and cave-chapels mark the traditional field of the shepherds. Across the Judean hills, low stone walls and rock-cut enclosures are still used as night folds for sheep.

Luke has shepherds first to hear the birth; Jesus later calls himself the good shepherd who knows his sheep, enters through the gate and lays down his life. 1 Peter 5:2-4 asks the elders to “be shepherds of God’s flock” and promises a crown when “the Chief Shepherd” appears, and 2:25 says the readers have returned to “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls.”
Caution: Several villages claim the shepherds’ field. The Gospel does not locate it.
f: Byzantine monastery remains; folds in use since antiquity

e.n: Old Cairo: the Holy Family’s tradition
t: In the district of Old Cairo, a Roman fortress called Babylon still has a surviving tower. Coptic churches, including the Church of St. Sergius, stand over a crypt traditionally said to be where the Holy Family sheltered.

Matthew says Joseph took Mary and the child to Egypt to flee Herod. Egypt had a large Jewish community, centered on Alexandria, so refuge there made sense. Coptic tradition holds that Peter’s “Babylon” (1 Peter 5:13) was this Roman fort in Egypt, where Mark is said to have taught. Most scholars read “Babylon” as Rome instead.
Caution: The Gospel names no place in Egypt. The fortress itself is later than Jesus’ day.
f: Roman fortress of Babylon (2nd–4th century); church traditions from the 5th century on

t: A village in the hills with two churches: the Church of the Visitation (1955) and St. John the Baptist, built on Byzantine and Crusader remains, marking where Elizabeth and Zechariah lived.
Luke says Mary travelled “into the hill country of Judea” to visit Elizabeth. The village has been honored as their home since the Byzantine centuries.
Caution: Luke names no village. Ein Karem’s link is traditional.
f: Byzantine and Crusader churches; modern churches from 1885 and 1955

e.n: The Tel Dan Stele: the “House of David”
t: In 1993–94 archaeologists found fragments of an Aramaic victory inscription carved into basalt. One line names the “House of David” and the “king of Israel”. It is the earliest known reference to David’s dynasty outside the Bible.
Matthew opens with “the son of David” and Luke ties Jesus’ birth to David’s town. The stele shows that David’s dynasty was known to Israel’s neighbors centuries before Jesus.
Caution: The text is fragmentary, and scholars still debate its wording and which king wrote it.

e.n: The Temple Mount and the Western Wall
t: Herod doubled the size of the platform to about 36 acres (14.4 hectares), faced it with enormous cut stones (some 13 m long, hundreds of tons), and added stairways, shops and gates. The lower courses of the Western Wall are Herod’s work. Broad stairs rise to the sealed Huldah Gates on the south.

This is the temple Jesus entered, taught in and predicted would fall. John records that it had been under construction for “forty-six years”, a timeline that fits Herod’s building campaign. Ephesians 2:20-22 pictures believers as “a holy temple in the Lord,” built on the apostles and prophets with Christ as the “cornerstone.” The Temple of Herod was a building every Jew knew, with its huge corner stones. Second Thessalonians 2:4 speaks of a man who will “seat himself in the temple of God.” Some readers think this is the Temple on this mount, and others think it is the church. Hebrews never describes Herod’s Temple. It speaks of the tabernacle of Moses and of priests who serve at “a copy and shadow” of the heavenly things (8:5). Scholars differ on whether the present tenses (priests “offer” gifts, 8:4) show that the Temple was still standing, or are only the way the writer speaks of the law. James 2:21 recalls Abraham offering Isaac on the altar. Genesis 22 places the offering in the region of Moriah, and 2 Chronicles 3:1 says that Solomon built the Temple on Mount Moriah, so Jewish and Christian tradition has long placed it on the Temple Mount. The Samaritans hold that Mount Gerizim is the place.
Caution: Nothing of the temple building itself survives; what remains is the platform around it.
f: Herod’s rebuilding began about 20–19 BC; destroyed AD 70

t: At the foot of the Western Wall, archaeologists found Herodian paving covered by massive stones hurled down by Roman soldiers in AD 70. One fallen block, carved “to the place of trumpeting”, once marked a spot where a priest sounded the Sabbath trumpet.

Jesus told his disciples that not one stone would be left on another. The rubble lies exactly as it fell, still on the street where Jesus’ contemporaries once walked. 1 Peter 2:4-8 calls Jesus the “living stone” and the “cornerstone” in Zion, rejected by the builders (Psalm 118:22; Isaiah 28:16). The enormous Herodian blocks at the corner of the Temple Mount show what builders meant by a cornerstone: a large, squared stone set first, which fixed the line of the walls.
f: South-west corner of the Temple Mount

t: A limestone block carved in Greek warns any foreigner not to pass beyond the barrier around the inner courts on penalty of death. It was found in 1871, and a second fragment was found in 1935. The first is in Istanbul, the second in Jerusalem.

The Jewish historian Josephus described this stone barrier. Jesus drove the traders out of the outer court, the Court of the Gentiles, the only part non-Jews could enter. Ephesians 2:14 says Christ “has made the two one and has torn down the dividing wall of hostility.” The Temple had such a barrier. A Gentile who passed it risked death, and Paul says Christ has taken it away.

e.n: The Tyrian shekel and the Temple tax
t: The Temple tax had to be paid in Tyrian silver (a heavy, pure coin stamped with Melqart and an eagle). Money changers set up in the Temple courts to exchange common currency for it, and thousands of these coins turn up in Jerusalem.
This explains the money changers whose tables Jesus overturned, and the “shekel” Peter finds in the fish’s mouth to pay the tax for both of them.

Tiny bronze coins, weighing a gram or two, were minted by the Hasmonean kings and found in huge numbers in Judea. In Greek they are lepta, “thin ones”; Mark says two of them make a quadrans, the smallest Roman coin.

The poor widow dropped in two lepta, perhaps the smallest coins in circulation, and Jesus said she gave more than all the rich donors. Paul’s rule in 2 Corinthians 8:12, “the gift is acceptable according to what one has,” echoes her story.

e.n: The denarius: the tribute penny and the day’s wage
t: The silver denarius of Tiberius shows the emperor’s head with the words “Tiberius Caesar, son of the divine Augustus”. It was the coin of a soldier’s pay and a laborer’s day. Greek silver drachmas were roughly equal in value.

When opponents asked about paying taxes to Caesar, Jesus asked for a coin and “whose image and inscription is this?” The same coin is the “denarius” of the workers in the vineyard and the lost drachma in Luke 15. In 2 Corinthians 13:5-7 Paul tells the Corinthians to “test yourselves” and speaks of who has “stood the test.” The Greek word for “approved” was also used of a coin tested and found genuine.

e.n: The Pilate Stone and Pilate’s coins
t: In 1961, Italian archaeologists at Caesarea’s theater found a carved block with a Latin dedication naming “Pontius Pilatus, prefect of Judea”. It is the only inscription from his lifetime naming him. Bronze coins he issued with pagan cult symbols still turn up.

It confirms Pilate as a real governor, with the title prefect, and Caesarea as the Roman capital where he lived. The Gospels move him between Caesarea and Jerusalem at Passover. First Timothy 6:13 speaks of “Christ Jesus, who made the good confession in His testimony before Pontius Pilate.” The Pilate Stone shows that Pilate was a real prefect of Judea.
Caution: The original is in the Israel Museum; Caesarea displays a copy.
In 1990 construction work uncovered a burial cave with twelve ossuaries. Two bear the name “Joseph son of Caiaphas” and one, richly decorated, held the bones of a man of about sixty.

Josephus calls the high priest “Joseph, who was called Caiaphas”. If this is his tomb, it is the closest we get to the man who presided over the interrogation of Jesus. Hebrews 7:23-28 says many priests followed one another because death stopped each, while Jesus holds his priesthood forever. A family tomb like that of Caiaphas shows how many priestly families succeeded one another in the Temple.
Caution: Most scholars accept the identification, but some doubt it.

e.n: St Peter in Gallicantu and the high priest’s house
t: A church on the slope of Mount Zion stands over rock-cut rooms, cisterns and a pit-like prison cell. Nearby is an ancient stepped street, often dated to the 1st century, linking the lower city to Mount Zion.
Pilgrims from the Byzantine period honored this as the house of Caiaphas, where Jesus was questioned and Peter denied him before the rooster crowed.
Caution: The wealthy mansions excavated in the Upper City are better candidates for a high priest’s house. This one is a tradition.
f: Church from 1931; site tradition from the 5th century

e.n: The mansions of the Upper City and the Burnt House
t: Digs in the Upper City found grand houses with mosaics, painted plaster, stone tables, ritual baths and private courtyards. In the “Burnt House”, charred wood, a spear and a weight inscribed “of Bar Kathros” show the fire of AD 70.

This is where the priestly families lived. John describes the high priest’s courtyard, a fire in it, a doorkeeper and Peter warming his hands, details that fit a mansion of this kind. Hebrews says that high priests were taken from among men and had to offer for their own sins, and that there were many of them because death kept them from continuing (7:23). The wealthy houses in the Upper City show how a priestly family lived in Jerusalem before AD 70.
In 2004, while repairing a sewer pipe, workers uncovered a large stepped pool with three tiers of stairs. Coins and pottery date it to the Second Temple period. It was fed by Hezekiah’s Tunnel.

In John 9 Jesus sends a blind man to wash in the pool, and John adds the meaning of its name (“Sent”). It was also the starting point of the water ceremony in the feast of Tabernacles that frames John 7.
Caution: A later Byzantine pool, further downstream, was long mistaken for the one in John.

A water tunnel, 533 m (1,750 ft) long, cut through solid rock from the Gihon Spring to the Pool of Siloam. An inscription found in the tunnel, in ancient Hebrew, records the moment the two teams dug toward each other and met. You can still wade through it.
The tunnel brought water to the Pool of Siloam, the pool where Jesus sent the blind man, and it supplied the water used at Tabernacles.
Caution: The tunnel is 700 years older than Jesus. It matters for what it fed.
f: Jerusalem, from the Gihon Spring to Siloam

e.n: The Pilgrim Road from Siloam to the Temple
t: A stepped, paved street about 600 m long ran from the Pool of Siloam up toward the Temple, with shops and drains along the way. Coins found under its pavement suggest it was built about AD 30.
This is the street pilgrims took when they came for the festivals; Jesus and the Twelve would have walked it with the crowds.
Caution: The date comes from a limited number of coins and is not accepted by everyone.
f: City of David and the Temple Mount

t: Two huge pools lay side by side, separated by a rock wall, with colonnades on all four sides and on the dividing wall, five porticoes in all. Later a Roman healing shrine (an Asklepieion) was built beside them.
John 5 begins with “a pool in Jerusalem, near the Sheep Gate, called Bethesda, which has five porticoes”. The discovery matches the detail, one of the Gospel’s most exact descriptions.
Caution: The healing shrine was added after Jesus’ time.
f: North of the Temple Mount, near the Sheep Gate
Hasmonean–Herodian pools; Roman healing shrine 2nd century AD

e.n: A scale model of Jerusalem in Jesus’ day
t: A 1:50 scale model of Jerusalem at its height just before AD 70, built from excavations and from the descriptions of Josephus, shows the walls, the Temple, Herod’s palace and the theater.
It is useful for seeing how the places in the Gospels fit together: the Temple, the Antonia, Herod’s palace, the pools and the garden east of the city.
Caution: It is a reconstruction. New digs keep changing details.
Large paving stones, some scratched with gaming boards, lie under the Sisters of Zion convent. They were long said to be the courtyard where Pilate judged Jesus.
John 19:13 says Pilate sat “at a place called the Stone Pavement, and in Aramaic Gabbatha”. The pavement is among the sites visited on the Via Dolorosa.
Caution: Most archaeologists date this pavement to the time of Hadrian, a century after Jesus. John names a real place, but this particular pavement is a later work.
f: Pavement from about AD 135; traditional since the Middle Ages

t: At the Citadel by the Jaffa Gate, the base of one of Herod’s three towers and parts of his palace walls survive. The palace stood in the city’s highest part and became the governor’s residence in Jerusalem.
Many scholars think Pilate judged Jesus at this palace, not at the Antonia fortress. Josephus and Philo say the governors stayed there when in Jerusalem.
Caution: The location of the trial is a scholarly argument: Herod’s palace or the Antonia fortress.

e.n: The Mount of Olives and the road from Bethphage
t: A long ridge east of the city, its slope covered by about 150,000 Jewish graves, some from Jesus’ own time. Chapels mark the Lord’s Prayer, the weeping over Jerusalem (Dominus Flevit, where first-century tombs were found) and the Ascension.
The road from Bethphage, over the summit and down into the Kidron Valley, is Jesus’ route on Palm Sunday. From here you look straight across to the Temple Mount, where he predicts its fall.
Caution: Individual chapels are traditional; the mountain itself is exactly as described.
f: Cemetery in use from the First Temple period; churches from the 4th century

t: The Aramaic name means “oil press”. A modern church stands over the rock honored as the place of Jesus’ prayer, and ancient olive trees in the garden are among the oldest in the region. A nearby cave with an olive press and cisterns is also venerated.

All four Gospels set Jesus’ arrest in an olive garden across the Kidron, just east of the city. The name fits both the trees and the oil presses that processed their harvest. Hebrews 5:7 speaks of prayers and cries and tears offered to the one who could save him from death, which many readers link to Gethsemane. The letter does not name the garden or say when, so it may also gather up other times of Jesus’ prayer.
Caution: Studies date the oldest trees to about 900 years, and Rome cut down the trees around Jerusalem in AD 70.
f: Foot of the Mount of Olives
Church of All Nations 1924, over a 4th-century church

e.n: The Cenacle: the traditional Upper Room
t: A Gothic hall on Mount Zion, built by the Crusaders over earlier churches that go back to the 4th century. Below it is a shrine long venerated as the tomb of David.

Mount Zion has been remembered as the place of the Last Supper and Pentecost since the early church. The Gospels say only that Jesus sent two disciples to prepare “a large upper room, furnished and ready”.
Caution: The room you visit is medieval. A first-century upper room could have stood near here, but no evidence confirms it.
f: Crusader hall (about 12th–14th century) over a 4th-century church

e.n: The tombs of the Kidron Valley
t: Along the valley between the city and the Mount of Olives stand monumental rock-cut tombs with names such as Absalom’s Pillar, the Tomb of Zechariah and the Tomb of Bnei Hezir, the last carrying an inscription naming priests of the Hezir family.

Jesus denounces scribes who “build the tombs of the prophets and decorate the graves of the righteous.” These tombs are exactly that kind of memorial, and Jesus crossed this valley to Gethsemane. Christian tradition has long called the Tomb of Bnei Hezir the Tomb of St James, but its inscription names a priestly family, and Hegesippus (quoted by Eusebius) says that James was buried near the Temple. Nothing ties these tombs to James the brother of Jesus.
Caution: The traditional names (Absalom, Zechariah) are later labels; they are not the original owners.

The steep Hinnom Valley wraps around the south of the old city. On its far slope are many first-century rock tombs and the Greek Orthodox Monastery of St. Onuphrius, built on the traditional “Field of Blood”.
Jesus uses the Hinnom Valley (Gehenna) as an image of judgement. Matthew says the chief priests bought a potter’s field with Judas’s returned silver and called it the Field of Blood.
Caution: The spot is traditional. Gehenna is an image drawn from the valley’s history.

e.n: The Church of the Holy Sepulchre
t: Constantine’s builders cut away a hillside to expose a tomb identified by the local Christian community, and built a church around it. Under the church are first-century burial caves, and the 2016 renovation of the shrine briefly exposed the original rock bench of the tomb.

John says Jesus was crucified “near the city”, in a garden with a new tomb. This site was a quarry outside the city wall in Jesus’ day, later turned into tombs, which matches the Gospel details. Hebrews 13:12 says that Jesus suffered outside the city gate, and verse 13 asks the readers to go to him outside the camp. The Gospels also say that Jesus was crucified outside the city (John 19:20), and the traditional site of the Holy Sepulchre lay outside the walls of the time.
Caution: Many scholars find it plausible, but there is no inscription naming the tomb. The case rests on early local memory.
f: First-century quarry and tombs; church begun about AD 326

t: A peaceful garden with a rock-cut tomb north of the Old City. It was popularized as Jesus’ tomb in the 19th century and remains a place of prayer for many Protestants.
It offers a picture of what a garden tomb looked like, with a rock-cut chamber, a low entrance and a long groove in front (its original purpose is debated).
Caution: Most archaeologists date the tomb to the Old Testament period, so it cannot be Jesus’ tomb.
f: Tomb cut in the Iron Age (about 8th–7th century BC); identification from 1883

e.n: Rolling-stone tombs of the Herodian period
t: Some wealthy tombs around Jerusalem, among them Herod’s Family Tomb and the Tomb of the Kings, were sealed with a great round stone that rolled in a groove across the entrance. Most burial caves were closed with a square block.

The Gospels say a great stone was rolled to close Jesus’ tomb and rolled away at Easter. These tombs show what that looked like and that such a tomb belonged to someone of means (Joseph of Arimathea was rich).
Caution: The Gospels say “rolled”, but don’t describe a disc; a square stone can also be rolled.

For about a century before AD 70, Jerusalem families collected a loved one’s bones after the flesh had decayed and put them in small limestone boxes, often scratched with names. Hundreds are known, with names such as Mary, Joseph, Simon, Jesus and Lazarus.

It shows how ordinary the Gospel names were. Jesus’ burial in a tomb, and the Gospels’ concern about uncleanness from graves, make more sense against this background. An ossuary with an Aramaic inscription naming James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus, was announced in 2002. Its inscription is disputed, and the box has no recorded findspot (see “The James ossuary”).
Caution: An ossuary reading “Jesus son of Joseph” is real but means little: both names were common.

e.n: The crucified man of Giv’at ha-Mivtar
t: A heel bone from an ossuary in a Jerusalem tomb was pierced by an 11.5 cm iron nail, with traces of olive wood still attached. The ossuary was inscribed “Yehohanan”. It is the only skeletal remains of a crucified man known from Roman Judea.

It shows that crucifixion in Judea involved nails, as in John’s account of the marks on Jesus’ hands and feet, and that the victim could be buried by his family in a family tomb. Paul says “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20), that Christ was “clearly portrayed as crucified” (3:1), and that he became “a curse for us,” quoting “Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree” (3:13). Ephesians 2:16 says Christ reconciled both groups “to God in one body through the cross,” and 5:2 says Christ “gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God.” The cross was not a symbol to the first readers but a Roman execution. Philippians 2:8 says Christ “became obedient to death,” even “death on a cross.” The nail through a heel bone from Jerusalem shows what that death was for real people.
Caution: Original claims about how he was positioned were revised in 1985. Its date and the nail’s role are still debated.

A deep well inside a Greek Orthodox church marks the traditional spot, honored since at least the 4th century. It is fed by groundwater and was once about 40 m (130 ft) deep. A church was built here around AD 380 and rebuilt several times.
John says the woman was surprised that Jesus, with no bucket, could draw water: “the well is deep.” The site is also in the heart of Samaritan country, between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal.
Caution: This is one of the few Gospel sites with a continuous, undisputed tradition.
f: Church from about AD 380; well deep in antiquity

t: Excavators found a large sacred precinct on the summit with a temple platform, altars and hundreds of inscriptions in Aramaic and Hebrew. John Hyrcanus destroyed it about 111 BC. The Samaritans still make Passover offerings on the mountain.
The Samaritan woman asks Jesus whether people should worship on “this mountain” or in Jerusalem. The hostility behind that question was centuries old.
f: Temple precinct built about 200 BC; destroyed about 111 BC

t: Herod rebuilt the old city of Samaria as Sebaste, honoring Augustus, with a temple, a forum, a stadium, a colonnaded street and strong walls. Its Roman ruins still stand on a hilltop.
Jesus travelled “between Samaria and Galilee,” and Samaria was home to the people he made the heroes of two stories. The Gospels never name this city.
Caution: It shows Samaria’s Roman-era setting; no Gospel event happens here.
A large Greek-style city below a mound, with a well-preserved Roman theater, a colonnaded street, bathhouses and a hippodrome. It was the only Decapolis city west of the Jordan.

The Gospels say crowds from the Decapolis followed Jesus, and the healed man proclaimed his story across the region. These cities were Greek in culture, showing a different world from the Jewish villages of Galilee.
Caution: Gospel texts do not mention Scythopolis by name.
The Roman city at Tyre has a vast hippodrome, a long colonnaded road and large cemeteries. It was a great Phoenician port long before and after Jesus.
Jesus withdraws to the district of Tyre and Sidon and meets a Gentile woman whose faith he praises. He also remarks that Tyre and Sidon would have repented had they seen the signs he did in Galilee.
Caution: Most of what is visible is later than Jesus.
f: Roman city; excavated colonnades from the 2nd–4th century

t: Emmaus-Nicopolis (Imwas) has a Roman city and Byzantine church, Abu Ghosh a Crusader church, Qubeibeh a Franciscan shrine over a Roman villa. Another candidate, Motza, is only about 6 km from Jerusalem.
Luke says Emmaus was “about seven miles from Jerusalem” (60 stadia), though some early manuscripts say 160 stadia. The village’s identity is unsettled.
Caution: Nobody knows which Emmaus it was.
f: Roman and Byzantine remains at several sites

t: Two tiny rolled silver amulets, found in a burial cave, carry the priestly blessing “The Lord bless you and keep you” in ancient Hebrew script. They are the oldest known fragments of any biblical text.
The blessing is the one priests spoke over the people. In Luke, Zechariah is a priest, and the risen Jesus lifts his hands in blessing as he leaves.
Caution: They are from the First Temple period, long before the Gospels.

Excavations at the mounds of Kuyunjik and Nebi Yunus uncovered the palaces of the Assyrian kings and the library of Ashurbanipal, with tens of thousands of clay tablets. Parts were badly damaged in 2014–17.
Jesus says the people of Nineveh will stand up at the judgement because they repented at Jonah’s preaching, and “something greater than Jonah is here”.

e.n: Papyri, contracts and phylacteries from the Judean desert
t: Dry caves have preserved legal papyri: marriage contracts, land deeds and certificates of divorce, along with tiny leather phylactery boxes holding Scripture, used for prayer.

They show how often marriage and divorce were a legal matter, which sheds light on the Pharisees’ question about divorce. Phylacteries and tassels explain Jesus’ remark about people who make theirs wide. Colossians 2:14 says God took away “the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us,” nailing it to the cross. The Greek word for the written note of debt (cheirographon) was used for a signed IOU, and the legal papyri from the desert show how debts and promises were written down and kept.

e.n: Stone vessels: cups and jars that stay clean
t: Cups, mugs and large jars were turned or carved from soft chalkstone, which Jewish law considered immune to ritual impurity. They appear in huge numbers in Jerusalem, Galilee and Judea in Jesus’ time. The big jars hold roughly 80–120 liters.
John mentions six stone water jars used for purification at the wedding in Cana. They are right for the setting and for the amount of wine Jesus made.

Hundreds of stepped, plastered pools have been found in Jerusalem, Qumran, Sepphoris, Magdala and Gamla, with private ones in rich houses and public ones near the Temple. Most have a divided stairway, one side for going down, one for coming up.
They were used to become ritually clean. They explain the washings the Gospels mention, the question about hand-washing and the baptism of John.
Small, hand-sized clay lamps, with a round body and a pinched spout (the “Herodian lamp”), are among the most common finds. A lamp burned a little olive oil for an hour or two.
Jesus’ images of lamps are everyday ones: lamps are put on a stand, kept filled while waiting for the bridegroom, and used to see the room.

e.n: Wine and oil presses, vineyards and terraces
t: Rock-cut treading floors with collecting vats, watchtowers and stone terraces survive across the hills of Judea and Galilee, along with stone olive-crushing basins and beam presses.

Vineyards and olive groves were common, so Jesus’ parable of the tenants builds a wall, a winepress and a tower for the vineyard, as every listener would have known. Vines, figs and olives were the staple crops of the land (Deuteronomy 8:8), which is why James 3:12 asks whether a fig tree can grow olives or a vine figs. Olive oil was also used on the skin and for wounds, and in James 5:14 the elders anoint the sick person with it; Luke 10:34 and Mark 6:13 also mention oil used on the sick and wounded.
Smooth, rock-cut circles on hilltops were used to thresh and winnow grain, and rock-cut pits and stone-lined silos stored it.

John the Baptist’s picture of wheat gathered into the barn while the chaff burns, the parable of the weeds, and the rich man’s plan to build bigger barns all use these familiar scenes. Paul says whoever “sows sparingly will also reap sparingly,” and that God “supplies seed to the sower and bread for food” (2 Corinthians 9:6, 10). In Galatians 6:7 Paul says, “Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return,” and in 6:9, “in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up.”
Heavy basalt rotary querns, turned by hand or hourglass mills turned by donkeys, are common finds. A great millstone weighed as much as a person could carry.

Jesus’ warning about anyone who causes a child to stumble, that it would be better to have a great millstone hung around the neck, and his picture of two women grinding at the mill, use daily household tools.

Galilean homes were small basalt or fieldstone rooms around a shared courtyard, with flat roofs of beams, branches and packed clay, reached by an outside stair. In Jerusalem’s Upper City, wealthy homes had mosaics, dining rooms and private baths.

A paralyzed man’s friends can tear through a roof, a woman can sweep her house for a lost coin, and a wise builder digs down to rock, because Jesus’ audience lived in houses like these. First Timothy 3:4-5 says an overseer “must manage his own household well” and asks, “if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he care for the church of God?” The household was the basic unit of society and the place where churches gathered.
Rome paved and marked key routes, with milestones, and Herod’s sons collected tolls where roads crossed borders. Capernaum lay on the road between Antipas’s Galilee and Philip’s territory.

This is the world of Levi (Matthew) sitting at his toll booth, of Zacchaeus the chief tax collector, and of the soldier who could make you carry his pack one mile. James 4:13 pictures traders who say they will go to this or that city, spend a year there and make a profit. Roman roads, with their milestones, and the sea lanes made that kind of planning possible, and tolls were taken where goods crossed borders.
Caution: Customs stations are described in writing; none from the Gospel period has been excavated at Capernaum.

Wealthy houses in Jerusalem’s Upper City had dining rooms with frescoed walls, mosaic floors, private ritual baths and imported tableware. Jewish custom at Passover was to recline on couches around the table. Josephus says the priests counted over 250,000 lambs offered one year.

John 13–17 is set around the Last Supper, and John says one disciple was “reclining next to Jesus”. The farewell conversations in John 14–17 take place within this meal setting. 1 Peter 1:18-19 says the readers were redeemed “with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot,” a picture of the Passover lamb, which had to be without defect (Exodus 12:5). Josephus’s count of the lambs shows how many families in Jerusalem knew the sight.
Caution: The Gospels do not say whose house it was or where. This shows only what a dining room of the time looked like.

e.n: The Nicanor ossuary and the Temple gates
t: A limestone ossuary inscribed in Greek and Hebrew with the name “Nicanor of Alexandria, who made the doors.” The Mishnah says a man named Nicanor of Alexandria donated the bronze doors of one of the temple gates.

Acts 3 says the lame man sat at the Temple gate called Beautiful. Many scholars link that name with the gate of Nicanor, which opened from the Court of the Gentiles into the court of the women. The ossuary shows that Diaspora Jews from Egypt gave gifts to the Temple and are remembered for it.
Caution: The Beautiful Gate is not identified for certain; some scholars prefer the Shushan Gate on the east. The link between the ossuary and the Mishnah’s Nicanor is probable, not proven.
f: Jerusalem (found on Mount Scopus in 1902; now in the British Museum)

t: The Mishnah names the “Chamber of Hewn Stone” in the temple precinct as the Sanhedrin’s seat, and Josephus mentions a council house near the Xystus, west of the temple. Excavations along the temple’s western and southern sides have not identified either building.

Acts has the apostles and Stephen stand before “the council” (Peter and John 4:5-22, the apostles 5:27-40, Stephen 6:12-7:60, Paul 22:30-23:10). The question where they stood helps picture how close the courts were to the temple courts.
Caution: No remains of the council chamber have been identified. Scholars debate whether the Sanhedrin moved from the Chamber of Hewn Stone to the city before AD 30.
f: South-west of the Temple Mount, Jerusalem

t: The Empress Eudocia built a large church north of the walls in about AD 460 to honor Stephen. Its remains lie under the Dominican basilica of St Stephen at the École Biblique, finished in 1900. Another old tradition puts the stoning east of the city near the Kidron Valley.
Acts says only that Stephen was dragged “out of the city” and stoned (7:58). The two traditions show how early the church kept his memory.
Caution: Luke does not name a place. The site is traditional.
f: North of the Old City, Jerusalem (St Stephen’s Basilica)
Church of the 5th century and a modern basilica

e.n: Mount Zion: the first church in Jerusalem
t: Epiphanius, writing in the 4th century, says a small “church of God” stood on Zion when Hadrian visited Jerusalem in AD 130. The Byzantine church Hagia Sion later rose on the hill, and the Crusader hall called the Cenacle stands on it today.

Acts places the first believers in Jerusalem, in an upper room, in homes, and in the temple courts. The Zion tradition suggests where the Jerusalem church (and James and the elders) remembered meeting.
Caution: The memory is old but the exact buildings of AD 30-60 are not identified.

e.n: The Tomb of the Kings and Queen Helena
t: A large rock-cut tomb with a sunken courtyard, a stepped entrance and a rolling-stone door. A sarcophagus found there was inscribed with the name “Queen Tsaddan.” Josephus says Queen Helena of Adiabene, a convert to Judaism, was buried in Jerusalem, and that she bought grain from Egypt and figs from Cyprus for the poor during the famine.

In Acts 11:27-30 the prophet Agabus predicts a world-wide famine “in the days of Claudius,” and the believers at Antioch send relief to Judea. Josephus puts a famine in Judea in about AD 46 and names Helena as a donor. Paul asks Corinth to finish its gift for the poor believers in Jerusalem (2 Corinthians 8-9), another relief gift like the one the Antioch believers sent in Acts 11. In Galatians 2:10 the Jerusalem leaders ask Paul and Barnabas “to remember the poor,” “the very thing I was eager to do.”
Caution: Most scholars take this tomb to be Helena’s, but the identification is not certain.
f: North of the Old City, Jerusalem

e.n: The coins of Herod Agrippa I
t: Bronze prutot minted for the king Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, showing the name “Great King Agrippa.” One type shows a royal canopy, another shows three ears of barley.
Acts 12 calls him simply “Herod the king.” He had James killed, jailed Peter and then died at Caesarea (12:23). Josephus says he died in AD 44 after the crowd shouted he was a god.
Caution: The coins show his office and his dates; they say nothing about the events in Acts.

e.n: The house of Mary, mother of John Mark
t: The Syriac Orthodox church of St Mark in the Old City claims to stand over the home of Mary, where Peter went after the angel freed him. An inscription in the church dates its tradition from the 6th century.

Acts 12:12 says “many were gathered together and were praying” at the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark. It shows that the Jerusalem believers met in homes large enough for a gate, a courtyard and a servant girl. Peter ends his first letter with greetings from “my son Mark” (1 Peter 5:13). If this is John Mark, he is the son of the Mary named in Acts 12:12.
Caution: Luke gives no street. The identification is a tradition.
f: Syriac Orthodox church of St Mark, Jerusalem
A church there since at least the Middle Ages

t: Herod rebuilt an older fortress at the Temple’s north-west corner on a rock outcrop and named it for Mark Antony. Josephus describes four towers, barracks and stairs down into the temple courts. The cut rock scarp can still be seen, and the large paving stones beneath the Sisters of Zion convent are now thought to date to the 2nd century.

In Acts 21:31-40 the Roman tribune takes Paul up the steps into “the barracks” and lets him address the crowd from the stairs. The fortress overlooked the Temple courts so soldiers could answer a riot quickly.
Caution: Little of the fortress survives. Not all scholars agree on its exact footprint.
f: North-west corner of the Temple Mount, Jerusalem
Rebuilt by Herod about 35-20 BC; destroyed AD 70

t: Two main roads ran from Jerusalem to Gaza, one by Hebron and one by Beth Guvrin. A Byzantine church by a spring near Hebron (Ain Dirweh) was remembered as the place of the Ethiopian’s baptism.
Acts 8:26 says the road was “desert” or “desolate.” A man traveling it in a chariot would have been in no hurry and able to read aloud.
Caution: Luke does not name the spot. The traditional site is a later memory.

e.n: Meroë and the Candaces of Kush
t: The capital of the kingdom of Kush, on the Nile north of Khartoum, has more than 200 steep pyramids and royal temples. Greek and Roman writers record that Kush was ruled by queens whose title was Kandake, rendered “Candace.”
The official in Acts 8:27 served “Candace, queen of the Ethiopians” as her treasurer. “Ethiopia” meant Kush, the land south of Egypt, not modern Ethiopia.
Caution: Acts does not name the queen or her city.

The long east-west Roman street (Via Recta) still runs through the old city, now partly under modern shops. A Roman arch survives along it. A small underground chapel nearby is honored as the house of Ananias.

Acts 9:11 says the Lord told Ananias to go to “the street called Straight” and ask for Saul at the house of Judas. Luke names a street, which his readers could check. In Galatians 1:17 Paul says he went “into Arabia and later returned to Damascus,” so the city is where his new life began and where he came back to. Philippians 3:12 says Christ Jesus “took hold of me.” Paul does not name the place, but Acts 9 and 22 tell of the encounter on the road to Damascus.
Caution: The chapel of Ananias is a later tradition, and the street is not as straight now as in Paul’s day.

e.n: Bab Kisan and Paul’s escape from Damascus
t: A walled-up gate called Bab Kisan, with a modern chapel beside it, is honored as the place where Saul was lowered in a basket. The present walls are medieval over earlier Roman walls.

Acts 9:25 says the disciples let Saul down “through an opening in the wall, lowering him in a basket.” Paul remembers the same story in 2 Corinthians 11:32-33, which adds that the governor of King Aretas was guarding the city. Paul uses the story as proof that he boasts in weakness: “I will boast of the things that show my weakness” (2 Corinthians 11:30).
Caution: The exact opening is unknown. The chapel is a modern marker.

e.n: King Aretas IV, Petra and Damascus
t: Aretas IV ruled the Nabataean kingdom for about 48 years. His capital Petra has rock-cut tombs and temples; inscriptions and many coins carry his name and the title “lover of his people.”

Paul writes that “the governor under King Aretas” watched the Damascus gates to seize him (2 Corinthians 11:32), which is why some date Paul’s escape about AD 37. Paul places the story at the end of his list of hardships in 2 Corinthians 11:23-33. Paul’s “Arabia” in Galatians 1:17 most likely means the Nabatean kingdom ruled by kings like Aretas, but the letter does not say where he went or what he did there.
Caution: How Aretas held Damascus is debated; no Roman coin of Damascus covers the years about AD 34-37.

e.n: Joppa: the harbor and a tanner’s house
t: Excavations in Old Jaffa have found Hellenistic and Roman houses and harbor remains. A building called the house of Simon the Tanner stands near the harbor, and a Russian church honors Tabitha.

Peter stays here “with Simon, a tanner” (9:43) and sees the vision of the sheet from the roof (10:9-16). Tanners worked with dead animals and lived near water and the edge of town, so Peter’s host was among those considered unclean.
Caution: The house of Simon the Tanner is a later tradition. Excavation shows that Joppa was a busy port in the first century.

Herod built a harbor (Sebastos) with breakwaters, a theater, a hippodrome, an aqueduct and a palace on the point, and named the city for Caesar Augustus. The Roman governors lived here. The Pilate inscription was found in the theater.
Philip settled here (Acts 8:40; 21:8), Cornelius lived here (10:1), Herod Agrippa went here before he died (12:19-23), and Paul was held here for two years (24:27).
Caution: Most of what stands now is Roman and later; the harbor is partly under the sea.
f: 22-10 BC; Roman capital of Judea until the 4th century

e.n: Herod’s palace at Caesarea: the praetorium
t: On a rocky point jutting into the sea, Herod built a palace with a long pool and courtyards. Excavators found a mosaic floor, a sunk pool and storerooms. The Roman governors took it as their residence and administrative headquarters.

Acts 23:35 says Felix kept Paul under guard “in Herod’s praetorium.” The same compound would be where Paul spoke to Felix, Festus and King Agrippa (24:1-26:32). Paul was also held at Caesarea for two years (Acts 24:27). Some scholars think the letters he wrote as a prisoner, Ephesians among them, came from here, though the letter does not say where he was. Caesarea has also been proposed as the place where Philippians was written. Herod’s palace there was the praetorium where Paul was kept (Acts 23:35), and the Greek word for it is the one translated “palace guard” in Philippians 1:13. Caesarea is a third place proposed for Philemon, since Paul was held there about two years (Acts 24:27). Paul’s hope that through Philemon’s prayers he will be “restored” to the church (verse 22) could fit any of the three places, and the letter does not name the one.
Caution: The palace is the likely building behind Luke’s phrase, but the text does not describe its rooms.
f: Built about 25-13 BC; used by Roman governors

t: An inscription names a unit, “Cohort II Italica of Roman citizens, volunteers,” as serving in Syria in AD 69.
Acts 10:1 calls Cornelius a centurion of “what was known as the Italian Cohort.” It shows that Luke names an actual kind of Roman unit, made of citizens, with officers like Cornelius.
Caution: No inscription places this cohort at Caesarea in the 40s, and some scholars say it was not in Judea until later.
f: Rome’s army in Syria (inscription found at Carnuntum, Austria)

e.n: Syrian Antioch: city of the first “Christians”
t: The ancient city lies mostly beneath modern Antakya. Excavations of the 1930s uncovered Roman villas with fine mosaics, now in the Hatay Archaeological Museum, which shows the wealth of the city. A cave church outside the walls is honored as an early meeting place.

Acts 11:19-26 says believers who fled Stephen’s persecution preached to Greeks here, and “in Antioch the disciples were first called Christians.” Barnabas and Saul taught here and from here the first journey was launched (13:1-3). In Galatians 2:11-14 Paul says Peter ate with Gentiles here until “certain men came from James,” and then “began to draw back and separate himself.”
Caution: The cave church is a traditional site, and little of the first-century city has been excavated.
f: Founded 300 BC; third city of the empire

t: Excavations have uncovered a Roman paved street and a large gate called Cleopatra’s Gate (a name of later tradition). The city sat on the Cydnus River where the road from the Cilician Gates reaches the sea, and was known for philosophy and linen weaving.

Paul says he was “a Jew, from Tarsus in Cilicia, a citizen of no obscure city” (Acts 21:39). Barnabas went to find him here (11:25), and he later revisited the churches of Cilicia (15:41). In Galatians 1:21 Paul says he “went to the regions of Syria and Cilicia.” Tarsus was the main city of Cilicia, though he does not name it.
Caution: The “Saint Paul’s well” is a modern marker. Excavation shows a city of philosophers and trade, which explains Paul’s ease with Greek.

The harbor city has a Roman gymnasium and baths with marble statues, a theater and a large forum. Just to the west stands the monastery of Apostle Barnabas, where tradition says his tomb was found in AD 477.

Barnabas was a Levite from Cyprus (Acts 4:36). Acts 13:5 has Barnabas, Saul and John Mark preach “in the synagogues of the Jews” at Salamis, and Acts 15:39 has Barnabas return here with Mark. Colossians 4:10 names Mark as “the cousin of Barnabas,” which links him to this island and to the family Barnabas came from.
Caution: No synagogue has been found at Salamis; the tomb of Barnabas is a tradition.
f: 11th century BC to the 7th century AD

e.n: Paphos: the Roman capital of Cyprus
t: Nea Paphos has a theater, an Odeon, a Roman governor’s residence and the famous mosaic villas (House of Dionysos, House of Theseus). In the church of Agia Kyriaki stands a stone column called St Paul’s Pillar.
Acts 13:6-12 has Paul and Barnabas cross the island “as far as Paphos,” where they meet the proconsul Sergius Paulus. “Proconsul” is the correct title for Cyprus’s governor in that period.
Caution: Paul’s Pillar is a medieval tradition, and Acts says nothing of a flogging there.

e.n: Sergius Paulus: inscriptions behind the proconsul
t: An inscription from Rome names Lucius Sergius Paullus as a curator of the Tiber under Claudius. A Cypriot inscription from Soloi mentions a proconsul “Paulus,” though its date is disputed. At Pisidian Antioch, inscriptions name members of a Sergius Paullus family.
Acts 13:7 says Paul met “the proconsul, Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence” on Cyprus. The finds show the family was prominent, and Pisidian Antioch is Paul’s next stop.
Caution: No inscription proves that these are the same man. The Soloi proconsul may be someone else.

Excavations uncovered the temple of Augustus on a high platform, a colonnaded street, a theater and an aqueduct. Fragments of a long Latin text of the emperor’s achievements (the Res Gestae) were found at the sanctuary, and the ruins of a 4th-century basilica stand on the supposed synagogue site.

Paul preached in the synagogue here (Acts 13:14-41) and the next Sabbath “almost the whole city” came (13:44). The Roman colony’s officials (“leading men of the city,” 13:50) were the ones who expelled Paul and Barnabas. If the “churches of Galatia” (Galatians 1:2) were in the south, this Roman colony is one of the first places Paul would have visited, and Galatians 4:13-14 may recall that visit. Second Timothy 3:11 puts Antioch first among the places where Paul suffered. Acts 13:50 says that Jews stirred up the leading women and men of the city and drove Paul and Barnabas out of the region.
Caution: The basilica sits on a tradition. No first-century synagogue has been found.
Perga has a Hellenistic gate with two towers, a long colonnaded street with a water channel down the middle, a theater and a stadium. Attalia (Antalya) keeps Hadrian’s Gate in its old harbor.
The missionaries landed at Perga, where John Mark left them (13:13); on the way back they preached at Perga and sailed from Attalia (14:25-26).
Caution: Most of what stands is from the 2nd century AD. Hadrian’s Gate is later than Paul.

The ancient city lay on the mound that is now Alaaddin Hill. Little of the first-century town is exposed because the modern city covers it, but finds include inscriptions and carved tombstones in the Konya museum.

Paul and Barnabas spent “a long time” speaking boldly (14:3). The city split between those for and against, and they fled when a plot to stone them formed. Second Timothy 3:11 lists Iconium among the places where Paul suffered. Acts 14:5-6 says a plot to mistreat and stone him there made him leave for Lystra and Derbe.
Caution: Almost nothing from Paul’s day has been excavated.

Lystra is a mound near Hatunsaray; excavations are slight. In 1909 explorers found a stone near Lystra dedicated to Zeus, and an altar to Hermes was found nearby, showing the two gods were worshiped together in the region.

In Acts 14:11-13 the crowds shout in “the Lycaonian language,” call Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes, and bring oxen and garlands. A temple of Zeus stood “at the entrance of the city.” Timothy came from here (16:1). If the Galatian churches were in the south, Lystra is one of them. Paul says they welcomed him “as if I were an angel of God” (Galatians 4:14), and he was stoned here (Acts 14:19), which some connect to “the marks of Jesus” (6:17). Neither link is stated in the letter. Timothy came from Lystra or its area (Acts 16:1-2), and Paul calls him “my true child in the faith” (1 Timothy 1:2). Paul says “Let no one despise your youth” (4:12), and Timothy was probably a young man when Paul took him along at Lystra. Second Timothy 1:5 names Timothy’s grandmother Lois and his mother Eunice, and 3:10-11 recalls Paul’s sufferings “in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra.” At Lystra Paul was stoned and left for dead (Acts 14:19-20), and Timothy came from this area (Acts 16:1-2).
Caution: The 1909 find shows the gods’ pairing in the region; it does not prove the Acts story.
In 1956 an inscription found on Kerti Hüyük named the town of Derbe, and most scholars now place Derbe on this mound. The mound has not been excavated much.
Paul and Barnabas preached the good news in Derbe and “made many disciples” there (14:20-21). Gaius from Derbe later travels with Paul (20:4).
Caution: The site of Derbe was disputed until the inscription was found, and some scholars still doubt it.

The excavated city has a large forum, a theater, the remains of two basilicas, an octagonal church and a Roman crypt venerated as Paul’s prison. West of the city a modern baptistery honors Lydia on the river bank.

Acts 16:12 calls Philippi “a Roman colony,” and 16:13 says Paul went outside the gate by the river, where women met for prayer. The magistrates were Roman “praetors” and had lictors with rods (16:35). In 2 Corinthians Paul meets Titus in Macedonia (7:5-7), praises the generosity of the Macedonian churches (8:1-5), and counts “imprisonments” (6:5) and being “beaten with rods” (11:25) among his hardships, as at Philippi in Acts 16:22-24. Philippians is addressed to the church Paul founded here, “To all the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, together with the overseers and deacons” (1:1). Paul tells them they are “encountering the same struggle you saw I had” (1:30), and says that “no church but you partnered with me in the matter of giving and receiving” (4:15).
Caution: The crypt is traditional, and the baptistery is a modern memorial.

This Roman highway ran about 1,100 km (700 miles) from the Adriatic to Byzantium. Paving stones, bridges and milestones survive. A stretch of the road lies exposed at Philippi, and another near Amphipolis.

Acts 17:1 says Paul and Silas “passed through Amphipolis and Apollonia” on the way to Thessalonica, which stood on the Via Egnatia. Travelers who crossed from Troas to Macedonia joined this road at Neapolis, and Paul went on to Macedonia in 2 Corinthians 2:13 and 7:5. Philippians 4:16 says that “even while I was in Thessalonica, you provided for my needs again and again.” The Via Egnatia joined the two cities, so gifts and messengers could pass along it. First Thessalonians 1:8 says the message of the Lord rang out from the church to Macedonia and Achaia, and 4:10 says the church shows love “to all the brothers throughout Macedonia.” The Via Egnatia ran through the city and linked the churches of Macedonia, so Christian travelers would pass through it.
Caution: Acts names the towns, not the road.
f: Amphipolis and the road across Macedonia, Greece

t: Inscriptions from Thyatira, in Lydia, mention guilds including dyers and wool workers. Roman purple was made from sea snails, and a cheaper dye was made from madder root.
Acts 16:14 introduces Lydia, “from the city of Thyatira, a seller of purple goods.” It places a woman of means among Philippi’s first believers.
Caution: The inscriptions come from Thyatira, not Philippi, and no inscription names Lydia.
The letter to Thyatira (Revelation 2:18-29) warns against the prophetess called Jezebel, whose teaching may have made room for guild feasts held in honor of pagan gods.
The ruins include a large bath-gymnasium, parts of the harbor, the city wall and a long aqueduct. The city served as the main port for travel between Asia and Macedonia.

Paul sees the vision of the man from Macedonia here (Acts 16:8-10), and later raises Eutychus here (20:6-12). He came here from Philippi in five days. In 2 Corinthians 2:12-13 Paul says “a door stood open” for him at Troas, but he had “no peace” because Titus was not there. Second Timothy 4:13 asks Timothy to bring “the cloak that I left with Carpus at Troas, and my scrolls, especially the parchments.” The letter does not say when Paul was there. Troas was the port Paul used on the road between Asia and Macedonia.
Caution: Most standing buildings are 2nd century or later.
A Greek inscription from the Vardar Gate lists the city’s “politarchs,” a title for local magistrates. Other inscriptions from Macedonia use the same word.

The word “politarch” is rare in literature, and Luke is the main writer to use it. Acts 17:6, 8 says the mob dragged Jason and others before the politarchs. The finds show that Luke used the right title for a Macedonian city. Paul praises “the churches of Macedonia,” which included Thessalonica, for giving out of “deep poverty” (2 Corinthians 8:1-2). Philippians 4:16 says the Philippians sent help to Paul “even while I was in Thessalonica,” and sent it more than once. Colossians 4:10 sends greetings from Aristarchus, Paul’s “fellow prisoner,” who came from Thessalonica (Acts 20:4; 27:2). In 1 Thessalonians 2:14 Paul says the believers suffered “from your own countrymen” the things the churches of Judea suffered. The magistrates who heard the charge against Jason in Acts 17:6-9 are the city officials the letters have in mind when they speak of pressure on the church.
Caution: The inscription lists six politarchs and dates to the 2nd century AD, about a century after Paul. The office is older: Thessalonica had politarchs in the time of Augustus.
f: Thessaloniki, Greece (found at the Vardar Gate, now in London)

t: A stone platform in the town, called the Bema, honors Paul’s preaching, with a mosaic from 1960. Remnants of the old Jewish quarter lie near the river.
The Bereans received the word “with all eagerness, examining the Scriptures daily” (17:11).
Caution: The Bema is a memorial, and the town has few first-century remains.
The Areopagus is a rocky hill north-west of the Acropolis. Stone benches are cut into the hill, and a bronze plaque with Acts 17:22-31 in Greek was fixed to the rock in 1964.

Acts 17:19 says the philosophers “took him and brought him to the Areopagus,” which may mean the council that met there or the hill itself. First Thessalonians 3:1 says that Paul was “left on our own in Athens,” which is the time of his speech on the Areopagus in Acts 17.
Caution: In Paul’s day the council may have met in the Royal Stoa in the Agora.

e.n: The Athenian Agora: philosophers and altars
t: The marketplace has the rebuilt Stoa of Attalos, the Altar of the Twelve Gods, the Stoa Poikile where the Stoics met, and the Temple of Hephaistos. Greek writers record altars “to unknown gods” in Athens, and an altar fragment from Pergamum carries the same words.

Acts 17:16-21 says Paul reasoned “in the marketplace every day” with Epicurean and Stoic philosophers. His speech quotes the Greek poets (17:28; the line “we are his offspring” is from Aratus). In 1 Thessalonians 3:1-2 Paul says that he waited in Athens and sent Timothy to Thessalonica from there.
Caution: No altar reading “To the unknown god” (singular) has been found in Athens.

e.n: Corinth: the city Paul stayed in
t: The excavated city has the Temple of Apollo, a large agora with shops, a platform called the Bema where officials judged, the Peirene fountain, and a stone meat market. A carved lintel reading “[Syna]gogue of the Hebr[ews]” was found nearby, though it is probably later.

Paul spent eighteen months in Corinth (Acts 18:11) and was brought “before the judgment seat” (bema) of Gallio (18:12). The shops in the agora fit the tentmaking work he shared with Aquila and Priscilla (18:3). In 2 Corinthians Paul writes to the church he founded here, tells of a painful second visit (2:1), and says he is coming “a third time” (12:14). Most readers think Paul wrote 1 and 2 Thessalonians from Corinth, since Silas and Timothy joined him there (Acts 18:5) and both are named in the greetings (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Second Timothy 4:20 says, “Erastus has remained at Corinth.” The city was where Paul had stayed longest after Ephesus, and the letter gives no reason for Erastus’ stay there.
Caution: The Bema is large enough to be the tribunal for the Gallio story, but Acts does not describe it. The lintel is probably later than Paul.
A paving block near the theater is carved in Latin: “Erastus, in return for his aedileship, laid [this pavement] at his own expense.”

Paul sends greetings to “Erastus, the city treasurer” (Romans 16:23), and Acts 19:22 names an Erastus among his helpers. The pavement shows that a man of that name held office in Corinth.
