The decree shows how freely the title “lord” was used for Nero, and Paul gives it to Jesus. 1 Peter 2:17 sets “fear God” beside “honor the king,” and 3:15 tells the readers to “sanctify Christ as Lord.” In the cities of Asia Minor, where the emperor was hailed with titles like “lord,” the letter keeps its highest allegiance for Christ.

Caution: The stone is from about five years after the most likely date of Philippians, and the hymn does not mention Caesar. “Lord” was also the ordinary word for a master, and Greek-speaking Jews used it for God. Scholars disagree about how far Paul meant a contrast with the emperor.
f: Archaeological Museum of Thebes, Greece (found at Akraiphia, Boeotia)

e.n: 4QMMT: “Some of the Works of the Law”
t: Six damaged copies of a long letter-like text found in Cave 4 at Qumran. It lists some twenty rulings on Temple sacrifice, priestly gifts and ritual purity, and it calls its readers to follow the writer’s understanding of the law. The scholars who first published it gave it the name 4QMMT, from a Hebrew phrase that means some of the works of the law.

Philippians 3:6 says that “as to righteousness in the law,” Paul was “faultless,” and 3:9 says he does not want “my own righteousness from the law” but “the righteousness from God on the basis of faith.” The phrase “works of the law” appears in Galatians 2:16 and Romans 3:20. This text shows how a Jewish group in the century before Paul spelled out what keeping the law should look like.
Caution: The text is about two centuries older than Paul, and it does not say anything about faith in Christ. Scholars disagree about how much light it sheds on his argument.
f: Found in Qumran Cave 4; fragments kept in Jerusalem
Composed about 150 BC; copies from about 75 BC to AD 50

e.n: Caesar’s household: tombs of the emperor’s slaves and freed people
t: Burial chambers on the roads out of Rome hold the ashes of slaves and freed people of the emperors. Their inscriptions record the jobs they held in the household, from cooks and gardeners to secretaries, and show how large and varied the emperor’s staff was.

Philippians 4:22 ends with greetings from “all the saints,” “especially those from the household of Caesar.” The household meant the emperor’s staff of slaves and freed people, not his family. Members of it had rank and pride within their world, and many were Paul’s contemporaries. The greeting says that believers were among them.
Caution: The tombs do not name any Christian. Imperial slaves and freed people also worked in the provinces, so the phrase alone does not prove that Paul wrote from Rome.

e.n: Hierapolis: hot springs, white terraces and the Plutonium
t: A hillside city built beside hot springs whose mineral water has laid down white terraces of travertine, now called Pamukkale. The excavated city has a long colonnaded main street, a large theater, baths and a great necropolis with hundreds of tombs. An Italian team has worked here since 1957. The Plutonium, a cave sanctuary of Pluto where gas from the earth killed animals, which the Greek geographer Strabo describes (Geography 13.4.14), has been identified at the site.

Colossians 4:13 is the only verse in the New Testament that names Hierapolis. Paul says Epaphras “goes to great pains for you and for those at Laodicea and Hierapolis.” The city was about 12 miles (20 km) from Colossae and across the river from Laodicea, so the three towns were close neighbors. The springs drew visitors, and the city was famous for its cloth and its dyes.

Caution: The letter gives no more than the name, so nothing is known about the church there. The city has a well-known Christian tradition, with a shrine of the apostle Philip from the 5th century, but this is later than Paul.
f: Founded in the Hellenistic period; rebuilt after an earthquake in AD 60

e.n: Hierapolis: the dyers and weavers who kept Jewish festivals
t: Tomb inscriptions of Hierapolis show that the city had guilds of workers in cloth. On a sarcophagus a man named Publius Aelius Glykon leaves 200 denarii to the guild of the purple-dyers, to be shared by its members at the festival of Unleavened Bread, and 150 denarii to the carpet-weavers, to be shared at the Kalends and at Pentecost. Another third-century tomb text threatens a fine to be paid to the Jews who live in Hierapolis and orders a copy to be put in their archive.

Colossians 2:16 says “let no one judge you by what you eat or drink, or with regard to a feast, a New Moon, or a Sabbath.” The Hierapolis texts show a Jewish community in the valley, mixed up with the town’s trade guilds, who kept Unleavened Bread and Pentecost. The valley was also known for its wool and dyes, which is the background of the clothing language in Colossians 3:9-14.
Caution: The inscriptions are from one to two centuries after Paul. Whether Glykon was himself Jewish is debated, and the texts do not mention the church or the Colossian teachers.
f: Necropolis of Hierapolis, near Pamukkale, Turkey
Tombstones of the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD

e.n: Chonai and the Archangel Michael: a later story from Colossae’s valley
t: The town of Chonai (modern Honaz) grew beside the old site of Colossae. Tradition says that the Archangel Michael once saved a church there from a flood by splitting a rock so that the river ran off. The story spread widely, and Michael was honored in this valley for centuries. The 4th-century council of Laodicea included a rule against Christians who “go away” to call on angels.

Colossians 2:18 warns against “the worship of angels.” Some scholars think the local stories show an old habit of calling on angels in this area, and others point out that they come centuries after Paul. They are included because they come from the same valley.
Caution: The story and the council rule are all later than the letter, and neither tells us what the teachers at Colossae did. The Greek of 2:18 can also mean worship that the angels offer to God.
f: Stories from the 4th century onward; the shrine was built later

e.n: The so-called Prison of Paul at Ephesus
t: A stone tower on the hill south of the ruins of Ephesus, part of the city wall that tradition ascribes to Lysimachus after 300 BC. Inside, the building has walls dividing it into small rooms and a second floor, so it has the look of a jail. Visitors have called it the Prison of Paul.

Colossians, Ephesians, Philippians and Philemon all say that Paul wrote in chains (Colossians 4:3, 18), but no letter says where he was. Rome is the usual answer. Ephesus is the other major suggestion, since Paul spent two or three years here (Acts 19:8-10), and he lists “more imprisonments” than his rivals (2 Corinthians 11:23). The tower is how some tourists picture that option. Philemon is another letter that may come from an Ephesian imprisonment. Paul asks Philemon to “prepare a guest room” (verse 22), which sounds like a trip he hopes to make soon, and Ephesus is only about 105 miles (170 km) from Colossae. The letter does not name the place.
Caution: No ancient text connects Paul with this tower, and Acts does not record an arrest at Ephesus. The name is a later tradition. Colossians does not say where Paul was held.
f: Tower in the Hellenistic wall of about 290 BC; the name comes from later tradition

e.n: Thessalonica: the city on the Via Egnatia, under modern Thessaloniki
t: Modern Thessaloniki sits on top of the ancient city. The excavated Roman forum lies in the center, with a covered colonnade, a small theater-like hall and shops, and the Arch of Galerius, built about AD 300, stands on the line of the main street. The Via Egnatia entered the city here, and today’s Egnatia Street still follows its route. The city was founded about 315 BC by Cassander, who named it for his wife Thessalonike, a half-sister of Alexander the Great.

Acts 17:1-9 says Paul came here along the Via Egnatia, reasoned in the synagogue for three Sabbaths, and was forced out by a mob. The two letters are addressed to “the church of the Thessalonians” (1 Thessalonians 1:1; 2 Thessalonians 1:1). Paul says the message of the Lord rang out from them to Macedonia and Achaia (1:8), which fits a church on the main road of the province. Thessalonica was the capital of Macedonia and a free city under Rome, and it was an important harbor. Second Timothy 4:10 says Demas, “in his love of this world, has deserted me and gone to Thessalonica.” Paul had named Demas as a companion in Colossians 4:14 and Philemon 24.
Caution: The Roman forum, the arch and most other buildings now visible are later than Paul. Little of the first-century city has been excavated because the modern city covers it.
f: Founded about 315 BC; the visible Roman buildings are later than Paul

e.n: The gods of Thessalonica: Serapis, Dionysus, the Cabirus and the emperors
t: A sanctuary of Serapis and Isis has been excavated in the center of Thessaloniki, and the city is known to have honored Dionysus and a local protector god called the Cabirus. Coins of the first century BC and AD show the emperors with titles that call them divine, and Rome and the emperors were honored here with temples and festivals. This is the religious world the converts came from.

First Thessalonians 1:9 says the believers “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God.” Acts 17:7 reports that the mob accused Jason of acting against the decrees of Caesar by saying that “there is another king, named Jesus.” Choosing to follow Christ meant giving up festivals, guild meals and civic honors, which may be part of the “great suffering” in 1:6 and the persecution in 2 Thessalonians 1:4.
Caution: The letters do not say which cults the Thessalonians had joined. The evidence comes from the city’s long history and is not tied to the people of the church.
f: Temples and coins from the 3rd century BC to the Roman period

e.n: The tombstone formula: “I was not, I was, I am not, I do not care”
t: Many Latin tombstones of the Roman world carry a short formula, “non fui, fui, non sum, non curo,” which means “I was not, I was, I am not, I do not care.” It is often cut as the first letters only (N F F N S N C). The formula appears on stones from Italy, Spain, North Africa and other provinces, and ordinary people used it, not only the educated.

First Thessalonians 4:13 says that the church should not “grieve like the rest, who are without hope.” The stones show one common attitude to death. Not every Greek and Roman thought that way, since many tombs speak of a shadowy afterlife or of hope in the gods, but the formula shows how final death could look to the people around the church.
Caution: The inscriptions come from all over the empire and are not from Thessalonica. They give one attitude among several and do not describe every pagan view of death.
f: Gravestones of the 1st to 3rd centuries AD

e.n: Parousia and apantesis: how Greek texts describe a king’s arrival
t: Greek papyri and inscriptions use parousia (“presence, arrival”) for the visit of a king, a governor or an emperor. The meeting party that went out of the city to greet the visitor and bring him in is called by a related word, apantesis. Cities prepared gifts, crowns and speeches for such visits.

The words “coming” (parousia) in 1 Thessalonians 2:19; 3:13; 4:15; 5:23 and 2 Thessalonians 2:1, and “to meet” (apantesis) in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 belong to this vocabulary. Acts 28:15 uses the same word for the brothers from Rome who traveled out “to meet us” when Paul was approaching the city. Some scholars think the picture in 4:15-17 is of a welcome that goes out to meet the king and escorts him in, and others think the language is only broadly similar.

Caution: Paul does not say that he is describing a royal visit, and scholars differ on how much of the civic background shapes 1 Thessalonians 4:15-17. The texts are not from Thessalonica in particular.
f: Greek cities of the Roman East
Papyri and inscriptions from the 3rd century BC to the 2nd century AD

e.n: Antiochus IV, “God Manifest,” and his coins
t: Silver coins of the Seleucid king Antiochus IV show his portrait and the Greek legend “of King Antiochus, God Manifest,” Theos Epiphanes. In 167 BC he took control of the Temple in Jerusalem, banned Jewish practice and set up an altar to Zeus there (1 Maccabees 1:41-64). The Jews who resisted him led the Maccabean revolt.

Daniel 11:36 says that a king “will exalt and magnify himself above every god.” Second Thessalonians 2:4 describes a man who will “oppose and exalt himself above every so-called god or object of worship” and “seat himself in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.” Many readers think Antiochus and then Caligula (AD 40) are the kind of ruler that Paul has in view, though Paul names neither. The Greek word epiphaneia, “appearance,” comes from the same family as the king’s title Epiphanes, “Manifest.” Titus 2:13 looks for “the blessed hope and glorious appearance of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ.”

Caution: Paul does not name Antiochus, and the coins say nothing about Paul’s meaning. Readers are divided on whether 2 Thessalonians 2:3-4 looks back to such a ruler, forward to one still to come, or both.
f: Silver tetradrachms minted in Antioch and other cities of the Seleucid kingdom

e.n: Ephesus: capital of Asia, and the Library of Celsus
t: In 27 BC Augustus made Ephesus the capital of the province of Asia, and Strabo called it second in importance only to Rome. The ruins today show a marble street, a theater, baths, fountains and the Library of Celsus, begun about AD 125, which once held nearly 12,000 scrolls. The facade was rebuilt between 1970 and 1978. Six luxury houses with mosaics and wall paintings stand on a hillside terrace.

The letter places Timothy at Ephesus (1:3), the city where Paul had spent more than two years (Acts 19:8-10; 20:31). Paul had warned the elders of Ephesus that “savage wolves” would come and that “men will rise up and distort the truth” even from their own number (Acts 20:29-30), and 1 Timothy 1:3-7 shows teachers of that kind at work. The city was large, rich and full of cults, with a great temple of Artemis, so the church lived in a crowded and public setting. Second Timothy 1:18 speaks of the help Onesiphorus gave Paul “in Ephesus.”
Caution: Most of the visible city, the library included, was built after Paul, in the 2nd century AD. The city of his time lies partly under and around it. The letter does not describe the city.
In 1 John: Early writers place John at Ephesus, and the letter’s closing “keep yourselves from idols” (5:21) fits a city of many temples.
f: Capital of Asia from 27 BC; most standing buildings are 2nd century AD

e.n: Plancia Magna and the women benefactors of Asia Minor
t: Inscriptions show that some wealthy women in the cities of Asia Minor held priesthoods and paid for public buildings. Plancia Magna of Perga, in the early 2nd century AD, was priestess of Artemis, high priestess of the imperial cult and priestess for life of the mother of the gods, and she held the city’s highest civil office, demiourgos. She paid for the restoration of the southern gate of Perga about AD 119-122.

First Timothy 2:9-10 says women should adorn themselves “with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God,” and 5:10 says a widow worth enrolling is “well known for good deeds.” Both passages are set in a world where some women gave publicly and were honored for it, and where dress and jewelry were a sign of rank. This is not a source for how to read 1 Timothy 2:11-15, which is debated.
Caution: The inscriptions come from Perga and other cities, not from Ephesus, and from a century after Paul. Women with civic offices were rare and mostly very wealthy.
f: Inscriptions of the 1st and 2nd centuries AD

e.n: Pliny’s letter: Christians sing “to Christ as to a god”
t: Pliny the Younger, governor of Bithynia and Pontus, wrote to the emperor Trajan about how to handle people accused of being Christians (Letter 10.96, about AD 110). He says they were in the habit of meeting before dawn on a fixed day and singing a hymn to Christ “as to a god.” It is one of the earliest outside reports of Christian worship.

The lines in 1 Timothy 3:16 (“He appeared in the flesh, was vindicated by the Spirit, was seen by angels”) are written in short, balanced clauses, and most scholars think Paul is quoting a hymn or creed the churches already used. Pliny’s report shows that singing to Christ was an early part of Christian meetings. Pliny governed Bithynia and Pontus, two of the provinces named in 1 Peter 1:1. His letter shows that about fifty years after Peter the name “Christian” itself could bring a person before the governor, which fits 4:14-16. The letter of Pliny also shows Christians being asked to give an account of themselves, as 3:15 describes.
Caution: Pliny wrote about forty years after the likely date of 1 Timothy and about northern Asia Minor, and he does not mention 1 Timothy. The letter says nothing about the content of the hymn.

e.n: The marriage laws of Augustus and the widows
t: Augustus passed laws to raise the birth rate. The laws penalized unmarried adults and those without children, for example in what they could inherit, and gave privileges to parents. They pressed widows and divorced women to marry again.

In 1 Timothy 5:11-15 Paul advises “younger widows” to “marry, have children, and manage their households,” and says that those who are not enrolled should be cared for by their families (5:4, 16). Marrying again was normal for a young widow in the Roman world, and the law encouraged it. Paul gives church reasons: the risk of idleness and gossip, and the “slander” the community might face.
Caution: The laws are a background to the advice and not its source. Paul gives his own reasons, and the letter does not mention the laws.
f: Laws of 18 BC and AD 9, in force in Paul’s time

e.n: Sacrifices for the emperor at the Jerusalem Temple
t: Josephus and Philo say that the Temple offered daily sacrifices on behalf of the emperor and the Roman people, and that the priests stopped them at the start of the revolt in AD 66 (Josephus, Jewish War 2.197, 2.409-410). The offering was made for the emperor, and not to him.

First Timothy 2:1-2 asks for “prayers, intercessions, and thanksgiving” for “kings and all those in authority,” as Jeremiah 29:7 told the exiles to seek the peace of the city where they lived. Jews and Christians prayed for the ruler without worshiping him, in a world where emperors were honored as gods, especially in Asia.
Caution: Josephus wrote after the war and describes the practice from his own view. The letter does not mention the Temple offerings.

e.n: Jannes and Jambres in Jewish tradition
t: The Old Testament does not name the magicians who opposed Moses (Exodus 7:11). Jewish tradition did. The Damascus Document, known from the Cairo Genizah and from fragments found at Qumran, says that Jannes and his brother stood against Moses and Aaron. The Targum of Pseudo-Jonathan on Exodus names Jannes and Jambres as Pharaoh’s chief magicians. A damaged Greek papyrus of the 3rd century AD, in leaves now in Dublin, Cologne and elsewhere, preserves part of a “Book of Jannes and Jambres,” and Origen knew a book of that name.

Second Timothy 3:8 says “Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so also these men oppose the truth.” Paul does not explain the names, which means Timothy and the church could be expected to know them from Jewish teaching. The comparison is about opposing the truth and foolishness that is finally shown up (3:9), and does not depend on details of the tradition.
Caution: All of these sources are later than Exodus and some are later than Paul. The letter does not say where Paul learned the names, and it does not quote any of these books.
f: Qumran (Damascus Document); Egypt (papyrus), Dead Sea and Nile
Jewish writings from the 2nd century BC to the 3rd century AD

e.n: Scrolls and parchments: books in Paul’s day
t: Most books in the Roman world were rolls of papyrus. Parchment was prepared animal skin, and ancient writers said it was developed at Pergamon, which is where the word “parchment” comes from. The Roman poet Martial, writing in the 80s AD, describes small parchment notebooks and a pocket edition of Virgil on parchment. Papyrus rolls, some burned black by the eruption of Vesuvius, were found in a villa at Herculaneum.

Second Timothy 4:13 asks Timothy to bring “my scrolls, especially the parchments.” The scrolls were probably rolls of papyrus and the parchments were skin, perhaps notebooks or copies of Scripture. The letter does not say what was written on them. Paul asks for them while he sits in chains and expects to die (4:6), which shows that he still wanted to read and write.
Caution: The finds come from other places and times. The letter does not describe the scrolls and parchments, and the Greek word for “parchments” (membranai) is a Latin loan word.
f: Papyrus rolls and parchment notebooks of the 1st century AD

e.n: Tacitus and 1 Clement on Nero and the Christians
t: The Roman historian Tacitus (Annals 15.44) says that after the great fire of Rome in AD 64 Nero blamed the Christians, and that a large number were arrested, mocked, and put to death, some by dogs, some by crucifixion and some burned as lights at night. 1 Clement, a letter from the church at Rome to Corinth about AD 96, says that Peter and Paul were among those who suffered, and that Paul reached the farthest limit of the west and gave his testimony before the rulers (1 Clement 5).

Second Timothy shows Paul in Rome in chains, expecting to be poured out “like a drink offering” (4:6). If Paul wrote it, as early Christian writers say he did, he was probably there in the 60s, when Nero had made Christians a target in Rome. The letter does not mention the fire or the persecution. Hebrews says its readers had suffered abuse and loss, and helped prisoners, but had not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood (12:4). Tacitus says that Nero in AD 64 put many Roman Christians to death, so some scholars think Hebrews was written before that, others that it is about a different place or later. 1 Peter 4:16 is one of the three places where the New Testament uses the name “Christian,” and it speaks of suffering “as a Christian.” Tacitus says the name was in use at Rome by AD 64. The letter does not say that its readers were being tried by Rome, and if “Babylon” in 5:13 means Rome, the letter was sent from the city where Tacitus says Christians were punished.
Caution: Neither source mentions Paul’s trial or says exactly when he died, and Tacitus does not name him. The date of Paul’s death is debated, with estimates from AD 64 to 68.
f: Tacitus about AD 116; 1 Clement about AD 96

e.n: Silver and clay vessels of a Roman house
t: In 1895 workers found 109 pieces of silver tableware, including cups, bowls and platters, hidden in a wine cistern at a villa at Boscoreale. The set is now in the Louvre. In the same households, simple clay jars, cups and lamps did the everyday work.

In 2 Timothy 2:20-21, “a large house contains not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay.” The vessels differ in use. Those who cleanse themselves become “a vessel for honor.” A wealthy house showed the whole range, from the silver set on the table to the clay jar in the kitchen.

Caution: The silver is from Italy and a decade or two after Paul. It shows what a rich house held, and not what Paul had in mind. Paul uses a similar picture of clay vessels in Romans 9:21-23 and 2 Corinthians 4:7.
f: Buried by the eruption of Vesuvius in AD 79

e.n: Roman rules for holding a prisoner
t: Roman jurists such as Ulpian, whose work is quoted in the Digest (48.3), describe ways to hold an accused person until trial: in the public prison, in the charge of a soldier, in the care of sureties, or under watch in a house. A prisoner could be bound with a chain to the soldier who guarded him. Acts 28:16 says Paul was allowed to stay by himself, with a soldier to guard him, and in 28:20 he speaks of “this chain.”

Second Timothy speaks of heavier treatment than Acts. Paul is “chained like a criminal” (2:9), his friend had to search “diligently” to find him (1:17), and no one stood with him at his first defense (4:16). A prisoner in this state depended on friends for food, clothing and company, which fits his request for a cloak (4:13). In Philemon Paul is “in chains” (verses 10, 13) yet has people with him: Onesimus ministering to him, and Epaphras, called a “fellow prisoner,” along with Mark, Aristarchus, Demas and Luke (verses 23-24). A prisoner held loosely could receive visitors and helpers.
Caution: The jurists wrote after Paul and the rules changed over time. The letter does not say how Paul was held.

Gortyn was the chief city of the Roman province of Crete and Cyrenaica. Excavations have uncovered the Roman governor’s residence (the praetorium), a theater, an odeon, baths and the ruins of a large early church of Saint Titus. Cut into the wall of the odeon is the Law Code of Gortyn, a long Greek inscription of about 450 BC with rules on marriage, divorce, property, inheritance and slaves.

Titus 1:5 says Titus was to “appoint elders in every town” of Crete but names no town. Gortyn was the seat of the Roman governor, so a mission to the island’s towns could well have used it, but that is a guess. Eusebius (Church History 3.4) says Titus was the first bishop of the churches on Crete, and the church of Saint Titus at Gortyn keeps that later memory.

Caution: The letter names no town on Crete. The church ruins are several centuries after Titus, and the law code is about five centuries older than Paul. It shows Cretan household law, not the churches of Titus.

Knossos was the center of the Minoan palace culture. Its huge Bronze Age palace, with painted frescoes and rows of storerooms, was abandoned long before Paul’s day. Rome made Knossos a colony in the first century BC, and Roman houses have been dug nearby.

Knossos is the town traditionally linked with Epimenides, the poet to whom later writers attribute the saying that Paul quotes in Titus 1:12. In Paul’s day it was a Roman colony and not the capital of the province. The letter does not say that Titus visited it.
Caution: The palace is more than a thousand years older than Paul and says nothing about Titus. Knossos is a pin for the poet, not a place named in the letter.
f: Bronze Age palace; Greek and Roman city

t: Epimenides is a half-legendary Cretan poet and seer. Later Greek writers tell that he slept for many years in a cave, that he was called to Athens to purify the city, and that he wrote poems of which only scraps survive. Clement of Alexandria and Jerome connect the saying that Cretans are always liars, evil beasts and idle bellies with him, and the opening words appear in the Hymn to Zeus of the poet Callimachus (3rd century BC).

Paul calls him “one of their own prophets” (Titus 1:12) and says, “This testimony is true.” He then tells Titus to “rebuke them sternly, so that they will be sound in the faith” (1:13), which treats the fault as one that can be corrected. The Greek word for “prophet” is used here of a poet-seer and does not make him an Old Testament prophet.

Caution: The letter does not name the poet. The link to Epimenides comes from later writers, and his dates and works are uncertain. The puzzle that arises when a Cretan says all Cretans lie is a later one; Paul does not use it.
f: Quoted by Clement of Alexandria and Jerome; Knossos in tradition
Poet of about 600 BC (traditional date); quoted from the 3rd to the 5th century AD

e.n: Saint Titus on Crete: tradition and relic
t: Church tradition says Titus stayed on Crete as its first bishop and died there. His memory is kept at the ruined church of Saint Titus at Gortyn and at the Church of Saint Titus in Heraklion, where a reliquary said to hold his skull was returned from Venice in 1966.

The New Testament says nothing about Titus after 2 Timothy 4:10, where he has gone to Dalmatia. Eusebius (Church History 3.4) says he was the first bishop of the churches of Crete, and the later tradition builds on that line.
Caution: The relic cannot be traced to the first century, and the New Testament does not tell of Titus’s later life or death.

Augustus founded Nicopolis, the City of Victory, after his defeat of Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC, and settled people from nearby towns there. Long stretches of the city wall, a theater, an odeon, a stadium and an aqueduct can still be seen, and on the hill north of the city lies the base of a victory monument whose wall once carried the bronze rams of captured warships. Games were held there every four years.

Titus 3:12 asks Titus to come to Paul at Nicopolis, “because I have decided to winter there.” Several cities had this name and the letter does not say which one Paul meant. Nicopolis in Epirus is the usual guess because it was a large and busy Roman city. Paul says in Romans 15:19 that he preached as far as Illyricum, which lies to its north.
Caution: Much of what can be seen was built or rebuilt after Paul’s day, and the letter does not say which Nicopolis it means.

e.n: Household duty lists in Greek and Roman writing
t: Greek writers organized the household as three pairs: master and slave, husband and wife, father and children. Aristotle sets this out in his Politics, and later Greek and Roman writers kept giving advice on how each person in a household should behave. Such lists are often called household codes.

Titus 2:1-10 gives short duties for older men, older women, younger women, younger men and slaves, and ties each to the gospel: “so that the word of God will not be discredited” (2:5), and slaves are to “adorn the teaching about God our Savior” (2:10). Similar lists appear in Colossians 3:18-4:1, Ephesians 5:22-6:9 and 1 Peter 2:18-3:7. Paul uses a form his readers knew and gives it a gospel reason. 1 Peter 2:18-3:7 follows the same pairs in order (servants, wives, husbands) and adds a reason in each case from the example of Christ and the hope of the readers. Unlike the Greek lists, it speaks first to slaves and to the wife of an unbelieving husband, and it asks the husband to honor his wife as a fellow heir.

Caution: The older Greek lists are advice for the head of a household. Titus speaks to each group and does not list duties for masters. Scholars debate how much of the form Paul borrowed and how the passages apply today.

Roman law treated a slave as his owner’s property. An owner could have a runaway (a fugitivus) hunted down, and a person who sheltered or hid one could be charged with theft. The Digest of Justinian, which collects the work of earlier jurists, has a whole title on fugitives (11.4). Recaptured runaways were often flogged, chained or branded, and some wore a metal collar with the owner’s name.

Philemon 10-18 deals with a slave who is away from his owner. If Onesimus was a runaway, Philemon had the right to punish him severely, and Paul asks him to give that right up and to receive Onesimus as a brother. Some scholars point to a rule recorded in the Digest (21.1.17.4) that a slave who went to a friend of his master to ask the friend to speak for him was not counted a fugitive. They suggest Onesimus came to Paul in that way. The letter does not say how he came to be with Paul.

Caution: The Digest was put together about 500 years after Paul, from jurists who wrote mostly in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, so it shows how the law worked over time and not exactly what applied at Colossae. Philemon never says that Onesimus ran away, or that he stole anything.
f: Roman law; the surviving texts are collected in the Digest of AD 533

e.n: Pliny asks a friend to forgive a freedman
t: Pliny the Younger, a Roman lawyer and later a governor, left ten books of letters. In Letter 9.21 he writes to a friend, Sabinianus, to ask him to forgive a freedman (a former slave) who had angered him and who had come to Pliny for help. Pliny urges mercy, says the young man is sorry, and tells Sabinianus that he may be angry again if the man deserves it. In Letter 9.24 Pliny thanks Sabinianus for pardoning him.

The letter is often set beside Philemon because both are written by a respected man to a friend, asking that an offender be received kindly. Paul goes further. He calls Onesimus “my child” and “my very heart,” offers to pay any debt, and asks Philemon to receive him as he would receive Paul himself (verses 10, 12, 17-18). Pliny’s man is a freedman and not a slave, and Pliny does not call him a brother or offer to pay.

Caution: Pliny wrote about 45 years after Paul’s letter, and the two cases are not the same. The resemblance shows how such appeals were worded in the Roman world, not that Paul knew of Pliny’s letter.
f: Rome; Pliny the Younger, Letters 9.21 and 9.24

t: About AD 110 Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, wrote to the church at Ephesus and named its bishop as Onesimus (Ephesians 1:3). He plays on the name in Ephesians 2:2, saying he hopes to have “profit” of him. Later church tradition says that Philemon, Apphia and Archippus died as martyrs at Colossae. Neither the New Testament nor Ignatius says that Paul’s Onesimus is the bishop.

Philemon never says what became of Onesimus. Some readers suggest that the bishop was the same man, since the name was common but the setting fits: Ephesus was the nearest large city to Colossae, and Paul sent Onesimus back to that region. One theory, proposed by Edgar Goodspeed in the 1930s, is that Onesimus later helped gather Paul’s letters at Ephesus, which would explain why so short a letter was kept. There is no direct evidence for it.
Caution: Onesimus was a common slave name. The link between the slave in Philemon and the bishop in Ignatius is a guess, and the stories of the martyrdoms come from much later.
f: Ephesus; Ignatius of Antioch, Letter to the Ephesians

e.n: The earthquake in the Lycus Valley
t: The Roman historian Tacitus (Annals 14.27) says that Laodicea was thrown down by an earthquake in Nero’s reign and rebuilt from its own resources, without help from Rome. Later Christian chronicles that rely on Eusebius add Hierapolis and Colossae to the list. The valley lies on an active fault, and the ruins of Hierapolis show repeated damage.

If Colossians and Philemon were written at Rome about AD 60-62, the earthquake would have struck the three towns about that time, yet neither letter mentions it. Some scholars take the silence as a reason to place the letters earlier, from an imprisonment at Ephesus or Caesarea. Others point out that the evidence for damage at Colossae is late and uncertain, and that a letter about a slave need not mention it.
Caution: Tacitus names only Laodicea, and the date is debated. The case for Colossae rests on later writers, so the silence of the letters proves little.
f: Laodicea, Hierapolis and Colossae, Lycus Valley, Turkey

t: A badly broken scroll found in Cave 11 in 1956, known as 11QMelchizedek or 11Q13. It reads the year of release in Leviticus 25 as a time at the end of days and gives Melchizedek a part in that release and in the judgment of the wicked. The writer uses verses from Leviticus, Isaiah and the Psalms.

Hebrews 7 builds its case from two Old Testament passages, Genesis 14:17-20 and Psalm 110:4. The scroll shows that other Jews of the time also thought about Melchizedek and gave him a large role. The writer of Hebrews calls Melchizedek “like the Son of God” (7:3) and makes him a picture of the Son, not a heavenly rival.

Caution: The scroll is full of gaps, and scholars disagree whether its Melchizedek is an angel, a divine figure or a human priest. Nothing shows that the writer of Hebrews knew this scroll; it shows only that the interest was in the air.
f: Qumran, Cave 11, near the Dead Sea

e.n: Philo of Alexandria and the Letter to the Hebrews
t: Philo was a Jewish writer in Alexandria who read the Greek Old Testament as pointing to unseen realities behind the visible world. He wrote on Melchizedek, called the divine Word (the Logos) a high priest, and spoke of the tabernacle as a copy of a heavenly pattern.

Hebrews also speaks of the earthly tent as a “copy and shadow” of heavenly things (8:5), and the letter shares many words and images with the educated Greek-speaking Judaism that Philo belongs to. Hebrews differs at the center: its high priest is a person who suffered and died at a particular time, not an idea.

Caution: Scholars debate how far Hebrews depends on Alexandrian thought. Shared language does not prove that the writer read Philo, and the Dead Sea Scrolls offer other parallels, for example in the thought of a heavenly temple.

e.n: The Greek Old Testament that Hebrews quotes
t: Two great Greek Bibles of the 4th century, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus, contain the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Old Testament made by Jewish scholars from about the 3rd century BC. The writer of Hebrews quotes this Greek text again and again.

Several arguments depend on the Greek words. Psalm 8 speaks of people made lower than “angels” in the Greek, where the Hebrew has a word that can mean God or gods (Hebrews 2:7). In Psalm 40 the Greek says “a body You prepared for Me,” where the Hebrew says that ears were opened or dug (Hebrews 10:5). The writer was clearly writing for readers who knew the Greek Bible.

Caution: The copies are 700 years or more later than the letter, and some differences may come from earlier forms of the Greek text, or from the writer adapting what he quoted, and not only from the translators.
f: Codex Vaticanus (Vatican Library) and Codex Sinaiticus (British Library and other libraries)
4th century AD copies of a much older translation

t: No remains of the tabernacle survive, but its measurements are given in Exodus, and builders have made models and full-size replicas from them. The court was 100 by 50 cubits (about 50 by 25 meters if a cubit is about half a meter), with a tent 30 cubits long and 10 wide, divided into a Holy Place and a Most Holy Place.

Hebrews 9:1-5 walks through the tent room by room, and chapter 8 says its priests serve at “a copy and shadow” of heavenly things. A model helps a reader picture the first room with the lampstand, table and bread, the curtain, and the inner room that the high priest entered once a year.

Caution: Details differ between reconstructions because Exodus does not give every measurement, and the contents of the inner room in 9:4 raise questions of their own. No excavation has found the tent of Moses.
f: Modern reconstructions, including a full-size replica at Timna Park in Israel
Built in modern times from Exodus 25-27 and 35-40

e.n: The Day of Atonement: Leviticus 16 and the Mishnah
t: Leviticus 16 sets out the rite once a year: the high priest, after offering for himself, takes the blood of a bull and a goat into the inner room and sprinkles it, with a cloud of incense, and a second goat is sent into the wilderness. The Mishnah (tractate Yoma) describes the day in much more detail, including the washings and the high priest’s changes of clothing.

Hebrews points to the yearly repetition twice (9:7, 25). In 10:1-4 the writer says the same sacrifices year after year can never make the worshipers perfect, because the offering has to be made again. The writer says that Christ entered once for all (9:12).

Caution: The Mishnah was put into writing about 130 years after the Temple was destroyed, so it records memory and not an eyewitness account. It also says the Holy of Holies in the Second Temple held no ark, only a stone, which bears on how 9:4 should be read. Hebrews itself follows the tabernacle and Leviticus, not the Temple of its day.
1 John 2:2 and 4:10 speak of Jesus as “the atoning sacrifice for our sins.”
f: Leviticus (the Law); Mishnah tractate Yoma, about AD 200

t: Josephus describes a great woven curtain hanging before the doors of the sanctuary, made of blue, fine linen, scarlet and purple, with a picture of the heavens embroidered on it. He says it was a Babylonian tapestry.

Hebrews uses the curtain as a picture of the barrier between the people and God’s presence. The “second” curtain of the tabernacle hides the inner room (9:3), hope enters “behind the curtain” (6:19), and the new and living way is opened “through the curtain of His body” (10:20). Mark 15:38 says the Temple curtain was torn at Jesus’ death.

Caution: Josephus describes the curtain at the entrance to the sanctuary, and the Mishnah and others mention an inner one, so scholars differ over which curtain is meant in the Gospels. Hebrews speaks of the tabernacle and does not say which curtain of the Temple it has in mind.
f: The Jerusalem Temple; Josephus, Jewish War 5.212-214
Josephus wrote about AD 75, describing the Temple before AD 70

t: A spring-fed oasis in the Negev, the largest spring for many miles, with the remains of a fortress from the time of the Judean kings. It is the most favored candidate for the biblical Kadesh-barnea, and Ain Qadis nearby is another.

Numbers 13-14 places Kadesh-barnea where the spies came back and the people refused to enter the land. Hebrews 3:7-4:13 quotes Psalm 95 about hardened hearts and the failed entry into “rest,” and says that the promise of rest still stands for the readers.
Caution: The fortress dates from centuries after the exodus, and nothing proves where Israel camped. The identification is probable and not certain.
f: Negev, near the border of Egypt and Israel
Iron Age fort; Israel’s time at Kadesh is told in Numbers

t: Second Maccabees tells how the aged scribe Eleazar was beaten to death rather than eat pork, and how a mother and her seven sons were tortured and killed one by one under Antiochus IV, each refusing to break the law and speaking of resurrection. The book uses a word for an instrument of torture, the tympanon, in the story of Eleazar.

Hebrews 11:35 says that “Others were tortured and refused their release, so that they might gain a better resurrection.” The Greek verb for “tortured” comes from the same word as the tympanon in 2 Maccabees 6. Many scholars think the writer has this story in mind, along with other martyrs.

Caution: Hebrews does not name the martyrs. “Women received back their dead” also fits the stories of the widow of Zarephath and the Shunammite (1 Kings 17; 2 Kings 4). Second Maccabees is part of the Greek Old Testament, but Protestant Bibles do not include it, so readers differ on how to treat it.
f: Jerusalem and Antioch; told in 2 Maccabees
Events about 167-164 BC; 2 Maccabees written about 124 BC or later

e.n: Isaiah sawn in two: a Jewish tradition
t: A Jewish story, preserved in the first part of a text called the Martyrdom (or Ascension) of Isaiah, says that King Manasseh had the prophet Isaiah sawn in two. The Talmud and Christian writers such as Justin Martyr repeat the tradition in some form.
Hebrews 11:37 says that some were “sawed in two.” The writer does not give a name, and many readers think the tradition about Isaiah is one of the things he may have in mind.
Caution: The Old Testament does not say how Isaiah died. The story comes from later writings of uncertain date, and the writer of Hebrews names no one in this verse.
f: Jerusalem; the Martyrdom of Isaiah and later Jewish and Christian writers
A text from about the 1st century BC or AD; later writers repeat it

t: Pompeii has the remains of many small inns and taverns, with counters, rooms, wall paintings and scribbled graffiti. The poet Horace (Satires 1.5) and other writers describe the poor beds and noise of inns along Roman roads.

Hebrews 13:2 tells the readers to “show hospitality to strangers.” Travelers, including traveling Christian teachers, often stayed in a believer’s home, since inns had a poor name. 1 Peter 4:9 tells the readers to “show hospitality to one another without complaining.” In the Roman world, the roadside inns were noisy and unsafe, so a believer’s house open to a travelling brother mattered.
Caution: The best evidence comes from towns such as Pompeii. The letter does not say where its readers lived, and country inns may have been worse.
For 3 John: verses 5-8 praise Gaius for taking in traveling brothers who were strangers to him. A Christian home spared such workers the cost and the rough company of the inns.
f: Pompeii, Italy, and other Roman towns

e.n: Origen and Eusebius on who wrote Hebrews
t: Eusebius reports a homily of Origen on Hebrews. Origen says that the thoughts are those of Paul, but that the wording and composition belong to someone who remembered the apostle’s teaching and wrote it down, and that only God knows who actually wrote the letter. He mentions that some people said Clement of Rome and others said Luke.

The letter names no author. Around AD 200 Tertullian, in North Africa, named Barnabas. Churches in the East came to treat Hebrews as Paul’s, while many in the West doubted this until the 4th century. In modern times Apollos, Priscilla and others have been suggested.

Caution: These are the opinions of later writers, not evidence from the author’s time, and nothing in the letter decides the matter. The ending, with Timothy and a blessing, is why Paul’s name was attached, and the style and Greek differ from Paul’s other letters.

A limestone ossuary of the kind Jerusalem families used before AD 70, carrying an Aramaic inscription that reads “James, son of Joseph, brother of Jesus.” It was announced at a press conference in Washington on 21 October 2002. The owner, Oded Golan, said he had bought it from an antiquities dealer in the 1970s, so it has no recorded findspot.

If the inscription is ancient and names the James of the New Testament, it would be an early written mention of Jesus’ family. Paul calls James “the Lord’s brother” (Galatians 1:19), and Josephus names him as the brother of Jesus. The letter of James itself calls its writer only “a servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (1:1).

Caution: In June 2003 a committee of the Israel Antiquities Authority judged the inscription a modern forgery; other experts disagreed. In March 2012 a Jerusalem court acquitted the owner of the forgery charges, but the judge said that this did not prove the inscription genuine. James, Joseph and Jesus were all common names, and with no findspot the box cannot be tied to any particular family.
f: Jerusalem area; no known findspot; now in a private collection in Israel
Limestone bone box of the late Second Temple period; the inscription is disputed

e.n: Josephus and Hegesippus on the death of James
t: The Jewish historian Josephus tells that after the death of the Roman governor Festus, and before the next governor arrived, the high priest Ananus convened judges and brought before them James, the brother of Jesus who was called Christ, and some others. He had them stoned as lawbreakers. Josephus adds that the most fair-minded citizens objected and that Ananus lost his office. Hegesippus, whom Eusebius quotes, tells a different story: James was thrown from the Temple wall, survived the fall, and was beaten to death with a fuller’s club.

Both accounts treat James as a well-known leader of the Jerusalem church, which fits the picture in Acts and Galatians (Acts 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 2:9). If the letter comes from this James, it was written before his death, dated by Josephus to about AD 62.

Caution: The two accounts do not agree on how James died or who ordered it. Most scholars accept the Josephus passage on James as his own writing, though some think a Christian copyist added to the wording. Hegesippus wrote about a century later and his story has legendary features. Hegesippus also says James was buried near the Temple, but no one has found the spot.
f: Jerusalem; Josephus, Antiquities 20.200; Hegesippus, quoted in Eusebius, Church History 2.23
Josephus about AD 93; Hegesippus about AD 170; Eusebius about AD 325

e.n: Early papyri of James (P20, P23 and P100)
t: Three fragments of papyrus codices found in the rubbish mounds of Oxyrhynchus carry parts of James. Papyrus 20 (Princeton University Library) has James 2:19 to 3:9, Papyrus 23 (Spurlock Museum, University of Illinois) has 1:10-12 and 15-18, and Papyrus 100 (Ashmolean Museum, Oxford) has 3:13 to 4:4 and 4:9 to 5:1.

They show that the letter was copied and read in Egypt by the 200s, about the time Origen cites it by name. The sections they preserve include the passage on the tongue (3:1-12) and the section on the two wisdoms (3:13-18).
Caution: The dates come from handwriting and can only be given to about a century. The fragments contain no title or author, and they say nothing about who wrote the letter or when.
f: Oxyrhynchus, Egypt (now in Princeton, Urbana and Oxford)
Early 3rd century (P20, P23); late 3rd or early 4th century (P100)

t: The Greek word dipsychos, “double-minded,” is not found in earlier Greek writing that survives, and in the New Testament it occurs only in James (1:8; 4:8). It then turns up in early Christian writings: in a saying quoted in 1 Clement 23 and 2 Clement 11 (“Wretched are the double-minded”), in the Didache and the Epistle of Barnabas, and many times in the Shepherd of Hermas.

James may have coined the word, or taken it from a Jewish teaching that did not survive. In James the double-minded person is the one who asks God for wisdom but doubts (1:6-8), and the “double-minded” who must purify their hearts are those trying to be friends of God and of the world at once (4:4-8).

Caution: The dates of these writings are uncertain (Hermas is placed anywhere from the late 1st to the mid-2nd century), so it cannot be shown who borrowed from whom. The quotation in 1 and 2 Clement is introduced as “the word of the prophets” or “Scripture” but matches no known biblical text.
f: Rome and elsewhere; 1 Clement, 2 Clement, the Didache, Barnabas and the Shepherd of Hermas

e.n: A harvester’s complaint from Mesad Hashavyahu
t: A pottery fragment (an ostracon) found in 1960 at a small Judean fortress on the coast carries a Hebrew letter in which a field worker appeals to the commander. He says he is a reaper, that he finished his harvesting, and that an official took his garment; he asks to have it returned.

James 5:4 says that the wages held back from the workers who mowed the fields “are crying out,” and that the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts. The Law protected the poor worker’s cloak and his daily wages (Exodus 22:26-27; Deuteronomy 24:12-15), and the ostracon is a written complaint of the kind a poor man would bring.

Caution: It is some six centuries older than James and comes from a military post, not from a landowner’s estate. Scholars differ on parts of the reading and on why the garment was taken. It is evidence of what a harvester’s complaint could look like, not of what James’s readers faced.
f: Mesad Hashavyahu, near Yavne-Yam on the Mediterranean coast; now in the Israel Museum

t: A small limestone tablet carries a short inscription naming the farm work of the year in periods of one or two months: a time of ingathering, two months of planting, two of late planting, a month of cutting flax, a month of barley harvest, a month of harvest and measuring, two months of pruning, and a month of summer fruit.

The farmer of James 5:7 waits “for the fall and spring rains.” The tablet does not mention rain, but it shows the farm year in the hills of Israel, which depended on the early rain to start the planting and the late rain to fill the grain (Deuteronomy 11:14).
Caution: The tablet was not found in a layer that fixes its date, and scholars have argued about its language and purpose. It lists work, not weather.
f: Gezer, between Jerusalem and the coast; now in the Istanbul Archaeology Museums
About the 10th century BC (found in 1908; not firmly dated)

e.n: Philo on the Jewish communities of the Dispersion
t: Philo, a Jewish writer in Alexandria, quotes a letter from King Agrippa I to the emperor Gaius. It says that Jerusalem is the mother city of Jewish settlements in Egypt, Phoenicia, Syria, Pamphylia, Cilicia, most of Asia as far as Bithynia and Pontus, and in Europe Thessaly, Boeotia, Macedonia, Attica, Corinth and much of the Peloponnese, as well as the islands and the lands beyond the Euphrates.

James writes to “the twelve tribes of the Dispersion” (1:1). The word diaspora was used for the Jews living outside the land, and Philo’s list shows how widely they were scattered about a generation before the letter could have been written.

Caution: The list comes from a political appeal to an emperor and may be made to sound as large as possible. James names no places, so the list does not tell us where his readers lived, and some think “the twelve tribes” is a title for the church as a whole and not only for Jews.

e.n: Gold rings and rank in the Roman world
t: In Rome a gold finger ring marked a person’s rank. Pliny the Elder, writing about AD 77, traces the history of the right to wear one: first reserved for senators, then extended to the equestrian order, then granted by emperors to favored freedmen. He complains that in his day too many people wore them.

James 2:2 pictures a man who comes into the meeting “wearing a gold ring and fine clothes.” The Greek word for his gold ring (chrysodaktylios, “gold-fingered”) occurs only here in the New Testament. The picture is of a visitor whose clothes and jewelry would earn him a seat of honor.

Caution: Pliny describes Rome, and the rules may not have held in the provinces. James does not say that the man in his example held any rank, only that he looked wealthy, and the story may be a made-up example and not a real event.
f: Museums in Italy and Britain; written evidence in Pliny the Elder, Natural History 33

e.n: The Ben Sira scroll from Masada
t: A Hebrew scroll of the Wisdom of Ben Sira (Sirach) found at Masada in the 1960s preserves a long run of the book, from chapter 39 to chapter 44. It shows that the book was read in Hebrew in Judea before the time of Jesus.

James reads like the teaching of Ben Sira in several places. Sirach 2:1 warns that serving the Lord means being tested, Sirach 5:11 tells the reader to be quick to hear, Sirach 15:11-20 denies that God causes people to sin, and Sirach 28 is a long warning about the tongue. These match the topics of James 1:2-4, 1:19, 1:13 and 3:1-12.

Caution: The Masada scroll covers only chapters 39-44, so it does not contain those parallels; it shows only that the book was known. Sirach is in the Greek Old Testament and in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, but not in Protestant ones, and James does not quote it by name.
f: Copied in the 1st century BC; the book was written about 180 BC

e.n: Mount Carmel: Muhraqa, the traditional place of Elijah’s contest
t: A Carmelite monastery stands on the southeastern end of Mount Carmel at a place called Muhraqa, “the burning place,” which tradition names as the site where Elijah met the prophets of Baal. The terrace has a view across the Jezreel Valley to the Kishon stream below.

James 5:17-18 says Elijah prayed that it would not rain, and then prayed again and the sky gave rain. First Kings 18 puts the final scene on Carmel, where Elijah bowed down with his face between his knees and sent his servant to watch the sea for a cloud.

Caution: The identification is traditional. Carmel is a long ridge, and the Bible does not name the exact spot. James also says the drought lasted three and a half years, a figure that Luke 4:25 repeats; 1 Kings 18:1 says that the rain came in the third year.
f: Southeastern end of Mount Carmel, overlooking the Jezreel Valley
Tradition; a Carmelite monastery was built there in the 19th century

e.n: The Armenian Cathedral of St James, Jerusalem
t: A church in the Armenian Quarter of Jerusalem honors two apostles named James: James the son of Zebedee, killed by Herod Agrippa I (Acts 12:2), and James the brother of the Lord, called James the Just. The building seen today is mostly from the 12th century.

Acts and Galatians show James the brother of Jesus as a leader in Jerusalem (Acts 12:17; 15:13; 21:18; Galatians 2:9), and a long Christian tradition calls him the first bishop of the city. The letter of James does not describe his role.
Caution: The church is a memorial to a tradition, not evidence from the first century. Nothing ties the present building, or any other place in Jerusalem, to James’s own time.
f: Present church mainly 12th century; the tradition is older

e.n: Papyrus 72: the oldest copy of 1 Peter
t: A small papyrus book that carries 1 Peter, 2 Peter and Jude along with other Christian writings, among them the Nativity of Mary, a homily of Melito, and Psalms 33 and 34. It belongs to the group of Greek and Coptic papyri bought in Egypt in the 1950s and named after the Swiss collector Martin Bodmer. They are said to have come from near Dishna in Upper Egypt.

It is the earliest surviving copy of 1 Peter, and it shows the letter was in circulation in Egypt within about two centuries of its writing. At 1 Peter 3:15 it reads sanctify Christ as God where most manuscripts read “as Lord” (the wording in this app), and the scribe’s changes show how an early reader handled the text. Psalm 34, which is also in the volume, is the psalm Peter quotes in 2:3 and 3:10-12.

Caution: The dates come from handwriting and are given to within a century or so. Scholars are not agreed whether the pieces were bound together as one book from the start or whether it was a collection assembled for one reader. It says nothing about who wrote 1 Peter.
In 2 Peter: Papyrus 72 also holds 2 Peter, so it is the earliest surviving copy of that letter as well, though Eusebius says some Christians did not accept it.

The same little book holds the oldest nearly complete copy of Jude. At Jude 5 its scribe wrote that “God Christ” saved the people from Egypt, where other old copies read “Jesus” (as the BSB does) or “the Lord.”
f: Egypt (the Bodmer papyri); now divided between the Bodmer Library near Geneva and the Vatican Library

e.n: The Vatican excavations under St Peter’s
t: Between 1940 and 1949, archaeologists dug beneath the floor of St Peter’s Basilica and found a Roman burial ground of the 2nd and 3rd centuries with rows of mausoleums. Under the high altar they found a small monument of about AD 160, set against a red plastered wall, with a niche over a simple grave. Around it, graffiti and later walls cluster closely. Pope Pius XII announced in 1950 that the tomb of Peter had been found, and in 1968 Pope Paul VI said that some bones from the site had been identified as his.

A priest named Gaius, writing at Rome about AD 200, says he can show the trophies of the apostles on the Vatican and on the Ostian Way (quoted in Eusebius, Church History 2.25). The monument on the hill matches the kind of trophy he meant. The people of Rome had remembered the spot for a century and a half. The letter says it was sent from “Babylon,” and the Rome of Peter’s last years is the likeliest place the early church had in mind.

Caution: The excavators and later scholars disagree on how to read the evidence. The shrine is some ninety years after Peter’s death; the bones came from a wall cavity and had been moved in the past. The grave in the shrine was found empty. Neither the Vatican nor the excavators claim proof that Peter lay there, and most historians would say only that the Christians of Rome believed it by the middle of the 2nd century.
2 Peter 1:14-15 has the writer expecting his death soon, “as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me.”
f: Vatican Hill, Rome (under the basilica of St Peter)
Roman cemetery of the 1st to 4th centuries; the shrine dates to about AD 160

e.n: Early writers on Peter and Mark at Rome
t: Several early Christian writers place Peter at Rome. The letter 1 Clement, written from the church at Rome about AD 96, tells how Peter endured many hardships and bore his witness, and puts Paul with him. Ignatius, writing to Rome about AD 110, says he will not command the church there as Peter and Paul did. Dionysius, bishop of Corinth about AD 170, says both apostles taught in Italy and were martyred about the same time. Eusebius, about AD 325, quotes Papias as saying that Mark was Peter’s interpreter, and tells that the first letter of Peter was written at Rome, calling the city Babylon in a figure.

The letter ends with greetings from “the church in Babylon” and from “my son Mark” (5:13). If “Babylon” means Rome, as these writers took it, Peter, Silvanus and Mark are with him in the capital. The Mark of Acts 12:12 (John Mark) and Peter in this company would also fit the Gospel tradition of Mark as Peter’s interpreter.

Caution: These writers are all from 30 to 250 years after Peter’s death, and none of them says in so many words that Peter wrote from Rome in AD 62-65. The New Testament does not describe Peter in Rome. The older city of Babylon on the Euphrates and the Roman fort of Babylon in Egypt have also been proposed, and Eusebius’s account of Papias on 1 Peter is a report of a report.
In 2 Peter: 1 Clement says Peter suffered many hardships and went to his place of glory, which fits 2 Peter 1:14-15, where the writer expects to lay aside “this tent” soon.
f: Rome; 1 Clement 5 (about AD 96); Ignatius, Romans 4; Dionysius of Corinth and Irenaeus (2nd century); Papias and Eusebius

t: Excavators at Sardis found a small industrial area beside the Pactolus stream where workers separated gold from silver and other metals. They uncovered clay furnaces, small cups for heating the ore, and traces of gold dust in the debris. The refinery dates from about the time of King Croesus (reigned about 560-546 BC), whose kingdom was famous for its wealth and which is credited with the first coins of nearly pure gold and silver.

Sardis was in Asia, one of the five provinces named in 1 Peter 1:1. Peter says the proven character of your faith is “more precious than gold, which perishes even though refined by fire” (1:7). Refining gold in a furnace to burn off its impurities is also the picture in Proverbs 17:3 and Malachi 3:3, and the people of Sardis could have seen the work done within living memory of the hill.

Caution: The refinery is five or six centuries older than the letter and does not belong to the early church. Peter does not mention Sardis, and the picture of the furnace was already common in the Old Testament.
The letter to Laodicea counsels buying “gold refined by fire” (Revelation 3:18), and the letter to Sardis speaks of soiled and white garments (3:4-5).
f: Sardis (Pactolus valley), Lydia, in the Roman province of Asia

e.n: Enoch’s Watchers among the Dead Sea Scrolls
t: Fragments of about eleven Aramaic manuscripts of the Book of Enoch were found in Cave 4 at Qumran. They include the section called the Book of the Watchers, which retells the story of Genesis 6:1-4: angels called Watchers came down, took wives, and fathered giants, and God had them bound in prison until the judgment. Enoch is told to carry God’s sentence to them.

1 Peter 3:19 says Christ “preached to the spirits in prison,” who “disobeyed long ago when God waited patiently in the days of Noah.” Many modern commentators read this through the Enoch story, in which the rebel angels of Noah’s day are bound in prison, and 2 Peter 2:4 and Jude 6 speak of angels held in darkness. Jude 14 quotes from the Book of Enoch.

Caution: The scrolls show the Enoch story was known to Jews in the land two centuries before Peter. They do not prove that Peter had it in mind in 3:19-20, and the older readings (Christ preaching through Noah, or to the dead) are still held. The New Testament never calls Enoch Scripture.
2 Peter 2:4 says God put the angels who sinned “in chains of darkness to be held for judgment,” as the Enoch story tells of the Watchers.

For Jude the book matters twice over: verse 6 speaks of angels who left their proper dwelling and are kept in chains under darkness, as the Watchers are in the Book of Enoch, and verses 14-15 quote the opening vision of the book.
f: Qumran, Cave 4, above the Dead Sea (now in the Israel Museum and the Rockefeller Museum, Jerusalem)
Copied about 200-100 BC; the book itself is older

e.n: Flood stories on clay tablets from Mesopotamia
t: Babylonian stories tell of a great flood sent by the gods. In Tablet XI of the Epic of Gilgamesh, Utnapishtim builds a boat, loads it with his family, craftsmen and animals, and rides out the storm; when the boat grounds on a mountain he sends out a dove, a swallow and a raven. An older version, the Atrahasis story, goes back to about 1700 BC. A tablet published in 2014 describes a round boat of reeds and ropes, built to a stated size.

1 Peter 3:20 recalls “the days of Noah while the ark was being built,” when “only eight souls” were saved through water. Genesis 8:4 puts the ark on the mountains of Ararat. The tablets show that the flood story was told in the lands of the Bible long before Genesis was written down, and they give the closest outside parallels.

Caution: The stories have the same outline but differ in the reason for the flood, the gods, the size of the boat and the end of the story. Scholars disagree on whether Genesis drew on the Mesopotamian tradition, shares an older source with it, or tells the true events the others remember. The tablets say nothing about 1 Peter.
2 Peter 2:5 and 3:6 recall the flood.
f: Nineveh (Ashurbanipal’s library, now in the British Museum); older versions from Babylonia
Gilgamesh XI about 650 BC (Nineveh copy); Atrahasis about 1700 BC

e.n: Urartu and the mountains of Ararat
t: Assyrian kings from the 13th century BC record campaigns against a land they call Uruatri and later Urartu, in the mountains around Lake Van. By the 9th century BC the kingdom of Urartu had a capital at Tushpa, a rock fortress above the lake, and left cuneiform inscriptions and large fortresses across the region. The Hebrew name “Ararat” is the same word. The Bible uses it for a land: the sons of Sennacherib fled to the land of Ararat (2 Kings 19:37).

Genesis 8:4 says the ark came to rest on the mountains of Ararat, a range or region and not one peak. The mountain now called Ararat (Agri Dagi, 5,137 m) took the name later. 1 Peter 3:20 recalls the ark and the people saved in it, and so the pin for the flood scene falls in this country.

Caution: Urartu shows where the biblical writers placed Ararat, but it cannot tell us where the ark landed. Several mountains and sites have been claimed, and no expedition has produced evidence of a boat. Jewish and Christian traditions also name other places, such as Mount Judi east of the Tigris.
2 Peter 2:5 and 3:6 recall the flood but do not name the mountains.
f: Lake Van region of eastern Turkey and Armenia; the fortress of Tushpa (Van)

e.n: Hairstyles of Roman women on portraits and coins
t: Portrait busts and coins of women in the families of Augustus and his successors show hair dressed in waves, curls, braids and pins, and in the later 1st century in high tiers of curls. The poet Ovid, about 1 BC, advises women in his Art of Love that there are far more styles than he could name and that each should choose the one that suits her face. Wealthy women employed a slave hairdresser.

1 Peter 3:3 tells wives that their beauty “should not come from outward adornment, such as braided hair or gold jewelry or fine clothes.” A similar warning is in 1 Timothy 2:9. Peter is not forbidding braids as such. He puts the real beauty in “the inner disposition of your heart” (3:4), a point that moralists of his day also made when they criticized display.

Caution: Most surviving portraits are of rich or imperial women, and the styles in the provinces of Asia Minor may have been simpler. Peter’s list is a contrast, not a rule against hairstyles or clothes.
f: Museums in Rome and elsewhere; written evidence in Ovid, Art of Love 3
Late 1st century BC to 1st century AD

t: Small marble statues of a young man carrying a sheep across his shoulders were made in the 3rd century for Christian tombs and houses, and the figure was painted in the catacombs and in the house church at Dura-Europos. The type had been used for centuries in Greek and Roman art for a man bringing an offering animal, and Christians took it over for Christ.

1 Peter calls Jesus “the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls” (2:25) and “the Chief Shepherd” (5:4), and asks the elders to “be shepherds of God’s flock” (5:2). Peter had heard Jesus’ words to him about feeding his sheep (John 21:15-17). Christians of the following centuries chose this picture for Christ more often than the cross.
Caution: The statues are one to two centuries later than the letter. The same pose was used in pagan art, so a statue without a Christian setting does not prove who made it.
f: Vatican and Lateran collections, Rome (from catacombs and houses)

e.n: Resident aliens (paroikoi) in the cities of Asia Minor
t: Greek inscriptions from the cities of Asia Minor use the word paroikos for people who lived in a city or on its land without being citizens. Citizens had a vote, a share in civic rites and, in some cities, a claim to public handouts; a resident alien could be taxed, could not hold office, and could usually not own land. Inscriptions from several cities list such people separately from the citizens.

1 Peter calls its readers “exiles” in 1:1 and “foreigners and exiles” in 2:11, using this word paroikos. Some scholars argue that many of the readers were literally resident aliens or newcomers on the edge of civic life, and that the letter tells them God has given them a place as his own people (2:9-10). Others think the words are only a picture of the church’s life in the world.

Caution: The inscriptions show how the word was used, not who the letter’s readers were. The letter’s own phrase “exiles of the Dispersion” (1:1) also echoes the Jewish scattering abroad, which suggests a picture in two senses at once.
f: Greek inscriptions from Ephesus, Sardis and other cities of Asia Minor

t: Josephus says priestly families kept careful written genealogies.
Stone benches in first-century synagogues show where Jews prayed and gathered.
Many excavated homes rest on bedrock or stone, the kind the wise builder chose.
Ancient terraces and presses show how central grapes and figs were to Galilee.
Ruins at Umm Qais include a theater, a colonnaded street and tombs.
Small bronze coins like the assarion are what Jesus says buys a sparrow.
Early synagogues have been found across Galilee, at places like Gamla and Magdala.
A boat found in the lake mud in 1986 shows how Jesus could teach from one.
Ruins at Al-Mina include Roman columns and a wide colonnaded road.
Excavations show Roman streets, columns and a huge hippodrome.
Roman-era ruins show a wealthy port city whose people came to hear Jesus.
Large stone jars, made to avoid impurity, are common in Jewish homes of this time.
Large stone jars, used for purity and wine, are common finds in Jewish homes.
At Banias, a cave and temple niches honor Pan beside a spring below Mount Hermon.
Banias digs show Roman-era baths and a temple Herod built for Augustus.
Herod’s temple platform still stands, with huge stones in the Western Wall.
The platform that Stephen discusses is still visible in Jerusalem.
Tyrian silver coins, like the one in the fish, are common finds in Jerusalem.
Ancient weights show how large sums were measured, a talent being about 75 pounds.
Surviving first-century papyri include marriage contracts and divorce certificates.
Silver denarii with Tiberius’ image have been found across Judea.
Excavated palaces show the wealth of the road’s last stop.
Palaces at Tulul Abu el-Alayiq show the wealth of Herod’s winter capital.
Excavated winter palaces near Jericho show how rich the town was.
Tyrian silver shekels, used for the temple tax, are common finds in Jerusalem.
Monumental tombs in the Kidron Valley, like Zechariah’s, honor Jerusalem’s dead.
Tiny leather cases with Scripture scrolls were found in the Judean desert.
Small clay lamps with a spout are common finds across Judea.
An ossuary inscribed with Caiaphas’ family name was found in Jerusalem.
A heel bone pierced by a nail was found in a Jerusalem tomb of this era.
A heel bone with an iron nail was found in a Jerusalem tomb of this era.
A crucified man’s heel bone, with a nail, was found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1968.
Round stones that rolled in a groove sealed some Jerusalem tombs.
Round stones in a groove sealed some Jerusalem tombs.
Rock-cut tombs of the time were sealed with rolling disk stones, as in the story.
A later white limestone synagogue stands over the first-century basalt one.
An early house church was built over a home in Capernaum.
Capernaum houses were small basalt homes around shared courtyards.
Customs stations stood along the lakeshore road near Capernaum.
Early synagogues at Gamla and Magdala show where such teaching happened.
The shoreline near Tabgha has ancient harbor structures.
A fifth-century church holds a mosaic of loaves and fish on the shore.
A church beside the lake honors the breakfast Jesus served.
Cave tombs cut into hillsides are common around the lake.
Rich men’s rock-cut tombs near Jerusalem show how wealth marked even burial.
A cave and spring below Hermon preserve niches for the god Pan.
Tiny bronze coins of this era are common finds in Jerusalem.
Built under Constantine, rebuilt in the 6th century.
Small perfume flasks like the woman’s are common finds from first-century sites.
Rock-cut pits and silos show how large landowners stored their grain.
Wealthy homes in Jerusalem had dining rooms built for reclining guests.
Silver drachmas like the lost coin were worth about a day’s wage.
Stone olive presses across Galilee show how important oil was for trade.
Stone presses are found at many excavated sites in Israel and Greece.
Stone presses found at sites around the Mediterranean show how olive oil was made. It was used for food, for light and for healing.
Ancient Jericho’s mound is among the oldest cities known, but Jesus’ Jericho lay nearby.
Herod’s winter palaces near Jericho have been excavated, with pools and gardens.
Herod’s builders cut enormous blocks, some weighing hundreds of tons.
Tiny bronze lepta have been found in Jerusalem, many no bigger than a fingernail.
Several places claim to be Emmaus, including Emmaus-Nicopolis and Abu Ghosh.
Stepped ritual baths are found across Jerusalem from this period.
Excavations on Gerizim uncovered a Samaritan temple platform.
Two large pools with colonnades were found near St. Anne’s Church.
Later Roman shrines to Asclepius stood nearby.
Broad stairs on the south side led pilgrims up to the temple.
Broad steps on the temple platform’s south side lead to the old Huldah Gates.
Wide stairs south of the Temple Mount lead to the entrances.
Chambers along the Court of Women held the offering chests.
The eastern wall of Herod’s platform stands near where Solomon’s Porch was.

The great Temple platform in Jerusalem was Herod’s work, and the Temple stood until the Romans burned it in AD 70, about twenty years after this letter. Whether “the temple of God” in 2:4 means that building, the church, or something else is debated.
Rock-cut folds and cisterns survive in the Judean hills.
A rock-cut tomb in al-Eizariya has been honored as Lazarus’ tomb since early times.
Alabaster flasks for costly perfume are found in Jerusalem tombs.
The ancient road down the Mount of Olives into the city still survives in part.
Stone and clay basins for foot washing are found in wealthy Jerusalem homes.
Houses in Jerusalem’s upper city had multiple rooms around a courtyard.
Rock-cut presses and vats appear in vineyards across Judea.
A golden vine decorated the temple entrance, a symbol of Israel.
Early synagogues at Masada and Herodium show how Jewish communities gathered.
Breastplate stones of twelve tribes are described in Exodus 28.
Excavations on Mount Zion reveal large first-century homes of the priestly aristocracy.
Rock-cut tombs with rolling stones are found around Jerusalem.
Rock-cut tombs cover the Mount of Olives, which was a Jewish cemetery.
Akeldama is traditionally placed in the Hinnom Valley south of the city.
Dozens of stepped ritual pools near the Temple suggest where crowds could be baptized.
Herod’s huge stone platform still stands, including the eastern wall.
A first-century bone box with the name Caiaphas was found in Jerusalem.
An ossuary inscribed “Yehosef bar Qafa” was found in 1990 in a tomb south of the Old City. Many scholars identify the man as Joseph Caiaphas, the high priest from AD 18 to 36.
An inscription naming Pilate was found at Caesarea in 1961.
The city had guard rooms near the Temple and the Antonia fortress.
A Greek stone in Jerusalem records a first-century synagogue built for visiting Jews.

A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem in 1913 records that a priest named Theodotus built a synagogue for the reading of the Law and the teaching of the commandments, with a guesthouse for visitors. Most scholars date it before AD 70.
Jerusalem tombs name families from Cyrene and Alexandria.
Excavations show the city where Abraham first built an altar in the land.
The southern road to Gaza was a main trade route to Egypt.
Tanning pits near the sea at Joppa have been uncovered.
Herod’s artificial harbor was one of the largest in the Mediterranean.
Roman villas in Antioch yielded splendid floor mosaics.
A long main street lined with columns ran through the city.
Bronze coins of Agrippa I show him as a friend of Rome and of the Jews.
Coins of Agrippa II show him with the title of king.
The Roman theater by the sea is where Herod likely gave the speech.
Villas and mosaics show the wealth of the Roman capital of Cyprus.
A Greek dedication to Zeus and Hermes was found near Lystra in 1909.
First-century letters open with the same Greek greeting used in verse 23.
The wealthy upper city where leaders met has yielded large stone houses.
The excavated forum and its steps show the colony’s Roman character.
The ruins of the Roman colony where Paul had been jailed.
The civic center of the colony, laid out on two terraces beside the Via Egnatia. Most of what stands was built after Paul’s time.
The raised platform in the forum is where officials judged cases.
A later seat inscription names a place for Jews and God-fearers.
Alexandria Troas was a Roman colony and a key crossing point for Paul.
A Greek stone warns that foreigners who enter will be killed.
Stairs from the Temple to the fortress allowed soldiers to rush down.
A stone-paved street from this era runs along the Temple’s western wall.
The Roman road at Tarsus led through the Cilician Gates.
The coastal road past Antipatris was a major Roman highway.
The palace on Caesarea’s shore later became the Roman governor’s residence.
A Roman chariot track on the shore is still visible.
Bronze coins dated to the governor’s term circulated in Judea.
The audience hall of Herod’s palace could hold a royal court.
Herod’s palace on the sea included large halls and pools.
The Roman port of Andriake has a large granary from the empire.
Later house churches in Rome left inscriptions, though none from Paul’s day survive in place.
Greek inscriptions from Jewish catacombs in Rome show a large Greek-speaking Jewish community.
Scrolls like those found at Qumran show how a Jew “rested in the law” by studying it.
Excavated cities where Abraham’s family lived, now in Iraq and Turkey.
The oaks where Abraham camped near Hebron, the place of the promises, are a pilgrimage site today.
The Ara Pacis, a huge altar to Augustan peace in Rome, shows the claim Paul’s readers lived under.
