Arches celebrated military victories. Paul describes a different kind of victory.
Stone tablets with the commandments are described in Exodus 20 and later copied on synagogue walls.
Excavated workshops in Jerusalem and Corinth show the scale of the trade.
Egyptian records of Pharaohs show the setting for the exodus story Paul quotes.
Greek inscriptions called Augustus “savior” and “lord,” showing the claim Paul’s words challenged.
Olive trees in Gethsemane and elsewhere in Israel are very old, a picture of a living root.
Roman inns were rough, which is why Christians welcomed travelers in homes.
Inscriptions in Asia list the Roman customs duties collected on goods.
Coins and statues of the emperor were everywhere, a constant reminder of who ruled.
Roman meat markets such as the one at Pompeii show where meat was sold and where questions arose.
Corinth’s meat market stood in the forum, with shops for butchers and fishmongers.
Pig bones are absent from Jewish towns in the land of Israel, showing a distinct diet.
The main Roman road in Spain, from the Pyrenees to Cádiz, which Paul would have used.
A paving stone at Corinth reads that “Erastus laid this pavement at his own expense” as aedile (a city official). This may be the same man.
Excavations at Cenchreae, the port Phoebe came from, have uncovered warehouses and sea walls.
The speakers’ platform in the Corinth forum, where Paul probably stood before Gallio (Acts 18:12).
Quarried stone was used on public buildings in Corinth’s forum.
Large foundation blocks survive on the hill above Corinth.
A large theater and an arena in Corinth show the entertainment world Paul alludes to.
Storage buildings near the harbor remind us how important Corinth’s trade was.
Ancient writers described Corinth as a city of loose morals, and “to act like a Corinthian” was slang for immorality.
Excavated law courts in the forum were the sort of place these lawsuits would be heard.
Papyri record sales of slaves and the price paid, behind Paul’s “bought with a price.”
Papyri of marriage agreements show the economic side of Roman marriage.
Stones often honor a spouse after decades of marriage.
Corinth’s healing sanctuary had dining rooms for worshipers, an example of what Paul describes.
The excavated Isthmian stadium and the starting line of the track survive.
A paved track across the isthmus where ships were hauled between the seas.
Rooms with couches and tables have been excavated at the Asklepieion in Corinth.
Excavated villas show the divide between dining room and courtyard.
The Callixtus catacombs include early meal pictures.
Votive feet, hands, and eyes found at Corinth’s Asklepieion show how people prayed for healing.
Greek dedications show religious devotion in the city.
Contains bronze and pottery from the Roman city.
The temple of Apollo at Delphi, with its famous oracle.
A small covered theater in Corinth shows a space used for performances.
First-century Jerusalem tombs had rolling-stone doors, like the one described in the Gospels.
A grand building in Ephesus from a few decades after Paul, showing the city’s importance.
The great theater in Ephesus, where the riot of Acts 19 took place, still seats thousands.
Clay seal impressions have been found in many archives.
The port of Troas, with city walls and a bath complex, lies on Turkey’s northwest coast.
Stone tablets from antiquity illustrate what “written on stone” meant.
A stone from Corinth bears the inscription “Synagogue of the Hebrews,” perhaps from a later period.
Large cylindrical jars from Qumran, in which scrolls were stored.
Locally made oil jars and lamps are common finds in Corinth.
The platform in Corinth’s forum, where Paul faced Gallio.
Goat-hair tents are still used by Bedouin today.
Wooden yokes and plowing scenes appear on Greek pottery.
A healing temple with banquet rooms.
Corinth minted its own bronze coinage, some of which was in circulation in Paul’s day.
Greek inscriptions mention grain shortages in the East during Claudius’s reign.
Excavated granaries in Corinth show how seed was stored.
Sowing scenes appear in Greek and Roman art.
The Roman siege ramp at Masada is a famous example of ancient siege works.
Houses built into the city wall, like those in Bab Kisan, are shown as the traditional escape site.
The old city wall still shows Roman and later work.
The fasces were the symbol of Roman magistrates.
Apocalyptic texts such as 2 Enoch describe a series of heavens.
Regions where Paul spent years before his missionary journeys.
Metal was assayed in fire to prove its purity.
The eastern harbor of Corinth, where Paul sailed from.
The Nabatean kingdom around Petra and Bosra may have been where Paul went.
Little remains of the ancient city, but mosaics survive.
A cave church traditionally tied to the first Christians of Antioch.
Greek vase paintings and carvings show adult attendants walking with boys who carry writing tablets.
Crucifixion remains are rare. A heel bone with a nail was found in Jerusalem.
Paul links Hagar with Sinai in Arabia.
Two inscriptions found near Lystra in 1909 name priests of Zeus and a statue of Hermes. They are often set beside Acts 14:12, where the crowd called Barnabas Zeus and Paul Hermes.
Surviving papyrus letters show how a scribe wrote and the sender signed.
The huge stones around the Temple Mount are Herod’s work.
Acts 19 says converts burned magic scrolls. Ephesian letters, amulets, and papyri show magical practice.
Paul lived in a rented house under guard.
Marketplace ruins show the daily life of the city.
Early Christian baptisteries have been found around the Mediterranean.
Houses in Pompeii show where the family lived and met.
Latin and Greek tombstones record married couples’ affection.
Helmets, swords, and breastplates survive from many Roman camps.

Paul pictures faith and love as a breastplate and the hope of salvation as a helmet (5:8). Segmented plate armor came into use in his time, and a Roman cavalry helmet of the 1st century AD was found at Hallaton in England. Isaiah 59:17 has the same picture of God as a warrior.
The Roman legionary shield (scutum) was a large curved oblong, roughly three and a half to four feet tall.
A vaulted chamber at Philippi is traditionally shown as Paul’s prison. The tradition is later than Paul, and Acts 16 does not say where the jail stood.
The theater goes back to the Macedonian city and was reworked in Roman times. It sits below the acropolis.
Paul’s party likely traveled the Via Egnatia, which runs through Philippi and on toward Thessalonica (Acts 16:12; 17:1).
Acts 16:13 says a prayer meeting met by a river outside the gate. The Gangites is the traditional candidate, and the exact spot is uncertain.
The main mound of Colossae, near modern Honaz, is mostly unexcavated. Reports say a survey began in 2021 and excavation in 2025; check recent news for finds.
Laodicea, about 9 miles (15 km) from Colossae, has colonnaded streets, a stadium, theaters, baths and fountains. Most of what stands was built after Paul’s time.
Hierapolis (modern Pamukkale) stands above hot, mineral-rich springs that have built white terraces of travertine. Paul says Epaphras worked for the believers here (4:13).

Strabo describes a cave at Hierapolis, the Plutonium, that gave off deadly fumes (13.4.14). Excavators have identified it beside the Temple of Apollo. The temple that stands is from the 3rd century AD.
Tomb inscriptions from Hierapolis, mostly of the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD, name guilds of dyers and weavers. They show how large the cloth trade of the valley was.
Wealthy homes in the cities of Asia had courtyards, mosaics and wall paintings. The Terrace Houses at Ephesus, far to the west, are the best-excavated example.
Laodicea had no good spring of its own and brought its water in by pipe. Pipes found there carry heavy lime scale, a sign of the mineral-rich water of the valley.
This is often given as the background of Revelation 3:15-16, where the church is neither cold nor hot but lukewarm.
No papyrus letter from Colossae is known. Papyri from Egypt show the usual shape: sender, greeting, thanks, body, closing greetings, and a last line in the writer’s own hand, as in 4:18.
The Arch of Galerius was built about AD 300, some 250 years after Paul. It stands over the main east-west street of the city, on the line of the Via Egnatia.

An inscription from the Vardar Gate of Thessalonica, now in the British Museum, lists six politarchs. It dates to the 2nd century AD, after Paul, but the city had politarchs earlier, and the title Luke uses in Acts 17:6, 8 is the one found in Macedonian inscriptions.

Roman shops were small rooms opening onto the street. Rows of them survive at Corinth, where Paul worked as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3). Little of the first-century street level of Thessalonica has been excavated, because the modern city covers it.
Excavated shops, such as the west shops at Corinth, were small rooms opening onto a colonnade. Paul’s example of hard manual work (3:8) belongs in this setting.

The Agora lay below the Acropolis and was the marketplace and civic center. Acts 17:17 says Paul reasoned there every day. The Stoa of Attalos on its east side was rebuilt in the 1950s and is now a museum.
Many Latin tombstones carry a short formula, often written only by its initials: “I was not, I was, I am not, I do not care.” Not every Roman held this view, but it shows how some spoke of death.

Christian burial inscriptions in Rome, mostly from the 3rd century on, often say “in peace” (in pace) and speak of the dead as sleeping. They are later than Paul but use the language of 1 Thessalonians 4.

e.n: Peace in Stone: the Ara Pacis
t: The Ara Pacis Augustae, the Altar of Augustan Peace, was dedicated in Rome in 9 BC. Its carvings of a peaceful, fruitful empire are some of the best surviving examples of Roman peace imagery.

Thessalonica lay at the head of the Thermaic Gulf and had a harbor as well as the Via Egnatia, which made it a major trading city. Remains of the Roman harbor lie under the modern city, near Frangon Street.

Many Greek and Latin inscriptions survive from Thessalonica, among them decrees, tomb inscriptions and the lists of politarchs. They show a city with civic offices, associations and many cults. Many date after Paul.

Coins of Antiochus IV (175-164 BC) call him Theos Epiphanes, “God Manifest.” In 167 BC he set up an altar to Zeus in the Temple, the abomination that makes desolate in Daniel 11:31. Paul’s wording in 2:4 resembles Daniel 11:36-37.

Inscriptions from Thessalonica come from private associations that met for meals and worship, including cult groups of Dionysus and Sarapis. Associations in other cities were often formed by members of one trade.

A marble-paved colonnaded street ran from the theater to the harbor and was the main approach to the city from the sea. Today it is often called the Arcadian Way, after the emperor Arcadius (AD 395-408), who rebuilt it. Most of what stands is later than Paul, but the street itself is older.

Statues of Artemis of Ephesus show her with rows of rounded shapes on her chest. Ancient and modern writers disagree about what they are: breasts, eggs or other ornaments. Her cult dominated the city (Acts 19:27-28). Some scholars suggest it shaped the problems behind 2:9-15, but the letter never mentions her, so this stays a suggestion.

Paul says “physical training is of some value” (4:8). Ephesus had a stadium and large bath-gymnasium complexes where men exercised. The surviving buildings are mostly Roman and many are later than Paul, but they show how central athletics were to the life of a Greek city.

Greek and Latin epitaphs praise women who stayed with one husband. The Latin word is univira, “a one-man woman.” The phrase in 5:9, “the wife of one husband,” sounds like this kind of praise, though many surviving examples are later than Paul and from Rome.

City inscriptions in Asia Minor honor wealthy donors for gifts of money, grain, oil and public feasts. Scholars note that such gifts usually went to the city or its citizens as a whole, not to the poor as a class, which makes the church’s care for its widows (5:3-16) stand out. This is a general picture, not a record from Ephesus.

Coins of Ephesus often show Artemis, her temple or her symbols, such as the stag and the bee. Under Rome the city took pride in being the temple-warden (neokoros) of Artemis, and later of the emperors.

The Carcer Tullianum, now called the Mamertine Prison, stands at the foot of the Capitoline Hill in Rome. Later tradition, not the New Testament, says Peter and Paul were held there. Second Timothy does not name Paul’s prison, and it speaks of his chains (1:16; 2:9).

Bronze military diplomas were small folded bronze tablets given to soldiers of auxiliary units and fleets on discharge, recording a grant of Roman citizenship. The earliest known date from the reign of Claudius, and most surviving ones are from the 2nd century AD, later than Paul.

Prizes at the Greek games varied: olive at Olympia, laurel at Delphi, pine at Isthmia and celery at Nemea, and at the Panathenaic Games a jar of olive oil. Paul’s picture of the athlete who receives the crown (2:5) uses a word from the same family as the crown of righteousness in 4:8.

The New Testament does not describe Paul’s death. Church tradition says he was executed in Rome under Nero and buried on the road to Ostia, and the place usually named for his execution is Tre Fontane. Gaius, a Roman churchman about AD 200, says the trophies (victory monuments) of Peter and Paul were at the Vatican and on the road to Ostia (Eusebius, Church History 2.25).

The basilica stands beside the road to Ostia and, by tradition, over Paul’s tomb. The first church was built in the 4th century, and much of the present building was rebuilt after a fire in 1823. In 2009 Pope Benedict XVI announced that bone fragments from the sarcophagus under the altar had been dated to the 1st or 2nd century. That does not prove whose they are.

Gortyn was the capital of the Roman province of Crete and Cyrenaica, and its ruins include the governor’s residence, a theater, an Odeion and the large church of Saint Titus, built in the 6th century. Tradition, not the New Testament, ties Titus to Gortyn. Titus 1:5 names no town.

The Law Code of Gortyn is a long Greek inscription of the early 5th century BC, about 500 years before Titus. Its rules cover marriage, divorce, property, inheritance and slaves. The Roman Odeion at Gortyn was built around it. It shows how Cretans ordered family life long before Paul, but Titus does not refer to it.

Roman houses with mosaics and painted walls have been dug at Knossos and Gortyn. Most of what survives is from the 2nd century AD or later, after Paul. They show what a well-off household on the island looked like, but the letter does not describe any house.

Long stretches of the city wall, a theater, an Odeion, an aqueduct and a stadium survive at Nicopolis near Preveza. Most of the city dates from its founding by Augustus, and the walls seen today are largely late Roman and Byzantine.

On the hill north of the city lies the base of Octavian’s victory monument for Actium. Its terrace wall has cuttings where the bronze rams of captured warships were fixed. Augustus built it to mark the victory over Antony and Cleopatra in 31 BC.

The ruins of Colossae lie beside the modern town of Honaz in southwestern Turkey. The Roman town is mostly unexcavated. It has a large mound and a theater that is almost completely buried. A Turkish university team began a survey in 2021 and started excavation in 2025. Few houses of the Roman town are known, so Philemon’s house has not been identified.

e.n: Angels in the Dead Sea Scrolls
t: The Songs of the Sabbath Sacrifice, found at Qumran and copied in the 1st centuries BC and AD, describe angelic priests serving in a heavenly sanctuary. Hebrews shares the interest in angels and a heavenly sanctuary, but argues that the Son is above them all.

Hebrews usually quotes the Greek Old Testament. That text survives in great Greek Bibles of the 4th century such as Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus and in older papyri. Codex Vaticanus is also one of the oldest copies of Hebrews itself.
Papyrus 13 is a roll from Oxyrhynchus in Egypt, from the 3rd or early 4th century. Hebrews is written on the back of a roll that held a summary of Livy. One fragment contains Hebrews 4:2-12.
A fragment of Papyrus 13 contains Hebrews 10:8-22. The papyrus is 3rd or early 4th century and was found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt.
Roman short swords such as the Mainz type have been found at military sites across the empire.

Excavations in Jerusalem’s Upper City uncovered large, richly decorated houses from the time of Herod, some probably owned by priestly families. A stone weight in the Burnt House is inscribed “of bar Kathros,” the name of a priestly family known from the Talmud.
Christians in Rome drew anchors on tombs and in the catacombs. The anchor is often taken as a sign of hope, and in some drawings its shape also suggests a cross.
Stone and metal anchors survive from ancient harbors and wrecks, including a limestone anchor from Paphos on Cyprus.
The ridge south of the Temple Mount where ancient Jerusalem began. Many identify Salem, Melchizedek’s city, with Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2).
Full-scale models, such as the one at Timna Park in Israel, show the layout of the desert tent from the description in Exodus. No remains of the tabernacle itself have been found.

e.n: The Day of Atonement in the Mishnah
t: The Mishnah tractate Yoma, written down about AD 200, describes how the Day of Atonement was kept in the Second Temple. It records memories of rituals that Hebrews knew only from Scripture and from tradition.
Believers who were “publicly exposed” (10:33) may have been mocked in a theater or arena. Roman crowds loved gladiator games, and a cemetery of gladiators has been found at Ephesus.

Tell es-Sultan, the mound of ancient Jericho, was excavated by John Garstang in the 1930s and Kathleen Kenyon in the 1950s. It holds one of the oldest known towns, with a stone tower from about 8000 BC.

Stadiums have survived at Olympia, Delphi, Ephesus and other cities of the Greek world. Their long, narrow tracks with stone seats on the slopes are the setting the writer’s picture of the race would have called to mind.

Today the name Mount Zion is given to the hill southwest of the Old City, where the Dormition Abbey stands. In the Bible Zion usually means the Temple hill or the city of David. In Hebrews 12:22 it means the heavenly city, not a place to visit.
Roadside inns at places such as Pompeii and Ostia had small rooms, shared dining areas and a rough reputation. This explains why believers were urged to take travelers into their homes.

The Church of the Holy Sepulchre stands on the place that Christian tradition since the 4th century has marked as Golgotha and the tomb. In the time of Jesus this ground lay outside the city wall, which fits Hebrews 13:12.

Papyrus 23 is a leaf from a codex found at Oxyrhynchus in Egypt and dated to the 3rd century. It has James 1:10-12 on one side and 1:15-18 on the other. It shows that James was being copied in Egypt by the 200s.
Papyrus 20, from the 3rd century and now in Princeton University Library, has James 2:19-3:9. It includes the closing words of the argument about faith and works in 2:26.
The back of the Princeton leaf of Papyrus 20 has James 3:3-9, the passage about the bit, the rudder and the tongue that no one can tame.

Bronze and iron horse bits survive from many ancient sites, including a Greek bit of the 4th or 3rd century BC in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. A steering oar from a 1st-century Roman river boat, found in Germany, is in Cologne. Seagoing ships were steered by oars of this kind at the stern.
Wrecks and cargoes on the Mediterranean seabed show how much trade moved by sea in Roman times. A fresco of the merchant ship Isis Giminiana, about AD 200-250, is in the Vatican Museums.
The synagogue at Ostia, the port of Rome, shows that Jewish communities lived in the trading cities of the Mediterranean. James names no city, but his readers lived in settings like these.

A pottery fragment of the 7th century BC from a Judean fort on the coast records a reaper’s complaint that an official took his garment. It is much older than James, but it shows a harvest worker appealing for justice.
Excavations at Sardis found a large gold refining workshop.
The dramatic rock landscape of central Turkey.
Herod’s masonry, with huge cut stones.
Dedicatory stones in Roman cities.
Marble busts show elaborate hairstyles.
Early Christian pools.
Triclinia in excavated villas.
Tradition places Peter’s martyrdom and tomb near the Vatican.
The site of Nero’s games where Christians were killed.

In 1967 a Dutch expedition at Tell Deir ‘Alla, in the Jordan valley east of the river, found fragments of a plaster wall covered with writing in black and red ink. The text is in a language close to Hebrew and Aramaic. It begins as the book of Balaam son of Beor, a seer of the gods. In the story the gods come to him in the night and announce a coming disaster, and Balaam weeps and tells the people what he has seen.

2 Peter 2:15 says the false teachers follow “the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the wages of wickedness.” Numbers 22-24 tells of Balaam, a foreign seer hired to curse Israel, and the donkey that spoke. The wall text shows that a seer called Balaam son of Beor was remembered in the Jordan valley about 800 BC, long before the New Testament, as a man who saw visions and spoke for the gods. His name is the same as the one in Numbers.

Caution: The inscription does not mention Israel, the donkey, or Moab’s king, and Balaam is a seer of the gods in it, not a prophet of the LORD. Scholars agree that the name is the same but disagree on how the two traditions are related. The text is broken, and many of its readings are debated. The date rests on the writing and on the layer where it was found.
Jude 11 says the intruders “have rushed headlong into the error of Balaam.”
f: Tell Deir ‘Alla, Jordan Valley, Jordan (now in the Jordan Archaeological Museum, Amman)

e.n: Bab edh-Dhra and the towns of the Dead Sea plain
t: A walled town of the Early Bronze Age beside a very large cemetery with many thousands of tombs, among them shaft tombs and buildings for bones. Excavations from 1965 to 1979, first under Paul Lapp and then under Walter Rast and Thomas Schaub, found that the town was abandoned about 2350 BC, and at some sites in the plain nearby (Numeira, for example) there is burnt debris. Four other sites lie along streams to the south, which has led some to count five towns on the plain.

2 Peter 2:6 says God condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah, “reducing them to ashes as an example of what is coming on the ungodly.” Genesis 13-19 places Sodom and Gomorrah in the plain of the Jordan at the Dead Sea, and Genesis 14:3 puts them in the valley of Siddim, by the Salt Sea. Bab edh-Dhra is one of the candidates for Sodom, and Numeira for Gomorrah.

Caution: No inscription names Sodom here, and the identification is a proposal. The Early Bronze date is earlier than most dates given for Abraham and Lot, which fall in the Middle Bronze Age, and the cause of the end of the towns is not certain. Another proposal puts Sodom at Tall el-Hammam, northeast of the Dead Sea, and that too is disputed. The Bible does not say where the cities were.
Jude 7 uses the same example: Sodom and Gomorrah and the cities around them “are on display as an example.”
f: East of the Dead Sea, Jordan, near the Wadi Kerak

e.n: Early doubts about 2 Peter: Origen, Eusebius and Jerome
t: Three early writers say that some Christians doubted that Peter wrote 2 Peter. Origen, in the first half of the 3rd century, says that Peter left one letter that is acknowledged, and perhaps a second, “for it is doubted” (quoted by Eusebius, Church History 6.25.8). Eusebius, about AD 325, says he has been taught that the second letter is not part of the New Testament, yet it has seemed useful to many and has been studied with the other Scriptures (3.3.1); he lists it among the disputed books (3.25.3). Jerome, in 392, says that many deny the second letter is Peter’s because its style is unlike the first (On Illustrious Men 1). Athanasius lists it among the books of the New Testament in his Easter letter of AD 367.

2 Peter 1:1 calls the writer “Simon Peter, a servant and apostle of Jesus Christ.” These writers show that the question of authorship is old, and that doubts about the letter did not keep it out of the New Testament for good. The doubts are the same ones that modern scholars raise: how unlike 1 Peter it is in Greek, its use of Jude, and how late it first appears in the writings of the church.

Caution: These are reports of what other people thought, not evidence about who wrote the letter. Origen and Jerome were themselves ready to accept it; Jerome says some think the style difference came from another secretary. The letter’s earliest known copy is Papyrus 72, of the 3rd or 4th century.
f: Caesarea in Palestine (Origen and Eusebius) and Bethlehem (Jerome)
3rd to 4th century AD; the letter accepted by about AD 367

t: A single leaf of papyrus found at Oxyrhynchus, a town in Egypt whose rubbish heaps gave up many thousands of papyri, published as Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 402. It carries parts of 1 John 4:11-12 and 4:14-17, and is catalogued as Papyrus 9. The writing is a plain hand of the 3rd century.

It is one of the oldest surviving pieces of 1 John, and it holds the verses about God’s love sent in His Son and the perfected love that drives out fear. It shows that the letter was being copied and read in Egypt, far from Asia Minor, within about a century or two of when it is usually dated.
Caution: A single leaf holds only a few verses, so it cannot show how the whole letter looked or settle disputed wording. The date comes from the handwriting and is given to within a century or so.

e.n: The Basilica of St. John at Ephesus and the memory of John
t: On the hill above Ephesus stand the ruins of a large church, built in the 6th century under the emperor Justinian over a smaller earlier church. Local Christians honored the spot as the grave of John. Excavations in the 20th century found a tomb under the central part of the church.

The letter does not name its writer or its place, but a line of early writers says that John lived in Ephesus in his last years. Irenaeus, who grew up in Asia, says John stayed in Ephesus until the time of Trajan (Against Heresies 2.22.5; 3.3.4). Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus about AD 190, wrote that John, who had leaned on the Lord’s breast at the supper, lies buried there (in Eusebius, Church History 3.31.3).

Caution: The building is more than four centuries after John, and no inscription in the tomb names him. Some scholars think the Ephesian John may have been John the Elder, a separate person mentioned by Papias (Eusebius, Church History 3.39.4), and not the apostle; others hold that the tradition rests on the apostle. The pin on the map follows the tradition and is a judgment call.

For 2 John: Jerome (On Illustrious Men 9) says that some ascribe 2 and 3 John to John the presbyter, and that a second tomb of John was shown at Ephesus in his time, though some took them for two memorials of one man.
For 3 John: like 2 John, it comes from “the elder,” whom tradition places at Ephesus.
f: Church of the 4th century; large basilica built under Justinian, 6th century AD

e.n: The Muratorian Fragment and the letters of John
t: A damaged Latin list of books received in the church, found in a Milan library and published by Ludovico Muratori in 1740. It names the four Gospels, Acts and the letters of Paul, and says of John’s Gospel that when his fellow disciples urged him to write, he asked for a fast. It then quotes the opening of 1 John: what we have seen with our eyes and heard with our ears and handled with our hands.

The list is early evidence that the first letter of John was read as the apostle’s, and as a letter that goes with his Gospel. Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria and Tertullian also quote 1 John by name.

Caution: The Fragment is missing its beginning and its end, and the date and place are debated. It names “two” letters of John, which is usually taken to be 1 and 2 John, or 1 John and a letter that counted 2 and 3 as one.
For 2 John: the Fragment says that two letters with John’s name are accepted in the church. Whether it means 2 and 3 John (since it has already quoted 1 John) or counts 1 John among them is debated.
For 3 John: if the Fragment’s two letters are 1 and 2 John, it does not know 3 John at all; if they are 2 and 3 John, it is the earliest list to include it. The wording does not settle the matter.
f: Written about AD 170-200 by most scholars; some argue for the 4th century

e.n: Papyrus 52: the earliest scrap of the Gospel of John
t: A fragment about the size of a credit card, with parts of John 18:31-33 on one side and 18:37-38 on the other. It was bought in Egypt in 1920 and identified in 1934. It is a piece of a codex, a book with pages, not a roll.

The letter of 1 John reads as written by someone who knows the Gospel of John and its words, and the Gospel may have been written first. This fragment shows that the Gospel was read in Egypt, a long way from Asia Minor, by roughly the first half of the 2nd century, which fits a late 1st-century writing in Asia.

Caution: It carries only a few verses of the Gospel and nothing from the letters. The dating rests on the handwriting and is given as a range; some scholars would put it later in the 2nd century. It does not show the order in which the Gospel and the letter were written.
f: John Rylands Library, Manchester, England (found in Egypt)

e.n: The Community Rule from Qumran: sons of light and spirits of truth
t: The Community Rule (1QS) is a scroll of rules for the community at Qumran. One section (3:13-4:26) describes two spirits that God put in humankind, the spirit of truth and the spirit of falsehood, and divides people into “sons of light” and “sons of darkness.” It says that those who walk in the ways of light do so by the spirit of truth, and that the angel of darkness leads others astray.

1 John 4:6 speaks of “the Spirit of truth and the spirit of deception,” and 1:5-7 pairs light with darkness and “walking” with truth. The Rule shows these pairs were already at home in Jewish thought a century or more before the letter. The Gospel of John uses the same vocabulary of light, darkness and truth.

Caution: The writer of 1 John never mentions the Qumran community, and the two writings differ a great deal: the Rule describes a closed group and a strict code, while 1 John speaks of love for the brother and the confession of Jesus Christ. Scholars debate whether the parallels come from direct contact or from a shared Jewish background.
f: Cave 1 at Qumran, northwest shore of the Dead Sea (now in the Shrine of the Book, Jerusalem)
Copied about 100-50 BC; the teaching is older

e.n: Cerinthus and the departed teachers: what the early church said
t: Irenaeus (about AD 180) says that Cerinthus, a teacher in Asia, held that Jesus was the son of Joseph and Mary, that “the Christ” came down on him at his baptism and left him before the cross, so that Jesus suffered and rose again while the Christ stayed impassible (Against Heresies 1.26.1). He also tells of Polycarp's report that John once left a bathhouse at Ephesus on seeing Cerinthus inside (3.3.4). Ignatius, about AD 110, writes to the churches of Asia against those who said Christ only seemed to suffer (Smyrnaeans 2-7; Trallians 10).

1 John 2:18-23 says that “many antichrists” have gone out from the community and deny that Jesus is the Christ, and 4:2-3 and 5:6 say that Jesus Christ has “come in the flesh” and “by water and blood.” Some readers see Cerinthus’s teaching in those verses, others see an early form of docetism, the view that Christ only seemed to have a body.

Caution: The letter does not name the teachers or say what they taught, and Irenaeus wrote about a century after the letter. The bathhouse story reaches us third hand, and some scholars think it is a later tale. How closely the opponents of 1 John match Cerinthus is debated.
f: Ephesus (reports by Irenaeus of Lyon and others)
Reports of the 2nd century AD about teachers of the late 1st century

e.n: The imperial temple of Ephesus (the Temple of the Sebastoi)
t: At the north side of the upper market stand the remains of a large temple, begun under the emperor Domitian and dedicated to the Sebastoi, the imperial family. Its platform and part of a colossal statue were found; the head and arm of the statue are in the Ephesus museum. After Domitian’s death in AD 96 the Roman senate condemned his memory, and the temple was rededicated to his father, Vespasian.

It made Ephesus a “temple warden” (neokoros) of the emperors in addition to its temple of Artemis. A writer in Ephesus in the 90s would have lived among the shrines of Artemis, of the emperors and of other gods, which gives a setting for the closing words of 1 John, “keep yourselves from idols.”

Caution: The letter does not mention the emperor or the temple, and the date of the letter is debated, so the link is background and not an argument. The building is a ruin, and the statue fragments are much larger than life.

e.n: Polycarp and Ignatius: early echoes of 1 John
t: Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, writes to the church at Philippi that anyone who does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is an antichrist (Philippians 7:1). That is close to 1 John 4:2-3 and 2 John 7. Ignatius of Antioch, on his way to Rome, writes to the churches of Asia that Christ truly suffered and was truly raised, and that his opponents say it was only in appearance (Smyrnaeans 2; 4-5).

Polycarp’s sentence is the earliest known use of the idea in the letters of John, and Papias, a bishop of Hierapolis, is said by Eusebius to have used 1 John (Church History 3.39.17). These writers show the letter in the circle of the churches of Asia within a generation or two of its writing, and they show that the “flesh” of Christ was still the question.

Caution: Polycarp does not name 1 John in the sentence, and scholars debate whether he quotes the letter or the same teaching that stood behind it. The earliest manuscripts of his letter are from the Middle Ages.

For 3 John: the letters of Ignatius (about AD 110) show one bishop leading each church of Asia, and some scholars see in Diotrephes, “who loves to be first” (3 John 9), an early step toward that kind of single leader. The letter itself only says that he pushed himself forward.
f: Smyrna (Izmir) and Antioch; letters written about AD 110-135

t: A short early church manual, “The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles,” known from a manuscript of AD 1056 found in Constantinople and published in 1883, and from older fragments. Chapters 11 to 13 give rules for visiting apostles and prophets: they may stay one day or two, they must not ask for money, and a prophet who teaches the truth but does not live it is false.

1 John 4:1 tells believers to “test the spirits” because “many false prophets have gone out into the world,” and the Second and Third Letters speak of traveling teachers (2 John 10; 3 John 5-8). The Didache shows how a church of the time handled visiting teachers, with tests of doctrine and of conduct that match the two tests John gives.
Caution: The Didache is not the Bible and its date, place and relation to the New Testament are debated. It does not mention 1 John.
2 John 10-11 and the Didache agree that hospitality has limits set by the teaching a visitor brings, and 2 John is the sharper of the two.
For 3 John: verses 5-8 show the other side of the same custom. Gaius is praised for taking in traveling brothers who were strangers to him and is asked to send them on with what they need.
f: Written in Syria or Palestine; the main manuscript was found in Constantinople

e.n: The added words in 1 John 5:7-8 (the Comma Johanneum)
t: Some older English Bibles read in 1 John 5:7-8, “For there are three that bear record in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Holy Ghost: and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness in earth...” The extra words about heaven are missing in the early Greek manuscripts, among them Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, and in nearly all Greek copies. They appear in some Latin manuscripts and in a few late Greek ones.

The BSB, like most modern versions, reads only “the Spirit, the water, and the blood,” as in 5:6-8. Erasmus left the extra words out of his first two Greek editions (1516, 1519) and put them into his third (1522) after a Greek copy that contained them was shown to him; the King James Version followed that text.

Caution: The doctrine of the Trinity does not depend on these words, and it is taught in many other passages. The added words are sometimes called the Comma Johanneum. Where and when they entered the Latin text is still debated.
f: Latin manuscripts of the West, and a few late Greek copies
Absent from the early Greek manuscripts; in some Latin copies from the early Middle Ages

e.n: Early Christian care for the needy: Aristides, Lucian and Tertullian
t: Aristides of Athens, in an Apology to the emperor of about AD 125-140, says that Christians love one another, do not turn away from the widow and rescue the orphan, and that a man with something gives to the one who has nothing. Lucian of Samosata, about AD 165, mocks the Christians in his Passing of Peregrinus because they hurry to help a brother in prison and treat one another as brothers, and Tertullian (Apology 39, about AD 197) describes a common fund for the poor.

1 John 3:17-18 asks: “If anyone with earthly possessions sees his brother in need, but withholds his compassion from him, how can the love of God abide in him?” These writers, one a friend of the faith and one an outsider, show that the practice of caring for a fellow believer in need was a mark of the churches within the century after the letter.
Caution: These are later writings by outsiders and defenders, not records of John’s own churches, and they describe the church at large. Lucian wrote to mock, and his picture is a satire.
f: Athens, Syria and Carthage (writers of the 2nd and 3rd centuries)

t: Irenaeus, bishop of Lyon, grew up in Asia Minor and as a boy heard Polycarp speak. In his book Against Heresies he quotes 2 John at least twice and ascribes it to John, the Lord’s disciple: verses 10-11, about not even greeting a false teacher (1.16.3), and verses 7-8, about deceivers who deny that Christ came in the flesh (3.16.8). The work survives mainly in an old Latin translation, with parts of the Greek kept by later writers.
He is the earliest writer known to quote 2 John and to name John as its writer, and he knew it as John’s letter in Gaul in the late 2nd century. That sets the letter well before AD 180.

Caution: Irenaeus does not number the letters, and in 3.16.8 he quotes 1 John and 2 John in one run, so some scholars ask whether he knew them as a pair or as one letter. The Latin translation cannot always be checked against his Greek.
For 3 John: Irenaeus never quotes it. A private note about hospitality gave teachers little to quote, which may be why it is not heard of until Origen.
f: Lyon, France (writing in Greek; preserved mostly in an old Latin translation)

e.n: Eusebius and Origen on the disputed letters of John
t: Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, sorted the books of his day in Church History 3.25. He put 1 John among the books accepted everywhere and 2 and 3 John among the disputed ones, asking whether they came from the evangelist or from another John. He also reports (Church History 6.25.10) that Origen said John left one letter of a very few lines and perhaps a second and a third, since not everyone held these two to be genuine, and that the two together do not run to a hundred lines.

It shows that 2 John was known and read in the 3rd and 4th centuries but was not yet on every church’s list, and that the doubt was about who wrote it and how widely it was known, not about its teaching. Athanasius’s Easter letter of AD 367 names all seven General Letters, and the African councils of the late 4th century list three letters of John.

Caution: “Disputed” does not mean rejected: Eusebius still counts these letters among the books the church knew. His own guess about the two Johns is a view, not a fact, and he gives it with a purpose of his own about Revelation.
For 3 John: Origen’s remark, from the first half of the 3rd century, is the earliest clear mention of the letter that survives. No earlier writer is known to quote it.
Eusebius lists Jude with James, 2 Peter and 2 and 3 John among the disputed books that most people still knew.
f: Church History finished about AD 325; Origen’s remark from about AD 230-250

e.n: Papias of Hierapolis and “John the Elder”
t: Papias, bishop of Hierapolis, wrote five books on the Lord’s sayings that are lost except for quotations. In a passage Eusebius quotes (Church History 3.39.3-4), Papias says that he asked travelers what Andrew, Peter, Philip, Thomas, James, John and Matthew had said, and also what Aristion and the elder John were saying. Eusebius thought this might point to two men named John.

Since 2 John and 3 John begin with “the elder,” some scholars think this elder John wrote them and that he was a separate person from the apostle. Jerome (On Illustrious Men 9) says that many think the second and third letters are by John the presbyter, and that two tombs were shown at Ephesus, though some took them for two memorials of one John.

Caution: Papias is known only through Eusebius, who used the passage to suggest that the elder and not the apostle wrote Revelation, so his reading may serve that aim. Whether there were two Johns, and who wrote these letters, is still argued; the pages note both views.
For 3 John: the letter opens with the same title, “The elder,” so the question of the two Johns touches it as much as 2 John.
f: Papias wrote about AD 100-130; his words are known from Eusebius in the early 4th century

e.n: The Syriac Peshitta and the missing General Letters
t: The Peshitta, the standard Bible of the Syriac-speaking churches, at first held only James, 1 Peter and 1 John among the General Letters. It left out 2 Peter, 2 John, 3 John, Jude and Revelation. These books were added in later Syriac translations made in the early 6th and 7th centuries.

It is a clear case of the doubt that short letters could meet in a region where few copies had arrived, and of how the later versions filled the gap. 2 John was not in the New Testament of these churches for some centuries.

Caution: The history of the Peshitta text and its date are debated, and the later versions survive in few manuscripts. The gap in the Peshitta is a fact about that Bible, not a judgment by the whole church.
For 3 John: it was one of the five books missing from the early Peshitta.
Jude was another of the five books missing from the early Peshitta.
f: Edessa (Şanlıurfa), Turkey, and the Syriac-speaking churches
Peshitta in use by the early 5th century; later Syriac versions in AD 508 and 616

e.n: The Apostolic Constitutions: Gaius at Pergamum, Demetrius at Philadelphia
t: The Apostolic Constitutions is a church manual in eight books, put together in Syria, probably near Antioch, about AD 375-380 and written as if the apostles were speaking. One chapter (7.46) lists the first bishops of many cities. For Pergamum it names Gaius, and for Philadelphia it names Demetrius, appointed by John.

It is the only early statement about where the Gaius and Demetrius of 3 John ended up, and it is why the map sets a pin at Pergamum. It shows that by the 4th century some Christians in the East linked both men with the churches of Asia near Ephesus.

Caution: The list was written nearly three hundred years after the letter, and no earlier source backs it. Its names may have been taken from the New Testament and matched to cities. 3 John names no town, and Gaius and Demetrius were both common names.
f: Pergamum (Bergama), Turkey; the text was compiled in Syria

e.n: The letter of Apion: a prayer for health at the start of a letter
t: Apion, a young Egyptian who had joined the Roman fleet at Misenum in Italy, wrote home to his father Epimachus in the village of Philadelphia in the Fayum. The papyrus (BGU II 423), now in Berlin, opens with his greeting and then a prayer that his father is well and will go on in good health and good fortune, along with his sister and brother. He thanks the god Serapis for saving him from danger at sea, and he ends with greetings to people at home by name and to his friends.

3 John 2 follows the same letter custom: after the names comes a wish for the reader’s health and well-being. The elder turns the custom into a Christian prayer by tying it to the health of the soul. The close of 3 John, with greetings to the friends by name, also matches ordinary letters like this one.
Caution: Apion was a worshiper of Serapis, and his letter is a parallel in form only. The health wish was so common that by itself it says little about how sick or well a reader was.
f: Philadelphia in the Fayum, Egypt (written from Misenum, Italy)

e.n: A letter of recommendation on papyrus (P.Oxy. 292)
t: A man named Theon wrote to Tyrannus, an official, on behalf of his brother Heraclides, who carried the letter. Theon asks Tyrannus to take Heraclides under his care, says he has written to another man about him as well, and closes with a wish for unbroken health and prosperity. The papyrus was found at Oxyrhynchus and published in 1899.

3 John 12 does the same for Demetrius: the elder vouches for a man who is probably carrying the letter, so that Gaius will receive him. Such letters were the way a stranger got a welcome in a town where no one knew him, and Paul writes one for Phoebe (Romans 16:1-2).
Caution: The papyrus is an ordinary request for a favor and has no link with the church. That Demetrius carried 3 John is a reasonable guess, and the letter does not say it.

e.n: Codex Bezae: a Latin page with the end of 3 John
t: Codex Bezae is a manuscript of the Gospels and Acts with Greek on the left-hand pages and Latin on the right. Many leaves are lost. Just before Acts begins, one page survives with the Latin of 3 John 11-15, the last lines of the letter, and a note that the third letter of John ends and the Acts of the Apostles begins.

The page shows that this book once held some or all of the General Letters between the Gospels and Acts, and that 3 John was being copied in Latin as Scripture by about AD 400. It is one of the oldest Latin witnesses to the letter.

Caution: Only the last verses are left, in Latin and not in Greek, and no one knows which other letters stood in the lost pages. The date and first home of the manuscript are debated. It was at Lyon in the 16th century, and Theodore Beza gave it to Cambridge in 1581.
f: Cambridge University Library, England (earlier at Lyon, France)

e.n: A begging servant of the Syrian goddess (the Kefr Hawar inscription)
t: A Greek inscription found at Kefr Hawar in Syria and published in 1897 was set up by a man who calls himself a slave of the Syrian goddess. He says that he was sent out by the goddess and that each of his journeys brought back seventy bags. The scholar Adolf Deissmann drew attention to it as a picture of religious begging in the Roman East.

3 John 7 says the Christian workers went out for the Name and accepted nothing from the pagans. The inscription shows the kind of collecting they did not want to be confused with, and why the churches had to support them from their own homes.
Caution: The inscription is not dated exactly, and it concerns one cult in one region. 3 John does not mention it; it is background for what traveling servants of other religions were known to do.
f: Kefr Hawar, near Mount Hermon, Syria

e.n: Hegesippus on the grandsons of Jude before Domitian
t: Hegesippus, a Christian writer of the 2nd century, is quoted by Eusebius (Church History 3.19-20 and 3.32). He says that the emperor Domitian was told of two grandsons of Jude, who was called the Lord’s brother according to the flesh, and had them brought before him as men of David’s line. They told him that between them they owned a small farm, which they worked with their own hands, and they showed him their hard, calloused hands. Asked about Christ’s kingdom, they said it was not of this world but would come at the end of the age. Domitian let them go as simple men of no danger, and Hegesippus adds that they became leaders in the churches and lived until the time of Trajan.

Jude 1 calls the writer “a brother of James,” and the Gospels name a Judas among the brothers of Jesus. This is the only early account of Jude’s family after the New Testament. It shows that the relatives of Jesus were remembered as farmers in the land of Israel and as leaders among the Jewish Christians there, and it suggests that Jude himself had died before the reign of Domitian.

Caution: Hegesippus wrote about eighty years after the event, his work survives only in quotations, and parts of the story may be legend. It says nothing about the letter, and it does not show where or when Jude wrote.
f: Galilee (the family home was Nazareth); the hearing is set before the emperor Domitian
Written about AD 170, of events about AD 90-96

e.n: The Book of Enoch in Ethiopic, Greek and Aramaic (the source of Jude 14-15)
t: The Book of Enoch, also called 1 Enoch, is a Jewish collection of visions and warnings set in the mouth of Enoch. The whole book survives only in Ge‘ez, the old church language of Ethiopia, where the Ethiopian Orthodox Church counts it as Scripture; the oldest Ethiopic copies known are of about the 15th century. The Scottish traveler James Bruce brought three copies to Europe in 1773. In the winter of 1886-87 a small parchment book was found in a grave at Akhmim in Egypt with the first 32 chapters in Greek. Pieces of about eleven Aramaic copies came from Cave 4 at Qumran, the oldest from the 2nd century BC, and one of them (4Q204) has part of the very sentence Jude quotes.

Jude 14-15 quotes 1 Enoch 1:9: the Lord comes with his holy ones to judge everyone and to convict the ungodly. Jude’s Greek is close to the Greek copy from Akhmim, with some differences, so the book he quotes can be laid beside his letter. The same book lies behind the angels who left their place (Jude 6) and the wandering stars (Jude 13).

Caution: Jude quotes one sentence. He says that Enoch “prophesied,” and he does not call the book Scripture or say that all of it is true. Jews did not include it in the Hebrew Bible, and most churches have not included it in theirs. In Jude the one who comes is “the Lord”; the Enoch text says only “he.”
f: Akhmim (ancient Panopolis), Egypt; also Ethiopia and Qumran
Written 3rd-1st century BC; copies from the 2nd century BC to the 15th century AD and later

e.n: The Testament of Moses and the lost story of Michael and the body of Moses
t: In 1861 Antonio Ceriani published a Latin text he had found in the Ambrosian Library in Milan, on parchment that had been scraped and written over. It is a farewell speech of Moses to Joshua, and it is usually called the Testament of Moses or the Assumption of Moses. It breaks off in the middle of a sentence, before the death of Moses. Clement of Alexandria and Origen, about AD 200-230, say that Jude’s story of Michael and the devil comes from a book they call the Assumption or Ascension of Moses, and later Christian writers pass on pieces of the story: the devil claimed the body, calling Moses a murderer for killing the Egyptian, and Michael answered, “The Lord rebuke you!”

Jude 9 tells of the archangel Michael disputing with the devil over the body of Moses, a story that is not in the Old Testament. These texts show that it stood in a Jewish book known to Jude’s first readers. Deuteronomy 34:6 says that the Lord buried Moses and that no one knows the grave, and the story grew around that verse.

Caution: The Milan copy does not contain the story, because its ending is lost. Whether the Testament and the Assumption of Moses were one book or two is debated, and the story has to be pieced together from later writers.
f: Written early 1st century AD; the one copy is of the 6th century

e.n: Papyrus 78: Jude on a tiny charm (P.Oxy. 2684)
t: A single folded sheet of papyrus from Oxyrhynchus, a few centimeters high and wider than it is tall, with Jude 4-5 and 7-8 in Greek. Its odd shape and small size suggest that it was made to be worn or carried as a charm for protection. It was published in 1968 and is kept with the Oxyrhynchus papyri in Oxford.

With Papyrus 72 it is one of the two oldest copies of Jude. It shows that the letter was being copied in Egypt by about AD 300, and that someone valued these verses about judgment enough to carry them.
Caution: Only four verses survive, in part, and the copying is careless. That it was a charm is a deduction from its shape, and the date rests on the handwriting.

e.n: Mount Nebo and the memorial of Moses
t: A ridge east of the north end of the Dead Sea, about 700 meters high, with a wide view over the Jordan valley to Jericho. Deuteronomy 34 says that Moses climbed Mount Nebo, saw the land, and died there in Moab. Christians built a small church on the summit in the 4th century, and the pilgrim Egeria, who came in the 380s, was shown the place where the monks said Moses was laid. The church was enlarged in the 5th and 6th centuries and has fine floor mosaics; Franciscan archaeologists have dug there since 1933.

Jude 9 speaks of a dispute over the body of Moses. Deuteronomy 34:6 says the Lord buried him in a valley in Moab and that no one knows where his grave is. That silence is the starting point of the story Jude uses.
Caution: The church marks a memory, and no tomb has been found. Which summit of the ridge is the Nebo of Deuteronomy is uncertain.

e.n: The love feast in Ignatius and Tertullian
t: Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the church at Smyrna about AD 110, says that it is not allowed to baptize or to hold a love feast without the bishop (Smyrnaeans 8). Tertullian of Carthage, about AD 197, describes the meal (Apology 39): its name is the Greek word for love; it begins and ends with prayer; people eat only what satisfies hunger; the poor are fed; and afterward each is asked to sing to God. Paintings of shared meals in the Roman catacombs, of the 3rd century, may show such gatherings or meals for the dead.

Jude 12 says the intruders are “hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you.” These writers show what the meal was: a real supper of the whole church, at which rich and poor ate together. Paul corrects abuses at such a supper in 1 Corinthians 11:17-34. Jude’s complaint is that men who cared only for themselves sat at the table of love.

Caution: Both writers are later than Jude and describe their own cities. How the love feast and the Lord’s Supper were joined in Jude’s day is not known, and the catacomb paintings can be read in more than one way.
f: Carthage (Tunis), Tunisia; also Smyrna and Rome

e.n: Early witnesses to Jude: Clement, Tertullian, Origen, Eusebius and Jerome
t: Clement of Alexandria, about AD 190-200, quotes Jude by name and wrote short notes on it. Tertullian, about AD 200, appeals to Jude, whom he calls an apostle, as a witness for the Book of Enoch (On the Apparel of Women 1.3). The Muratorian Fragment lists the letter of Jude as received. Origen calls it a letter of few lines but full of the strong words of heavenly grace (Commentary on Matthew 10.17), and he knows that some doubted it. Eusebius, about AD 325, places it among the disputed books that are still known to most (Church History 3.25.3) and says that few of the early writers mention it (2.23.25). Jerome, in AD 392-393, writes that because Jude quotes the Book of Enoch many reject it, yet by age and use it has gained authority and is counted among the Holy Scriptures (On Illustrious Men 4).

Jude was known and quoted in Egypt, North Africa and Italy by about AD 200, earlier and more widely than 2 Peter or 2 and 3 John. The doubts came later, and Jerome gives the reason: verses 9 and 14-15 use Jewish books outside the Old Testament.
Caution: The date of the Muratorian Fragment is debated. Clement’s notes survive only in a Latin version. The early Syriac Bible did not include Jude.
f: Alexandria, Egypt; also Carthage, Caesarea and Bethlehem

e.n: Patmos: the Cave of the Apocalypse and the Monastery of St John
t: Patmos is a small volcanic island in the Aegean, about 13 km long, some 60 km from the coast of Asia Minor. Pliny the Elder mentions it in his list of islands, and inscriptions show that it had a town, a gymnasium and a temple of Artemis in Roman times. Halfway up the hill between the harbor and the main town is a cave shown since the Middle Ages as the place where John received his visions, now inside a chapel. In 1088 the monk Christodoulos founded the fortified Monastery of St John the Theologian on the summit, with a grant from the Byzantine emperor. The monastery, the cave and the town are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

John says he “was on the island of Patmos because of the word of God and my testimony about Jesus” (1:9), and there he heard the voice that told him to write to the seven churches. Early writers say he had been banished to the island and was later released. From Patmos the cities of Asia lay just across the water.

Caution: The cave is a place of memory; nothing shows that it is the actual spot. Revelation does not say why John was on the island. Banishment is the early tradition and fits Roman practice, and that Patmos itself was a penal colony or a mine is a later guess.
f: Tradition from late antiquity; monastery founded 1088

e.n: Smyrna: the agora, and the death of Polycarp
t: Smyrna, the modern Izmir, has been lived in without a break, so little of the ancient city can be dug. The main remains are the state agora, with its vaulted basement and colonnades, rebuilt by the emperor Marcus Aurelius after an earthquake in AD 178. The city prided itself on its beauty and its loyalty to Rome: it built a temple to the goddess Roma in 195 BC and in AD 26 won the right, over ten rival cities, to build Asia’s temple to the emperor Tiberius (Tacitus, Annals 4.55-56). A letter from the church of Smyrna tells how its bishop Polycarp was burned in the stadium about AD 155, after refusing to swear by the fortune of Caesar and to curse Christ.

The letter to Smyrna tells a poor church, “Be faithful even unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (2:10). The death of Polycarp, who by tradition had known John, shows the same pressures two generations later: accusation before the governor, and a demand to honor the emperor.

Caution: The agora as seen today is later than Revelation. The account of Polycarp was written to honor him and shapes the story to recall the death of Jesus. Its hostile picture of the Jews of Smyrna reflects the quarrels of that time and should be read with care.
f: City refounded about 300 BC; agora rebuilt after AD 178

t: A huge altar platform, about 36 by 34 meters, built on a terrace of the acropolis of Pergamum under King Eumenes II. A marble frieze over 110 meters long runs around its base and shows the gods of Olympus fighting the giants, some with snakes for legs. The German engineer Carl Humann excavated it from 1878 to 1886, and the frieze was rebuilt in Berlin, where it gave its name to the Pergamon Museum. The altar is usually thought to have been sacred to Zeus, perhaps with Athena.

Christ says to the church at Pergamum, “I know where you live, where the throne of Satan sits” (2:13). The altar, which looked from the plain like a great throne on the hillside, is one of the things proposed as that throne. The others are the temple of Augustus and Rome, the first temple of the emperors in Asia; the shrine of the healing god Asclepius, whose sign was the snake; and the seat of the Roman governor.

Caution: Revelation does not say what the throne was, and scholars have not settled it. Most now think the worship of the emperor is the likeliest meaning, with the altar as one part of a city crowded with temples. The temple of Augustus is known from coins and has not been found.
f: Bergama, Turkey; the altar is in the Pergamon Museum, Berlin

e.n: Sardis: the citadel, the temple of Artemis and the synagogue
t: Sardis lay below a steep, crumbling citadel rock at the foot of Mount Tmolus. It was the capital of the Lydian kings, and the stream Pactolus brought down the gold that made Croesus proverbial. Herodotus tells how the Persians took the citadel in 546 BC by climbing a face left unguarded, and Polybius tells of a similar night climb by the soldiers of Antiochus III in 214 BC. Excavation since 1958 has uncovered the great temple of Artemis, never finished, a bath and gymnasium complex, and a very large synagogue of the 3rd and 4th centuries AD, over 80 meters long, in the middle of the city. An earthquake destroyed Sardis in AD 17, and Tiberius paid for rebuilding.

The church at Sardis is told, “you have a reputation for being alive, yet you are dead,” and is warned to wake up or Christ will come like a thief (3:1-3). A city twice captured because its watchmen were careless would feel the point. The half-built temple also suits the words, “I have found your deeds incomplete in the sight of My God.”

Caution: The links with the city’s history are suggestions by modern scholars; the letter does not make them. The synagogue is later than Revelation, though it shows a large and settled Jewish community.
f: Lydian capital from the 7th century BC; Roman city

t: Philadelphia was founded by the kings of Pergamum in the 2nd century BC on the road from Sardis to the interior, beside a volcanic district the Greeks called the Burnt Land, which grew fine vines. The geographer Strabo, writing soon after the great earthquake of AD 17, says its walls cracked daily and that most people lived out in the country for fear of the tremors. In thanks for the emperor’s help it took the name Neocaesarea for a time, and later Flavia. The modern town covers the ancient city; the brick piers of a Byzantine church of St John are the main remains.

The promise to this church fits such a place: “The one who overcomes I will make a pillar in the temple of My God, and he will never again leave it,” with a new name written on him (3:12). A people used to fleeing their houses, in a city that had changed its name, are promised a fixed home and a lasting name.
Caution: The connections are modern suggestions. Almost nothing of the first-century city has been excavated.
f: Founded 2nd century BC; earthquake of AD 17

e.n: Megiddo and the plain of battles
t: A mound of about twenty layers of cities at the mouth of the pass that carries the main road from Egypt to Syria through the Carmel ridge into the Jezreel plain. Whoever held it controlled the road, and battles were fought here from the campaign of Pharaoh Thutmose III about 1457 BC to that of General Allenby in 1918. In the Bible, Deborah and Barak defeated the Canaanites “by the waters of Megiddo,” Solomon fortified the city, and King Josiah was killed here by Pharaoh Neco in 609 BC. Excavations have uncovered gates, palaces, stables or storehouses, and a deep water tunnel. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Revelation 16:16 says the kings are gathered “in the place that in Hebrew is called Armageddon.” The usual explanation is Har Megiddo, the mountain of Megiddo: the famous battlefield stands for the last gathering of the nations against God.

Caution: Megiddo is a mound on the edge of a plain and has no mountain, so the name is a puzzle. Other explanations have been offered, such as “mount of assembly.” Many readers take the name as a symbol, and Revelation 19, which describes the end of the kings, names no place. By John’s day the city had long been deserted.

e.n: The goddess Roma on the seven hills: a coin of Vespasian
t: A bronze sestertius struck at Rome in AD 71 under the emperor Vespasian. The reverse shows the goddess Roma, in armor, seated at ease on seven hills, with the river god Tiber beside her and the she-wolf with Romulus and Remus below. Roman poets from Virgil on call Rome the city of the seven hills, and a yearly festival, the Septimontium, was named for them.

Revelation 17:9 explains that “The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits,” and 17:18 that she is “the great city that rules over the kings of the earth.” The coin shows how the empire pictured its own capital: a woman seated on seven hills. John’s vision turns the proud image into a prostitute.

Caution: The coin shows that the picture was familiar; it does not show that John knew this coin. Readers who take Babylon as Jerusalem, as a future city, or as a symbol of all proud empires explain the seven hills differently.

e.n: Papyrus 115: an early copy that reads 616
t: Twenty-six small pieces of a papyrus book of Revelation found at Oxyrhynchus and published in 1999 (P.Oxy. LXVI 4499). They preserve parts of chapters 2-15. At 13:18 the number of the beast is written in Greek numeral letters as 616, where most copies have 666. The 5th-century Codex Ephraemi has 616 too.

Revelation 13:18 says the number of the beast “is the number of a man, and that number is 666.” Irenaeus, about AD 180, already knew copies with 616 and judged 666 to be right. Both numbers fit one answer: “Nero Caesar” written in Hebrew letters adds up to 666 when spelled in the Greek way (Neron) and to 616 when spelled in the Latin way (Nero).

Caution: That both numbers fit Nero is a strong argument but not a proof, and Revelation does not explain the number. Other solutions have been proposed in every century. Most early copies, including Papyrus 47 and Codex Sinaiticus, read 666.

e.n: The oldest copies of Revelation: Papyrus 98 and Papyrus 47
t: Papyrus 98, a scrap in Cairo with parts of Revelation 1:13-20, is usually dated to the 2nd century and is the oldest known piece of the book. Papyrus 47, in the Chester Beatty Library in Dublin, is ten leaves of a 3rd-century book with Revelation 9:10-17:2. The whole book is found in Codex Sinaiticus (4th century) and Codex Alexandrinus (5th century); Codex Vaticanus lacks it. About 300 Greek copies of Revelation survive, far fewer than for the Gospels.

The papyri show that Revelation was being read in Egypt within a century or so of its writing. The smaller number of copies reflects the book’s slower acceptance in the Greek-speaking East, where it was not read in church services.

Caution: The date of Papyrus 98 rests on its handwriting. Because copies are fewer and the Greek is unusual, the wording of Revelation is less certain in places than that of other New Testament books.
f: Egypt; now in Cairo and Dublin

e.n: Babylon: the fallen city behind the name
t: Babylon on the Euphrates was the largest city of its age under Nebuchadnezzar II, who built its double walls, the Ishtar Gate, the temple tower of the god Marduk and the palaces. His armies destroyed Jerusalem and its temple in 586 BC and carried the people of Judah into exile. Babylon fell to Cyrus of Persia in 539 BC without a siege. It declined under the Greek kings, and by the first century it was largely empty: Strabo applies to it the line that the great city has become a great desert, and the emperor Trajan, visiting in AD 116, found mostly mounds. German excavators under Robert Koldewey dug the site from 1899 to 1917.

When Revelation announces, “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!” (18:2), it uses the words of Isaiah 21:9 about this city. For the prophets Babylon was the power that destroyed the temple, exiled God’s people and boasted that it would last forever. John gives the name to the great city of his own day.

Caution: Hardly any reader thinks John means the city in Mesopotamia, which was a ruin when he wrote. Most take Babylon in Revelation as Rome, as 1 Peter 5:13 probably does; others take it as Jerusalem, as a city yet to come, or as a picture of every such power.

e.n: The Euphrates frontier and the Parthians
t: In the first century the Euphrates was the border between the Roman Empire and the Parthian Empire, which ruled from Mesopotamia to India. The Parthians fought as mounted archers and armored lancers. They destroyed the army of Crassus at Carrhae in 53 BC, and they were the one neighbor Rome could not subdue. After Nero’s death in AD 68, stories spread that he was alive and would return from the East with Parthian armies, and at least two pretenders claiming to be Nero appeared (Tacitus, Histories 2.8; Suetonius, Nero 57).

Twice in Revelation trouble comes from this river: four angels are released “at the great river Euphrates” with a vast force of horsemen (9:14-16), and the river is dried up “to prepare the way for the kings of the East” (16:12). For people in Asia, the east bank of the Euphrates was where an invasion would come from.

Caution: The horsemen of chapter 9 are described as monsters and are not a Parthian army. The frontier explains why the picture frightened; it does not tell us what John foresaw. In the Old Testament the Euphrates was already the direction from which Assyria and Babylon came.

e.n: Ostia and Portus: the harbor of Rome
t: Ostia, at the mouth of the Tiber, was the port of Rome. The emperor Claudius began a great artificial harbor just to the north, finished under Nero, and Trajan added a six-sided inner basin. Warehouses line the streets of Ostia, and the mosaic floors of the Square of the Corporations show the ships and trade marks of shippers from Africa, Gaul, Sardinia and Egypt. In Rome itself, Monte Testaccio is a hill some 35 meters high made of broken oil jars, the remains of tens of millions of jars of olive oil, most of them from Spain. A fleet of grain ships from Alexandria fed the city.

Revelation 18:11-13 lists the cargoes that “the merchants of the earth” sold to Babylon, from gold and silk to wheat, cattle and slaves, and verses 17-19 give the lament of “Every shipmaster, passenger, and sailor, and all who make their living from the sea” The ruins of Ostia show the scale of the trade the chapter describes.

Caution: Revelation 18 is built from Ezekiel’s lament over Tyre (Ezekiel 27) and names no port. The match with Rome’s trade supports reading Babylon as Rome and does not prove it. Trajan’s basin is a little later than the book.
f: Harbors built AD 42-64 and about AD 110

e.n: The worship of the emperors in Asia
t: The cities of Asia asked for the right to worship the emperor and competed for the title “temple warden.” Pergamum received the province’s first temple, to Augustus and Rome, in 29 BC; Smyrna a second, to Tiberius, in AD 26; and Ephesus a third, to the Flavian emperors, about AD 89-90. Inscriptions record the provincial council, its high priests, and festivals with processions, sacrifices, games and hymns sung by choirs. Emperors are called “lord,” “savior” and “son of god” on stones and coins. About AD 112 the governor Pliny, in the province to the north, tested people accused of being Christians by having them offer incense and wine to the emperor’s statue and curse Christ.

In Revelation 13 a beast from the land makes the earth “worship the first beast,” sets up its image, and causes those who refuse to be killed. The picture fits the local leaders who promoted the worship of the emperor in the very cities John writes to. The praise of God and the Lamb in chapters 4-5 uses the forms of such ceremonies and gives them to the one who deserves them.

Caution: Evidence for an organized persecution under Domitian is thin, and many scholars now think the pressure was local and social more than official. Revelation names few who had died: Antipas, and the souls under the altar. Futurist readers see chapter 13 as a ruler still to come.

e.n: Justin and Irenaeus on John, the date and the number
t: Justin Martyr, who had lived at Ephesus, writes about AD 155 that a man of the church named John, one of the apostles of Christ, prophesied in a revelation that believers would spend a thousand years in Jerusalem (Dialogue with Trypho 81). It is the earliest statement about who wrote the book. Irenaeus, who grew up in Asia and became bishop of Lyon, quotes Revelation often. He says the vision was seen not long before his own time, toward the end of the reign of Domitian (Against Heresies 5.30.3), and he discusses the number of the beast, noting that the best and oldest copies read 666 while some read 616, and declining to name the man.

These are the main early witnesses for the author and date printed in most Bibles: John the apostle, about AD 95. They also show that within eighty years the book was read from Asia to Gaul and that the thousand years of chapter 20 were then taken as a coming reign on earth.

Caution: Some scholars take Irenaeus’s sentence to mean that John, and not the vision, was seen in Domitian’s time; most do not. A minority date the book to the late 60s. That the John of Revelation is the apostle was questioned in the 3rd century on grounds of style.
f: Lyon, France; also Ephesus and Rome

e.n: Dionysius, Eusebius and the slow acceptance of Revelation in the East
t: Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria about AD 247-264, wrote against Christians who read the thousand years as a time of earthly pleasures. He accepted Revelation as the work of a holy and inspired man named John but argued, from its vocabulary, its grammar and the way it names its author, that it was not by the writer of the Gospel and letters of John (Eusebius, Church History 7.25). Eusebius, about AD 325, lists it both among the accepted books and among the rejected, leaving the choice open. Cyril of Jerusalem and the list attached to the Council of Laodicea leave it out; Athanasius includes it in AD 367. The early Syriac Bible lacked it, and the Greek churches never gave it a place in their cycle of readings.

This is why Revelation stands last and came last. The West, where Irenaeus, Tertullian and Hippolytus used it freely, never doubted it. The East hesitated for centuries, partly over its author and partly over the use some made of chapter 20.
Caution: Dionysius’s points about style are still discussed. They show that the Greek of Revelation differs from that of the Gospel of John; they do not settle who wrote either.

Victorinus, bishop of Poetovio, who died in the persecution of Diocletian about AD 304, wrote the oldest commentary on Revelation that survives. He noticed that the seals, trumpets and bowls do not simply follow one another in time but go over the same ground again, an idea called recapitulation. Tyconius in North Africa, about AD 380, read the book as a picture of the church’s struggle in every age, and Augustine followed him on the thousand years. In Greek the first commentaries are those of Oecumenius, in the 6th century, and Andrew of Caesarea in Cappadocia, about AD 611, whose work became the standard in the East. In England the monk Bede wrote his commentary about AD 710.

The main ways of reading Revelation today all have roots in these writers: the book as a forecast of the end, as a set of visions that repeat and deepen, and as a picture of the church’s life between the two comings of Christ.
Caution: These are interpreters, centuries after John, and they disagree with one another. They are witnesses to how the book was read, not to what its first readers knew.
Betrothal was legally binding, so ending it took a formal divorce.
Jewish family lists usually named fathers only, so Matthew’s four women stand out.
Magi were scholar-priests who studied stars and dreams, likely from Persia.
Gold, frankincense and myrrh were costly gifts, fit for a king.
John’s camel-hair clothes and leather belt matched Elijah’s, a deliberate prophetic sign.
Locusts were a clean food under the Law and a common desert meal.
Flat round loaves were the daily staple, so turning stones to bread meant ending hunger.
Fishermen cast round nets by hand, then mended them on the shore.
A rabbi sat to teach with authority, so Jesus visibly takes that role.
Anointing the head with oil was normal grooming, so fasting should look ordinary.
Spices honored the dead and eased the smell, they did not preserve the body.
1 John 2:20 and 2:27 use anointing as a picture of what God has given every believer, not oil on the body: “the anointing you received from Him remains in you.”
Walled towns had narrow gates, so the road through one was tight and easy to miss.
Sudden rains turned dry riverbeds into torrents that swept away poor foundations.
A healed leper brought offerings to the priest, as the Law of Moses required.
Banquet guests lay on couches, so “reclining with Abraham” pictures a feast of honor.
Flat roofs of beams and clay could be opened, as when friends lowered the paralytic.
Roofs were beams covered with branches and clay, so a crowd could open one.
Flute players and wailing mourners were hired at a death, so they were already there.
Traveling light made the Twelve depend on each town’s hospitality.
Shaking dust from the feet marked leaving non-Jewish land, so here it was a solemn warning.
Shaking dust off the feet marked leaving non-Jewish land, so here it was a pointed warning.
Village children played at weddings and funerals, the image Jesus uses for a stubborn crowd.
Pharisees counted plucking grain as reaping, work the Sabbath forbade.
Most rabbis allowed rescuing a sheep on the Sabbath, which Jesus uses in His answer.
The weeds were likely darnel, which looks like wheat until it matures.
A public oath was hard to break without losing face, so Herod gave the order.
The fourth watch came before dawn, so Jesus reached them in the last hours of night.
Ritual hand washing before meals was a tradition, not a command of Moses.
Pharisees washed before meals for purity, so Jesus skipping it was noticed.
Declaring money “Corban” set it aside for God, a loophole to avoid supporting parents.
Calling goods “Corban” dedicated them to God, which some used to avoid helping parents.
Keys marked a steward’s authority over a house, as in Isaiah 22.
Peter’s offer of shelters recalls the booths built at the Feast of Tabernacles.
Peter’s offer to build shelters recalls the booths of the Feast of Tabernacles.
A stater was a silver coin worth four drachmas, enough for two men’s temple tax.
Children had no status in the ancient world, so honoring one was a shock.
1 John calls its readers “little children” again and again (2:1, 12, 28; 3:7, 18; 4:4; 5:21), and speaks of believers as “children of God” (3:1-2, 10; 5:2).
In 2 John, the writer speaks of the church’s “children” three times: “her children” (1), “some of your children walking in the truth” (4), and the “children of your elect sister” (13).
In 3 John 4 the elder says, “I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.” Gaius seems to be one of them.
A husband gave a written divorce certificate, which let the wife remarry.
The camel was the largest animal in Galilee, so the image is deliberately absurd.
The day counted from sunrise, so the eleventh hour was near sunset.
A king on a donkey meant peace, not war, unlike a king on a war horse.
Spreading cloaks and branches on the road honored a king.
Guests were expected to dress properly for a wedding feast, as a sign of respect.
