A childless widow married her husband’s brother to carry on the family line.
A childless widow married her husband’s brother to continue the family line.
Tombs were whitewashed so travelers wouldn’t touch them and become unclean.
Flat roofs were living space with outside stairs, so fleeing meant not going back inside.
Travel on the Sabbath was limited, which would make a Sabbath flight harder.
Small clay lamps burned only a short while, so spare oil was needed.
A talent was a huge sum, roughly many years of a laborer’s pay.
At Passover guests reclined at table, so a dipped bowl was shared closely.
Guests reclined at the table, so those beside Jesus shared the same dish.
Guests reclined at meals with feet to the side, so the woman could reach Jesus’ feet.
A prisoner was released at the festival, a gesture to calm the crowds.
Bodies were wrapped in cloth and laid in rock-cut tombs sealed with a stone.
Women’s testimony carried little weight in court, yet they are first at the tomb.
Spices and perfumes were brought to honor the body, not to preserve it.
Camel hair and a leather belt recalled the prophet Elijah.
Teachers usually quoted earlier rabbis, but Jesus spoke on His own authority.
Roofs of beams, branches and clay could be opened from above.
Roofs were living space with outside stairs, so fleeing meant not going back in.
Old skins grew stiff and would burst if filled with fermenting wine.
Many rabbis allowed healing on the Sabbath only to save a life.
Family was a person’s greatest loyalty, so Jesus’ words shocked.
Farmers scattered seed by hand before plowing it under.
The curved shore works like an amphitheater, carrying a voice across the water.
Hillside caves served as tombs, and touching the dead made one unclean.
A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and kept apart.
Shaking dust off one’s feet signaled a break with a town.
A king could not easily take back a vow made in front of guests.
Washing hands, cups and couches was a Pharisaic tradition, not a Mosaic command.
A little leaven spreads through all the dough, standing for hidden influence.
Saliva was a folk remedy, though Jesus needed no such help.
Teachers were often given children to bless, though disciples tried to block them.
Spreading cloaks and leafy branches on the road honored a king.
A king on a donkey came in peace, not on a war horse.
Landowners often leased vineyards, collecting a share of the fruit.
The smallest coins in use, worth a fraction of a day’s wage.
Roman time divided night into four watches, and servants stayed alert.
Prisoners were beaten before crucifixion, often weakening them.
A written charge was fixed above the condemned person on the cross.
Work stopped from Friday sunset, so the women waited until Sunday.
Priests drew lots for the rare honor of burning incense in the holy place.
Boys were named at circumcision on day eight, and neighbors expected the family name.
Poorer families offered two birds instead of a lamb.
Farmers tossed grain into the wind so the wheat fell and the chaff blew away.
The “year of the Lord’s favor” echoes Jubilee, when debts were erased and slaves freed.
A leper lived apart and was ritually unclean, so Jesus’ touch broke a strong taboo.
Pharisees counted rubbing grain by hand as work, which the Sabbath forbade.
The dead were carried on an open bier and buried the same day, followed by mourners.
Seed was scattered by hand before plowing, so some landed on paths, rock and thorns.
Seed was scattered by hand across the field.
Her bleeding made her ritually unclean, so touching Jesus’ cloak was a bold risk.
Sitting in groups of fifty matched the orderly pattern of a pilgrim meal.
A priest or Levite touching a corpse became unclean, which may explain why they avoided him.
Sitting at a teacher’s feet was the place of a disciple, usually a man’s role.
A village home had one room, so waking for a late guest meant waking the whole family.
Sparrows were the cheapest bird sold for food, five for two small coins.
Servants waiting for a master’s late return kept their robes tucked up and lamps lit.
Many Jews allowed leading an animal to water on the Sabbath, which Jesus uses in His answer.
Both were everyday items, so small things growing large was easy to picture.
Seats nearest the host were places of honor, and guests competed for them.
A dinner was expected to be repaid, so inviting the poor broke the pattern.
A father rarely divided his estate while alive, so the younger son’s request was an insult.
Dignified older men didn’t run, so the father’s sprint broke every social rule.
Managers often added a commission to debts, which this manager may have cut from his own share.
Lazarus lay at the gate with dogs licking his sores, showing how complete his neglect was.
A priest had to declare a leper clean, so going to him meant trusting before healing.
Lepers had to stay away and call out “unclean,” so these men stood far off.
Pharisees fasted Mondays and Thursdays and tithed carefully, so his claims were real.
Chief tax collectors bought the right to collect for Rome and kept the extra.
Spreading cloaks on the road honored a king, as when Jehu was crowned.
Thirteen trumpet-shaped chests held offerings, so large gifts were heard dropping in.
Two lepta were the smallest coins, worth a tiny fraction of a day’s wage.
The meal recalled Israel’s rescue from Egypt, with unleavened bread, bitter herbs and wine.
Gethsemane means “olive press,” from the oil pressed on that hillside.
Burial had to happen before the Sabbath began, so the women prepared spices later.
Spices honored the body, so the women did not expect a resurrection.
About seventy-five pounds of spices were wrapped with the linen.
The host broke and blessed bread to start a meal, when they recognized Him.
The Lord’s Supper was part of a shared meal on Sunday.
Lambs were offered daily and at Passover, a picture of sacrifice.
Weddings lasted days, and running out of wine shamed the host.
Large stone jars held water for ritual washing, since stone stayed pure.
Teachers often studied by night, away from crowds and scrutiny.
Hebrew and Greek use one word for wind, breath and spirit.
Women drew water in cool morning or evening, so noon hints she avoided others.
Jews often avoided Samaritan cups and bowls as unclean.
Carrying a mat on the Sabbath was counted as work.
Some believed an angel stirred the water to heal.
Barley was the poor man’s bread, a boy’s small lunch.
Jesus’ words sounded shocking, since the Law forbade drinking blood.
Pilgrims lived in leafy shelters for a week to remember the wilderness.
Priests poured water at the altar each morning of the feast.
Jesus wrote on the ground, and John never says what.
Giant lamps in the Court of Women lit the temple during Tabernacles.
Saliva was a folk remedy, though Jesus needed no medicine.
Water from Siloam was drawn each morning for the Tabernacles ceremony.
At night several flocks shared a pen, and each sheep knew its own shepherd’s voice.
Jews believed the spirit lingered three days, so four days proved real death.
Professional mourners and visitors comforted the family for a week.
Nard was an imported perfume worth about a year’s wages.
Palms were a national symbol, welcoming a hoped-for king.
Washing feet was the work of the lowest slave, not a teacher.
Giving a morsel to a guest honored him, which made the betrayal sharper.
A groom prepared a room at his father’s house before the wedding.
Peace was the usual Jewish greeting, meaning wholeness, not only calm.
Vinedressers cut back branches in winter so the vine bears more.
Dead branches were gathered and burned as fuel.
The prophets often used labor pains as a picture of pain turning to joy.
To ask in someone’s name meant coming with their authority.
Jews often prayed with eyes lifted toward heaven.
God’s name stood for His character and presence.
Soldiers claimed the executed man’s clothing, and cast lots for the seamless one.
Burial cloths and a separate face cloth lay neatly in the tomb.
Galilean fishermen worked at night, using nets let down from boats.
Bread and fish were the staple meal of the lakeshore.
About 1,100 yards, the farthest a person could walk on the Sabbath.
The feast of weeks, fifty days after the Passover offering.
About nine in the morning, when the pilgrims were awake but sober.
The sick and disabled sat by busy gates where worshipers gave alms.
About three in the afternoon, the time of the afternoon sacrifice.
The arrest came at evening, so the hearing waited until morning.
Land was a family inheritance, so giving it up was costly.
Verse 30 says Jesus was hanged on a tree, a phrase for crucifixion.
Thirty-nine lashes were the usual Jewish punishment for public offenses.
Widows received daily food, a duty Israel owed to the poor.
A sign of blessing and commissioning for a task.
The church commissions its missionaries with fasting and prayer.

Paul reminds Timothy of the gift given “through prophecy with the laying on of hands by the council of elders” (4:14), and 2 Timothy 1:6 says it came through Paul’s own hands. In Scripture the laying on of hands marks blessing (Genesis 48:14), setting apart (Numbers 27:18-23; Acts 6:6; 13:3) and healing. The two verses may describe one event or two.
A sign of rage, as in Psalm 35:16 and Job 16:9.
Witnesses removed outer robes to throw stones freely.
The word comes from Simon, who tried to buy the Spirit’s power with money.
People read aloud, which is how Philip could hear the Ethiopian.
Saul neither ate nor drank for three days, a sign of shock and repentance.
Their work was unclean, so Simon’s trade put him at the edge of society.
Jewish food laws kept Jews from sharing meals with Gentiles.
The sixth hour was a common prayer time, and roofs were quiet places.
Jewish believers were wary of eating with uncircumcised Gentiles.
Each disciple gave according to his ability, a model for later churches.
Four groups of four soldiers took turns, each guarding for three hours.
Early believers met in homes, and Mary’s house was large enough for many.
A gesture of rejection that Jesus taught his disciples (Luke 9:5).
Priests offered sacrifices with garlands at the city gates.
A sign of grief and horror at blasphemy, as in verse 14.
Official letters opened with “greetings” and named their senders.
Without a synagogue, Jews gathered near water for prayer.
A slave girl was thought to speak for the Pythian oracle.
The Bereans checked every claim against Scripture.
Ancient writers mention altars to unnamed gods in Athens.
Leatherwork and tent cloth were a common trade for Tarsus natives.
Paul says he worked “night and day” so as not to burden them, and to give an example (3:7-9). Acts 18:3 calls him a tentmaker. The Greek word is usually understood as a worker in leather or cloth.
A vow ended with cutting the hair, as in Numbers 6.
Spells were written on scrolls and sold for high prices.
Prayer on the shore was a physical sign of deep farewell.
Men finishing the vow shaved their heads and offered sacrifices.
Many Jewish believers were strict about the law, as James says.
A sign of anger or of readiness to throw stones.
They bound themselves by a curse to fast until Paul was dead.
The escort left at the third hour of the night, about nine.
Orators praised the judge before making their case.
Paul could receive visits from friends while being held.
A citizen could appeal to the emperor to stop a local trial.
Local rulers paid formal visits to new Roman governors.
Farmers prodded oxen with a sharp stick, and kicking back only hurt the ox.
Prisoners spoke in chains before the court.
The Day of Atonement fell in early autumn and marked the end of safe sailing.
Sailors dropped a weighted line to measure the depth near shore.
The twin gods were patrons of sailors and carved on ship prows.
A soldier was chained to the prisoner day and night.
“Slave” could be a humble word in Rome, but in Scripture it was used of God’s chosen leaders such as Moses.
Greeks divided the world into Greeks and “barbarians,” people who didn’t speak Greek. Paul says the gospel is for both (v.14).
Jews were to bind the law to their hands and foreheads. Paul says the real place for it is the heart.
People in Roman society boasted in family, rank, and achievements. Paul says faith leaves no room for it (v.27).
The Shema, “the Lord is one,” was the Jewish creed. Paul uses it to say that God must be the God of Gentiles too (v.29-30).
An accounting word. A sum is put to someone’s account. Paul says righteousness is put to the believer’s account.
Abraham’s name means “father of many,” given in Genesis 17:5.
The word in v.2 was used of being introduced to a king. Believers are brought into God’s presence.
Heroic friends sometimes died for each other, but Paul says Christ died for people who had nothing to offer (v.7-8).
Soldiers received a wage. Paul says sin pays its servants with death, but God gives life freely.
The word describes offering something as a sacrifice or reporting for duty.
The tenth commandment deals with desire, not action, which is where Paul says he saw his sin.
A woman was bound to her husband while he lived, and free to remarry after his death.
A Roman might adopt an adult to carry his name and inheritance. Paul says God does this for believers.
Romans adopted adult heirs to carry on a family name.
The firstborn son normally got the larger inheritance. God reversed that for Jacob and Esau.
Potters were common in towns, and Jeremiah 18 uses the image of clay shaped by the potter.
Early Christians publicly said “Jesus is Lord,” which could cost them in a world of emperor worship.
1 John 1:9 says, “If we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.” The same verb is used of confessing the Son (2:23; 4:2-3, 15).
In 2 John, the refusal “to confess the coming of Jesus Christ in the flesh” (7) is what marks the deceiver. Confessing here means saying openly what is true of Jesus.
A runner arriving with news of victory was welcomed with joy.
Olive trees took years to bear fruit and could live for centuries. They were a symbol of Israel (Jeremiah 11:16).
Rome collected direct taxes (tribute) and indirect ones such as customs duties. Both are named in v.7.
Jews kept Sabbath and festivals. Some Gentile believers may have had other days or none.
Daniel and his friends ate only vegetables in Babylon (Daniel 1:12), a model for staying clean.
“To be helped on my journey” (v.24) means to supply food, money, and companions for the next stage.
In 3 John 6 the elder asks Gaius to “send them on their way in a manner worthy of God,” the same term for supplying travelers.
Greetings mention groups meeting in homes: those with Aristobulus, Narcissus, and others.
Greek teachers had loyal students who defended them against rivals, a pattern Paul says has crept into the church.
Public speaking was an art form. Teachers like the Sophists traveled and charged fees for show.
Mystery cults offered hidden knowledge to initiates. Paul says God’s mystery is for all believers.
Gold and silver survive fire, while wood and straw do not.
Often a trusted slave who ran the household. His job was faithfulness.
A disciplinary tool. A father might use it on a child.
Before Passover, families searched the house with a lamp and removed all leaven.
The Jewish community could exclude a person. Paul asks the church to do the same.

In 3 John 10, Diotrephes “refuses to welcome the brothers and forbids those who want to do so, even putting them out of the church.” Here the power to exclude is misused by one man against people who had done right. The verb is the one used when the man born blind is thrown out in John 9:34.
Corinthians seem to have said “All things are lawful.” Paul quotes and qualifies it.
Another slogan: “Food is for the stomach.” Paul answers that the body is for the Lord.
Vv.36-38 may be about engaged couples or fathers giving daughters in marriage, and commentators disagree.
Paul says slaves should accept freedom if it comes, but not worry if it doesn’t.
Perhaps a third of urban people were slaves. Paul tells masters to stop threatening them.
Temples had dining rooms. Paul mentions someone “reclining at table in an idol’s temple” (v.10).
Isthmian winners got a wreath of pine (earlier celery), which wilted quickly.
Athletes swore to ten months of training. Paul uses it as a picture of self-discipline.
To eat at a god’s table was to share in his worship.
Sharing a meal signaled acceptance and equality.

e.n: Head Coverings in the Lord’s Supper
t: See chapter 11 for the next set of worship matters.
Respectable women usually covered their hair in public. Men prayed uncovered. The passage addresses local custom and creation.
The Roman dining room held about nine on couches. Others stood in the atrium.
The story of Menenius Agrippa, who calmed a revolt with a tale about the belly and limbs, was a Roman classic.
Terra-cotta body parts were offered at healing shrines in Corinth.
Ancient mirrors were polished metal, so the image was blurred.

Mirrors were usually made of polished metal such as bronze. They gave a recognizable reflection, but a less clear one than modern glass. James uses one for a man who looks at his face and then forgets what he looked like (1:23-24).
Paul compares himself to a child who has put away childish things.
A person who spoke in a tongue, or another, was to interpret it so all could say “Amen.”
Unbelievers might attend a house church, which Paul wants to be convincing and not confusing.
The practice in v.29 is obscure and debated. Paul mentions it without endorsing it.
A bare seed is buried and rises as something new.
Giving on “the first day of the week” (v.2) suggests that early Christians met on that day.
The Greek word arrabōn was a first installment guaranteeing the full purchase.
The Spirit is the pledge of the full inheritance.
Rome’s greatest victory ceremony, with captives, trophies, incense, and a parade to the Capitol.
After a great victory a Roman general led his captives through the streets in a procession. Paul pictures Christ leading the defeated powers this way (2:15).
Paul says rivals traded in God’s word, like merchants watering down wine.
A letter of introduction was a basic form of trust in the Roman world.
Jews read Moses in the synagogue, and Paul says a veil lies over their reading.
Cheap, breakable, and disposable. They show how plain the vessel is compared to what it holds.
Paul’s picture of being “struck down but not destroyed” sounds like a gladiator.
The Greek word is bēma, the raised platform on which a magistrate sat.
Two animals pulled a plow together, so mismatched pairs made the work harder.
The hearts and affections were thought to be in the chest and “cramped” or “wide.”
Paul speaks of the church clearing itself of blame.
Paul says the abundance of one meets the need of another (v.14), so that there is equality.
Paul has others handle the money so no one can blame him.
The Greek word is hilaros, from which we get “hilarious.” It means glad, not grudging.
Fortresses on hills in the ancient world, which siege engines battered.
Visitors came with credentials, and Paul says that’s not the same as being commended by God.
Jews stopped at 39 so as not to exceed the limit by miscounting.
Roman lictors beat with rods. Paul was a citizen, but not always spared.
Miracles and endurance, which Paul says he did among them.
Paul compares Christ’s crucifixion in weakness with his living by God’s power.
A greeting kiss was common among family and close friends.
Pharisees took pride in observing ancestral traditions.
A gesture of agreement and partnership.
Deuteronomy 21:23 said a hanged man was cursed. Paul reads that as Christ taking the curse.
A child was legally like a slave until the date set by the father.
A father decided when a son became an heir, in the Roman and Greek world.
Jewish feast days, months, and years were things Gentile believers were taking up.
The law as a way to earn favor was a heavy yoke.
The fruit was thought of as the natural result of a tree’s life.
Slaves and temple servants were sometimes marked. Paul says his scars show whom he serves.
Teachers could count converts as a proof of success.
A seal marked ownership and protection.
Roman citizenship was a high privilege. Paul says Gentiles now share in Israel’s commonwealth.
Kneeling was an earnest posture for prayer.
“Every family” (v.14) plays on the Greek words for father and family.
A victorious king gave gifts to his followers.
Greek ethics warned against unrestrained anger. Paul adds a time limit: do not let the sun go down on it.
The male head had legal authority over the family. Paul modifies it with love.
Believers sang psalms and hymns and spiritual songs to one another.
Believers taught each other with psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs.
Paul calls it “the first commandment with a promise” (Exodus 20:12).
Philippi was a Roman colony settled by veterans and governed by Roman law. Paul’s words for conduct (1:27) and citizenship (3:20) come from this civic setting.
A word meaning shared work and common cause.
A libation was wine or oil poured out for a god. Paul pictures his own life being poured out over the sacrifice of their faith (2:17).
A newborn Jewish boy was circumcised on the eighth day.
Paul pictures a runner straining toward the finish (3:13-14). Greek games gave a wreath to the winner, as at the nearby Isthmian Games.
The language of the sacrifices at the Temple.
A register of those who belong to God (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28). City rolls of citizens give a picture of what such a book meant.

Revelation speaks of the book of life six times (3:5; 13:8; 17:8; 20:12, 15; 21:27): names written from the foundation of the world, never erased for the one who overcomes, and the list of those who enter the new Jerusalem.

In Israel the firstborn son held the place of honor and received a double share of the inheritance (Deuteronomy 21:17). Psalm 89:27 calls the king God’s firstborn. Paul uses the word for Christ’s rank over creation (1:15).
The geographer Strabo says the Laodicea area had sheep with fine dark wool and that a color of wool was named for Colossae (12.8.16).
The Greek word in 2:14 means a handwritten record of debt. Papyrus IOUs could be canceled by crossing them out, and Paul says God wiped out the record and nailed it to the cross.
Paul pictures taking off the old self and putting on the new, like a change of clothes (3:9-10). Later churches gave new white robes at baptism, which is later than Paul.
Most people heard letters read in groups.

Inscriptions from Roman Thessalonica name cults of Dionysus, Sarapis, Zeus Hypsistos and others. Paul says the believers “turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God” (1:9), a break that probably cost them a place in the civic and family religion around them.
The Greek verb in 1:10 means to wait for or await someone. Paul describes the believers as people who serve God now while they wait for His Son from heaven.

Paul compares himself to a nursing mother caring for her own children (2:7) and, a few verses later, to a father who encourages and urges each child (2:11). Early manuscripts differ in 2:7 between “gentle” and “infants,” which changes the first picture.

Paul writes, “now we really live, if you are standing firm in the Lord” (3:8). The verb means to stand fast or hold one’s ground. He uses it for steadiness in several letters (1 Corinthians 16:13; Philippians 4:1; 2 Thessalonians 2:15).

Paul fears “the tempter” had tested them and his work would be in vain (3:5). In 2:18 he blames “Satan” for hindering his return. The Gospels use the same title for the devil who tempted Jesus (Matthew 4:3).

The Greek word in 4:17 (apantēsis) means a meeting. Some scholars think it pictures a city’s delegation going out to greet a visiting dignitary and escort him back. Others doubt that the word was a fixed term. Paul’s own picture is of being caught up “to meet the Lord in the air.”

Paul speaks of believers who “have fallen asleep” (4:13-15). Greek writers already used sleep for death, and Jesus used it of Lazarus (John 11:11). In these letters Paul uses it of believers, and the picture comes with waking.

“The day of the Lord will come just like a thief in the night” (5:2). Jesus used the same picture (Matthew 24:43; Luke 12:39). A thief gives no warning, so Paul tells believers to stay awake and sober (5:6).
The Greek word translated “rest” in 1:7 (anesis) means relief or easing. Paul uses it of relief from trouble in 2 Corinthians 2:13, 7:5 and 8:13.

In 1:5 the believers are “considered worthy of the kingdom of God,” and in 1:11 Paul prays that God would count them worthy of His calling. He ties it all to the grace of our God and the Lord Jesus (1:12).

Paul says “you know what is restraining him now” (2:6) because he told them in person (2:5), and he does not write it down. Readers have proposed Roman rule, the preaching of the gospel, the Spirit or an angel, but the text does not settle it.

Paul says that because people refused the love of the truth, God sends them a deluding influence so that they believe the lie (2:10-11). Compare the lying spirit sent to the prophets of Ahab in 1 Kings 22:22.

In Greek and Roman cities wealthy patrons supported dependents who gave them honor and service. Some scholars think the idle believers were leaning on rich members of the church in this way. Paul tells them instead to earn their own bread (3:12).

Paul tells Timothy to stop some people from devoting themselves to “myths and endless genealogies” (1:4) but does not say what these were. Suggestions include Jewish speculation about the patriarchs’ family lines, as in the book of Jubilees, and Greek stories about the founding of cities; Ephesus had its own legendary founder, Androclus. Scholars cannot tell which, if any, Paul has in view.

Paul says some have “shipwrecked” their faith (1:19) and names Hymenaeus and Alexander (1:20). He knew the sea well: he lists three shipwrecks in 2 Corinthians 11:25, and Acts 27 tells of another. Here the word is a picture of faith wrecked.

Paul wants men in every place to pray “lifting up holy hands” (2:8). Standing with the hands raised was the usual way to pray among Jews and Greeks (Psalm 28:2; 134:2), and early Christian art shows people praying this way. He adds that the prayer should be free of anger and quarreling.

Paul says women should dress with modesty and self-control, “not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothing” (2:9). First Peter 3:3 gives a similar warning. Writers such as Plutarch also criticize lavish display, and portraits of Roman women of the later 1st century show tall, built-up hairstyles. Paul sets the display against good works (2:10).

“The husband of one wife” (3:2) is debated. The Greek says literally “of one woman a man.” It may mean faithful to one spouse, no polygamy, not remarried after divorce, or not remarried after a wife’s death. First Timothy 5:9 uses the matching phrase for widows, “the wife of one husband.”

Paul says a man who cannot manage his own household well cannot care for God’s church (3:4-5). Churches met in homes (Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19), and 3:15 calls the church the household of God.

Paul tells Timothy to devote himself to “the public reading of Scripture, to exhortation, and to teaching” (4:13). Synagogues read the Law and the Prophets aloud (Luke 4:16-20; Acts 13:15), and Paul expected his letters to be read aloud to churches (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27).

No widow is to be “enrolled” unless she is at least sixty, “the wife of one husband,” and known for good works (5:9-10). The letter does not say what the list was for. It may have been a roll of widows receiving support, a group with a service role, or both. Scholars differ. Younger widows are told to marry (5:11-14).

Paul tells Timothy to “stop drinking only water” and to use “a little wine” for his stomach and frequent illnesses (5:23). Wine was an ordinary drink, usually mixed with water, and ancient doctors prescribed it for stomach complaints. The verse is a personal note that sits between lines on purity (5:22) and on sins that are plain or hidden (5:24-25).

Paul bursts into praise of “the King of kings and Lord of lords,” who “dwells in unapproachable light” (6:15-16). The same titles appear for Christ in Revelation 17:14 and 19:16. “King of kings” was a title of Persian and other eastern rulers; Paul gives it to God.
Jude 24-25 is one of the fullest doxologies in the New Testament: glory, majesty, dominion and authority are given to “the only God our Savior” “through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

Paul asks Timothy not to be ashamed of the testimony about the Lord or of Paul, His prisoner (1:8), and he praises Onesiphorus for not being ashamed of his chains (1:16). Being in chains carried public disgrace, so standing by a prisoner could cost a person his good name. The letter also says Onesiphorus had to search for Paul in Rome (1:17).

Paul asks Timothy to endure hardship like a good soldier (2:3) and says a soldier avoids civilian entanglements to please the one who enlisted him (2:4). Paul also calls Epaphroditus and Archippus “fellow soldier” (Philippians 2:25; Philemon 2). Roman soldiers swore an oath and lived under strict military discipline.

Paul says an athlete is crowned only if he competes according to the rules (2:5). Greek games had strict rules and officials. The Greek travel writer Pausanias (2nd century AD) says athletes at Olympia swore they had trained for ten months. Paul does not mention that; his point is that the prize goes to the one who keeps the rules.

Paul says Timothy has known the Holy Scriptures “from infancy” (3:15). Jewish writers such as Philo and Josephus say that children were taught the Law from their earliest years. The likely teachers were Timothy’s mother and grandmother (1:5), though the letter does not say so.

Paul says some will hold “a form of godliness” but deny its power (3:5). The phrase comes at the end of a long list of vices (3:2-4) that begins with lovers of self and lovers of money. The word “form” means outward shape or appearance.

Paul asks Timothy to bring the cloak he left with Carpus at Troas (4:13). The Greek word for cloak is rare, and it is used for a heavy outer garment. Paul also asks Timothy to come before winter (4:21), which may be why he wants it. The letter does not say why he left it at Troas.

Paul asks for his scrolls, “especially the parchments” (4:13). Parchments were sheets of animal skin, and they may have been notebooks. The letter does not say what the books and parchments were; suggestions include Scripture scrolls and Paul’s own papers.

Paul tells Titus to rebuke those who pay attention to Jewish myths and the commands of men who have rejected the truth (1:14), and then says that to the pure all things are pure (1:15). The letter does not list the rules. The mention of those “of the circumcision” (1:10) and of what is defiled suggests that purity and food rules were part of the dispute.

Slaves are to “adorn the teaching about God our Savior” (2:10). The Greek verb kosmeo means to put in order or to decorate, and it is also used for jewelry and dress (1 Peter 3:5). Slaves with no say in their circumstances are called to make the gospel attractive by honest, faithful work.

Christ gave Himself “to redeem us from all lawlessness” (2:14). The Greek verb is from the word family for a ransom price paid to free a captive or a slave. The Old Testament uses the idea for God’s freeing Israel from Egypt (Deuteronomy 7:8).

Titus 3:5 says God saved us through “the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit,” and not by the righteous deeds we had done. Many readers see baptism here, but the verse does not use the word, and some see the washing as the cleansing that comes with new birth.

Titus is to reject a divisive man after a first and second admonition (3:10). The Greek word hairetikos comes from a word meaning to choose, so it first meant someone who picks a party. The meaning “heretic” grew up later in church history.

The letter does not use the word “runaway.” It says Onesimus was parted from Philemon “for a while” (verse 15) and that he may have wronged him or owes him something (verse 18). Most readers take him to be a fugitive. An owner could have a runaway hunted down and punished harshly, and a person who sheltered one could be accused of theft. Some scholars think Onesimus went to Paul as a friend of his master to ask him to plead for him, but the letter does not say how he came to Paul.
To sit at the king’s right hand was to share his honor and rule (1 Kings 2:19; Psalm 110:1). Hebrews says the Son sat down there after he made purification for sins.
The Greek word charaktēr comes from the engraver’s tool and the mark it leaves, as on a coin or seal. The Son is the exact representation of God’s being (1:3).
The verb in 2:1 pictures something slipping past unnoticed, like a boat that drifts by the harbor because no one is paying attention.
The word in 2:10 (archēgos) can mean founder, leader or pioneer: someone who goes ahead and opens the way for others. It returns in 12:2.
The word “today” in Psalm 95 means that the time to respond is always now. The writer tells his readers to encourage one another daily “as long as it is called today” (3:13).
In Greek, a “house” can mean a household or family. Moses was a servant within the household. The Son is over it, as its builder and heir (3:2-6).
The word of God is said to be sharper than any double-edged sword (4:12). The Roman short sword, the gladius, was sharp on both edges and had a point.

The rare word in verse 13 (tetrachēlismena) comes from the word for “neck.” Scholars explain it as a wrestler’s hold that bends the head back, or as an animal’s neck held back for the knife. Either way, nothing is hidden from God.
A picture of infants and adults.
Priests did not choose their office.
People swore by something greater. God swore by himself.
In Jesus’ day people backed their words with oaths by heaven, the temple or the altar (Matthew 5:33-37; 23:16-22). James repeats the command to let a plain yes and no be enough (5:12).
A scout who ran ahead to prepare the way.
A tenth of the spoils was given to the priest.
The priesthood of Jesus was established with an oath.
Shadows show a shape without substance.
Contrasts with writing on stone tablets.
At Sinai Moses sprinkled the book and the people with blood (Exodus 24:6-8). Hebrews 9:19-21 adds that the tent and its vessels were sprinkled too.
The Greek word diathēkē means both “covenant” and “will.” Hebrews 9:16-17 plays on the second meaning: a will takes effect only when the one who made it has died.
The Greek word in verse 24 (paroxysmos) means to provoke or spur on. It is also used of sharp disagreement (Acts 15:39). Here believers are to provoke one another to love and good works.
Some had given up meeting (10:25), perhaps out of fear, since being seen with a persecuted group could cost a person dearly.
The walls fell after the people had marched around them for seven days (11:30). Excavators have disagreed for a century about what the Late Bronze Age city looked like at that time.
Greek foot races were run in a stadium before crowds. The writer pictures a runner who lays aside every weight, with a “great cloud of witnesses” around him.
The word paideia means the whole upbringing of a child. A Roman father held legal authority over his children, and discipline was a sign that a child was accepted as his own (12:5-11).
The writer says worship takes the place of animal sacrifice: the fruit of lips that give thanks to his name, doing good, and sharing (13:15-16).

Pliny the Elder (Natural History 33) says that in Rome the right to wear a gold ring marked rank: first senators, later the equestrian order. A visitor wearing one would look important, which is the point of James 2:2.
James says the rich oppress the poor and drag them into court (2:6). Debt and lawsuits were common, and the Law warned against taking advantage of the poor (Exodus 22:25-27; Deuteronomy 24:12-15).
A horse was steered by a bit in its mouth, and a ship by a steering oar at the stern. James uses both as pictures of a small part that directs a large body (3:3-4).
James asks whether a fig tree can grow olives, a grapevine figs, or a salt spring produce fresh water (3:12). Jesus also used trees and their fruit to show what a person is like (Matthew 7:16-20).
The Greek word atmis means vapor, steam or smoke. Hosea 13:3 uses similar pictures for things that quickly vanish: morning mist, early dew, chaff and smoke. James says that life is like this (4:14).
To cleanse the hands and purify the heart, and to be wretched, mourn and weep (4:8-9), is the language of repentance in the prophets (Isaiah 1:15-17; Joel 2:12-13).
The prophets often described Israel’s unfaithfulness to God as adultery (Hosea 2:2-5; Jeremiah 3:6-10; Ezekiel 16). James uses the same picture for believers who make friends with the world.

Olive oil was used on wounds (Luke 10:34), and the Twelve anointed many sick people with oil (Mark 6:13). James tells the elders to pray over the sick person and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord (5:14). Whether the oil is medicine, a sign, or both is debated.
The early rain of autumn softened the ground for planting, and the late rain of spring filled out the grain (Deuteronomy 11:14; Jeremiah 5:24). A farmer could do nothing to hurry them.
Gold was purified in fire and tested.
An unblemished animal was required.
Public respect was central to Roman society.
Fashion of wealthy women.
The Greek word apologia is the origin of “apologetics.”
Greek and Roman parties.
The same word is used of refining.
Daily routine of leading, feeding, and guarding the flock.

The letter closes its warning with two proverbs: “A dog returns to its vomit,” and, “A sow that is washed goes back to her wallowing in the mud” (2:22). The first is from Proverbs 26:11. The second is not in the Old Testament; a similar saying about a washed pig appears in the Story of Ahikar, a wisdom tale that was read widely in the ancient Near East. Dogs and pigs were unclean animals to Jews, and “dogs” was also a word for outsiders (compare Philippians 3:2).
Both proverbs describe an animal that goes back to what it was. They are used of people who have “escaped the corruption of the world” (2:20) and then returned to it.

e.n: Paper and ink: a letter on one sheet
t: The writer says “I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with paper and ink. Instead, I hope to come and speak with you face to face, so that our joy may be complete” (12). The “paper” is a sheet of papyrus, the writing material of the day, made from the pith of a reed; the “ink” was a black mix of soot and gum that was made up as needed and could be washed off. A letter of about 245 Greek words, as this one is, would fit on a single sheet. The phrase “face to face” is, in the Greek, “mouth to mouth,” the ordinary way of speaking of a talk in person.

A letter in this world was carried by a friend, who often added the news and could answer questions. The letter itself was a stand-in for the writer, and many writers of the time said they would rather be present. 3 John 13-14 has nearly the same words, with “pen” for “paper.” Paul sometimes added a closing line in his own hand, and the papyrus letters found in Egypt show a scribe writing and the sender adding a line at the end.
In 3 John 13 the words are “pen and ink.” The pen (kalamos) was a reed cut to a point; see the entry on pen and ink in 3 John.

“You will do well to send them on their way in a manner worthy of God” (6). The Greek verb, propempō, is a set term in the New Testament for equipping a traveler for the next stage of a journey: food, money, letters, sometimes a companion or a guide to the next town. The church at Antioch sent Paul and Barnabas on their way (Acts 15:3), Paul hoped Rome would do it for him on his way to Spain (Romans 15:24), and he asked Titus to see that Zenas and Apollos lacked nothing (Titus 3:13).

Travel was slow and inns had a bad name, so a traveler relied on friends, or on friends of friends, from town to town. A Christian worker who took nothing from outsiders (7) relied on the believers entirely. “In a manner worthy of God” sets the measure: they are to be treated as God’s own messengers. Jesus said that whoever receives the one he sends receives him (John 13:20).

e.n: A word for the bearer: Demetrius and letters of recommendation
t: “Demetrius has received a good testimony from everyone, and from the truth itself. We also testify for him, and you know that our testimony is true” (12). A stranger arriving in a town needed someone to vouch for him, and the usual way was a letter from a person the host knew. Many such notes survive on papyrus; one from about AD 25 asks an official to look after the bearer, the writer’s brother. Paul commends Phoebe to Rome in the same way (Romans 16:1-2) and speaks of letters of recommendation in 2 Corinthians 3:1.

Verse 12 does this for Demetrius, who was most likely carrying the letter and may have been one of the brothers Diotrephes would not receive. Three voices speak for him: everyone, the truth itself, and the elder’s own circle. “The truth itself” probably means that his life agrees with the message, so that the truth, so to speak, takes the stand for him. The last words are close to what the Gospel of John says of the disciple who wrote it, that his testimony is true (John 19:35; 21:24).

e.n: Pen and ink, and greetings by name
t: “I have many things to write to you, but I would prefer not to do so with pen and ink. Instead, I hope to see you soon and speak with you face to face” (13-14). The pen (kalamos) was a reed cut to a point and split, dipped in black ink made of soot and gum. The same wish closes 2 John, with “paper and ink.” A letter was thought of as a poor stand-in for a visit, and what the elder had to say about Diotrephes was better said in person.

The close has three short lines. “Peace to you” is the Jewish greeting, the word of the risen Jesus to his disciples (John 20:19). “The friends here send you greetings” uses a name for believers that is rare in the New Testament. “Greet each of our friends there by name” asks Gaius to go to each one, as papyrus letters often ask, and it shows how small and close the circle was. Many Bibles number these lines as verse 15.

Jude says the intruders are “hidden reefs in your love feasts, shamelessly feasting with you but shepherding only themselves” (12). The love feast (Greek agapē, the ordinary word for love) was the common meal of an early church. Believers gathered in a home, each brought what they could, rich and poor ate together, and the bread and cup of the Lord’s Supper were shared at the same table. Acts 2:46 shows the first believers breaking bread from house to house, and Paul corrects a church where the rich ate well while the poor went hungry (1 Corinthians 11:20-22).

Jude 12 is the one place in the New Testament where the meal is plainly called by this name; some copies of 2 Peter 2:13 have it too. Ignatius, about AD 110, and Tertullian, about AD 197, describe it. Over time the Lord’s Supper was separated from the meal, and church councils of the 4th century restricted love feasts in church buildings. At a table meant to show love, Jude’s intruders came to feed themselves.

Revelation begins with a blessing: “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and obey what is written in it, because the time is near” (1:3). The one who reads and those who hear are different people. Few could read, and books were costly, so a letter was read aloud by one person to the whole gathered church, as Paul expected his letters to be (Colossians 4:16; 1 Thessalonians 5:27).

Revelation was written to be heard in one sitting, with its sounds, repetitions and songs. It holds seven blessings in all (1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7; 22:14). The first and the sixth both bless those who keep what is written: the book is meant to be obeyed, not only decoded.

e.n: The white stone and the new name
t: To the church in Pergamum Christ promises, “To the one who overcomes, I will give the hidden manna. I will also give him a white stone inscribed with a new name, known only to the one who receives it” (2:17). In the Greek and Roman world small stones and tokens had many uses. Jurors voted to acquit with a white stone; tokens of stone or metal were used as tickets to feasts and games; some people wore stones inscribed with secret names as charms.

Readers have proposed each of these. The stone may be a verdict of acquittal, an invitation to the messianic banquet (with the hidden manna), or a pledge of a new identity known only to God and the one who receives it. The new name may be the believer’s own or the name of Christ (3:12; 19:12). The promise answers the pressure of a city where eating at idol feasts was the price of belonging (2:14).

e.n: A scroll sealed with seven seals
t: In the right hand of the one on the throne John sees a scroll that “had writing on both sides and was sealed with seven seals” (5:1). Writing was usually on one side only, so a scroll written inside and out was packed full. Important documents were closed with clay or wax seals; Roman wills were sealed by seven witnesses and could be opened only by the right person. Ezekiel saw a scroll written on front and back with laments and mourning (Ezekiel 2:9-10), and Daniel was told to seal up his book until the time of the end (Daniel 12:4).

Many take the scroll as God’s plan for history and for the redemption of the world, which only the slain Lamb is worthy to open. Some see it as a deed or will, the title to creation, or as the book of the covenant. As each seal is broken something happens, so the opening of the scroll and the events of history are bound together.

When Babylon falls, the merchants of the earth weep, because no one buys their cargo any more, and John lists it: gold, silver, jewels and pearls; fine linen, purple, silk and scarlet; scented wood and ivory, bronze, iron and marble; cinnamon, spice, incense, myrrh and frankincense; wine, olive oil, fine flour and wheat; cattle, sheep, horses and carriages; and at the end, the bodies and souls of human beings (18:11-13). The list follows the luxury trade that poured into Rome through the harbor at Ostia and the port of Puteoli.

The list draws on Ezekiel 27, the lament over the trading city of Tyre. Ending with human beings, John puts slaves last of all, after the animals. The kings, merchants and seafarers mourn from a distance, not for the city but for their profits (18:9-19). The chapter is a warning to the churches about sharing in a wealth built on idolatry and oppression: “Come out of her, My people” (18:4).

e.n: Laodicea: gold, white garments and eye salve
t: Christ says to Laodicea, “You say, ‘I am rich; I have grown wealthy and need nothing.’ But you do not realize that you are wretched, pitiful, poor, blind, and naked” (3:17), and he counsels the church to buy from him gold refined by fire, white garments, and salve for their eyes (3:18). Laodicea was a banking city; when an earthquake destroyed it in AD 60, Tacitus says, it rebuilt itself from its own resources without help from Rome. It was known for a soft black wool and for a medical school, and the geographer Strabo mentions a Phrygian eye powder.

Each part of the counsel answers something the city was proud of: its money, its cloth and its medicine. The famous lines about being lukewarm (3:15-16) are often explained by the city’s water, piped in from springs some miles away and arriving tepid, unlike the hot springs of nearby Hierapolis or the cold water of Colossae. The church thought itself rich; Christ stands outside its door and knocks (3:20).

Whenever the living creatures give glory to the one on the throne, the twenty-four elders fall down, worship him, and lay their crowns before the throne, saying, “Worthy are You, our Lord and God, to receive glory and honor and power, for You created all things” (4:10-11). In the Roman world a defeated or client king laid his crown before the emperor to show who ruled; in AD 66 the Parthian prince Tiridates knelt before Nero in Rome and received his crown from Nero’s hands.

The elders’ crowns are the victor’s wreath (stephanos), not a ruler’s diadem. Laying them down says that every honor they have comes from God. The cry “Worthy are You” also echoes the acclamations shouted to emperors as they entered a city; in heaven it is given to God and to the Lamb (5:9, 12).

Teachers who insisted Gentile believers must be circumcised.
Paul says the Philippians sent help more than once while he was in Thessalonica (4:15-16). He also says Macedonian believers supplied his needs in Corinth (2 Corinthians 11:9).

Tacitus says Laodicea was destroyed by an earthquake in Nero’s reign, about AD 60, and rebuilt from its own funds (Annals 14.27). Some later writers add Hierapolis and Colossae. The letter does not mention it.

The letter never names the teachers. It points to food, festivals and Sabbaths (2:16), visions and the worship of angels (2:18), and a “philosophy” of human tradition (2:8). Scholars still debate where it came from.
Greeks used barbarian for people who did not speak Greek and often thought of Scythians, from north of the Black Sea, as especially wild. Paul names both to show that no one is outside Christ (3:11).
Luke is called the beloved physician (4:14). Mark, the cousin of Barnabas (4:10), is usually identified with John Mark, who left Paul and Barnabas in Acts 13:13.

Thessalonica was a free Greek city that honored Rome and its rulers. Bronze coins of the city from the reign of Augustus show Julius Caesar with the legend THEOS, “god,” on one side and Augustus on the other.

Revelation is the New Testament book most shaped by the worship of the emperors. Five of the seven churches stood in cities with imperial temples, and the second beast makes the earth worship the first beast and its image (13:12-15).

Acts 17:5-9 says some Jews, jealous of Paul’s success, gathered men from the marketplace and a mob, attacked Jason’s house, and dragged him and others before the politarchs. Paul says the believers suffered “from your own countrymen” (2:14), so the pressure came from fellow citizens and not only from Jews.

Paul says he tried more than once to return, but “Satan hindered us” (2:18). Acts 17:9 says Jason and the others had to post bond. Some scholars think that bond kept Paul away, but he does not say what the hindrance was.

e.n: Death in Greek and Roman Thought
t: Greek and Roman writers describe death in many ways. Epicureans held that death was the end, many expected a shadowy afterlife, and some philosophers thought the soul lives on. Paul says the Thessalonians must not grieve “as the rest do who have no hope” (4:13).

Paul says God’s will is their holiness, so they are to abstain from sexual immorality (4:3). In the Roman world, men were widely allowed sex outside marriage with slaves and prostitutes, while Jewish teaching, and the church after it, held to marriage. The Greek of 4:4 can mean controlling one’s own body or taking a wife.

Rome presented its rule as bringing peace. Scholars disagree about “peace and security” in 5:3. Some hear Roman propaganda, while others hear the prophets’ warnings against false peace (Jeremiah 6:14; Ezekiel 13:10) and doubt it was a fixed Roman slogan.

Paul tells them not to “quench the Spirit” or “treat prophecies with contempt,” and to “test all things” (5:19-21). Prophecy was a gift of the Spirit in his churches (1 Corinthians 14), and what was said was to be weighed.
Paul praises their endurance in “all your persecutions and afflictions” (1:4). The pressure that began in Acts 17 had not ended, and the letter does not say who was applying it.
Paul says it is just for God to repay affliction to those who afflict them and to give relief to those who suffer (1:6-7). The wording of 1:8-9 echoes Isaiah (66:15; 2:10, 19).

About AD 40 the emperor Caligula ordered a statue of himself set up in the Jerusalem Temple. The governor Petronius delayed, and Caligula was killed in AD 41 before it was done (Josephus, Antiquities 18). Some readers think this memory shaped 2:4. Paul does not mention it.

Paul warns them not to be shaken by a letter “as if from us” saying the day of the Lord has come (2:2), and says he signs every letter himself (3:17). Some scholars think 2 Thessalonians itself was written by someone else. Others defend Paul as the author.

Paul tells the church to keep away from those living “in idleness” (3:6, 11). The letter does not say why they were idle. Readers suggest excitement about the Lord’s return, dependence on patrons, or contempt for manual work.
Paul writes the closing greeting himself and calls it “the sign in every letter” (3:17). He does the same in 1 Corinthians 16:21, Galatians 6:11 and Colossians 4:18.

Paul asks first for prayers for all people, including kings and all in authority (2:1-2). Jews prayed for foreign rulers (Jeremiah 29:7; Ezra 6:10), and Josephus says sacrifices for the emperor were offered in the Jerusalem Temple until they were stopped in AD 66. Early Christian writers such as Tertullian say believers prayed for the emperor.

Inscriptions from the cities of Roman Asia, Ephesus among them, name women who held civic and religious titles, paid for buildings and games, and were honored with statues. Wealthy women were visible in public life, which is part of the setting scholars raise for 2:9-15. How it bears on the instructions about teaching and authority in 2:12 is debated.

In Acts 20:17 and 20:28 Paul calls the same Ephesian leaders “elders” and “overseers,” and Titus 1:5-7 uses the two words for the same office. Here (3:1-7) he lists what an overseer must be. The letter does not say how many served in a church or how their work was divided.

The Greek word diakonos means servant. Paul uses it of Phoebe in Romans 16:1, and Philippians 1:1 greets the “overseers and deacons” together. First Timothy 3:8-13 gives their qualifications but not their duties.

Paul tells Timothy, “Let no one despise your youth” (4:12). Writers of the time used words for “youth” of men well into their thirties. Timothy was already a disciple when Paul first met him (Acts 16:1-3), so he could have been in his thirties when this letter was written, but no source gives his age.

Paul says elders who lead well are worthy of “double honor” (5:17). The word for honor was also used for payment, and in 5:18 he cites Deuteronomy 25:4 about the ox and a saying about workers deserving their wages (compare Luke 10:7). That fits support. Whether “double” means twice the pay, twice the respect or simply generous honor is unclear.

Ephesus was one of the busiest ports and commercial centers of Roman Asia, and ancient writers say the temple of Artemis held deposits like a bank. Paul warns about teachers who think godliness is “a means of gain” (6:5) and about those who want to be rich (6:9-10). The letter does not accuse any named person of greed.

Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he heard from Paul among many witnesses to faithful people who will be able to teach others as well (2:2). That makes four stages in handing on the message: Paul, Timothy, the faithful people, and those they teach.

Paul reminds Timothy of the persecutions and sufferings he met at Antioch, Iconium and Lystra (3:11). Acts 13:50, 14:5 and 14:19 tell of them, and at Lystra Paul was stoned and dragged out of the city. Timothy came from that region (Acts 16:1-2).

Acts 2:11 lists Cretans among the people in Jerusalem who heard the apostles at Pentecost. Acts does not record a mission to Crete. The only visit it tells of is Paul’s ship putting in at Fair Havens on the way to Rome (Acts 27:7-13). Titus 1:5 says Paul left Titus in Crete to set in order what was unfinished and to appoint elders in every town, so the work there came at some other time.

Greek writers such as Aristotle set out the duties of each person in a household. Titus 2:1-10 gives short duties for older men and women, younger women and men, and slaves, and ties each to the gospel: so that the word of God will not be discredited (2:5) and so that slaves may adorn the teaching about God our Savior (2:10).

Paul says the grace of God “has appeared” (2:11) and looks for the “glorious appearance” of our great God and Savior Jesus Christ (2:13). The Greek word epiphaneia was used in the Greek world for the arrival of a ruler or a god’s help. Antiochus IV took the title Epiphanes, “God Manifest.”

Augustus founded Nicopolis, the City of Victory, about 31-29 BC after his victory at Actium. Titus 3:12 asks Titus to come to Paul there because Paul has decided to winter there. Several cities were named Nicopolis, and the letter does not say which; the one in Epirus on the Ionian coast is the usual guess.

Titus is told to equip Zenas the lawyer and Apollos so they have everything they need (3:13). Apollos is known from Acts 18:24-28 and 1 Corinthians 1:12; 3:4-6; 16:12. Zenas is named only here. The Greek word for lawyer could mean an expert in either Jewish or Roman law.

Slaves were a large part of the Roman world. Historians’ estimates vary a great deal, often putting slaves at roughly one in ten to one in five of the empire’s people, and more in Italy and the big cities. The law treated a slave as the owner’s property. Slaves could be freed, and many freed slaves stayed close to their former owners. Philemon is a slave owner, since Paul speaks of Onesimus as his slave (verse 16), and Paul asks him to receive Onesimus “no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.”

In Jewish tradition the law was given through angels (Acts 7:53; Galatians 3:19). So the writer first shows that the Son is above the angels, then that he is above Moses and the priests who served under the law.

The letter quotes the Old Testament in its Greek form (the Septuagint) almost every time. Some quotations, such as the one in 1:6, follow the Greek wording and not the Hebrew. This fits readers who read Greek, in a city where Jews used the Greek Bible.

Writers of the time, such as the Epicurean poet Lucretius, argued at length against the fear of death, which suggests how common it was. Hebrews 2:15 says that Jesus frees those who were held in slavery by this fear.
Verse 17 is the first time the letter calls Jesus a high priest. He became “merciful and faithful” by sharing flesh and blood and by being tempted, so he can help those who are tempted (2:18).
Israel wandered forty years because of unbelief at Kadesh (Numbers 14:33-34). Hebrews 3:17 recalls those “whose bodies fell in the wilderness.”
God said Moses was faithful in all his house (Numbers 12:7). Hebrews grants this, then says a builder has more honor than the house, and a son over the house more than a servant in it (3:2-6).
Ancient Israel hoped for rest from enemies and from labor. Hebrews links the promise in Psalm 95 with God’s own rest on the seventh day (Genesis 2:2).
Verse 7 speaks of prayers “with loud cries and tears” in the days of his flesh. Many readers connect this with Gethsemane (Mark 14:32-42), though the letter does not name the place.

Hebrews 6:4-8 is one of several warnings in the letter (2:1-4; 3:7-4:13; 10:26-31; 12:25-29). Readers have understood it in different ways: as a warning about believers losing salvation, about people who looked like believers but never were, or about loss of reward. The writer follows it at once with confidence of “better things” (6:9).
Mediterranean ships carried several anchors. In Acts 27:29-30 the ship carrying Paul dropped four from the stern in a storm.
Probably Jerusalem (Psalm 76:2).
They died, so the office passed on. Jesus lives forever.

Hebrews says priests “offer gifts according to the law” (8:4), in the present tense. Some take this to mean that the temple still stood when the letter was written. Others think the writer is describing the system as Scripture sets it out and not what was happening at the time.
The new covenant was promised by Jeremiah in the early 6th century BC, around the time the temple fell to Babylon (Jeremiah 31:31-34).

Hebrews 9:4 lists the golden jar of manna, Aaron’s staff that budded and the tablets of the covenant as being in the ark. 1 Kings 8:9 mentions only the two tablets in Solomon’s time. After the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC the Bible does not say what became of the ark.
The ashes of a red heifer, mixed with water, were used to purify those made unclean by contact with a dead body (Numbers 19). Hebrews 9:13 says the blood of Christ does more.
The readers were publicly exposed to abuse (the word in verse 33 means being put on display, as in a theater), shared the sufferings of prisoners and had their property seized (10:32-34).

If the readers were in Rome, the earlier suffering might point to the troubles under Claudius, who expelled Jews from Rome about AD 49 (Suetonius, Claudius 25.4; Acts 18:2). This is a guess. The letter names neither the place nor the date.
Abraham lived in tents and never owned the land except a burial plot (Genesis 23). Hebrews 11:13-16 says the faithful were looking for a better country, a heavenly one.

Verses 35-38 speak of people tortured, mocked, stoned, sawn in two, killed with the sword, and living in caves. Many readers link 11:35 to the martyrs of 2 Maccabees 6-7. Being sawed in two matches a Jewish tradition about the prophet Isaiah, which the letter does not name.

Revelation honors those killed for their witness: Antipas (2:13), the souls under the altar (6:9-11), the two witnesses (11:7), and those beheaded for the testimony of Jesus who reign with Christ (20:4).
Esau sold his birthright for a meal (Genesis 25:29-34) and later found no way to change what he had done, though he sought the blessing with tears (12:16-17).
At Sinai the people begged that no further word be spoken to them (Exodus 20:19; Deuteronomy 5:25), which Hebrews 12:19 recalls.
The phrase “those from Italy send you greetings” (13:24) can mean Italians who are with the writer away from Italy, or believers in Italy. So it does not settle where the letter was sent from or to.

Paul calls James the Lord’s brother and names him with Cephas and John as one who seemed to be a pillar of the church in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:19; 2:9). Josephus (Antiquities 20.200) says that a high priest named Ananus had James stoned, about AD 62.
In Jesus’ day leading people loved the best seats in the synagogues (Luke 11:43; Matthew 23:6). James uses the same kind of scene to show a church repeating the world’s ranking.

Abraham was the father of the Jewish people, and Rahab was a Canaanite woman of Jericho who is called a prostitute in Joshua 2:1. James puts them side by side as people whose faith showed in what they did (2:21-25).
Teaching was honored work in the early church (1 Corinthians 12:28; Acts 13:1). James warns that those who teach will be judged more strictly (3:1), and he ties the warning to the tongue.
James traces fights among believers to desires that war inside them (4:1-3) and warns against speaking against one another (4:11-12). He does not say what the fights were about.

James imagines traders who say they will go to a city, spend a year there, do business and make a profit (4:13). Roman roads and Mediterranean sea routes made such journeys common for people with money to risk.
The Law said a day laborer must be paid before sunset (Deuteronomy 24:14-15; Leviticus 19:13). James says the wages that were held back are crying out (5:4), as Abel’s blood did (Genesis 4:10).

First Kings 17-18 tells how Elijah prayed for drought and for rain. James says it did not rain for three and a half years (5:17), and Luke 4:25 gives the same figure. First Kings 18:1 says the rain came in the third year, so the numbers are counted in different ways.
Peter writes at a time when Christians faced growing hostility.
Roman provinces in modern Turkey.
Roman temples were built of cut stone, and Peter says the church is God’s temple.
Household servants had little protection.
Whether to the dead, to fallen angels, or to Noah’s generation is debated.
Used in Antioch (Acts 11:26) and in Nero’s time as a charge.
Social events usually included idol worship.
Probably Rome, a code name for the capital.

In Revelation “Babylon the great” is the city of luxury, idolatry and persecution whose fall is announced in 14:8 and described in chapters 17-18. Most readers see Rome behind the name, as 1 Peter 5:13 already uses it; others see a future world city or a picture of every society set against God.
John Mark, who traveled with Paul and later with Peter.

e.n: Tartarus and the chains of darkness
t: Peter writes, “if God did not spare the angels when they sinned, but cast them deep into hell, placing them in chains of darkness to be held for judgment” (2:4). The verb behind “cast them deep into hell” (tartaroo) comes from Tartarus, the deep prison beneath the underworld in Greek myth, where the Titans were bound. It is found only here in the New Testament. Jesus’ word for hell, Gehenna, is a different word from a valley by Jerusalem.

The letter does not say which angels or what they did. Most readers link the verse to Genesis 6:1-4 and the Jewish Book of Enoch, in which rebel angels are bound in darkness until the judgment, as the Dead Sea Scrolls show was known in Israel. Jude 6 tells almost the same story. Some take it to speak of the fall of Satan and his angels, and 1 Peter 3:19-20 is often read beside it.
Jude 6 does not use the word Tartarus. It speaks of “eternal chains under darkness,” and its word for darkness (zophos) is the gloom of the underworld in Greek poetry.

e.n: Nero and the legend of his return
t: The emperor Nero killed himself in AD 68, and the empire fell into a year of civil war. Rumors soon spread that he was not dead, or that he would come back from the East at the head of a Parthian army. Tacitus and Suetonius tell of men who claimed to be Nero and drew followers, one as late as about AD 88, and Jewish writings of the time also speak of Nero’s return.

Many scholars think Revelation alludes to this legend: the beast has a fatal wound that was healed (13:3), and the beast “was, and now is no more, but is about to come up out of the Abyss” (17:8), with kings from the East and the Euphrates in the background (9:14; 16:12). If so, John takes a rumor his readers knew and turns it into a picture of evil that seems defeated and keeps returning. Other readers see no allusion to Nero and read these passages of a future ruler or of the persistence of evil.
Matthew, Mark and Luke, which share much of the same material and can be read side by side (“seen together”). John is quite different in structure and content.

Passages where two or more Gospels tell the same story. Reading them side by side shows what each writer includes, leaves out or emphasizes. The Parallels tab in the Study section puts them next to each other.

A hypothetical collection of Jesus’ sayings, from the German Quelle (“source”), proposed by some scholars to explain material found in both Matthew and Luke but not in Mark. It is a theory: no copy of Q has been found, and not all scholars accept it.
A work that explains the Bible passage by passage. Commentaries range from short devotional notes to scholarly volumes that discuss the original languages and history.
Drawing the meaning out of a text, by studying its original language, setting, genre and context. The opposite is eisegesis, reading something into the text.
The principles of interpretation: how to move from the words of an ancient text to understanding what it meant then and what it means now.
A link from one verse to another that touches the same subject, quotation or word. The cross-reference sections in the Deep Dive show where the Gospels quote or echo the Old Testament.
An index of every place a word occurs in the Bible. The word study view in the Verse Inspector works like a concordance for the Gospels, using Strong’s numbers.

Latin for “Golden Chain,” a commentary on the four Gospels compiled by Thomas Aquinas in the 13th century as a chain of quotations from the church fathers. The early church excerpts in the Commentary section come from it.
Early Christian writers from roughly the 2nd to the 8th centuries, whose writings shaped Christian theology and interpretation. Examples include Irenaeus, Origen, Augustine, Chrysostom and Jerome.
The list of books accepted as Scripture. The four Gospels were widely read and accepted as authoritative by the second century. Christian groups differ over some Old Testament books.

Jude was received early in the West and in Egypt (the Muratorian list, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian), was later questioned because it quotes the Book of Enoch, and was included in the lists of Athanasius (AD 367) and the councils that followed.
The study of ancient manuscripts to work out the wording of the original text. No original manuscripts of the Gospels survive, but thousands of copies do, and most differences between them are small.

A language related to Hebrew that was the everyday speech of most Jews in Judea and Galilee. Jesus probably spoke it daily. The Gospels preserve a few of his Aramaic words, such as Talitha cumi, Ephphatha, Abba and Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani.
The common Greek of the Mediterranean world in the first century, in which all four Gospels were written. The Greek word studies in this app use it.
A translation approach that stays as close as possible to the wording and structure of the original, even when it sounds less natural in English. Examples: KJV, ASV, NASB, ESV.
A translation approach that aims to convey the meaning of the original in natural English, even if the wording changes. Also called functional equivalence. Examples: NIV, NLT (in part).
A free restatement in the translator’s own words, more like a commentary than a translation. Examples: The Message, The Living Bible.
The Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, made in Alexandria from about the 3rd century BC. Most Old Testament quotations in the New Testament follow it.
The Latin Bible translated mainly by Jerome around AD 382 to 405. It was the Bible of Western Christianity for a thousand years.

The traditional Hebrew text of the Old Testament, copied and preserved by Jewish scribes (the Masoretes) between about the 7th and 10th centuries AD. Most English Old Testaments are translated from it.

Manuscripts found from 1947 in caves near Qumran, dating from about the 3rd century BC to the 1st century AD. They include every Old Testament book except Esther and show that the Hebrew text was copied very faithfully.

A 4th-century Greek manuscript containing most of the Old Testament and the whole New Testament, discovered at St. Catherine’s Monastery on Mount Sinai. One of the oldest and most important Bible manuscripts.
A 4th-century Greek manuscript of the Bible kept in the Vatican Library, among the oldest and most important surviving manuscripts.

The Greek New Testament text published by Erasmus in 1516 and revised by others, based on a handful of late manuscripts. The King James Version and NKJV are based on it. Most modern translations use a critical text drawn from earlier manuscripts.
A Greek New Testament assembled by scholars comparing thousands of manuscripts (Nestle-Aland, UBS). Most modern translations use it.

Older translations such as the KJV, ASV, WEB and YLT are in the public domain and can be built into an app. Modern translations such as the ESV, NIV and NLT are copyrighted and need a license, which is why they depend on a connection in this app.
Berean Standard Bible (BSB) was published in 2023.
New International Version (NIV) was published in 2011.
New Living Translation (NLT) was published in 2015.
English Standard Version (ESV) was published in 2016.
King James Version (KJV) was published in 1769.
American Standard Version (ASV) was published in 1901.
Young’s Literal Translation (YLT) was published in 1898.
World English Bible (WEB) was published in 2020.
Bible in Basic English (BBE) was published in 1965.
Christian Standard Bible (CSB) was published in 2017.
New King James Version (NKJV) was published in 1982.
New American Standard Bible (NASB) was published in 2020.
The Message (MSG) was published in 2018.
